Results: The final CFA model exhibited acceptable/good fit (RMSEA=0.046 and CFI=0.901) and described 12 QoL dimensions (i.e., factors): ‘psychological symptoms’, ‘social relations’, ‘physical functioning’, ‘emotional resilience’, ‘pain’, ‘cognition’, ‘financial needs’, ‘discrimination’, ‘Outlook on life/growth’, ‘public services’, ‘living environment’, and ‘control over life’. All dimensions were positively and significantly correlated to self-reported health and wellbeing, but the magnitudes and relative differences in associations varied considerably (e.g., ‘pain’ had the strongest correlation with overall health but among the weakest correlations with wellbeing). Conclusions: This study contributes to a broader understanding of QoL by exploring the dimensionality and relationships among various QoL measures. A number of the dimensions identified are HRQoL focused, with others covering broader constructs. Our findings offer insights for the development of comprehensive instruments, or use of instrument suites that capture multidimensional aspects of QoL. Further research should explore the relevance of the identified dimensions in different settings and populations, and in particular scrutinize the feasibility and appropriateness of measuring the identified dimensions to inform resource allocation.

Title: Measuring population health status at a time of national crisis
Abstract: The study collected EQ-5D-5L and 3L from the UK population in an online survey conducted in the early weeks of the coronavirus pandemic in 2 waves about a month apart. These data were compared with EQ-5D-5L data collected as part of the Health Survey for England (2017) survey. Additional 3L data were collected during both waves, including a modified form derived from 5L. The second wave also fielded EQ-HWB. Spin-off activity from this study continues in other derivative studies.

Title: Valuation of the EQ-5D in countries with limited research resources: investigating the potential of shrinkage analysis
Abstract: Introduction Resource-constrained countries have difficulty conducting large EQ-5D valuation studies, which limits their ability to conduct cost-utility analyses using a value set specific to their own population. When estimates of similar but related parameters are available, shrinkage estimators reduce uncertainty and yield estimators with smaller mean square error (MSE). We hypothesize that health utilities based on shrinkage estimators can reduce MSE and mean absolute error (MAE) when compared to country-specific health utilities. MethodsWe conducted a simulation study (1000 iterations) based on the observed means and standard deviations (or standard errors) of the EQ-5D-3L valuation studies from 14 counties. In each iteration, the simulated data was fitted with the model based on the country-specific functional form of the scoring algorithm to create country-specific health utilities (“naïve” estimators). Shrinkage estimators were calculated based on the empirical Bayes estimation methods. The performance of shrinkage estimators was compared with those of the naïve estimators over a range of different sample sizes based on MSE, MAE, mean bias, standard errors and the width of confidence intervals.ResultsThe MSE of the shrinkage estimators was smaller than the MSE of the naïve estimators on average as theoretically predicted. Importantly, the MAE of the shrinkage estimators was also smaller than the MAE of the naïve estimators on average. In addition, the reduction in MSE with the use of shrinkage estimators did not substantially increase bias. The degree of reduction in uncertainty by shrinkage estimators is most apparent in valuation studies with small sample size.Conclusion Health utilities derived from shrinkage estimation allow valuation studies with small sample size to “borrow strength” from other valuation studies to reduce uncertainty.

Title: Agreement of the Amharic EQ‐5D‐Y-3L and Y-5L self-report (by interview-administration and self-complete) and proxy‐report
Abstract: Introduction: Different modes of administration (MoAs) have been used to administer the EQ-5D-Y, including self-complete questionnaire (SC) and interviewer administration (IA). Proxy-report is recommended for those who are unable to self-report their HRQoL e.g. young children, cognitively impaired or poor literacy. Objective: To assess and compare agreement and psychometric properties between SC, IA and proxy-report of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L Tigrinya Version. Methods: Psychometric performance and agreement between SC, IA and proxy-report of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Tigrinya paper version was assessed and compared among children aged 8–18 years. First, children and adolescents self-reported their health state on the corresponding version and then through IA. Thereafter, parents/guardians completed the corresponding EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Tigrinya proxy-report version. Administration of the SC and IA versions was randomized and separated by an age-appropriate demanding cognitive task/problem- solving experiment. Agreement between MoAs was assessed at baseline only. Repeated measures were taken by self-report (SC and IA) and proxy-report to assess test-retest reliability (for unchanged health status) and responsiveness (for changed health status) after ten days and one month, respectively, using a one-item global rating (GRS) scale to assess change. MoAs were compared by analyzing agreement of dimension scores (using Gwet’s AC and agreement percentage) and for LSS and EQ-VAS (using ICC), test-retest reliability of dimension scores (using Gwet’s AC and Cohen’s) and for LSS and EQ-VAS (using ICC), known-group validity (using Kruskal-Wallis rank test), and responsiveness (using mean change, standardized effect size– SES, and area under the curve (AUC). Results: A total of 636 participants for EQ-5D-Y-3L and 644 participants for EQ-5D-Y-5L were included in the analysis. Most of the study participants in both EQ-5D-Y-3L (65.41%) and EQ-5D-Y-5L (68.63%) had a health condition. were school children/adolescents. The highest proportions of health problems were reported in the “Feeling worried/sad/unhappy” dimension for EQ-5D-Y-5L (level 2 to 5), whereas “Feeling worried/sad/unhappy” and “Having pain/discomfort” for EQ-5D-Y-3L (Level 2 to 3) across SC, IA, and proxy-report. For both EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L, proxy consistently reported fewer "no problems" responses compared to SC and IA responses (χ² > 100, p  270, p < 0.001 for both SC and IA of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L). Respondents showed similar preference for IA and SC in EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L. Regarding responsiveness the largest difference was detected in the SC and IA of both EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L with SES in EQ-5D-Y-5L between 0.48-1.01(SC) and 0.21-0.73 (IA); and in EQ-5D-Y-3L between 0.90-1.58 (SC) and 0.38-1.87 (IA). Conclusion: Both the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Tigrinya versions demonstrated good to excellent/almost perfect agreement and psychometric performance across SC, IA, and proxy-report versions. Proxy-reports showed a slightly lower in psychometric performance and lower agreement as compared to self-reports indicating some difference. The IA version could be recommended for children who are able to self-report but unable to self-complete the instrument due to poor literacy.

Title: Research visit to University of Auckland to facilitate collaborative working and engage with local stakeholders to promote routine PROM data collection and analysis in the New Zealand healthcare system.
Abstract: I visited the Universities of Auckland, Otago and Macquarie during the period 8th March to 18th April 2023. This visit was facilitated by Paula Lorgelly, Trudy Sullivan, Sarah Derrett and Yuanyuan Gu to whom I am grateful. Most of the time was spent at the University of Auckland, where I engaged with a number of staff members and explored opportunities for future collaborations on EQ-related topics (e.g. collecting and linking HRQoL data as part of national surveys).

Title: Establishing EQ-5D-5L value set for Serbia
Abstract: Serbia is a middle-income country located in South Eastern Europe, where the valuation set for health-related quality of life has never been done before. It is unknown how the Serbian population will value different health conditions and what their preferences are, which would be very important from the perspective of growing interest in the process of Health Technology Assessment (HTA) and valuation of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures.  The objective of this study is to produce a preference-based national value set for EQ-5D-5L instrument, strictly using an EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) protocol and hybrid techniques combining Time-Trade-Off (TTO) with a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE). According to the protocol, the required sample for a country valuation study is 1000 participants who are nationally representative in terms of age, sex, region, and type of settlement they live in (urban/rural area). Quota sample will be determined by the company for market research in Serbia who will also organize data collection in the field. Interviewers will be a mix of students and professional interviewers who will receive training from a previously trained Principal Investigator and another researcher from the core team, during ToT by EuroQoL Research Foundation. Training will be followed by practicing and piloting the study. Interviews will be done in a combination of face-to-face and online interviews. Every step of the process will be carefully monitored and supervised by members of our research team, on a daily basis, in order to ensure quality control. Meetings with national stakeholders are planned for the beginning and the end of the project. Three interim meetings with interviewers are planned during data collection, after achieving 25%, 50% and 75% of target sample, along with continuous consultations and reporting EuroQoL Research Foundation.

Title: EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, and ICECAP-A: A Comparative Study of Health and Wellbeing Measures in Ireland
Abstract: This study conducted a psychometric validation of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S instruments in an Irish general population sample, comparing them with the EQ-5D-5L and ICECAP-A. The analysis, based on data from 1,220 respondents, revealed that both EQ-HWB versions demonstrated good psychometric properties, including lower ceiling effects than EQ-5D-5L and ICECAP-A. The EQ-HWB showed strong correlations with EQ-5D-5L and moderate correlations with ICECAP-A, suggesting it captures both health-related quality of life and broader wellbeing aspects. Factor analysis identified a unique five-factor structure spanning health and wellbeing domains. While EQ-5D-5L showed higher sensitivity to health problems, EQ-HWB captured a wider range of wellbeing concepts. The study also provides insights into the potential effects of ongoing modifications to the EQ-HWB, particularly the rewording of positively framed items. These findings contribute to the growing body of evidence on the EQ-HWB's performance and inform its use in various healthcare and policy contexts.

Title: travel scholarship for Xueyun Zeng
QALY MICI (IBD QALY)
Abstract: QALY-MICI (IBD QALY) is a prospective observational transversal survey, the primary objective of which was to collect health states using EQ-5D-5L in the French context for patients who suffer from Inflammatory Bowel Disesase (IBD: Crohn’s disease and Ulcerative Colitis) and to provide utility values based on the French Value 5L set. EQ-5D data was associated to data on history of disease, past treatments, current treatments, activity scores. Socio-demographic data include type of activity and occupation, as well as size of residential area. EQ-5D data are compared to a specific QoL questionnaire for IBD, the Short Inflammatory Bowel Disease Questionnaire (SIBDQ).

Title: Relationship between behavioural risk factors for poor health and the EQ-5D: Prospective analyses in a New Zealand cohort
Abstract: Introduction: Physical inactivity, tobacco smoking, high body mass index and hazardous alcohol consumption are risk factors for poor health. However, their relationship with the EQ-5D, a commonly used measure of general health status, is poorly understood. This study examines the relationship between these factors, both individually and in combination, with the EQ-5D-3L. Methods: Data from the Prospective Outcomes of Injury Study (n=2856) was analysed using multi-variable logistic regression modelling to examine pre-injury relationships between physical activity, tobacco smoking, body mass index and alcohol consumption and each of the five EQ-5D dimensions. Logistic regression modelling was also used to calculate the predicted probability of problems within each of the EQ-5D dimensions for each possible combination of the four behavioural risk factors (i.e. 16 possible combinations were examined for each of the five dimensions). Graphs were produced to show the 16 combinations of risk factors with each of the dimensions. This appears to be a novel approach in terms of presenting EQ-5D findings. Results: Physical inactivity was associated with being more likely to have problems with mobility. Tobacco smoking was associated with being less likely to have problems with pain or discomfort whereas high alcohol consumption was associated with being more likely to have problems with pain or discomfort. Body mass index was not associated with any of the EQ-5D dimensions. However, the combination of obesity and physical inactivity (with or without the other behavioural risk factors) corresponded to a larger probability of problems in almost all dimensions. Conclusions: Our results support earlier findings that large scale population studies should consider collecting information about key behavioural factors alongside EQ-5D health outcomes. It also appears useful to consider specific combinations of behavioural risk factors when assessing general health status using the EQ-5D.

Title: Testing the validity of EQ-5D-5L respiratory bolt-ons in a large Australian dataset
Abstract: Objectives: The EQ-5D has been used to assess health related quality of life (HRQoL) in respiratory conditions including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma. However, the core descriptive system may not be sensitive to all the HRQoL impacts of respiratory conditions. To increase the sensitivity of the descriptive system, two bolt-on questions “Limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath” and “Breathing problems,” have been developed (EQ-5D-5L+R1 and EQ-5D-5L+R2). Psychometric comparisons are required to understand the performance and sensitivity added by the bolt-ons in comparison to other validated instruments. This is important to inform the work of the EuroQol group in the further development of bolt-ons, and the research agenda around bolt-ons. Therefore, this study tested the psychometric characteristics of the EQ-5D-5L+R using a large dataset collected in Australia. Take-away results: o The results show that adding the respiratory bolt-on to the EQ-5D-5L improved the instrument's descriptive sensitivity in a sample of people with respiratory conditions. o The bolt-on ‘‘breathing problems’’ did not have a high correlation with other dimensions which shows that it is a more independent dimension, than the physical activity limitation bolt-on. The “Limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath” domain might have an overlap with the other EQ-5D domain “usual activities”, which might cause limited sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L+R1. o The bolt-on instruments are not suggested to be used as a stand-alone instrument however, they can be used alongside the EQ-5D-5L to estimate so-called ‘‘bolt-on’’ QALYs in addition to the calculation of the standard QALYs to show the potential change in treatment impact when a condition-specific domain is included in the economic evaluation. The choice of bolt-on may be driven by whether overall problems or limitations are being measured. Implications and next steps: o Results suggest a level of validity of the bolt-ons in an Australian population, and therefore to facilitate further use, a value set would be beneficial. The values set can be used alongside the EQ-5D in the economic evaluation of new interventions and treatments for respiratory conditions. However, before using the values to measure QALYs (Quality-adjusted life years), future studies should check the validity and responsiveness of the bolt-ons in different respiratory conditions. o Further research is required to investigate whether the EQ-5D-5L+Rs will be more responsive to changes in the health status of patients longitudinally.

Title: No kidding: the validity of discrete choice experiments in children - a pilot study
Abstract: Objective: To assess the feasibility and validity of using adiscrete choice experiment format to elicit health preferences in children by comparing illogical choices and choice blindness rates between adults and children; and toexplore the relationship between personality traitsand health-state choices.Methods: A convenience sample of adults and children (8-17 years old) were recruited aroundChicago, USA. Apersonality inventorywas administered,followed by pairwise comparisons of6health-state scenarios. Health statedescriptionswere based ona simplified 3 dimension version of EQ-5D (mobility, pain, depression, each with 3 levels). For 2 scenarios, theinterviewer switchedthe respondent’s preferred choiceto identify choice blindness. Odds of choice blindnessand health-state choice among pairswas assessed using logistic regression.Results: One-hundred and onerespondents were recruited (44% adults). Comparing children to adults, there was no significant difference in the rate of illogical preferences, i.e. selecting a dominated state, (9% vs. 12%) or in preferring dead to the worst health-state (54% vs. 64%) (p>0.05). Choice blindness rates were significantly higherin children (35%) thanadults (9%) (p<0.01). Adjusting for gender and personality traits, the odds of choice blindness in children was 6.6(CI 95%: 1.8-23.8, p=0.004). Conscientiousness was significantly associated with health-state choice in 3 of the 6 models predicting health state choice (using p<0.1as a threshold).Conclusions: The results of this exploratory study suggest it is feasible to conduct choice experimentsin children; however, children are significantly more likely to demonstrate choice blindness.Psychological traits may be noteworthy predictors of health-state choices, withConscientiousness independently associated with severalhealth-state choices.

Title: Exploring non-iterative TTO (ENITTO)
Abstract: Background – Time Trade-Off (TTO) usually relies on “iteration”, which is susceptible to bias. Discrete Choice Experiment with duration (or DCETTO) is free of such bias, but respondents find this cognitively more challenging. This paper explores non-iterative TTO (NITTO). In NITTO respondents see a series of independent pairwise choices without iteration (similar to DCETTO), but one of the two scenarios always involves full health for a shorter duration (similar to TTO). Methods – We examine the performance of three different types of NITTO relative to DCETTO (i.e. four “Types” of choice tasks). Each Type is presented in two ways: (a) verbally tabulated (as in a DCE); and (b) with visual aids (as in a TTO). Thus, there are eight survey variants, each with 12 experimental choice tasks and a 13th task with a logically determined answer. Data on the 12 experimental choices obtained from an online survey of 6,618 respondents are modelled by variant using conditional logistic regressions. Results – The overall results suggest that NITTO seems feasible. Fewer respondents found the tasks difficult compared to DCETTO; the great majority of respondents “pass” the logical consistency test; and data can be modelled to produce interpretable coefficients. However, some relatively mild states appear to have almost implausibly low values, and the range of predicted values between state 22222 and 55555 seems narrow. A high proportion of respondents are non-trading, always choosing the shorter survival in full health over the longer survival in worse health.

Title: Health Related Quality Of Life Of Children And Adolescents With Cerebral Palsy, And The Spillover Effect In Their Caregivers. Cross-Sectional And Longitudinal Analysis, And EQ-5D-Y-5L And EQ-HWB-9 Psychometric Properties In This Population In Argentina.
Abstract: This cross-sectional and longitudinal study investigates the Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents with Cerebral Palsy (CP) and the consequential spillover effects on their caregivers in Argentina. Utilizing two EuroQol instruments,  the EQ-5D-Y-5L for children and the EQ-HWB-9 for caregivers, the research aims to explore both direct impacts and indirect influences on caregiver well-being due to prolonged caregiving roles. Set in the largest high-complexity pediatric environment of the Hospital of Pediatría Dr. J.P. Garrahan in Buenos Aires, Argentina, this study will analyze caregiver-child dyads to describe their HRQoL, as well as assess dynamic changes in HRQoL and spillover effect over time. The primary objectives include detailing HRQoL profiles, examining the nuanced relationship between child HRQoL and caregiver HRQoL, and evaluating the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-Y And EQ-HWB-9, including responsiveness. We plan to include 100-150 dyads, and have six month follow-up data of 50-75. By describing initial and six months follow up HRQoL, the study will provide a robust understanding of how children's health status impacts their caregivers' quality of life, incorporating factors like emotional, physical, and social well-being. In addition to descriptive and exploratory analyses of HRQoL profiles, the study will investigate differences in child HRQoL as related to CP severity and identify the most affected HRQoL domains among caregivers. Longitudinally, it will explore how changes in children’s health status influence caregiver HRQoL, aiming to validate the responsiveness of the EQ-HWB-9 in detecting shifts in caregiver burden over time. Furthermore, the research will utilize a comprehensive approach to correlate the EQ-HWB-9 findings with other caregiver-specific tools, such as the CarerQoL-7D, to assess their comparative effectiveness. By contributing to the validation of these instruments in a complex caregiver population, the study aims to illuminate the broader impacts of pediatric chronic illness on families, and contribute to the scarce body of evidence of EuroQol instruments in this population, thereby informing both internal EuroQol strategy as well as broader policy and supporting intervention strategies to assess spillover and mitigate caregiver burden.

Title: Non-parametric approach to valuing the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: In this study we compare a set of methodologies for generating value sets across EQ-VT survey data from eight countries. Across countries a variety of estimating specifications are present in the literature, here we seek to investigate the impact of these different specifications, and consider whether a uniform specification might be possible. We included the EQ-5D-5L valuation study data from 8 countries including Canada, China, Germany, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Singapore, and The Netherlands. We first used a set of standard parametric models frequently encountered in the literature, including the main effects model with and without additional interaction terms, Left-censored model with individual random effects, 8-parameter model using individual country’s data. We also pooled all countries’ data and used the same parametric models. Three types of non-parametric models were used: 1) optimal bandwidths using individual country's data and kernel smoothing using individual country's data (denoted NP models); 2) optimal bandwidths using pooled data and kernel smoothing using pooled data (denoted NPU models); and 3) optimal bandwidths using pooled data and kernel smoothing using individual country’s data (denoted NPUc models). All models were compared on the basis of goodness of fit statistics, mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE). Value sets were generated for each country using each model. Bland-Altman critical differences were generated to evaluate the difference from the value set generated using the model with the lowest MAE and RMSE for each country. Compared to the parametric models, the nonparametric models improved model goodness of fit across countries. The nonparametric model using the bandwidth optimized based on individual country’s valuation data performed slightly better than the nonparametric model pooling all countries’ data.

Title: Developing a localized electronic version of EQ-5D-Y-5L and evaluating its measurement properties for use in clinical settings: the case of Paediatric and Adolescent Wellness Service (PAWS)
Abstract: Background: The Paediatric and Adolescent Wellness Service (PAWS) at KK Women's and Children's Hospital (KKH), Singapore’s largest public hospital specialising in women’s and children’s healthcare, was established in 2022 for children and adolescents with mild to moderate mental health conditions. To enhance service evaluation and patient management, PAWS is interested in incorporating EQ-5D-Y into its routine patient-reported outcomes measures (PROMs) data collection. However, several practical concerns need to be addressed. First, the currently approved electronic formats of EQ-5D-Y are in the forms of REDCap, Qualtrics, and LimeSurvey, none of which is suitable for long-term data collection at KKH because of both data security and platform-related cost concerns. Like all other public hospitals in Singapore, PAWS has been collecting patient-/caregiver-reported data using Form-SG (https://form.gov.sg), a free and secure platform developed by the Singapore government. The EQ-5D-Y questionnaire implemented in Form-SG is similar to, but not exactly the same as the approved electronic versions. It is unknown if the Form-SG powered EQ-5D-Y questionnaire has acceptable measurement properties. Besides, it is necessary to specify the age thresholds for self-reported and proxy-reported EQ-5D-Y-5L. However, the minimum age at which children with mental health conditions or symptoms can reliably self-complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L—and the age below which it should be completed by a proxy—remain unanswered. This lack of guidance poses challenges for routine implementation in clinical settings and may lead to inconsistent use, reduced data quality, and limited comparability across settings and over time. In addition, the use of EQ-5D-Y in the paediatric setting often face the problem of transitioning from EQ-5D-Y to EQ-5D-5L when the child or adolescent grows into adultohood as understanding about the comparability between EQ-5D-Y and EQ-5D-5L is limited.  Aims: This proposal aims to support the integration of EQ-5D-Y-5L into the routine PROMs data collection at PAWS and to facilitate the transition from EQ-5D-Y-5L to EQ-5D-5L. The transition from EQ-5D-Y to EQ-5D is inevitable in longitudinal data collection from adolescents. Little research has been done to understand at what age the transition should start. While it is not a pressing issue for integrating EQ-5D-Y into PAWS, insight about the optimal transition age would be useful in the long term.  Therefore, there are three specific objectives: (1) to develop the Form-SG powered EQ-5D-Y-5L questionnaire, including both self-complete and proxy versions, in children who visit the PAWS clinic for treatment of mental health conditions or symptoms and to evaluate their measurement properties; (2) to explore the minimum age at which children with mental health conditions or symptoms can reliably self-complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L questionnaire; and (3) to assess the comparability between EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L among adolescents.  Methods: The project will be carried out in two phases. In Phase 1, we will develop Form-SG powered EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires, followed by a qualitative testing with children visiting PAWS and their caregivers. In Phase 2, we will incorporate the Form-SG powered EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires into PAWS’s current system for routine longitudinal data collection. The data collected in Phase 2 will be used to assess the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires including construct validity, test-retest reliability, responsiveness, and patient-proxy agreement. Besides, the data collected at Phase 2 will be used to compare the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L.

Title: Feasibility of the EQ-TIPS-5L Latent Scale DCE: A Qualitative Study in the UK and Singapore
Abstract: Background: he EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS-5L) instrument is a key advance in assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children aged 0–4 years. Its use in economic evaluation is limited by the absence of a validated valuation protocol and value set. Proxy valuation by parents or caregivers raises methodological, cognitive, and emotional challenges, underscoring the need for qualitative groundwork. This study aims to investigate the feasibility of applying DCE latent scale methodology to EQ-TIPS-5L valuation, examining how caregivers and general public respondents interpret dimensions, engage with choice tasks, and respond to alternative presentation strategies.Methods: We will conduct a qualitative, exploratory, multi-country study in the United Kingdom and Singapore, involving 30–40 participants (15–20 per site). The UK sample will focus on caregivers, whilst Singapore will include both caregivers and general public respondents to enable exploratory comparison of perspectives. Using a phenomenological approach, in-depth semi-structured interviews will combine cognitive debriefing, think-aloud techniques, and eight mock DCE tasks employing level overlap methodology to reduce cognitive burden. Cross-national comparison will assess both universal and context-specific influences on task interpretation and valuation.Implications and Future Directions: This study will generate critical qualitative evidence to inform a robust, internationally applicable valuation protocol for EQ-TIPS-5L. By incorporating perspectives from two culturally distinct health systems, it will strengthen the external validity of future quantitative valuation studies and lay the foundation for developing value sets that enable systematic inclusion of very

Title: A PhD grant to investigate the valuation of worse-than-dead health states
Abstract: A PhD project was completed to investigate the challenges in valuation of worse-than-dead EQ-5D health states and to explore methods that may improve the valuation of such health states. The project started with a study to investigate whether extending the lead time in the lead-time TTO tasks will mitigate the floor effects in negative TTO values in an EQ-VT study. A qualitative study of respondents participating in another EQ-VT study was conducted to understand why negative values were given in TTO tasks. Based on findings from these two studies, a new TTO variant was developed, tested, improved, and tested again. The new TTO variant was found to be able to better measure worse-than-dead EQ-5D health states compared to the composite TTO.

Title: The long CORona Follow-Up Study (long CORFU): long-term outcomes and health-related quality of life of long COVID patients
Abstract: Objectives Our project had two main objectives, i.e. to estimate the prevalence of post COVID at the long term and study its association with HRQoL, and to study the psychometrics of the EQ-5D-5L for its use in post COVID. Methods Data of the CORona Follow-Up study (CORFU) were used, with an additional follow-up questionnaire at 3 years after COVID-19 designed specifically for the present project (‘long CORFU’). Data were available of former COVID-19 patients with and without post COVID. HRQoL was quantified using the EQ-5D-5L. The EQ index was computed using the Dutch value set. To estimate the prevalence of post COVID over 3 years of follow-up and associations between post COVID and HRQoL, we used (generalized) linear mixed-effects regression. Multivariable linear regression was used to estimate differences between those with and without post COVID in change of HRQoL between 2 and 3 years, and to assess the association between baseline and diversity factors and change in HRQoL in only those with post COVID. For the objective on psychometrics of the EQ-5D-5L, we used longitudinal data to determine responsiveness, and for distributional characteristics the ceiling/ floor effects we used health profiles. Divergent and convergent validity were assessed using Spearman’s correlation, and we used multivariable regression to determine explanatory power. Known-group validity was assessed by testing differences in mean EQ-5D-5L aggregate scores between groups of different symptom severity, and responsiveness by estimating correlation coefficients. Results We used data of 1255 questionnaires to determine the prevalence of post COVID at 1, 2, and 3 years follow up (62.5, 63.6, and 64.9%), with no significant change over time. Post COVID was significantly associated with HRQoL: mean utility was 0.16 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.13, 0.18), p-value: 0.001) lower, adjusted for confounders. At two years after COVID-19, 66% met the definition of post COVID. The effect of having post COVID on change in VAS scores between 2 and 3 years was 1.6 points (95% CI -2.6, 5.8; P=0.4) and on change in utility -0.03 points (95% CI -0.07,0.02; P=0.3). Having social engagement problems was associated with greater positive changes in EQ VAS scores. For the psychometric properties, we observed a ceiling effect in 7.2%; no floor effect was detected. A total of 115 health profiles (3.7% of possible profiles) were observed. Significant correlation coefficients across EQ-5D-5L dimensions ranged from poor (0.24, for anxiety/depression and self-care) to moderately strong (0.62, for mobility and usual activities). A moderately strong correlation (-0.67; 95%CI -0.74, -0.59) was found between the EQ-5D-5L level sum score and EQ VAS. Usual activities and mobility together explained 39.0% of EQ VAS variance. Other dimensions did not significantly improve contribution. Mean (SD) EQ-5D-5L level sum score for the group with low, medium and high severity of symptoms was 8.1 (2.4), 9.3(2.9), and 12.3 (3.2), respectively. A poor correlation was found between change of level sum score and change of general health status, and between changes in general health and changes in usual activities, pain discomfort, and anxiety/depression. Conclusions From this project, we can conclude that the prevalence of post COVID did not change over time and that presence of post COVID significantly affected HRQoL. HRQoL remained stable for those with post COVID between 2 and 3 years, and improved only for those without post COVID. Any variation in changes within patients could not be attributed to sociodemographic or clinical characteristics. More studies may be needed to understand the variability in HRQoL changes in post COVID patients. We found promising psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L in post COVID, demonstrating sensitivity in distinguishing variations in health states and symptom severity. The dominance of mobility and usual activities in explaining general health suggests that the EQ-5D-5L may under-represent other health aspects important to post COVID, highlighting a potential value of bolt-ons.

Title: Travel support for the SEVQoL PhD student to the Priorities 2024 conference
Abstract: SEVQoL (SEVerity and Quality of Life, EQ no. 1340-RA) investigates whether people show a preference for prioritising the 'worse off' in hypothetical healthcare allocation scenarios, using individually calibrated EQ-5D-5L health state values. An abstract for the project's first article, "A Preference for the Better Off? A Discrete Choice Experiment Using Individually Calibrated EQ-5D-5L Health State Values", was accepted as a poster presentation for the Priorities 2024 conference in Bangkok on May 7.-11. hosted by The International Society for Priorities in Health. As there is no funding for the project beyond salaries for the PhD student, we apply for additional funding to cover 50% of the conference fee, travel and accommodation for Marius Torjusen, who is the first author and PhD student on the project.

Title: Interval TTO valuation approach (2nd revision)
Abstract: In our study, we evaluated the feasibility of interval Time Trade-Off (iTTO) as a potential TTO variant that permits response intervals rather than discrete indifference points. We aimed to determine if iTTO reduces the cognitive challenges often seen in regular cTTO (cTTO) without sacrificing data quality. In an EQ-5D-5L valuation experiment, 100 participants were randomly assigned to either cTTO or iTTO. The iTTO tasks were designed to terminate after 15 movements or when respondents cycled around a 0.1-width interval. Since the entire response paths were stored, we could explore different termination rules, specifically examining rules based on a maximum number of Iterative Steps and Interval Width (IS-IW) and the Two Directional Changes approach (TDC). Task complexity metrics were based on task completion time, movements, and participant feedback. We assessed inconsistencies and value clustering at 1, 0.5, 0, -0.5 and -1 across both arms. We assessed model performance using mean standard error, Akaike Information Criterion, and Bayesian Information Criterion though a 20-parameter hybrid model that combined cTTO and iTTO data with discrete choice experiment data from a previous study in the same population. Our findings indicate that iTTO led to faster task completion times, more movements, and enhanced self-reported comprehension. iTTO reduced value clustering with no significant differences in inconsistencies. The relative precision of models developed through both cTTO and iTTO methodologies was nearly identical. In conclusion, iTTO emerges as a promising alternative to cTTO for health state valuations. iTTO has the potential to improve participants' comprehension and efficiency in completing tasks while limiting the impact of satisficing and preserving model precision. Among the tested iTTO termination rules, we particularly recommend the TDC approach. Further research is needed to assess iTTO in diverse populations and with alternative iterative procedures.

Title: Extension to 20180300: What aspects of quality of life are important to people with experience of cognitive or visual impairment? A qualitative investigation
Abstract: There is a series of ongoing work on the development of descriptors for bolt-ons to the EQ-5D, driven by the need to capture domain-specific Qol not measured by the EQ-5D. One such project is currently underway exploring the development of bolt-ons for cognition and vision. As part of this project substantive qualitative data collection with individuals and carers experiencing these health conditions has taken place. The pre-planned analysis has revealed that a broad range of quality of life domains beyond those with a vision and cognition focus, and beyond the domains currently covered by the EQ-5D descriptive system, are important to these people. As such, we seek additional funding to explore these domains using a detailed qualitative thematic analysis, which is important to ensure content and construct validity of further quantitative work. The outcomes of this work will lead to a robust and comprehensive list of quality of life domains of importance for people with cognition and vision impairments. Moreover, it will provide a comparison of this list with existing measure of quality of life measures that cover the domains of cognition and vision (e.g. Adults Social Care Outcomes Toolkit (ASCOT)). Therefore, the project will deliver evidence about the suitability of the EQ-5D in these health conditions and inform its future development. This will yield important insights for future bolt-on development work as well as research seeking to develop broader quality of life descriptive systems, such as the E-QALY.

Title: Redundancy in HRQoL algorithms: conceptual and empirical challenges
Abstract: Objectives: Providing policy makers with value sets is a crucial part of EuroQol’s work and enables our instruments to be widely used in HTA and other settings. However, given the long history of EuroQol’s work, and the number of existing valuation studies, many of our value sets are now old, based on potentially outdated valuation methodology, and in popu-lations which no longer represent the contemporary population. Assuming EuroQol wants a role in endorsing approved value sets - or at least a way of identifying priorities for in-vesting in new value sets - having a clear strategy for identification and mitigation of re-dundancy is important to ensure policy makers retain confidence in their country-specific value sets. Methods Through discussion and iteration with our international authorship team, we have constructed a taxonomy of redundancy. We have explored how the different types of redundancy might be identified, and how the EuroQol group might work with local policy makers to address redundancy, and therefore ensure our instruments remain relevant for use. Results The taxonomy of redundancy consists of four main areas, based on both redundancy and obsolescence. These are that the value set no longer aligns with current normative HTA requirements; that the methods used to generate it are no longer considered robust or adequately close to best practice; that the population composition has moved too far from the population in which the original value set was derived; and that, even after controlling for population differences, preferences are likely to have changed since original data collection. Through identification of the type of redundancy that applies in a particular setting, we then suggest a range of possible solutions to each, ranging from recommending particular sensitivity analyses, through reweighting of existing data to better account for population differences, to collecting new data for an updated value set. Conclusion: Redundancy of existing value sets is driven by more than just time since data collection and is often a matter of judgment rather than based on a clear definition. Working closely with local policy makers, in manner appropriate to the local environment, to discuss the ongoing appropriateness of existing value sets is an important part of EuroQol’s ongoing role, and includes the consideration of updating value sets in contemporary populations using current best-practice methods. However, the benefits of updating value sets has to be balanced against the desire of policy makers for consistency in their local decision-making processes.

Title: Comparing the performance of the modified and experimental versions of the EQ-HWB Hopelessness item; a psychometric study using IRT and DIF using data from the Meditation Engagement Study
Abstract: The EuroQol Health and Wellbeing Full instrument (EQ-HWB) is an internationally developed instrument for evaluating the impact of health, public health and social care interventions on patients and carers.(1,2)  Whilst the wording of the EQ-HWB-9 short-form is now finalised, research is needed to evaluate the performance of the other 16 items and the proposed study aims to address this evidence gap.The Meditation Engagement Study (MES) study was undertaken by the Contemplative Studies Centre (CSC), University of Melbourne, and sought to measure engagement and utility in the use of mindfulness apps for addressing mental health concerns use for people who seek to improve their mental health.  In this study we included the modified and experimental versions of the EQ-HWB-9, randomised with more than 400 cases in each arm. We analysed this data with a EuroQol grant – 1872-RA and presented the findings at the EQ-HWB WG at the Vienna Plenary pre-meeting, thus contributing to the finalisation of the short form.In this study, we also included four extra hopelessness questions, the experimental and modified versions, plus a test item and an item from the WHOQol. An extra two hopelessness variables were contained in the SWEMWBS and K10 instruments, giving us 6 items suitable to measure the latent variable in IRT analysis. The study for which EuroQol funding is sought aims to examine the psychometric performance of the experimental and modified hopelessness questions. Specifically, we aim to conduct psychometric analysis on the experimental and modified hopelessness questions compared to 4 possible alternative questions, and conduct IRT and DIF analysis on the 6 questions.

Title: Alternative Wordings for the EQ-5D descriptive Systems: Optimising Measurement Excellence - Stage 1 (AWESOME 1)
Abstract: BACKGROUND: The AWESOME project aims to generate new evidence regarding challenges with the current wording of the four EQ-5D instruments and to identify possible wording improvements. Stage 1, detailed here, intended to provide empirical evidence, harvested from the cognitive debriefing (CD) reports of routine translation, to support the need for the larger project. OBJECTIVES AND METHODS Drawing on the VMC repository, cognitive debriefing (CD) reports were analysed to identify the range and nature of wording issues identified during translation. The specific objectives were to: a) Establish the range, nature and frequency of wording issues identified during CD. b) Identify the range and type of solutions offered to translators to overcome these problems, and to note how often and in which languages (and language groups) such solutions are implemented. d) Explore if certain respondent characteristics are related to these reported problems (e.g. age, health condition, etc.). A mixed methodology was used to analyse 87 cognitive debriefing (CD). These reports comprised eight 3L, 32 5L, 36 Y-3L and 11 Y-5L versions from 54 countries and included 55 unique languages and 633 respondents (296 adults and 337 children). RESULTS: Comprehension Issues: Approximately 47% of respondents provided one or more responses to probing questions indicating an interpretation of EQ-5D terms which deviated from the EuroQol’s official Definition of Concepts document. Four main problem types were identified: • Interpretation: Difficulties in understanding high register terms such as “mobility” or “anxiety”; broader interpretation of defined concepts. • Qualifier Comprehension: Variability in interpreting severity qualifiers, particularly the mid-level qualifiers (2nd level in the 3L versions and 2nd and 3rd level in the 5L versions). • Non-Health Centered Examples: E.g., responses influenced by developmental stages (mostly children) rather than health-centered examples, particularly in the Self-care dimension and Depression/Anxiety dimensions. • Dual constructs in the same dimension causing confusion: E.g., in the dimension heading (e.g. Pain or Discomfort) or dissonance between heading and level descriptors (e.g., Mobility and Walking about). Translatability Challenges: Difficulty in finding equivalent terms in the target language for concepts led to the use of alternate words to the English source in 61 of the 87 translations (70%) (e.g., Worried instead of Anxious in the adult versions). OUTCOMES As per the primary intended outcome, commonly misunderstood words and phrases and possible alternative words and phrases were identified to be tested in Stage 2. The results have been presented in the 2024 Copenhagen and Noordwijk EruroQol meetings and shared with the AWESOME Team and the VMC to inform the formulation of alternative versions to be empirically tested during Stage 2. Additionally, a comprehensive list of all words or phrases that have proved challenging, and the suggested alternative phrasing that was approved by reviewers, has been developed and these are in the process of incorporation into the Definition of Concepts document. This extended glossary will further assist in standardisation of any changes required to ensure cultural acceptability RECOMMENDATIONS: 1. Proceed with AWESOME Stage 2 to empirically test proposed alterations in collaboration with the VMC. This could potentially lead to simplified English wording more easily translated into other languages. 2. Work with the wider VMC to expand the VMC Definition of Concepts documents to include acceptable alternatives for semantic equivalence. CONCLUSION: EQ-5D instruments show overall linguistic and conceptual validity, yet the range and frequency of deviations from the defined concepts indicate the need for improvement to enhance cross-cultural comparability and age-appropriate continuity.

Title: Testing 4 cognition bolt-on items in a community dwelling elderly group
Abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of four candidate cognition bolt-on items and their combinations to the EQ-5D-5L. Methods Four cognition items (concentration, memory, calculation, and learning) were developed as separate questionnaire items, and were administered with the standard EQ-5D-5L to 640 individuals in a general population survey in China. From 4 items, 11 compound items were constructed, and the ‘worse level counts’ rule was used to achieve a compound item score. Psychometric performance of the cognition bolt-ons was assessed in terms of informativity, convergent validity, explanatory power, and discriminatory power. Results The tested four cognition bolt-on items improved informativity, convergent validity, explanatory power and discriminatory power of EQ-5D-5L, with calculation and learning yielding better psychometric performance. The compound bolt-on items that cover a range of cognitive functions demonstrated superior psychometric performance compared to single-aspect bolt-on items, with those items covering calculation and learning resulting in better psychometric performance. Conclusion This study confirmed the validity of the tested cognition bolt-ons in a general Chinese population. It supported the use of a compound bolt-on item covering a range of cognitive functions such as ability to calculate and learn.

Title: Development of an EQ-5D-5L Value Set for Adult Population in Nepal
Abstract: **Background** Health economists and other researchers in Nepal are using EQ-5D in their research with proxy value sets from different countries. The Ministry of Health and Population, Health Insurance Board, Social Security Fund and the Department of Drug Administration of Nepal are the key government agencies which have the potential to use cost-utility analysis and health technology assessment in their decision-making. Besides these agencies at the federal level, provincial and municipal governments also have the potential to use cost-utility analysis, particularly in redesigning the package of basic health services that are being provided universally free of user’s fee. Therefore, an EQ-5D-5L valuation study in Nepal can help address the gap and move forward with the adoption of the Health Technology Assessment (HTA) in the country. Additionally, evidence on the direct comparison between value set from Discrete choice Experiments with duration (DCEd) approach and commonly used composite time trade-off (cTTO) will guide researchers to adopt more convenient yet reliable approach for future valuation studies in lower-middle-income country setting. **Objectives** The objective of this study is two-fold: 1) to develop EQ-5D-5L value sets for the adult population in Nepal; and 2) to make a direct comparison between DCEd and cTTO valuation methods in Nepali context. **Methods** We will conduct 1,000 face-to-face interviews following the EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) protocol. We will apply a multi-stage cluster sampling technique and the sample will be allocated based on population distribution by age, sex, and geographical areas to represent the Nepal population. The research team consists of multidisciplinary expertise and Nepal team will lead the data collection with trained and qualified interviewers. A system will be established to continuously monitor quality of the collected data using EuroQol group’s tools and expert support from quality control officers. The respondents will complete cTTO, discrete choice experiments (DCE) (without a duration attribute) and split-triplet DCEd tasks during interview. Regression models will be employed for estimating values from the data collected using cTTO and DCE questions. The estimated values using cTTO and DCEd approach will be compared by using scatterplots and Bland-Altman plots. Ethical clearance will be obtained from Brunel University London, UK and Health Research Council, Nepal. **Output** The study will provide EQ-5D value sets for the adult population in Nepal. Additionally, this study will provide evidence on whether the DCEd approach delivers results similar to the commonly used cTTO method for eliciting health state utility values for lower-middle-income country settings. The findings will be published in scientific peer-reviewed journals. We will also conduct workshops, present the findings at conferences, and prepare policy briefs to communicate the findings to the relevant stakeholders in Nepal and internationally.

Title: Furthering the DCE research agenda: Comparing anchoring and design methods for the valuation of EQ-5D
Abstract: Objectives The DCETTO is a popular method to create value sets for the EQ-5D. There are two main approaches to the DCETTO, where either immediate death or full health for a shorter duration is included as the third option in a choice set. There are also two main DCETTO choice set construction methods i.e. generator-developed or efficient DCE designs. There is a lack of studies that directly compare the two approaches and two construction methods and their impact on value sets. It is also unclear whether alternative methods would have an impact on nonlinear time preferences and whether the impact would vary in value sets from different countries. This study seeks to investigate these issues. Methods A 4-arm study was used to provide a comparison of the two approaches and two choice set construction methods of the DCETTO. This was tested in a sample of respondents from Peru (n = 942) and Denmark (n = 988). Results There was evidence that DCETTO approach and construction method can impact value sets, particularly for more severe health states. Respondents generally exhibited nonlinear time preferences. Results were noted to be more variable in the Peruvian data set. Conclusion This is the first study to provide a comparison of the two commonly used DCETTO approaches and associated construction methods in valuation studies across two countries. Efficient DCE designs had slightly better performance across arms but require priors and are less convenient than generator-developed designs. Directions for future research are discussed.

Title: Exploring the content validity of the EQ-PSO bolt-ons in chronic skin conditions other than psoriasis
Abstract: Background: The objective of this study was to assess the content validity of the EQ-5D-5L and four bolt-ons: skin irritation, self-confidence, social relationships and sleep, for people with atopic dermatitis (AD) and chronic urticaria (CU). Methods: Adults with AD (N=15) or CU (N=15) in the United Kingdom, with varying levels of severity, participated in either online or in-person semi-structured interviews. During the interviews, participants were first asked about the symptoms and impacts of their condition. They were then asked to complete the EQ-5D-5L and four bolt-ons using ‘think-aloud’ and retrospective probing. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, then analysed using content and thematic analysis. Results: Participants spontaneously reported itch (AD: 100%; CU: 93%), self-confidence (AD: 100%, CU: 47%), sleep (AD: 53%; CU: 53%), and social relationships (AD: 27%; CU: 60%). The skin irritation bolt-on was the most important dimension for 60% of AD and 73% of CU participants. Social relationships was more frequently ranked as the least relevant among the other bolt-ons. Overall, 15, 9, 9 and 7 AD participants and 15, 9, 10 and 6 CU participants respectively supported adding the skin irritation, self-confidence, sleep and social relationship bolt-ons to the EQ-5D-5L. Few missing concepts were identified (e.g. treatment burden, appearance, anger or frustration). Conclusions: Our findings support the use of the skin irritation and self-confidence bolt-ons, originally developed for psoriasis patients, in AD and CU. Skin irritation, self-confidence and sleep bolt-ons showed good evidence of content validity in these two populations. The value of the social relationships bolt-on warrants further investigation.

Title: Preference heterogeneity in health valuation: Peru EQ-VT data
Abstract: Background: Preference heterogeneity in health valuation has become a topic of greater discussion among health technology assessment agencies. To better understand heterogeneity within a national population, valuation studies may identify latent groups that place different absolute and relative importance (i.e., scale and taste parameters) on the attributes of health profiles. Objective: Using discrete choice responses from a Peruvian valuation study, we estimated EQ-5D-5L values on a quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) scale accounting for latent heterogeneity in scale and taste, as well as controlling heteroskedasticity at task level variation. Method: We conducted a series of latent class analyses, each including the 20 main effects of the EQ-5D-5L and a power function that relaxes the constant proportionality assumption (i.e., discounting). Taste class membership was conditional on respondent-specific characteristics as well as their experience with the time trade-off tasks. Scale class membership was conditional on behavioral characteristics such as survey duration and self-stated difficulty level in understanding tasks. Each analysis allowed the scale factor to vary by task type and time (i.e., heteroskedasticity). Results: The results indicate three taste classes: a quality-of-life oriented class (33.35%) that placed the highest value on levels of severity, a length-of-life oriented class (26.72%) that placed the highest value on life span, and a middle class (39.71%) with health attribute effects lower than the quality class and life span effect lower than the length-of-life oriented class. The EQ-5D-5L values ranged from -2.11 to 0.86 (quality-of-life oriented class), from -0.38 to 1.02 (middle class), and from 0.36 to 1.01 (length-of-life oriented class). The likelihood of being a member of the quality-of-life class was highly dependent on whether the respondent completed the time-tradeoff tasks (p-value <0.001). The results also show two scale classes as well as heteroskedasticity within each scale class. Conclusion: Accounting for taste and scale classes simultaneously improves understanding preference heterogeneity in health valuation. Future studies may confirm the differences in taste between classes in terms of the effect of quality of life and life span attributes. Furthermore, confirmatory evidence is needed on how behavioral variables captured within a study protocol may enhance analyses of preference heterogeneity.

Title: An Irish valuation study for the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: The objective of this study is to derive a preference valuation set for the EQ-5D-5L health states from the Irish general public, following the standard protocol for such studies developed by the EuroQol Groupand examine variations across identifiable population groups in respect of preferences. A random sample (N=1,000) from the Irish population will be asked to value a standard subset of EQ-5D-5L health states,usingcompositetime-trade-off and discrete choices, in face to face interviews. Interviews will be conducted by a small team of postgraduate researchers with background knowledge of valuation methods, and who will be trained in the interviewing process and EQ-VT software.Regression analyses will be applied to the valuations of those health states. By means of the estimated regression coefficients, which together constitute the so-called Irish value set, valuations for all possible 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states willbe derived. This set of social health status preference valuations ensures the application of the EQ-5D-5L in cost-utility analysis for health care policy and clinical assessment in Ireland.Variations in preferences related to private health insurance status will be examined to shed light on potential differences in preferences for health. The study will provide an opportunity to investigate emergent methodological issues relating to EQ-5D-5Land Iand wewould welcome the opportunity for this study to facilitate this.

Title: Understanding the transitions and measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and EQ-5D-5L among adolescents aged 12-18 in China
Abstract: Objective Adolescence is a transitional period in which both youth-specific and adult health-related quality-of-life instruments may be appropriate. The EQ-5D-Y-5L is a new child-friendly HRQoL instrument with improvements in responsiveness and known-groups validity compared to EQ-5D-Y-3L. Both EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y (-3L and -5L) are suitable for use in older adolescents. However, evidence remains limited on transitions and comparative measurement properties across these instruments. This study aimed to examine the measurement properties and response redistribution of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and EQ-5D-5L among adolescents aged 12-18 years in China.Methods Data were obtained from the first wave of the Comprehensive Health and Relevant Factors Measurement among Chinese Children and Adolescents (CHARMING) study, a nationwide, geographically diverse survey using stratified quota sampling and paired parent-adolescent questionnaires. The EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-5L, CHU-9D, and EQ VAS were administered in randomized order. Level sum scores (LSS) were calculated for all EQ-5D instruments. Measurement properties were assessed using ceiling effects, Shannon’s index (H’), Shannon’s evenness index (J’), convergent validity, and known-groups validity. Paired response redistribution was examined between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L to assess the impact of expanding response levels, and between EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L to evaluate wording-related differences. Response redistribution was further compared between adolescents aged 12-15 years and 16-18 years, following the age ranges specified in the EuroQol user guides. Results This analysis included 5,062 adolescents (mean age, 14.9 years; 53.9% boys). Mean LSS were 5.337, 6.342, and 6.121 for the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and EQ-5D-5L, respectively. Ceiling effects were highest for the EQ-5D-Y-3L (73.2%), followed by the EQ-5D-5L (48.6%) and EQ-5D-Y-5L (41.2%). The EQ-5D-Y-5L had higher mean H’ (0.823) and J’ (0.355) than EQ-5D-Y-3L (H’: 0.294, J’: 0.186) and EQ-5D-5L (H’: 0.731, J’: 0.315). Correlations with EQ VAS and CHU-9D utility were strongest for the EQ-5D-5L LSS (r=-0.631 and -0.624), followed by the EQ-5D-Y-5L LSS (r=-0.589 and -0.599) and EQ-5D-Y-3L LSS (r=-0.319 and -0.367). All three instruments distinguished the prespecified MHS-CA, EQ-VAS, and BMI groups, with the strongest gradients across EQ-VAS groups. Large-step discordance between the youth versions was low for mobility (0.51%) and self-care (0.22%) but higher for usual activities (7.05%), pain/discomfort (7.35%), and emotional health (6.60%). For EQ-5D-Y-5L versus EQ-5D-5L, non-agreement ranged from 0.32% for MO to 28.09% for WSU. Compared with those aged 12-15 years, adolescents aged 16-18 years showed larger inconsistency or non-agreement in WSU.Conclusions Three EQ-5D instruments showed varied measurement performance across criteria among adolescents aged 12-18 years. EQ-5D-Y-5L showed the most favorable distributional properties and informativity, whereas EQ-5D-5L performed best in convergent validity. All three instruments demonstrated known-groups validity. Response redistribution analyses suggested that expanded response levels and wording differences mainly affected UA, PD and WSU. Adolescents aged 16-18 years showed greater divergence in WSU than those aged 12-15 years, possibly because richer health experiences made them more sensitive to wording and response-level differences in subjective dimensions.

Title: Pilot of the UK EQ-5D-5L TTO valuation to assess equivalence and feasibility of online interviews and face-to-face interviews during the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: Objective: Recent evidence has established the feasibility of generating time trade-off (TTO) utility values using online videoconference (video) interviews, but has not assessed whether the results are equivalent to values elicited via face-to-face in-person interviews, that were widely used prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines the equivalence, feasibility and acceptability of video and in-person interviews in generating TTO values. The study further aims to inform the choice of mode of administration for the new UK EQ-5D-5L valuation of the EQ-5D-5L and future valuation studies. Methods: Sample participants in Sheffield and Oxford, England were recruited using a blended approach of different methods to attract different people to be interviewed, and were sampled based on age, gender, ethnicity, and index of multiple deprivation. Participants were allocated to be interviewed either via video or in-person by 6 trained interviewers. Participants completed TTO tasks for the same block of 10 EQ-5D-5L health states using the EQ-VTv2 software. Feasibility, acceptability and equivalence was assessed across mode using: sample representativeness; participant understanding, engagement and feedback; participant preferred mode of interview; data quality; mean utility and distribution of values for each health state; and regression analyses assessing the impact of mode whilst controlling for the sociodemographic characteristics of participants. Results: The video and in-person samples had statistically significant differences in terms of ethnicity and income levels but were broadly similar across all other characteristics. Video interviews generated marginally lower quality data across some criteria. Participant understanding and feedback was positive and similar across modes. TTO values were similar across modes (mean and distribution for each state); whilst mean TTO values were lower for the in-person interviews for the most severe states, most noticeably the worst state, in most regression analyses the mode dummy was insignificant. There was no clear preference of mode across all individuals, though the characteristics of participants preferring to be interviewed across each mode differs. Discussion: The results demonstrate that video and in-person TTO interviews are feasible and acceptable. Both generated good-quality data, though video interviews had lower quality data across some criteria. Whilst TTO values differed across the modes for the more severe states, mode does not appear to be the cause. The sample is highly educated across both modes, and it is possible that data quality and TTO values by mode could differ in a less educated sample. The study results suggest that whilst TTO data collection using either mode is feasible, acceptable and will not in itself affect TTO values, the characteristics of people willing to be interviewed differs for each mode, and this in turn may impact on sample representativeness for some characteristics and the TTO values.

Title: Exploring the added value of the EQ-5D-5L in a VBHC setting: implementing and prediction
Abstract: Introduction  Value-Based Health Care (VBHC) principles are increasingly being adopted worldwide to improve healthcare quality. The Franciscus Gasthuis & Vlietland operationalizes the concept of value through the Quality Cost Indicator (QCI) framework. Central to QCI is Textbook Outcome (TO). TO is achieved when all predefined health outcome indicators are passed (score = 1) and is considered failed (score = 0) when at least one indicator is not passed. Next, Value in QCI is calculated as the percentage of patients achieving TO divided by the average healthcare costs. Using TO, a binary metric, may lead to over- or underestimation of value. This study aims to explore a graded optimal outcome approach using EQ-metrics, or estimations of EQ-metrics, using disease-specific outcomes to provide a more nuanced assessment of value.  Methods   Three patient populations were included: bariatric care, breast cancer care, and chronic kidney failure (later excluded due to low patient participation rates). Generic patient-reported outcomes (PROs) were assessed using EQ-5D-5L, disease-specific PROs via the already implemented ObesiQ (bariatric care) and EORTC-QLQ-BR23 (breast cancer). Hospital based healthcare costs and clinical outcome data were also collected from the electronic medical record. Improvements in PROs were analyzed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank (EQ-5D-5L, ObesiQ) and Bhapkar test (EORTC-QLQ-BR23). Univariate and multivariable regression analyses were used to explore associations between disease-specific outcome indicators, patient characteristics, and generic EQ metrics (tariffs, VAS, LSS). Cut-off values for graded optimal outcome, percentage TO, and QCI values were estimated. In depth interviews with healthcare professionals and managers were held to assess the role of EQ-5D-5L in VBHC at the micro and meso levels.  Results  Breast cancer population (n=33) No significant improvement in EQ metrics was observed. Patients reported significantly more arm (p = .03) and breast symptoms (p .01) post-surgery (EORTC-QLQ-BR23). Additionally, 79% of patients achieved TO based on clinical outcomes alone. Bariatric population (n=75) Significant improvements were observed in all EQ summary metrics (p .01) and ObesiQ domains (p .01). Furthermore, 68% achieved TO excluding comorbidities (64% including comorbidities).  Breast cancer population Body Image domain had the largest explanatory power on EQ metrics (R².24-.44), pre-surgery. Post-surgery, the Future Perspective domain had the largest explanatory power (R².12 -.21). Multivariable analysis indicated that disease-specific outcomes explained more variance of EQ-VAS (max R² = .49) than the EQ-tariff (max R² = .37) or unweighted sum scores (LSS, max R² = .37) at any time point. Bariatric population Pre-surgery, the Physical Functioning domain score had the largest explanatory power on EQ metrics (R².06- .31). Post-surgery, the Psychological Functioning domain score showed the largest R² (R².06- .11). Multivariable analysis indicated that disease-specific outcomes explained more variance of EQ-tariff (max R2 = .53) than EQ-VAS (max R2 = .37) at any time point. Post surgery, cut-off values for graded optimal outcomes based on EQ-VAS scores (p50) were 80 (breast cancer) and 82 (bariatric care); and 88 (breast cancer) and 92 (bariatric care) using EQ-tariffs (both scaled to a 0-100 scale). QCI cut-off values using optimal and graded optimal outcome (p50) ranged from 4.15 to 6.76 (breast cancer population) and 6.52 to 7.57 (bariatric population).  Discussion  EQ-5D-5L metrics provide information which can only be partially explained by the QCI-indicator set or any disease specific PROM. At the micro (patient physician) level, the EQ-5D-5L gives additional insights into the patient perceived health status. However, due to time constraints physicians prefer to limit consultations to disease specific PROMs and clinical outcomes. At the meso level, the EQ-5D-5L offers insights across patient populations, care paths and IPUs, but currently does not directly inform management decisions. The QCI model appears to be predominantly physician-oriented, with indicator selection being largely based on clinical relevance rather than patient-perceived value. To align the QCI model more closely with the principles of VBHC, a re-evaluation of the included indicators is needed, emphasizing outcomes that reflect what matters most to patients.

Title: Is the EQ-VT TTO Protocol Suitable for Use in 16- and 17-Year-Old Adolescents?
Abstract: Background: When valuing child health (e.g., generating EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L value sets) decisions need to be made on whose preferences and who respondents should think about. Emerging evidence from studies with the public, child valuation experts, and older adolescents themselves, suggests a majority consensual view that older adolescents (16-17-year-olds) should be involved in valuing child and adolescent health states imagining themselves living in impaired health, even when trading off life years as in time trade-off (TTO). However, limited research has assessed the feasibility and content validity of the existing EQ-VT valuation protocol, including TTO, for use in older adolescents. Aim: Using mixed-methods research, the overall aim is to assess the feasibility and content validity of the EQ-VT TTO protocol in the UK to value child health states, using the EQ-5D-Y-3L classification system in older adolescents (aged 16-17 years old). Methods: ‘Think aloud’ TTO interviews will be undertaken with 20 adolescents (50:50 16- and 17-year-olds; 50:50 male/female) valuing health states for themselves, following the EuroQol standardised valuation protocol using the EQ-VT system. Follow-up semi-structured interviews will elicit information on methodological questions relevant to using TTO in adolescents. Data will be analysed using qualitative framework analysis and quantitative analysis of TTO values, designed to assess the feasibility and content validity (comprehensibility, appropriateness, relevance) of using the EQ-VT TTO protocol in 16- and 17-year-olds. Quantitative and qualitative findings will be triangulated to provide further insights. Recommendations will be made for any potential modifications to the EQ-VT TTO protocol for use in older adolescents.

Title: Exploring the relationship between EQ-5D-5L and PROMIS-29
Abstract: The PROMIS set of measures represent an important body of work and there is increasing use of them both in the US and further afield, including in the UK and Australia. They are accompanied by utilities via PROPr. Both EQ-5D and PROMIS-29 are potential candidates for use in evidence for HTA. However, our literature review (paper 1 from this project) revealed there is very little evidence about how they compare in terms of measurement and valuation. In paper 2, we compared all theoretical values generated by PROPr based on PROMIS-29 instrument and compared these with the EQ-5D-5L value sets for US, Australia and England. There are very substantial differences in the properties of these values, and PROPr utilities have some unusual characteristics. In Paper 3 we examine and compare the psychometric performance of PROMIS-29 and EQ-5D-5L in a cross-section sample of patients with diverse health problems. The measurement and valuation properties of each instrument interact in complex ways. We conclude that which instrument is chosen is likely to have an important bearing on QALY estimates but how they compare depends on the nature and severity of the condition of interest.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Valuation, Populations and Health Systems

Title: A Randomised Controlled Trial of the effect of Short-Stretch Inelastic Compression bandages on Knee Function following total knee arthroplasty: Comparison of EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: Objectives: The aim of this research is to undertake a comparison of differentEQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets (UK, SP, NL) in a population of 2600patients withknee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis in the UKover a 12 month period. Methods:The comparison will take place as part of arandomised controlledtrial which aims to assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a two layer compression bandage versusstandard bandage post-operatively on patient reported outcomes in total knee arthroplasty patients. The trial aims to recruit 2600 participants and as part of the trial EQ-5D-3L data will be collected at baseline (pre-operatively)and 6 months (via theUKNHS Patient Reported Outcome Measures(PROMs)programme) and at 12 months(via a questionnaire). There is the opportunity toalso collect data on the 5L version in this population of patients, in order to undertake a comparison of the value sets, i.e. the 3L value sets versus the 5L value sets. The proposed research will assess the sensitivity to change of the 5L value setsby administering boththe3L and 5L versionsat baseline and at 12 monthsvia paper-based questionnaires. The projectwill be the firstto compare the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5Lvalue sets using panel data forthis population of patients, to our knowledge. The comparison will assess whether the new value sets for the 5L version aremore sensitive to the changes compared with the previous 3L value sets.

Title: Health utilities used in economic evaluations of cancer treatments
Abstract: Background: Tremendous health resources are needed to treatment patients with cancer. Health utility is a key input used to perform cost-utility analysis (CUA), which is increasingly used to inform resource allocation decisions. Objective: To identify the sources and elicitation methods of health utilities used in CUAs in oncology and to understand to what extent the EQ-5D has been used in these CUAs. Methods: We used the Tufts Cost-Effectiveness Analysis Registry to identify oncology CUAs published in Medline between 1976 and 2021. Eligible CUAs had to include an oncology population (based on ICD-10 codes), report health utilities, and be published in English. The references of cited health utilities were traced to identify the original study and the method of utility elicitation. Characteristic of included CUAs were summarized and the methods to derive health utilities were compared. Results: A total of 1,512 CUAs in oncology were identified. The majority of CUAs (n=1,428, 94.4%) were model-based. Malignant neoplasm of female genital organs (i.e., breast, vagina, cervical, and ovarian) were the most common population considered (n=424, 28.0%). Among these CUAs, 8,714 health utilities were identified. Upon review, the sources of 2,096 (24.1%) health utilities could not be traced. Of the remaining 6,618 health utilities, 1,718 (26.0%) used original data often derived from expert opinion (n=547, 31.8%) or EQ-5D (n=479, 27.9%). The 4,900 health utilities that were cited from external studies were most often derived using the standard gamble (n=1,258, 25.7%) or EQ-5D (n=1,190, 24.3%). Conclusion: Published health utilities are widely used in oncology CUAs, especially for model-based analyses. The EQ-5D has been the mostly widely used utility-based instrument in these CUAs.

Title: Advancing EuroQol Research and Collaboration in Saudi Arabia: A Visit to King Saud University (KSU)
Abstract: This visit to King Saud University (KSU) in Saudi Arabia aimed to explore opportunities for advancing the use of EuroQol instruments in research, clinical practice, and health policy.
