In all dimension, there is a much better distribution of responses across the levels in the 5L version compared to the 3L version, especially in the mobility, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression dimensions. Overall, quality control indicators were similar between literate and illiterate respondents. Although not significantly different, number of non-traders (those who do not trade any years for any health state irrespective of severity) was slightly higher in illiterate respondents. DCE estimates suggested that impact of health impairment on usual activities imposed highest influences on how respondents made their choices. And, presence of moderate problems in mobility was most likely led to respondents avoid choosing to be in that particular health state. The range of TTO values for the two groups was somewhat similar. Majority ofthe respondents reported that religion had noimpact on their responses(literate or illiterate). In addition, literate respondents indicatedthatno response of cultural beliefs on their responses while most of the illiterate respondents highlighted the impact of cultural norms on their responses, especially self-care. Conclusion:The results of this pilot study indicate that using the preference elicitation methods (TTO and DCE) is feasible, practical and acceptable with the Pakistani population. The usefulness and practicality of graphical illustrations of health dimensions/states and preference elicitation exercises with illiterate respondents has also been proven successful; however, incorporating these graphics in the electronic EQ-VT/PVT platform would be more useful.

Title: Mixed logit estimation of QALY tariffs corrected for non-linear time preferences
Abstract: Aim: We aimed to create a model estimation tool that will enable EuroQol researchers to efficiently analyze their discrete choice experiment (DCE) with duration data with mixed logit (MIXL) choicemodels that accommodate non-linear time preferences. Methods: The MIXL choice models are optimized using Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation techniques, with the integration over the respondents’ preferences performed using Simulated ML instead of Laplace approximations. After estimation, the software provides the end-user with parameter estimates, standard errors, 95% confidence intervals, and the QALY tariff. Software implementation: The software is bundled into an easily distributed R package. The underlying computational engine of the software is programmed in an efficient, low-level language (C++), and an R interface enables users to analyze their data directly in R - similar to any other R function.

Title: Assessing psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB-S for outcome monitoring in populations under regular surveillance for gastrointestinal cancers and under treatment for prostate cancer
Abstract: Background: Cancer contributes to a significant disease burden worldwide, with gastrointestinal (colorectal and oesophageal) and prostate cancer among the top five cancers. There are existing surveillance programs for individuals at above-average risk of developing colorectal cancer with colonoscopy, and endoscopy surveillance for oesophageal cancer. Treatment for prostate cancer includes hormonal therapy or surgery and active surveillance in early-stage disease. Under surveillance and following treatment, individuals have regular encounters with the health care system to monitor the presence of pre-cancerous lesions, cancer progression or cancer recurrence. These encounters affect patients' quality of life (QoL), specifically anxiety over the fear of cancer. While QoL is a required input for economic evaluations informing the efficient allocation of health care resources, existing recommended generic QoL measures often lack sensitivity in cancer surveillance populations. The EQ Health and Wellbeing short (EQ-HWB-S) is a new generic utility-based measure of health and wellbeing covering nine dimensions, including control, anxiety and being sad/depressed. Given its broader coverage of wellbeing aspects, the EQ-HWB-S may offer a more sensitive and suitable alternative for capturing QoL impacts in cancer surveillance settings. Aim: To assess the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB-S as an outcome measure in individuals under regular surveillance for gastrointestinal cancers and following a diagnosis of prostate cancer. Methods: Participants in surveillance will be invited from two existing pre-cancer registries for oesophageal (≈250) and colorectal (≈1000) and one post-diagnosis registry for prostate cancer (≈1600). The EQ-HWB-S will be completed alongside the EQ-5D-5L, as well as the cancer-specific EORTC QLQ-C30 and the prostate cancer-specific EPIC-26. Convergent/divergent validity, known-group validity and feasibility will be assessed. Sensitivity will be assessed by exploring ceiling/floor effects and responsiveness. Expected outcomes and significance: The EQ-HBW-S is expected to demonstrate strong psychometric validity in this population, given its broader coverage of wellbeing dimensions such as anxiety, control, and sadness, which are highly relevant to individuals undergoing cancer surveillance. We anticipate that our results will support the wider adoption of the EQ-HWB-S in routine care, which will provide more sensitive and accurate inputs for health economic evaluations of interventions in cancer surveillance settings.

Title: PhD dissertation funding request for a novel valuation method: Feasibility and application of the single profile preference elicitation (SPP) method to value bolt-on items. (Revised application)
Abstract: Bolt-on items can be appended to the EQ-5D core dimensions in order to improve its performance in applications to certain patient populations. Valuation studies have been conducted in order to obtain utility values for the health states described by the EQ-5D classifier appended with a bolt-on. However, the valuation methods used in these valuation studies require large sample sizes and are associated with a high cognitive burden to respondents. A new valuation method, currently referred to as Single Profile Preference Elicitation (SPP), is emerging as a plausible alternative for the valuation of extended descriptive systems. Feedback from testing of SPP in small-scale experiments suggests high user acceptance, ease of administration, and a comparatively low cognitive burden compared to regular DCE. Additionally, preliminary simulation studies indicate that SPP should provide more information per task than regular DCE, which should translate into improved precision or lower sample size requirements. Our project's primary aim was to examine the feasibility and acceptability of using SPP to value multidimensional measures when adding dimensions to existing measures. To achieve this goal, we first conducted a qualitative study (n=17) to explore the feasibility acceptability of using the SPP to value bolt-on items. This information helped us to refine the protocol used in the valuation stage. The second aim of this project was to apply the SPP method to value bolt-on dimensions while retaining the scaling of the reference EQ-5D-5L value set. In the subsequent valuation stage, a sample of 1008 members of the general population completed an online survey, administering regular DCE and SPP for EQ-5D + a bolt-on item, for head-to-head comparison. The results obtained in this stage will lead to the estimation of the preference weights for the bolt-on item and the examination of the precision of the estimates yielded by the SPP compared to regular DCE.

Title: UK valuation of the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: The aim of this study was to generate a new UK value set for the EQ-5D-5L using a representative sample of the UK general public. In total 1200 interviews were conducted, of which 1102 were conducted via videoconference using Zoom and 98 interviews were undertaken in-person. The sample of 1200 participants were representative of the UK population for age, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic group as set according to quota groups. The sample is also proportionally representative for the four nations. Participants were interviewed using the time trade-off technique to elicit preferences for EQ-5D-5L health states. The data was modelled to generate utility values for every health state defined by the EQ-5D-5L. The study has benefitted from governance from a study Steering Group, with input from an EQ-VT support team from the EuroQol Group, a Quality Control team independent of the study team, advice from the EuroQol Valuation Working Group, and patient and public involvement.

Title: EQVT iteration experiment
Abstract: TTO data from recent EQVT valuation studies displays troubling patterns, including spikes at 1, .5, 0, -.5, and -1; a lack of non-integer year responses; high levels of logically inconsistent responses, and possible censoring of values below .5 or 0 for a number of respondents. The (ping-pong) routing, has been suggested as part of the reason for the observed spikes. This proposal is submitted under the umbrella of the ongoing effort to improve the EQ-VT system, and aims to determine if two approaches to altering the routing procedure may improve the data quality, particularly in terms of reduced spikes and reduced level of inconsistent responses The alternative procedures are based on the observation that the spikes of elicited values correspond to respondents stating indifference very early in the current TTO routing. At least two distinct effects may contribute to this: satisficing (i.e. respondents stating indifference early in order to shorten the task), anda form of sequential anchoring (inadequate adjustment from the values presented in the TTO task). The two modifications we suggest testing are1) Randomized starting point and routing:Reducing the danger of routing-specific bias through randomizing respondents to a range of different routing procedures. If anchoring and satisficing is at play in all conceivable routing procedures, introducing a variety of routes will distribute the overall bias, so that the common variance across different routing procedures should be a less biased measure of net preferences.As a benefit, varied routing may enable analyses to determine to what extent values are censored at 0.2) Non-stopping TTO:Satisficing is a problem in TTO because the procedure ends as soon as respondents state indifference, creating an incentive for stating indifference at values corresponding to early choices. The second modification attempts to remove this incentive through forcing respondents to perform the same amount of work for all possible elicited values. This is achieved by not stoppingthe preference elicitation once a point of indifference is identified. Deliverables: (1) report to the Exec/VMWG with description findings and suggestions for how to handle routing in the EQVT, (2) Scientific paper on routing bias and satisficing effects in TTO valuation, (3) paper on a non-stopping TTO, and (4) paper on censoring.

Title: A qualitative examination of the content validity of the EQ-5D in patients with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
Abstract: This qualitative study aimed to examine the content validity of the EQ-5D in a sample of Chinese patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). The research team collaborated with Beijing Dear Mom & Dad DMD patient centre, China's largest DMD patient organization, to recruit participants. Thirty participants—15 adult patients and 15 children and adolescent patients—who met the inclusion criteria were invited to participate in web-based one-on-one, in-depth interviews. The interviews included concept elicitation to identify patient-perceived DMD impact, and cognitive debriefing to assess the relevance and acceptability of the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y, respectively. Overall, DMD patients' health and quality of life were affected in three areas: physical health, mental well-being, and social relationships. Nearly all patients agreed that the EQ-5D represents most aspects affecting their quality of life, but it may lack components such as social relationships. Moreover, items related to physical health were not very appropriate for patients with DMD, which could affect the use of EQ-5D in this population, especially for adult patients.

Title: General public EQ-5D measurement before and during general Covid-19 quarantine in Spain
Abstract: Abstract Please provide a short summary of your completed work. This information will be included in the EuroQol database on funded research and may also be presented on the research section of the EuroQol website Objectives The COVID-19 pandemic forced many countries to implement confinement measures to limit the spread of the virus. Measuring the loss in terms of quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) may provide a commensurable basis for comparison of the impact of COVID-19 and related factors to health and well-being. The aim of this research was to explore the impact of the first 28 days of COVID-19 related confinement measures on the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of the Spanish general population. Methods We implemented a quota-based online survey to collect age, gender, region and EQ-5D-5L data. The data collection was conducted in four waves with 500 general population respondents each: one conducted shortly before the lockdown and 3 follow-ups conducted every consecutive week. Each wave of sampling was independent, and any overlap of respondents between waves would be coincidental. EQ-5D-5L responses were described using the proportion of respondents reporting each level of functioning on each dimension over the follow-up period. Utility values were retrieved from the Spanish EQ-5D-5L value set. For comparison with pre-covid responses, data from the 2011-2012 National Health Survey (NHS) was taken as reference. We calculated the QALY loss over the 21 days of the follow-up period as the difference between utility values from the reference sample and the corresponding values for the 4 waves of our data collection. QALY loss for the entire duration of the lockdown was estimated taking the mean QALY-loss for the 4 waves. For comparison, we estimated the total QALY-loss associated with premature deaths due to COVID-19 in Spain until the end of the study, assuming that they would otherwise have lived to the estimated life expectancy for their corresponding age/sex group, with values corresponding to their respective mean utilities based on the reference sample. Results Comparing the baseline results to the follow-up results shows little change with respect to the distributions of reported problems in any of the 5 dimensions during the follow-up period. However, results for anxiety/depression show a 32% increase in the proportion of reported problems (most prominently for level 2, from 9% to 35%). The Spanish population was estimated to accrue a total of 1,994,216 QALYs over the study period. Based on the corresponding reference data, the population should have accrued 2,054,737 QALYs, leading to a loss for the general Spanish population of 60,520 QALYs over 21 days. If the situation observed were to continue for the entire lockdown, the corresponding loss would be 285.310 QALYs. For comparison, the estimated lifetime loss associated with the 15,956 individuals who had died from COVID-19 by the end of the study would have tallied 146,584 QALYs. Conclusions A population under a lockdown situation reported higher rates of anxiety/depression problems than in a regular situation. On a country-wide scope, this may lead to a substantial loss in terms of QALYs, especially over longer periods of time.

Title: Formatting the EQ Health and Wellbeing 9 (EQ-HWB-9): Qualitative assessment of acceptability of the digital version
Abstract: Currently there is only a paper version of the EQ-HWB-9 questionnaire. YPrime was contracted to create a digital prototype that included 3 routes of the item-by item EQ-HWB-9 layout and to test it on appropriate users. The project gathered patient feedback on the digitised EQ-HWB-9 through moderated 1:1 user testing sessions. Focus areas included task completion, user sentiment, device behavior, accessibility, and design variances. Sixteen participants interacted with the prototypes on their personal mobile (69%) or tablet device (31%). Participants were over 60 years old (range 62-81 years) and had one or more qualifying conditions/disabilities, which included limited hand mobility to health condition, stroke or injury (7/16); colour vision deficiency (4/16); difficulty with concentration (3/16); reading disability (3/16). Data privacy agreements were signed, and verbal consent was obtained for recording interviews. All participants were able to independently complete the testing. They found it easy to engage with, reported acceptability of the instructions, were satisfied with the length of the questionnaire, and expressed some preferences. The digital designs adhered to the Electronic Clinical Outcome Assessment (eCOA) Consortium best practice recommendations surrounding electronic data. Fonts and approach used were consistent across all screens; no items were preselected when the respondent opened the questionnaire or any screen within it; scrolling should be allowed but all response options on a given screen must be viewed before the navigation button becomes available;  skipping should also be allowed but a validation message should be in place to have the participant confirm if they chose to skip intentionally or if they did so in error.

Title: A mixed methods approach to testing alternative recall periods for EQ-5D (2nd revision)
Abstract: Background: EQ-5D-5L with its recall time of “today” may limit its ability to capture episodic symptoms and exacerbations in chronic obstructive airway diseases (OAD). We examined whether longer timeframes and changing the intensity response scales to frequency scales could improve the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L. Methods: We used a mixed method design starting with in-depth interviews with 20 patients and clinicians to elicit preferred timeframes using concept elicitation techniques and content analyses. We then administered the top four preferred variants using one- & four-weeks’ timeframes with the original intensity or an alternative frequency response scale alongside EQ-5D-5L and St George Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) to OAD patients during two different visits. We compared the ceiling effects and construct validity by testing a priori hypotheses in relation to SGRQ and clinical outcomes via correlation and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses, respectively. Follow-up patients were categorized into “better”, “stable”, and “worse” groups to assess reliability using intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) or Cohen’s Kappa (k), and responsiveness using ROC analysis. Results: 184 patients (mean [SD] age: 54[18]; female: 37.0%) completed baseline assessments.120 patients also completed follow-up assessments (mean [SD] interval: 2.8 [1.7] months). The ceilings were lower in the variants compared to EQ-5D-5L (p<0.001). Reliability of the variants were comparable to or higher than EQ-5D-5L. The c-statistic values derived from ROC analyses of the variants were consistently higher than EQ-5D-5L. Conclusions: Use of longer timeframes with the original intensity or the frequency response scales may improve EQ-5D-5L’s psychometric properties in OAD patients.

Title: Exploring the use of EQ-5D-3L in measuring population health and studying health inequalities in China: evidence from National Health Services Surveys (2008, 2013 and 2018)
Abstract: This project aimed to generate EQ-5D-3L population norms for China; to investigate inequalities in health across social determinants of health; and to describe changes in population health between 2008 and 2018. We had planned to use three waves of the largest national representative population health survey data – National Health Services Survey (NHSS). We had obtained data access (oral) approval from NHSS data PI (also co-investigators on this project: Yaoguang Zhang and Ling Xu) at the time of submitting the proposal (Oct 2020). However, our access to the data was delayed due to several rounds of domestic COVID-19 outbreaks in China and domestic travel restrictions, particularly to Beijing. The NHSS data centre is located in Beijing and all the analyses are required to be done on-site at NHSS data facilities. In November 2021, China released new regulations on data sharing and data security, particularly for projects supported by international organization/funds. All NHSS data access approvals have been escalated to Vice Minister level. During the similar period, the NHSS PI has been promoted to other departments and left NHSS data center. We have made every effort to explore a number of options for completing the project as proposed, including: our Chinese colleagues undertaking the analyses on-site at Ministry of Health secure data facilities, under supervision, and strictly limiting any sharing to results tables/statistical output; providing an official support letter from Nanjing Medical University (where co-PI Jiaying is based) to the NHSS data center for internal clearance; and several efforts at personal correspondence with MoH officials. Unfortunately, the circumstances appear to restrict all potential uses of NHSS data for research purposes (i.e. for both domestic and international research), and all avenues of further enquiry have been exhausted. In August 2022 we informed the senior scientist and our advisors about these issues, and in Oct 2022 we submitted a memo to the Exec on this issue. We considered a number of options for using alternative regional data sets, but none would have allowed us to fully achieve what we had originally proposed to do before access to the national health survey data was denied. We consider the best option is to cancel the project so the funds can be released for other uses. We have had made quite a bit of progress in producing an SAP, hosting the first advisory group meeting (in June 2021) and quite detailed outline/draft papers, up until the point the data access was withdrawn. We have included those materials as attachment, in case they are useful for future projects. We thank the Exec and office for their understanding about the circumstances affecting this work.

Title: Development of the Turkish Value Set for the EQ-5D-5L Quality of Life Instrument: A Nationally Representative Valuation Study Using the EQ-VT Protocol
Abstract: This project aims to develop the first nationally representative EQ-5D-5L value set for Türkiye by applying the standardized EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) protocol. Although the EQ-5D-5L instrument is widely used in health technology assessment (HTA), cost-effectiveness analysis, and health policy design globally, Türkiye currently lacks a locally validated value set, which undermines the relevance of utility-based evaluations in national decision-making. To address this gap, we plan a cross-sectional valuation study targeting a nationally representative sample of 1,000 adults. Data collection will be carried out in seven geographical regions of Türkiye, each represented by its most populous province to ensure regional diversity and operational feasibility. Two trained interviewers will be assigned to each region (14 in total), with each interviewer expected to complete approximately 70–75 interviews. Our aim is to obtain complete and high-quality data from 1,000 adult respondents. The EQ-VT protocol will be used, applying both composite time trade-off (cTTO) and discrete choice experiment (DCE) methods. Data will undergo rigorous quality control aligned with EuroQol standards and analyzed using models that correct for heteroskedasticity, including Tobit regression and hybrid modeling techniques that integrate cTTO and DCE data. The resulting Turkish value set will serve as a robust, culturally relevant foundation for HTA, reimbursement decisions, and public health planning. Additionally, it will enable Türkiye’s formal integration into the international EuroQol data network, facilitating cross-national comparability and collaboration. All project outputs, including value sets, documentation, and training materials, will be openly accessible to promote transparency, reproducibility, and widespread use.

Title: The role of attention allocation in health state valuation with time trade-off: an exploration of the decision processes underlying correction for prospect theory.
Abstract: Background: In EQ-5D valuation, time trade-off (TTO) is applied under strict assumptions about decision-making about health that are violated for many individuals, e.g. each year has the same value. Earlier work has shown that when these assumptions are relaxed, e.g. by applying cumulative prospect theory (CPT), TTO utilities are similar to those derived with standard gamble (SG). This work, referred to as the corrective approach, requires measuring or approximating differences between individuals’ decision-making for life duration, such as differences in sensitivity to losses and discounting life years. These CPT measurements are used to estimate parameters reflecting this loss aversion and discounting, used for ‘correcting’ TTO utilities Aim. When CPT parameters are used for correction, it is assumed that the decision-making processes they capture are also apparent in TTO. For example, for an elicited loss aversion parameter, which captures increased sensitivity to losses in life duration in CPT measurement, to be applicable to TTO, we should see similar sensitivity to giving up life duration in TTO. We aim to explore if this is true. Methods: We will study decision processes by using mouse tracking software. By tracking which information is studied and for how long, we can get insight into how people decide in TTO. Mouse tracking will be used when eliciting TTO utilities for 4 health states and CPT measurement. We also incorporate SG tasks for the same 4 health states, as this will allow us to evaluate the validity of corrected TTO utilities.

Title: Exploring the validity of EQ-5D-5L in Indigenous people of Canada
Abstract: Background. Worldwide, there is a need to recognize the distinct health needs of Indigenous people, address inequalities of health experienced by Indigenous people, and improve the appropriateness of health care services and measures of chronic disease. In the context of colonized countries, there is need to examine current (colonized) systems of measuring health-related quality of life and traditional approaches to measuring and valuing health to establish relevance of these approaches to, and appropriateness for, Indigenous people. This will improve recommendations for the use of preference-based measures (PBMs), such as the EQ-5D-5L, in Indigenous people and their application in evaluating effectiveness of healthcare. Objectives. This study aimed to (1) review the literature reporting the use of indirect or direct PBMs for Indigenous people, in terms of application of direct or indirect measures (which PBMs have been used, for which Indigenous groups), development or translation, or performance (validity, reliability), (2) explore validity of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Quality Appraisal Tool in the context of Indigenous Peoples in Canada, (3) explore the validity of the EQ-5D-5L (Canadian version) and how well it represents health-related quality of life for Indigenous people in Canada, and (4) explore conceptual feasibility of traditional choice-based valuation tasks and how these techniques align with Indigenous worldview. Methods. The first project was a systematic review, following standard methodological protocols including support of an expert librarian, a search of multiple major databases (n=13), and screening by two reviewers. Elements of ethically engaged research were considered indicators of quality. To address the absence of a widely adopted quality appraisal tool to assess ethically engaged research, an Australian quality appraisal tool was subsequently mapped to select existing national and regional ethical guidance for research with Indigenous people in Canada. QAT questions were mapped to source concepts, and cross tabulated in visual form. Convergence and gaps were identified. In the second project, qualitative description and Two-Eyed Seeing guided exploration of validity of the EQ-5D-5L and valuation techniques with urban Indigenous participants. Recruitment, data collection, analysis, and dissemination approaches were co-designed with Indigenous research partners. Participants were First Nations, Inuit, or Metis people living in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, or nearby urban center (urban Indigenous) working in health, policy, leadership, or community positions, and willing to share their individual knowledge of Indigenous health and wellness. Semi-structured interviews were co-facilitated with an Indigenous research partner. Concurrent data collection and analysis included member-checking, peer debriefing, reflexivity journals, and an audit trail. Findings. The systematic review demonstrated a large number of recent publications in diverse areas of research reporting the use of PBMs in Indigenous people. It also showed relatively little evidence on their performance in various Indigenous populations, and none in Canada. Similarities and a few gaps were found between the Australian Quality Assessment Tool for Indigenous-engaged research when mapped to ethical guidance in Canada. There may be space for more Indigenous specific instruments or domains, and a shift to strength-based wording within the EQ-5D-5L. The context of colonization and colonial impacts on Indigenous health and ways of living must also be considered when measuring HRQL. In the second study, participants expressed concern for inaccurate measurement and potential for negative impact on Indigenous people. Conceptualization and feasibility of the TTO and DCE may be affected by the content of the descriptive system presented, and the ability to envision the choice options as realistic. Lastly, the concept of “trading all” raised questions for participants. Discussion/Significance. This research indicates there is work to be done to improve performance (starting with face validity) of HRQL instruments, such as the EQ-5D-5L, currently in use in Canada for Indigenous people. This study can inform conversations about how the EQ-5D-5L and traditional valuation tasks should be used (or not) to advise health policy decisions affecting Indigenous Peoples in Canada.

Title: Measurement Issues in EQ-5D Use in Older People Living with Dementia: Comparing the Dimensional Coverage of EQ-5D of Self and Proxy Reports
Abstract: Background: Persons living with dementia (PlwD) make up a growing proportion of the elderly population. Their healthcare use is relatively high, making HRQoL outcomes for healthcare decisions important. Although generic preference-based instruments like the EQ-5D are widely used, there are some specific measurement issues in this patient group. These instruments  may inadequately capture domains relevant to dementia, such as cognition, emotional well-being, and social participation/relationships. Additionally, proxy reporting due to cognitive impairment introduces potential misalignment with patient experiences.Objective: To explore the dimensional coverage of the EQ-5D in assessing HRQoL and the impact of proxy-reporting  in older people living with dementia, comparing self-reported and proxy-reported data.Methods: Using the multinational Actifcare dataset (N=902), which includes both self-reported and proxy-reported HRQoL data from community-dwelling individuals with dementia (n=451) and their carers (n=451), we will conduct exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses (EFA and CFA) to assess the dimensional structure of EQ-5D alongside co-administered instruments (DEMQOL-U, QoL-AD, and ICECAP-O). Subgroup-specific factor analyses will identify structural differences between respondent types (i.e., PlwD vs proxies). Building on these findings, we will apply structural equation modeling (SEM) to quantify the incremental explanatory value of non-EQ-5D dimensions in predicting overall HRQoL, as measured by the EQ VAS. Model fit and statistical significance will be rigorously evaluated using appropriate estimators and nested model comparisons.Relevance to the EuroQol Group: Through our inclusion of an increasingly important older people subgroup and our focus on dimensionality to inform bolt-on selection, this project will directly respond to the DSWG’s call for secondary analyses to explore measurement issues of the EQ-5D in diverse older people subgroups. In addition, this study will provide critical insights into the overlap and differences in dimensional performance of EQ-5D when it is self-reported by PlwD compared to when it is proxy reported by informal carers. Such findings are relevant to inform the selection of potential bolt-ons to use across the spectrum of dementia care (ranging from contexts where self-reported HRQOL is feasible to situations where only proxy reports are feasible).

Title: Does rapid fluctuation of health over time affect the actual time span that is used by trauma patients when thinking of ‘your health today’?
Abstract: The standard reference period of the EQ-5D is ‘your health today’. However, the ‘true’ reference period that is used by the respondent when filling out the EQ-5D may be shorter or longer than ‘your health today’, or may focus on specific (peak) health experiences in that time period. The aims of this study were to determine the actual reference period that was used by trauma patients when thinking of 'your health today' and the heuristic "aggregation of time" rule that was used to combine the full experience of that actual reference period in one overall 'signifying' number or level. A total of 531 trauma patients completed the 1 week, 3 month and 12 month questionnaires. The 3 and 12 month questionnaires included the EQ-5D-3L and cognitive debriefing questions. The most frequently reported reference time span when reporting health status was either "the last 24 hours" or "today". Most patients reported their health as an average moment. Age and education level were key factors influencing the reference period and heuristic rule, respectively. These findings highlight the importance of considering time reference and individual factors, such as age and education level, when interpreting EQ-5D data.

Title: Travel grant for ISPOR Europe 2025 to give an oral presentation of work for SG-1792.
Abstract: This grant was used to support the dissemination of research findings through an oral presentation at the ISPOR Europe 2025 Conference, which took place on 9th-12th Nov 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland. The study linked to SG-1792, entitled “Utilizing LLMs to Enhance Patient-Reported Outcome Measures: Application to the EQ-5D and Bolt-ons", was presented as one of 4 presentations in the session of 12 Nov at 10:00 entitled "Patient Preferences in Clinical Trials and HTA". This project (SG-1792) was funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation as a Seed Grant. The session was attended by approximately 100 ISPOR Europe attendees, including experts from academia, government, and industry with interests in HTA/HEOR methods, quality of life research, patient reported outcomes, etc. Submitted abstract for the presented research: OBJECTIVES: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising applications in healthcare, yet little is known about their potential to improve the measurement of patient-reported outcomes, which are central to inform decision-making across health system levels. We explored the use of LLMs to develop or extend patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) based on information from patient-reported free-text data. METHODS: The GPT-4o model was used to analyze data from 1,977 members of the Dutch Celiac Association who completed the EQ-5D-5L and narratively described the impact of celiac disease on their lives. Prompts to the LLM were designed to identify possible additional dimensions (i.e., ‘bolt-on’ dimensions) to the EQ-5D-5L, and to produce preliminary bolt-on item wordings for selected dimensions. Evaluation of the approach comprised: comparisons of dimensions identified by two alternative approaches (i.e., qualitative analysis and topic modelling);text-entry level agreement (i.e., Cohen’s Kappa) on identified dimensions; suitability of LLM-generated bolt-on wordings assessed against existing criteria using Likert scales; and a critical appraisal consisting of face validity assessments and a SWOT analysis. RESULTS: The LLM identified 12 potential bolt-on dimensions to the EQ-5D-5L, of which 9 were also identified using qualitative analysis, and 5 using topic modelling. Text-entry level agreement between the LLM and qualitative approaches was ‘substantial’ or ‘almost perfect’, with two exceptions of poor/fair agreement (median Kappa=0.70, IQR=0.44-0.89). The LLM-generated potential bolt-on wordings for the 4 most common dimensions (i.e., ‘Dietary restrictions’, ‘Fatigue’, ‘Social participation’, and ‘Gastrointestinal symptoms’) scored 4/5, 4.4/5, 4.3/5, and 4.2/5 respectively when assessed against existing criteria. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the promising potential of LLMs to inform the development or modification of PROMs based on patient-reported text data. A limitation to generalizability and reliability is the approach’s dependency on prompt quality. Further research should assess the approach’s transferability across disease areas and different data sources (e.g. social media, EHRs).

Title: Case-mix adjustment of EQ-5D health profiles for the purpose of hospital performance assessment
Abstract: There is increasing interest in using routinely collected EQ-5D data to compare the performance of healthcare providers in terms of their patients’improvementsin health-related quality of life. An essential condition forsuch comparisons to be valid is that they shouldadjust for differences between providers in thecharacteristics of thepatients that they treat; a process known as case-mix adjustment. The prevalentapproach is to estimate a case-mix adjustment model that relates patient and provider characteristics directly toEQ-5D valuesand to use thisto generate provider-specific outcomesin terms of changes in adjusted EQ-5D values. However, this approach haslimitations. For example,it does not make full use of the information provided by the underlying EQ-5D profile data,and it generates results that are specific to the value set used. We propose an alternative approach that will generatefor providers the mix of EQ-5D profilesadjusted for patient and provider characteristics, with associated probabilities. These can then be used to generate EQ-5D valuesor analysed in profile formfor use in performance comparisons. This approach relies on predicting dimension-specific case-mix adjusted responses using a multivariate regression framework. In this project we will use a simulation study to investigate the statisticalproperties of both methods, how well they can identify performance variation, and which context-specific factors should guide the choice of methodology in applied research. We will follow this up with real-world case studies to establish feasibility of the proposed method in commonly-encountered performance assessment settings.

Title: Performance of the EQ-5D in the European aging population – A study on measurement properties, population norms, health inequalities and determinants of health in a large representative sample of European adults aged 55+ using the SHARE-data
Abstract: The primary deliverables are the results from three secondary data analyses based on the fourth wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), as described in the study proposal. Major findings will be published in international (open access) journals and presented on international conferences and the EuroQol plenary meeting. Two manuscripts are currently submitted, and a third manuscript is being prepared. Based on the planned analyses, we investigated the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-3L in the (SHARE) population of elderly Europeans (I), developed country-specific EQ-5D-3L norms stratified by age-groups and gender for the elderly Europeans (II), studied health inequalities using single and combined indicators of socioeconomic status (SES) and their relative importance as determinants of health in the ageing European population (III).

Title: Patient Reported Outcomes in Quality of Care. A systematic review with specific attention to barriers and opportunities for EQ-5D in orthopedic surgery
Abstract: **Background** The use of the EQ-5D in recent years has been broadened to its use as a PROM. These broader applications include: assessment of quality of care (mainly in clinical registries), large scale (sub)population health assessment (such as the recent covid-studies), and use in clinical decision making or provider's choices, as exemplified by Bansback (orthopedic surgery choices), and Parkin & Devlin’s work on NHS data. **Aims** The aim of the study is to investigate the utilization of the EQ-5D as a PROM in quality of care applications, notably in orthopedic surgery, elaborating on a pre-existing generic study into empirical evidence on PROMs in general. Barriers and opportunities will be investigated, including different medical cultures across the globe. **Methods** A systematic review will be conducted, combined with interviewing/surveying specific stakeholders (a.o. OECD, and EQ-Network; orthopedic registry stakeholders in particular). The systematic review will start from preparatory work from a Master thesis of the applicant. Part of the work expediates on materials from the September 2019 EQ Workshop in Brussels. **Deliverables** * List of strengths and weaknesses of the EQ-5D (to improve; maybe suggestions for data processing [casemix control, dashboards], for opportunities to apply so-called 'deep dive' technology or insert bolt-ons, adaptation of reference time [now: today], desired supportive information) in this context; in particular to research/network groups like Canada, Sweden, UK. * Input for a EQ-5D dissemination strategy on PROM use * Input for a.o. the OECD platform, and national specialist's platform (like FMS Netherlands)

Title: Joint North American EuroQol Regional meeting and 10th Annual APERSU End-user meeting
Abstract: The 2025 joint meeting of the EuroQol North American Regional Meeting and the Alberta PROMs and EQ-5D Research and Support Unit (APERSU) 10th Anniversary and End-User Meeting was held at the Malcolm Hotel in Canmore, Alberta. This milestone event convened a diverse group of stakeholders, including EuroQol members, APERSU staff and students, patient partners, representatives from the Alberta Government, Alberta Health Services, Primary Care Networks, and PROMs users from across Canada. The meeting celebrated a decade of APERSU’s role as an intermediary organization connecting the EuroQol Research Foundation with non-commercial users of EQ-5D, supporting licensing, education, training, implementation, and research to advance the use of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in health systems.The two-day meeting brought together researchers, clinicians, policy leaders, patient partners, and international collaborators to explore innovations in EQ-5D and PROMs, with approximately 60 in-person and 10 virtual participants per day. Evaluation findings from 31 respondents demonstrated high overall satisfaction (mean 4.1/5), particularly among in-person attendees (4.3/5), with 98% indicating they were likely or very likely to attend future meetings. Most frequently cited topics of interest included the future role of EQ-5D and PROMs in decision-making, next-generation instruments and bolt-on dimensions, and implementation examples featuring patient engagement.Key strengths included strong participant engagement, appreciation for the breadth of expertise and topics, and positive feedback on interactive discussant-style poster sessions. Constructive feedback highlighted opportunities to strengthen policy- and system-level content, enhance poster session logistics, broaden clinical and patient representation, and increase time for discussion and networking. Looking ahead, participants identified priorities for APERSU’s next decade, including supporting policy and system-level PROMs use, enhancing patient-level applications, and expanding PROMs integration in primary care. Overall, the joint meeting both celebrated APERSU’s achievements and reinforced its leadership in fostering collaboration, innovation, and patient-centered PROMs use in Alberta and beyond.

Title: Validation of the Chichewa versions of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L in Malawi
Abstract: Objectives The EuroQol Group has developed an extended version of the EQ-5D-Y with five response levels for each of its five dimensions (EQ-5D-Y-5L). The psychometric performance of the three response level version (EQ-5D-Y-3L) has been reported in several studies involving both healthy children as well as clinical populations, but that of the EQ-5D-Y-5L has only been reported in a few studies. This study aimed to translate and psychometrically evaluate the Chichewa (Malawi) versions of both the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L. Methods The EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL™ 4.0 self-report Chichewa versions were administered to children and adolescents aged 8-17 years in Blantyre, Malawi. Both the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L were evaluated using gold standard psychometric methods, including missing data, floor/ceiling effects, reliability (internal consistency) and validity (convergent, discriminant, known-group and empirical). Results A total of 289 participants (95 healthy, and 194 chronic and acute) self-completed the questionnaires. There was little problem with missing data (0.7). Convergent validity tested with PedsQL™ 4.0 self-report was found to be satisfactory (correlation >0.4). However, correlation between some of the dimensions for both versions of the EQ-5D-Y and the PedsQL™ 4.0 sub-scales was mixed. While there was evidence of discriminant validity with respect to gender and age (no association with EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L sum and utility scores), it was not evident for school grade (p<0.05). As regards empirical validity, the EQ-5D-Y-5L was 31%-91% less efficient than the EQ-5D-Y-3L at detecting differences in health status using external measures. Conclusions The EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were both found to be reliable and valid for use among children and adolescents although with some limitations. Further, psychometric testing is required for test re-test reliability and responsiveness that could not be carried out in this study due to COVID-19 restrictions.

Title: (Proposal extension) An online DCE study to support the development of an EQ-5D-Y value set for the UK: including an adolescent arm in the study
Abstract: Introduction: Currently, no value sets exist to support the use of EQ-5D-Y health states in cost-effectiveness analyses. One of the challenges associated with generating these value sets is that standard valuation methods are cognitively demanding and may not be appropriate for younger individuals to complete. However, asking adults to complete a valuation task from the perspective of a child/adolescent presents its own challenges. In this study we collected adolescent and adult responses to a discrete choice experiment (DCE). The aim was to evaluate whether there are systematic differences in preferences between these two groups when they make choices between EQ-5D-Y health states.Methods: An online survey was designed containing a DCE plus background and debrief questions. The DCE comprised 15 pairwise choices between EQ-5D-Y health states. A sample of UK adults was asked to consider the health of a 10-year-old child when completing the tasks. In contrast, a sample of UK adolescents (11-17 years) received the same survey and completed the tasks considering their own health. Mixed logit models with correlated parameters were estimated for both samples based on prior research. To understand whether preferences between the two groups were different,accounting for any scaledifferences,we conducted the Swait-Louviere test. To ensure the comparisons accounted for potential differences in scale between the two samples, we used the relative 2parameter importance of the attribute levels and an examination of differences in predicted choice probabilities. Results: In total, 1,000 adults and 1,005 adolescents completed the survey. The relative importance of the levels attached greatest disutility to level 3 in pain/discomfort (PD3) followed by anxiety/depression (AD3)in both groups. The third-worst level differed: mobility (MO3)for adolescents; and usual activities (UA3)for adults. Modelling results indicate that there are significant differences in preferences between the two samples. The Swait-Louviere test confirmed that model coefficients were different and that such differences cannot be explained entirely by differences in scale.Analysis of predicted probabilities suggest that there were fewer predicted/observed probabilities around 0.5 in the adult sample, suggesting that adolescents were perhaps less confident in their choices. Discussion/Conclusion: Resultsthat adolescents’ preferences differ from those of adults taking the perspective of a child. It may be that these differences exist due to the relative experience of adults, who might have a better understandingof ill health and its effects. However, a normative argument can be made that adolescents’ preferences should be considered in any decision-making that is directly relevant to them. Whilst the cognitive demands of other valuation methods may have ruled this possibility out, this study provides evidence to suggest that adolescents are capable of completing a DCE.

Title: The relationship between the EQ-5D-5L “anxiety/depression” dimension and anxiety and depression symptoms
Abstract: Background and aims: The EQ-5D-5L “anxiety/depression” (A/D) dimension is a composite dimension. The forced single response relies on the respondent's ability to endorse a response option when the levels of the anxiety and depression problems, taken apart, may differ. The aims of this study were to investigate the relationship between the composite A/D dimension, separate anxiety (here referred to as “A dimension”) and depression (here referred to as “D dimension”) dimensions and anxiety and depression symptoms as measured with the Generalized Anxiety Disorder–7 (GAD-7) and Patient Health Questionnaire–9 (PHQ-9) respectively. Methods: This study is a secondary data-analysis of data from the POPCORN study. The data were collected using a web-based survey among general population samples from nine countries. The primary outcome measures of our study were the EQ-5D-5L A/D, A and D dimension level scores (5L) and the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 (sum)score. In part 1 of the analysis, we examined the frequency of reported problems on the composite A/D dimension and A and D dimensions. We used Spearman rank correlation coefficients to examine the strength of association between the A/D dimension and the A and D dimension and the GAD-7 and the PHQ-9 score. In part 2 of the study, we calculated the performance of the A/D dimension using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) and compared to having anxiety (GAD-7≥8), depression (PHQ-9≥10) and both versus none for the total population and sub-groups. Results: Of the 23,622 respondents, 48.7% reported problems on the standard A/D dimension, versus 46.4% on the A dimension and 34.8% on the D dimension if presented separately. A total of 15.7% gave non-consistent answers on the A/D dimension versus the separate A and D dimensions. Spearman rank correlation coefficients of the A/D dimension and A and D dimensions were 0.712 and 0.657, respectively. The performance of the A/D dimension in the total sample was good (AUROC>0.8) and did not differ significantly between diagnostic groups. The performance differed significantly between the age groups, with worse performance in the younger groups, and differed between those with a singular chronic condition, with worse performance in those indicating having an anxiety or depression disorder. The performance did not differ significantly by gender, education, nor total chronic conditions. Conclusions: The combined EQ-5D-5L A/D response is consistent with A and D dimension if presented separately. Convergent validity between the AD, A and D dimension and the GAD-7 and the PHQ-9 score was high. The A/D dimension captures symptoms of anxiety, depression or both equally well. Performance is worse in the younger population.

Title: Acute and Chronic Episodes (ACE) Project
Abstract: In health valuation, respondents are commonly asked to choose between episodes with problems described by EQ-5D-5L attributes. A chronic episode describes health problems until the person dies. Preferences over chronic episodes may differ from those of acute episodes (i.e., when a person returns to their original health trajectory). Currently, the paired comparison tasks in the EQ-VT describe health states (i.e., generic episodes), omitting the timing attributes such as when they start, their duration and how they end. The aim of the proposed study is to examine whether preferences differ when the 1-year episodes are acute, chronic, or generic. Differences in value between acute, chronic, and generic episodes are relevant for health technology assessments (HTAs). HTA agencies may evaluate chronic interventions separately (i.e., persons who are likely to die within 12 months). They may also consider evidence on acute episodes when assessing curative therapies. In the future, EQ-5D studies may commonly assess acute and chronic episodes.

Title: Assessing the suitability of the EQ-5D-Y for children and adolescents with intellectual disability
Abstract: Background: Approximately 3% of children worldwide have intellectual disability (ID). This population is highly heterogeneous. These children have poorer health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and higher healthcare costs than the general population, as ID is associated with various co-morbidities, (e.g., behaviour disorders, epilepsy). Aims: To examine the test-retest reliability, concurrent validity, and content validity of the EQ-5D-Y-5L for children with ID. Methods: There were 2 studies: a survey and a qualitative interview study. In the survey study, caregivers of children with ID were invited to complete an online questionnaire. To examine the concurrent validity of the EQ-5D-Y-5L, the questionnaire included the EQ-5D-Y-5L and scales validated for children with ID, for each of the 5 dimensions of Mobility (MO); Self-Care (SC); Usual Activities (UA); Pain and Discomfort (PD); and worry, sadness, unhappiness (AD), as well as an overall measure of HRQoL: the Quality of Life Inventory-Disability (QI-Disability). To examine test-retest reliability, a subgroup of participants completed the EQ-5D-Y-5L again within a month. The qualitative interview study involved cognitive think-aloud interviews with caregivers of children with ID. Participants completed the EQ-5D-Y-5L for their child while commenting on the rationale for their scores. They were also asked about the content validity (relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness) of the questions for this population. Results: The survey was completed by 234 caregivers of children with ID (aged 4–17 years), 21 of whom completed the EQ-5D-Y-5L twice, on average 18.6 days apart (range: 9-32 days). Qualitative interviews were completed with caregivers of 28 children with ID (aged 8–22 years). Survey data indicated that: • test-retest reliability was moderate to excellent for the 5 EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions, but poor for the 100-point EQ-5D-Y-5L visual analogue scale (VAS). • concurrent validity was moderate to good for MO, SC, PD, AD, and VAS, but poor to moderate for UA. Interview data indicated that: • comprehensibility was excellent for all questions. • participants considered that UA, PD, AD were all relevant to HRQoL, but opinions differed regarding the relevance of MO and SC. • mapping of rationales for responses to EQ-5D-Y-5L scores was moderate to good for all but the VAS. • interview participants thought the EQ-5D-Y-5L insufficiently comprehensive to capture the HRQoL of children with ID, and recommended adding questions about communication, social engagement, supports and equipment required, and broader questions about mental health. Conclusions: The EQ-5D-Y-5L is a brief measure of HRQoL for children with ID that is easy to understand and complete. It has generally moderate concurrent validity against ID-specific scales. Test-retest reliability may be affected by true fluctuations in health states in this population. It lacks the comprehensiveness of longer scales, and may usefully be supplemented by additional questions about communication, social engagement, supports, and mental health.

Title: Measuring Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in the Youngest Population
Abstract: The Toddler and Infant (TANDI) HRQoL measure for use in children aged 0-3 years is designed for completion by proxy and was developed in English in South Africa. It was based on the EuroQol model of health status and aimed to be part of the EuroQol family of instruments to allow measurement and valuation of health across the lifespan. The TANDI was developed following a rigorous process which included the generation and refinement of the item pool through review of the literature (EQ Project 2014_200), cognitive interviews with caregivers of children, a round table meeting with paediatric experts (EQ Project 2016_180) and two rounds of an online Delphi panel with international experts in paediatric health and HRQoL (14). A preliminary set of 11 items (dimensions) were quantitatively tested in children with and without illness and reduced, according to a priori criteria to six dimensions and a Visual Analogue scale measuring general health (15). The final version of the TANDI includes six dimensions: movement, play, pain, relationships, communication and eating, with (currently) three levels of severity in each (Appendix B). The measure has retained the EQ-VAS (15). Content validity and psychometric properties of the TANDI have only been tested in South Africa with good results. Concurrent validity of dimensions showed moderate to strong correlations to instruments measuring similar constructs. Internal consistency reliability was good (α= 0.83). The TANDI was able to discriminate between known groups (children with acute illness, chronic illness and those from the general population). Test-retest results showed no variance for dimension scores of movement and play, and high agreement for pain (83%), relationships (87%), communication (83%) and eating (74%) and the VAS scores were highly correlated (ICC = 0.76; p < 0.001). Intellectual property (IP) of the TANDI has been transferred to the EuroQol Research Foundation and it is currently classified as an experimental version.

Title: Understanding the ceiling effects phenomenon of EQ-5D instruments: a systematic investigation into possible reasons, existing evidence, and future research directions and priorities
Abstract: Cross-cultural studies of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using generic or disease-specific instruments have consistently reported higher ceiling effects (i.e., the proportion of respondents reporting full health or no problems across all dimensions) among people from Asian cultures compared with Western populations. A recent meta-analysis found the ceiling effect in East/South-East Asia was higher than in Europe by 26% in EQ-5D-3L and by 7% in EQ-5D-5L (Cheng et al 2024). China appears to be the country that suffers most from this phenomenon. However, there has been no systematic investigation into the contributing factors or synthesis of existing hypotheses and empirical evidence. In this project, we synthesised relevant theories, models, and empirical evidence from multiple disciplines to develop a general conceptual framework explaining the ceiling effect phenomenon in HRQoL instruments across Asian and Western cultures. The framework, described from an Asian perspective, organises key factors across macro-, exo-, meso-, and microsystem levels: (1) Cultural factors (macrosystem), including holistic thinking, the view of health as the unity of mind and body, and collectivist social orientation; (2) Structural factors (exosystem), including socioeconomic conditions, social support networks, stigma, and healthcare systems; (3) Ways of perceiving, coping with, and reporting health problems (mesosystem); and (4) HRQoL instrument characteristics (microsystem) and (5) data collection processes (microsystem), including conceptual and semantic equivalence, question framing, recall period, mode of administration, sample representativeness, and intended data use. We further discussed how these factors interact and contribute to differences in the likelihood of reporting full health, and proposed several testable hypotheses for future research. We highlighted the importance of accounting for multilevel cultural and contextual influences when comparing HRQoL data across populations. The framework we developed has the potential to be applied to understand cross-cultural differences in health and wellbeing measurement and valuation We hosted an advisory meeting to seek advice on the framework with EuroQol Group members and external experts from China, Japan, Singapore, Australia, US and the UK. A poster has been presented at 2024 EuroQol Academy, and a manuscript has been prepared for submission to journal.

Title: Exploring the measurement strengths and gaps of the EQ-5D-5L in older populations
Abstract: Background: As populations age, robust measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in older adults has become increasingly important. Although the EQ-5D-5L is widely used to measure HRQoL, older adults may differ in the relevance of certain domains (e.g., fatigue, relationships, cognition, sensory function) and in how they interpret response options (e.g., due to adaptation with age), potentially undermining the validity of the EQ-5D-5L and risking measurement non-invariance. Although previous research has explored the use of the EQ-5D in elderly populations, most of it has focused on the EQ-5D-3L, not explored the potential added value of bolt-ons, and did not explore differential item functioning (DIF) [1, 2].Aim: To explore the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-5L in older people to identify both its strengths and possible limitations, specifically in terms of (i) informativity, (ii) target constructs (dimensionality) and (iii) item functioning.Methods: We will conduct secondary analyses of two large datasets (total N≈ 31,000 adults ≥18 years old, including N≈7,000 older adults ≥ 65 years old): EQ-DAPHNIE multi-country general-population samples (including multiple HRQoL/well-being instruments, bolt-ons, and anchoring vignettes), and W-MIC population data (including multiple HRQoL/well-being instruments). Analyses will comprise: (i) descriptives and informativity (ceiling/floor, missingness, Shannon’s indices); (ii) dimensional coverage via factor analyses and structural equation models regressing EQ VAS on the five EQ-5D items plus latent non-EQ-5D domains to quantify incremental explanatory value (ΔR²); and (iii) item response theory (IRT) using two-parameter graded response models to assess discrimination, thresholds, information, and DIF. Assessments of DIF will follow an anchor-based multi-group IRT approach in all datasets and, additionally in EQ-DAPHNIE, with HOPIT models using the anchoring vignettes. Prespecified subgroups include age bands, sex, comorbidities, health/social care use.Relevance to the EuroQol Group: The study will map the EQ-5D-5L’s strengths and gaps in older adults, identify candidate dimensions that may improve sensitivity (e.g., fatigue, cognition, sensory function), explore potential issues with composite items (anxiety/depression; pain/discomfort), and provide guidance on relevant bolt-ons. These outputs directly respond to section 3 of chapter 2 (DSWG) of the 20th RFP calling for secondary data analyses to explore the measurement issues relating to the measurement of HRQoL in older populations. The included datasets were explicitly selected to meet the call’s preference for datasets that include HRQoL dimensions considered in the Bolt-on Toolbox. Furthermore, the project is aligned with EuroQol’s strategic objectives 14 and 20 about research on elderly populations.  Deliverables will include 1-2 open-access manuscripts, conference presentations, and openly shared R code.

Title: Scientific international exchange project in the context of the EQ-sponsored PhD project (PHD-287) on inequality research with orthopedic registry data.
Abstract: I had the privilege to perform research at the department of population health sciences and orthopedic surgery in a world-renowned hospital (Mount Sinai Hospital, New York), with one of its focus being registry data analysis. The director dr. J. Poeran, an epidemiologist with Dutch origins, of whom Gouke Bonsel was his original PhD advisor, personally supervised this project. We primarily aimed to explore analytical techniques used to analyze health inequalities, specifically the concentration index and accompanying decomposition analysis. Secondarily, we aimed to understand the organizational structure of the visited research institute, the perspective of clinicians on end-user registry data, and the potential incorporation of the EQ-5D. Key scientific results: we selected the Medicare dataset with different outcomes, which can easily be substituted by the EQ-5D (see below for an elaborate explanation on this choice). We studied socio-economic inequalities in the use and effectiveness of regional anesthesia in patients undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty. We found a strong relation between hospitals and socioeconomic status, which complicated the use of concentration indices for analyzing health inequalities. Instead, adjusted Population Attributable Risks (PARs) were calculated and a quasi-moderation analysis was performed to determine the effect of socioeconomic and hospital-level factors on the use and effectiveness of regional anesthesia. We consider the adjusted PAR calculation to be a valuable analytical technique for EuroQol research, potentially aiding in determining the relationship between variables of interest and improvements or deteriorations in EQ-5D scores after arthroplasty. Deliverables: one manuscript is being prepared for submission to a high-impact anesthesiology journal, focusing on the presence of access and outcome inequalities of regional anesthesia in hip or knee arthroplasty. The key findings of the secondary aims were: 1. That there is a gap in the current routine collection of PROMs: PROMs are not routinely collected of conservatively treated patients. Promoting the collection of PROMs in this group will open the door to further research, including the use of PROMs in selecting candidates for surgery. Moreover, it will further promote the wide-spread use of PROMs (EQ-5D) in routine care. 2. At the Mount Sinai Hospital, the collection of PROMs is in its early stages, with discussions ongoing to streamline the process within the Orthopedic Surgery department. Furthermore, the routine clinical use of the EQ-5D is limited in the USA. In clinical studies, however, the EQ-5D can be additionally collected. The Mount Sinai Hospital, with its large Orthopedic Surgery department, could serve as a valuable candidate hospital for multicenter studies. 3. Regarding the competitiveness of the EQ-5D compared to other generic PROMs, it is worth noting that US statisticians consider the availability of value sets a clear strength of the EQ-5D. However, in current US policy-making, cost-effectiveness data using quality of health measures are not mandatory nor regarded vital from a clinical point of view. Only if this policy matrix changes in the future, the role of the EQ-5D in the USA could significantly expand. New collaborations/next steps: the exchange project fostered mutual interest between the department of Orthopedic Surgery at Erasmus Medical Center and the visited department at Mount Sinai Hospital. A number of future collaborations are being considered, particularly in utilizing Dutch Orthopedic Registry (EQ-5D) data. In all, I regard my visit as a very fruitful exchange. Valuable delivrables were created as were many opportunities for future collaborations on EuroQol related research in the field of orthopedic outcome research, and on doing advanced inequality analysis in particular. I was pleased that the hosting institute expressed their high esteem of the achievements made. Also, I believe that my personal research skills have markedly developed due to the stimulating environment. I want to thank the EuroQol group and members of the Exec for their support in this work. Without their support, this work would not have been possible.

Title: Comparative Assessment of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Interviewer-administered versions in Children Aged 5–8 Years: Feasibility, Comprehension, and Psychometric Properties.
Abstract: Background: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) capture individuals’ perceptions of their health, including Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL). The EQ-5D-Y is a widely used instrument for children and adolescents, but evidence on its feasibility and psychometric performance in 5–8-year-olds, as well as the comparison of the 3L and 5L versions, is limited.Objectives: To evaluate comprehension, feasibility, validity, and reliability of the Interviewer-administered (IA) EQ-5D-Y (3L and 5L) versions of in children aged 5–8.Methods: A mixed-methods study will be conducted in the largest pediatric hospital in Argentina (Hospital Garrahan). 1) Qualitative component: After piloting the interview guide, cognitive interviews with 15 children with an oncological diagnosis will assess comprehension and response differentiation in the Y-3L and Y-5L, as well as VAS interpretation. 2) Quantitative component: a) After piloting the interview and procedures, thecross-sectional psychometric testing will involve personal interviews with 100 children (50 hospitalized, 50 outpatients) with oncological conditions, each completing IA EQ-5D-Y –3L and 5L in a random order,  PedsQL Cancer Module, a Global Health Measure, and an ad-hoc comprehension test. b) Test–retest reliability will be assessed after 2 days to 2 weeks in a sub-sample of 50 stable children. Qualitative interviews will be recorded, transcribed and analysed thematically, to understand feasibility and comprehension qualitatively. Quantitative analysis will assess convergent validity between HRQoL measures with Pearson Correlation, ANOVA, as well as known-group validity, as well as test-retest reliability using ICC and Kappa. Feasibility and comprehension will also be assessed in this quantitative phase (both by directly observing child behavior during the interview as well as by the ad-hoc comprehension test). Due to our ongoing work in children with cancer with the Garrahan Hospital team, the study feasibility is high. Expected Outcomes: The results of this study will inform the EQ-5D-Y 3L and 5L user guides to inform the age range where self-report is valid and reliable by IA. It will further provide useful evidence on whether young children are able to understand and recall the expanded 5 levels of report of the Y-5L as compared to the Y-3L.

Title: An investigation of differential item functioning related to age, gender and education in the EQ-5D-5L using ordinal logistic regression
Abstract: Objectives: The EQ-5D-5L is commonly used in population health studies, clinical trials and economic evaluations as a measure of health. A key assumption for the validity EQ-5D-5L data is measurement invariance, meaning that its items and response options are interpreted in the same way across respondents. If measurement invariance is violated, the EQ-5D-5L would exhibit differential item functioning (DIF), whereby individuals from different groups with the same underlying health respond to it differently. This study investigates whether the EQ-5D-5L is affected by DIF using ordinal logistic regression (OLR). Methods: Data from the Multi-Instrument Comparison (MIC) study was used to investigate DIF, across the following groups: older adults aged 65+ versus younger adults aged 18-64; women versus men; and individuals with different levels of education attainment (high school versus diploma/technical training or university education). OLR was used to investigate whether individuals across groups had different expected EQ-5D-5L scores, despite having the same underlying health. Effect size measures were used to assess whether identified DIF indicated meaningful differences in scores. Analyses were completed on purified and unpurified EQ-5D-5L sum scores and on split-half samples to test the stability of results. Results: No meaningful DIF relating to gender or education was observed for any item. The anxiety/depression item exhibited meaningful age-related DIF, with older adults being less likely to report problems with anxiety and depression. Mobility exhibited age-related DIF to a lesser extent but did not meet the threshold for meaningful DIF. Findings were stable across purified and unpurified analyses. Conclusion: The EQ-5D-5L did not exhibit DIF for gender or education, suggesting response behaviour is generally stable across these groups. Meaningful age-related DIF was found for anxiety/depression and, to a lesser extent for mobility. These findings are consistent with those of a previous study. It is important to further understand causes of DIF in older populations as this may bias estimates of burden of illness and treatment effectiveness. Further research is also required to understand how to control for such DIF.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: An investigation into the psychometric performance of the EQ-PSO in patients with atopic dermatitis in the UK and Germany
Abstract: Introduction: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition impacting quality of life, with itch identified as the main symptom affecting daily life. EQ-5D measures are widely used to assess the impact of treatments and conditions on health-related quality of life, but they may not perform well in all conditions due to their brevity and generic nature. Bolt-on versions, such as the EQ-PSO, may improve their performance in certain conditions. This study assesses the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-PSO, EQ-PSO+sleep in AD patients. Methods: An online survey in the UK and Germany was administered to 306 adults with moderate-to-severe AD, collecting POEM, DLQI and EQ-PSO+sleep. Convergent validity was analysed by evaluating the item and sum score correlations between the different versions of the EQ-5D (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-PSO and EQ-PSO+sleep) and two condition-specific measures (DLQI and POEM). Hierarchical models evaluated the explanatory power of EQ-5D-5L, EQ-PSO and EQ-PSO+sleep to predict EQ-VAS, DLQI and POEM scores. Known-group validity was assessed using ANOVA to test whether the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-PSO and EQ-PSO+sleep level sum scores (LSSs) distinguish between known groups defined by POEM severity categories. Factor analysis was conducted to examine the structural validity of the EQ-PSO and the impact of the addition of sleep. Results: The EQ-5D-5L showed good convergent validity, correlating strongly with both condition specific measures. Convergent validity was better between the two EQ bolt-on versions and the POEM, but not between bolt-on versions and the DLQI. The bolt-on versions improved the explanatory power of the EQ-5D-5L, when predicting POEM and VAS scores, but not the DLQI. All EQ measures could distinguish between known groups defined by POEM severity categories, with bolt-on versions performing better than EQ-5D-5L. Conclusion: While the EQ-5D-5L performed acceptably in AD, the EQ-PSO and EQ-PSO+sleep offered improvements in psychometric performance over the EQ-5D-5L, capturing symptom severity and QoL impairments specific to AD.

Title: Testing EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons in patients with sleep & sleep breathing disorders: an exploratory study for making EQ-5D a clinically attractive patient-reported outcomes measure.
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D-5L may not adequately capture the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of patients with sleep disturbances. We examined whether the addition of four sleep-related bolt-ons could enhance the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L. Methods: We employed a mixed methodology involving in-depth interviews with 23 patients and clinicians to test the face validity of “sleep”, “cognition”, “tiredness” and “relationship” and refine the bolt-ons. We then administered the four bolt-ons, appended to EQ-5D-5L, together with three condition-specific patient-reported outcome measures (cPROMs), i.e., Sleep Apnea Quality of Life Index (SAQLI), the Functional Outcome Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ) and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) questionnaires during two clinical visits. We compared ceiling effects and construct validity by testing a priori hypotheses in relation to the cPROMs and polysomnographic characteristics via correlation and areas under the curves (AUC) analyses, respectively. We examined responsiveness among “treated/improved” participants using standardized response means (SRM) and AUC analysis, and reliability among “untreated/no change” participants using intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) or Cohen’s Kappa (k). Results: 110 participants (mean [SD] age: 47[13]) were recruited of 90 returned for their review assessments (mean [SD] interval: 2.2 [2.1] months). The absolute ceiling reduction was 42.7%. The bolt-ons were better correlated with cPROMs and possessed higher discriminatory power and responsiveness, with comparable reliability to EQ-5D-5L. A combined module of the four bolt-ons provided better results than individual bolt-ons. Conclusions: Adding the four sleep-related bolt-ons improved EQ-5D-5L’s psychometric properties among patients with sleep disturbances.

Title: Completion of the Covid-stranded Norwegian EQ-5D-5L valuation study
Abstract: Purpose: To develop the Norwegian value set for the EQ-5D-5L based on interviews with a representative sample of the Norwegian adult population. Methods: Random and quota sampling were used to recruit the sample of adults (age > 18 years) representative of the Norwegian general population. Data collection followed EQ-VT 2.1 undertaken before and after the COVID-19 pandemic from November 2019 to December 2022, using PC-assisted and video conferencing interviews, respectively. Each respondent valued 10 health states using composite time trade-off (cTTO) and 7 health states using a discrete choice experiment (DCE). Different statistical models were assessed for logical consistency and predictive accuracy using cTTO and DCE data alone or in combination as hybrid models.
