Results: Of the 1,321 respondents, 1,237 met inclusion criteria. All statistical models demonstrated logical consistency. The weighted hybrid model combining both cTTO and DCE data was preferred and had the highest predictive accuracy. Predicted values ranged from - 0.453 to 1, and the dimension of anxiety/depression was the most highly valued by respondents, followed by pain/discomfort, self-care, mobility, and usual activities. These findings are not dissimilar to those for most Western European countries, and regression coefficients are closest to those for other Scandinavian countries. Conclusion: This study provides the Norwegian value set for the EQ-5D-5L based on health state values obtained from members of the adult general population in Norway. This is an important contribution to economic evaluation and the broader application of the EQ-5D-5L in Norway including clinical and health services research, and quality measurement.

Title: What contributes to variations in self-reported health for the general population and for ten condition-specific patient groups in England? - An empirical analysis using repeated cross-sectional general practice data with 2.9 million patient records.
Abstract: Background Significant variations in the UK’s population health have been widely observed. Little is known about individual and health service factors associated with these variations in health or about how much of the unexplained variation is at patient and health service levels. Aim This report explores which factors explain the variation in patients’ self-reported health, measured by the EQ-5D-5L instrument, for the English general population and for ten patient groups with self-reported chronic conditions. We quantify how much of the variation that observed factors could not explain can be attributed to patients, general practice, and Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) characteristics and whether they differ across the general population and ten patient groups. Methods We linked data from three data sources - the NHS’s General Practitioner (GP) Patient Survey, Quality and Outcomes Framework, and GP workforce databases, over five years between 2012/13 to 2016/17. The resulting dataset covers almost all GP practices in England, with a nationally representative sample for the general population (N=2,913,294). Additionally, we generated ten subsamples for each chronic condition. We use ordinary least squares, mixed-effects, practice fixed- and random-effects models to identify factors associated with EQ-5D-5L index variation for the general practice population and for groups of patients with one of ten specific conditions. We also calculate ICCs using variances estimated from mixed-effects models to decompose the unexplained variation in the EQ-5D-5L index to patient, GP, and CCG levels. We explored the impact of missing values on mixed-effects models using multiple imputation. Results Some explanatories (such as multimorbidity, gender, deprivation, employment status, smoking status, satisfaction with access to the practice and good overall experience with the practice) had similar and plausibly signed effects for all 11 sets of individuals. But there were differences for those with different conditions. For example, those reporting their ethnicity as Black had lower EQ-5D-5L index if they had Alzheimer/dementia or angina but higher EQ-5D-5L index if they have asthma, diabetes, hypertension, or mental health problems. Better clinical quality for specific conditions was associated with better patient reported health only for three conditions (asthma, diabetes, epilepsy). For the general practice population, the unexplained variation in the EQ-5D-5L index was almost entirely at patient level (99.57%) with very small general practice (0.29%) and CCG (0.14%) contributions. Ten condition-specific patient groups shared similar findings for the decomposition of unexplained variation as that from the general population. Conclusion The findings from our study identifies factors that explain the variation in health for the general population and patient groups with chronic conditions in England. Policymakers could develop interventions to reduce or eliminate the effects for some of those factors in our list, such as smoking and deprivation status of individuals, or patient satisfaction with access to their general practice, to improve health and to reduce variation in health.

Title: Deriving social values using the EQ-5D-5L in the general population of Uruguay.
Abstract: The results of this study have been published here: Augustovski F, Rey-Ares L, Irazola V, Garay OU, Gianneo O, Fernández G, Morales M, Gibbons L, Ramos-Goñi JM. An EQ-5D-5L value set based on Uruguayan population preferences. Qual Life Res. 2016 Feb;25(2):323-333. doi: 10.1007/s11136-015-1086-4. Epub 2015 Aug 5. Erratum in: Qual Life Res. 2016 Feb;25(2):335. PMID: 26242249.

Title: Bolt-ons and EQ VAS: a study to inform the development of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox user guide
Abstract: Order bias in survey question sequencing can influence responses, potentially distorting data and limiting comparability across studies. The EQ-5D, a widely used health-related quality of life measure, traditionally places the EQ VAS after the descriptive system, a legacy design that may introduce context effects. With the EuroQol Group developing the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox, the placement of bolt-on items relative to the EQ VAS remains unstandardized and underexplored. Limited evidence suggests that bolt-on positioning may affect EQ VAS scores, yet systematic investigation is lacking. This study aims to address this gap by examining order effects in a general population sample. We propose a cross-sectional study in China with 1,200 participants, randomized into four arms with varying sequences of the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, EQ VAS, and three bolt-on items (cognition, fatigue, vision). Participants will be recruited via a survey company’s online panel, with soft quotas ensuring demographic representativeness. Data quality will be ensured through CAPTCHA, time analysis, and cross-validation. EQ VAS score differences across arms will be analyzed using ANOVA, ANCOVA, and regression models, with sensitivity analyses to assess robustness. This study will provide evidence on whether bolt-on placement impacts EQ VAS scores, offering initial evidence for optimal sequencing. Findings will inform recommendations for the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox user guide, enhancing data consistency and comparability. By funding this project, the EuroQol Group will gain critical insights into order bias, supporting the strategic development and standardization of bolt-ons as outlined in the 2024-28 Strategic Plan, ultimately strengthening the utility and reliability of EuroQol instruments.

Title: The ceiling effects of EQ-5D in general population health surveys: A systematic review and meta-regression
Abstract: Objectives: This review aims to examine the ceiling effects of EQ-5D-3L (3L) and EQ-5D-5L (5L) in general adult populations and identify the factors influencing these effects. Methods: We searched 8 databases for observational studies published in English from inception to 24 July 2023. Ceiling effects were calculated by dividing the number of participants reporting full health at dimension or profile level by the total sample size. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression using the metafor package in R software were performed. Results: We identified 94 studies from 70 articles, including 4 543 647 adults across 37 countries. The global pooled proportion of individuals reporting full health ("11111") was 56% (95% CI 51%-62%) for 3L and 49% (95% CI 44%-54%) for 5L. The self-care dimension showed the highest ceiling effects (3L: 97%; 5L: 94%), whereas pain/discomfort had the lowest (3L: 69%; 5L: 60%). The ceiling effects in East/South-East Asia were higher than in Europe by 25% (95% CI 18%-32%) in 3L and 9% (95% CI -2%-20%) in 5L. Adjusting for mean age and proportion of males, significant regional differences persisted in the overall profile level of 3L, in all 3L dimensions (except for self-care), and 5L dimensions (except for pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression). Conclusions: This review highlights significant ceiling effects in the EQ-5D, especially in Asian populations. The 5L version exhibited fewer ceiling effects than the 3L, indicating its superiority for general population surveys. Further research is crucial to understand the disparities in self-reported health outcomes between Asians and other populations.

Title: Generating an EQ-5D-3L value set for the Hashemite kingdom of Jordan
Abstract: PCR174 VALUATION OF THE EQ-5D-3L IN JORDAN Al Rabayah AA,1 Purba F,2 Rencz F,3 Roudijk B,4 Jaddoua S,5 Siebert U6 1King Hussein Cancer Center, UMIT - University for Health Sciences, Medical Informatics and Technology, Institute of Public Health, Medical Decision Making and Health Technology Assessment, Hall in Tirol, Austria, Hall in Tirol, Austria, 2Faculty of Psychology, Padjadjaran University, West Java, Indonesia, 3Department of Health Policy, Corvinus University of Budapest, Budapest, Hungary, 4EuroQol Research Foundation, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, 5King Hussein Cancer Center, Amman, Jordan, 6UMIT - University for Health Sciences, Medical Informatics and Technology, Hall i.T., Austria. ONCOTYROL - Center for Personalized Cancer Medicine, Innsbruck, Austria. Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA Objectives: Cost-utility analysis is an important tool for health technology assessment and decision-making about health technologies in Jordan, however no national value set is available for any preference-accompanied health utility measure. To develop a value set for EQ-5D-3L based on the preferences of the Jordanian population. Methods: A representative sample of the Jordanian general population was obtained in 2021 through stratified quota sampling involving age, gender and region. Participants aged above 18 years, were interviewed by online videoconferencing using the EuroQol Valuation Tech- nology web based LimeSurvey. Four trained interviewers completed data collection. The data were closely monitored through the QC protocol of Euro- QoL. Participants completed 10 composite time trade-off (cTTO) and 10 discrete choice experiments (DCE) tasks. In addition, participants completed the feed- back module. Values for the EQ-5D-3L health states were estimated using regression modeling. The cTTO and DCE data were analyzed using linear and logistic regression modeling, and hybrid models combining the DCE and cTTO data. Results: A total of 301 participants with complete data were included in the analysis. Only one interview was flagged. All regression models showed both logical consistency and significance with respect to the parameter estimates. The hybrid model corrected for heteroskedasticity was selected as it included data from both the cTTO and the DCE tasks which provided a comprehensive value set. Utility decrements due to mobility had the highest weight followed by anxiety and depression. The lowest weight was assigned to usual activities. Conclusions: This study provides values for EQ-5D-3L health states for the Jordanian population. This value set can be used in health technology assessments for health policy planning by the Jordanian health sector’s decision makers.

Title: Addressing the challenge of recall periods for the proxy version of the EQ-HWB in dementia
Abstract: Aims: Recall periods are an important aspect of content validity for measures about health and well-being. The literature on recall periods for proxy-reported versions of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) is poorly developed compared to the literature on recall periods for PROMs. This project aimed to evaluate the perceptions of carers with dementia on the 7-day recall period for the proxy version of the EQ-HWB-9. Methods: Two mixed-methods studies were conducted with carers of people living with dementia in Australia, evaluating the recall period for the proxy version of the EQ-HWB-9 (V1.0 and V2.0). Think-aloud interviews were used for the qualitative studies, and participants were prompted to reflect on their interpretation of the recall period, the proxy perspective they used. Thematic analysis was used. To evaluate the content validity of V2.0, framework analysis was used, with a pre-defined framework mapped against components of content validity. In the quantitative studies, participants were randomly assigned to the EQ-HWB-9 with a 7-day or 1-day (“today”) recall period. At the end of the survey participants were asked to indicate the proxy perspective and recall period they used when completing the questionnaire. Results: Forty-one participants completed interviews (19 for V1.0, 22 for V2.0) and 282 participants completed online surveys (147 for V1.0, 135 for V2.0). In the qualitative studies, most carers were able to recall relevant observations of the person with dementia within the 7-day recall period across the EQ-HWB- domains. Events occurring outside the recall period or the normality of the past 7 days were also considered by carers. The EQ-HWB-9 (v2) was comprehensible, though specific items were more difficult for carers to answer as proxies due to the constructs being less observable. In the quantitative studies, adherence to the recall period was not consistent. Most participants used a 7-day period regardless of assignment. Adherence was slightly higher in the survey using V2.0. In all studies, participants reported using a mix of proxy perspectives. Conclusion: The findings provide support for the use of the 7-day recall period used in the EQ-HWB-9 proxy version in dementia. Repetition of the recall period, as seen in the  EQ-HWB-9 (V2.0) proxy version, may help promote adherence. The use of a mix of proxy perspectives suggests that clear instructions regarding perspective-taking may be beneficial.

Title: Exploring dimension-specific components and aging (EDCA): a secondary data analysis
Abstract: **BACKGROUND:** Within the EuroQol, a deep-dive module is a multi-layered measure of one of the EQ-5D dimension. Among the items within a deep-dive module, some may be components of the original items and others may not be listed directly. For example, the self-care item (SC) is a global composite item with two components (washing self and dressing self); yet, an SC deep-dive module may include items beyond those two components (e.g., eating). So far, many studies have examined components of pain/discomfort(PD) and anxiety/depression(AD), but this study is the first to examine the components of SC as well as one of the largest component studies. Also, little is known about their construct validity across age groups, particularly among older adults. **AIMS:** This secondary data analysis examined the relationships between the composite items (namely SC, PD and AD) and their components as a precursor to the development of deep-dive modules. Its results address questions on convergent validity and dimensionality of component items: Aim 1: Are the response levels/patterns of the component items associated with respondent characteristics and EQ-5D-5L responses? Aim 2: Does the global composite item (e.g., self-care) capture the same underlying construct as the two component items (washing self, dressing self)? Furthermore, we assessed each aim in the overall population and by 6 age-specific groups (i.e., differential item functioning). **METHODS:** A 2024 survey of US adults (Dynata) included the EQ-5D-5L and 6 component items of SC, PD and AD. Using these secondary data, we calculated descriptive statistics and conducted onvergent validity analyses examining the association between the component items and other key variables such as EQ-5D-5L responses and respondent characteristics (Aim 1). Furthermore, we assessed whether the global composite items capture the same underlying dimension as their component items (Aim 2). Each analysis was conducted in the full sample (N=6,022) and in 6 age-specific groups (N=802 to 1268) and followed the existing framework for assessing the measurement performance of bolt-ons(Mulhern et al. 2022). The aims of this study complement ongoing work within the DSWG on the development of deep-dive modules, particularly into the psychometrics and limitations of composite items, and a new measure of HRQoL in older adults.

Title: Alternative approach to value set construction – accounting for interpersonal utility comparisons taboo based on axiomatic approach
Abstract: Background Interpersonal utility comparisons are challenging. Meanwhile, in health valuation studies, the utilities elicited with time trade-off method (TTO) are simply averaged, somewhat thoughtlessly. Such averaging is theoretically unfounded and it violates the relative preference inversion property (RPI). A recent solution, using relative utilitarianism approach, addresses this problem but violates the independence of irrelevant alternatives property (IIA). Aim I aimed to propose a health state utility aggregation method preserving the RPI and IIA. Methods In the economic literature, it was shown that for strictly positive and ratio-scale measurable utilities, geometric mean should be used to aggregate preferences. I show how to adapt this approach to health valuation by calculating the geometric mean of disutilities relative to 11111 (non-trading is assumed to result from limited granularity of TTO). I estimate a new value set for Polish EQ-5D-5L valuation study TTO data. Results The proposed method has the RPI and IIA, however, it violates the unanimity for risky prospects. The estimated level 5 disutilities amount to: 0.19 for mobility, 0.19 for self-care, 0.141 for usual activities, 0.478 for pain/discomfort, and 0.175 for anxiety/depression. The estimated value for 55555 amounts to −0.174, as compared to −0.392 for the standard approach and to −0.106 for the relative utilitarianism approach. Conclusion The challenges of interpersonal utility comparison are largely neglected in valuation studies. Theoretically sound methods are available in the economic literature and can be applied to valuation studies. Correctly addressing the interpersonal utility comparisons reduces the range of utilities.

Title: panel presentation titled "Putting Patients at the Centre of Health Care: The use of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in the Healthcare System” for CAHSPR annual conference
Abstract: The presentation has been held
Working Group: Populations and Health Systems, Education and Outreach

Title: Public health impact of the COVID-19 pandemia: inequity of its effects and the role of health policies.
Abstract: The Population health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic (POPCORN) study, sponsored by the EuroQol, explored the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on health-related quality of life (HRQL) and mental well-being of the general adult population of nine countries and investigate the role of individual and country level factors. Data were collected in the first phase of the pandemic (Spring 2020). Results showed that stringency of government response (at country level) had a small positive relation with HRQL and a strong negative relation with mental well-being, although the magnitude of effects differed for healthy persons and diseased persons. Moreover, the youngest age group (18-29 years old) had lowest mental well-being. Results among a sub-group of respondents from New York State showed that the negative impact of the pandemic was aggravated in diseased persons, in part through limited access to health care.

Title: Testing the ordinal relationship between TTO utilities and the ranking of EQ-5D health states : examining the commensurability of preferences in the MVH dataset
Abstract: Estimation models based on 5L valuation study data combine data from DCE and TTO in a single "hybrid". This approach is not what was intended when the EQ-VT protocol was initially specified. As originally planned, DCE responses would enable the creation of a set of latent scale values for 5L states, with these being transformed to the conventional 0-1 format using TTO preferences. The combination of DCE and TTO preferences relies on a critical assumption - that they are commensurate and in effect, measure the same construct. Unfortunately, the EQ-VT protocol does not collect data that allows us to test this property. Luckily, the original MVH protocol enables us to precisely target the problem. Despite being based on the analysis of 3L preferences, the (definitive) UK 3L valuation study provides an ideal benchmark for the investigation of respondent-level ordinal consistency. The proposed study will examine the extent to which the rank order of EQ-5D health states as explicitly determined by each respondent, is consistent with the ordering of the SAME states as inferred from the TTO values subsequently assigned to them.

Title: Quantitative Psychometric Investigation of Adding Four Bolt-ons to the EQ-5D-5L in Patients with Psoriasis or Atopic Dermatitis
Abstract: Background: In recent years, new treatment options for psoriasis and atopic dermatitis (AD) have advanced significantly. However, their high costs impose significant financial burdens on patients and healthcare systems, underscoring the need for cost-utility analyses. EQ-5D, the most widely used instrument for measuring health-related quality of life worldwide, has been found to be deficient in capturing important health aspects in chronic skin conditions. Therefore, this study aimed to  investigate the psychometric properties of adding four bolt-ons (skin irritation (SI), self-confidence (SE), social relationships (SR), and sleep(SL)) compared to the standard EQ-5D-5L, PROMIS-29 and Skindex-16 instruments in adult patients with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis (AD).Methods: This study comprised two sequential phases. The first phase focused on translation of four EQ bolt-ons into standard Arabic following the EuroQol's translation guidelines and evaluation of their content validity. The second phase collected health-related quality of life data from patients with psoriasis and AD using the EQ-5D-5L, EQ bolt-ons, PROMIS-29, and Skindex-16. Participants self-completed the questionnaires at baseline, after 3–7 days for test–retest reliability, and after 12 weeks for responsiveness. Psychometric analyses at baseline examined ceiling effects, informativity, validity, explanatory power, known-group differences, feasibility, and general performance using both dimension-level and standardized Level Sum Scores (LSS).Results: The standard Arabic version of the four EQ bolt-ons was well understood and culturally appropriate. Their inclusion expanded the EQ-5D’s content coverage from 55% to 81%, with SI and SL identified as the most relevant. A conceptual overlap was noted between the SI bolt-on and the Pain/Discomfort dimension in four out of five interviews. Feasibility was confirmed by the absence of missing responses. The greatest reduction in the ceiling effect occurred with SI (100%), followed by SL (61.8%). The highest informativity was achieved when all four bolt-ons were included (Hʹ = 7.83). Known-group validity analyses showed superior relative efficiency compared to the standard EQ-5D-5L. In psoriasis, EQ-5D-5L+SI had the strongest explanatory power for EQ-VAS variation (51%), while in AD, the version with all four bolt-ons explained 39%. EQ-VAS and standardized LSS showed good reliability across all versions in psoriasis, and moderate to good reliability in AD. Adding the bolt-ons, particularly SI alone or all four combined, improved the responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L in the “improved” group, reaching medium to large effect sizes. Discussion: Overall, the addition of the four bolt-ons enhanced the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L, although the extent of improvement differed by bolt-on and condition. In AD, the inclusion of SL had a greater impact on improving EQ-5D-5L psychometrics than in Ps. This is expected since sleep problems are highly prevalent in AD, often driven by nocturnal itching and pain. In contrast, SI had the greatest impact in Ps. Conversely, SE and SR provided smaller beneficial effect which may be partly explained by the fact that 72% of our sample had low-to-medium educational levels. Previous research has shown that educational and socioeconomic differences can influence self-esteem, with individuals of higher education often reporting lower self-esteem. Moreover, their moderate responsiveness also aligned with patients’ feedback during content validation phase that improvements in these dimensions would occur only after lesion clearance. Given that few patients who achieved complete recovery within 12 weeks, a longer follow-up may reveal stronger responsiveness.   The addition of the four bolt-ons improved the EQ-5D-5L’s ability to discriminate between smaller orders of improvement, complementing prior evidence of enhanced responsiveness observed in EQ-PSO (which includes the Skin Irritation and Self-Confidence bolt-ons) in clinical trials. However, the inclusion of bolt-ons had minimal impact on responsiveness among patients whose conditions worsened. Although the mean standardized LSS declined significantly, the effect size remained smaller than that of the standard EQ-5D-5L. This reduced sensitivity can be attributed to the high proportion of patients who, at baseline, already reported moderate-to-extreme problems on the Skin Irritation and Sleep dimensions, creating a floor effect that limited responsiveness to further deterioration.Conclusion: The findings support the clarity, cultural appropriateness, and comprehensibility of the four Arabic bolt-ons, even among individuals with lower educational levels. Adding the bolt-ons to EQ-5D-5L eliminated the ceiling effect, improved absolute informativity, enhanced explanatory power for VAS variation, and increased discriminatory ability across disease severities. Also, responsiveness to smaller health changes over a three months follow-up period improved while maintaining good feasibility and test-retest reliability.

Title: Pilot valuation of the EQ-HWB-S using the VWG DCE with duration protocol
Abstract: Background: A recent study has piloted the use of the EQ-VT valuation protocol for valuing EQ-HWB-S. (Mukuria et al, 2022) While the EQ-VT protocol is a mature valuation protocol, there are several signs that the EQ-VT protocol may not be the most suitable method for valuing the EQ-HWB-S. For example, the costs of an EQ-VT cTTO study for EQ-HWB-S are prohibitive, which is directly related to the large representative sample and several interviewers that are required to complete the required face to face cTTO/DCE interviews. Furthermore, even with a large number of health states in the the EQ-VT protocol, realistically only a small subset of the total number of the 1.95 million EQ-HWB-S health states can be valuated. This results in substantial extrapolation uncertainty. Therefore, it is important to investigate other candidate valuation methods that are more promising for the valuation of EQ-HWB-S. More specifically, EuroQol’s valuation Working Group is currently piloting their DCE-duration protocol in a study in Trinidad and Tobago, for which the results will be available in Q1 2023, after which a final protocol version will be developed. This final protocol is also a promising candidate for the valuation of EQ-HWB-S. Aims: This study aims to perform a pilot valuation of the EQ-HWB-S using the DCE-duration valuation protocol as developed by EuroQol’s Valuation Working Group, to test the feasibility of this stand-alone DCE (i.e. without TTO) protocol for a more complex instrument such as EQ-HWB-S. Furthermore, this study aims to test the agreement between the results of the pilot of valuing EQ-HWB-S using EQ-VT by Mukuria et al. (Mukuria et al, 2022) Methods: An online administered DCE-Duration will be conducted in a representative sample of respondents from the UK. Each will be presented a set of 18 split triplets, which means that every respondent will make a total of 36 paired comparisons. The exact content of these split triplets will depend on the decisions made in the final DCE-Duration protocol, and a small pilot in which qualitative evidence is collected on the feasibility of the survey. The study will start with an informative prior design, which will be updated up to 6 times after a set number of responses (e.g. 10% of data collection, 20%, etc.). Mixed logit models with utility functions that allow for non-linear time durations will be used to model the data. The results of the current study will be compared to the EQ-HWB-S EQ-VT valuation pilot results, using Bland-Altman plots, to assess whether the estimated values are similar.

Title: Using EQ-5D-Y to measure the health of patients for multiple paediatric health conditions: a project to validate the self-complete, interviewer-administered and proxy administered versions of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in China
Abstract: There has been rapid progress in validating the experimental version of the Y-5L and producing the Y-3L values sets worldwide. For Y-5L, it is in experimental stage and requires more psychometric evidence to move it to the next stage. In the penultimate (14th) round of RFP, the YPWG was calling for proposals to assess the psychometric evidence of these two instruments in different health condition groups and different modes of administration, like self-complete, interviewer-administered (IA) and proxy versions, with an emphasis on research in younger aged group (<8 years). In the last (15th) round of RFP, the YPWG simulates prioritized data collection of the 3L and 5L version of the EQ-5D-Y in children with a high burden of disease. In this resubmission proposal for the penultimate (14th) round of RFP, we have included parallel 3L and 5L data collection, in accordance with the requests made in the last (15th) round of RFP. We will include inpatients with sufficient disease burden and a sample size of 120 dyads (patients and caregivers) for each of following 3 disease groups (n=120 for each group): • Pneumonia: 50% severe pneumonia. • Paediatric central nervous system (CNS) solid tumour: Neuroblastoma or Wilms tumour: 33% category 1, 33% category 2a and 2b; 33% category 3 and 4 and beyond. • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura, ITP, with 33% mild, 33% moderate and 33% sever.  Notably, the cross-sectional data collection at baseline of this project will be covered by another proposal entitled ‘Extending the crosswalk dataset for EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L: proposal to fund multiple new inputs’ (1721-RA, revise and resubmit). As we collect patients mainly administered as inpatient at the hospital with high burden, this data set will be valuable for the cross-walk exercise as prioritise in the (15th) round of RFP, and will help to get good evidence for the psychometrics like responsiveness as requested in the second last (14th) round of RFP.  We will share our 3LY 5LY parallel data with the 1721-RA team as soon as the first cross sectional data from the baseline observations are available. As our research group is an established clinically group, we have direct access to the patient data, and the suggested deadline for the crosswalk data collection of Q3 2024 is feasible. The budget of the cross-sectional data collection at baseline will be covered by 1721-RA and this proposal only ask the budget for conducting the follow-up survey.

Title: Can EQ-5D capture the impact of climate change? A study of the health impact of heatwaves
Abstract: We conducted a cohort study in Fuzhou, China to assess the health and wellbeing of community-dwelling older adults in spring, summer, and autumn in 2023. Data collection was conducted in two residential areas. We performed analysis to assess the validity and responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB to the impact of heatwaves. We also performed a head-to-head comparison between EQ-5D_ and EQ-HWB and explored the demographic factors affecting the impact of heatwaves on older adults' heath-related quality of life.

Title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Content Validation of Vision Bolt-ons for EQ-5D-5L: Exploring Wording Variations, Conceptual Overlap, and Cultural Relevance
Abstract: Background:The EQ-5D-5L is a widely used measure of health-related quality of life; however, it may not fully capture the impact of vision problems on daily functioning and well-being. To address this limitation, vision and vision-related activities bolt-ons have been proposed to enhance its sensitivity in populations with visual impairment. Further work is needed to adapt these bolt-ons across different cultures, assess their relevance, comprehensiveness, and comprehensibility, and determine whether alternative wording (e.g., “vision” vs. “seeing”) affects their interpretation. Cultural adaptation is particularly important in Arabic-speaking settings, where language and context may influence how individuals perceive and report visual difficulties. Aim:This study aims to conduct cross-cultural adaptation and explore the content validity of vision bolt-ons from the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. Objectives include exploring wording variations, assessing cultural relevance, importance, comprehensiveness, comprehensibility and examining potential conceptual overlaps between these bolt-ons and the existing EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Methods:Vision bolt-ons (best available and exploratory) will first be translated following the EuroQol VMC translation and adaptation guidelines as two forward and two back translations, followed by cognitive debriefing interviews to establish consensus on conceptual and linguistic equivalence of the final Arabic version of the tested bolt-ons. Afterwards, semi-structured interviews will be conducted with adults diagnosed with cataract, age-related macular degeneration, or diabetic retinopathy. Using a think-aloud approach and retrospective probing, participants will complete the EQ-5D-5L and the four bolt-ons while providing feedback on clarity, relevance, comprehensiveness, and preferences for wording alternatives. All interviews will be recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using content and thematic analysis to identify key concepts, cultural relevance, and potential overlaps. Findings will inform final recommendations on item wording and the appropriate use of the bolt-ons in populations with visual impairment.

Title: Exploring subjective constructions of quality of life as defined by EQ-HWB in patients, carers and the healthy general publics: a Q-methodological study
Abstract: Objective The overall aim of this study was to explore similarities and differences in perceptions of QoL, as defined by EQ-HWB, among different groups of populations, including patients, carers and the healthy general publics. Methods This study used Q-methodology to investigate the subjective constructions of QoL across the groups. We developed a list of 34 Q-sample items (24 EQ-HWB items + 10 unique Chinese QoL items) that can be used in the Q-sort ranking activity to elicit participants preference across various aspects of quality of life (QoL). We collected a total of 151 Q-sort data for use in the standard by-person factor analytic procedure designed for Q-methodology. We also conducted post-sort interviews and obtained qualitative information about why they ranked the statements in certain ways, which can help the interpretation of the output data. Results We were able to identify four distinct viewpoints: Factor 1: Eat well, sleep well, be well; Factor 2: Positive relationships, belongings and well-being; Factor 3: My own feelings matter for well-being; Factor 4: Physical health is the foundation of well-being. While Factor 4 was equally valued across all three categories of participants, Factor 2, which places a high value on positive relationships, was predominantly represented by carers. In contrast, patients tended to emphasise Factor 3, which focuses on individual feelings—particularly emotional and physical distress. Items related to pain, discomfort, and sleep, which are part of EQ-HWB, were consistently identified as the most important across all four identified views. Nearly all EQ-HWB items were rated as highly relevant by at least one view in our study, which further supports the relevance of EQ-HWB in capturing individuals’ QoL. Conclusion This study presents the similarities and differences of the subjective constructions of QoL across patients, carers and the healthy general publics. It provides conceptual evidence to show that EQ-HWB can have a variety of targeting audiences. It also implies the variances of preferences in evaluating QoL, and such variances can consequently affect the measurement and evaluation of QoL.

Title: How do HTA practitioners and researchers in Asia perceive EuroQol instruments? A qualitative study
Abstract: Background: While Asian HTA agencies accept or recommend EQ-5D instruments, they are continuously exploring better ways of measuring health-related quality of life. This study addresses a critical knowledge gap by engaging directly with Asian HTA practitioners and researchers to understand their views on EuroQol instruments.Methods: We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with 22 HTA practitioners and researchers across 10 Asian countries (China n=4, India n=1, Indonesia n=2, Japan n=2, Malaysia n=3, South Korea n=2, Thailand n=2, Taiwan n=2, Singapore n=2, Philippines n=2). Interview transcripts were systematically coded using a comprehensive 18-category framework covering current use, strengths/weaknesses, implementation challenges, cultural considerations, future recommendations, evidence gaps, and collaboration expectations.Findings: EQ-5D-5L has achieved strong institutional adoption (mandated or de facto standard in 90% of agencies), but significant implementation gaps prevent optimal utilisation. The "Philippines paradox" exemplifies this: a locally-developed value set exists but remains underused due to capacity constraints. Three critical barriers emerged: (1) fundamental capacity gaps in basic methodologies blocking QoL expertise development, (2) awareness deficits regarding value sets, bolt-ons, and registration processes, and (3) absence of utility infrastructure (databases, guidelines, quality assurance protocols). Cultural factors may significantly impact measurement validity—mental health stigma limits EQ-HWB adoption, toxic positivity/religious coping inflates wellbeing scores, and complex family structures complicate pediatric proxy validity. Priority needs cluster around: ecosystem-wide training (HTA staff + academics + external researchers), regional LMIC utility databases, EQ-5D-Y value sets (highest priority across all countries), and methodological guidance on transferability/proxy use for adaptive HTA contexts.Implications: EQ-5D is institutionally entrenched but operationally underutilised. The highest ROI interventions are: (1) comprehensive training programmes targeting entire research ecosystems, not just HTA agencies, (2) development of maintained utility databases/registries aligned with national HTA priorities, (3) prioritisation of EQ-5D-Y value sets given universal paediatric gaps, and (4) creation of methodological guidance for adaptive HTA contexts where primary data collection is infeasible. Regional collaboration through HTAsiaLink offers scalability, and individual country partnerships (particularly collaboration with universities) could be more effective due to legal/institutional constraints.

Title: Developing and delivering a workshop for promoting the use of the EQ-5D as a PROM for improving clinical and shared decision-making in routine care in Asia
Abstract: On 30th May 2023, Drs Nick Bansback and Nan Luo conducted a workshop at the National University of Singapore on using the EQ-5D as a PROM for improving clinical and shared decision-making. The workshop was designed based on feedback from a number of clinical groups in Singapore who have been collecting the EQ-5D and interested in how they can use the results more to improve patient centred and value based care. The workshop was split into 3 sections. The first section, led by Nan described what PROMs are and how to choose a PROM for different clinical use. This focused on using the EQ-5D as a PROM but also described how condition specific PROMs could be used in combination. The second section, led by Nick then described how PROMs could be used for clinical management and shared decision making. A number of case studies were used, including how the EQ-5D has been used to create an individualized decision aid for knee replacement surgery. The last section provided information about how to obtain the EQ-5D, and how to use and analyze it. The workshop was attended by 55 clinicians, clinical researchers, graduate students, and industry reps from Singapore.

Title: Health-related quality of life in patients with COVID-19: a protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis of EQ-5D studies
Abstract: Introduction: COVID-19 affects millions of persons worldwide, with a significant proportion experiencing long-COVID and impaired health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Despite numerous primary studies, the impact of COVID-19 on patients, as measured by the EQ-5D instrument, has not been examined using a systematic review and meta-analysis. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to identify and summarize the currently available evidence on the HRQoL in patients with COVID-19, measured using EQ-5D. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for English-language studies published between December 2019 and January 2023. The included studies were peer-reviewed and assessed HRQoL of COVID-19 patients using the EQ-5D. Quality and bias were evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pooled estimates of health utility values were analyzed using a random-effects model, with further subgroup analyses conducted. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. Predictors of poor HRQoL were identified from each article and narrated qualitatively. Results: Our search identified 1797 references, resulting in the selection of 87 studies involving 25,711 participants. The majority of studies used the EQ-5D-5L (79.3%) instrument. The pooled mean EQ-5D utility score for COVID-19 patients was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75-0.84; I2 = 99.8%), and the pooled EQ-5D VAS mean score was 71.73 (95% CI: 69.35 – 74.12; I2 = 99.2 %). Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression were the dimensions most affected, with pooled estimates of 49% (95% CI: 41-56) and 44% (95% CI: 35-53), respectively. Subgroup analysis revealed significant differences based on age subgroups and continents. We identified 42 studies that reported on predictors of HRQoL among COVID-19 survivors. The most common predictors were demographic factors such as older age and female gender, as well as clinical factors such as disease severity, comorbidities, and post-COVID-19 symptoms. Conclusion: This study presents a comprehensive summary of evidence concerning HRQoL in patients with COVID-19. Our analysis revealed a reduction in HRQoL, as indicated by EQ-5D utility scores among COVID-19 patients compared to general population. These findings will aid healthcare professionals and policymakers in better understanding the groups that may experience a greater burden due to COVID-19. The mean utility value derived from this study can assist in calculating Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs).

Title: The impact of COVID-19 on EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-TIPS, EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-S in Chinese children and their parent carers
Abstract: [Objectives] The serious impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in China provided a unique opportunity to test the newly published Chinese EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets and EQ-TIPS in a very large sample of young patients with COVID-19 and children affected by the lockdown. Additionally, we compared the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-S and the EQ-5D-5L in capturing health status and well-being in parental carers of children with COVID-19, and identified spillover effects of the disease of children with COVID-19 towards their parents and other factors associated with lower worse health status. [Methods] 861 patients with COVID-19 completed the baseline survey in the hospital. Of this sample 311 patients needed outpatient treatment or were temporally hospitalised completed a follow-up survey after 2-3 weeks in the hospital. The EQ-TIPS, Y-3L, EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB-S, and overall health assessment (OHA) were digitally administered. 231 healthy children and their parents were recruited as health controls using a snowball method and were administered online at home. Clinical data were collected from medical records. The analysis included assessment of known-groups validity, by comparing the proportion of dimension responses, the Level Sum Score (LSS) for EQ-TIPS and EQ-HWB-S, the index score for Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L, and EQ-VAS across children with different health status using effect sizes. Test-retest reliability and child-parent agreement were also evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Responsiveness of four EQ instruments to changes in respondents with improved health status was assessed using standardized effect sizes (SESs). Associations between patient’s health condition and lower parent’s HRQoL was examined by multivariate linear models. [Results] • Regarding distributional properties, children with COVID-19 experienced more problems across all dimensions compared to non-infected children, except for “communication” for EQ-TIPS; Parents' physical functions were more impacted by child’s infection than emotional functions; EQ-HWB-S demonstrated a lower ceiling effect in dimensions that overlap with EQ-5D-5L. • Regarding known-groups validity, children with COVID-19 (and their parents), those with more severe disease, or poorer OHA reported higher EQ-TIPS LSS, lower EQ-5D-Y/EQ-HWB-S/EQ-5D-5L index scores and lower EQ VAS compared to those non-infected, with milder disease severity, or with poorer OHA, supporting a good known-groups validity (ESs: 0.60-1.91); Self-completed EQ-5D-Y performed better than proxy version; EQ-5D-5L differed in relation to more child’s health conditions than EQ-HWB-S. • ICC was 0.866 for EQ-TIPS LSS, 0.726 for self-completed EQ-5D-Y index, 0.845 for proxy EQ VAS, 0.764 for EQ-HWB-S index, 0.769 for EQ-5D-5L index, 0.702 for parent’s own EQ VAS; Gwet’s AC1for EQ-HWB-S ranged from 0.33 (anxiety) to 0.79 (mobility); and from 0.41 (anxiety/depression) to 0.76 (mobility) for EQ-5D-5L, demonstrated good test-retest reliability. ICC ranged from 0.653 to 0.823, and Gwet’s AC from 0.470 to 0.738 demonstrated moderate to good child-parent agreement for EQ-5D-Y. • EQ-TIPS was responsive to health improvement (SESs: 0.98 - 1.75). Proxy Y-3L performed better responsiveness than the Self-report version (SESs: 1.16-2.29 vs 1.13- 1.98). Most of the items and scores for the EQ-HWB-S performed similar and good responsiveness as the EQ-5D-5L to improved children’s or their own health condition (SESs: 0.23-0.91 vs 0.4-0.91), and was more sensitive for the physical dimensions. • Both EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L could estimate spillover effects associated with child’s different health conditions related to COVID-19 infection, as well as their health improvement; EQ-HWB-S exhibited better discriminate ability to children with or without COVID-19, while EQ-5D-5L showed better sensitivity to child’s improvement. • Patients with a longer duration of disease and more severe disease condition, including gastrointestinal issues, exhibited a correlation with a lower EQ-HWB-S LSS score. An extended disease duration in conjunction with COVID-19-related pneumonia or conjunctivitis was linked to a reduced EQ-5D-5L index score. Additionally, when a patient had a lengthier disease duration and their parent had contracted COVID-19, it was associated with a lower EQ VAS score for the parent. [Conclusion] The results of this large study support the reliability, validity and responsiveness for the EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L in assessing health outcomes of young patients affected by COVID-19. The EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L performed good with comparable construct validity and responsiveness among parental carers. These findings highlight their potential as promising instruments for estimating the spillover effects associated with a child's health condition in relation to COVID-19 infection.

Title: IHEA Pre-congress session on EQ-5D as a measure of population health, plus sponsorship of 7 LMIC ECR delegates to attend IHEA
Abstract: The project delivered a pre-congress session at the International Health Economics Association (IHEA) meeting in Cape Town in July. The pre-congress session was led by the Population and Health Systems Working Group and focused on EQ-5D as a measure of population health. Trudy Sullivan, Des Scott and Kompal Sinha presented EuroQol funded work on POPQOL, DAPHNIE and IndiQol, respectively. The session was moderated by Paula Lorgelly. In addition to providing funding for the pre-congress session, the grant also supported six ECRs from LMICs to attend the IHEA Congress.

Title: 2nd EuroQoL African Regional Academy (Virtual)
Abstract: Aims: To expand on the gains of the first African Academy Meeting in 2020 in building capacity in the field of measurement of HRQoL, stimulating interest in the continued and expanding use of the EQ-5D and creating opportunities for researchers in Africa. (Long term) Outcomes: : Greater utilization of the EQ-5D as a patient-reported outcome (PRO) measure across different countries and contexts; improved methodology, analysis and reporting of studies using the EQ-5D; establishment of researcher networks within and between countries; possible interest in doing national or language valuation studies; greater attention to methodological research about EQ-5D; and an increased interest in Health Technology Assessment (HTA) and Cost Utility Analysis (CUA) by health economists and policy makers.

Title: Evaluating the validity of the EQ Health and Wellbeing short (EQ-HWB-S) in a large general population sample.
Abstract: Objectives: The EQ Health and Wellbeing Short (EQ-HWB-9) is a generic, preference-weighted instrument with an interim value set for assessing quality of life across health, social care, and informal caregiving. This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the experimental (2022) version and compared its performance with established measures of health and wellbeing.Methods: Data were drawn from a large cross-sectional online survey of the UK general population (n = 11,383). Ceiling/floor effects were assessed at item (>50% extreme responses) and instrument (>15% at min/max score) levels. Construct validity was evaluated through convergent validity using Spearman correlations between EQ-HWB-9 items and conceptually similar items from the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (SWEMWBS), the ICEpop CAPability measure for Adults (ICECAP-A), the Health Utilities Index Mark 3 (HUI3), and the Office for National Statistics Four Personal Wellbeing Questions (ONS-4). Pearson correlations were used for utility scores. Known-group validity was assessed using effect sizes to examine differences by mental wellbeing, disability, life satisfaction, caregiving status, self-reported health, and age. Agreement with comparator instruments was assessed using Bland–Altman plots and Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient (CCC).Results: Ceiling effects were noted for EQ-HWB-9 mobility and activity items, but not at the instrument level. Strong correlations (rs ≥0.5, P.001) supported convergent validity with SWEMWBS, ICECAP-A, HUI3, and ONS-4. The EQ-HWB-9 effectively distinguished between relevant population subgroups (effect sizes ≥0.8). Agreement was lower with HUI3 utilities compared to others.Conclusions: The EQ-HWB-9 shows strong psychometric performance and is supported for use in UK health and wellbeing assessments.

Title: ISPOR Issue Panel on child health valuation
Abstract: Title: Valuing health in children –where are we now, and what further work is needed?Issue: To facilitate the HTA of interventions for younger patients, utilities are needed that reflect the value of health in children and adolescents. However valuing health in children is challengingand raises questions about methodology, ethics and social values. For example: Which preference elicitation techniques should be used? Whose preferences should count (e.g. adults, parents, adolescents)? Under what perspective should those preferences be elicited (e.g. adults valuing health states for themselves or for a child)? Should we aimfor consistency between child and adult health valuation, in terms of both methods and values? Recent research has provided insights on some of these issues, but uncertainties and disagreements remain about the best way forward. Overview: In this issue panel, Koonal Shah will moderate and summarise emerging international research that addresses some of the key challenges. Elly Stolk will describe the development of the first international protocol for valuing the EQ-5D-Y, the youth version of the EQ-5D, and its recent application in Japan. This protocol combines time trade-off (TTO) and discrete-choice experiments to elicit adult preferences, but differs from the protocol for valuing the adult EQ-5D-5L. Donna Rowen will explain her concerns about the use of TTO in this setting and examine what alternative approaches are possible, focusing on how other measures such as CHU9D have been valued. She will also highlight current research gaps. Rosie Lovett will provide the perspective of an HTA agency exploring whether to issue guidance to companies about measuring and valuing child health. She will focus on questions about consistency and outline what further work would help agencies like NICE to make methodological recommendations. Following the brief presentations, 30 minutes will be reserved for panel and audience discussion, with questions and suggestions on how to reach consensus particularly welcomed.

Title: The impact of recent health events and fluctuations in health status on the assessment of health today using the EQ-5D-5L: A mixed-methods study among people with dementia and their caregivers
Abstract: Background: This project aimed to quantify the frequency of health fluctuations over time, identify affected HRQoL dimensions and evaluate whether past fluctuations are considered in assessing today's health using the EQ-5D-5L in people living with dementia where spells of good and bad days are common. Methods: This study was an explorative, single-group, observational study with daily measure points that combined quantitative and qualitative (mixed) methods. Caregivers of persons with dementia completed a daily diary for 14 days, documenting health fluctuations and the affected HRQoL dimension. Also, caregivers and patients completed the EQ-5D-5L (proxy- & self-reported) on days one, seven and 14. Subsequently, caregivers were interviewed about documented health fluctuations and whether these fluctuations were considered in the EQ-5D-5L assessment of today's health. Results: Health fluctuations occurred in 96% of cases and every second day (50% of daily assessments). The most frequently affected HRQoL dimensions were memory and mobility, followed by concentration, sleep, pain/ discomfort, and usual activities. A higher fluctuation in the diary was associated with a higher EQ-5D-5L health state variation. Patients with a moderate to high fluctuation had the highest LSS and health utility change and the highest non-adherence to the EQ-5D-5L recall period (31% vs 17%) compared to patients with a low health fluctuation. The non-adherence to the EQ-5D-5L recall period of today was also significantly higher in patients with improved health states than in patients with deteriorated health states (37% vs 9%), which was confirmed by qualitative interview data. Conclusion: Health state fluctuations frequently occur in dementia. A higher fluctuation was associated with larger changes in health utilities and non-adherence to the EQ-5D's recall period of today. However, the results are based on small sample size, limiting its generalizability. Therefore, further research is needed to confirm demonstrated results. Secondly, future research should evaluate if longer recall periods, like those of the EQ-HWB(-S), capture recurrent health fluctuations more appropriately, resulting in higher reliability and recall period adherence.

Title: Assessing the Content Validity of EQ-5D Vision Bolt-Ons in People with Diabetic Retinopathy
Abstract: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a common complication of diabetes that can cause vision impairment and blindness. The health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of people living with DR is substantially reduced, yet evidence shows that generic HRQoL instruments such as the EQ-5D may not be sufficiently responsive in this population. Previous studies have demonstrated that EQ-5D often fails to discriminate across DR severity and can produce counterintuitive results. EuroQol Group has developed the Bolt-on Toolbox, which is designed to enhance the responsiveness and sensitivity of the EQ-5D across a range of health conditions, including those that affect vision. This study aims to explore the content validity of vision bolt-ons in the context of diabetic retinopathy, assessing whether they improve the EQ-5D’s responsiveness and identifying which version(s) offer the most meaningful measurement properties from the perspective of people living with DR.The study will adopt a qualitative design using 25 semi-structured online interviews with individuals diagnosed with DR. This sample is intended to provide at least five participants for each type of DR: (1) non-proliferative (early stage) and (2) proliferative (advanced stage).Interviews will follow a think-aloud protocol with some cognitive debriefing. All interviews, conducted via MS Teams, will be transcribed, coded, and analysed using framework analysis developed by van Leeuwen et al., which has previously been applied in studies using think-aloud methods to test the validity of EQ-5D-5L.The purpose of this study is to establish a foundation for a prospective psychometric property analysis of the vision bolt-on. The research team plans to develop a proposal for this subsequent study, targeting the 21 EuroQol Request for Proposals (RFP). No need for citations in the abstract unless they’re really crucial. Think-aloud (on its own) is generally seen as being insufficient because participants struggle to fully articulate everything that we want to know during the process of completion. It is best to combine the think-aloud protocol with some cognitive debriefing.

Title: National EQ-5D Symposium and Valuation Workshop
Abstract: A total of 18 potential interviewers were selected to undergo the three‐day valuation workshop. Two esteemed EuroQol Board Members, together with the Investigator Team moderated the workshop. The entire workshop was held at Universiti Sains Malaysia, Penang. On the first day of the workshop, held at the Main Meeting Room of the School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, the participants were exposed to the various concepts and interview techniques pertaining to the Valuation Study. A series of comprehensive lectures were delivered by experts from the Investigator Team and by one of the invited representative from EuroQoL. The participants were also familiarized to the interview script by are corded mock session of the interview (Appendix1), besides practising the script among colleagues. These cond day of the workshop included mock interview sessions organized at the lobby are alocated beside the university’s Main Library. Each participant interviewed a minimum of five individuals using the official script of the Valuation Study. The Investigator Team evaluated each participant’s performance to ensure only well‐prepared interviewers are selected to participate in the Valuation Study. The final day of the workshop included a round‐table discussion held again at the Main Meeting Room of the School of Pharmaceutical Sciences. The participants had a chance of sharing their experience of conducting the mock interviews and raise any queries pertaining to the interviews. Generally, the participants shared that they enjoyed their new experience of interviewing and encountering interviewees from different walks of life. The invited guests from EuroQoL were generous in sharing their expert advice and experience in conducting such interviews. Additionally, the performance of the participants’ mock interviews was also formally reviewed using official quality control methods adopted by EuroQoL. Each of the 18 participants passed the performance review and were selected to represent the Valuation Study Team of Interviewers. Overall, the moderators of the workshop were very satisfied with the participation, enthusiasm, and energy of the participants of the workshop and hoped that that would follow through the entire Valuation Study.

Title: Use of EQ-5D in elderly populations (Call for proposal 1)
Abstract: INTRODUCTION:At present the world is undergoing a demographic revolution, with a sizeable and ongoing increase in the absolute and relative numbers of older people in both developed and developing countries. According to the fact that chronic illnesses and disabilities has a high prevalence between the elderly, it further emphasises the importance of appropriate assessment of health related QoL (HRQoL) within the elderly. The aim of the review was to identify to what extent the QoL/wellbeing of these patients can be measured with the EQ-5D generic instrument. This paper reviews the use of EQ5D in elderly populations (not specific disease groups in old age) with special attention given to the distinction between frail elderly and non-frail elderly and between users and non-users of social/long-termcare. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted using the PubMed, EBSCO, JSTOR, Springerlink, Science direct and Wiley online library databases to identify articles that examined the EQ-5D questionnaire in connection to with the elderly. RESULTS: 23 articles, which address the EQ-5D questions in connection to the elderly, have been found. The presentation of the results is prepared from different angles. Firstly, the results are presented according to the countryof research, then according to the type of the study and then according to the target population of the study(i.e. frail elderly in comparison to non-frail elderly and users vs. non-users of social/long term care). The latter division is described in details with special attention given to EQ-5D instrument. CONCLUSION:It can be summarized that EQ-5D is a good instrument to assess HRQoL and also a useful predictor of mortality and first hospitalization. Therefore it can be confirmed that EQ-5D can help to find differences between frail and non-frail elderly and users and non-users of social/long term care.

Title: An Empirical Ethical Evaluation of Population Health using EQ-5D data
Abstract: This research explores an empirical ethical framework for evaluating population health. We apply sequential stochastic dominance to compare population health distributions across five countries, using EQ-5D health-related quality of life data and life table mortality statistics. Sequential stochastic dominance relies on ethical principles — anonymity, Pareto efficiency,  diminishing positive welfare returns to quality of life that decline by age — without imposing restrictive functional forms. In comparing health distributions, it allows to take an ethical stance to age-prioritization of health improvements. Our findings show that sequential dominance provides a nuanced comparison of population health between countries, highlighting differences that are obscured by averages. The graphical exposition of sequential stochastic dominance offers a transparent and ethically grounded tool for health policy evaluation, showing why population health in one country is preferred. Sequential dominance therefore complements existing summary measures.

Title: Health-Related Quality of Life in Bangladeshi Children and Adolescents: Population reference data and Comparison of EQ-5D-Y-3L Value Sets
Abstract: Background:Measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among children and adolescents is essential for understanding their physical, mental, and social well-being from their own perspectives. The EQ-5D-Y, developed by the EuroQol Group, is a validated, child-friendly, preference-based instrument that captures HRQoL across five dimensions. The instrument has been recently piloted in Bangladesh and found to be feasible and acceptable. Establishing national reference data is therefore crucial to support policy development, economic evaluations, and child health planning.Objectives:This study aims to (1) generate EQ-5D-Y-3L population reference data for Bangladeshi children and adolescents, (2) examine variations in HRQoL reporting by age, sex, and socio-economic characteristics, and (3) explore the impact of applying different international value sets on the derived utility scores.Methods:A cross-sectional study was conducted between December 2024 and February 2025 alongside the adult EQ-5D valuation study in Bangladesh, implemented by the ARK Foundation following the EuroQol Group’s EQ-VT protocol. Using a multistage stratified quota sampling method, 1,023 households were surveyed across the eight administrative divisions. Of these, 535 households with children aged 8 to 17 years were eligible, yielding 712 valid EQ-5D-Y-3L responses.  The Bangla version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and visual analogue scale (VAS) were completed by children, while adult respondents provided socio-demographic data.Descriptive statistics will summarise socio-demographic characteristics and HRQoL responses across dimensions. Differences by demographic variables will be tested using chi-square, t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, and ANOVA, as appropriate. Logistic regression models will assess associations between socio-demographic factors and reporting problems in each EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension.  As Bangladesh lacks a country-specific value set, available international EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets will be applied to estimate health state utilities. Additional analyses will compare results across 10 available international value sets using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman plots to assess agreement. Expected Outcomes:This study will provide the first nationally representative EQ-5D-Y-3L reference data for Bangladeshi children and adolescents and offer methodological insights for developing a local value set. Findings will inform HRQoL research, child health policy, and future economic evaluations in Bangladesh.

Title: Population Health Primary Data Collection Project
Abstract: Year 1 completed work: • Established Project Team (held 6 meetings to date), created project team terms of reference document • Established EQ-DAPHNIE Executive Committee (held 13 meetings to date) • Established advisory panel, created advisory panel terms of reference document (held 2 meetings with 2 advisors to date) • Established charter for data management/sharing, in alignment with the EuroQol Office SAVED initiative • Created authorship guidelines • Invited EQ membership to propose research questions/measures • Created sub-teams for population norms and instrument comparison research objectives • Established contract with Maths in Health (MiH) • MiH purchased and configured EQ-DAPHNIE servers • Finalized modules for pilot survey in the United Kingdom • Draft programming of pilot survey completed by MiH • A webinar was held (Dec. 7, 2021) on the research objectives, project team, methodological plan, data charter and project timelines • Interactive presentations were held during the 2022 EuroQol Academy Meeting, including breakout sessions for the population health and instrument comparison research domains Year 2 completed work: • MiH programmed the pilot survey Title: Investigating the development of a multi layered “Deep Dive” measure of health-related quality of life based on the EQ-5D: A pilot study
Abstract: This Descriptive System Working Group led pilot study was the first step in exploring the potential development of deep-dive modules for the EQ-5D-5L. The Deep Dive approach includes a higher-level preference- accompanied measure (i.e., the core EQ-5D descriptive system), and a set of items associated with each dimension (the deep-dive). As part of this exploration we have considered the conceptual basis, and the potential advantages and disadvantages of deep-dive modules, and also the methodological process for developing the modules, building on similar approaches used by other developer groups that we have identified. This resulted in an introduction paper outlining the approach (Mulhern et al 2022). The introduction paper provided the basis for a detailed consultation process with EuroQol stakeholders from key groups, including the Board, Executive Committee, Office, Working Groups and the Version Management Committee. Finally, we have conducted analysis of existing datasets including a range of HRQoL instruments to explore potential methodological approaches to develop deep-dive modules based on EQ-5D-5L dimensions. The results of this pilot work have been used to inform discussions about the broader programme. This has taken the form of ongoing discussions between the DSWG and Executive Committee. A draft memo titled “Deep-dive modules for the EQ-5D – What, why and how?” was recently put forward for the Exec based on this work (see attachments). This memo includes more advanced thinking around the overall deep-dive initiative that has developed since the original pilot study, and is therefore included here. This document is outside the remit of this pilot study but is important contextual information for the broader program, and the consideration of this final report.These discussions have led to a deprioritisation of the programme, but with renewed focus on methodological research and possible exploration of certain elements (e.g. one individual dimension or specific methodological aspects). This pilot work already contributes to this process, and the secondary data analysis has been reframed as informing the broader agenda of the DSWG and the wider group focused on the use of IRT methods (as part of a broader mixed methods protocol) to test and develop current (eg EQ-HWB-25) and future EuroQol instruments
