Title: Psychometric Evaluation of the EQ-5D-5L in Sepsis Patients
Abstract: Background and objectiveSepsis is one of the leading causes of death worldwide and a major challenge in intensive care medicine. Survivors frequently experience markedly reduced Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL), with persistent physical and functional impairments long after discharge. Despite this, HRQoL assessments such as the EQ-5D-5L are rarely conducted during the acute phase of sepsis, and evidence on their psychometric properties in this population remains scarce.The overall aim of the proposal is to test the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L in critically ill patients using a sample of sepsis patients. Specific objectives are to assess feasibility, floor and ceiling effects, construct validity by examining convergent and known-groups validity, and responsiveness. The secondary aims are to (1) compare self- and proxy-reported EQ-5D-5L assessments in sepsis patients, examining effects of administration mode on psychometric properties, and (2) evaluate the longitudinal stability of these properties across three time points.Proposed methodsThe proposed project is a secondary data analysis of existing clinical trial data. Data was collected during a randomized, controlled, interventional, open-label, multi-center trial that included patients with sepsis or septic shock from 03/2022 to 08/2023 in the medical and surgical ICUs of 24 maximum care hospitals.Next to response distribution, feasibility (absolute numbers and percentage of missing values) and floor/ceiling effects (profiles of “11111” and “55555”), construct validity in terms of convergent (Pearson correlation coefficients) and known-groups validity (t-tests, analysis of variance or non-parametric alternatives and effect size) will be assessed. Finally, responsiveness will be determined by effect size and standardized response mean.

Title: Health-Related Quality of Life in children attending specialist health services
Abstract: Background: The development of the EQ-5D-Y-5L (Y-5L) has created a demand for mapping the EQ-5D-Y-3L (Y-3L) values to the Y-5L while the international protocol for valuation of the EQ-5D-Y-5L is developed. One of the challenges identified with mapping is having sufficient data across the severity spectrum. This study aimed to recruit patients, and their caregivers attending specialist health services, with presumed severe health profiles, to contribute paired Y-3L and Y-5L responses for the purposes of mapping. The secondary aim was to assess the psychometric performance of the Y-3L, Y-5L and EQ-TIPS in this cohort of children. Methods: Caregivers of children aged 0-18 years, were recruited from specialist outpatient clinics at Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital in South Africa. The performance of the EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y 3L and 5L versions was determined by comparing feasibility with the absolute reduction in the ceiling effect (111111). Discriminatory power was evaluated with Shannon’s H’ index for absolute informativity and Shannon’s J’ index for relative informativity or spread of responses. The redistribution of dimension responses between the 5L and 3L versions was evaluated for inconsistency. If a 5L response is two or more levels removed from a 3L response, that response pair is classified as inconsistent. Known group severity was calculated for the 5L and 3L LSS scores according to severity groupings by PedsQL total score (≤74.2) and EQ VAS (≤80). Results: EQ-TIPS: Data from 176 children aged 0-4 years were included, with a median age of 29 months and more males (n = 95, 54%). The majority of respondents were mothers (n = 137, 81%). Children were grouped by disease category: epilepsy (n = 15, 9%), neuromuscular disease (n = 13 ,7%), chronic gastrointestinal disease (n = 19, 11%), renal disease (n = 48, 27%) and oncological or haematological diseases (n = 72, 41%). The ceiling effect (111111) decreased minimally by 4% from the 3L to 5L. Absolute informativity (H’) of dimensions improved by 0.115 on the 5L, with retention of the spread of responses for all dimensions. Convergent validity was similar, with strong correlations on paired 3L and 5L dimensions. The 3L and 5L were similarly able to significantly differentiate between known groups based on PedsQL and EQ VAS severity cut-offs. EQ-5D-Y: Proxy report data from 328 children aged 5-18 years were included, with a mean (SD) age of 9.8 (4.3) years and more males (n=173, 53%). The majority of mothers were mothers (n=245, 75%). Children were grouped by disease category: epilepsy (n = 55, 17%), neuromuscular disease (n = 59, 18%), chronic gastrointestinal disease (n = 36, 11%), renal disease (n = 73, 22%) and oncological or haematological diseases (n = 105, 32%). The ceiling effect (111111) decreased by 7% from the 3L to 5L. Absolute informativity (H’) of dimensions improved by 0.05 on the 5L, with the greatest improvement in pain/discomfort, with retention of the spread of responses for all dimensions. The 3L and 5L were similarly able to significantly differentiate between known groups based on PedsQL and EQ VAS severity cut-offs. Conclusion: The five-level versions of the EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y have similar or superior performance to the three-level version.

Title: Improving DCE design efficiency with (automated) design updates
Abstract: Background: Even though it is well-established and common practice for DCE design efficiency to be improved through sample-specific design updates, the EQ-VT (5L/Y) continues to rely on a 'one-single-design-fits-all-countries' approach. Based on existing literature it is unclear whether the EuroQol Group should revise this approach and, if so, how much efficiency would be gained.  Aim: To systematically investigage the design efficiency improvements obtained for a range of possible DCE design update strategies, including the option of an update strategy based on multiple pilot samples that can be automated for online data collection.  Methods: The relative design efficiency achieved through seven different design update strategies is evaluated in a simulation study for eight different scenarios. Four synthetic scenarios are used to allow for systematic variation in the degree of choice consistency and preference heterogeneity, and four real-life scenarios cover a wide range of DCE design dimensions, including the EQ-5D-5L instrument. All achieved design efficiencies are averages achieved across 10 independent runs and proposed to be expressed on a scale that ranges from 0% to 100%, with 0% denoting the design efficiency achieved based on the most simplistic model without making use of any prior information and 100% denoting the design efficiency of the most advanced MIXL design combined with on full prior knowledge of the respondents' preferences. Further technical details are provided in the research strategy.

Title: Developing a value set for the EQ-5D-5L in United Arab Emirates
Abstract: We completed a valuation study for the EQ-5D-5L in United Arab Emirates (UAE) following the EuroQol EQ-5D-5L Valuation protocol. The study was conducted as proposed and was completed according to timelines. The value set was derived using a hybrid model using an analytical sample of 1005 participants representative of the general UAE population.

Title: Values for severe states: a methodological and cultural view
Abstract: Introduction: Scaling severe states can be a difficult task. First, the method of measurement affects whether a health state is considered better or worse than dead. Second, in discrete choice experiments, different models to anchor health states on 0 (dead) and 1 (perfect health) produce varying amounts of health states worse than dead. Research question: Within the context of the QALY model, this paper provides insight into the value assigned to dead and its consequences for decision making. Our research questions are: 1) What are the arguments set forth to assign dead the number 0 on the health-utility scale? 2) What are the effects of the position of dead on the health-utility scale on decision making? Methods: A literature review was conducted to explore the arguments set forth to assign dead a value of 0 in the QALY model. In addition, scale properties and transformations were considered. Results:The review uncovered several practical and theoretical considerations for setting dead at 0. In the QALY model, indifference between two health episodes is not preserved under changes of the origin of the duration scale. Ratio scale properties are needed for the duration scale to preserve indifferences. In combination with preferences and zero conditions for duration and health, it follows that dead should have a value of 0. Conclusions: The health-utility and the duration scale have ratio scale properties and that dead should be assigned the number zero. Furthermore, the position of dead should be carefully established, as it determines how life saving and life improving values are weighed in cost-utility analysis.

Title: Psychometric Evaluation of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in Vulnerable Child Populations: Implications for Assessing Health-Related Quality of Life
Abstract: Background: Assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in vulnerable young populations is essential for informing policy and improving healthcare services tailored to their needs. South Korea has been selected as the study site because no validation work has been conducted on EQ-5D-Y in this context so far. The EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L are preference-weighted instruments designed for measuring HRQoL in children and adolescents, yet their applicability in specific vulnerable subgroups remains underexplored. This study aims to validate two HRQoL questionnaires among vulnerable young populations, with a focus on children and adolescents residing in orphanages. We will culturally adapt the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, two generic, preference-based instruments designed for measuring the HRQoL of children and adolescents, for use in South Korea and assess their validity and reliability in children and adolescents residing in orphanages. Methods: The project consists of two phases. Phase 1 will focus on the cultural and linguistic adaptation of the EQ-5D-Y (English to Korean) to ensure its relevance and comprehensibility. The study will consult the EuroQol Version Management Committee to verify whether a validated Korean version of both EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L exists. If necessary, a rigorous translation and cross-cultural adaptation process will be undertaken. Cognitive interviews will be conducted to assess content and face validity, ensuring that the translated versions are conceptually equivalent to the original instrument and appropriate for use in the target population.Phase 2 will involve the psychometric evaluation of both EQ-5D-Y versions in vulnerable young populations residing in orphanages. This will include assessing construct validity (convergent and known-groups validity) and test-retest reliability (over 1–2 weeks). A head-to-head comparison between the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L will be conducted for both self-reported and proxy-reported versions. Additionally, this study will explore HRQoL outcomes in this population and identify associated predictive factors. Findings from this research will contribute to methodological advancements in HRQoL measurement and provide evidence for selecting the most suitable EQ-5D-Y version for vulnerable young populations.

Title: Better understanding of the transition between Y and adult instruments: taking both measurement and valuation differences into account
Abstract: IntroductionThe EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L descriptive systems share the same five dimensions. However, they differ in terms of their wording of dimensions (e.g. Anxiety/Depression versus Worried, Sad or Unhappy), number of response levels, and level descriptors e.g for the worst level, “extreme”/”unable to”  in the 5L versus “a lot”/”cannot” in the Y-3L. Value sets for EQ-5D-Y-3L also have different properties compared to EQ-5D-5L value sets: Y-3L value sets are generally observed to have higher minimum values; contain a lower proportion of values < 0; and have a different order of dimension importance, compared to corresponding 5L value sets. These discrepancies may affect longitudinal HRQoL assessments in patients transitioning between the youth instrument and adult instrument, potentially leading to changes in index values without any change in underlying health. Systematic differences in measurement and values between age-specific instruments also raise potential concerns about the comparability of QALYs (e.g. in HTA) derived from youth and adult instruments. This study investigates whether these differences in value set characteristics and descriptive systems for the adult and youth instruments lead to overall differences in HRQoL (i.e. index values) when transitioning between them.MethodsWe pooled 4 datasets containing EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L responses  from the same respondents: a sample of South African children aged 12-19, half of which had a known condition (n=624); a sample of Australian children aged 12-18 with known conditions (n=591); and two general population young adult (ages <25) samples from the Netherlands (n=203) and Hungary (n=125). We report the distribution of responses for both instruments, and applied value sets to the response data, for the 10 countries that both have an EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value set (dyads). The difference between index values was compared between the instruments, for each dyad. ResultsCeiling effects were high and similar between the two instruments for all dimensions except anxiety or depression/worried, sad or unhappy. EQ-5D-Y-3L level 2 responses translated to levels 1-3 responses in EQ-5D-5L in 96% of cases. EQ-5D-Y-3L level 3 responses translated to level 3-5 responses on the EQ-5D-5L in 80% of cases. The differences in index values between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L were normally distributed but varied by country. Using EQ-5D-5L to report their own health led to higher index values using the value sets of 2 countries compared to their corresponding value on the EQ-5D-Y-3L (Indonesia and Japan; mean difference of 0.079 and 0.052, respectively). For the Netherlands and China, no difference was found. For the remaining countries (Australia, Belgium, Germany, Hungary, Slovenia and Spain), the use of the EQ-5D-5L instrument led to lower index values on average (0.052, 0.043, 0.078, 0.056, 0.077 and 0.068 respectively). DiscussionWe found differences in index values for the same respondent depending on whether EQ-5D-Y-3L or EQ-5D-5L was used. In 2 out of the 3 Asian countries, using EQ-5D-Y-3L led to lower index values for the same respondent, while for 5 of the European countries and Australia, the opposite was true. While the mean difference was smaller than 0.1 for all countries, overall the results suggest an effect of moderate size. This suggests that these differences in index values could lead to a substantial difference in QALYs accrued over multiple years for some value set dyads, although for 2 out of 10 value set dyads, the difference was negligible. Our sample contained more respondents with mild health problems, and further testing in more severe samples may be warranted.

Title: Adults' socio-demographic characteristics, valuation perspective, and TTO valuation of child EQ-5D-Y-3L health states: exploring the role of psychological distance
Abstract: Objective: In the valuation of EQ-5D-Y-3L health states with composite time trade-off method (cTTO), the joint impact of adult socio-demographic characteristics (parental status and sociocultural variables) and the perspective used (depicting a child as more or less distant from the adult) remains unclear. The current study aimed to fill in this gap. Methods: We recruited a sample of 108 Polish adults. First, their parental status, collectivism, conservatism, religiosity, and pro-euthanasia attitude were measured with a self-administered online survey. Then, the respondents were interviewed and completed cTTO tasks for 5 EQ-5D-Y-3L states using a self-perspective and for a hypothetical child in three perspectives: unknown, known but not own, and own. For each perspective, we measured the perceived psychological distance from the child. We used linear regression models to study the impact of perspective and adults' characteristics (1) on the psychological distance, (2) on the cTTO-elicited utility, and (3) the impact of perspective, adults' characteristics, and psychological distance on the cTTO-elicited utility. Results: Changing the perspective (from own to unknown) increased psychological distance as perceived by adults. This increase was larger in parents. Psychological distance also increased with adult collectivism. Adult conservatism was positively related to utility, especially in farther child perspectives and for a larger psychological distance. Conclusions: How the child is depicted in valuation studies should be carefully chosen, especially in samples consisting of parents. Adults’ conservatism and collectivism should be controlled in those studies.

Title: Scale and rate heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L valuation.
Abstract: Scale and Rate Heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L Valuation - This study aims to determine US EQ-5D-5L values by estimating quality-adjusted life year (QALY) scores based on individual preference evidence. Choice analyses are commonly used for this purpose, involving additional parameters like scale factors and discount rates. We investigate the impact of allowing variation in these scale and rate parameters on the estimation of US EQ-5D-5L values in our research. Comparing the Conditional Logit Estimates and True parameters under Preference Heterogeneity: A Simulated Discrete Choice Experiment - This article focuses on Health Preference Research (HPR), a subfield of health economics that aims to understand the value of health-related objects through observational or experimental methods. Specifically, the study uses a simulated Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) to investigate how interpersonal heterogeneity affects the estimation of coefficients, willingness-to-pay (WTP), and choice predictions in the context of choice probabilities described by logit functions with fixed individual-specific parameters. The simulation results indicate that when heterogeneity is ignored in health preferences, Conditional Logit (CL) estimates may be biased, leading to substantial differences in true and estimated WTP (up to 20%). However, despite this bias, the CL and true choice probabilities remain relatively similar to each other (difference less than 0.08). This suggests that CL estimates may differ from their true means under preference heterogeneity, leading to underestimation of WTP and potentially impacting the value of treatment and quality of care in health economics research. The study emphasizes the importance of recognizing and addressing preference heterogeneity in health economics studies, especially when using CL, a widely used model in practice. Comparing the Mixed Logit Estimates and True parameters under Informative and Uninformative Heterogeneity: A Simulated Discrete Choice Experiment - This study explores the impact of unobservable heterogeneity in discrete choice experiments (DCEs) on the estimation of mixed logit models. Unobservable heterogeneity refers to latent factors that influence individuals' choices but are not directly observable. These factors can be modeled using correlated (informative heterogeneity) or uncorrelated (uninformative heterogeneity) individual-specific parameters in a logit model. The researchers conducted simulations to compare the results of maximum simulated likelihood (MSL) estimation for correctly specified and mis-specified mixed logit models. The findings indicate that MSL estimates are biased and significantly deviate from the true parameters, even when the model is correctly specified. The study recommends that choice modelers conduct simulation analyses before estimating a mixed logit model to assess potential biases and identify the model specification that minimizes bias in the estimates, especially in terms of variances and correlations.

Title: A Chinese value set for the EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: The first attempts to make national value set for the EQ-5D-Y are on their way as the Exec has agreed upon proposals for Spain, the UK, the Netherlands and Germany. This valuation task arrives at a latent scale though DCE in an online sample. These value sets studies also included a methodological research question about the age dependency of EQ-5D-Y values. Age dependency was found in Spain, the UK, and Germany, but not so clear in the Netherlands. The Dutch study also assessed another methodological question of whether the relative value of life years over quality of life is related to whom the tradeoffs apply. The study found the presence of a latent variable affecting differently on the tradeoff ratios for adults and children. In the present study we developed the first comparable value set for China, and further explored the two methodological questions in China. In order to make the results compatible with the studies done in Spain, the UK, the Netherlands and Germany, we used the similar protocol, notably the Dutch and work in close cooperation with the original researchers. The Dutch study was administered using an online survey. It includes three tasks: latent scale DCE, DCE duration questions, and questions assessing preference towards different kinds of QALY compositions (e.g. 2 years in full health, or 4 years in utility of 0.5).All respondents will receive the same tasks but will be randomized into three arms for three hypothetical persons in different ages(10-years, 15-years or 40-years). Our study translated the survey into Chinese language version, and add an additonal arm (70-years) as well as localize questions (e.g. the demographic questions). The survey provided data to addressed three aims, including: 1. Derive the preliminary value set of the EQ-5D-Y for China. 2. Assess age dependency of EQ-5D-Y values 3. Explore the presence of a latent variable affecting differently on time trade-off ratios for adults and children in China

Title: ‘Decolonizing health’: Perception and development of a conceptual health framework among children and adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa and its content comparison with the EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: Purpose Most health measurement instruments are based on a conceptual framework developed either in a western culture or with adults or both. Few investigators have considered how health is perceived by children and adolescents in low-income countries (LICs) particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aimed to understand how health is thought about by children and adolescents in Malawi, develop a conceptual framework, and compare its content with that of the EQ-5D-Y. Methods Four focus group discussions (FGD) were conducted in 2019- 2020 among children and adolescents aged 8-17years from schools around Blantyre urban, Malawi. After consent/ assent from both parents and children, a semi-structured discussion in each group explored how participants understood health and what it meant to them. Each focus group was recorded and transcribed verbatim in English and thematic coding undertaken to identify concepts and sub-concepts of the conceptual framework. Results The final sample had a total of 37 participants- 21 females and 16 males (8-17 years). Qualitative analysis identified seven concepts (existence/functionality, self-care, strength/energy, peace of mind, absence of illness, God-given, and acceptance of illness). Comparison with the EQ-5D-Y showed that four of the five EQ-5D-Y dimensions were captured by the conceptual framework. The dimension of “pain or discomfort” was not covered by the new conceptual framework. Further, the new conceptual framework had five concepts that are not in the EQ-5D-Y (absence of illness, acceptance of illness, existence/functionality, strength/energy, and God-given). Conclusion A new conceptual framework of health developed among children and adolescents in Malawi has seven concepts some of which go beyond the EQ-5D-Y. The EQ-5D-Y is a valid utility instrument for use in economic evaluation, but it may not fully represent the concept of health held by children and adolescents in LICs such as Malawi.

Title: EQ-5D-5L VALUATION IN POLAND
Abstract: Objective Cost-utility analysis gain importance also in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). We aimed to develop Polish utility tariff for EQ-5D-5L health states.Methods Face-to-face, computer-assisted interviews were collected in the representative sample. Each respondent followed a standardizedprotocol to collect 10composite time trade off (cTTO) and 7discrete choice experiment (DCE) observations. In the Bayesian approach, several model specifications were compared based on model fit, the usabilityof the final value set, and how they reflect the elicitation procedure (e.g. censoring). A hybrid approach (using cTTO and DCE data) was employedin the final set, which wascomparedwith the existing ones: EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L cross-walk.ResultsData from 1252 respondents (11,480 cTTO valuations and 8764 DCE pairs) were collectedin June-October, 2016. The final model accounted for random parameters, error scaling with fattails, censoring at -1, unwillingness to trade in TTO by the religious, and Cauchy distribution in DCE. Pain/discomfort impacts the utility most: disutility equal to 0.575 when at level 5. In the value set, 4.4% of EQ-5D-5L states are worse than dead. Thenew value set has a comparable range (minimum at -0.590 compared to -0.523) and same ordering of the first three dimensions (pain/discomfort, mobility, self-care) as EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L cross-walk value sets. Moreover,it is more sensitive to mild health worsening.Conclusions The new value set guarantees consistency with past decisions in cost-utility studies,while offering betterassessment of even mild health gains. It can be an option for CEE countries lacking own value sets.

Title: Translating the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox  (Best Available, EV1.0 & Exploratory set of items, EV1.5) into Polish (for Poland)
Abstract: This study aimed to translate the 31 items of the Experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox (versions EV1.0 and EV1.5) into Polish for use in Poland, in accordance with the EuroQol Group Experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox Translation Guidelines (October 2025). An additional experimental item within the FATIGUE domain (“Persistent Fatigue”) was also translated. The resulting Polish version is intended for use in the EQ-DAPHNIE survey planned in Poland in Q1–Q2 2026 and for future methodological research involving the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox.The translation process followed the official EuroQol methodology and included two independent forward translations, two independent backward translations, Cognitive Debriefing (CD), and linguistic proofreading. Four bilingual translators fluent in English and Polish participated in the forward and backward translation stages. The translation subsequently underwent a VMC light review process.Cognitive Debriefing interviews were conducted face-to-face by a single interviewer in February and March 2026 with eight respondents recruited from the general population (4 women, 4 men; aged 20–74 years). The sample was heterogeneous with regard to age, education, and occupational background. All participants were native Polish speakers residing in Warsaw. Interviews were conducted in quiet home environments and lasted approximately three hours on average due to the extensive questionnaire burden. Respondents completed the EQ-5D-5L, both versions of the Experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox, the additional fatigue item, and the EQ VAS.The CD process identified seven linguistic issues related to the Polish translation. One inconsistency identified in the FATIGUE items was corrected in the third consensus version, while the remaining issues were resolved in consultation with a Polish language specialist. The final Polish translation demonstrated good comprehensibility and conceptual equivalence with the source version.

Title: Do EQ-5D valuations differ in palliative care settings? A discrete choice experiment
Abstract: This study investigated whether EQ-5D-5L health state valuations differ when framed within a palliative care needs context through a large-scale discrete choice experiment (DCE) conducted across Australia (n=2,082), Ireland (n=1,280), and the UK (n=2,009). The research examined how factors like limited life expectancy and available support levels influence how people value different health states. This work contributes important empirical evidence to the ongoing debate about the appropriateness of using standard value sets in palliative care decision-making and highlights the need for more nuanced approaches to health state valuation in end-of-life contexts.

Title: Exploring the content validity and acceptability of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L among children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes in Ethiopia A qualitative-study
Abstract: AbstractBackground: The EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L are widely used generic measures of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents. However, evidence on the content validity and acceptability of the instruments among adolescents with chronic conditions, particularly in low-income settings, remains limited. This study aimed to assess the acceptability and content validity of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L among adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) in Ethiopia.Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with adolescents aged 12-17 years who were diagnosed with T1DM and had visited the diabetes clinic at Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital. Purposive sampling was used to recruit a breadth of participants with variation in age and sex. Interviews were conducted using an interview guide. First, concept elicitation was used to explore adolescents’ understanding of health and the aspects of health important to them. Then, adolescents completed the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and EQ VAS, followed by cognitive interviewing to examine the comprehension, comprehensiveness, and relevance of the instruments. Interview data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis, and identified health concepts were mapped against the EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L descriptive system to assess comprehensiveness.Results: A total of 25 adolescents with a mean age of 14.6 years participated, and 13 (54.0%) of them were male. Adolescents primarily conceptualized health in terms of physical health, emotional and psychological well-being, functioning and daily activities, disease management and control, dietary management, and social functioning. Most of these concepts aligned well with the EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L dimensions. Both the Y-3L and Y-5L versions were generally perceived as easy to understand and complete, indicating good acceptability. However, some misinterpretations, including broad interpretations of the mobility and looking after myself dimensions, challenges with the recall period (“today”), and difficulty selecting precise values on the EQ VAS were noted. Several important health aspects were identified as missing from the EQ-5D-Y, including diabetes self-management, dietary management, treatment burden, and social relationships. Most participants preferred the EQ-5D-Y-5L due to its greater descriptive detail, while some favoured the EQ-5D-Y-3L for its simplicity.Conclusion: The EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L demonstrate good acceptability and capture key generic aspects of health relevant to adolescents with T1DM in Ethiopia. However, for this patient group, important diabetes-specific and social aspects of health are not captured within the EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L descriptive system. These findings support the use of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L as generic measures of HRQoL and could be beneficial to combine with disease-specific instruments in this population.

Title: A visit to APERSU in Alberta for learning and exploring research collaborations aiming to establish an EQ-5D support unit in SIngapore
Abstract: A team of EuroQol researchers from National University of Singapore including Nan Luo, as the mentor, and three PhD students including Rachel Tan, Jia Jia Lee and Meixia Liao visited Canada from to 15 to 25 Oct in 2023. The team first reached Calgary to attend the APERSU 7th end-user meeting on 16-17 Oct and then the ISOQOL 30th annual conference on 18-21 Oct. Several EuroQol studies were presented by the students in the ISOQOL conference. Afterwards, the team travelled to Edmonton to visit the APERSU office on 23-24 Oct. During the visit, the team shared their studies and discussed research collaborations with Jeff Johnson, Fatima Al Salah and the APERSU team.

Title: Unravelling the puzzle of low TTO values for establishing a trustworthy EQ-5D-5L value set for Singapore
Abstract: We used EuroQol's 'lite' valuation protocol to collect cTTO data from 500 individuals in Singapore. We used this data to estimate an EQ-5D-5L value set for Singapore. We compared the values with those collected in a previous EQ-VT study in Singapore. We also investigated the socio-demographic factors affecting the values.

Title: Startup & support cost for the UK 5L valuation study

Applying for travel scholarship to attend the 2023 ISPOR Europe Meeting: Testing the Psychometric Properties of Several EuroQol Instruments for Measuring the Impact of COVID-19 in a Large Sample of Chinese Children and their Parent Carers
Abstract: In my completed work, I attended the ISPOR Europe 2023 Conference to present my poster titled "Testing the Psychometric Properties of Several EuroQol Instruments for Measuring the Impact of COVID-19 in a Large Sample of Chinese Children and Their Parent Carers." The study evaluated the Chinese EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets and EQ-TIPS in young patients with COVID-19 and compared EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-S in parent carers, exploring the spillover effects of children's COVID-19 infection on their parents. The presentation took place during the ISPOR Europe 2023 conference in Copenhagen, Denmark, from November 12 to November 15, with the 'Poster Presentation Session' occurring on November 13. During the poster presentation, I engaged in discussions with the audience, providing additional context and insights into the study's methodology, results, and implications. The exchange of ideas with conference attendees, including healthcare professionals, researchers, and practitioners, enriched the overall experience and fostered valuable connections within the academic and research community. The presentation contributed strategic value to the EuroQol Group by extending the application of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) to assess COVID-19's impact on pediatric health. It provided insights into PROMs' effectiveness, aiding instrument selection, and promoting global relevance. The findings enhanced patient-centered research and decision-making, attracting diverse attendees interested in health outcomes assessment, PROMs, pediatrics, and the impact of COVID-19 on health. I also engaged in valuable academic activities, including connecting with the PhD Student Network, attending a relevant short course, and participating in breakout sessions to enhance my understanding of measuring HRQoL in pediatric populations facing life-limiting conditions.

Title: Population health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic (POPCORN): longitudinal effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on individual's health-related quality of life
Abstract: Background: In 2020-2021, several countries faced another peak of COVID-19 infections, with renewed restrictive policies, continued disruption of daily life, social isolation, economic uncertainties and discontinuation of usual health care. The POPulation health impact of the CORoNavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (POPCORN) study was set up to investigate the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on health-related quality of life (HRQL) and to study the role of determinants of health. This abstracts pertains to the second wave part of the POPCORN-study, with multiple measurements in the same groups of persons. Methods: We administered a web-based survey repeatedly to participants from Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Sweden and the United States. Primary outcome measures were HRQoL (measured by EQ-5D-5L) and mental well-being (measured by WHO-5). Linear regression analyses were performed to estimate the impact of determinants on HRQoL and well-being. In total, 8,097 respondents completed the questionnaire at T1 (April-May 2020) and T2 (May-June 2021). Results: For all countries combined, 33% showed improved HRQoL at T2, whereas 31% deteriorated. In terms of mental well-being, 44% improved and 41% deteriorated. The effect of negative life events on HRQoL and mental well-being was larger than the effect of positive life events. Approximately one in five respondents reported insufficient healthcare access. Respondents with chronic disease, those aged 18–34 and 35–54 years old and respondents from Greece and the UK reported insufficient healthcare access more often compared to their counterparts. Respondents with insufficient healthcare access had both more improved and deteriorated HRQoL compared to respondents with sufficient healthcare, whose HRQoL remained unchanged. We did not find significant interactions between age, gender, socio-economic status (SES) and/or chronic disease status with healthcare access at onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Title: ISOQOL Annual Conference, Calgary, October 18 - 21; Symposium 7: Measuring and valuing health in children using EuroQol instruments – Challenges and Opportunities
Abstract: ISOQOL Annual Conference is the leading conference in the world in the area of Quality of Life and PROMs/PREMs. This group of EuroQol researchers (Arto Ohinmaa, Nancy Devlin, Mickael Herdman, Feng Xie and Deborah Marshall) got a symposium accepted to ISOQOL Calgary conference between October 18 and 21. The symposium title was "Measuring and valuing health in children using EuroQol instruments – Challenges and Opportunities" and it was based on EQ-5D-Y related research projects and their findings. It was also designed to provide educational material and opportunities for the audience to ask questions related to measurement and valuation related issues in pediatric HRQOL measurement. The presentation was on Saturday 21st October at 8.30 am (75 min). The structure of the symposium was: - Introduction of the symposium by Arto Ohinmaa (moderator of the symposium) - Measuring health in younger populations: EQ-5D-Y and beyond; Michael Herdman, MSc, Insight Consulting & Research, Mataró, Spain - Methods for valuing child HRQoL: value sets for EQ-5D-Y-3L and related methods challenges; Nancy Devlin, BA(Hons) PhD, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia - Validating the EQ-5D-Y-5L in childhood arthritis: the UCAN precision health study; Deborah Marshall, PhD, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada - Entering the child’s mind: qualitative and quantitative evidence in valuing youth health in Canada; Feng Xie, PhD, McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada The symposium speakers provided the current state of play in measuring and valuing health using EuroQol instruments, discussed key challenges and opportunities in advancing the measurement and valuation of health and validation of these instruments in children across a range of diseases, and shared examples from large projects being conducted around the world. All presentations were about 12 to 15 min long followed by a short questioning period. In the end we had a questioning period where audience made several interesting questions related to pediatric HRQOL measurement and valuation. Many of these questions were related to EQ-5D-Y instruments and their valuation issues.

Title: Two small DCE projects
Abstract: Background:Although much progress has been made on identification efficiency in the design of discrete choice experiments (DCE; e.g., D-efficiency), less is known about allocation efficiency, such as number of pairs and number of responses per pair. The aim of this project was to investigate the effectof number of pairs and pair-specific sample sample size on the variability in DCE results(i.e., standard deviation and error). Methods: We examined data from three DCEvaluation studies for the EQ-5D-5Lfrom the Netherlands: two of the studies used face-to-face interviews and onewas an online self-completed survey.This analysis was conducted in three steps:First, we conducted a series of analyses to create a “base case” specificationto act as the primary comparator forsimulationson variability. In these analyses, we applied2 cumulutative density function (CDF) specifications(sigmoidal[logit]and ratio-based[Bradley-Terry]) and 3 estimation techniques (Weighted least squares (WLS) using the observed choice probabilities, WLS using the predicted choice probabilities and Maximum Likelihood). Theresulting base case included 186 pairs with a mean of 183 observations per pair, weighted according to mode of administration(30% face-to-face; 70% online)and specifieda 20-parameter main effects logitCDF estimated by maximum likelihood. Second, we simulated 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 responsesper pairfor 186 pairs and estimated the base-case model. For each of the 1000 bootstrap iterations, we compared the results to the base caseusing three criteria: median coefficient standard error, the number of rejected predictions, and chi square of predictions. Third, weran aBayesian efficient design algorithm that takeslevel balance into account to generate design sizes of 25, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100 and 150 pairs drawn from the 186 pair design of the base case.We simulated 30, 50 and 70 responsesper pair for each design sizes:25, 50, 100 and 150 pairs(similar to the second step). Results:Among the findingsfrom this brief study, three results areparticularly noteworthy for the EuroQol Group: (1) future attempts tomanuallyenterpairs should take scale into account(i.e., adding the 10 mild pairs to the EQ-VT DCE may have created a bias in logit estimates); (2)the concept of the “pragmatic p” may serve as the basis for determining number of responses per pair and range of pair probabilities in future studies; and (3) Infuture EQ-VT studies, the number of responses per pair should increase (>50) and the number of pairs should decrease (~150).

Title: Translation of the EQ-HWB-9 EMV2.1 and seven EQ-5D bolt-on items (fatigue, cognition and sleep) from EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox into Standard Arabic Language
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol Health and Wellbeing instrument (EQ-HWB) and EQ-5D Bolt-ons Toolbox represent recent developments within the EuroQol instrument family, designed to capture broader aspects of health and wellbeing. Although EQ-5D instruments have been widely translated, validated, and used in Arabic-speaking populations, the EQ-HWB-9 and generic bolt-on items for sleep, cognition, and fatigue were not yet available in Standard Arabic for Egypt. Given the large Arabic-speaking population and the growing use of EuroQol instruments across the Middle East and North Africa region, producing culturally appropriate Arabic versions is important for future validation, population health measurement, and health outcomes research.Aim: This project aimed to translate and culturally adapt the EQ-HWB-9 EMV2.1, two versions of the EQ-HWB VAS, and seven bolt-on items from the EQ-5D Bolt-ons Toolbox Sleep (items 1 and 2), Fatigue (items 2 and 5), and Cognition (items 1, 3, and 4).Methods: The project followed EuroQol translation guidance for the EQ-HWB and EQ-5D Bolt-ons Toolbox. Two independent forward translations were produced, reconciled into a consensus Arabic version, back-translated into English, and reviewed by the research team to ensure conceptual equivalence and consistency with existing Arabic EuroQol terminology. Cognitive debriefing interviews were conducted with two groups of eight native Arabic-speaking adults: one group tested the EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-HWB VAS versions, and the other tested the seven bolt-on items. Participants represented variation in age, sex, education, socioeconomic background, and health status. Interviews explored clarity, interpretation, preferred wording, and the effect of the VAS preamble and 7-days recall period.Results: The Arabic EQ-HWB-9 iwas generally well understood and culturally appropriate, requiring. Key challenges were identified around the Arabic interpretation of “wellbeing,” the instruction sentence, frequency descriptors, “feel exhausted” item and  “lack of control” item. The EQ-HWB VAS without preamble was understood by respondents, although many performed only one of the two required tasks. Preferences for the VAS with versus without preamble were split, and the 7-day recall period was preferred by most respondents. The seven bolt-on items were also generally clear and acceptable. Cognition items were well understood, although some conceptual overlap was observed between memory and concentration. The tiredness item was more culturally challenging because the Arabic term may also refer broadly to illness, pain, or being unwell, whereas the fatigue 2 item preserved the intended meaning more clearly. Both sleep items were well understood, with equal preference for the version including explanatory wording.Conclusion: This project produced Standard Arabic for Egypt versions of the EQ-HWB-9 EMV2.1, EQ-HWB VAS with and without preamble, and seven bolt-on items. The translated versions provide a foundation for future psychometric validation, EQ-DAPHNIE-related work, and clinical research.

Title: Validity and Responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-5L Instruments in the Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Abstract: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common type of arthritis among children and youth. It can cause pain and permanent physical damage to joints, which affects mobility, pain, and daily activities. Current effective treatment methods have improved the health status and health-related quality of life of many JIA patients so that during remission they may not have any severe symptoms and thus their HRQOL during that period may be relatively good. The 3-level self-report version of EQ-5D-Y has been validated in JIA, but the validity and responsiveness of the 5-level version remains under investigation. In Arthritis Society of Canada funded work, our team has studied the validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-5L parent-proxy instrument. In this proposal, we aim to build upon this previous work and examine the psychometric properties (validity and responsiveness) of the EQ-5D-Y-5L self-report versions among children with JIA and compare the results to parent-proxy version using both matched and unmatched datasets. Both validity and responsiveness results from the child-report will be compared to parent-proxy analysis results to identify potential differences between the results and if they are correlated to any of the background variables.  The results of the analysis will address a gap in the literature in terms of validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-5L self-report version in a population with a range of health states including relatively severe health states, and using a longitudinal dataset with detailed clinical, physician reported and condition specific measures.

Title: REDCap Evaluation: Instrument Construction
Abstract: On 5 October 2016, Benjamin M. Craigand Juan Manuel Ramos Goñiconducted a brief evaluation of REDCap (1-week trial license) for discrete choice experiments (DCEs).Based on its findings, Arnd Jan Prause led a team to install REDCap on a virtual Unix server licensed by the EuroQol Research Foundation (https://mq-rc.codedose.com/). Installation was completed on 28 November 2016.The aim of thisfast-track proposal is to extend the evaluation by constructing two survey instruments for EQ-5D-5L valuation using DCEs (United States and Germany). This entails three steps: (1) the construction of the data dictionaries and randomization lists in English; (2) the translation of these files into German; and (3) the installation these files into REDCap. Each instrument will have three components: screener (consent, demographics), health (EQ-5D-5L and EQ VAS), and DCE (28 paired comparisons; two sets of 14 pairs).If this project is successful, we will further extend this evaluation and propose that (1) the instruments be fielded using online samples of 350 U.S. and 350 German respondents to collect 50 responses for each of the 196EQ-VT pairs (50 × 196/28 = 350); (2) that hyperlinks to the instruments be placed on the EuroQol website to aid in dissemination and feedback; (3) that an abstract on REDCap valuation be submitted to the Plenary meeting; and (4) that we visit Vanderbilt Universityto demonstrate the instrumentsand to solicit their counsel on the design. The longer term objective is to provide an alternative platform for future valuation research.

Title: The uniqueness and overlap of the EQ-HWB and the EQ-5D-5L in four diseases, healthy subjects, and caregivers
Abstract: Through comparison of the EQ-HWB with the EQ-5D-5L in the Chinese population in healthy subjects, patients, and healthy caregivers, we explored the overlap and uniqueness of the preliminary version of the EQ-HWB. In this research, we explored the distribution, convergent and divergent validity, known group validity, and exploratory factor analysis. Our research found that the EQ-HWB could measure health-related quality of life as the EQ-5D-5L. But it was more sensitive in measure mental disease burden than the EQ-5D-5L. Also, the EQ-HWB possessed the capability for discriminating the caregiving burden, which achieved the aim of the EQ-HWB. In general, the EQ-HWB has the ability for measuring the intervention outcomes across heath care, social care, and public health.

Title: A head on comparison of EQ-VT and crosswalk based EQ-5D-5L value sets.
Abstract: This study found poor agreement among existing crosswalk and EQ-VT value sets. Our findings suggest that these should not be used interchangeably, except under circumstances where it is not possible or feasible to conduct a direct EQ-5D-5L valuation study- for example countries with populations of less than 250,000.

Title: Valuing EQ-5D-5L and Cognition bolt-on attributes using DCE with Kaizen tasks (VECK): a feasbility study
Abstract: **BACKGROUND** Each bolt-on item (and its response options) may be transformed into an attribute and appended to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system for a health valuation study. Although many have shown that it is technically feasible to produce de novo value sets for bolt-on attributes, this approach seems impractical given the possible number of bolt-ons. At present, the EuroQol Group lacks a valuation method for bolt-ons that does not rely on potentially invalid assumptions (e.g., scale-factor model). **AIMS:** The primary aim of this study is to assess the feasibility of DCE with kaizen tasks for bolt-on valuation. Furthermore, this feasibility study addresses two questions in bolt-on valuation: (1) Whether a bolt-on attribute is more or less important than the core dimensions (i.e., importance)? (2) Does a bolt-on attribute overlap with the other core dimensions or attenuate their importances (i.e., shrinkage)? More specifically, the proposed study examined two descriptive systems with cognition bolt-ons: (5D+1) an EQ-5D-5L system with a single composite bolt-on attribute: Memory/Concentration: (no, slight, moderate, severe, extreme) problems remembering things or concentrating. (5D+2) an EQ-5D-5L system with two component bolt-on attributes: Memory: (no, slight, moderate, severe, extreme) problems remembering things. Concentration: (no, slight, moderate, severe, extreme) problems concentrating. These bolt-ons were selected largely for pragmatic reasons. The levels are on a severity scale as recommended by Mulhern et al. 2022 and their descriptors were adapted from Sampson et al. 2020. METHODS: Following a published protocol, we conduct six surveys (N=1268), each with 2 discrete choice experiments (DCE) back-to-back. The DCEs differed by their attributes: EQ-5D-5L only, EQ-5D-5L with 1 bolt-on (Memory/Concentration), EQ-5D-5L with 2 bolt-ons (Memory, Concentration). For each DCE, we estimated US values on a quality-adjusted life year (QALY) scale for 10-year episodes by maximum likelihood using conditional logit models and compared them with prior US value sets. In response to the US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, we also produced EQ-5D-5L values on an experience scale.

Title: Assessment and comparison of the feasibility and measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L self-complete versions in the Tigrinya language
Abstract: Objectives: The objectives of this study are to assess and compare the feasibility, distributional characteristics, discriminatory power, and measurement properties of the Tigrinya versions of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in healthy children and children with a range of health conditions.Methods:The EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L were adapted into Tigrinya (a semitic language spoken by approximately 9 million native speakers, primarily in Ethiopia and Eritrea) following the EuroQol Version Management Committee guidelines. The feasibility, distributional properties, discriminatory power, and known groups’ validity, and children’s preferences for Y-3L and Y-5L were tested in samples of acute and chronic patients, and a general population sample. Test-retest reliability and responsiveness were assessed in a sub-group of the initial sample who reported unchanged health status and changed health status) after 10 days and one month, respectively, using a one-item global rating (GRS) scale to assess change in health status. Test–retest reliability was assessed using Gwet’s agreement coefficient (Gwet’s AC) and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Kruskal-Wallis rank test was used to examine known-group validity and responsiveness was evaluated using standardized effect-size (SES).Results: A total of 480 participants were included in the study. The mean (SD) age was 13.20 (3.05) years. Most of participants reported no problems, with the highest ceiling observed in the SC/LAM and Mob dimensions. The A/D/WSU and P/D dimensions showed the highest proportion of reported problems compared to other dimensions. EQ-5D-Y-3L consistently showed higher ceiling effects than the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D- 5L across all dimensions. highest inconsistencies were showed in the P/D and A/D dimensions, indicating challenges in cross-walking across severity levels. In the testing of known groups’ validity, all versions of EQ-5D (Y-3L, Y-5L, 5L) were able to differentiate between children with and without health conditions and within rheumatic heart disease and acute limb fracture groups according to NYHA class and type of assistive device (p<0.001). EQ-5D-Y-5L demonstrated higher discriminative power than the EQ-5D-Y-3L, with ΔH′ values ranging from 0.28 (Mob) to 0.36 (P/D) and Evenness values (J′) were generally similar across instruments. Healthy children and those with T1DM generally showed high test-retest reliability (0.83 and 0.96) and the LSS demonstrated excellent reliability across all versions (0.85–0.89). In patients reporting improvement on the GRS (n=86), significant reductions in LSS were observed across all measures, with large effect sizes (SRM = -1.48 for Y-3L, -1.88 for Y-5L, and -1.69 for 5L). Among the worsened group (n = 19), all three instruments captured significant increases in LSS with moderate-to-large effect sizes (SRM = 0.70–0.79). When asked about their preferences for the two Y versions, 53% said they preferred EQ-5D-Y-3L, while 46% preferred EQ-5D-Y-5L.Conclusion:This is the first study to explore the psychometric properties of the Tigrinya versions of the Y-3L and Y-5L in acute and chronic patient populations in an Ethiopian setting. These are also the first generic preference-weighted measures available for use in younger populations in this setting. Both versions of EQ-5D-Y showed generally satisfactory psychometric properties in this study suggesting they are suitable for use in this context, though further research in other patient populations would be warranted.

Title: Exploring differential item functioning in EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB, and PROMIS-10 using EQ-DAPHNIE data
Abstract: Background: International health surveys such as EQ-DAPHNIE (The EuroQol Data Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation) support cross-country comparisons of population health. For such comparisons to be valid, participants across countries should interpret health status measures consistently. However, the validity of such cross-country comparisons may be threatened by heterogeneity in how patients with the same underlying health status interpret and respond to questions about their health and quality of life, a phenomenon also known as differential item functioning (DIF). The presence of differential item functioning (DIF): individuals with the same underlying health respond differently by country, will compromise the comparability. The EQ-DAPHNIE dataset provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the differential item functioning across multiple health status measures and across countries and languages. Our pilot work using this dataset identified moderate to large country-related DIF in several EQ-5D-5L dimensions, primarily mobility, self-care, and usual activities, and particularly across non-English-speaking countries. However, these analyses focused solely on the EQ-5D-5L, and they did not address population composition differences across countries with respect to confounding factors such as age and sex.Aims: This project seeks to build on our pilot work by:Assessing the presence and magnitude of country-related DIF in EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB-9 and PROMIS-10 across multiple countries using the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset;Comparing the magnitude of country-related DIF with other sources of DIF (e.g., age, sex) to contextualize the relative impact of country-level differences; andSide-by-side evaluating country-related DIF across EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB-9, and PROMIS-10, providing insights on which instrument has more cross-country measurement invarianceMethods: This study will use advanced psychometric methods on the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset to evaluate DIF in EQ-HWB-9, PROMIS-10, and EQ-5D-5L items. Specifically, ordinal logistic regression analysis framework, and modern item response theory (IRT) modelling framework will be used to evaluate DIF on these measures. We will first estimate DIF for EQ-HWB-9 and PROMIS-10, and then compare their DIF patterns with EQ-5D-5L to identify which instrument shows the most measurement invariance. To contextualize country-related DIF, additional analyses will compare its magnitude with DIF associated with factors such as age and sex. Analyses will be conducted both on the original dataset and on matched subsamples (e.g., generated using propensity-score matching) to improve comparability and reduce confounding from sociodemographic and health-utilization factors. Benefit of the research: This project directly addresses Populations and Health Systems Working Group Priority #3 by systematically investigating response-scale heterogeneity across multiple EQ instruments. It will provide a reproducible framework for analyzing DIF to support capacity building, ultimately strengthening the use of EuroQol instruments in population health assessment.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems, EQ-HWB

Title: Responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L self and proxy ratings in dementia diseases (ReDem)
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D-5L has been criticized for limited responsiveness in detecting health changes in people living with dementia (PlwD). This study assessed its responsiveness compared to the disease-specific Quality of Life in Alzheimer's Disease (QoL-AD) scale using longitudinal data from a cluster-randomized controlled intervention trial.Methods: Data were derived from the German InDePendent trial, which evaluated a model of collaborative care. Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) was measured at baseline and at the six-month follow-up using the EQ-5D-5L, EQ Visual Analogue Scale (EQ VAS), and QoL-AD, through both self-reports and proxy reports. Responsiveness was analyzed using effect sizes (Cohen's d), which were anchored to intervention effects and changes in cognitive status, depressive symptoms, and care needs, and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.Results: PlwD [mean age: 80.6] were predominantly female (56%) and mildly to moderately cognitively impaired (89%). Self-reported HRQoL scores were consistently higher than those reported by proxies. The intervention group showed modest but significant improvements in the EQ-5D-5L (d = 0.206) and EQ VAS (d = 0.160), but not in the QoL-AD (d = xx). In subgroups with cognitive improvement or reduced care needs, the EQ-5D-5L (d = 0.268) and EQ VAS (d = 0.415) also outperformed the QoL-AD (d = XX). For those with reduced depressive symptoms, all instruments were responsive, with the QoL-AD showing the strongest effect (d = 0.314). Responsiveness of proxy-reported changes was generally smaller.Conclusion: The EQ-5D-5L, as a generic measure of HRQoL, demonstrated sufficient responsiveness in dementia, particularly among patients receiving the collaborative care intervention and those experiencing cognitive or emotional improvement over 6 months. The EQ-5D-5L's simplicity and acceptability suggest practical utility in dementia research. In contrast, proxy ratings were less sensitive to change, possibly due to contextual factors, and, therefore, should be used with caution.

Title: EQ-5D as an add-on generic measure in psoriasis, when excellent disease-specific measures are present: its psychometrical and clinical value in a representative Swedish cohort
Abstract: **Background** Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory disorder affecting the skin and other organs. As a systemic disease, psoriasis can have a severe negative impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI; clinical) and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI; patient-reported) are widely used instruments for measuring psoriasis severity. However, these methods may be insensitive to the generic impact of psoriasis on HRQoL. We tested whether the generic instrument EQ-5D provides evidence on addressing this limitation. **Objective** To determine whether the generic EQ-5D-3L (mobility (MO), self-care (SC), usual activities (UA), pain/discomfort (PD) and anxiety depression (AD) covers additional information in psoriasis patients compared to disease-specific instruments (PASI and DLQI). **Method** The Swedish National Quality Register for Systemic Treatment of Psoriasis (PsoReg) is a national register for systemic treatment (synthetic or biological systemic drugs) of moderate to severe psoriasis. All patients included between 2006 and 2022 were incorporated in the present study. Spearman rank correlations (summary scores, domains/items) and exploratory factor analysis methods were used to assess to what extent the PASI, DLQI and EQ-5D-3L measure the same, or different, constructs and which components of the EQ-5D, if any, provide additional information. **Results** In total, 16 887 patients were identified at baseline. Cross-sectionally, a moderate association was found between the PASI score and the DLQI summary score (rank correlation 0.51). The DLQI summary score was moderately correlated with the EQ LSS (0.55) and the EQ index (-0.58). The association between the PASI and the EQ LSS was moderate (0.26) as was between the PASI and the EQ index (-0.26). At the domain level association of the EQ-5D with the DLQI domains was stronger (range 0.13-0.46) as with the PASI domains (0.01-0.17). By applying factor analysis to the pooled items of the PASI, DLQI, and EQ-5D, a six-factor solution was found to be the best and most parsimonious. All DLQI items plus the AD domain of the EQ-5D were represented by the strongest factor (factor I), with high inter-item correlations. The remaining four EQ-5D items (MO, SC, UA, PD) together represented the second factor (factor II). The PASI items were grouped into the four different factors (factor III-VI) according to body location (arms, legs, head, and trunk), with no overlap with the EQ-5D or DLQI. EFA were also performed for the split data, according to the severity of PASI score (mild, moderate, severe), and loading pattern was similar to the entire sample results. Additionally, we included age, sex, BMI, alcohol and tobacco consumption, and psoriasis-arthropathy in the model, the loadings of the DLQI, PASI and EQ-5D items were similar to what was observed in the previous models. Age, sex and lifestyle variables loaded weakly mainly onto factors I and II, except that smoking also loaded on factor III (PASI items related to induration and scaling at the leg and arms area). The items related to psoriasis-arthropathy were loaded moderately onto factor II. **Conclusion** This study shows that the PASI, DLQI and EQ-5D-3L cover different constructs: the PASI describes skin lesions, the DLQI describes experienced disturbance in general (despite the specific items), and the EQ-5D describes the impact on five HRQoL domains, of which mood (EQ-5D-AD) coincides with the DLQI. The three instruments provide largely different, yet valuable information about patients with psoriasis: the DLQI proves that personal disturbance goes beyond skin extension, while the EQ-5D shows that psoriasis impacts multiple domains of HRQoL beyond this disturbance. Therefore, the three instruments should be employed as complementary measures. Our study confirms the need to combine a generic instrument with a condition-specific instrument for measuring HRQoL.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Methodological improvements in health-state valuations using discrete choice experiments.
Abstract: The proposed project aims to strengthen the cooperation and share knowledge between the EuroQol Group on the one hand and the Erasmus Choice Modelling Centre (in terms of methodological expertise) and the Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management (in terms of experience with the valuation of large instruments using stand-alone discrete choice experiments) on the other. As such, the proposed plan is strongly methods-oriented and aims to improve existing and introduce new methods while also focusing on making state-of-the-art discrete choice experiment methods more easily accessible.

Title: Applying Large Language Models to Identify EQ-5D Bolt-ons Based on Patient Text Data
Abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising applications in healthcare, yet little is known about their potential to improve the measurement of patient-reported outcomes, which are central to inform decision making across health system levels. We explored the feasibility of utilizing LLMs to develop or extend patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) using information from patient-reported free-text data. Methods: The GPT-4o model was used to analyze data from 1,977 members of the Dutch Celiac Association who completed the EQ-5D-5L and narratively described the impact of celiac disease (CD) on their lives. Prompts to the LLM were designed to identify possible additional dimensions (i.e., ‘bolt-on’ dimensions) to the EQ-5D-5L, and to produce preliminary bolt-on item wordings for selected dimensions. Evaluation of the approach comprised: comparisons of dimensions identified with two alternative approaches (i.e., qualitative analysis, and topic modelling); text-entry level agreement (i.e., Cohen’s Kappa) between LLM and qualitatively identified dimensions; suitability of LLM-generated bolt-on wordings assessed against existing criteria using Likert scales; and a critical appraisal of the approach consisting of face validity assessments and a SWOT analysis. Results: The LLM identified 12 potential bolt-on dimensions to the EQ-5D-5L, of which 9 were also identified using qualitative analysis, and 5 using topic modelling. Text-entry level agreement between the LLM and qualitative approaches was ‘substantial’ or ‘almost perfect’, with two exceptions of poor/fair agreement (median Kappa=0.70, IQR=0.44-0.89). The LLM-generated potential bolt-on wordings for the 4 most common dimensions (i.e., ‘Dietary restrictions’, ‘Fatigue’, ‘Social participation’, and ‘Gastrointestinal symptoms’) scored 4/5, 4.4/5, 4.3/5, and 4.2/5 respectively when assessed against the existing criteria (Mulhern et al. 2022).  Conclusions and Relevance: This study demonstrates the promising potential of LLMs to inform the development or modification of PROMs based on patient-reported text data. A limitation to generalizability and reliability is the approach’s dependency on prompt quality. Further research should assess the approach’s transferability across disease areas and different data sources (e.g. social media, electronic health records).

Title: Comparison of the Afaan-Oromo language version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L performance among children and adolescents in Ethiopia
Abstract: Introduction: EQ-5D-Y is one of the commonly used generic health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures. As has been done before, cultural adaptation and testing the psychometric properties of the instruments have crucial implications for measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL) outcomes, resource allocation, and the planning of healthcare interventions in child and youth populations in Ethiopia. This study aimed to assess and compare the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L among school children and adolescents, as well as those with a range of health conditions. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted to collect data among children and adolescents aged 8-15 years. Data were collected from mainstream schools and government hospitals in Addis Ababa. All the participants self-completed the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and the self-rated health question. Both instruments were compared for their feasibility, ceiling effect, redistribution, informativity, test-retest reliability, and known groups’ validity. Cohen’s Kappa agreement and ICC were used to assess the test-retest reliability and ANOVA with post hoc Tukey test was used to confirm the known-group validity of the instruments by comparing groups with prior expected differences. Data was analyzed using IBM SPSS statistics 26, where a p-value of <0.05 was considered significant. Results: A total of 473 children and adolescents (comprising those with diagnoses of CHF, asthma, acute leukemia, and also school children and adolescents) with a mean (SD) age of 14.62 (1.89) years completed both instruments. There were a few missing values of 3.8% for Y-3L and 4.2% for Y-5L, suggesting comparable feasibility. The ceiling effect was reduced from 52% for Y-3L to 45.8% for Y-5L (by 12.0% in general). The proportion of inconsistencies was relatively low (4.4%-7.0%) across dimensions moving from Y-3L to Y-5L, and redistribution was cross-checked for all 35 3L-5L-level combinations. Regarding informativity, the Y-5L demonstrated more discriminatory power, indicated by having a higher Shannon diversity index in all domains of the Y-5L compared with the Y-3L. Both Y-3L and Y-5L showed moderate to substantial agreement on test-retest reliability across dimensions, EQ-VAS, and LSS scores. The known-group validity was confirmed for both the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L i.e., both instruments seemed to do well at detecting differences between healthy (school) children/adolescents and patients with disease conditions (p<0.05). Conclusion: The Afaan-Oromo language version of the Y-5L appears to improve the measurement properties; reducing the ceiling effect, improving discriminatory power, and achieving higher test-retest reliability agreement compared to the Y-3L. Both instruments had similar feasibility and confirmed known-group validity.

Title: Revisiting EQ-5D-3L tariffs – An international collaboration between Slovenia end Portugal
Abstract: Introduction: The two primary objectives were (a) to develop first logically consistent TTO based EQ-5D-3L value sets for Slovenia and (b) to revisit earlier developed VAS-based EQ-5D-3L value sets. Methods: Between September 2005 and April 2006, face-to-face interviews with 225 individuals in Slovenia were conducted. Protocols from the Measurement and Value of Health study were followed closely. Each respondent valued 15 health states out of a total of 23. Model selection was informed by the criteria monotonicity/logical consistency. Predictive accuracy was assessed in terms of the mean square difference between out-of-sample predictions and corresponding observed means, as well as Lin’s Concordance Correlation Coefficient. Results: Modelling was based on 2,717 VAS and 2,831 TTO values elicited from 225 respondents. A 6-parameter a constrained regression model with a supplementary power term was selected for VAS and TTO value sets, as it produces monotonic values, and proved superior in terms of out-of-sample predictive accuracy over the tested alternatives. Conclusion: This is the first EQ-5D-3L TTO-based value set in Slovenia and the second in Central and Eastern Europe (besides Poland). It is also the first monotonic and logically consistent VAS value set in Central and Eastern Europe. Comparisons with Polish and UK TTO values show considerable differences, mostly due to mobility with having a substantially greater weight in Slovenia. The UK value set generally produces lower values and the Polish value set higher values for mild states.

Title: Assessment of psychometric properties of EQ-HWB and Comparative Analysis with EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT, and QOL-ACC in the Australian context.
Abstract: Objective: Evidence regarding the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB including its reliability, dimensionality, and structural validity and its associations with other quality of life (QoL) instruments is emerging. However, a comprehensive evaluation of its measurement properties is required to establish robust evidence of its reliability and validity. This study aimed to use existing data to assess the measurement properties of the EQ-HWB in comparison with both EuroQol and non-EuroQol instruments. Specifically, the study examined the validity, reliability and measurement relationships between EuroQol instruments (the EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L) and non-EuroQol measures of quality of life (Adult Social care Outcomes Toolkit (ASCOT) and Quality of Life- Aged Care Consumers (QOL-ACC). In addition, the study investigated the underlying dimensionality of the EQ-HWB using factor analysis.Methods: A secondary analysis of existing longitudinal data collected in 2023 was conducted to evaluate the psychometric performance of four QoL instruments in a general Australian population: the EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT, and QOL-ACC. Descriptive analyses were undertaken to examine response distributions and the presence of ceiling effects for the EQ-HWB, with comparisons made across instruments. Convergent validity were assessed by examining correlations between EQ-HWB items and conceptually related and unrelated items from the EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT, and QOL-ACC. Known-groups validity was evaluated by testing the ability of the EQ-HWB to discriminate between predefined subgroups. Test–retest reliability of the EQ-HWB was assessed. The measurement performance of the 25-item and 9-item versions of the EQ-HWB was compared using regression models. Finally, the dimensionality of the EQ-HWB was explored using exploratory factor analysis.Results: A total of 1,505 participants completed the survey, of whom 453 respondents aged ≥65 years completed all four instruments, as QOL-ACC was administered only to this age group. In this subsample, mean index scores were comparable across instruments (EQ-5D-5L: 0.88; EQ-HWB: 0.82; ASCOT: 0.88; QOL-ACC: 0.81). In the overall general population sample, a ceiling effect was observed for the EQ-5D-5L (23.3%). At the item level, the strongest correlations were observed between conceptually aligned EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB items, particularly pain (ρ = 0.77–0.78) and mobility (ρ = 0.66). ASCOT dignity items showed weakest correlations with EQ-HWB items (ρ = 0.03–0.20). Known-groups validity analyses were statistically significant across instruments, with the EQ-HWB demonstrating stronger discriminatory ability. Test–retest reliability for EQ-HWB was comparable to EQ-5D-5L (ICC 0.79 vs 0.73), and higher than ASCOT (ICC=0.64). Comparative regression analyses using backward stepwise linear regression showed that the EQ-HWB-25 explained a greater proportion of variance in external index scores than the EQ-HWB-9 (EQ-5D-5L: Adj R²=0.70 vs 0.65; ASCOT: 0.56 vs 0.48; QOL-ACC: 0.72 vs 0.58).Exploratory factor analyses were conducted separately for the EQ-HWB-25 and for each instrument (EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT, and QOL-ACC), with all analyses yielding a four-factor structure. EFA of pooled items across all instruments indicated that a five-factor structure provided a better model fit. The five factors identified were emotional functioning, self-care and usual activities, leisure and enjoyment, cognition and senses, and pain. EFA of pooled EQ-HWB-9 items with the other three instruments identified a four-factor structure. All items loaded on at least one factor, except for the ASCOT “food and drink” item, which did not load on any factor. The four factors were conceptually interpretable and reflected domains of pain, emotional functioning, physical functioning and independence, and social roles and engagement.For the general population sample (n = 1,505), EFA was conducted using three instruments (EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, and ASCOT), as QOL-ACC was administered only to participants aged 65 years and over. The analysis identified a five-factor structure, with all ASCOT items loading on a single factor except for the ‘dignity’ item, which did not load on any factor. The first factor comprised items related to emotional functioning, while a second factor was dominated by ASCOT items and was interpreted as reflecting social care related quality of life. Items from the EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-5L relating to activities and functioning loaded on a third factor, items capturing pain and discomfort loaded on a fourth factor, and positively worded items loaded on a separate factor representing positive wellbeing.Conclusion The EQ-HWB demonstrated robust psychometric performance in an Australian population, showing moderate reliability, strong convergent validity with the EQ-5D-5L, and meaningful discrimination between known groups. The 25-item version consistently explained more variance in external QoL measures than the 9-item version. Factor analyses indicated interpretable multidimensional structures for both versions, with the EQ-HWB capturing domains of pain, emotional functioning, physical functioning and independence, and social roles and engagement.
