These findings support the EQ-HWB as a valid and reliable measure of broad QoL in Australian adult population.The results of this study will inform the EQ-HWB Working Group by providing evidence on the measurement properties of the EQ-HWB instruments, particularly in the Australian populations.

Title: An EQ-5D-5L value set for the Swedish population
Abstract: The aim of this proposal is to develop a Swedish value set for EQSD-SL. We will do it by using standard data collection methods developed by the EuroQol group. Participants will be recruited in four regions in north, south and central of Sweden. Rural and urban participants will be included. 20% will be over 65 years and 80% in working age. Age, gender and rural/urban will reflect the Swedish population. The 800 informants will answer cTTO- and DCE-questions in face-to-face interviews. PI will conduct first 50 interviews before the training of interviewers. Training of 12 interviewers will be conducted according to EuroQol procedures. The analysis will have the possibility to use both TTO and DCE data (hybrid model)

Title: Estimating the EQ-5D-5L Value Set for the Philippines
Abstract: The Philippine National Formulary Executive Committee, a body tasked to selecting which medicines can be bought by the Philippine government, has been conducting health technology assessments. In the past, the group uses DALYs or QALYs weighted using Thai value sets. The group would like to standardize assessments and utilize QALYs weighted using the Philippine value set. The goal of this research is to generate the Philippine EQ-5D-5Lvalue set. The value set will be estimated using the standard methodology using the EQ-VT software translated to appropriate local languages. A purposive sample of 1,720 Filipino adults will be recruited to valuate 86 health states using TTO and 196 health state pairs using DCE. Previous modelling approaches as well as the hybrid approach will be explored to generate the valuation model. An exploratory study to assess equivalence of the translated software will be also done through a survey of bilingual speakers who will valuate the same set using two different languages.

Title: Valuation of the EQ-5D-Y-3L in Poland
Abstract: Background: Measures of health-related quality of life require country-specific value sets to inform cost-utility analyses. Although Polish value sets exist for adult EQ-5D instruments, no value set is available for the EQ-5D-Y-3L.Aim: To estimate the Polish EQ-5D-Y-3L value set and examine methodological issues related to composite time trade-off (cTTO) valuation.Methods: Preferences were elicited from adults in Poland considering EQ-5D-Y-3L health states for a hypothetical 10-year-old child. Standard cTTO interviews were conducted with 204 respondents, and DCE survey data were collected from 1,185 respondents. An additional experimental cTTO arm tested a modified procedure omitting the comparison with immediate death. The final value set was estimated using a Bayesian model combining cTTO and DCE data, accounting for left-censoring at −1, repeated observations, preference heterogeneity, heteroscedasticity, response granularity, and non-normality of cTTO values.Results: The selected hybrid model without a constant showed satisfactory convergence and face validity. Pain/discomfort was the most important dimension, with a level 3 disutility of 0.725, followed by anxiety/depression, while self-care had the smallest impact. Level 2 contributed substantially less than level 3 across all dimensions. The utility of the worst health state, 33333, was −0.443. The experimental cTTO arm improved distributional properties for worse-than-dead states but was not used in the final value set for consistency with earlier EQ-5D-3L/5L value sets.Conclusion: This study provides the EQ-5D-Y-3L value set for Poland, complementing existing adult EQ-5D value sets and enabling cost-utility analyses in paediatric populations. The findings also support methodological refinements in future child health valuation studies.

Title: Impact of mode of administration on responses and measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L and other pediatric preference weight measures: a systematic review
Abstract: Background: Different modes of administration (MoAs) have been used to administer EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L and other health-related quality of life (HRQoL) pediatric measurement scales, including self-administered ((e.g., paper and pencil, and digital survey) and interviewer-administered (e.g., face-to-face, telephone, and computer-administered). However, the impact of using different MoAs on health state reporting in children and adolescents is unclear. Objective: This scoping review mapped and characterized available evidence on health state score level of agreement and other assessed measurement properties between different MoAs of the EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L and other pediatric HRQoL measurement scales to assess the impact of MoAs on health state score. Methods: A scoping review of studies that compared health state scores agreement and measurement properties across different MoAs for the EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L or other HRQoL pediatric measurement scale was conducted. We searched eight databases from inception up to 30 August 2025 for studies reporting the health state scores, distributional characteristics and other measurement properties between different MoAs of EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L and other HRQoL pediatric measurement scales. All titles/abstracts and full texts were reviewed by two reviewers independently using an online software platform called Covidence. Any disagreement regarding eligibility was discussed and resolved through group discussion between reviewers. Data were extracted in duplicate using a form developed and tested by the research team. Information on study characteristics, the types of analyses conducted, and the types of measurement property assessed between different MoAs was assessed. Results: We identified 18 studies, of which only two (11%) studies used the EQ-5D-Y measurement scale. These studies varied in design, measurement scales, recall periods, and the measurement properties evaluated. Twelve studies used MoA in the category of digital/internet vs paper based, five in the category of self-administered/self-complete vs interviewer administered and one study use both categories. A broad range of measurement properties (including feasibility, response distribution, reliability, and validity) were used to assess health state responses agreement and measurement properties between different MoAs of the EQ-5D-Y-3L/-5L and other pediatric HRQoL measurement scales. Nine studies (50%) did not assess feasibility, five (28%) did not report any agreement statistics, eight (44%) did not report either validity or reliability, and none of the included studies assessed responsiveness. Feasibility, validity, and reliability differed more between SC and IA MoA than between digital and non-digital modes. Using different MoA can influence measurement property outcomes in paediatric health state assessments, with greater discrepancies observed between SC and IA MoA than digital and paper versions. Conclusion: Despite the widespread availability of pediatric HRQoL measurement scales, evidence on the impact of MoA remains limited. Greater discrepancies between SC and IA MoA than digital and non-digital MoA suggest that the data collection MoA choices may influence health state reporting outcomes. Rigorous longitudinal studies, particularly those assessing responsiveness are important before different MoAs can be used as interchangeable.

Title: Monthly measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) from early pregnancy to postpartum: An Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) of the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: Pregnant people represent a specific population group with changes in health states throughout pregnancy, from conception to postpartum. The EQ-5D-5L instrument has been used previously to describe such changes in the health states of pregnant population (by the same group of investigators as well as others) and findings have been published. At the same time, previously published work has been based on cross-sectionally collected data, and no study to date has evaluated monthly changes in HRQoL from pregnancy through postpartum. The concept of intertemporal health measures has been increasingly discussed due to its relevancy and importance in health care decision making. Furthermore, whether instruments like the EQ-5D-5L can be used to detect or predict health issues during pregnancy remains uncertain. Thus, we aim to verify our previously reported findings using a longitudinal assessment of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) with the EQ-5D-5L in a national sample of pregnant people. That way, we are able to assess self-reported HRQoL changes month by month by pregnant persons during their journey from early pregnancy to postpartum (Aim 1). In addition, longitudinal measures permit the assessment of the EQ-5D-5L’s responsiveness to and ability to predict health changes in this particular cohort (Aims 2a & 2b). We expect that results from this longitudinal study will further validate the EQ-5D-5L performances in this unique cohort at a granular level of measuring the monthly changes.

Title: EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB: Assessing Distinctiveness of Frequency vs. Severity Response Scales in Pain and Discomfort & Instruments Convergent Validity in the Context of Self-Reported Chronic Conditions
Abstract: This study provided the first comprehensive psychometric evaluation of frequency versus severity response scales in pain and discomfort assessment using the EQ-HWB instrument. Analysis of data from 1,008 U.S. participants employed multiple complementary methods to examine scale properties and performance. Frequency scales demonstrated superior informativity (Pain: H'=2.28 vs H'=2.06; Discomfort: H'=2.18 vs H'=2.00) and better measurement across trait levels, while severity scales showed higher discrimination at upper trait levels (a=6.23 for pain severity). DIF analysis revealed significant scale differences for pain (ΔR²=0.24) but not discomfort (ΔR²=0.001), suggesting different measurement approaches may be needed for these constructs. Health condition-specific analyses showed distinct patterns of scale performance, with frequency scales being particularly informative for conditions characterized by recurring symptoms (e.g., immunologic conditions OR=3.21, 95% CI: 1.97-5.24). These findings support using frequency scales in shorter instruments like EQ-HWB-S, while suggesting both scale types provide valuable information in comprehensive assessment. The results offer important empirical evidence for response scale selection in health measurement instrument development and highlight opportunities for condition-specific measurement optimization.

Title: Order effects in the EQ-5D item responses
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D has threeversions: threelevel (EQ-5D-3L), child-friendlyversion (EQ-5D-Y),and fivelevel (EQ-5D-5L). Generally, each version begins by asking about mobility (MO) followed by questions on self-care (SC), usual activities (UA), pain or discomfort (PD), and anxiety or depression (AD). This study examineswhether changing the order of the EQ-5D questions changes their responses.Methods: As part of a national survey, adults from the general population (N=4747) were asked the 15 EQ-5D questions(3 versions, 5 questions each)in random order. The majority (4272; 90%) completedall questions. Wefirst assessedthe influence of question positionon responses using chi-squared testsand piece-wise linear probability models. Furthermore,we testedwhether respondent characteristics―includingage, gender, race/ethnicity, education, household income, and self-reported general healthon a 5-level scale and 101-point visual analogue scale―modifiedthe ordereffect(if any).Results: A quarter of all EQ-5D responses (25.0%) were greater than Level 1 (no problems), but this likelihood was 2.5% higher when asked first (27.5%). Overall, the likelihood of reporting problems appearedto decreaseup to the tenth position (0.4% for each position) then flattened; however, thiseffect is largely attributedtothePD and AD questions. For example, the likelihood of reporting PD problems increasedfrom 26% to 28% whenPD was asked first(AD changedfrom 48% to 51%). However, the effect appearedto be largely among respondents who report “Good” health or better.Conclusions: Advancing the PD or AD questions to be asked firstled to a smallincreasein reportinga problem, particularly among healthy respondents. Although it is important to recognize that the current EQ-5D question order may weakly underrepresentPD and AD problems, the findings from this study appear tosupport maintaining the current questionorder (i.e., no randomization).Further research is needed in clinical populations.

Title: NA
Abstract: Relative to other countries, Bermuda has achieved above-average performance on several health indicators. Despite this, the health system in Bermuda faces some challenges. These include high levels of expenditure on healthcare, rising prevalence of non-communicable disease and inequality in access to healthcare. The Ministry of Health of Bermuda has outlined a strategy for dealing with these challenges over the medium term. A decision has been taken to create an EQ-5D value set for Bermuda which can support policy and clinical decision-making by allowing at the policy level: economic evaluation of health interventions and programmes, measuring burden of disease, and tracking health inequality. At the clinical level EQ-5D can be used to monitor and track patients’ health outcomes through a treatment or an illness and to compare the performance of healthcare interventions. EQ-5D is used for these purposes in many countries and is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) in the United Kingdom as the preferred health outcomes measure for economic evaluation. A protocol that included a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) and composite Time-Trade Off (cTTO) component was developed based on recent developments in EQ-5D valuation methods. 366 adults in Bermuda completed the valuation tasks in on-line interviews with an experienced EQ-5D valuation interview team in Trinidad. A bootstrapping approach was used to estimate a DCE-cTTO hybrid model based on which an EQ-5D-3L value set was created. An EQ-5D-5L crosswalk value set was developed based on the EQ-5D-3L value set. There were challenges in recruiting respondents for the survey resulting in a sample that was not fully representative of the Bermuda population in age and sex. This is due in part to the small population requiring surveys from a sample approaching 1% of the adult population. Analytical methods were employed to overcome the representativeness of the sample such that the resulting model would reflect the preferences of the adult population of Bermuda. The EQ-5D-3L value set and the crosswalk EQ-5D-5L value set created for Bermuda are presented in the Appendices.

Title: Content validity of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in caregivers of paediatric individuals with autism spectrum disorder
Abstract: Caregivers of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often face substantial challenges and may experience reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and wellbeing. This study examined the content validity of five EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB long form among caregivers of pediatric individuals with ASD. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 31 caregivers of children and adolescents aged 8–17 years with ASD in China. The interviews assessed the relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness of the EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB. For the EQ-HWB, relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness were generally rated positively. The most relevant items were “feel anxious?”, “feel frustrated?”, “feel sad or depressed?”, “feel lonely?”, and “have problems with your sleep?”, reflecting key aspects of caregivers’ HRQoL. Sixteen participants considered the measure to capture the main impacts of caregiving on health and wellbeing. However, some physical functioning items were seen as less relevant, certain examples lacked contextual fit, and caregiving-specific social impacts, particularly reduced social participation, were not fully captured. Some conceptual overlap between items was also noted. Response options were generally acceptable, although some participants preferred a longer recall period. For the EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons, the five bolt-ons were generally regarded as relevant, comprehensible, and useful. In terms of perceived relevance and importance, the priority order was sleep, happiness, tiredness, cognition, and social relationships. Compared with the EQ-5D-5L alone, the EQ-5D-5L plus bolt-ons was seen as more comprehensive, particularly through better coverage of sleep, fatigue, mood, and cognitive burden. Nonetheless, social support and financial concerns remained the most frequently identified missing domains, and the response options for the happiness bolt-on were most often seen as needing revision. These findings have two main implications for EuroQol. First, they provide supportive evidence for the relevance and coverage of the EQ-HWB in a caregiver population, helping to strengthen the empirical basis for its finalisation. Second, they suggest that selected EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons may improve the relevance and comprehensiveness of the core measure in caregivers, informing the development of an EQ-5D bolt-on toolbox for use in specific populations and contexts.

Title: Developing an interviewer administered version of O-PUF (Online Personal Utility Function): a first step involving co-design with members of the public.
Abstract: The Online Personal Utility Functions approach (O-PUF) has gained prominence in health state valuation studies, yet concerns regarding data quality, particularly among older respondents, have emerged. To address these challenges, we propose the creation of an Interviewer-guided O-PUF/CAPI (Computer-Assisted Personal Interview) approach, integrating standardised interviewer training, scripts, prompts, feedback and quality control processes. This approach aims to improve respondent understanding and data quality, particularly for complex instruments like EQ-HWB. Public Involvement (PI) is pivotal to the success of this initiative. We acknowledge that PI members offer invaluable insights into user experiences and ethical considerations. Collaboration with PI members, spanning diverse age groups, will ensure that the development of the interviewer-guided O-PUF/CAPI is well-informed and aligns with the requirements of both researchers and respondents. This seed project was the initial phase of this endeavour, beginning with a commitment to integrate PI members fully into the process. To enable meaningful PI within the overall project it is imperative to provide opportunities for training and involve PI members from early planning stages. This seed project recruited and provided extensive and appropriate training to two members of the public who were then able to work with the project researchers to co-produce a protocol for the larger project. The seed project culminated in a submission of a comprehensive research protocol for developing an interviewer script, feedback mechanisms, and quality control procedures for O-PUF, co-designed with PI members.

Title: Developing a value set for the child-friendly EQ-5D Health-related Quality of Life instrument EQ-5D-Y in Hong Kong
Abstract: Report Findings from CUHK’s Research Team (PI: Professor Eliza Wong) based on CUHK recruitments Developing a value set for the child-friendly EQ-5D Health-related Quality of Life instrument EQ-5D-Y in Hong Kong Background: The EQ-5D-Y is currently used to assess health-related quality of life of health states experienced by youth populations. However, there is no country-specific EQ-5D-Y value set available currently for the local Chinese population. Recent research indicates that using adult value sets to EQ-5D-Y states is inappropriate. However, developing valuation studies for the child population presents challenges. This study aimed to develop a value set for the EQ-5D-Y by the local adult population in a child perspective in HK following the recommended valuation proposal for EQ-5D-Y studies by the EuroQol Group. Methods: A cross-sectional valuation survey was conducted between December 2021 and July 2023 among the adult Chinese population aged 18 or above. During the interview, the participants either completed a discrete choice experiment (DCE) exercise or a composite time-trade off (C-TTO). The DCE was applied to estimate the relative importance associated with each EQ-5D-Y level in each dimension, while the C-TTO was used to anchor the latent scale DCE value set into the quality-adjusted life years (QALY) 0-1 scale. Both the DCE and the C-TTO were administered through computer-assisted personal interviews using the EQ-PVT platform, following the international valuation protocol for EQ-5D-Y-3L established by the EuroQol Group. The respondents answered either DCE and C-TTO questions from a child perspective to obtain their preferences. Hong Kong’s value set was estimated based on the responses of the DCE and C-TTO collected from the valuation survey. Results: A total of 1,396 HK Chinese adults aged 18 or above responded to the study, with a response rate of 22.0% (1,396/6,340). However, missing values were identified among 161 respondents. Thus, the responses from these 161 respondents were excluded, leaving a total of 1,235 respondents with complete information were included in the study, comprising of 1,030 completed DCE exercises and 205 completed the C-TTO valuation tasks from a child perspective. The value set model of EQ-5D-Y is established for the HK children population. Conclusions: This study elicits health preferences of the adult Hong Kong population from a child’s perspective using EQ-5D-Y-3L and the generated value sets, allowing the implementation of a cost-utility analysis for the youth population in Hong Kong. Report Findings from HKU’s Research Team (Dr. Carlos Wong) Comparisons of Preferences Towards EQ-5D-Y-3L Health States Between Adult Own and Child Perspectives Objectives: The international valuation protocol for EQ-5D-Y-3L recommends elicitation of utilities using adults’ preference for a hypothetical 10-year-old child. Published studies have reported preference difference in adults when valuing for a child and valuing for themselves. This study aimed to obtain EQ-5D-Y-3L preferences in Hong Kong and understand the preference difference between the adult own perspective and the child perspective. Methods: We recruited 1,000 and 200 adults in Hong Kong to value EQ-5D-Y-3L health states using discrete choice experiment (DCE) and composite time trade-off (cTTO), respectively. DCE respondents were randomized to complete tasks from either adult own perspective or child perspective. cTTO respondents completed valuation from the child perspective. Relative attribute importance (RAI) scores were compared between perspectives. Utility values were obtained by anchoring on the worst health state for both perspectives. Results: Both perspectives had similar RAI scores, rankings of dimensions, rescaled coefficients, and elicited values. Rank order of five dimensions, from highest to lowest importance, was ‘having pain or discomfort’, ‘doing usual activities’, ‘feeling worried, sad, or unhappy’, ‘mobility’, and ‘looking after myself’ for both perspectives. The most important and least important dimensions were ‘having pain or discomfort’ and ‘looking after myself’ respectively, consistent with published EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets. Conclusions: This study reported no remarkable preference difference for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states between the adult own and child perspectives, offering insights to the development of EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol. Adherence to the current international valuation protocol is recommended.

Title: Full Title: Population norms and inequalities based on EQ-5D-5L general population surveys (POPS 2)
Abstract: After the POPS 2 pilot demonstrated feasibility for the full POPS 2 project, the aim of this proposed project is to obtain and archive EQ-5D-5L general population datasets and produce a new edition of population health data, including norms and inequality indicators based on EQ-5D-5L surveys conducted in representative samples of general populations. Specifically, the following are the key objectives: Component 1: a) create a database archive of EQ-5D-5L data from general population surveys b) standardize the data structure and document a user guide Component 2: a) generate EQ-5D-5L population norms b) generate basic inequality indicators, both from epidemiological and economic origin c) make basic cross-country comparison of EQ-5D-5L population data Component 2 of the project will be supported by a separate methods pilot project (EQ Project 1600-RA) which began earlier in 2023 to establish the analytic and reporting approach for the main project. The major deliverables are 1) the POPS 2 data archive, 2) documentation for archive data use, 3) a report reporting the standardized country-level EQ-5D-5L norms, and 4) at least one publications in peer reviewed journals. The POPS 2 archive can drive future research activities for the HISIG, such as in-depth analyses of health inequalities and cross-country comparisons. The project would also have implications for other working Groups, such as the Valuation and the Education & Outreach Working Groups. This project will also collaborate actively with other ongoing EuroQol funded efforts to use EQ-instruments on the population level.

Title: A Systematic Review of the Validity, Reliability, and Responsiveness Studies of EQ-5D-5L: Methodological Insights and Future Directions
Abstract: Background: Over the past few decades, preference-based Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) measures, notably the EQ-5D developed by the EuroQol Group, have gained prominence. Despite numerous studies of measurement properties published in the literature, there is a lack of guidelines for validating preference-based measures and knowledge about the methodological quality of such studies. Aim: This study aims to systematically review and evaluate the methods used in published validity, reliability, and responsiveness studies of EQ-5D-5L across various health conditions. Methods: Adhering to the PRISMA and COSMIN guidelines, our approach involves meticulous identification of research questions followed by a three-pronged search strategy across prominent databases. Selected articles will undergo a rigorous review process, with data extracted systematically and summarized narratively and/or quantitatively. A tool will be developed and used to evaluate the appropriateness and quality of the identified studies Impact: This review provides the first insights into the variations, appropriateness, and quality of methods used to evaluate the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L. It will contribute to the Descriptive Systems Working Group’s psychometric research programme, aimed at developing guidelines for psychometric validation studies of EuroQol instruments.

Title: EQ-5D-5L in pregnancy. Antenatal and postnatal HRQOL, the impact of poor out
Abstract: The general aim of this study is to describe, in terms of the EQ-5D5L: (A) the health in pregnancy and the maternity period, using a representative large nationwide dataset (n>8000), which - apart from the EQ data - have been used for developing an international instrument to study care delivery in pregnancy/maternity units. (B) describe health inequities along several criteria (income class, education, living area, ethnic background) using conventional direct methods, in general and after subdivision into clinically relevant subgroups. (C) to predict in women without antenatal clinical problems (>80%), postnatal health from 1. antenatal health, 2. personal characteristics, 3. delivery course, 4. the reported health of the baby, and, 5. facility/pregnancy unit. We will apply some known group comparisons to establish sensitivity of EQ-domains for common clinical conditions (episiotomy and ceasarean section: pain/discomfort; ceasarean section: mobility; poor outcome child: anxiety&depression).

Title: Retrospective measurement of EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons: a study on recall bias among patients with post COVID-19 condition.
Abstract: Background/Context: The EuroQol 5D-5L instrument is widely used to assess the impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among COVID-19 survivors and individuals with Post-COVID Condition (PCC). Efforts to refine the EQ-5D-5L include the addition of bolt-ons (i.e. dimensions that can be appended to the EQ-5D-5L to benefit its use in a particular population) to better capture specific health dimensions. However, the presence and influence of recall bias in retrospective measurements using the EQ-5D-5L and its bolt-ons, particularly in post-acute infection syndromes (PAIS) like PCC, is not well understood. Recall bias is commonly observed in individuals with long-term illness or a history of pain. Additionally, the adoption of coping mechanisms is prevalent in these populations and may directly influence the accuracy of how they recall health experiences. Given that symptoms in PCC often persist for years after the initial infection, we hypothesize that the potential for recall bias in PCC patients is substantial. Addressing this methodological challenge is therefore critical for improving HRQoL assessments. Moreover, understanding the role of coping mechanisms and how they contribute to recall bias is essential for improving the accuracy of retrospective health measurements for this population. Addressing these challenges is key to ensuring reliable interpretations of HRQoL changes in treatment, care, and longitudinal studies using the EQ-5D-5L. Objective/Aim: This PhD proposal has two main aims. First, to explore the presence of recall bias based on perceived change assessed at three year follow-up using the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-on symptom questions in patients with a previous SARS-CoV-2 infection with and without PCC. Second, to explore the different types of coping mechanisms used by individuals with PCC and assess whether these mechanisms influence the health domains of the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons, and how they contribute to recall bias when retrospectively reporting on HRQoL. Methodology: Secondary analyses will be performed on the combined data from the CORFU and Long CORFU studies (EQ Project 1569-RA). This is a longitudinal dataset containing data of several former COVID-19 patient groups (at home, admitted to the hospital, either general ward or the intensive care unit) up to 3 three years after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Data were collected using questionnaires, including the EQ-5D-5L for HRQoL assessment and 13 symptom questions that were rated using the same 5 level Likert scale as the EQ-5D-5L. The three year follow-up questionnaire included retrospective questions on changes (compared to 12 months before), on the EQ-5D-5L dimensions and symptoms. The EQ-5D-5L dimensions and symptoms measurements collected prospectively at two and three years and retrospective measurements will be used to assess the presence and magnitude of recall bias. Differences will be tested across dimensions and bolt-ons. Moreover, we collected data on the use of coping mechanisms associated with perceived improved health at three years follow-up, making an analysis of associations with recall bias possible. Frequencies of coping mechanisms will be described and associations with recall bias tested using multivariable regression models. Analysis will be done for PCC and non PCC individuals, and other subgroups of interest.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Implementation of a digital survey, and development of an EQ-based patient platform (dashboard) in national longcovid study (CORFU) focussing on quality of life
Abstract: This project was not a research project in the conventional meaning, with relevant research questions to be addressed by data. Instead, the primary goal was to facilitate/support implementation of a digital survey system to collect data from patients with long covid. This project (645-RA) was tied to the so-called CORFU study, funded by ZONMW in The Netherlands. Corfu can be described as a prospective cohort study on the scope and severity of post-COVID symptoms across diverse patient groups in the Netherlands-insights from the CORFU study. A connection between CORFU and EuroQol was made in project 645-RA to ensure that a survey instrument and data collection structure developed in context of other projects (popcorn and 512-RA) could also be leveraged in this ambitious project.

Title: Response heterogeneities in EQ-VAS within identical EQ-5D-5L profiles: Investigating potential underestimation of the education-health gradient
Abstract: From the abstract of the published paper Measuring inequality in quality of life: Why the EQ-5D may underestimate it. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11136-025-04087-7 :The EQ-5D is increasingly being used in studies of health inequalities, providing further evidence of a social gradient in health; i.e. consistent positive associations between a socioeconomic indicator and health. However, the steepness in the social gradients in HRQoL differs depending on which of the two EQ-5D measures is used; whether based on respondents’ EQ-5D-5L descriptions or by their direct valuation in EQ VAS. This study aims to provide new knowledge as to why the two HRQoL measures suggest different degrees of health inequalities. Based on two large unique data sets (Tromsø Study Wave 7, N= 21,083; MIC study, N= 8,022), cross-sectional analyses were conducted. We identified the most prevalent EQ-5D-5L profiles. Within each of ten EQ-5D-5L profile groups, we examine response heterogeneities in EQ VAS scores using linear regressions, as explained by respondents’ level of educational attainment, controlling for age and sex.We showed significantly increasing EQ VAS scores along with educational attainments. For instance, in the most prevalent health state (11121), a consistent education-health gradient was observed: compared to individuals with primary education, the EQ-VAS was 1.7 higher among those with secondary education; 2.6 higher among individuals with short tertiary education; and, 3.7 higher among individuals with long tertiary education. This paper provides new insights into the use of EQ-5D in health inequality studies by suggesting an additional underlying education gradient in HRQoL than what is revealed through the EQ-5D-5L values. Broader psychosocial domains and aspects of adaptation should be considered when monitoring health inequalities.From an additional follow-up study, based on the EQ-DAPHNIE data: Measuring inequality in quality of life: Further evidence that the EQ-5D-5L may underestimate itAfter completing the planned work, we wanted to investigate the generalizability of our results – based on another large dataset. Two research questions were addressed: i) is there supportive evidence in other datasets for a hidden education–health gradient among respondents with identical EQ-5D-5L profiles?, ii) does a similar pattern emerge if, instead of educational attainment, we use a different socioeconomic proxy, such as income status? For reason of comparability with datasets used in our first paper, we chose eight rich countries: Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, UK, and US, and an age range of [25-79] years (N = 33,281). Educational attainment was reported using country-specific categories and harmonized into three levels for cross-country comparability. As an alternative socioeconomic proxy, we use income status, capturing financial strains that are particularly relevant in cross-country analyses where absolute income levels and purchasing power differ substantially. Income status was measured by a subjective indicator, ‘how you feel about your household’s income nowadays’, reported along four levels: comfortable, coping, difficult, and very difficult. Due to relatively few responses in the bottom category, the last two were combined and reverse-coded. Regression results show a clear educational gradient in EQ VAS within identical EQ-5D-5L profiles, consistent with our first study. Within the 11121 profile, EQ VAS scores were 1.1 and 2.4 points higher among respondents with medium and high education, respectively, than among those with low education. Tertiary education was associated with higher EQ VAS scores in nine of ten profiles, with seven statistically significant effects. Income status exhibited an even stronger gradient. In the same profile (11121), EQ VAS scores were 2.4 points higher among respondents coping with their income and 5.0 points higher among those living comfortably, compared to those reporting financial difficulties. Overall, significant income gradients were observed in nine of the ten profiles. This study provides strong cross-national supportive evidence of a “hidden” socioeconomic gradient in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) that is not fully captured by the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system. Among individuals reporting identical EQ-5D-5L profiles, both education and—more prominently—income status, were systematically associated with higher EQ VAS scores. These findings suggest that individuals with lower socioeconomic status experience worse overall health than reflected by the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, highlighting limitations in the instrument’s ability to capture socioeconomic disparities in HRQoL. The results have significant implications for health measurement and policy evaluation. Reliance on EQ-5D-5L values alone may underestimate socioeconomic health inequalities, challenging its use in equity-oriented policy analyses and health inequality monitoring. More research is needed on which factors might help explain these heterogeneities; dimensions of HRQoL (‘bolt-ons’) beyond those included in the EQ-5D, and demographic characteristics.

Title: Travel Grant Application for the 2024 ISPOR Meeting in Atlanta GA, USA-Yared Belete Belay
Abstract: I participated in the ISPOR 2024 meeting held May 5-8 in Atlanta, GA, USA. I presented two posters from projects funded by The EuroQol Research Foundation. Poster 1: "A Qualitative Study on Respondents’ Interpretation of the EQ-Vas in Ethiopia," findings from EQ project 327-RA. Poster 2: "Health-Related Quality of Life and Utility Values Among Patients with Anxiety and/or Depression in a Low-Income Tertiary Care Setting: A Cross-Sectional Analysis," from EQ project 229-RA. I received valuable feedback on my abstracts from meeting participants. This conference provided an opportunity to share insights on the utilisation of EQ-5D-5L in low-income settings and to receive constructive feedback on my work. Additionally, as an early-career researcher and PhD student, attending this conference allowed me to learn from experts in the field of outcome research. It also facilitated networking with fellow researchers, practitioners, and students, enriching my academic and research journey. I attended podium presentations, discussions, and preliminary sessions, further gaining knowledge and experience.

Title: extension of 20190150: Exploring non-iterative time trade-off methods for valuation of EQ-5D-5L health states: an on-line experiment
Abstract: Objectives In our previous investigation of two non-iterative Time Trade-Off (TTO) methods - open TTO and non-stopping TTO - we found indications that EQ-5D health states could be evaluated using approaches with reduced burden on both interviewers and interviewees compared to the cTTO method. Inspired by recent developments in online TTO assessments, we devised a self-administered TTO method (referred to as sTTO), combining elements of the two non-iterative TTOs. Our aim was to evaluate the feasibility of sTTO by comparing it with the conventional TTO (cTTO) in a sample of the general population. Methods We developed a computer-based tool similar to EQ-VT for the valuation of EQ-5D-5L health states using sTTO. Thirty EQ-5D-5L health states, chosen from an orthogonal array, were evaluated by individuals from the general population in Guizhou Province, China. Participants were provided with a pre-recorded video explanation of the valuation task before completing 11 sTTO tasks independently, without assistance from interviewers. For comparison with cTTO, we utilized data collected in a previous study following the EQ-VT protocol. We compared the burden of administration, logical consistency, value distribution, acceptability and modeling performance of the two methods. Results A total of 324 participants contributed data, with 143 using the cTTO method and 181 using the sTTO method. On average, the time taken to complete the survey and a single valuation task was 26 minutes and 1.5 minutes shorter, respectively, with sTTO compared to cTTO. We observed logical inconsistencies in 78% of participants using sTTO, with 51% showing severe inconsistencies, compared to 1.4% and 14% respectively for cTTO. The mean health-state value for sTTO (0.293) was slightly higher than that for cTTO (0.256). However, cTTO values displayed a smoother and more continuous distribution with fewer spikes and gaps, and a wider range of unique values. Additionally, cTTO outperformed sTTO in all criteria of modeling performance. Participant feedback indicated moderate challenges with sTTO compared to cTTO. Conclusion While the sTTO method proved to be significantly more time-efficient for valuing EQ-5D-5L health states, suggesting acceptable administration burden, the data quality was inferior to that of cTTO data collected with trained interviewers. Participant feedback also suggested that sTTO presented moderate challenges, slightly less acceptable than cTTO. These findings indicate that the current design of sTTO may not be feasible for valuing EQ-5D health states when self-administered. Future research could explore its feasibility for use in group interviews and investigate alternative designs for self-administered TTO valuation.

Title: Valuing health‐related quality of life: An EQ‐5D‐5L value set for Morocco
Abstract: Background: There is a growing interest in health technology assessment (HTA) in Morocco. An EQ-5D-5L value set allows the computation of Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) in economic evaluations of healthcare interventions to support decision making. Although context-specific HTA is needed, a value set for the EQ-5D-5L based on the preferences of the general Moroccan population is not yet available. Objective: The aim of this study was to develop a Moroccan value set for the EQ-5D-5L based on data from a representative sample of the Moroccan adult population. Methods: A nationally representative sample using quota stratified sampling based on gender, age category, and urban/rural residence was approached based on the last general population and housing census data in Morocco. Data were collected using the international valuation protocol developed by the EuroQol Group (EQ-VT) to elicit the health preferences using: (i) composite time trade-off (cTTO) and (ii) discrete choice experiment (DCE). The cTTO includes 86 EQ-5D-5L health states grouped into 10 blocks, each block with 10 health states. The DCE comprises 196 pairs EQ-5D-5L health states grouped into 28 blocks, each block with 7 choice pairs. Each respondent valued 1 block of health states using cTTO, and 1 block of DCE pairs. The cTTO and DCE data were modeled using a Tobit model and a conditional logit model, respectively. In addition, these models were combined using a hybrid model. Model performance was compared using AIC and BIC criteria. Results: A total of 1006 respondents were included in the study. Responses from 30 participants (3%) were flagged according to the 4 quality control criteria. The cTTO distribution was similar across interviewers and there were only minor interviewer effects. The most common health problem reported by participants was anxiety/depression (44.53%), and the least frequent health problem was self-care (15.71%). The mean ± standard deviation of the EQ VAS score was 77.25 ± 17.05. The hybrid model was considered the preferred model, i.e., the estimated coefficients attributed to the levels of severity were logically consistent. The pain/discomfort dimension had the largest effect on health state preference values, followed by anxiety/depression, mobility, self-care and usual activities. The hybrid model was in relative agreement with the cTTO and DCE models regarding the order of dimensions that affect the HRQOL. Conclusion: Morocco is the second country in the MENA region (following Egypt) with an EQ-5D-5L value set. This study supports the use of EQ-5D-5L data for healthcare decision-making in the Moroccan context. The availability of the EQ-5D-5L value set will facilitate health technology assessment in Morocco. Moreover, it will be used to implement patient-reported outcomes measures for routine clinical practice to improve the monitoring and management of patients and thus provide more evidence for decision-makers in healthcare systems in Morocco.

Title: Assessing TIPS Attributes using DCE with Kaizen Tasks: a feasibility study
Abstract: The five-level EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) is under development as a health-related quality of life (HR-QoL) measure for toddlers and infant populations, aged 0 to 36 months. Each of its seven items (and response options) can be transformed into an attribute with five levels for a health valuation study. However, it is unclear whether severity (i.e., order of the five levels) concords with preferences along each EQ-TIPS domain. Furthermore, the EuroQol Group lacks a method for EQ-TIPS valuation, particularly one that works well in small samples. The primary aim of this feasibility study was to assess EQ-TIPS attributes using DCE surveys. This methods research will address three questions critical for EQ-TIPS development: (1) Whether severity concords with preferences along each EQ-TIPS domain? (2) To what extent do the EQ-TIPS attributes influence preferences? (3) To compare the performance of kaizen tasks and paired comparisons for EQ-TIPS valuation

Title: Examining the desirability, feasibility, and impact of involving children in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states
Abstract: Background: The valuation of EQ-5D-Y (-3L/-5L) health states by adults has been a subject of ongoing discussion, particularly after publication of the valuation protocol in which adults perform valuation tasks for a 10-year-old child. Recent evidence indicates that the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states may be influenced by adults’ fear of underestimating health problems when performing valuation tasks for a child or adolescent. Adults feel uncomfortable not knowing the health-state preferences of the child or adolescent and anticipate what their preferences might be. In fear of making a wrong choice, being considered a bad parent, or others bearing a grudge against them, adults compromise between their own preferences and the anticipated preferences of the child or adolescent. Furthermore, adults struggle with the responsibility of stating preferences for a child or adolescent. They believe that adolescents are able—and should be enabled—to make such decisions for themselves and that children should at least be consulted or (somehow) involved in these decisions. Adults’ belief that children and/or adolescents should be involved in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states runs parallel to the increased interest of researchers and policymakers to involve stakeholders in decisions on health and healthcare to improve the quality, relevance, and outcomes of research and policies, empower stakeholders, and promote the transparency and legitimacy of decisions. Nonetheless, insight into the desirability, feasibility, and needs of stakeholders (potentially) involved in and affected by the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states, and the impact of their involvement on the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states is currently lacking.  Aims: To provide insight into the desirability, feasibility, and impact of involving children (8–18 years) in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states by addressing four evidence gaps in successive work packages (WPs): • WP A provides insight into the theoretical/normative and empirical underpinning of involving stakeholders, in particular children, in decisions on health and healthcare. • WP B provides insight into whether and (further explores) why child and adult members of the public, and policymakers in healthcare believe that (somehow) involving children in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states would be desirable and feasible. • WP C provides insight into the various ways in which children can (potentially) be involved in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states, and into the necessary conditions and stakeholder support for putting these ways into practice. • WP D provides insight into the impact of involving children on the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states.  General methods: To achieve the abovementioned aims, a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods will be applied; targeted review of the theoretical/normative and empirical literature, and (health) policy reports on stakeholder involvement (WP A), semi-structured interviews with children (8–18 years), adults, and policymakers (WP B), identification and description of the various ways in which children can be involved in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states based on previous results and semi-structured interviews with experts on child (mental) health and well-being (WP C), and impact assessment of the most promising way for involving children on the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states (WP D).

Title: Uncertainty around EQ-5D values used in cost effectiveness analysis: identifying types of uncertainty & strengthening the methods to address them
Abstract: A key feature of modern approaches to economic appraisal is the treatment of uncertainty, particularly in the context of probabilistic sensitivity analysis used within cost-effectiveness studies (Briggs, Sculpher and Claxton, 2006). However, an underexamined area is variability in health state values and the consequent uncertainty when they are used to estimate QALYs. This project represents the first step toward a wider research programme to address this for values for Euroqol's instruments. The principal methods we used were (a) a scoping review leading to a comprehensive account of sources of variability, from valuation studies, through valuation modelling, to the use of values in specific contexts; and identification of how such variability is currently dealt with as a source of uncertainty in decision analysis modelling. We then (b) created a framework in which the principal sources of variability in EQ-5D values are identified and categorised, drawing on the literature. We discuss the appropriate means by which such variability can be dealt with in the context of uncertainty in valuation studies and in decision analysis modelling. In the course of our work we identified (c) a means of calculating the standard error around values for EQ-5D profiles which has not previously been used. This was demonstrated using data from the MVH 3L valuation study, which we obtained from the ESRC data archives. The MVH modelling sample was replicated, and the covariance matrix produced and used to demonstrate how standard errors can readily be produced for health state profile values. The worked example and tools for producing these standard errors were provided via the LSHTM website: https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/research/centres/global-health-economics-centre/methods-addressing-uncertainty-around-eq-5d-values. Our work has been presented as a paper at the 2023 plenary as an ISPOR Europe 2023 poster. Each element of our work is now being prepared for submission to journals. Finally, our team has additionally produced a memo for the Executive Committee, outlining the future research which could be pursued to strengthen the way uncertainty around HRQoL valuation is handled and reported.

Title: Estimating EQ-5D-Y-3L Value Set for the kingdom of Saudi Arabia using DCE and c-TTO Values
Abstract: Introduction: EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation studies are now being conducted in several countries. The idea of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is multifaceted and focuses on how a health condition and its treatment affect a person's daily life. Assessing young people's HRQoL will be crucial for the evaluation of treatments and for public health research, just as it is for the adult population. Even though the EQ-5D-Y version is receiving more attention, there are few data on the health of the youth population, particularly in the Middle East. The measurement and valuation of HRQoL outcomes, resource allocation, planning of healthcare interventions, and policy decision making for Saudi populations will all be significantly impacted by this research. Objectives: to estimate a value set for EQ-5D-Y-3L among Saudi Arabia's Youth population (8–15 years old) in terms of population health status. Methods: The study will employ a discrete choice experiment (DCE) exercise to ascertain the relative importance of each EQ-5D-Y level in each dimension using the valuation approach, as recommended by the EuroQol Group for EQ-5D-Y research. The latent scale DCE value set will then be anchored into the quality-adjusted life years (QALY) 0–1 scale using a data from a sample of composite time-trade off (C-TTO) interviews. A representative sample of 1000 adults interviews from the general community will be conducted as an online discrete choice experiment (DCE) to elicit preferences for the EQ-5D-Y health state, and 200 interviews will be done in a face-to-face interview using composite time trade-off (cTTO). The EQ-VT survey will take into account any Arabic translations. The questions will ask respondents to imagine a 10-year-old child living with the health problems described by the health state that is being valued. Responses from DCE and c-TTO will be collected through adults from the general population taking a discerned perspective: adults responding the elicitation tasks from what they would prefer for a 10 years old child perspective.

Title: Developing an online person trade-off survey for determining the weight between child and adult QALYs based on the preferences of the general public: the phase-1 study
Abstract: We developed an interactive survey tool similar to the design of the cTTO and tested its feasibility and acceptability. We tested the first version with 5 laypersons and used their feedback to improve the survey tool. We tested the improved tool with 5 more laypersons. Their feedback suggested the survey tool is ready for use in an online survey to estimate the value of child QALY relative to adult QALY using the person trade-off method.

Title: Psychometric properties, feasibility and usefulness of the extended EQ-5D-Y-5L in children with prevalent disease conditions in Ethiopia
Abstract: Background: Type 1 Type-1 diabetes mellitus and heart diseases are the most common medical problems among children in Ethiopia. Children's health-related quality of life (HRQoL) outcome measure are currently receiving attention. EQ-5D-Y-5L health survey in children has been used in different countries. Objective: To assess the psychometric properties of the Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Experimental version and, thereby, to test whether the measure is feasible, reliable, and valid to use among healthy and children with prevalent disease conditions. Methods. Data were collected using a pen-and-paper survey that presents the self-complete Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Experimental version and EQ-VAS. A cluster sampling strategy was used to select 200 school children study participants from ten sub-cities in Addis Ababa city, Ethiopia. A supervisor selected one class from the elementary school of each sub-city using simple random sampling techniques. Within each class (n=40-60), 20 students between the age of 8 and 12 were randomly selected and invited to complete a self-complete Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Experimental version and EQ-VAS. For children with the prevalent disease conditions (Type-1 diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, rheumatic heart disease) participants were identified from Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital (TASH) of diabetic and cardiac clinics. A sample of 55 study participants (23 congestive heart failure, 17 rheumatic heart disease, and 15 Type-1 diabetes mellitus) who had unchanged health state based on the general health item received the questionnaire again 10 days after the first task for the test-retest procedures to investigate reliability of the instrument. Ceiling was compared in between paired versions with the X2 test and the absolute reduction in proportion scoring was calculated. The test-retest method was used to determine stability. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare the mean (SD) LSS scores for each instrument between groups with known health conditions to assess known group validity. Results. The mean (SD) age of the participants in this study was 10.35 (1.42) years of which 51.00% were female. A sample of 450 participants (200 school children, 65 Type-1 diabetes mellitus, 70 Rheumatic heart disease, and 115 congestive heart failure) were recruited and 437 participants (200 school children, 62 Type-1 diabetes mellitus, 66 Rheumatic heart disease, and 109 congestive heart failure) were included in the sample for analysis. All of the EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions and the EQ-VAS had strong intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), which fall within the range of good agreement for all respondents (ICC ranges from 0.52-0.77, p 0.001). The differences in self-complete Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Experimental version and EQ-VAS scores between disease groups demonstrate the self-complete Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Experimental version's significant known group validity. Conclusion: The Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L Paper EXPERIMENTAL Self-Complete appears to be a suitable measure for assessing HRQoL in various child population groups in Ethiopia, according to this study.

Title: Estimating the relative importance of health when being a child vs when being an adult at an individual respondent level
Abstract: Eliciting health state utilities with the time trade-off (TTO) method relies on assessing the relative importance of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) versus longevity. Adults typically assign higher utilities when considering a hypothetical child than when considering their own HRQoL. We aimed to decompose this effect by comparing the importance attached to survival and to HRQoL in adolescence versus adulthood.We developed and used a method that employs intrapersonal choices between lotteries involving health problems that differ in age of onset or probability of occurrence, thereby avoiding ethical concerns about interpersonal comparisons. Respondents chose from the perspective of a hypothetical 10-year-old and 20-year-old facing HRQoL worsening or death. They also completed TTO tasks from both perspectives, as well as tasks intended to measure probability weighting.We piloted the method in a convenience sample of 100 respondents. Our results suggest that the respondents value the nearest 10 years more than subsequent years; the implied annual discount rates range from 0.26% to 9.49%, depending on the health problem. Crucially, this increase of importance does not vary by perspective. Thus, we find no evidence that hypothetical adolescents receive greater weight on either HRQoL or survival than hypothetical adults. TTO results are consistent with these findings. Probability-weighting tasks yielded ambiguous patterns and were excluded from the main analysis.We conclude that higher TTO utilities when adults value a hypothetical child’s health versus their own are unlikely to be driven by adolescent years receiving special value. Instead this effect may be driven by the change from self- to other-perspective.

Title: Travel Grant to visit the University of Sheffield for Qualitative analysis of EQ-TIPS qualitative data on content validity.
Abstract: Dr Verstraete travelled to the University of Sheffield and ISPOR Barcelona to 1) analyse data and a draft manuscript on the multi-national content validity testing of the EQ-TIPS and 2) present EQ-TIPS work at ISPOR Europe. The research visit was fruitful as key changes to the EQ-TIPS descriptive system were discussed and could be finalised with public and patient engagement representatives and expert stakeholders. Version 3.0 of the EQ-TIPS descriptive system is currently being tested for psychometric validity.

Title: Comparison of the psychometric properties of self-complete and proxy version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L in Ethiopian children with prevalent acute illnesses
Abstract: Evidence regarding parent-child agreement in pediatric health-related quality-of-life assessments is scarce. This study aimed to explore the agreement between child/adolescent self-reports and parent proxy reports using the EQ-5D-Y-3L tool, along with the tool’s convergent validity and responsiveness. For younger participants aged 4-7 years, administer-assisted surveys were implemented to ensure accurate and child-friendly administration. The follow-up interviews were conducted before patient discharge, typically about 2-4 weeks after treatment. The repeated measure designed was intended to observe changes in health status over time and to assess the responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-3L measure. Separate interviews were conducted for caregivers and children/adolescents in distinct settings - nurses' offices for caregivers and pediatric wards for children/adolescents- to ensure comfort and privacy, thereby enhancing the quality of the data collected. The analysis involved examining the differences in EQ-5D-Y-3L health profiles and EQ VAS scores between self-complete and proxy reports using Chi-square tests for categorical data and t-tests or ANOVA for continuous EQ VAS scores, focusing on sociodemographic groups with known health disparities. Weighted kappa agreement coefficient and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) were employed to assess the level of agreement between self-complete and proxy versions of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, with subgroup analysis by sociodemographic characteristics like age and gender. The psychometric performance of both versions was evaluated in terms of convergent validity (correlation of EQ-5D-Y-3L index scores with EQ VAS scores using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient), and the responsiveness to health status changes over time. Responsiveness analysis was assessed at the dimension level using percent reduction of problems across each dimension. At individual level, the Paretian Classification of Health Change (PCHC) was employed. According to PCHC analysis, an EQ-5D-Y-3L health state is considered 'better' than another if it is better on at least one dimension and no worse on any other dimension. And an EQ-5D-Y-3L health state is considered 'worse' than another if it is worse in at least one dimension and no better in any other dimension. Furthermore, the change in EQ-5D-Y-3L index (computed using the Zimbabwe value set), and the EQ VAS scores were examined using a paired t-test analysis to assess the instruments performance in detecting change in health status. Participant characteristics o A total of 985 pediatric inpatients and their caregivers participated in baseline and follow-up interviews. 28 dyad responses were excluded due to incomplete data, resulting in analysis with 957 (97.1%) dyads. o Boys: 504 (52.7%), average age 10.7 years (SD = 4.4 years, range 4–18 years) o Girls: 453 (47.3%), average age 10.6 years (SD = 4.2 years, range 4–18 years) o Various health conditions identified including respiratory infections (e.g., pneumonia, pharyngitis), urinary tract conditions (e.g., UTIs, glomerulonephritis), neurological conditions (e.g., meningitis), vector-borne diseases (e.g., malaria), and nutritional problems (e.g., severe and moderate acute malnutrition). o Median length of hospital: 10 days (IQR 7-15 days), consistent for both boys and girls. o HRQoL problems increased with age, especially in dimensions of Looking After Myself (LAM), Doing Usual Activities (UA), Pain/Discomfort (PD), and Worried, Sad, or Unhappy (WSU). o Oldest age group (12-18) reported the highest frequency of problems in these dimensions. o Gender differences were not significant in most dimensions. o Family income significantly impacted emotional well-being, with children from families with inadequate income reporting more problems in the WSU dimension. o Urban versus rural residence showed a statistically significant difference in the mobility dimension, suggesting environmental factors may influence physical health components. Agreement between children/adolescents and caregiver reported measures o Significant trends noted in agreement over time across the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions, index, and EQ VAS scores:  Fair agreement on the EQ-5D-Y-3L dimension levels at baseline/admission and follow-up/discharge, with exception of poor agreement for WSU dimension at discharge.  Increase in exact agreement percentage observed from baseline/admission to follow-up/discharge.  Weighted kappa coefficients indicate consistent convergence over time. o Agreement level on index, and EQ VAS scores.  EQ-5D-Y-3L utility values and EQ VAS scores at admission and discharge within acceptable range.  EQ-5D-Y-3L index ICCs: 0.582 (admission), 0.498 (discharge).  EQ VAS scores ICCs: 0.671 (admission), 0.676 (discharge).  Gender-Based Analysis:  Boys exhibit higher ICC values compared to girls for both EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS scores.  Boys: ICC values of 0.625 (admission), 0.493 (discharge) for index; ICC values of 0.689 (admission), 0.688 (discharge) for EQ VAS scores.  Age-Stratified Analysis:  Younger children (ages 4-6) and older adolescents (ages 16-18) showed lower ICC values, indicating lower agreement between child and caregiver reports.  Children aged 7 to 15 years exhibited higher ICC values, suggesting more consistent agreement between child and caregiver reports.  Residence-based comparisons:  Rural residents displayed slightly higher ICCs compared to urban counterparts, particularly at discharge, indicating more consistent health status reporting in rural settings. Convergent validity and responsiveness o Significant correlations observed between child/adolescent and caregiver reported EQ-5D-Y-3L index and EQ VAS scores at admission and discharge (p < 0.01).  Child/adolescent reports: correlation coefficient of 0.453 at admission, increasing to 0.514 at discharge.  Caregiver reports: correlation coefficients of 0.512 at admission and 0.520 at discharge. o Marked decrease in reported problems across all dimensions of EQ-5D-Y-3L from admission to discharge was observed for both child/adolescent and parent/caregiver reported measures. Dimensional improvements o Children/adolescents reported most pronounced improvement in 'Looking After Myself (LAM)' dimension (76.2% decrease), followed by 'Mobility (MO)' and 'Worried, Sad or Unhappy (WSU)' dimensions (75.2% and 75.4% reduction respectively), compared with caregiver reported outcomes. o Caregiver reports highlighted 'Worried, Sad or Unhappy (WSU)' dimension as most significantly improved (85.1% reduction), followed by 'Looking After Myself' (83.5%) and 'Mobility' (82.0%) dimensions. Paretian Classification of Health Change (PCHC) Analysis o Significant majority (91.4%) of children/adolescents demonstrated health improvement according to PCHC criteria in both measures, which was as expected as their treatment at the hospital was effective upon discharge.  Hence, instances of unchanged health status was rare (1.4% in children/adolescents' reports, 2.1% in caregivers' reports), and declines in health status were remarkably low (2.9% in children/adolescents' reports, 0.4% in caregivers' reports). EQ-5D-Y-3L Index and EQ VAS Scores o Substantial increments in the EQ-5D-Y-3L index scores from admission to follow-up for both measures. o Mean scores significantly increased for children/adolescents (from 0.422 to 0.810) and caregivers (from 0.350 to 0.844). o From admission to discharge, the EQ VAS scores also exhibited significant changes, increasing for both children/adolescents (from 36.2 to 72.1) and caregivers (from 36.3 to 79.5).

Title: A convergent parallel mixed methods study to assess the feasibility of using discrete choice experiments among Canadian youth
Abstract: Background: During consultations on the development of the EQ-5D-Y value set, Canadian stakeholders recommended that preferences be elicited from children and adolescents using discrete choice experiments (DCEs).  Objective: To understand the feasibility of directly eliciting health state preferences from Canadian children and adolescents using DCE. Methods: A convergent parallel mixed methods study was conducted among a purposeful sample of Canadian youth (13-18 years) separated by age and sex. First, participants completed an online survey with the EQ-5D-Y-5L, 13 DCE tasks using EQ-5D-Y-5L health states (all participants), and three DCE with duration tasks (15-18 years only). Then, they engaged in a focus group discussion on their experience with the online survey. Quantitative data on DCE feasibility indicators (i.e., incompletion, speeding, flatlining, violation of dominant choice task) were analysed using descriptive statistics. Qualitative focus group data were analysed using content analysis. The findings from the qualitative and quantitative components of the study were integrated narratively. Results: Six focus groups with a total of 36 children and adolescents (n = 6 per focus group) were conducted. The average time to complete all DCE tasks was 7 minutes (range 3 – 12). In the focus group discussions, all participants reported that they understood both the DCE and DCE with duration tasks, and had minimal issues with engagement and use of the online technology. This was confirmed by the quantitative data on feasibility indicators, which found no incomplete tasks, speeding, flatlining, or wrong answers to the dominant choice task. A few participants mentioned challenges in imagining hypothetical health states, but most of the group discussions focused on minor issues with the presentation (e.g., not noticing the bolding that differentiates health states) and framing (e.g., imagining someone older instead of themself in a health state) of the DCE tasks. Participants reported that these issues could cause them to answer the survey questions differently. Conclusion: Both the qualitative and quantitative data indicate that the direct use of DCE and DCE with duration is feasible among Canadian children and adolescents. There are minor issues with the presentation and framing of DCE tasks, which have the potential to cause heterogeneity in preferences, and could be improved. These findings can inform the design of the EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation study in Canada.

Title: Analysis of the measurement properties of the Brazilian-Portuguese version of the health-related quality of life instruments EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in children and adolescents
Abstract: BACKGROUND: The EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L are friendly-child versions of the EQ-5D instruments that measures health-related quality of life in children and adolescents aged 8-15 years. However, the measurement properties of both instruments have not been tested in Brazilian kids yet. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to test the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L in Brazilian children and adolescents with and without disabling musculoskeletal pain. METHODS: This is a methodological study with test-retest of 7 days interval. We included children and adolescents with disabling musculoskeletal pain (who reported pain in the back, neck, arms, or legs that lead to school absenteeism and/or interference with normal and/or recreational activities) and without any musculoskeletal pain from public and private schools in Sao Paulo state. Children and adolescents answered the self-reported versions of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L. We tested test-retest reliability using Kappa coefficient for descriptive system and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for EQ-VAS, construct (convergent) validity (classified as sufficient if at least 75% of the results were in accordance with our pre-specified hypothesis) using the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory questionnaire version 4.0 (PedsQLTM) and the Child Health Utility 9D (CHU9D), the ceiling and floor effects of the instruments using the dimensions’ descriptive system and health profile, and the feasibility by the missing responses. RESULTS: From 356 children and adolescents included in this study, 181 reported disabling musculoskeletal pain and 175 did not report any musculoskeletal pain. Most children and adolescents were boys (53%) with a mean age of 11.5 years-old (standard deviation [SD]: 2.9). In the descriptive system, reliability was inadequate ranged from 0.25 to 0.48 for the EQ-5D-Y-3L, and 0.20 to 0.49 for the EQ-5D-Y-5L, considering children and adolescents with and without musculoskeletal pain. Reliability for the EQ-VAS ranged from moderate (ICC: 0.40, 95% CI: 0.24 to 0.53, for children and adolescents without musculoskeletal pain) to substantial (ICC: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.72 to 0.87, for children and adolescents with disabling musculoskeletal pain). Construct (convergent) validity was sufficient for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L compared to the PedsQLTM for children and adolescents with disabling musculoskeletal pain, but insufficient for those without any musculoskeletal pain. Construct (convergent) validity was insufficient for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and sufficient for the EQ-5D-Y-5L when compared to the CHU9D for two subsamples of children and adolescents. There was lower ceiling effect of the EQ-5D-Y-5L compared to the EQ-5D-Y-3L for almost all the dimensions of the descriptive system, and also for the health profile (11111). The missing responses rate ranged from 0.6% to 1.7% for the EQ-5D-Y-3L, 0% to 12.7% for the EQ-5D-Y-5L, and 4% to 5.5% for the EQ-VAS. CONCLUSION: The reliability for the descriptive system was inadequate for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L, and the EQ-VAS presented moderate to substantial reliability. Both instruments presented sufficient construct (convergent) validity when compared to PedsQLTM for children and adolescents with disabling musculoskeletal pain. When compared to the CHU9D, the EQ-5D-Y-5L had sufficient construct (convergent) validity, considering the two subsamples. The Brazilian-Portuguese version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L can be used in research and in the clinical practice to assess the health-related quality of life, especially of children and adolescents with disabling musculoskeletal pain. Furthermore, the EQ-5D-Y-3L can be recommended in future economic evaluations conducted in Brazil.

Title: Assessment of the use of EQ-5D and other generic health-related quality of life measures to evaluate the health outcomes associated with extreme weather events and related climate change impacts: A systematic review
Abstract: Background and aim: Climate change presents a major public health concern globally. Extreme weather events and related climate change impacts including extreme heat, cyclones, bushfires, floods, and droughts have become more frequent and intense, posing significant challenges to global health. As health risks from climate change increase, understanding the appropriateness of using health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures such as EQ-5D to evaluate the health impact associated with climate change is important. This systematic review will describe the extent to which EQ-5D and other HRQoL measures have been used in the evaluation of HRQoL and assess their measurement properties, in the context of climate change, focusing on the health impacts of extreme heat, cyclones, bushfires, floods, and droughts.  Methods: This review will consider studies published from January 1990 to January 2024. Databases such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science will be searched for relevant literature. The review process will adhere to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Generic HRQoL measures, including both preference-based and non-preference-based instruments for use in adult and youth populations, will be considered, and their measurement properties will be summarized in terms of feasibility, validity, sensitivity, and reliability. Results: The review is expected to identify how the EQ-5D and other generic HRQoL measures have been implemented and what evidence exists concerning their measurement properties in the evaluation of HRQoL that could be impacted by climate change extreme weather-related event across different populations and settings. Conclusion: This systematic review aims to provide a better understanding of the appropriateness of using EQ-5D in the context of climate change. It will identify strengths and limitations in the current implementation of EQ-5D compared to other generic HRQoL measures and offer insights into developing a more robust EQ-5D instrument.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Psychometric performance of an EXtended version of the EQ-5D-5L in a cohort of German health care workers with AND without late consequences of SARS-CoV-2 infection (EXPAND)
Abstract: This study investigates an extended version of the EQ-5D-5L in a cohort of health care workers and medical workers, who reported a work-related COVID-19-infection. About 20,000 randomly selected persons from an ongoing research project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research will answer an online-questionnaire including the EQ-5D-5L, two bolt-on items (cognition, social participation, EQ-5D+), and several other health- and infection-related questions such as vaccination status, present health state and health state 12 months before the most severe COVID-19 infection, Long COVID symptoms (bolt-on-like items), chronic conditions, ability to work, need for rehabilitation. Persons with ongoing symptoms will be surveyed after a 12 month follow-up, which allows for longitudinal analysis of the EQ-5D+ and other variables.
