Psychometric analysis of the EQ-5D+ comprise analyses of:  distributional properties (i.e., ceiling of EQ-5D-5L, EQ-5D+, each single dimension, and bolt-on-like items) feasibility (proportion of missing responses on each dimension and bolt-on(-like) item) construct validity (correlation with other measures supposed to assess a (dis-)similar construct) known groups (comparisons between subgroups according to level distribution of responses across dimensions and the mean EQ VAS with formulated hypothesis regarding differences between groups) responsiveness of EQ-5D, bolt-on(-like) items, EQ VAS, EQ-5D index values, in the subgroup of HCWs and medical workers with ongoing symptoms dimensional dependency  multivariable regression analysis on the impact of the 5 dimensions, and bolt-on(-like) items and to predict group membership (e.g., persons with and without Long COVID) Results will be compared with other COVID-19 cohorts (e.g., POPCORN, CORFU) and will gain insight into the suitability of two candidate bolt-ons and bolt-on-like items in a German COVID-19 population, presumably as well as infectious diseases in general.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: TTOFU is good for health (valuation)! - Time Trade-Off Follow-Up questions in measuring the discounting, fear of death, and value of life per se
Abstract: The usual assumptions made when using the time trade-off method (TTO) to elicit prefernces for health states are increasingly subject to discussion. The present study focused on three issues: 1) discounting; 2) the special status of the task with comparison with immediate death (ID); 3) the increased willingness to accept a severe state if it only lasts a short time (referred to as value of life per se or maximal endurable time hypothesis, MET). I aimed to devise a method to measure the three above phenomena at the individual respondent level by asking TTO follow-up questions (TTOFUs) after the regular composite TTO task (cTTO) has ended. In total, 7 TTOFUs were designed, Q1--Q7. Q1--Q3 were aimed at identifying the discounting functional form (exponential, hyperbolic, or power) and direction (positive, negative, or none). Q4 and Q5 were aimed at measuring the fear of ID, i.e., the additional unwillingness to accept a state as worse than dead (WTD). Q6 and Q7 were aimed at detecting the increased acceptance of living in a severe state when duration is shortened (or vice versa: decreased acceptance when duration is longered, as usually interpreted in MET). Q1--Q3 were asked if a state was valued in cTTO as better than dead with utility >0.1. Q4 was asked for states equivalent to being dead or with utility = 0.05 or 0.1. Q5--Q7 were asked for states WTD. Data from 148 respondents were collected via online interviews. Eeach respondent valued 6 EQ-5D-5L health states. Regarding discounting, no standard functional form seems to fit the observed pattern of responses. Depending on the TTOFU, either positive or negative time preference seems to prevail. These findings can be explained when QALY model is disregarded and it is assumed that quality-of-life and longevity are aggregated in an additive, not multiplicative, way, and that the durations are compared in a relative, not absolute, way. Regarding the fear of ID, it seems that is is equivalent to about 1.5 years in full health in the standard QALY model. This can explain at least partially the observed gap in the slightly negative values elicited with cTTO. Regarding MET, it was confirmed that shortening the duration increases the acceptance of a state, both when compared to ID and when comparing two different durations in the same state.

Title: Evaluating the Sensitivity and Validity of EQ-5D-Y-5L in Measuring HRQoL Among Obese and Non-Obese US Children: Insights from the Little Rock Green Schoolyard Initiative
Abstract: Background: The relevance of the EQ-5D-Y-5L may be limited for specific population groups due to potential shortcomings such as content validity, sensitivity, and its ability to discriminate between known groups, such as children with moderate/severe obesity or those with normal weight. This study aims to address these challenges by providing essential insights that could enhance the instrument's effectiveness and application. Research Objectives:  Examine how physical activity, sleep, and obesity status impact health-related quality of life (HRQoL), as measured by the EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-Y-3L, and Kidscreen-27 instruments, and analyze these effects across different age groups. Assess if changes in the obesity status of children from Fall 2024 to Spring 2025 correspond to changes in EQ-5D-Y-5L scores. Evaluate whether the EQ-5D-Y-5L can effectively differentiate between children with moderate/severe obesity and those of normal weight. Investigate the concurrent validity of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and Kidscreen-27 alongside established measures of physical activity and sleep, using both accelerometry and biometric data.  Study Population: Data will be collected from 243 children in grades 3-5 attending four community schools in the Little Rock School District participating in a green schoolyard program. Data Collection: Measures will include the EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-Y-3L, Kidscreen-27, physical activity, and sleep quality assessed through actigraphy. Additional physical activity data will be gathered through direct observations during recess and outside of school hours. Project Context: This study is part of a larger project funded by the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities, NIH (Award Number R01MD018192), now in its second year. Biannual data collection for HRQoL, school climate, and other observations is planned for Fall 2024 and Spring 2025. The study has successfully recruited 243 child-parent dyads, with enrollment of up to 10 per grade per school. This sample size will enable us to successfully achieved stated research objectives, consistent with the most recent COSMIN guidelines. The children's ages range from 8 to 12 years. Methods: State-of-the-art econometric and psychometric methods will be utilized to address the study's objectives. Expected Results: This research program will produce several high-quality publications for leading health economics journals and provide innovative insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the EQ-5D-Y-5L, addressing existing research gaps and aligning with EuroQol's research priorities.

Title: Testing the validity and responsiveness to change of the EQ-HWB-S in a 4-week online study evaluating the effects of mindfulness training for meditation app users with a range of mental health statuses; The Medito Study.
Abstract: BackgroundThe EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a new generic questionnaire designed to measure quality of life across healthcare, public health, and social care. A shorter version with nine questions (EQ-HWB-9) has been developed, but it needs to be tested in different populations to ensure it works as intended.In this study, we aimed to test the EQ-HWB-9 among adults who had downloaded a meditation app and were likely experiencing poorer mental health. We also examined whether proposed modifications to the questionnaire affected how well it performed. These changes included switching the order of the first two items and making three minor adjustments to the response options.MethodsThis study was conducted as part of a larger project investigating engagement with a free meditation app. Participants were randomly assigned to complete either the original version of the EQ-HWB-9 (from 2022) or a slightly modified version (from 2024). We assessed how well the questionnaire performed using standard psychometric tests, including how responses were distributed, whether the measure could distinguish between known groups, how closely it aligned with related measures, and how sensitive it was to change over time.ResultsParticipants completing the original and modified versions of the EQ-HWB-9 were similar in terms of their demographic characteristics at both baseline (n = 865) and follow-up (n = 130). Overall, the results showed that the EQ-HWB-9 performed well in this population. Changing the order of the first two questions appeared to be beneficial: when the activities question was presented first, it produced higher average scores, greater variation in responses, and stronger relationships with psychosocial items. No meaningful differences were found for the other minor changes made to the questionnaire.ConclusionsThese findings add to the growing evidence that the EQ-HWB-9 is a suitable tool for measuring quality of life across a wide range of settings. They also support a hypothesis from earlier qualitative work suggesting that when the activities question followed the mobility question (original version), respondents tended to think of activities in more physical terms. Placing the activities question first (modified version) seemed to encourage a broader interpretation, consistent with the intentions of the measure’s developers. On this basis, changing the order of the items appears justified. The other modifications had little impact, indicating that further qualitative research may be needed to guide such decisions. Overall, the results suggest that the instrument is ready for wider use, and that developing country-specific value sets will be essential to support its application in economic evaluations.

Title: EuroQol’s Data for the Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE) – A Bridge Grant
Abstract: The EQ-DAPHNIE Project aims to establish infrastructure for the EQ Group to assess population health using EQ instruments. It was funded for 3 years (2021-2024), with an intention to consider a second 3-year phase depending on the success of Phase 1. We have completed Round 1 survey in 5 countries, with predominantly English-speaking populations. This request is a 1-year bridge grant to maintain momemtum on the EQ-DAPHNIE project. Requested funds would support the EQ-DAPHNIE Team in 3 areas: 1) survey development and depolyment for Round 2 countries; 2) EQ member access to EQ-DAPHNIE data; 3) data analysis & knowledge translation. Remaining funds for the original EQ-DAPHNIE 3-year Phase 1 grant will be used to support the ongoing data collection for the planned 10 countries in Round 2.

Title: A travel grant to support a clinical application of PROMs in pediatrics with a focus on EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL
Abstract: The travel proposal would allow us to further in-depth study the application of the EQ-5D-Y as a PROM in children, and would allow me to extent my expertise using an international environment. My living costs are to a large extent covered by a grant from the Sino-Dutch Bilateral Exchange Scholarship. However, traveling abroad and working temporary elsewhere cannot be accommodate by this sources. Therefore, I would like to apply for a travel grant, so I can continue my research in the rich international environment the EuroQol network offers.  Exploring an international environment has been very beneficial for me so fare. As a PhD student supervised by Professor Jan Busschbach at Erasmus University Rotterdam, I specialize in validating EuroQol instruments for paediatric patients and their parental carers. With a background as a paediatrician at a Shanghai hospital, I aim to bridge clinical practice with research. Inspired by Professor Nancy Devlin's work at the University of Melbourne, I seek to explore the use of PROMs in clinical practice and health systems. I propose a visit to Melbourne, from June 2024 to March 2025, focuses on two objectives: conducting research on the clinical application of generic HRQoL instruments, notably the EQ-5D-Y in paediatric patients with rare diseases. This visit will then allow me to foster a research partnerships between Erasmus University Rotterdam, my hospital in Shanghai, and the University of Melbourne. Through this visit, I aim to gain insights into the potential role of PROM in clinical practice, enhance opportunities for the use of EQ-5D-Y in China and facilitate collaborations on future research projects relevant to my PhD studies and professional trajectory. During this 9-months study visit, I am keen to learn paediatric PROM co-design principles, embedding within an Electronic Medical Record (EMR), development of supporting clinical materials, and implementation skills which are all being progressed in the Australian context. I aim to immerse myself in the QUOKKA research projects, engage with the research team, attend seminars and meetings, and participate in discussions with PROMs end-users. Furthermore, I will have the opportunity to collaborate with several PhD students from the University of Melbourne's Health Economics team, who are also members of the EuroQol PhD network like myself. This will offer abundant collaboration opportunities, foster mutual learning among us and help establish a long-term partnership that extend beyond our graduation. Most importantly, I intend to contribute to a specific research project which outlined is describe below: Title: Exploring the Clinical Application of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) in Paediatrics: a Focus on the EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL  • Background: Despite the enthusiastic efforts and promising results of researchers, integrating PROMs into clinical practice poses challenges. For instance, a standard PROM scoring system does not exist and medical providers find it difficult to make clinical decisions using normative-based scores. Second, structural barriers within healthcare systems, including limited consultation time, lack of implementation recommendations, and prioritization of laboratory outcomes, may impede the seamless integration of PROMs. Third, successful integration relies on genuine co-design to meet the needs of clinicians and patients, as well as addressing challenges in embedding PROMs in the EMR, including feedback presentation formats to patients and clinicians. Moreover, using validated PROMs that have undergone psychometric processes to ensure that the PROM measures what is intended. Therefore, PROMs that are ideal for use in clinical practices are those that both assess important outcomes for patients and providers and are valid, reliable, and specific to the context of use for the disease under study. • Research Aim: The aim of this research is to study and explore how generic health-related quality of life instruments, such as the EQ-5D-Y-5L and Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL), can be used in routine clinical care as PROMs in paediatric patients with rare disease (ITP) or cancer (Neuroblastoma or Wilms tumour). Specifically, the study will focus on codesigning preferences for PROM integration with perspectives from patients, parental carers and clinicians, and piloting the use of PROMs in paediatric inpatient and outpatient settings. The following questions will be studied: a) Are generic measure of quality of life, like EQ-5D-Y-5L helpful in clinical consultation with individual patients? b) What is the added values of generic PROMs over disease specific measure? c) What are favourable characteristics of generic measure of quality of life needed to ensure usefulness? d) To what extent does the EQ-5D-Y-5L meet such characteristics? e) Are generic HRQoL measure helpful when assessing oriented related research and application, such as a measure of the productivity of the clinical unit and the effectivity of the interventions given? • Proposed methods: a) Study Design: we propose to conducted a longitudinal study including two time points, before and after treatment, and will employ a mixed-methods approach, incorporating both qualitative and quantitative methods. b) The local ethics approval will be applied once the funding has been approved. c) Participants: we aim to recruit paediatric patients and their parental carers in China from various disease severity levels, as determined by two clinical diagnosis: paediatric central nervous system solid tumour (Neuroblastoma or Wilms tumour), and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).Our goal is to enrol a total of 240 dyads consisting of children/adolescents and their parental carers at the baseline, i.e., 120 dyads for each disease group, with a follow-up rate of 70%. d) Data Collection: Patients will be asked to complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L and Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) during their clinic visits or hospital stays. Parents will be asked to complete the EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L. e) Data Analysis: In addition to validating the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL, our primary focus will be on investigating the acceptability and usefulness of these measures from the perspectives of both families and clinicians. We will prioritize assessing feasibility, response distribution, and construct validity, alongside exploring stakeholders' perspectives on PROM integration and utility in clinical care through qualitative data analysis of interviews and focus groups. Additionally, we will compare the performance of EQ-5D-Y instruments with PedsQL to understand their relative efficacy in paediatric clinical settings.

Title: From Routine Collection to Routine Care: Understanding the Barriers and Facilitators to Greater Adoption of PROMs in Clinical Practice
Abstract: Patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) that collect patients’ perspectives of their symptoms, quality of life (QoL) and functionality are increasingly being used in routine clinical settings, including oncology services. However, challenges in the implementation and uptake of PROMs and using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in the delivery of routine care remain. Collecting PROMs data without subsequently discussing the PRO results with the patients can demotivate them to answer subsequent questionnaires. In December 2020, the Northern Region Head and Neck Cancer Service began collecting PROMs: EQ-5D-5L as a generic measure and FACT-H&N as a more disease-specific measure of functional outcome. PROMs are routinely collected by the service across the duration of the patient's follow-up (at baseline around the time of diagnosis, then 6, 12, 18 and 24 months follow-up) but we have identified challenges in effectively using PROs in the routine clinically setting when discussing treatment and management. The primary objective of this study is to investigate factors that may be influencing (positively or negatively) the integration of PROs into routine clinical care. The study will also address the role of healthcare professionals in integrating PROMs and PROs into the clinic routine. We will use a qualitative research method, with focus group discussions using a semi-structured interview guide. The study population will be healthcare professionals (surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, pathologists, dentists and nurse specialists) from the northern region of Aotearoa New Zealand. The factors that we hope to identify from this study may be generalisable to other head and neck oncology services and, also oncology services more broadly. The findings of this study may be relevant to non-oncology services looking to implement PROMs successfully and use PROs at their routine clinic. We also expect the study to identify a number of other research questions and therefore 'seed' further research on the use of PROMs in clinical care.

Title: An international comparison of the impacts of COVID-19 using EQ-5D
Abstract: An effective vaccine is a key strategy for ending the COVID-19 pandemic, but even when vaccine is found and approved for use, most countries will have insufficient initial stockpiles to cover all those who would ideally be vaccinated. Consequently, choices will need to be made as to which groups are prioritised to receive a vaccine. One important criterion is the maximisation of individual health benefits. Evidence that allows decision makers to employ QALYs alongside other metrics (e.g. lives saved) when making difficult resource allocation decisions, such as prioritization of a COVID-19 vaccine, is crucial. Nested into a wider multi-country project to collate and elicit public preferences for prioritising access to a COVID-19 vaccine in up to 12 countries around the world, this project will focus on a key component of the QALY, which is to have contemporary values for population norms that reflect the impact of COVID-19 (e.g. the current social distancing measures) on aspects of health-related quality of life. We will assess the current and pre-COVID-19 health status of individuals using the EQ-5D and explore how health-related quality of life can be used as a metric for the prioritisation of vaccination for COVID-19. These will be achieved through primary data collection and appropriate statistical methods (before/after methods, pooled-data/ panel regression analysis; choice models) of international community survey data (including a choice experiment to identify public preferences for vaccine prioritisation).

Title: Head-to-Head Comparison of the Psychometric Performance of the EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, and Re-QoL in the general population and people with mental health problems
Abstract: Objectives: The EQ-Health and Wellbeing Short version (EQ-HWB-S) is a newly developed measure designed to assess health and wellbeing outcomes in economic evaluations of healthcare, social care, and public health interventions from the perspective of service users, patients, and their caregivers. As a comprehensive measure of health and wellbeing, it is essential to evaluate the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB-S, particularly in the context of mental health. This study aims to directly compare the performance of the EQ-HWB-S with two commonly used instruments: the EQ-5D-5L, a widely used generic measure of health-related quality of life, and the Recovering Quality of Life – Utility Index (ReQoL-UI), a condition-specific measure developed for individuals with mental health conditions. Comparisons are conducted in both the general population and among individuals with self-reported mental health problems. Methods: Data were used from an online survey administered to a representative sample of Australian general population aged 18 years and more including those with a mental health problem. Respondents completed the EQ-HWB-S, ReQoL-UI, EQ-5D-5L and Kessler psychological distress 6 items (K6) in a random order, followed by demographic questions, questions about current and past experience with mental health problems. We compared the measures in terms of convergent validity at instrument and item levels using Spearman’s rank correlation based on a validated clinical measure of psychological distress (Kessler 6 items). Known-group validity was assessed between groups with and without mental health problems using self-reported mental illness and the K6 scores with a clinical threshold of 19 or higher. Item Response Theory analysis was conducted based on graded response models after an explanatory factor analysis. Results: The psychometric analysis was conducted using a representative sample of 3,052 Australians. The EQ-HWB-S, ReQoL and EQ-5D-5L demonstrated convergent validity when compared against the K6. Notably, the EQ-HWB-S exhibited superior convergent validity, with all items of K6 moderately or highly correlated with the psychological items of EQ-HWB-S. Regarding the known-group validity, most EQ-HWB-S, ReQoL, EQ-5D-5L items demonstrated discriminative ability among known groups with mental health problems. Item Response Theory (IRT) analysis indicated that most items of the EQ-HWB-S, ReQoL and EQ-5D-5L had well-functioning response categories; however, several items showed evidence of differential item functioning. Conclusion: Preliminary findings using a large representative sample of Australians aged 18 and above support the legitimacy of the EQ-HWB-S as a potential outcome measure for mental health and well-being. Specifically, our findings show a convergence between EQ-HWB-S and the K6 while the EQ-HWB-S performed well in differentiating among individuals with mental health problems.

Title: Validity of breathing and cognition bolt-ons for the EQ-5D instrument in non-hospitalized patients after COVID-19
Abstract: The EQ-5D has been criticized for lacking dimensions for breathing and cognition. In acute COVID-19 and Long COVID, breathing problems and cognitive complaints are common. This study evaluated the inclusion of EQ-5D-5L (bolt-on) items that assess these dimensions.    In a follow-up of community-based non-hospitalized patients with COVID-19 in 2020 (n = 450), we used respiratory and cognitive bolt-on items alongside other questionnaires about 30 months later (n = 220). We assessed data quality and construct validity for the bolt-ons, including comparison with concurrently used instruments’ domain and item scores. Bolt-on scores were correlated with pulmonary function tests and tablet-based cognitive tests about 1 year earlier. Finally, we assessed the contribution of the bolt-ons to variability of the EQ VAS.   Most patients had none or slight problems with breathing and cognition. The breathing problems bolt-on had an 8% lower ceiling effect, but otherwise a similar response distribution to the mMRC. Cognition bolt-on and four DSQ-SF item scores relating to frequency and severity were similar, except 2–13% higher ceiling effects for the former. The breathing bolt-on had a rank correlation of 0.54 with mMRC scores and higher correlations with Dyspnoea-12 scale scores. EQ-5D-5L dimensions explained 54% of variation in EQ VAS scores; the breathing bolt-on contributed a further 2%, but the cognition bolt-on contributed very little.   The results support the validity of the two bolt-ons in follow-up of non-hospitalized patients after COVID-19. Adding items of respiratory and cognitive symptoms may enhance the EQ-5D's appropriateness in respiratory and cognitive research and clinical practice.

Title: Exploration of patient self-perceived burden to caregivers as a construct captured by existing EQ measures and assessing measurement properties of EQ-HWB as a measure for caregivers
Abstract: Aims: Self-perceived burden (SPB), a patient's perception of the burden their illness imposes on caregivers, is an emerging construct distinct from but related to caregiver burden. This project aimed to advance the understanding of SPB and its measurement, validate the EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S for assessing caregiver health and well-being, and explore novel approaches for capturing caregiver spillover effects. Methods: A prospective survey was conducted with 504 patient-caregiver dyads in the United States. Exploratory factor analysis was used to examine dimensionality of SPB in relation to EQ-5D, EQ-HWB, ASCOT-Carer, and Carer-QoL. Intraclass correlation coefficients were employed to assess the level of agreement between care recipients' two perspectives of SPB (their own assessment of SPB and their assessment of caregiver burden, called caregiver burden proxy) and caregivers' self-reported burden. The suitability of care recipients as proxies for caregivers was evaluated by examining the agreement between care recipient proxy assessments and caregiver self-assessments using EQ-5D-5L. Additionally, the measurement properties of EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S/EQ-5D-5L for caregivers were investigated in relation to other preference-based measures used for caregivers: ASCOT-Carer, Carer-QoL, and EQ-5D. Results: SPB emerged as a distinct construct, moderately related to EQ measures. Care recipients tended to underestimate the burden they impose compared to caregiver assessments but demonstrated potential to serve as proxies when adopting the caregiver's perspective for SPB (caregiver burden proxy) or assessing caregiver health-related quality of life using EQ-5D-5L. The findings supported the construct validity of EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S for assessing caregiver health and well-being. Notably, care recipient proxy assessments introduced a novel approach for capturing caregiver spillover effects in economic evaluations. Conclusion: This work advances EuroQol's research priorities by validating EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S for caregivers in the US, and exploring care recipient proxy assessments as an innovative method for capturing spillover effects.

Title: Randomised equivalence study to compare online interviews versus face-to-face interviews to value the EQ-5D-5L using cTTO: Australian arm
Abstract: Introduction: Valuation studies using composite time trade-off (cTTO) interviews have historically been conducted face-to-face. The COVID-19 pandemic forced a number of valuation studies to conduct their interviews online via videoconference. These studies reported that online interviews appeared feasible and acceptable; however, participants were not randomly allocated and there was no reporting of cTTO value equivalence. This study builds on its sister study from the UK and aims to assess the acceptability and equivalence of in person face-to-face interviews with online videoconferencing interviews on cTTO valuation outcomes and explore the impact of interview mode on attendance and on data quality. Methods: Participants were recruited via an external market research company from Greater Melbourne and Regional Victoria. A multi-stage stratified sampling approach was used, with quotas based on Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data for age, gender, geographical location, education level and income. Consenting participants were randomly allocated to complete a cTTO interview face-to-face or online with 1 of 4 trained interviewers. Participants who refused the interview after randomisation were contacted to offer reasons. Participants completed cTTO tasks for the same 10 EQ-5D-5L health states using EQ-VTv2 software. Mean and SD cTTO value overall and for each health state, participant understanding, data quality, demographic characteristics, participant preference, participant engagement and participant feedback were all compared across interview mode. Statistical equivalence for cTTO values for each state was tested using two one-sided t-tests by mode. Finally, regression analysis was completed to assess the impacts of interview mode on cTTO value while controlling for demographic characteristics of the participants. Results: Mean cTTO values were shown to be equivalent for mild health states and showed no significant difference for serious health states. Regressions analysis showed that mode of interview did not have any significant impact on mean cTTO values (p=.817). The proportion of individuals who did not accept their interview in the face-to face group (21.6%) was significantly larger than the proportion in the online group (1.8%) (p<0.0001). No between group difference in demographic characteristics was found. No significant difference was found between groups for participant engagement, understanding or feedback. No significant difference was found between groups for any indicators of data quality. Overall, 151 (37.4%) participants reported that they would have chosen to be interviewed online if given the choice, 51 (12.7%) would have preferred to be interviewed face-to-face and 201 (49.9%) did not mind. Discussion: The results from this study indicate that cTTO values obtained from face-to-face and online interviews are statistically significantly equivalent for mild health states. Regression analysis found no statistically significant association between health state value and mode when all the ten health states were combined. The data generated by both interview modes was of high quality and showed no significant difference. The majority of participants had no preference for interview mode however a larger proportion of participants preferred to be interviewed online rather than face-to-face, this preference was supported by the larger proportion of participants who did not accept their interview when randomised to face-to-face. Both online and face-to-face interviews appear to be equivalent and acceptable for conducting cTTO interviews.

Title: Response Scale Heterogeneity in the EQ-5D: Interpreting Response Categories Across Chronic Disease Populations in Argentina
Abstract: Background: Response scale heterogeneity (RSH) in the EQ-5D occurs when individuals systematically differ in how they interpret and use response categories, producing health self-assessments that are not comparable even when underlying health is equivalent. Qualitative evidence on the mechanisms underlying RSH remains sparse, and is virtually absent from low- and middle-income countries and non-English-speaking populations. Chronic conditions represent a particularly important context, as prolonged illness exposure and recalibration of internal standards can systematically alter how patients interpret response categories over time.Aim: This study aims to explore how patients with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and heart failure in Argentina interpret the response categories of the validated Spanish-language EQ-5D-5L, and to identify the individual and illness-related factors — including disease severity, disease duration, and age — that contribute to heterogeneity in this interpretation.Methods: An interpretive qualitative design will be used, comprising individual semi-structured interviews (n = 30–36) integrating an illness narrative, concurrent think-aloud EQ-5D-5L completion, and anchoring vignette exploration. Purposive sampling will ensure variation in disease severity, duration, and age, with at least 40% of participants aged 65 or older. We will use thematic analysis with a hybrid a priori and inductive codebook, conduct a systematic comparison across conditions, severity strata, disease duration, and age as a central analytical objective.Expected contribution: This study will generate the first qualitative evidence on EQ-5D-5L response category interpretation from a Spanish-speaking, Latin American population, with direct implications for data comparability, instrument administration, and the generalisability of EQ-5D value sets.

Title: Visit to National University of Singapore to complete and develop EuroQol projects
Abstract: This travel grant supported a visit to Singapore to meet with stakeholders interested in using PROMs including the EQ-5D in the Singapore health system, and researchers conducing studies using routine collected EQ-5D to inform clinical decisions with PROM based decision aids. This was facilitated by a research rounds presentations at the NUS School of Public Health, and Singhealth Primary Healthcare.

Title: Organizing an EQ-5D-Y workshop in Asia at the ISPOR Asia Pacific Summit 2022 (a virtual event)
Abstract: Substantial research efforts have been devoted to validate the EQ-5D-Y and to establish its value sets in Asia. It is also crucial to inform the users and researchers about the progress and the availability of this instrument. ISPOR Asia-Pacific Summit provides a great platform to present this instrument and its use to users and researchers from this region. After discussion, this team decided to deliver an introductory workshop to the attendees of 2022 ISPOR Asia-Pacific Summit. In this workshop, we aimed to help the users and researchers in this Asia-Pacific region to know about EQ-5D-Y and the research progress within this region. We also aimed to provide researchers practical guidance and tips on obtaining and using this instrument in their studies. The workshop entitled ‘The EQ-5D-Y(Youth) in the Asia-Pacific: What is it, how to get it, and how to use it?’ was accepted and in total, we delivered a one-hour workshop covering 4 pre-recorded pitches, two presentations and a Q&A session. The pre-recorded pitches were prepared incorporating the EuroQol whiteboard animations and were subtitled with both Chinese and English. As a virtual event, the workshop was recorded and can be played by registered attendees. After the meeting, the 4 pitches were placed online at Zhihu.com (similar to Quora, which shares knowledge), which can be accessed by researchers, students, and clinicians in China and beyond. In total, we counted 20+ live attendees and 229 hits on Zhihu.com (from 20 Sep to 05 Nov 2022). The number of attendees viewed the workshop at ISPOR was not formally recorded.

Title: Terror Management Theory: a new observation window on TTO and VAS
Abstract: Background: Several factors influencing the Time Trade-off (TTO) health measure are known. In TTO studies, respondents report thoughts related to death. According to Terror Management Theory (TMT), mortality awareness gives rise to anxiety and increases death thought accessibility (DTA), which can be mitigated by secure attachment. This explorative study aims to find additional factors influencing the TTO and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) health measures. Based on TMT, the role of DTA and attachment is explored. Research questions: 1) Does DTA occur in TTO and VAS methods, 2) How are DTA and attachment related to TTO and VAS measures. We hypothesize that 1) DTA is higher when respondents are confronted with TTO or VAS measures and, 2) TTO scores are higher in those with a better attachment style. Methods: In an online experiment, members of the general public were randomised to one of four conditions: 1) TTO, 2) VAS, 3) Mortality Salient (MS), and 4) control. In conditions 1 and 2, TTO and VAS valuation methods were used to obtain scores for a hypothetical wheelchair health state, and for self-experienced health. The MS and control conditions served as manipulation checks. ANOVAs were performed to compare the four conditions, correcting for multiple comparisons. Pearson’s correlations were used to assess the relationship between TTO/VAS and DTA/attachment. Results: 4572 respondents were included. The MS condition showed elevated DTA. Unexpectedly, DTA levels in the TTO condition tended to be lower than in the control condition. Associations between DTA and TTO were absent. Associations between DTA and VAS scores were negative for the wheelchair health state (p < .013), and for self-experienced health (p < .005). Attachment was associated with the health measures for self-experienced health (TTO and VAS, p < 0.001), but not with scores for the hypothetical wheelchair state. Conclusion: DTA emerged as a novel factor influencing hypothetical and self-experienced VAS scores. Attachment was identified as a novel factor influencing self-experienced TTO and VAS scores. All associations were weak in the order of -0.15. Unexpectedly, the DTA in the TTO condition tended to be lower than in the control condition. Reasons for these results are discussed.

Title: Mapping EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L to EQ-5D-Y-5L in Young Children to Enable Preference-Weighting EQ-TIPS Using EQ-5D-Y Value Sets
Abstract: Introduction EuroQol plans to take EQ-TIPS from its current ‘experimental’ status to launch as an approved version – but this requires establishing robust methods for preference weighting EQ-TIPS data. However, both existing (EQ-VT) and emerging (non-linear DCE methods) methods used by EuroQol to generate anchored values for its instruments are likely to be problematic in eliciting (anchored) values for EQ-TIPS states (Devlin et al., Forthcoming). EuroQol’s YPWG and VWG have therefore identified response mapping between the EQ-TIPS-5L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L as a potential solution. Aim The primary aims of this study are: (a) To explore a range of different mapping approaches between the EQ-TIPS-5L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L, and (b) drawing on an international data set (which is the basis of a separate proposal), to produce a mapping function that can be used internationally to preference weight EQ-TIPS-5L data using local EQ-5D-Y-5L value sets. Data Exploratory methodological work can begin immediately using the Australian Paediatric Multi-Instrument Comparison (P-MIC) study, which includes EQ-TIPS-3L Version 2 (V2) — available only in a 3-level format — alongside adapted and original EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L data. As there are n=140 paired EQ-TIPS-3L (V2) and EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L responses and n=400 paired EQ-TIPS-3L (V2) and EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L adapted responses for children aged 2-4 years all of these pairs will explored in the exploratory work. Although the final mapping will rely on the latest version of EQ-TIPS-5L Version3 (V3), P-MIC provides a valuable foundation for early proof-of-concept and methodological development. Methods tested using P-MIC data (and other, new data as they become available) will be used to develop a final mapping, which will use new international datasets with parallel EQ-TIPS-5L V3 and EQ-5D-Y-5L data from Australia, Canada, and Argentina. [Note: Parallel data collection of the EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y will be coordinated by the EuroQol office and the YPWG; a proposal outlining multiple data collection studies will be submitted separately]. Methods The primary focus will be on estimating and evaluating the performance of models using a range of response mapping techniques—including multinomial logit regression, ordinal logistic regression, and non-parametric approaches—to predict EQ-5D-Y-5L responses from EQ-TIPS-5L responses, allowing Y-5L value sets to be used to preference weight EQ-TIPS-5L. The final dataset will be split into estimation and validation samples. Model selection will primarily be based on predictive accuracy in the validation sample, with additional consideration given to performance across different severity levels. In addition to statistical mapping, we will explore two complementary approaches to support and validate the relationship between EQ-TIPS-5L (V3) and EQ-5D- Y-5L: vignette-based assessment and VAS-based analysis. First, qualitative methods will be used to derive comparative utility estimates by asking clinical experts in paediatrics and early childhood development, alongside caregivers, rate hypothetical child health scenarios described using EQ-TIPS-5L (V3) and EQ-5D-Y-5L descriptors—an approach similar to that used in the Health Utilities Preschool (HUPS) study for mapping to HUI3 utilities (Furlong et al., 2023). Second, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) data, available in both instruments, will be used to explore descriptive consistency. A descriptive analysis of the EQ-TIPS-5L V3 and EQ-5D-Y-5L profiles that correspond to each of the VAS digit clusters will also be examined, supported by data visualisations. This combination of statistical, qualitative, and descriptive methods will help triangulate the validity of the utility estimates generated through mapping and strengthen the credibility of the resulting value set for EQ-TIPS.

Title: Exploring the use of multi-dimensional Item Response Theory to analyse EuroQol Instruments
Abstract: Objective: Psychometric evaluation of the EQ-5D-5L to date has largely relied on classical test theory or unidimensional item response theory approaches that do not account for its multidimensional structure. This study evaluated the dimensionality, item performance, and stability of the EQ-5D-5L using multidimensional item response theory (MIRT) models reinforced with items from other patient-reported outcome measures.Methods: Confirmatory factor analysis and MIRT were applied across two datasets: the Multi-Instrument Comparison (MIC) study (n=5,487) and the E-QALY psychometric survey (n=903). Each dataset was conceptually mapped to identify relevant non-EQ-5D-5L items to overidentify each EQ-5D-5L domain in a MIRT model. EQ-5D-5L IRT parameter stability was assessed by removing non-EQ-5D-5L items, either one-by-one with replacement, or sequentially without replacement and estimating the change in standardised discrimination parameters and visually inspecting information curves. Results: Both datasets supported three-dimensional EQ-5D-5L MIRT structures (Physical Function including EQ-5D-5L mobility/self-care/usual activities and separate Pain/Discomfort, and Anxiety/Depression dimensions) with good model fit. EQ-5D-5L items demonstrated strong standardised discrimination parameters (MIC: 0.886-0.971; E-QALY: 0.780-0.916). Parameter stability varied by the conceptual breadth of factors. EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort was stable even with few anchoring items, reflecting narrow conceptual focus. Physical Function and Anxiety/depression exhibited greater sensitivity when item pools diminished, as imbalances occurred in how well the EQ-5D-5L concepts were covered.Conclusions: MIRT models reinforced with non-EQ-5D-5L items provide a feasible approach to inform psychometric evaluation of the EQ-5D-5L. Parameter stability requires sufficient item coverage reflecting EQ-5D-5L content, with attention to both total item number and conceptual breadth within factors.

Title: Psychometric Evaluation of EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y in Malaysian Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
Abstract: Background: Measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children is a global priority, yet major evidence gaps remain in low- and middle-income countries, particularly in multi-ethnic Southeast Asia. The EQ-5D-Y is available in a three-level version (Y-3L) and, since September 2024, a formally approved five-level version (Y-5L). Whether the Y-5L offers meaningful advantages over the Y-3L in neurodevelopmental conditions remains unclear. No study has simultaneously examined responsiveness, proxy-child agreement, and cross-ethnic measurement equivalence of both EQ-5D-Y versions in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).Methods: We propose a comprehensive psychometric study of EuroQol paediatric instruments in Malaysian children with ASD across the full age range (n≈400). Children aged under 3 years will be assessed using EQ-TIPS-5L (proxy only). Children aged 5–17 years will complete the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, by proxy only for ages 5–7 years and by both self-report and proxy for ages 8–17 years. A transition cohort aged 3–5 years will complete both EQ-TIPS-5L and EQ-5D-Y by proxy to examine transition between instruments. The PedsQL 4.0 Generic Core Scales and proxy-reported Quality of Life in Autism Spectrum Disorder scale will serve as comparators. Data will be collected at baseline, 2-week follow-up, and 3-month follow-up.Impact: Psychometric evaluation will include construct validity, reliability, responsiveness, ceiling effects, proxy-child agreement, instrument transition, and exploratory cross-ethnic measurement equivalence. Findings will address EuroQol Younger Populations Working Group priorities and inform guidance on paediatric instrument selection in diverse populations.

Title: As if there were (no) tomorrow: the association between time perspective profile and self-reported health on the EQ-5D
Abstract: Objectives: Few previous studies reported significant associations between EQ-5D responses and different psychological characteristics, such as personality, locus of control and optimism. Time perspective (TP) is a psychological construct that describes how one subjectively focuses on the past, present and future. TP has been found to be associated with several health-related behaviours, including healthy eating, smoking and adherence to medications. It is possible that two people with different psychological traits and the same health status rate their health differently, which is commonly referred to as response heterogeneity. Cut-point shift, a form of response heterogeneity, occurs if certain subgroups of respondents use systematically different category thresholds when self-reporting health. In this study, we aim to examine the associations of TP profile with self-reported health on the EQ-5D and to detect which EQ-5D domains display cut-point shift for TP. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of EQ-5D-5L data from a representative general population sample in Hungary (n=996). The 17-item Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory was used to measure individuals' TP on five subscales: past-negative (PN), past-positive (PP), present-fatalist (PF), present-hedonist (PH) and future (F). The associations between TP subscales and EQ-5D-5L domain scores were analysed by using partial proportional odds models adjusting for socio-demographic (age, gender, education, income) and health status (12 chronic health conditions). We used an iterative procedure to allow the parallel-lines constraint to be relaxed for those TP subscales that drive response heterogeneity. The results are reported in odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. The associations between TP subscales and EQ VAS and EQ-5D-5L index scores were analysed by multivariate linear regressions adjusting for socio-demographic and health status. Results: Respondents that scored higher on the PN and PF and lower on the PH and F subscales were more likely to report more health problems in at least one EQ-5D-5L domain (p<0.05). Adjusting for socio-economic and health status, three EQ-5D-5L domains exhibited significant associations with various TP subscales (usual activities: PF and F, pain/discomfort: PN and F, anxiety/depression: PN, PF, PH and F). The anxiety/depression domain showed evidence of cut-point shift; individuals with higher PH or F scale scores were less likely to report moderate-to-extreme problems vs. no or slight problems (PH: 0.58, 95%CI 0.40-0.86 and F: 0.42, 95%CI 0.26-0.69) relative to slight-to-extreme problems vs. no problems (PH: 0.90, 95%CI 0.73-1.10 and F: 0.75, 95%CI 0.57-0.99). Adjusting for socio-demographic and health status, EQ VAS scores were associated with PN, PF, PH and F and EQ-5D-5L index scores with PF and F subscales. Respondents’ TP profile increased the explained variance in EQ VAS from 26.6% to 30.2% and in EQ-5D-5L index from 30.9% to 32.6%. Conclusions: This is the first study to explore the association between individuals’ TP and self-reported health on the EQ-5D and also the first to identify response heterogeneity (cut-point shift) stemming from psychological characteristics in the EQ-5D. These findings increase our understanding of the non-health-related factors that affect self-reported health and the potential sources of bias in QALYs and cost-effectiveness outcomes.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Impact of EQ-5D-5L Arabic level 4 changes on preferences. Are corrections needed for value sets?
Abstract: BackgroundThe Version Management Committee (VMC) has identified a potential issue with the Arabic versions of EQ-5D-5L, whereby the label for level 4 was translated in a way that more closely corresponds to “acute” rather than “severe”. To address this issue, all Arabic versions will be updated with revised level 4 labels that more accurately reflect the intended meaning. Several EQ-5D-5L value sets developed in Arabic speaking countries, including Egypt, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, were originally based on the version containing “acute” label. At present, it is unclear whether the revised wording will have any impact on these existing value sets. The VMC has therefore requested that the VWG investigates whether the label change results in any meaningful differences in valuation outcomes.ObjectivesTo assess whether the relative position of the level 4 labels on a preference-based scale differs significantly between the original and revised labels.MethodsOnline latent scale DCE surveys will be conducted in two Arabic-speaking countries: Egypt and Saudi Arabia. In each country, a representative sample of 1000 respondents will be included, with half completing valuation tasks using the original level 4 labels (Group A), and the other half using the revised labels (Group B). Each respondents will complete 12 DCE choice pairs as used in the EQ-VT DCE design. Data from each country will be analyzed separately using mixed logit models with supplementary scaling parameters to identify differences between groups A and B. These supplementary parameters will allow us to determine whether there are significant differences in the relative importance assigned to level-dimension combinations, whilst accounting for differences in scale and response consistency between the groups.Potential ImplicationsIf no significant differences are observed between the two groups in either country, it is unlikely that the revised labels will materially affect existing EQ-5D-5L value sets. However, if significant differences are identified, it may become necessary to adjust existing value sets developed using the original Arabic level 4 labels. The current study is explorative in nature, and is intended as an initial assessment of whether meaningful differences exist. If that is the case, the VWG will prepare a follow-up proposal outlining potential approaches for revising existing value sets.

Title: Data collection to support developing a crosswalk between EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: Background With the EQ-TIPS descriptive system nearly finalized, the next step is to develop value sets. Given that existing valuation protocols require major adaptation for young children, mapping to the EQ-5D-Y is being explored as a viable alternative. Mapping is widely used when instruments share similar measurement properties and is the preferred strategy of both the Valuation and Youth Working Groups for EQ-TIPS value development. Objective This proposal aims to support value set development through mapping by collecting a dataset aligned with the final EQ-TIPS descriptive system. Methods An online cross-sectional survey will be conducted among parents of children aged 24 to 59 months with a chronic health condition confirmed by a healthcare professional. The survey will use infrastructure from the EQ-DAPHNIE project and include both the EQ-TIPS-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, presented in random order. The questionnaire will follow a modular format, with 4–5 modules (60–70 items), covering demographics, child health, family impact, and optional topics such as healthcare use or methodological enhancements. Participants will be recruited by Dynata in 10 countries where both instruments are available in a local language. Screening, consent, and quota management will ensure a balanced sample across severity and disease types. Data Handling and Quality Control The survey will be hosted by Maths in Health, with respondent IDs deleted after panel rewards are confirmed. As this is not a research project, only data cleaning will be performed, including attention checks, response consistency, and other quality indicators.

Title: Psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L, bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB
Abstract: Aims of the PhD proposal The overall aims of this PhD proposal is to allow a PhD student to gain theoretical knowledge of and practical experience in the following three topics: 1) assessing the psychometric performance of bolt-on items alongside the EQ-5D-5L, and 2) explore psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-S and the relationship with other instruments that measure health and well-being across countries and within sub-groups of countries.  Data-analysis and datasets The PhD student will gain practical experience with a range of data-analysis techniques, including techniques to explore psychometric performance and factor analysis. We will use the POPCORN dataset. The POPCORN study is a multi-country longitudinal study. Data were collected among an adult general population sample at T1 (April-May, 2020), T2 (May-June, 2021) and T3 (May-June, 2022). The POPCORN questionnaires have core modules that include several instruments to measure health and well-being. In the design of the POPCORN survey, extra questions (e.g. bolt-on items) have been added for methodological purposes, outside the primary research objectives of POPCORN study itself.  Supervision Bas Janssen and Juanita Haagsma will be the lead supervisors of the PhD candidate. Juanita Haagsma has 10 years of experience supervising PhD students.  Employment of PhD student During the PhD trajectory, the PhD student will be employed at the Department of Public Health, section Health Technology Assessment and Implementation, of the Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, The Netherlands. Duration The duration of the PhD proposal is three years. This time period is needed to reach the criteria to qualify for the PhD according to Department of Public Health standards. Deliverables The PhD project will result in at least 5 peer-reviewed international academic publications; out of these, 4 as first-author and 1 second-author, at least one (poster) presentation at the EuroQol Academy meeting and at least one (poster) presentation at an international conference and a PhD thesis (open access on the Erasmus University website) that meets the criteria of the Department of Public Health, Erasmus MC.

Title: Potential applications of the EQ Health and Wellbeing Short in health technology assessment (HTA)
Abstract: The following was presented as a workshop at ISPOR Europe 2024 in Barcelona Spain. ISPOR Europe is a health economic and outcomes research (HEOR) conference that is attended by those working in industry, academia, government and more. This year ISPOR Europe 2024 had more than 6,5000 attendees. This is the abstract that was submitted to ISPOR: Going Beyond Health-Related Quality of Life: Towards a Broader QALY Measure for Use Across Sectors: Introducing the EQ Health and Wellbeing Short (EQ-HWB-S) Discussion Leader: Aureliano Paolo Paolo Finch, PhD, The University of Economic Studies, Amsterdam, NH, Netherlands; Discussants: Jeremy Dietz, MSc, Science Policy & Research Programme, National Institute for Health and Care Excelllence, Bristol, BST, UK; Reva Efe, MD, MSc, Geneesmiddelenbeoordeling, Zorginstituut Nederland, Diemen, NH, Netherlands; Andrew Lloyd, DPhil, Acaster Lloyd, London, London, UK PURPOSE: ‘Value measurement: Assessing Value and QALY Alternatives’ remains a key trend in health economics and outcomes research. The goal of this workshop is to raise awareness of the EQ-HWB (EQ Health and Wellbeing instrument). The workshop will also explore the opportunities and strengths perceived by the speakers and audience on using the EQ-HWB-S, both from the perspective of health technology assessment (HTA) agencies and industry. DESCRIPTION: The EQ-HWB has been designed as a standardised measure of broader aspects of quality of life related to health, social care and informal carers enabling assessment of interventions that are delivered in health, including public health, and social care. A short version, the EQ-HWB-S, can be used to generate QALYs for HTA. The instrument has experimental status which has enabled collaborators and researchers to assess its performance in diverse populations. ZIN, the HTA agency for the Netherlands, has named it as a potential measure for use when evaluating interventions in chronic conditions. Understanding the views of those who will use the tool and appraise it are important to consider. In this workshop, Mr. Dietz will discuss the NICE reference case in relation to where deviations from the EQ-5D are allowed (10 minutes). Mr Finch will introduce the EQ-HWB and how it was developed and emerging evidence on its performance (10 minutes). Dr Efe will talk about ZIN’s decision to include the EQ-HWB in their methods document, ‘Guideline for economic evaluations in healthcare (2024 version)’ (10 minutes). Mr Lloyd will discuss their plans to use the EQ-HWB and provide an industry perspective (10 minutes). The workshop will allocate 20 minutes for an interactive audience discussion, including question and answer sessions. Audience views of the instrument and its potential use will be sought using polling to encourage active participation and engagement.

Title: A systematic literature review of the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-5L in conditions with itch to support the IP dossier of the ‘psoriasis bolt-ons’
Abstract: IntroductionItch is a burdensome symptom across dermatological and non-dermatological systemic conditions which can impact health-related quality of life (HRQoL). In some countries, patients’ access to treatments is partly dependent on data from EQ-5D-5L to demonstrate the HRQoL benefits of a treatment. Therefore, the instrument’s sensitivity to itch is important. This systematic literature review aimed to identify and summarise published evidence relating to the EQ-5D-5L’s measurement properties in conditions where itch is a key symptom in adults.MethodsA systematic literature search was conducted using Ovid (Embase and MEDLINE) according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines in February 2025 (PROSPERO No.: CRD420250650978). Included articles underwent quality assessment using two quality assessment tools, an adapted Grading of Recommendations Assessement, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) for quantitative studies and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist for qualitative studies.ResultsSearches identified 73 articles for final data extraction. Studies were conducted across 25 countries, covering 17 different dermatological conditions (e.g. psoriasis) and 9 non-dermatological (e.g. kidney diseases) conditions. Twenty-four publications were dedicated to the evaluation of psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L. No studies were excluded based on quality assessment. All n=5 included qualitative studies were ‘Acceptable’ quality (CASP). Within quantitative studies (n=68), n=15, n=52, and n=1 were graded as high, medium, and low quality respectively (GRADE). Qualitative investigations of content validity (n=5) reported that the EQ-5D-5L was comprehensible and relevant. Of three studies exploring missing concepts, social relationships was most commonly highlighted as missing. Itch was reported missing in one study and was the most frequent spontaneously reported symptom in another study.Evidence was found for convergent validity (n=32), known-groups validity (n=25), responsiveness (n=20), ceiling effects (n=20), and test-retest reliability (n=1). The EQ-5D-5L demonstrated some evidence of being able to discriminate between known-groups defined by symptom presence or condition severity. There was mixed evidence for convergent validity between the EQ-5D-5L and other HRQoL measures as correlations varied from weak to strong associations. There was also insufficient evidence to support the responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L, many articles reported change over time however only few studies assessed the change in EQ-5D-5L against changes in other validated measures.ConclusionsThis review identified a large number of studies demonstrating mixed evidence of psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L in conditions where itch is a key symptom, predominantly in dermatological conditions. Further studies are needed to strengthen the evidence base for under-researched measurement properties and to assess the potential value of the skin irritation (itch) bolt-on from the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox across different conditions.

Title: An EQ-5D multilayered measure of HRQoL: what are the perspectives of key stakeholders?
Abstract: In response to the limitations of the EQ-5D descriptive system, approaches such as addition of condition specific ‘bolt-on’ are being explored with the aim of improving the measurement sensitivity and relevance of EQ-5D in specific disease contexts. The Descriptive System Working Group (DSWG) of the EuroQol Group has proposed a different approach where the EQ-5D will be developed as a multi-level hierarchical instrument, where dimension specific items (or Dimension Specific Modules (DSM)) will be developed and nested below each of the existing five core dimensions. This project seeks to understand, from the perspective of key prospective users, the relevance, and expectations from such an instrument. This will be done via semi structured interviews with key international stakeholders from industry, government, academia and decision making contexts. The interviews will be guided by ‘mock DSMs’ for Mobility and Pain/Discomfort which will be developed using existing items from other instruments measuring the same, or overlapping constructs, identified by a targeted literature review. The ‘mock DSM’ will be used to facilitate the planned interviews, provide an example, and generate appropriate responses from study participants. We are proposing this approach on the basis that, provision of a ‘mock DSM’ during the interviews will put the subject matter in context and generate appropriate responses from study participants. Key prospective users of a DSM will be recruited internationally. Interviews will be conducted virtually, recorded, and transcribed for analysis. Thematic and content analysis of the transcribed data will be conducted, and the results presented in a de-identified manner.

Title: Testing the feasibility and acceptability of the EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol in adolescents and adults in Pakistan
Abstract: This 18-month study (Project 344-VS), funded from 1 July 2022 to 1 January 2024, aimed to develop Pakistan’s first nationally representative EQ-5D-Y-3L value set. The primary objective was to generate youth-specific utility weights to support equity-focused health technology assessment (HTA) and inform Universal Health Coverage (UHC) decision-making in the country. The valuation study followed a mixed-methods design in accordance with the EuroQol Group’s standardized protocol, incorporating both discrete choice experiments (DCE) and composite time trade-off (cTTO) tasks.The study was implemented in two sequential phases. The first phase involved a national stakeholder consultation held in Islamabad to contextualize the EQ-5D-Y-3L framework, introduce HTA principles, and emphasize the importance of valuation data in guiding resource allocation. Twelve stakeholders from across Pakistan and diverse professional backgrounds participated in a 3.5-hour session. Discussions focused on the need for a national youth value set, appropriate sources of health preferences (adults vs. adolescents), ethical concerns related to valuing life-years, and implementation challenges. Stakeholders acknowledged that while QALYs are not yet widely adopted in Pakistan’s health system, instruments like EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L are increasingly used for research and evidence generation. There was consensus that adolescents aged 11 and above could meaningfully engage in valuation tasks and should be included in data collection. One-third of stakeholders (4 out of 12) recommended using adult preferences initially due to technical and financial constraints. The remaining participants supported involving adolescents, either concurrently or in future phases. Ethical concerns regarding life-year trade-offs for children were not viewed as significant barriers. Parents or caregivers were considered the most suitable proxies when self-reporting by children was not feasible. Key challenges identified included limited awareness of QALYs among policymakers, scarce local utility data, technical capacity gaps, and restricted health budgets.In the second phase, a sample of 1,000 respondents for DCE and 1,000 for cTTO was recruited from the general population (aged 18+) across six major cities Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar, Quetta, Islamabad, and Rawalpindi representing all four provinces and the federal capital. Participants were drawn from both urban and surrounding rural areas and stratified by residence, age, gender, religion (Muslim, Hindu, Christian), and ethnicity (Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashtun, Balochi, Kashmiri, and others) to reflect national demographics. Initial data collection was completed within the grant period. However, to enhance data validity during the analysis phase, supplementary data collection was undertaken at no additional cost with approval from the EuroQol Executive Board. This led to a minor timeline extension, and the overall study was completed by mid-June 2025. Data cleaning and analysis followed immediately. The most frequently reported health problem was anxiety/depression (54.9% in the cTTO sample), while self-care had the fewest reported issues. Pain/discomfort had the greatest influence on preference values; usual activities had the least. Mean EQ VAS scores were slightly higher in the DCE sample (81.02) than the cTTO sample (78.27). All models demonstrated logical consistency. The Pakistani EQ-5D-Y-3L values ranged from –0.34 (worst health state: 33333) to 1.00 (full health: 11111), with 11112 valued at 0.96. All planned deliverables were produced.

Title: Online Personal Utility Function (OPUF) estimation based on Adaptive Discrete Choice Analysis with sign and monotonicity constraints
Abstract: This project aims to a) extend individually adaptive D-efficient DCEs with sign and monotonicity constraints to be able to elicit individualized preferences for the EQ-5D-5L, b) to estimate individual preferences for the EQ-5D-5L - with or without making use of the exact same sign and monotonicity constraints to increase statistical power in the estimations as well, and c) to provide internal validation of the preference estimates by asking respondents to reflect on summary graphs of their estimated preferences. The ultimate goal of this project is stand-alone individual-level preference estimation for the EQ-5D-5L; however, it should be emphasized that the same methods could also provide a valuable extension to the upcoming DCE with duration protocol, given that it would accomodate the estimation of heterogeneous time preferences and statistical identification of low-quality respondents in DCE valuation studies of larger instruments, such as the EQ-HWB.

Going beyond life expectancy– Examining health inequalities in quality adjusted life expectancy (QALE) in Australia
Abstract: We undertook a study to examine the potential health inequality using quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE) as an index for future public health policy formulation. Via surveying over 2000 participants, it was found that the gap in QALE is wider than that in life expectancy when comparing the major cities with the remote/very remote areas in Australia. There appeared some intersectional differences in utility values, life expectancy and QALE.

Title: Extending the QALY Valuation Study in England
Abstract: Objective: The first aim was to test the feasibility of using time trade-off (cTTO) and discrete choice experiment (DCE) administered using the EuroQol Valuation Technology research protocol to derive utilities for the EQ-HWB-S. The second aim was to review the acceptability of the new measure for decision-making with informed members fo the public. Methods: EQ-HWB-S utilities were elicited using cTTO and DCE tasks with adaptations to fit the new measure. Participants (target n=600) from the UK general population were sampled based on age, sex and ethnicity. Interviews were undertaken using video-conferencing. Quality control (QC) steps were used to assess interviewers’ performance throughout the study. Data were modelled using linear, Tobit, probit and hybrid models. Feasibility was assessed based on the evaluation of the distribution of cTTO data, QC assessment and regression modelling results. Regression results were assessed based on theoretical considerations, monotonicity and statistical significance. For the second aim, members of the NICE Public Involvement Programme Expert Panel were invited to participate, with volunteers selected to represent varying age, gender, health and caring responsibilities. To familiarise the group with the measure and the source of the weights, each person completed a valuation interview (time trade-off (TTO) and discrete choice experiment (DCE)). This was followed by a cognitive debrief and information giving group session, where the weights from the feasibility valuation study were presented. Two subsequent separate focus groups obtained views regarding the measure, the utility weights, the sample (including exclusions) and the methods used. All sessions took place online. Focus groups were recorded, transcribed, and analysed using a framework approach. Results: There were 521 participants who provided cTTO and DCE data. The demographic characteristics were broadly representative of the UK general population although participants were more educated and there were slightly more females. Interviewers met QC requirements. cTTO values ranged between -1 to 1 with increasing disutility associated with more severe states. The hybrid Tobit heteroscedastic model had values ranging from -0.384 to 1. Pain, mobility, daily activities, sad/depressed had the largest disutilities followed by loneliness, anxiety, exhaustion, control and cognition in this model. Twelve people (50% female, aged 28-74) completed the interviews and nine attended the focus groups to assess feasibility. EQ-HWB-S was viewed positively due to the inclusion of dimensions such as exhaustion and loneliness. Some missing dimensions were identified (e.g. coping, sleep), but existing dimensions were considered to cover some of these (e.g. sleep covered by exhaustion). There was surprise at the small utility decrements for anxiety, control and exhaustion relative to other dimensions. Weights were seen as reflecting societal norms, respondent experience or knowledge, the composition of the sample and the interpretation of items. There were concerns that the valuation survey sample was not diverse or large enough to adequately represent the values of those who would be impacted by decisions based on EQ-HWB-S. Participants only supported data exclusions where it could be evidenced by multiple sources that the respondent did not understand or fully engage in the exercise. Other exclusions were considered problematic either because the data could reflect true preferences or for ethical reasons. DCE was preferred to TTO, but participants suggested TTO could be improved by providing more background information, different practice states, particularly the wheelchair state, and offering post-survey debriefs.

Title: Evaluating Changes to the EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S: Examining the Psychometric Properties Using Modern Test Theory of Merged Double-Barreled Items (Concentrating/Thinking Clearly and Walking Inside/Outside) in the EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S among Patients and Caregivers
Abstract: This study evaluated the psychometric properties of two specific composite items in the EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S compared to their single-domain counterparts from the E-QALY project: (1) "Concentrating/Thinking Clearly" versus the separate "Concentrating" and "Thinking Clearly" items, and (2) "Walking Inside/Outside" versus the separate "Walking Inside" and "Walking Outside" items. Using a combination of classical and modern psychometric analysis of 504 US caregiver-patient dyads, we examined convergent validity, structural validity, item response characteristics, and differential item functioning. Results demonstrated strong correlations (r=0.70-0.78), substantial agreement (κ=0.69-0.79), robust factor loadings (0.877-0.976), and comparable information functions across the latent trait continuum. Both composite items showed acceptable discrimination parameters and minimal differential item functioning across caregiver and patient populations, supporting their validity for measuring cognitive and mobility constructs while offering potential for enhanced efficiency in health utility assessment.

Title: Psychometric properties of the EQ-5D in rare ataxia diseases (EQ-5D-ATAX)
Abstract: Background: There is a lack of evidence about the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-3L in patients with rare diseases. To address this gap, we assessed the acceptability, validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-3L in patients with rare Spinocerebellar Ataxia (SCA) and Friedreich Ataxia (FA). Methods: We analyzed data from three prospective, longitudinal observational ataxia cohort studies that recruited patients from various European and US clinical study centers. We evaluated the EQ-5D-3L in terms of acceptability, distributional properties, convergent and known-groups validity, reliability and responsiveness. Additionally, we analyzed the EQ-5D-3L's ability to capture health changes by analyzing factors influencing the patient's HRQoL progression using multivariate panel data regression models. Results: The EQ-5D-3Ls non-item response was low (<5%). Convergent validity was satisfied by comparing EQ-5D-3L/EQ-VAS with ataxia severity (SARA) and functional impairment (FARS-ADL). EQ-5D-3L discriminates well between age groups and ataxia severity, and responsiveness analyses yielded small to moderate effect sizes. Test-retest reliability indicated tolerable results. Multivariate regression analyses revealed that a more intensive progression of ataxia severity, mental health problems and obesity caused a more severe decline of patients' utility index over time, especially in male patients with an earlier disease onset. Conclusion: The analyses results satisfy acceptability, reliability, validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-3L in patients with rare ataxia diseases. Furthermore, the EQ-5D-3L measures HRQoL adequately, besides well-established clinical ataxia-specific instruments. Further research is needed assessing the performance of the EQ-5D-5L version in this disease area. A stronger focus on factors influencing HRQoL derived from longitudinal data analyses could help clinical evaluations and treatment.

Title: Comparison of DCE duration and EQ-VT in EQ-5D-Y-5L in the Netherlands
Abstract: Background: The VWG and YPWG are jointly working on a protocol for the valuation of the EQ-5D-Y-5L. In the context of valuations of the EQ-5D-Y-5L instrument, we envisage that either an expanded version of the existing EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol will be used, or a protocol that relies on DCE with a duration attribute. However, it has never been tested whether these methods produce similar results when valuing paediatric utility instruments. This study aims to make such a comparison and to develop a value set for the EQ-5D-Y-5L. Methods: Three samples will be collected: 1) a sample of n=1000 respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 DCE split triplets. 2) a sample of n=500 respondents that are interviewed in a personal interview, with each respondent completing 10 cTTO tasks. 3) a sample of n=1000 respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 latent scale DCE pairs. The DCE duration data will be analysed using a mixed logit model with an exponential discount rate. The latent scale DCE data is analysed using a mixed logit model. Predicted latent scale DCE values are anchored on the QALY scale using a mapping onto the mean observed cTTO values of each state included in the cTTO design. A value set is selected based consistency and discussion with the YPWG and VWG.

Title: Illustrating the empirical impact of applying different value sets: easy-to-read graphs and tables for stakeholders
Abstract: Introduction: The growing variety of Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) measures and value sets calls for methods and tools to assess which alternative is most sensitive to change in a particular target population. We introduce the valueSetCompare R package, which facilitates theoretical and empirical comparisons across different measures and value sets. We validate this tool with two case studies: (1) comparing EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets across 15 countries, and (2) assessing EQ-5D-5L, SF-6D, and HUI3 value sets in the United States. Methods: The valueSetCompare package allows theorical and empirical comparisons of value sets. Empirical comparisons require cross-sectional data incorporating utility scores from two or more different measures, and an independent severity variable.
