The package introduces a novel empirical methodology to assess the sensitivity of value sets to changes in health severity. To do so, a large number of simulated datasets are generated using resampling where the likelihood of sampling is a function of the severity proxy score. Mean scores and confidence bands along the severity for each instrument are presented in a ribbon plot. Results: In the first case study, we observed substantial differences between 3L and 5L value sets. Generally, 5L sets demonstrated smaller utility differences between health states, enhanced sensitivity to severity changes, and stronger interval measurement properties. In the second case study, the EQ-5D-5L and HUI3 demonstrated better responsiveness to severity variations compared to SF-6D. However, no significant differences in discriminative power were found among the three instruments. Conclusion: The valueSetCompare package offers a standardized and flexible framework for comparing HRQoL value sets, allowing for intuitive graphical representation of the sensitivity of different instruments, as well as standardized statistical tests. The package promotes transparency and rigor in the selection of the best-suited value set to capture treatment effects in populations of interest.

Title: Going beyond health related quality of life – towards a broader QALY measure for use across sectors
Abstract: Abstract Please provide a short summary of your completed research. This information will be included in the EuroQol database on funded research and may also be presented on the research section of the EuroQol website Quality adjusted life years (QALYs) are widely used around the world to inform health care decisions, such as the reimbursement of pharmaceutical products. Existing measures for estimating QALYs are mostly limited to health-related quality of life and focused on physical health. This will miss aspects of quality of life shown to be important to many patients, particularly those with long terms conditions and those reviewing social (i.e. non-medical) care. Furthermore, these measures are not designed to assess the impact on informal carers. We have developed a new generic measure of the impact of health and social care interventions on the lives of services users and their carers. The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) and a short version called the EQ-HWB-s (based on a sample of items from the longer version) were developed using qualitative evidence from service users (health and care services) and carers, along with psychometric evidence, collected in six countries.

Title: Research visit to University Technology Sydney, Macquarie University, Monash University and National University of Singapore to facilitate collaborative working on existing and planned research projects and build new networks.
Abstract: I visited four universities (UTS, Monash, Macquarie and NUS) during in November/December 2024. This visit was facilitated by EQ members Brendan Mulhern, Rosalie Viney, Lidia Engel and Nan Luo to whom I am grateful. As part of this visit, i co-developed a research proposal (with Mulhern), learnt about challenges of using EQ instruments in long-term care settings (with Engel), and explored opportunities for EQ-related research in Asia (with Luo).
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems, Education and Outreach

Title: Using the EQ-5D to understand how health impacts on preventative behaviour in rural Ghana as part of large randomized experiment of incentives for TB screening
Abstract: This project examined the feasibility of collecting measures of health-related quality of life, through the EQ-5D-5L instrument, in a large field experiment in rural Ghana, and explored how self-reported health (as per EQ-5D-5L) relates to preventative health behaviour in those settings. We used data from a randomised controlled trial (RCT) that explored incentives (i.e. a health message video; a health message with a telephone reminder; and a health message with $3.00) for tuberculosis (TB) screening through pop-up clinics in 78 villages. Univariate and multivariable regression analyses showed that neither self-reported health nor cash incentives or telephone nudges), had any significant impact on compliance (i.e. participation in TB screening). This may be due to the fact that by setting up pop-up clinics in each of the villages, we significantly reduced the costs of compliance.

Title: Investigating alternative methods for linking bolt-on and base instrument value sets
Abstract: In some clinical conditions, it may be worthwhile to extend the EQ-5D instruments by adding bolt-ons to the core five domains. In view of a multitude of possible bolt-ons, it is important to develop a reasonably cheap, reliable, and consistent valuation approach. Currently, the most developed idea is the scaling factor approach (SFA). However, SFA can be operationalized in various manners, but there is limited evidence to compare these. We seek to provide evidence in three areas. First, we plan to compare three strategies for linking the bolt-on to existing EQ-5D value set: (a) standalone bolt-on valuation; (b) estimating the SFs by comparing bolt-on preference data with pre-existing core domains importance; (c) estimating the SFs entirely within the new bolt-on valuation study (to account for changes in preferences across studies). Second, we plan to compare the two types of discrete choice experiments (DCE): with and without duration (to reduce the cost, we disregard the time trade-off method in the current proposal). Third, to assess the possibility of applying different SFs for the five core domains. Data will be collected through computer-assisted web interviews in Poland and China, with respondents valuing EQ-5D or EQ-5D+bolt-on health states using DCE with or without duration (hence, four arms). We plan to recruit 3000 respondents in each country (1000 in each of bolt-on arms, 500 in each of EQ-5D arms). We plan to compare the resulting models based on the convergence of estimation, estimation errors, face-validity of the results (e.g., inconsistencies).

Title: Research visit Melbourne School of Population and Global Health of the University of Melbourne.
Abstract: PhD candidate Ava Hoogenboom (EuroQol PhD network member) visited Kim Dalziel and the Health Economics Research group at the Melbourne School of Population and Global Health of the University of Melbourne for two weeks in October and November 2024. Ava works on project 1462-PHD aimed at examining the desirability, feasibility, and impact of involving children in the valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states. The project provides insight into the theoretical/normative and empirical underpinning of involving children in decisions on health and healthcare and into the various ways in which children can (potentially) be involved. This visit to Melbourne has yielded several results. Firstly, Ava expanded her knowledge on child health state valuation (HSV) by learning first-hand from researchers in Melbourne who are currently working on child HSV (e.g., the QUOKKA research project). For example, Ava met with Kim Dalziel and several of her PhD students on multiple occasions, exchanging knowledge and research experiences and brainstorming about how children could be involved in HSV. More specifically, it was explored what kind of tasks (TTO and others) children would be able to complete. In addition, Ava attended several presentations related to health technology assessment, and visited the children's hospital to learn more about how healthcare workers include children in decisions and policy making regarding child health and how the hospital implements local and national policies regarding children's involvement. This visit gave Ava the opportunity to exchange expectations and ideas on how to involve children, by learning from experts how they involve children in their own care and in research related to child health. For example, it was discussed how researchers should tailor their work to the needs and desires of children. After this visit, it was agreed that Ava and the researchers at the children’s hospital would stay in touch to continue to exchange knowledge on the topic. Secondly, the visit provided the occasion and possibility to further elaborate on the contents and designs of the remaining work packages in Ava's PhD project. Meetings with other researchers from Australia and also from Sweden emphasized that lessons can be learned from researchers and healthcare professionals that specialize in involving children in a broader sense, rather than focused on health state valuation. As a result, Ava and her supervisor Vivian Reckers-Droog explored options to expand the scope of some studies in the PhD project. That is, a planning for the remainder of Ava’s PhD trajectory was made that allows Ava to take a broader approach on the involvement of children in HSV by also considering methods used to involve children in their own care or in policy assessments. Thirdly, an additional (unplanned) visit to the Health Economics Group at Monash University took place, during which Ava spoke with multiple researchers (both PhD candidates and more senior staff). During this visit, Ava also attended presentations and got a chance to meet EuroQol (PhD network) members. Fourthly, during her visit to Melbourne, Ava strengthened and broadened her network (both with non-members and members of EuroQol) by meeting researchers from Australia, as well as other visiting researchers from the US and Sweden. This might result in future collaborations, especially with a group of researchers that focuses on involving children in policy making in a clinical setting.

Title: Translating EQ-5D into Hausa and validating the new version in hip replacement.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: The EQ-5D-5L is a questionnaire used for the measurement and economic valuation of a wide range of health conditions, which necessitates its existence and adaptation in different languages. Currently, the tool does exist in Hausa language but there is no psychometric validation of the Hausa version of the questionnaire. This study aimed to cross-culturally adapt, and determine the reliability and validity of the Hausa version of the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. OBJECTIVE: This study was aimed to determine the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L Hausa version in patients with hip replacement in National Orthopaedic Hospital Dala, Kano Nigeria. METHOD: This is a cross-sectional study aimed at determining the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L Hausa versions in patients with Hip replacement in national Othopaedic Hospital Dala, Kano Nigeria. For this study, 79 participants were found to complete the questionnaires; they comprised both male and female patients receiving treatment both the in and out patients department of National Orthopaedics Hospital Dala, Kano, Kano State, Northwest Nigeria. Only participants who meet the inclusion criteria were considered for the study. RESULT: The mean age of the respondents was 55.86 ± 18.447 years. The internal consistency was found to be 0.9 chronbach’s alpha. The test retest reliability of the EQ-5D Hausa was significantly correlated. The factor analysis yielded one factor. CONCLUSION: The EQ-5D-Hausa was successfully translated into Hausa language and is a valid tool for the measurement of health status among Hausa speaking populations.

Title: Testing two alternative TTO methods for valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states by trading life years in adulthood
Abstract: Introduction: One drawback of the current cTTO method for the Y valuation is that it works by asking respondents to consider shortening a 10-years-old child’s life for better health. Although it is hypothetical, the cTTO task could be upsetting and abhorrent to some respondents. Also, there is concern that adult respondents are unwilling to trade child life years, and consequently many studies reported cTTO values of Y valuation studies higher than the cTTO values of corresponding adult states. In order to overcome this potential issue, we conceptualized, and pilot tested two alternative TTO variants named the Parent TTO (PTTO) and lag-time TTO (LTTO). Both methods ask respondents to trade adult life years. We hypothesized that they have higher acceptability and would generate lower values compared to cTTO. Method: We collected PTTO and LTTO data for the 10 health states included in the EQ-5D-Y valuation protocol from a general population sample in China. The data collection was piggybacked on the China EQ-5D-Y valuation study, using three interviewers with experience using EQ-VT (two interviewers participated in the China Y study, one interviewer participated in two methodological study). For comparison, the cTTO data, including cTTO values, feedback questions and time etc. were drawn from the China EQ-5D-Y study. We compared the methods in terms of acceptability (using three feedback questions: easy to understand, easy to tell the difference, easy to make the decision), feasibility (time to complete the practice task, time to value the 10 states) and characteristics of TTO values (mean and data distributions). Results: In total, 304 participants were included (cTTO: 100; LTTO: 102; PTTO: 102) in this study. On a 5-point Likert scale, the mean score of the ‘easy to understand’ question was 1.18 (SD: 0.58), 1.45 (SD: 0.91) and 1.65 (SD: 1.02) for cTTO, LTTO and PTTO respectively. The mean score of the ‘easy to differentiate’ question was 1.45 (SD: 0.91), 1.94 (SD: 1.08) and 1.86 (SD: 1.24) and the mean score of the ‘difficult to decide’ question was 3.61 (SD: 1.29), 2.97 (SD: 1.33) and 3.02 (SD: 1.50) respectively. The mean (SD) time spent on the wheelchair example was 276.34 (147.51), 350.33 (140.28) and 454.44 (139.92) seconds for cTTO, LTTO and PTTO, respectively. The mean (SD) time spent on valuing each of the 10 states was 102.97 (29.48), 134.66 (49.69), 141.72 (47.07). The mean (SD) TTO values of all 10 states were 0.463 (0.494), 0.387 (0.555) and 0.123 (0.710). All tests were significantly different when using cTTO method as references, except that the mean value comparison between cTTO and LTTO. LTTO and PTTO showed clear clusterings at 0 and -1 respectively; PTTO had more values on the negative value range. Discussion: By designing and testing these two alternative TTO methods to trade-off life adult years, we found participants did not find the TTO tasks more acceptable and feasible, but these two methods do produce values that are more similar to the EQ-5D-5L values. We also found the TTO values may be affected by the parental status and age of the respondents suggesting that researchers to pay attention to the sample representativeness when conducting an EQ-5D-Y valuation study.

Title: ISPOR 2024 Dissemination: Advancing Understanding of Psychometric Validation in EQ-5D-Y Instruments and Health State Valuation
Abstract: This project aimed to disseminate findings from two studies at the ISPOR 2024 Conference through poster presentations in the "Pediatrics" and "Patient-Centered Research" sections. The first study, titled "Construct Validity and Test-Retest Reliability of the Three-level and Five-level Versions of the EQ-5D-Y" (SA65), systematically reviewed the psychometric performance of the three-level (Y-3L) and five-level (Y-5L) versions of the EQ-5D-Y instrument. Using a head-to-head comparison approach, the study assessed key properties such as construct validity and test-retest reliability. The findings support the adoption of the Y-5L for paediatric health assessments, especially in contexts requiring more precise measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL). These results align with EuroQol’s goal to enhance the applicability of its tools and were strategically timed to complement the launch of the Y-5L version. The second study, "Who Prefers Death to Life in Composite Time Trade-off Interviews and Why" (PCR43), is a secondary analysis of data collected from the Singapore EQ-5D-5L valuation study. It explored the motivations and characteristics of respondents who expressed a preference for death over living in states of poor health during composite time trade-off interviews. The analysis uncovered that middle-aged individuals, particularly those with dual caregiving roles, were more likely to consider health states as worse than death. These findings offer critical insights into the socio-demographic and cultural factors influencing valuation preferences, which can be used to refine valuation methods and inform resource allocation decisions. Both studies demonstrate strategic value to the EuroQol Group by advancing the scientific robustness, cultural sensitivity, and practical utility of EQ-5D instruments.

Title: Travel scholarship request to attend ISPOR Europe 2024 for findings dissemination.
Abstract: I delivered a podium presentation and a poster presentation at the ISPOR Europe 2024 Conference held between 17 and 20 November 2024, in Barcelona, Spain. My first study, “EQ-5D-Y in Children With Asthma or Eczema: Does Perspective Matter in Proxy-Reported Outcomes Assessment of Pediatric Populations?” was identified as Top 5% Finalist for the ISPOR Europe 2024 Research Presentation Awards. The podium presentation has won the best student podium research presentations award. This study evaluates the measurement properties of two different proxy versions (proxy-proxy and proxy-patient versions) of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, as reported by caregivers or legal guardians of pediatric patients with asthma or eczema. The project is partially funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation (EQ Project 188-2020RA; total project value: 22,120 euros [without a budget for conference]), and preliminary findings were presented at the EQ Early Career Meeting 2022. My second study, “Is a Longer Recall Period Better? A Study of EQ-5D-5L With a “1-Week” Recall Period in the General Population” [MSR31], compared the psychometric properties of two EQ-5D-5L versions differing in recall period (today vs. 1 week) in a Singaporean general population aged 15 and above (n=592) who participated in a nationwide household survey. This project is not funded by EuroQol.

Title: Testing the development of a Dimension Specific Module using cognition – Extending the Deep Dive pilot study
Abstract: The EQ-5D descriptive system includes dimensions that are measured using a single item for amenability to valuation. Such an approach to instrument design facilitates the generation of utility values but limits the possibility of collecting rich profile information about the patients’ status on each dimension. To address this gap the Descriptive Systems Working Group have proposed an extension to the core instrument that combines the benefits of both preference-accompanied and profile measures. This is a multi layered approach to measuring health and quality of life that generates Dimension Specific Modules (DSMs). The Executive Committee previously funded the Deep Dive Pilot study that includes an empirical exploration of developing a DSM in existing data that includes the EQ-5D-5L and other measures of HRQoL such as the SF-36 and PROMIS-29. The analysis of existing data included in the pilot study is informative in terms of exploring the development of DSMs. However it is limited due to the use of items from non EuroQol instruments as those tested within each DSM. Another strategic and methodological issue relates to which EQ-5D-5L dimension, or dimensions, should be used to provide further proof of concept for a DSM. An alternative approach would be to focus testing solely on experimental instruments and modifications in the EuroQol suite. For example, exploring DSMs using bolt-on constructs that meet the criteria for a DSM (i.e. a global construct with evidence of sub domains such as Cognition). The aim of this proposal is to leverage an ongoing cognition bolt on data collection, and to explore how a DSM could be constructed psychometrically when all items follow the EuroQol format, and also when all items are owned by EuroQol (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-5D-5L bolt on and sub domains and EQ-HWB items). The benefit of this is that the analysis will extend that done in the DSM pilot study as all items tested will be owned by EuroQol. Two cognition specific DSMs will be formed and tested across all analyses conducted. The analysis used will combine classical psychometrics, factor analysis and modern test theory (IRT) to explore the most appropriate approaches to develop a DSM. This will include assessing construct validity, dimensionality and item performance, linking items within a DSM, and associated score generation. The results from the psychometric methods will be triangulated to provide insight into the feasibility of developing DSMs within a multi-layered approach.

Title: Three weeks research visit to University of Melbourne, Monash University and University Technology Sydney to: facilitate collaborative work on two RFPs; present EQ-based papers at various seminars, and; revise a grant application investigating relevant bolt-ons for older adults.
Abstract: Funding was granted to allow me to visit University of Melbourne, Monash University and University Technology Sydney to: i) facilitate collaborative work on two RFPs; ii) present EQ-based papers at various seminars, and; iii) revise a grant application investigating relevant bolt-ons for older adults.

Title: New methods for analysing the distribution of EQ-5D observations in data sets
Abstract: Background: EQ-5D profile data are often under-analysed, but can yield important insights into levels of and changes in patient and population health. One characteristic is the extent to which they cluster together in a small number of profiles or are dispersed evenly over many profiles. This can have implications for interpreting statistical analysis of the corresponding EQ values (Index)data, and for clinical management of patients.Aims:This paper aims to develop methods for describing observed distributionsof EQ-5D profiles and to explore the properties of the new methods compared with existing ones (e.g. Shannon’s Index). We investigate the methods using both real, from the EnglishNHS, and simulated EQ-5D data, and show how they can be used to generate new insights into, for example, the differences between the three-and five-levelversions of the EQ-5D with respect tohow profile data are clustered. Methods: We report three methods we have developed to characterise and summarise the distribution of health states in patient reported outcome (PRO) data within a sample or population of patients: the Health State Density Index(HSDI), Health State Density Curve(HSDC)and estimated Power Law functions (PLFs).We compare these andexisting methods from information theory (e.g. Shannon’s Index), in examining the distribution of EQ-5D health profilesin three data sets:across three groups of patients in Cambridgeshire Community Services NHS’s electronic patient records for the EQ-5D-5L; the Health Survey for England 2014 for the EQ-5D-3L; andthe NHS PROMs programme for theEQ-5D-3L. The properties of the various methods are further examined using simulated data sets. Results:Each method has different properties and will give different insights into patients’ data. For example, the Shannon index (absolute and relative) is not sensitive to random variations but decreases slowly with “rare health states”. The HSDI decreases slowly with random variations and is strongly affected by “rare” health states with largedecreases towards zero (total inequality).Conclusions:These methods can be used by researchers to better understand the characteristics of EQ-5D profile data. They can also be used by clinicians to understand the degree to which their patients’ needs are homogeneous or characterised by distinct sub-groups, with implications for treatment planning. Finally, the methods can also be used as a way of comparing differences between instruments, such as the 3L and 5L, in measuring health. Acknowledgements and disclaimersThis project was funded by a research grant from the EuroQol Research Foundation. All views expressed are those of the authors, and not necessarily those of the EuroQol Research Foundation.The authors are grateful to Nils Gutacker, Thomas Kohlmann,and participants at the Health Economists’Study Group (HESG) Winter Meeting (Birmingham 2017)and the 34thEuroQol Plenary (Barcelona 2017), and to Nigel Rice, for helpful comments onearlier versionsof this paper.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Evaluating the psychometric properties of bolt-ons in breast cancer patients
Abstract: Objectives: We aimed to evaluate the psychometric performance of existing EQ-5D-5L-format bolt-ons and selected EQ-HWB items as bolt-ons, comparing them in patients with breast cancer. Methods: A secondary analysis was conducted on a longitudinal dataset of 300 female patients with breast cancer. Outcome measures included EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, and four EQ-5D-5L-format bolt-ons (bodily appearance [BA], social relationships, sleep [SL], fatigue [FA]). Fourteen EQ-HWB items were selected for testing as potential bolt-ons: sleep (SP), exhaustion (EX), loneliness (LO), unsupported (UN), memory (ME), cognition (CO), unsafe (US), frustration (FR), look forward (LF), no control (NC), coping (CP), accepted (AC), feel good (FG), and wanted to (WA). Psychometric properties assessed included ceiling reduction, validity (convergent/divergent and known-group), explanatory power, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness. Results: The EQ-5D-5L ceiling (35.0%) was reduced by adding EQ-5D-5L-format bolt-ons (0.7%-10.7%) or EQ-HWB items (0.3%-18.3%). No strong correlations were found between bolt-ons and core EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Adding FA, SL, EX, SP, CO, FG, or WA (or combinations) improved EQ-5D-5L’s known-group validity. In direct comparisons, EX and SP outperformed FA and SL in relative efficiency for distinguishing known-groups. EX outperformed FA in increasing the explanatory power of EQ-5D-5L for EQ VAS, Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General and Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale scores. Adding BA, SL, CO, LF, NC, or US slightly improved EQ-5D-5L test-retest reliability, while WA slightly increased the responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L in patients with worsened health. Conclusion: EQ-HWB items outperformed existing EQ-5D-5L-format bolt-ons in overall psychometric performance, with sleep and exhaustion emerging as promising bolt-on candidates in breast cancer. Further research is recommended to guide their adoption.

Title: Comparative Study of TTO-based, Hybrid, and DCE with duration Value Sets for EQ-5D-5L in Qatar
Abstract: This study has two primary objectives: first, to develop a value set for EQ-5D-5L health states reflecting the preferences of the general population in Qatar; second, to compare value sets derived from TTO-based, hybrid, and DCE with duration (DCEd) methodologies, in order to assess the consistency and agreement among these valuation approaches. This will be a cross-sectional population-based study involving interviewer-administered online interviews following the EuroQol EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol and using modified version of the EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT). The latent scale DCE in the current EQ-VT will be replaced by the DCE with duration. A representative sample of 1000 adults will be recruited from the Qatari general population using a two-stage quota sampling, first by population distribution across the country, and then by age and sex distribution. Sampling will also take into account the population distribution of nationals and expatriates. Interviews will be conducted online by trained research assistants. EuroQol quality control processes will be followed to ensure high quality data. Data collection will be paused at 20%, 40%, and 60% to evaluate the DCE with duration data and update the experimental DCE design.  This study will provide a country-specific value set of the EQ-5D-5L for Qatar, and will add to the body of evidence on the comparative performance of the cTTO/EQ-VT approach vs. DCE with duration for generating a value set for the EQ-5D-5L.

Title: Testing the validity of the EQ-HWB-S in a clinical setting with patients with rare neurological conditions, and their carers
Abstract: **Background:** The EQ-Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB-S) is a newly developed generic instrument that assesses the impacts of health, social care and being an informal carer on quality of life. It was developed to be brief and amenable for use in economic evaluations. The instrument is currently considered ‘experimental’ whilst evidence of its validity in future users is generated, and potential further modifications that have arisen in initial testing are considered.Sheffield Teaching Hospitals is a centre of excellence for neuromuscular (NM) patient care with a large group of NM patients. Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) and Myasthenia Gravis (MG) are two rare neuromuscular conditions which have considerable health related quality of life impacts, particularly in areas of mobility, fatigue and relationships. It is anticipated that the EQ-HWB-S, which captures these domains, may be suitable to measure quality of life in these patients. **Methods:** This is a mixed methods study in which the validity and suitability of the EQ-HWB-S will be explored using both qualitative and quantitative methods. Cognitive debriefing interviews with patients and their carers will be undertaken in a clinical setting to explore their understanding of the EQ-HWB-S instrument, and how well they think it reflects relevant aspects of their health or carer related quality of life. This will include consideration of the proposed modifications to the EQ-HWB-S. The EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L will be included into the package of patient reported and clinician reported outcome measures collected during clinic visits for a 12 month period. This data will be analysed to assess the psychometric performance of the instruments, through for example, comparing the generic instruments (EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-S) to condition specific measures and clinical outcomes.

Title: Development of EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set for India
Abstract: Background: India lacks an EQ-5D-Y value-set to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among children and adolescents, despite recommendations in national economic evaluations to use EQ-5D tools. This gap has significant implications for HTA studies focusing on pediatric interventions and can compromise the accuracy of quality adjusted life years (QALY) estimates in HTA studies concerning children. To address this gap, the Indian Health Technology Assessment agency (HTAIn) approved funding for a nationwide study to develop an EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set, which will be commenced soon. While the EQ-5D-Y-5L instrument, launched in September 2024, has superior psychometric properties compared to the older EQ-5D-Y-3L, no valuation protocol exists for EQ-5D-Y-5L. Therefore, first, a pilot study is being conducted currently, with an aim to assess the potential valuation methods, including the expanded Ramos-Goñi protocol and Discrete Choice Experiments (DCE) with a duration attribute. The design finalized by the EuroQol Foundation using the findings of this pilot study will subsequently be used in developing the Indian EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set. Developing an EQ-5D-Y-5L value set for India will allow for the estimation of child-specific health utility scores grounded in the values and preferences of the Indian population. This is vital for producing accurate assessments of health-related quality of life in economic evaluations of pediatric healthcare interventions. Embedding culturally appropriate perspectives into these evaluations will enhance the integrity of policy decisions, promoting fairness and relevance in child health policies. Methods: This study will employ a cross-sectional design involving face-to-face, computer-assisted interviews with a representative sample of 2,600 adults from six Indian states, selected using a multi-stage, stratified sampling approach to capture economic, health, and geographical diversity. The valuation protocol to be used—either the expanded Ramos-Goñi protocol or discrete choice experiment (DCE) with duration—will be finalized based on the findings of an ongoing pilot funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation. Valuation interviews will be conducted using EQ-5D-Y-5L translated into five Indian languages (Hindi, Gujarati, Tamil, Odia, and Assamese, as well as in English). Translation support in this regard is requested from the EuroQol Foundation. Depending on the final protocol, which is to be decided after completion of the ongoing pilot, data will be collected using either DCE with duration or the EQ-VT platform incorporating composite time trade-off (cTTO) and latent scale DCE methods. Data quality will be assured through interviewer training, standardized quality control procedures, and exclusion of invalid responses. The data will be analyzed using mixed logit models and Tobit regression as appropriate, with anchoring of latent values on the QALY scale, enabling derivation of an Indian EQ-5D-Y-5L value set based on societal preferences.

Title: Translation of EQ-TIPS into 10 most requested language versions
Abstract: **Background and aim**: The EuroQol Toddler and Infant (EQ-TIPS) measure of HRQoL is currently an experimental measure which has undergone modifications and testing in a large multinational research project (EQ 365 and EQ1928). Results of the final testing of the EQ-TIPS-3L and 5L are expected at the end of 2025. Thereafter, the descriptive system will be finalised, and a dossier of evidence will be submitted to support its transition from experimental to approved status. Approved versions of any instrument require formal linguistic review and translation by translation agencies based on the appropriate forward and back translation (FT and BT), cognitive debriefing and proofreading. In a recent joint EuroQol Board and Executive meeting, the decision was made to prioritise office resources to move the EQ-HWB-9 to an approved version before focusing on the EQ-TIPS. To ensure that the EQ-TIPS is ready for launch and the timeline is not protracted, this project aims to support the translation of the definitive EQ-TIPS version, of the ten most requested language versions and reduce the associated burden on the office staff. A secondary aim is to support researcher-led translations. **Methods:** The ten most requested language versions (English - UK, USA, Australia, Canada; Spanish - Spain, USA; German, Simplified Chinese, French, Italian) have been identified by the Version Management Committee (VMC). An ISO-certified translation agency will be engaged to undertake formal translation of the finalised descriptive system of the EQ-TIPS-5L. In all instances, the EQ-TIPS-5L will be translated or linguistically validated and cognitively debriefed, and the EQ-TIPS-3L will be extracted. In each language, linguistic review or translation will cover the self-complete (SC) (digital and paper) and interviewer-administered (IA) versions. The initial translation will be for an English UK version, which will be used as the source version for the other nine languages. Following a gap analysis by the VMC-liaison available, translated language versions will undergo linguistic review without FT and BT, subject to there being no changes in the English source version, otherwise, full translation will be required. Cognitive debriefing will be undertaken with eight participants (caregivers of infants and toddlers of mixed ages, mixed gender and different socio-demographic strata and health conditions). VMC reviewers will support the translation process by reviewing reports from the translation agency at each stage of the translation. Researcher-led translations will continue to be supported for languages that are not available. Researchers will undertake translations using EQ translation guides and processes developed by the VMC. This involves FT and BT, CD and reporting on the findings, including populating templates. VMC reviewers will undertake a light review of the results of the researcher-led translations before approval for use by the VMC liaison. **Outcome:** Agency translations will be available for the EQ-TIPS-5L and EQ-TIPS-3L for the ten most requested language versions with two modes of administration (SC and IA). Each translation will be delivered for quality control and approval by the EQ office ahead of the launch of the instrument.

Title: Brendan Mulhern - Study visit to Canada (hosted by Simon Fraser University, and the University of British Columbia)
Abstract: This application is for a 5 week study visit to Canada. I will be primarily based in Vancouver, and hosted by David Whitehurst (Simon Fraser University), Nick Bansback and Stirling Bryan (both University of British Columbia). I will also visit other EuroQol members including Feng Xie (McMaster), Jeff Johnson and Fatima Al Sayah (University of Alberta). All have agreed to my visit This research visit will focus on developing collaborations and proposals, the following EuroQol activities will be worked on: - Developing EuroQol proposals focused on the recall period of EQ instruments, and testing exclusion criteria and data quality in preference elicitation studies (with Whitehurst) - Developing a proposal around the use of EQ-HWB data in routine outcome assessment (with Bansback) - Developing further links between Australian and Canadian institutions with strong EuroQol connections - Strengthening collaborations between the DSWG (which i chair) and the PHS WG (Bansback is a member) - Strengthening links between the DSWG and Exec (Xie is a member) - Working on EQ-DAPHNIE related projects (with Johnson and Al Sayah - Giving seminars on ongoing EuroQol related research

Title: Assessing Content Validity in Generic Adult and Paediatric Preference-Weighted Measures: A Scoping Review to Identify Current Practice
Abstract: **Background:** Content validity is considered a fundamental measurement property. While guidance exists for assessing content validity of patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) as a whole, there is no best practice guidance for assessing content validity in generic preference-weighted measures (PWMs), and EQ instruments in particular, which represent a ‘special case’ of PROMs. This may lead to inaccurate conclusions that generic PWMs do not have satisfactory content validity in particular health conditions because they are evaluated inappropriately. **Aim:** Developing best practice methodological guidance is iterative. This review contributes to ‘Phase 1’ and aims to: (i) identify contemporary examples of qualitative work assessing content validity in generic adult and paediatric PWMs, including EQ measures; and (ii) map what has been done against recommendations to identify examples of good practice and gaps for future work. Guidance recommendations will be evaluated to assess whether they are appropriate for assessing content validity in generic PWMs (and in what form). **Methods:** A scoping review will be conducted using a robust search strategy developed by an Information Specialist. Eight databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Science and Social Sciences Citation Indexes, Econlit, Tufts CEA Registry, and MATHSCINET) will be searched. Contemporary qualitative content validity studies in generic adult and paediatric PWMs will be included and relevant data extracted. A descriptive narrative synthesis will be conducted mapping content validity studies onto existing guidance and appraised in the context of the unique challenges that exist in assessing content validity in generic PWMs.

Title: EQ-5D-3L as an outcome indicator: analysis of its performance in a longitudinal study of patients receiving palliative care
Abstract: It is well recognised that quality of life as measured by patient-reported outcomes (PROs) deteriorates near the end of life. This deterioration can be captured using the EQ-5D-3L, however, the extent to which the EQ-5D-3L dimensions and EQ-VAS are prognostic in advanced incurable cancer is unknown. This project encompassed three elements: - Using a simple prognostic model we demonstrate that the EQ-5D-3L self-care dimension alone can replace clinician-assessed performance status in predicting survival in advanced incurable cancer with bone metastases. Further, we illustrate that whilst the prognostic value of the self-care dimension is greatest for those with short survival, this diminishes in those with longer prognosis. Conversely the EQ-VAS offers greater prognostic separation at these later time points. The optimal measures for inclusion in future models will need to optimise model performance in line with the time points relevant to the clinical decision problem. - A one day inter-disciplinary workshop was convened to build a consensus on the use and challenges to including PROs in prognostic and predictive modelling in cancer care. Our consensus highlights the crucial need, particularly relevant in PRO models, to identify the decision problem and consider challenges of implementation at the earliest possible stage in model development. Beyond this we highlight key challenges to PRO capture in routine care and consider the impact of these challenges on prognostic and predictive models. - Finally, using longitudinal EQ-5D-3L data from patients undergoing palliative radiotherapy for bone metastases, we identify how the relationship between the EQ-5D-3L dimensions and the EQ-VAS changes with proximity to death. This analysis informs the wider discussions about the need to reconsider the evaluative space when appraising care outcomes for patients near the end of life.

Title: Travel Grant to support EQ PhD network member to present EQ-HWB research on iHEA meeting and to visit National University of Singapore for learning and exploring research collaborations.
Abstract: The funded project was successfully completed, supporting international dissemination and academic exchange around EuroQol-funded research on  EQ-HWB instrument and its application in elderly rehabilitation care.A central component of the grant was participation in the 2025 iHEA World Congress, where Haode Wang delivered an oral presentation on EuroQol-funded work related to preference elicitation using discrete choice experiments (DCE), and also co-chaired a session on QoL and PROMs research. This provided an important platform to disseminate findings, engage with leading international experts in health economics, and obtain high-quality feedback to refine ongoing and future research. The presentation has been arranged as the first presentation of QoL valuation and its methodology section. Haode was the only ECR researcher presented on the session. Around 47 international scholars, including Nancy Delvin, participated in the session activity. Apart from QoL researchers, the conference also facilitated networking with researchers and stakeholders interested in the application of EQ instruments in both clinical and policy settings.Haode also participated in the EuroQol-funded young children QoL pre-session, hosted by Nan Luo, where Haode and Nan had a thorough discussion about project 1963-RA. Although the originally planned institutional visit to the National University of Singapore (NUS) was not completed, key objectives related to academic exchange were still achieved. This iHEA interaction enabled meaningful discussion on the ongoing EQ-HWB (1963-RA) project, including methodological considerations such as the use of proxy versions, longitudinal data collection design, and potential approaches to estimating minimally important differences (MID). These discussions provided valuable expert input that will directly inform the next phase of the project.Importantly, the revision of the travel plan—specifically the cancellation of the NUS visit—resulted in a reduced overall expenditure, thereby generating cost savings for the EuroQol Group while still achieving the majority of the intended scientific and collaborative objectives. Overall, the project contributed to strengthening international academic exchange, enhancing methodological rigor in EQ-HWB research, and supporting the broader goal of promoting the application of EQ instruments. The knowledge gained and connections established are expected to lead to further collaborations, improved study implementation, and future research outputs, including publications and potential joint grant applications.

Title: Composite time trade-off valuations for EQ-5D-Y-3L: exploring perspective differences within respondents
Abstract: The EQ-5D-Y-3L International Valuation Protocol specifies that health states be valued from the perspective of a hypothetical 10-year-old child, rather than adults valuing the states for themselves. This use of perspective has been shown to influence valuation outcomes, affecting comparability of health utilities. Our study explored within-respondent differences in values between adult and child perspectives using data from Central and Eastern Europe. A secondary analysis was conducted using composite time trade-off (cTTO) data from the Hungarian EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation study. Two hundred adults valued 10 health states from the child perspective and four from the adult perspective. The cTTO values for the matched health states (valued from both perspectives) were compared, with differences analyzed using t-tests and random-intercept regression. We found differences in cTTO values between perspectives, particularly for more severe health states. The child perspective yielded significantly lower values for worse-than-dead observations, but higher values for better-than-dead observations. After adjusting for within-subject variation and respondent characteristics, perspective was not a significant predictor of cTTO values. Differences were partially explained by education, region of residence, parental status, and the view that a child’s life is more valuable than an adult’s. Our findings highlight the importance of considering individual-level attributes in pediatric health valuation.

Title: QUALITATIVE EXPLORATION OF THE NEED FOR A STRENGTHS-BASED FOCUS WITHIN THE EQ-5D-Y-5L: UNDERSTANDING MARKET THREATS AND POSITIONING
Abstract: Background: Few HRQoL instruments for children use ‘strengths based’ language but recently the ICECAP-CYS has been launched with strengths-based language having been heavily developed with consumers, parents and children which could pose a market-threat to the EQ-5D-Y-5L. The EQ-5D-Y-5L has recently launched after considerable EuroQol investment and was adapted from the adult instrument with limited consumer ‘co-design’ input. Like many HRQoL instruments it relies self or proxy reporting concerns and problems. This can be challenging for the inclusion of some children (and their families), such as those with children with severe conditions or complex disabilities that are not expected to cure or improve. A deficits focus can threaten child participant’s self-esteem and produce ethical concerns. There are several paediatric HRQoL measures that use positively worded language (e.g. KIDSCREEN and KINDL-R- which are non-preference weighted, and ICECAP-CYP which is preference weighted). There is a key opportunity to explore whether strengths-based adaptations are needed from the perspective of consumers and whether potential threats to the EQ-5D-Y-5L market exist. If a need is identified then any adaptations could be co-designed with patients/families to work in with existing EuroQol projects such as 1) changes to self-report/proxy recommendations for some children, 2) a deep dive on one or more EQ-5D-Y-5L items using strengths-based language, 3) one or more strengths-based bolt-ons to sit alongside existing EQ-5D-Y-5L items and/or 4) mapping for one or more EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions using alternative strengths based language. There is a pressing and strong ethical imperative and opportunity to position the EuroQol as a global leader in inclusive research practices securing its market positioning. Recent, and ongoing investments in the EQ-5D-Y-5L make this a strategic priority.  Aims: (a) To qualitatively explore the views and experiences of parents and young people regarding current item wording of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and perceived item-level needs (if any) for alternative strengths-based wording. (b) To understand paediatric and disability expert views on wording including for which items, paediatric populations and settings strengths-based adaptations may confer inclusive advantages including which children may be at-risk of harm through self-report using current wording. (c) To feedback information to EuroQol to inform strategic positioning of the EQ-5D-Y-5L in the market and inform whether future developments/enhancements are needed, and what consumers’ direction indicates for partnering with EuorQol work streams (e.g. DeepDive, Bolt-ons). This qualitative project would, together with patients and families, set the desired direction for such research if it was deemed necessary.  Methods: To explore the views and experiences of parents and young people, 3 online focus groups will be conducted in Australia with each of the following groups: parents of children with life limiting conditions or complex disabilities, and adolescents with life limiting conditions or complex disabilities. Participants will be recruited from The Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne and not-for-profit organisations representing rare childhood conditions. Additional interviews will be conducted with 6 paediatric experts (from clinicians, psychologists, disability experts, allied practitioners, or developmental/education specialists) to determine their views. Qualitative data will be coded and thematically analysed. We aim to understand whether EQ-5D-Y-5L strengths-based adaptions are required from a consumer perspective, which dimensions (if any) from the EQ-5D-Y-5L require a strengths-based approaches, and if so how development of a new version could progress (e.g. changes to recommended child self-report, deep dive, bolt-on, mapping to one or more dimensions).  Deliverables: A draft manuscript will be produced reporting qualitative findings along with a presentation prepared for a EuroQol audience to inform the development of future strategy around market position and need for future research for the EQ-5D-Y-5L in regard to strengths-based positioning. *Note that the intention of this project is NOT to produce or position for a new instrument or research program. The intention is to collaborate with consumers to understand whether further strengths-based research is needed for the EQ-5D-Y-5L and how to position this for partnering with existing EuroQol work streams.

Title: Systematic Review on Empirical Testing of Constant Proportionality-Linear Utility Function in Preferences for Individual or Societal Health
Abstract: Background. Constant proportionality (CPTO) — the assumption that individuals trade aconstant proportion of life duration for a proportional health improvement regardless of thetime horizon — is a foundational premise of the linear quality-adjusted life year (QALY)model and is closely related to time-trade-off (TTO) valuation methods. Departures fromCPTO and from linear utility of time have been reported in the literature; if theseassumptions do not hold empirically, values from standard elicitation may be affected, withimplications for EQ-VT methods and for all EuroQol-instrument valuation work. Whileindividual discounting in the monetary domain has been the subject of extensive cumulativemeta-analytic work, discounting and other CPTO violations in the health domain had notbeen systematically synthesised across elicitation methods.Objectives. To systematically review empirical evidence testing CPTO and the relatedassumption of linear utility of time in health preferences, summarize reported violations ofCPTO/linear utility (e.g. discounting behaviour), compare alternative functional forms head-to-head, and assess relevance for EuroQol valuation research.Methods. We searched PubMed, Scopus, EconLit and the Cochrane Library from inceptionto September 2025 for experimental or survey-based studies directly testing CPTO orestimating time-preference parameters in health-valuation tasks. Dual independentscreening and structured extraction captured sample characteristics, framing, elicitationmethod, time horizon, reported discounting direction and magnitude, and head-to-headcomparisons of alternative functional forms. Risk of bias and certainty were not formallyassessed (PROSPERO CRD420251019603).Results. We identified 77 publications (78 study records — one publication, Mulhern 2014,contributed two sub-studies), with ~36,700 participants across 24 countries. Samplesincluded general-population respondents, students, patients and proxies. Studies groupedinto four broad lines of evidence challenging CPTO: direct axiomatic tests, discounting / non-constant time preference (the dominant cluster), prospect-theoretic violations and other non-linear patterns. Across studies, CPTO was usually not supported, most commonly throughevidence of non-constant discounting. Positive discounting was the dominant direction(range 0%–93% of respondents within studies); zero/neutral discounting — the only directionstrictly consistent with CPTO — ranged 0%–56%; and negative discounting, an unusualpattern in health preferences, was nonetheless reported in 34/78 studies (44%). Among the8 studies formally comparing discounting model families head-to-head, non-exponentialspecifications (most often hyperbolic) provided better fit in 6/8 studies, withexponential/constant discounting preferred only in 2/8, using fit criteria such as AIC/WAIC,RMSE and R²/adjusted R². A quantitative synthesis of comparable discount-rate estimates iscurrently underway and will be reported in the accompanying manuscript.Conclusions. This is, to our knowledge, the largest systematic synthesis of empiricalevidence on CPTO and linearity in health preferences. The balance of evidence is largelyinconsistent with strict CPTO: departures are commonly observed across methods andvaluation contexts, with non-constant discounting accounting for the majority of thedocumented violations and non-exponential models typically outperforming exponentialdiscounting in head-to-head comparisons. These findings are directly relevant to EuroQolvaluation research — particularly to TTO interpretation, EQ-VT design and ongoing work onpaediatric and long-term outcome valuation. They suggest that CPTO and linear utilityshould be treated as empirically testable rather than self-evident assumptions, and that themagnitude and shape of observed time-preference effects, rather than their mere presence,should inform whether and how non-linear preferences are accommodated in value-set derivation — including through the corrective and generalised approaches now available inthe methodological literature.

Title: Testing a content validity and acceptability of respiratory bolt-on
Abstract: Constantly improving the EQ-5D descriptive system is one of the key mandates of EuroQol. To achieve this, specific dimensional bolt-ons were developed, offering a more fine-tuned approach to assessing the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in patients diagnosed with various diseases. This study will focus on a bolt-on dimension that was specifically developed to improve the responsiveness of EQ-5D in assessing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma. Despite the various studies addressing the importance and feasibility of bolt-ons through psychometric comparisons, and some through valuation studies, research on the acceptability and content validity of these bolt-ons is equally crucial. Such studies ensure that the instrument adequately captures the relevant aspects of the concept under investigation. Evidence from these studies enhances the global applicability of the instrument, especially when tested in non-Western environments, where cultural and contextual differences may affect the relevance of HRQoL assessments. Thus, the present study proposal aims to evaluate the acceptability and content validity of the EQ-5D 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) in asthma patients in Kazakhstan, where limited evidence on the use of EQ-5D-5L is available. Few studies have measured HRQoL using the EQ5D instrument in Kazakhstan, specifically in patients with hepatitis (Polukchi & Slavko, 2024), depression in older population (Papageorgiou et al., 2022), hereditary coagulopathies (Vorobyev et al., 2011), and HIV (Zhakipbayeva et al., 2019). Notably, there are no studies involving patients with COPD, despite its status as one of the leading causes of death in the country (Gulis et al., 2021). Additionally, there are no investigations into the content validity of the instrument in Central Asia. Therefore, the proposed content validity check will help ensure that the instrument accurately reflects the lived experiences and health concerns of patients in a non-Western setting, ultimately contributing to its broader global use and relevance. This qualitative study will add to the existing body of EuroQol research by evaluating the applicability of the EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons for asthma patients. Content validity will be assessed through semi-structured, one-to-one interviews with 40 adult asthma patients in Kazakhstan. All 40 participants will first undergo interviews using the concept elicitation method to uncover patient-perceived impacts of asthma, offering deeper insights into how they experience the disease. Following this, the cognitive-debriefing method will be employed to evaluate the acceptability and practical application of the EQ-5D-5L bolt-on, ensuring that the instrument accurately reflects the patients’ HRQoL. The practical usefulness of this study is in its potential to refine the EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons, ensuring they are more sensitive to the specific experiences of asthma patients, particularly in non-Western contexts like Kazakhstan. By assessing the acceptability and content validity of the bolt-ons, the study will provide critical insights into whether this tool accurately captures the HRQoL in asthma patients.

Title: Testing the EQ-HWB-S modifications in a multi-country mixed population
Abstract: Grant 1927-RA assessed the content validity of proposed modifications to the EQ-HWB-9 through qualitative cognitive debriefing interviews in the United States (n=34) and Germany (n=25), and quantitative data collection in the Netherlands -(n=3,783 as an add-on to the W-MIC study). The study also implemented a coordinated international effort across ten countries, which included Argentina, Australia, China, Indonesia, Ireland, Hungary, Slovenia, and the UK.Both qualitative arms recruited adults with chronic health conditions, unpaid caregivers, and social care users and followed parallel protocols developed by the UK team, and based on COSMIN content validity methodology. The German arm conducted interviews in two waves: wave 1 (n=18) tested both the modified and experimental versions (EV1.1 and EMV1.2), and wave 2 (n=7 elderly care recipients) tested the Vienna version (EMV2.1). Findings from the US and Germany were broadly consistent in supporting the content validity of the modified instrument, with most items demonstrating strong comprehension and relevance in both countries, though some items (notably anxiety in Germany) showed lower comprehension in one setting than the other.Evidence from the US, and in several cases also from Germany, favoured specific modifications: “difficulty” over “trouble” for the cognition item, “lacked control” over “no control” for the control item, “moderate difficulty” over “some difficulty,” and “a little of the time” over “only occasionally.” Persistent comprehension challenges were identified with the mobility item, where parenthetical examples led some participants to interpret the item as applicable only to users of mobility devices. These findings informed finalization of the EQ-HWB-9 (EMV2.1. the “Vienna version”) and contribute to the evidence base supporting the transition of the EQ-HWB from experimental to approved status.A large quantitative dataset was also collected in the Netherlands and US. The data collection followed the quantitative testing international protocol developed in the UK. Findings are reported elsewhere, as part of a separate grant.

Title: Testing of the ranking exercise -EUQ2137080 (TRF2191) - English (US) | Face Validity Results
Abstract: This project is undertaken by EuroQol’s version management committee. The aim of the project is to test how respondent will rank order the preliminary severity levels of the EQ-5D-Y-5L. The deliverables of this project are: 1) a definitive protocol for testing the ranking of the qualifiers during translation of the EQ-5D-Y-5L which may well be adapted for use in the adult 5L version as well; 2) a strong paper on the development of the ranking exercise; 3) an indication of how the EQ-5D-Y-5L performed generally in different languages. This information could assist the Exec in making a decision whether to promote the EQ-5D-Y-5L from a beta to an improved version; 4) a validated exercise which could be added to studies validating the EQ-5D-Y-5L and the EQ-5D-5L in future.

Title: Exploring potential innovations in hybrid modeling (REVISED)
Abstract: The aim of this project was to incorporate the power function into the estimation of cTTO-based weights and to test the effect of the power function on the 20-parameter model between countries (the Netherlands, Spain), response interpretation (point, interval), heteroskedasticity (constant, hetero) and censoring (none, -1). Examination of the formulae results revealed two limitations with cTTO responses: power cannot be estimated using cTTO responses alone and there is an overlap/or gap between BTD and WTD errors, which prevents interval estimation using the power function and cTTO responses. The benefits of relaxing the constant proportionality assumption is largely a shift in the values up, smaller confidence intervals, and improved face validity (e.g., fewer negative effects-coded coefficients). An exploratory analysis was conducted to attempt to address the two limitations by widening the intervals and incorporating DCE dead data. These pragmatic techniques appear successful and suggest specific changes to the EQ-VT protocol and hybrid analyses.

Title: Psychometric testing of the EQ-5D-5L and four bolt-ons in chronic urticaria in the US
Abstract: IntroductionChronic Urticaria (CU), characterised by hives and angioedema, can be spontaneous (CSU) or inducible (CIndU). Previous research has reported a substantial impact of CU on health-related quality of life (HRQL). However, research has also shown substantial ceiling effects in the EQ-5D-5L in chronic dermatological conditions. This study aimed to assess whether four existing bolt-ons can improve the EQ-5D-5L’s psychometric properties in CU.MethodsAn online survey was conducted (August-September 2025) with adults with CU, based in the United States. This included the EQ-5D-5L and four bolt-ons (skin irritation and self-confidence from the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox and two previously developed bolt-ons: sleep and social relationships). The survey also included some condition-specific measures: Chronic Urticaria Quality of Life Questionnaire (CU-Q2oL), Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and the Urticaria Control Test (UCT). Analyses explored the distribution of bolt-on responses and EQ-5D-5L ceiling reduction with bolt-ons. Known-groups discrimination by UCT disease control status and hives presence on the day of survey completion was investigated. Convergent validity between bolt-ons and items or total scores of condition-specific measures (CU-Q2oL, DLQI) and divergent validity between bolt-ons and EQ-5D-5L dimensions were also assessed.ResultsThe final sample (N=189; 77% completion rate), were 85% (n=161) female, 13% (n=25) non-white, and on average 40 years old (range: 20-72 years). Representative of the population, 60% (n=113) had CSU, 22% (n=41) CIndU, and 19% (n=35) had both.Of the five EQ-5D-5L and four bolt-on dimensions, problems were most frequently reported for skin irritation (n=168, 89%), and least frequently for self-care (n=46, 24%). Notably, n=28 (15%) reported problems on skin irritation and no problems on pain or discomfort. Full health on the EQ-5D-5L was reported by n=23 (12%), indicating no ceiling effect. The addition of any bolt-on reduced the EQ-5D-5L’s ceiling, however the largest absolute reduction was observed for skin irritation (9%-points).EQ-5D-5L level sum scores (LSS) were not significantly different when comparing those with current hives to those without hives. However, the addition of skin irritation yielded statistically significant group difference (p=0.036). The EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons effectively discriminated between poorly and well controlled disease (UCT). The addition of the skin irritation item in particular increased efficiency approximately fourfold (RE=3.96), which was further increased (RE=5.02) when both skin-irritation and self-confidence bolt-ons were included. The EQ-5D-5L LSS had weak to moderate positive correlations with the DLQI (0.16) and CU-Q2oL total scores (0.32). The addition of any bolt-on increased the strength of correlations, and skin irritation had the largest impact (increasing the correlation coefficient to r=0.27 (DLQI) and r=0.42 (CU-Q2OL), respectively). No strong correlations (≥0.5) were observed between any bolt-ons and EQ-5D-5L dimensions, suggesting divergent validity. ConclusionThe skin irritation bolt-on from the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox had the greatest impact on the EQ-5D-5L’s measurement properties, supporting its addition for this population. Some evidence was shown for the inclusion of further bolt-ons; however, these did not notably improve the EQ-5D-5L’s measurement properties in CU.

Title: Valuing Health-Related Quality of Life: An EQ-5D-5L Value Set for Belgium: Request for budget extention
Abstract: The aim of this study is to generate a value set for Belgium by means of 1000 computer-assisted face-to-face interviews in a representative sample of the general Belgian population. To both ensure the representativeness of the sample and avoid a too wide and scattered spread of individuals to be interviewed, a multistage, stratified, cluster samplingwith unequal probability design will be applied, with provinces and municipalities used as clusters and age and gender used as strata.Health state values will be elicited using both the composite time trade-off (cTTO) and the discrete choice experiment (DCE) tasks. Different models will be tested. For the DCE task alone, a conditional logit regression model will be used. For the cTTO task alone, a modelling strategy similar to the one used in the reassessment of the English value set (Feng et al, 2016){Feng, 2016 #11}will be followed, taking into account censoring-like characteristics of the TTO scale, coefficient order of magnitude consistency, semi-continuous nature of the TTO scale, and the heterogeneity of the respondents ‘personal’ TTO scale. A Tobitmodel similar to the one used in the Dutch value set (Versteegh et al, 2016),{Versteegh, 2016 #10}taking into account censoring-like characteristics of the TTO scale, will also be considered. Finally, the hybrid cTTO and DCE model described in Feng et al, 2016{Feng, 2016 #11}and Ramos-Goni et al, 2017{Ramos-Goni, 2017 #7}will be used. The performance of the models will be assessed on the basis of internal consistency, goodness of fit and parsimony.

Title: Preference heterogeneity in health valuation: Dutch BWS data
Abstract: Background Respondents in a health valuation study may have different sources of error (i.e., heteroskedasticity), tastes (differences in the relative effects of each attribute level), and scales (differences in the absolute effects of all attributes). Although prior studies have compared values by preference-elicitation tasks (e.g., paired comparison [PC] and best-worst scaling case 2 [BWS]), no study has yet controlled for heteroskedasticity and heterogeneity (taste and scale) simultaneously in health valuation. Methods Preferences on EQ-5D-5L profiles were elicited from a random sample of 380 adults from the general population of the Netherlands, using 24 PC and 25 BWS case 2 tasks. To control for heteroskedasticity and heterogeneity (taste and scale) simultaneously, we estimated Dutch EQ-5D-5L values using conditional, heteroskedastic, and scale-adjusted latent class (SALC) logit models by maximum likelihood. Results After controlling for heteroskedasticity, the PC and BWS values were highly correlated (Pearson's correlation: 0.9167, CI: 0.9109-0.9222) and largely agreed (Lin's concordance: 0.7658, CI: 0.7542-0.7769) on a pits scale. In terms of preference heterogeneity, some respondents (mostly young men) failed to account for any of the EQ-5D-5L attributes (i.e., garbage class), and others had a lower scale (59%; p-value: 0.123). Overall, the SALC model produced a consistent Dutch EQ-5D-5L value set on a pits scale, like the original study (Pearson's correlation:0.7295; Lin's concordance: 0.6904). Conclusions This paper shows the merits of simultaneously controlling for heteroskedasticity and heterogeneity in health valuation. In this case, the SALC model dispensed with a garbage class automatically and adjusted the scale for those who failed the PC dominant task. Future analysis may include more behavioral variables to better control heteroskedasticity and heterogeneity in health valuation.

Title: Translating the ‘Methods for analysing and reporting EQ-5D data’ into Chinese
Abstract: The use of EQ-5D in health research has been steadily increasing in China, but many studies published in Chinese journals lack proper guidance in analyzing and reporting EQ-5D data. To address this gap, we undertook the translation of the book “Methods for Analysing and Reporting EQ-5D Data into Chinese”, making this essential resource accessible to Chinese-speaking researchers. The project was carried out by a team of bilingual EuroQol members, who collaborated closely to ensure the accuracy and consistency of the translation. Despite the team's expertise, challenges arose due to inconsistencies in language across sections drafted by different authors, which complicated the translation process. The use of AI tools, such as “Claude,” during the typesetting stage helped identify and correct grammatical errors and inconsistencies, significantly improving the final version. We also encountered terminological variations in the original text, such as "health state" vs. "health profile" and "EQ-5D index" vs. "EQ-5D value" vs. "EQ-5D utility," which prompted the suggestion of a standardized glossary for future work. Through this translation project, we aim to enhance the quality of EQ-5D research in China by providing researchers with clearer guidelines for analysis and reporting. Ultimately, this effort may improve the rigor and reliability of Chinese EQ-5D studies, fostering better health research and decision-making in the region.

Title: Travel scholarship request to attend ISPOR Europe 2024 for findings dissemination.
Abstract: This grant provided funding to support the dissemination of research findings through a poster presentation in the “Patient-Centered Research” section at the ISPOR Europe 2024 Conference which was held between 17 and 20 November 2024, in Spain. The study, “Can EuroQol Instruments be Used to Study Climate Change? Validity and Responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S to Measure Health and Wellbeing Impact of Heatwaves Among Older Adults” [PCR299], assesses the validity and responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S for measuring the health and wellbeing impact of heatwaves among older adults. The study uses data from a cohort of Chinese residents aged 60 and above, surveyed four times in 2023. The study found that the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S demonstrate satisfactory known-groups validity, though limited responsiveness, in measuring the health and wellbeing impact of heatwaves. The project is funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation (1599-RA). The study provides strategic value to the EuroQol Group by generating important evidence on the psychometric performance of EQ-5D instruments. It is particularly significant as it supports the introduction of the EQ-HWB-S and EQ-HWB, aligning with the symposium at ISPOR Europe 2024 Conference, “Going Beyond Health-Related Quality of Life: Towards a Broader QALY Measure for Use Across Sectors: Introducing the EQ Health and Wellbeing Short (EQ-HWB-S) ”. Furthermore, this research contributes to the growing field of climate change studies, which represents one of the most pressing public health challenges of the century. This contribution will enhance the EuroQol Group’s reputation beyond the traditional healthcare research community. The travel grant significantly supported my ability to disseminate important findings at ISPOR Europe 2024, contributing to the broader discussion on the role of EuroQol instruments in addressing global challenges like climate change. The experience has also fostered my professional growth.

Title: Recent experiences using the EuroQol EQ-5D instrument In Latin America: The 3L & 5L; Public Health And Economic Evaluations; Newer Time Trade Off Variants And Discrete ChoiceExperiments
Abstract: EQ-5D research has been presented in all six previous meeting of the ISPOR Latin America Consortium, starting on 2007 in Cartagena (Colombia) with two workshops: 1) HEALTH VALUATION RESEARCH IN LATIN AMERICA: AN AGENDA FOR CHANGE (Kind&Zarate), 2) EQ-5D: PERSPECTIVES AND POSSIBILITIES FOR LATIN AMERICA(Zarate&Badia&Kind&Augustovski), followed by several poster and oral presentations performedthrough the years during the followregionalmeetings.Inthe last ISPOR LA meeting, which took place inSantiago (Chile)in 2015, two EuroQol members received best oral presentations awards (Augustovsky&Zarate) for EQ-5D research performed in Uruguay and Chilei.Given thestrong influence of the EuroQol group in the Region, there have been many EQ-5D valuation studies performed in Argentina, Chile, Brazil, Uruguay, Colombia and recently in Ecuador. EQ-5D 3L has been included in national population surveys in Argentina (2005) and Chile (2016),bothinitiatives were organized by their local Ministriesof Health in each nation.Despite the steady increase of EQ-5D research, that have seen almost 100 publications related with Latin Americain Pubmedii, there are stillmany countries in Latin America where there should bea highinterest to measure and value self-perceived health, but alow level of knowledge about how to do it properly based on the best scientific evidence. For the coming 2017 ISPOR LA Regional meeting, a group of EQ-5D members and non-member hassubmitted oneworkshop and fourpresentations (one of them already selected for an award). All activitiesaim to provide crucial information to Latin American decision makers regarding the different uses of the EQ-5D instrument in Public Health and Economic Evaluation, as well as give examples of such activities performed in different countries in Central and South America.The Conference expectsclose to 1.000 attendees and we aim to cover at least 10%-20% of them by direct contactthough our fivepresentations already confirmedby the ISPOR LA ConferenceCommittee.

Title: Cross-Country Qualitative Analysis of EQ-HWB Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Three Positively-Framed Items Responses From Indonesia, Germany, Slovenia, and Hungary
Abstract: Background: The EQ-HWB and its short form, EQ-HWB-9, were designed to capture both health and broader aspects of wellbeing across health and social care contexts. A Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) is being considered to complement the descriptive system by providing a respondent-centred summary rating of overall health and wellbeing. However, transferring the VAS concept from the EQ-5D to the EQ-HWB raises conceptual and methodological challenges, as the construct extends beyond health, involves multiple user groups (patients, social care users and carers), and must function equivalently across languages and cultures. In parallel, the EQ-HWB Working Group is reviewing item polarity. In the experimental (2022) version of EQ-HWB long form, there were three positively framed items ( felt accepted, felt good about self, and could do things as wanted to) that were revised as negatively framed in the modified (2024) version to ensure consistency across the items of the instrument. The wording of the “nothing to look forward to” item was also revised to “felt hopeless”. These      refinements require qualitative evidence to inform instrument development decisions.Objectives: This study aims (1) to explore respondents’ understanding and interpretation of potential EQ-HWB VAS versions across different languages and cultural contexts, (2) to qualitatively examine the relevance and comprehensibility of both the positively and negatively framed versions of the three modified EQ-HWB items, and (3) to investigate participants’ interpretations of the revised “hopeless” item, given that the final wording has not yet been determined.Methods: This cross-country qualitative study will conduct a pooled secondary analysis of existing interview data collected during the EQ-HWB modification studies in Indonesia, Germany, Slovenia, and Hungary. Across countries, semi-structured interviews were conducted with patients, informal carers and social care users, who completed and discussed the EQ-HWB descriptive system and the VAS versions. Probing questions explored what respondents thought the VAS was asking them to do, what recall period or reference they considered, whether the VAS was a meaningful summary of how they overall felt, how they interpreted alternative anchor labels (health, health and wellbeing, health and quality of life, and quality of life), and how they understood and related the concepts of health, quality of life and wellbeing. In countries where polarity testing was conducted (Indonesia, Slovenia, and Hungary), additional probes examined comprehension and relevance of the positive and negative item versions, including the “hopeless” item. Thematic analysis will be conducted centrally, with harmonized coding frameworks and iterative team discussions. Analysis will focus on cross-country and cross-group comparisons by examining similarities and differences by respondent type (e.g., caregivers, patients, social care users) and linguistic or cultural context.

Title: Using routinely collected EQ-5D-5L to evaluate Workers' Compensation Board programs and predict return-to-work outcomes
Abstract: The integration of patient perspectives into healthcare is essential for improving care quality and effectiveness. Despite global recognition of this need, there remains a challenge in adequately measuring outcomes that matter most to patients. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are standardized tools designed to capture patients' health status from their own perspective. One prominent PROM, the EQ-5D, is widely used to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) across various dimensions such as mobility, self-care, and pain/discomfort.
