In Alberta, the EQ-5D-5L has been incorporated into healthcare assessment frameworks and surveys to evaluate the effectiveness of health services and ensure they meet patient needs. This project builds upon our previous collaboration with the Workers' Compensation Board (WCB), which focused on evaluating the performance of two key patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in assessing Return-to-Work (RTW) programs. Our prior work involved a comparative analysis of the EQ-5D and the SF-36, with the goal of providing WCB with insights into the transition from SF-36 to EQ-5D for RTW assessments. The findings indicated that the EQ-5D outperforms the SF-36 in capturing the nuanced health status of workers, demonstrating greater relevance and accuracy. This analysis has been documented in a detailed report shared with Millard Health, presented at the EuroQol Academy meeting in Copenhagen in March 2024, and will be featured in an upcoming manuscript. Globally, the EQ-5D is a leading instrument for measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Endorsed by Alberta Health for self-reported health status assessments, the EQ-5D is integrated into various outcome measurement initiatives across Alberta Health Services, and its use in WCB return-to-work surveys aligns with provincial and national PROMs initiatives led by the Canadian Institute of Health Information (CIHI) and similar OECD efforts. Our proposed project aims to utilize the extensive EQ-5D data collected through WCB surveys to enhance quality improvement initiatives for RTW programs. Specifically, we will: 1) assess the impact of WCB programs on injured workers' HRQoL as measured by the EQ-5D; 2) compare these HRQoL outcomes to Alberta population norms; and 3) evaluate the predictive validity of the EQ-5D for forecasting RTW outcomes. This research is expected to provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of health programs and inform targeted interventions to improve workers' return-to-work experiences, thus contributing significantly to evidence-based quality improvement in health and social care.

Title: Valuation of the EQ-5D-Y in Hungary
Abstract: Background: The Hungarian health technology assessment guidelines recommend the use of the EuroQol instrument family in quality-adjusted life year calculations. However, no national value set exists for the EQ-5D-Y-3L or any other youth-specific instrument. Objective: This study aims to develop a national value set of the EQ-5D-Y-3L for Hungary based on preferences of the general adult population. Methods: This study followed the international valuation protocol for the EQ-5D-Y-3L. A representative sample of the Hungarian general adult population in terms of age and gender was recruited. Overall, 996 respondents completed online discrete choice experiment (DCE) tasks and 200 respondents completed composite time-trade-off (cTTO) tasks by computer-assisted personal interviews. Adults valued hypothetical EQ-5D-Y-3L health states considering the health of a 10-year-old child. DCE data were modeled using a mixed logit model with random-correlated coefficients. Latent DCE utility estimates were mapped onto observed mean cTTO utilities using ordinary least squares regression. Results: For each domain, the value set resulted in larger utility decrements with more severe response levels. The relative importance of domains by level 3 coefficients was as follows: having pain or discomfort>feeling worried, sad or unhappy>mobility>doing usual activities>looking after myself. Overall, 12.8% of all health states had negative utilities in the Hungarian value set, with the pits state (33333) having the lowest predicted utility of -0.503. Conclusion: This study developed a national value set of the EQ-5D-Y-3L for Hungary. The value set enables to evaluate the cost-utility of health technologies for children and adolescents based on societal preferences in Hungary.

Title: Legitimacy, use (and mis‐use) of Minimally Important Differences (MIDs) with the EQ-­‐5D: A systematic review
Abstract: We conducted a systematic review on minimally important difference for EQ-5D. We worked together with a librarianand established comprehensive search strategies for MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, and Cochrane Library. Subject headings and textwords relating to ‘minimally important difference’ and ‘EQ-5D’were searched in the aforementioneddatabases. No language restrictions were applied. Studies with at least one original estimated MID of the EQ-5D were included.We hired two research assistances (PhD students) to conduct screening and data extraction together with two APERSU research team members. MID estimationsidentified in our reviewwere summarized based onEQ-5D components, estimation methods, patient population, baseline health status and direction of change. We also took a close look at allanchor-based approachestimations, and conducted a critical review focusing on methodological limitations regarding this approach.

Title: Examining carer outcomes using the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB: Evidence from the EQ DAPHNIE Survey
Abstract: Objectives: Despite growing interest in incorporating carer outcomes into health economic evaluation, evidence on the performance of utility-based measures among informal carers remains limited. This study aimed to assess the performance of the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 in capturing outcomes relevant to informal carers.Methods: Data were drawn from the EQ-DAPHNIE survey conducted in English-speaking countries (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States). The EQ-HWB-9 (UK pilot value set) and EQ-5D-5L (country-specific value sets) were evaluated. Feasibility, distributional properties, convergent validity, and known-group validity were assessed using predefined hypotheses. Subgroup analyses were undertaken by age (≥60 vs <60 years) and financial situation (coping vs financially strained).Results: The sample comprised 6,743 informal carers from Australia (n=1,447), Canada (n=1,265), New Zealand (n=1,435), the United Kingdom (n=1,337), and the United States (n=1,259). A notable ceiling effect (>15%) was observed for the EQ-5D-5L, but not for the EQ-HWB-9. Although most respondents reported no problems on the EQ-5D-5L mobility, self-care, and usual activities dimensions, at least 60% reported problems in the pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression dimensions. For the EQ-HWB-9, impairments were most frequently reported in pain, loneliness, cognition, feeling sad or depressed, anxiety, and control. Both instruments demonstrated moderate correlations with the WHO-5, PROMIS-10, OPQOL-brief, PHQ-2, and GAD-2, and showed good known-group validity across indicators of physical and mental disability, chronic conditions, sleep quality, social support, and the perceived impact of caring on carers’ own health. Findings were consistent across country-specific EQ-5D-5L value sets and remained robust in subgroup analyses.Conclusions: Both the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 appear suitable for assessing outcomes among informal carers. However, evidence on responsiveness remains limited and is needed to more fully evaluate the performance of these measures in this population. Further research is warranted.

Title: Investigating the effect of interaction terms in modelling EQ-5D value set and its impact on sample size requirements using three VAS saturated data
Abstract: Objective: The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of incorporating interaction terms in EQ-5D valuation models and to examine the implications of health state coverage and sample size allocation for future valuation studies. By leveraging three saturated datasets—EQ-5D-3L datasets from the Netherlands and the UK, and an EQ-5D-5L dataset from China—we aimed to determine optimal model specifications and assess whether expanding the number of health states in the design improves predictive accuracy. Methods: We first estimated main-effects models and models with interaction terms to assess their predictive performance, using root mean squared error (RMSE), Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and R² as model evaluation metrics. We then systematically tested different health state selection strategies, including reducing the number of health states or observations per state, to examine the impact on model accuracy and feasibility. The study also explored whether specific universal interaction effects could be identified across the three datasets. Results: The inclusion of interaction terms significantly improved model performance, with RMSE reductions of 51% in the Netherlands dataset, 37% in the UK dataset, and 17% in the China dataset. However, the effect of interactions varied across datasets, with no universal interaction term consistently identified, except for PD3AD3, which captures the combined effect of severe pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression. Additionally, we found that increasing health state coverage (rather than increasing the number of responses per health state) yielded better prediction accuracy. Specifically, when the total sample size was fixed, doubling the number of health states while halving the number of responses per state improved RMSE without compromising model validity. Discussions: These findings suggest that the optimal model specifications differ by EQ-5D version: for EQ-5D-3L, the best-performing model includes N3 and D1, while for EQ-5D-5L, N45 and D1 provide the best fit. The results also highlight the importance of broader health state coverage in experimental design—current valuation studies that allocate 100 observations per health state may achieve better predictive accuracy by halving observations per state and doubling the number of health states in the design. The study demonstrates that interaction effects play a crucial role in EQ-5D valuation, particularly for severe health impairments. Future valuation studies should consider incorporating key interaction terms while optimizing health state selection strategies to balance model parsimony and predictive accuracy. These findings have practical implications for the design of future EQ-5D valuation studies and may inform methodological refinements for valuing newer instruments such as EQ-HWB-S, where health state coverage is a critical concern.

Title: PROMs and PREMs, their interaction: bias or added value? On the dependency between EQ5D5L (stand alone PROM), and validated PREMs in a large sample of recently delivering women, ranging from healthy to severely affected
Abstract: IntroductionThe study aim is to investigate the mutual cross-sectional relationships between PROMs (EQ-5D-5L) and PREMs (Picker, ReproQ-8D) with and without case-mix adjustment (socio-demographic, clinical, process of care, socio-economic status [SES] variables) in antenatal and postnatal care (Dutch healthcare system), using different instruments (EQ research priority). The research questions were (see proposal):AIM 1: Investigate whether EQ-VAS scores depend primarily on underlying EQ-5D PROMs information, particularly domain-wise, where substantial explanatory power is hypothesized.Embedded we checked the need for context-specific bolt-ons and the relevance of socio-demographic casemix factors, if these outcomes are used for quality of care (performance) purposes. AIM 2: Investigate whether Picker scores primarily reflect specific PREM information (ReproQ domains), where substantial explanatory power is hypothesized. Embedded we could check the need for casemix adjustment.AIM 3: Estimate for the EQ-5D-5L PROMs (domain scores, index, LSS) and EQ-VAS the influence of PREM measures (carry-over effect) where it is hypothesized that this effect should be minimal. And, reversely, the carry-over effect of the same PROMs for the PREMs (Picker, ReproQ8D), where it is hypothesized that this effect should be minimal.AIM 4: Study the role of SES in case-mix adjustment. I.e., to test whether the findings from AIMS 1-3 are essentially unrelated to deprivation/low SES, which is a pre-condition for straightforward use by clients of PROM and PREM data in monitoring quality of care.AIM 5: Test whether the relation between covariables and EQ-VAS (PROM) in the upper part of the VAS scale is different from relations in the lower part of the VAS scale; and the same for Picker score (PREM). Rationale of AIM 5 is that both PROMs and PREMs are statistically difficult to explain from underlying factors, even with a comprehensive predictor set. Hypothetically, relations are not equivalent across the range of the outcome. For example, for groups in rather good health EQ-VAS scores are possibly explained by an array of non-medical factors while for groups in poor health EQ-VAS is mainly explained by health-related factors (confounding).  The following sub-aims were added: 1) a longitudinal analysis (paired EQ-ANTE /EQ-POST data); 2) the adjustment of socio-economic status educational level as individual characteristic vs. composite SES indicator based on ZIP-code); 3) study of the well-known but difficult to understand poor explanatory performance of EQVAS as PROM compared to the Picker PREM models.METHODSData. We used data from a nationally representative cohort of >8000 pregnant women (covering 70% of perinatal care units), with longitudinal outcome data on: (1) PROMs (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS, condition specific maternal PROMs, condition specific newborn PROMs, obtained via maternal report and administrative routes); (2) PREMs (ReproQ-8D, an 8-dimensional validated WHO-based questionnaire; Picker score); (3) socio-demographic characteristics; and (4) complete clinical and process of care profile. This high-quality dataset was sufficiently large for analysis of subgroups of respondents/women with serious medical conditions.Datasets. Five specific datasets were created: Four cross-sectional datasets (EQVAS-ANTE (=antenatal), EQVAS-POST (=postnatal), PICKER-ANTE, PICKER-POST as dependent variables), and one longitudinal dataset for analysis of differences (paired EQ-ANTE and EQ-POST). The clinical and process of care variables differ between the ANTE and POST datasets. Analysis. 1. Univariable and multivariable linear regression (OLS, with/ without transformation of the dependent variable, forced entry of covariables) as point of departure. STEPWISE OLS (with/without transformation) was used to investigate the relative importance of predictors. 2. Dependent variables: EQ-VAS score (ANTE, POST) in AIM1; Picker-score (ANTE, POST) in AIM2; and all four outcomes in AIM3 and AIM4; and the difference (POST–ANTE) score in AIM5.3. For each AIM a large set of models was estimated, with the same structure (ANTE/POST, summary scores (Picker, EQVAS, EQ-Index, EQ-LSS, ReproQ Personal and Setting summary scores vs. EQ-5D and ReproQ-8D domain scores), with/without transformation, different covariable/clinical factors sets, ENTER/STEPWISE). Model changes were partially carried out to test systematically the role of (i) the selected variable set, (ii) transformation of the dependent variable, (iii) confounding (regular vs. stratified multivariable models) and (iv) multilevel effect. 4. Alternative models were compared in terms of R2 (proportion of variance explained) of the PREM effect (in PROM models; AIM 1) or PROM effect (in PREM models; AIM 2). Adjusted R2 were always 0.01-0.02 smaller than absolute R2 due to large sample size and were avoided (lack of relevance).5. The multivariable analyses were structured as follows:- a. We compared for the EQ-VAS models (AIM 1) the impact of EQ-PROM info (3 variants) as covariables, PREMs (3 variants), socio-demographic and clinical and process of care variables (1 variant), and socio-economic status (2 variants); together 3*3*2 =18 models (see T9+T10+T11).- b. Next, we repeated a., using different transformations of the dependent variable (root, square, natural logarithm, exponent). These transformations neither provided additional insight, nor improved the R2 values importantly.- c. Next, we used stratified analysis for (1) the dependent variable (focusing on the lower range outcomes to avoid the possible ceiling effect; cut-off 85%); and (2) the PREMs (cut-off 85%).- d. Finally, the dependent variable was dichotomized (1/0 variable) based on the same cut-off as in c., and multivariable logistic regression analysis was applied.For AIM2, the roles of PREMs and PROMs were reversed.-e. Finally we added multilevel analysis for EQ-VAS, with perinatal unit as multilevel effect.6. Sensitivity analysis was done for (a) the impact of SES (educational level vs. ZIP-based composite SES index); and (b) the potentially modifying effects of SES (comprehensive regression model vs. stratified analysis; i.e. confounding).RESULTS/DISCUSSIONThe key results are summarized in a Table book (56 tables, 7 Appendices). AIM1: The gain in explanatory power of PREMs (irrespective of precise measure) on EQVAS invariably is small; R2-change is +0.01-0.02 and coefficient size was low. Model adaptations sometimes increased or decreased R2 but never altered the PREM impact. The statistical results are supported by the XY-plot of Picker and EQ-VAS both ANTE and POST (Table Appendix 1). AIM2: The explanatory power of adding PROMs to PREMs is slightly larger than the reverse, yet small (R2 change +0.02-0.03; note that PREM models in general perform better). The type of PROM measure mattered somewhat; EQVAS had slightly more impact than EQ-5D and its derivatives. Model adaptations some­times impacted R2, but never the PROM impact. See also XY-plot of Picker and EQ-VAS (Table Appendix 1).SUBAIM OF 1. AND 2. CASEMIX adjustment Considering the minimal R2 values and the generally small coefficient sizes, casemix adjustment for potential PREM differences is not needed for the evaluation of quality of care performance with EQ5D/EQ-VAS as reference. The same applies for the reverse case. AIM3: Of the EQ-5D-domains, self-care has largest impact on PREMs, particularly for self–care levels L3-5. Overall the impact is small in terms of R2.AIM4: A head-to-head comparison between self-reported educational level and an official ZIP-based composite SES index showed that the association between both indicators is weaker than expected. This suggests that prosperity and living in a high-quality area does not strongly depend on a pregnant woman’s own level of education. Yet, the R2 of both indicators (in multivariable models) was comparable; if anything, the ZIP-based index performed slightly better. In terms of coef­ficient size, the gradient of higher EQ-VAS with higher SES-level was small relative to the scale, and standard errors were large. Using stratified analyses (3 strata for SES) showed a strong effect from stratification, i.e. demonstrated strong confounding: PROM and PREM models improved substantially, with stratified models with highest R2 seen at the extreme upper and extreme lower end of the SES scale. This cannot be explained by overspecification (large sample). Usually the model with low R2 was the model that included all SES-strata. We conclude that EQ-VAS and Picker models behave differently according to SES stratum. This should be analysed using stratified analyses. This cannot be covered by treating the SES as independent covariate nor as interaction term. While confounding is the likely cause, we cannot exclude effects from response heterogeneity. INCIDENTAL FINDINGS of AIM1 and AIM2: EQVAS models perform better (in terms of R2) in strata with lower PREM scores, and, reversely, Picker models perform better in strata with lower EQ5D/EQVAS scores. This suggests that the performance of EQ-VAS models is strongly affected (lower R2) by the presence of satisfied (!) respondents who add/subtract EQ-VAS points, not on the basis of their perceived health but for other reasons. AIM5: Stratified analysis (five EQ-VAS strata in AIM1; five Picker strata in AIM2) showed that the performance (in terms of R2) of any of the 5 stratified models was worse compared to the combined model. These results are opposed to the analysis of SES. INCIDENTAL FINDINGS1.There was no multilevel effect of perinatal care unit for the EQ-VAS ANTE data. Analysis of the EQVAS-POST data showed a low to modest multilevel effect, with impact on the coefficients related to process of care (indicators of high perinatal risk: secondary care only and referral from primary to secondary care) but not the other variables. Change of model log-likelihood and change of AIC were both ≈ 0.5%. Despite strong arguments to apply multilevel analysis with perinatal care unit as level, the effect for model performance was (very) modest.2.The analysis on difference scores suggests that (individual) difference scores are accessible for analysis, even with inclusion of difference scores of co-factors (when these factors can be subject to change over time). 3.Two surprising findings were:A. Overall, PREM-models showed better performance (in terms of R2) than the PROM-models, despite the skewed Picker distributions and less potential PREM cofactors.B. Overall, the EQVAS ANTE models showed better performance (in terms of R2) than the EQVAS POST models despite considerably more relevant covariables for EQVAS POST analyses.There are two non-mutually exclusive explanations for this observation:Firstly, postnatally mothers exhibit various very specific symptoms/complaints, adding to heterogeneity, that are hardly covered by the EQ-5D domains: e.g., breast-related symptoms, problems of urination and defaecation, psychological symptoms [not at all covered by AD domain]. The antenatal phase is characterized by fewer symptoms in general, and e.g. the psychological ones fit bitter to the AD domain.The relatively poor performance of EQVAS models in persons with a condition may be the result of underspecification of the model (practically: lack of bolt-ons).Secondly, having a specific disease condition (that might impact EQ5D scores) vs. experiencing non-wellbeing (extending to EQ5D impact) reflects very different pathways. Presence or absence of a specific disease condition could be another case of confounding (support from the POPCORN study). The same might be true for severe vs. mild disease or symptoms. If true, this phenomenon might affect the results of descriptive as well as valuation studies.4. Overall, the L1 vs L2-L5 dichotomy performed inferior to the L1-L2 vs L3-L5 dichotomy in our case. Conclusions: see highlights

Title: Measuring Health-Related Quality of Life in Orthopedic Clinical Practice
Abstract: This PhD-project investigated the broad potential of the use of EQ-5D and other PROMs in routine clinical care application in orthopedic surgery. The use of PROMs covered both of quality enhancement endevours and empirical research into specific problems. While doing so, several methodological challenges were addressed. First, (1) we conducted a systematic review on the use of EQ-5D and other PROMs in quality improvement tools; the scope was extended to other clinical fields (1 paper accepted). Next, (2) we used Dutch Arthroplasty Registry data to study the presence, patterns and pathways of socio-economic inequalities in total hip and knee arthroplasty patients. This research illustrated the meaningful performance of EQ-5D as indicator of inequalities along other PROMs via multiple techniques (1 paper published; 1 submitted). With the same dataset, we (3) quantified the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on EQ-5D and other PROMs, illustrating the performance of EQ-5D as public health indicator of a health disaster with national magnitude (1 paper published). (4) We compared head-to-head the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in adolescents with scoliosis, where the hypothesis to reject was that they are incomparable (1 under review). Finally, we (5) conducted a quality of care data analysis using national Medicare (US) data on arthroplasty interventions, in the context of a scientific exchange program supervised by dr. J. Poeran (NY, US). The relative importance of hospital, patient, and socio-economic factors, and their interaction, was addressed (1 paper published). The PhD-manuscript incorporating these studies has been submitted for evaluation, and is expected to be publicly defended in the first half of 2025 at Erasmus University Rotterdam. Its title runs “Patient-Reported Outcomes in Orthopedic Surgery: Enhancing Care Quality and Reducing Socioeconomic Inequality”. Over the course of the PhD trajectory, the candidate has contributed in several ways to the scientific processes both at Erasmus MC (dpt of Orthopedic Surgery) and the EuroQol Research Foundation, both related to the topics of the project, and unrelated (the EuroQol PhD network).

Title: Second Annual End-user and Scientific Advisory Committee Meeting
Abstract: Our proposalwas to host a meeting, notundertakea study. Through our meeting we educated and informed attendees on theuse ofEQ-5D and PROMs,including HQCA and AHS partners, Alberta Health Ministry Representatives and researchers from universities and organizations across Alberta and Canada.This has paved the way for more end-users of the EQ instrument which will lead to increased applications and more data being generatedand therefore, moreinformation to potentially call upon for future research.We also gained insight from end-users, particularly in the primary care setting, as to important implementation research questions to address. This input helps to inform our research agenda, about how EQ-5D is applied in PROMs programs.For our 3rd Annual APERSU End-User meeting, we will put the call out earlier to obtain a keynote speaker. We were waiting for a very long time to for a response from one of the people we contacted, in hindsight, we should have looked for alternates sooner. We have had comments from some potential attendees that the dates of our meeting conflicted with other meetingsbut with the diverse group of potential participants, it is difficult to get a time that would suit all.

Title: Travel Grant for IAHPR Presentation during the EuroQol Sponsored Session
Abstract: This grant contributed toward my meeting registration, train/bus fare, and hotel accommodations for the 16th IAHPR Meeting.  At this Meeting, I gave a 25-minute podium presentation on "Preference Reliability" during a session sponsored by the EuroQol Research Foundation. This secondary analysis utilized existing EQ-5D-5L data but was not part of any funded project. Multiple EuroQol members were in attendance, including Rosalie Viney, Exec Chair.

Title: EQ-5D health inequalities in orthopaedic patients. A Dutch registry-based study.
Abstract: **Aims** To assess the presence and extent of Health Inequalities (HIs) measured through a.o. the EQ-5D in all Dutch patients (n>150.000) treated by hip&knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis in 2016-2020. This project builds on preliminary evidence on best way to express those inequalities (EuroQol-Equimetrics (Haagsma, Janssen, Bonsel)) and the results on best econometric indicators (Bailey&Janssen 2020) under the HISIG umbrella. **Methods** Data is retrieved from the Dutch National Orthopedic Registry (LROI), with compulsory registration. Hip&knee arthroplasty patients report outcome data (EQ-5D, EQ-VAS, validated international disease-specific measures) before, shortly after, one-year after surgery. Recorded characteristics are age, gender, BMI, regional features, teaching vs. general/private hospital. Whilst maintaining privacy, SES is assigned to patients through their postal code. **Analyses** Simple and more advanced (standardized) table analysis, primarily on tLSS/index/VAS. Gini, Kakwani index (cf. advice Bailey&Janssen); Slope II & Relative II (cf. Equimetrics) Standard logistic/multivariable analysis; decomposition analysis (from Szende et al., 2014). Domain response analysis. If outcomes relate on the individual level: dedicated longitudinal analysis. Otherwise, cross-sectional analysis for inequities at 3 time moments. Above is repeated for disease-specific questionnaires (HOOS-PS, KOOS-PS, OHS/OKS). **Hypotheses** Better outcomes and higher surgical gain with higher SES levels; lower outcomes in teaching hospitals Larger HIs with EQ-5D LSS and index compared to VAS (adaptation). Results will be discussed among clinical experts to identify explanations. **Collaboration gains** Methods will be shared specifically with HISIG; other EQ-members may join with national datasets (appended project). APERSU (F. Al Sayah) group expressed willingness to accommodate a subsequent study on-site, using same methods/LROI.

Title: Exploring the content validity of the self-confidence and skin irritation bolt-ons in alopecia areata and vitiligo
Abstract: Background: Several bolt-ons have been developed for the EQ-5D, including two developed initially for psoriasis: skin irritation (SI) and self-confidence (SC). These dimensions may be relevant in other skin conditions, such as alopecia areata (AA) and vitiligo, however currently there is no evidence of their content validity in these conditions. Objectives: To conduct qualitative research to explore the content validity of the EQ-5D-5L and the SI and SC bolt-ons in two chronic dermatological conditions: AA and vitiligo. Methods: A qualitative study will be conducted to explore the content validity of the SI and SC bolt-ons in AA and vitiligo; other bolt-ons will also be considered, based on the findings of a rapid literature review. Individual interviews will be conducted until data saturation is reached, which is expected to be when approximately 15 interviews with patients with each condition have been conducted. Recruitment will aim to include patients with different severities of each condition in the UK. In order to evaluate the content validity of the EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons, the interviews will aim to assess the comprehensiveness, comprehensibility and relevance. Interviews will consist of concept elicitation questions to explore important areas of health-related quality of life in AA and vitiligo and cognitive interview questions about the relevance of and potential overlaps between dimensions and appropriateness of the wording and important health concepts not captured by the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons. Data will be analysed using thematic and content analysis.

Title: Measuring family spillover effects with EuroQol instruments over time associated with the care of babies with necrotising enterocolitis
Abstract: The impact of neonatal care interventions on health outcomes affects not only the newborn but their mothers and other family members. These spillover effects are seldom included in economic evaluation of neonatal care technologies because data to evaluate these wider benefits are rarely collected. The ongoing withholding enteral feeds around blood transfusion (WHEAT) study is a multi-centre randomised controlled trial comparing withholding milk feeds before, during and after blood transfusion in preterm infants to reduce the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC). WHEAT is funded by the Canadian Institute for Health Research (CIHR), as an international, randomised trial across the UK and Canada. An economic evaluation alongside the trial was not originally funded but investigators have now secured additional funding from the Bukhman Foundation to collect the relevant data for a cost analysis associated with NEC and an economic evaluation in the UK. In addition to resource use, planned data collection will include EQ-TIPS (for newborns), EQ-5D-5L (for parents), EQ-HWB (for parents) and EQ-5D-Y-3L (for siblings) at neonatal discharge, 6 months and 1 year follow-up. This longitudinal design will provide an excellent resource to understand whether EuroQol instruments used in the family context are able to capture spillover effects over time. This proposal has two main aims: 1) to secure the additional funding needed to successfully conduct this study over a year period, and 2) to formally assess the health spillovers on main carers and other family of babies who survived NEC.

Title: VMC proposal for developmental work to support development of gender neutral language in the EuroQol suite of measures
Abstract: (Note: This project has been discussed by email between the VMC (Sarah and Jennifer) and Elly and Bernhard. The project is being entered in to the portal so their is a project number allocated to it ad a budget stated for the external researchers and advisors to invoice against). The VMC wish to explore the use of gender-neutral terms in PROMS generally and in the EuroQol instruments in particular and is thus seeking funding to undertake this work. At the 2021 Strategic Planning Meeting the VMC agreed in principle that one of the roles of the Committee is to ensure that the EuroQol instruments are as inclusive as possible. In recent years there has been an increasing realization that gendered language may alienate certain respondents and may exclude some groups from participating in surveys. However, before the VMC proceeds to alter existing wording or introduce new phrases, there needs to be a strong theoretical foundation upon which to make these changes. The need for this strong foundation has become evident with each of our VMC/RWS meetings where the complexity associated with gender neutrality is evident. This proposal is requesting support for external-to-VMC expertise to undertake a scoping review with VMC members. Specifically: 1) For a researcher (external to the VMC) to lead a scoping review of published literature to identify, describe and understand the strategies used by others in addressing gender inclusiveness/neutrality in questionnaires 2) Engage advisors to provide specialist advice. We would like at least one advisor to come from the LGBTQIA+ (Rainbow) community to help ensure findings are interpreted in a non-discriminatory manner and one advisor from a region where there may be cultural/policy challenges to the use of gender neutral/inclusive language. Apart from providing the VMC with a theoretical foundation on which to base any further action on this topic, the project will deliver: A paper prepared for submission to a peer-reviewed journal, a survey of EuroQol members, and a report to the VMC and Executive.

Title: A qualitative approach to understanding what aspects of health are important to people Ð Australian extension
Abstract: This was an Australian extension to an existing project conducted in the UK. The attached final report reports results from both countries. We developed and administered a survey to identify what aspects of health and quality of life are important to people in the UK and Australia, and analysed these using content analysis to identify themes. The survey asked people list as many aspects of health and quality of life as they could The sample included individuals in UK and Australia (n=200 in each country) with one of four conditions (asthma, diabetes, depression and skin cancer), or no condition. We found that respondents described many of the dimensions included in generic preference based measures. Relationships, activities, social aspects and enjoyment appeared far more frequently in the quality of life data than in the health data. There were some differences between UK and Australian respondents - UK respondents more frequently mentioned quality of life aspects related to freedom, enjoyment, and absence of restrictions. Australian respondents more frequently mentioned aspects related to mental functioning, peace and contentment, and independence. There were also differences between patient sub groups.

Title: Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of the Chichewa (Malawi) EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) Measure of Health Related Quality of Life
Abstract: Objectives: The EuroQol Toddlers and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) was developed as a generic health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instrument for children aged 0 - 3 years. While the EQ-TIPS V3 has been used in various high-income settings across different disease with promising results, research in resource-poor settings has been limited. The aim of this work was to crossculturally adapt and validate the EQ-TIPS into Chichewa for Malawi. Methods: EQ-TIPS was forward translated into Chichewa and back translated into English by two sets of translators. The translated version was reviewed by a member of the EuroQol version management committee and after several iterations, an agreement was reached for a consensus version. The version was piloted through cognitive debriefing with five caregivers of infants and children aged 0-3 years two of which tow were at home and three in hospital. Changes were made accordingly based on their feedback to inform the next version. Results: The translation process was relatively straightforward although two items: “managing emotions” and ”interacting with others” were found to be difficult concepts to translate accurately. Further, we found that adding a pronoun such as he/she to response levels was necessary in comparison with the source language standalone options. Cognitive debriefing (CD) indicated that combining both “kumasuka (freeness)” and “kulankhulana (speaking)” would be ideal to accurately translate “interacting with others” which was also noted during translation. Additionally, CD identified issues with translation of ”sleep”, “pain”, and “managing emotions” items. For sleep, some respondents suggested that the examples included to explain the concept referred to different phases of sleep thereby making it difficult to rate it. Kuphwanya m’thupi (pain) was suggested to be replaced with ‘kupweteka’ or ‘kuwawa’ which also refers to pain but thought to be more age-appropriate translation for infants and toddlers. The EQ-5D-Y versions, however, uses “Kuphwanya m’thupi” for “pain” because they carry the thought of someone ably expressing pain for themselves as opposed to a proxy version. Lastly, it was suggested that “dongosolo la malingaliro” (managing emotions) may benefit from expansion of examples. For example, adding ‘ngati mwana amatha kuonetsa mkwiyo (unhappy), chisoni (sadness), chisangalalo (happiness)’ would enrich the meaning. Conclusion: These are only preliminary results of the EQ-TIPS Chichewa version for Malawi. The next steps will be to refine the items and come up with a final approved version. As this is the first study, to the knowledge of the team, attempting to establish a conceptual and linguistic equivalence of the EQ-TIPS into an African spoken language outside South Africa, this work will not only be useful to EuroQol’s Strategic Plan but also other settings. The study found that observable items were more easier to translate and understand as opposed to emotional items. The underlying cause for this could be due to a limited vocabularly of the Chichewa language which may be a common thread for the Bantu languages spoken in most of the sub-Saharan 2 of 3 Africa. As such, some emotional concepts such as pain, may be adapted with more examples for younger children in these settings.

Title: Building values sets based on TTO results by averaging model predictions and actually observed means
Abstract: To inform cost-utility analysis of health technologies, health states are assigned index values measuring their attractiveness for a given population. The values are constructed based on preference elicitation tasks. For EQ-5D-5L instruments, the index values are typically derived from time trade-off method (TTO), either alone, or in combination with discrete choice experiment (DCE). For practical reasons, only a limited number of EQ-5D-5L health states can be used in valuation studies, and extrapolations using econometric models are needed. However, also for the states valued in TTO, the index values are typically based solely on the econometric model, in this sense ignoring the actual direct observations. I aim to measure the benefits of using the direct observation in value set building. I propose a novel method of using the direct observation for neighbouring states (defined using Manhattan distance in EQ-5D-5L space) and averaging it with the econometric-model-derived values. I show it has promising statistical properties and it can help mitigate the problem of non-monotonicity of preferences which is often observed in actual valuation studies (i.e., level denoting more severe problems being assigned lower disutility). To value a given state, the direct observations of similar states are used, which helps to ac-count for the idiosyncrasies in the description of these states, e.g., interactions between select-ed dimensions. In the Bayesian setting, I show how the proposed method can also account for censoring in the TTO values as collected in standard EQ-5D-5L valuation studies. The results suggest that extending the usual design of 86 TTO states may be beneficial as it would yield more information on preferences for local regions of the space of all EQ-5D-5L states. Future studies could explore if the approach based on neighbouring states can narrow the gap between TTO and DCE results.

Title: Intercept investigation: Does the value drop from full health to any EQ-5D problems reflect preferences, or is it an artefact of the valuation method?
Abstract: Background: Time trade-off (TTO) is a class of methods designed to elicit preference values for health states on a scale appropriate for use in quality-adjusted life year (QALY) calculations. TTO variants are the primary preference elicitation methods used valuation studies for the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L health-related quality of life instruments. A common, and unfortunate, characteristic of TTO-based values is a disproportionate difference between full health (conventionally set to 1) and the mildest health states describable in e.g. the EQ-5D, compared to similar decrements added to imperfect health states. A disproportionate initial drop could lead to overspending on interventions targeting relatively trivial health problems. This study was designed to investigate whether the observed drop from full health is specific to full health, or better reflects a general tendency to contrast the presented health states, i.e. a form of end point aversion induced by the TTO format. Methods: 120 general population respondents were administered lead-time TTO for a fixed set of EQ-5D-5L health states (12111, 11122, 12122, 13224, and 24445), each traded off against 11111 and all dominating states, for a total of 14 comparisons presented in random order. For all triplets of states in logical dominance order (A, B, and C), we compared four statistical models for expressing the value of C in terms of A vs. through B: 1) no end aversion, u(C, A) = u(C, B)*u(B, A) End aversion for full health only, u(C, A) +α = u(C, B)*(u(B, A)+α), 3) End aversion in all TTO values, u(C, A) +α = (u(C, B) +α)*(u(B, A)+α), and 4) Proportional end-aversion u(C, A) *(1+α) = u(C, B) *(1+α)*u(B, A)*(1+α). Results: The worst performing model was the one assuming no end-aversion (1), and the best was model, assuming end aversion for all comparisons. Conclusions: The findings indicate that TTO values tend to be distanced from the top, which could reflect a contrasting effect. If this is observed in TTO-based valuation studies, the result would be a downward bias for all imperfect health states, suggesting that it may be appropriate to rescale TTO values, e.g. by removing the intercept.

Title: Demonstrating the feasibility and operational value of the routine measurement of health status in community mental health services: exploring the use of EQ-5D in an operational NHS setting
Abstract: This project was envisaged as developing a tool for real-time decision making by clinicians, specifically mental healthcare professionals working in an NHS community out-patient clinic. A data collection procedure was agreed in which patients completed an EQ-5D questionnaire whilst in the waiting room. This was then entered by the clinician into a bespoke analysis program with a menu of standardised reports, for example demonstrating changes in dimension response levels over time, alterations in EQ VAS and age/sex comparisons against population norms. The analysis system was expected to "learn" over time, so that new patients could be compared against cohort of patients who had previously attended the clinic. Software was designed, commissioned and delivered to the NHS provider who had jointly agreed the project. Practical issues immediately became apparent, notably the requirement to operate all software behind the NHS firewall. Despite initial progress in dealing with such implementation problems, the software was deemed a technical success. The project effectively collapsed when the NHS co-PI unexpectedly relocated. Efforts to resuscitate the project were ultimately unsuccessful. The software package (EQ5Drt, where the subscript rt indicates Real Time) was subsequently made available to colleagues in Hong Kong for use as a real-time application with MSK patients/

Title: Comparing DCE with duration split triplet and EQ-VT in valuing EQ-5D-Y-5L in Canada
Abstract: Study 1: Quantitative comparison of DCE with duration and EQ-VT in EQ-5D-Y-5L in Canada Following the methodology used in the Netherlands, three samples will be collected: 1) a sample of n=1000 adult respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 DCE with duration (“split triplets”); 2) a sample of n=500 adult respondents that are interviewed in a personal interview, with each respondent completing 10 cTTO tasks; 3) a sample of n=1000 respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 latent scale DCE pairs. All tasked will be framed from a 10-year-old child’s perspective. The DCE duration data will be analyzed using a mixed logit model with an exponential discount rate. The latent scale DCE data will be analyzed using a mixed logit model. Predicted latent scale DCE values will be anchored on the QALY scale using a mapping onto the mean observed cTTO values of each state included in the cTTO design.  Study 2: Qualitative think aloud interview study with adults (n = 20) and adolescents (n = 10) To obtain additional insight into the trade-offs made in DCE with duration split triplet vs cTTO, a qualitative study using Think Aloud cognitive interviews will be conducted among a separate sample of n=20 adults and n=10 adolescents in Canada. During the interview, adults will complete 3 cTTO and 3 DCE with duration tasks from their own perspective, and then the same tasks from a 10-year-old child’s perspective. Adolescents will complete the same tasks from their own perspective only. All participants will be instructed to verbalize their thought process. All interviews will be audio recorded and transcribed verbatim. The data will be analyzed using thematic analysis.

Title: Can adding routinely collected EQ-5D-5L administrative data improve predictions about who will be a high-cost user of healthcare?
Abstract: Abstract: Purpose: Patients with complex care needs are vulnerable to poor quality care and adverse health outcomes, and incur substantial costs for the health care system. A key to improving the outcomes for high-cost users (HCUs) is being able to accurately predict who will become a HCU before they have incurred substantial, avoidable costs. Data on self-reported health status may improve predictions about who will become a HCU. The objectives of this study are to: 1) develop models to predict individuals at risk of becoming future HCUs, and 2) compare the performance of predictive models with and without EQ-5D-5L data. Methods: We used data from respondents to two PCM surveys conducted in British Columbia, Canada (acute inpatient survey and emergency department survey) and linked health administrative data. Our outcome of interest was becoming a high-cost user (HCU) in the year following completion of a PCM survey. We conducted person-level costing following best practice guidelines for costing using British Columbia administrative databases and identified cost thresholds for HCUs, defined as those incurring costs in the 5th percentile and above among those with non-zero costs. We developed two sets of predictors, including a ‘standard’ set consisting of demographic, clinical, and resource use and cost predictors and an ‘enhanced’ set which added in EQ-5D-5L data. We imputed missing data using multiple imputation with chain equations, and compared five types of models, including 1) logistic regression, 2) least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), 3) elastic-net, 4) random forests, and 5) artificial neural network (ANN). Ten-fold cross-validation was used to assess how our results would generalize to an independent dataset. We assessed model performance based on discriminative ability (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUROC), cost capture) calibration (calibration curve), and clinical usefulness (decision curve analysis). We also identified which predictors were most important to model performance (relative importance analysis). Results: Using administrative data from over 5 million British Columbians, we found that approximately 40% of the population incurs no health care costs, while the top 5% incur 63% of health care expenditures and the top 1% incur 33% of health care expenditures. The final sample size was 11,964 for the inpatient care survey and 11,144 for the emergency department survey. Broadly speaking, discrimination was similar across model types (e.g., logistic versus LASSO), while the addition of EQ-5D-5L data improved discrimination. This improvement in AUROC curve was small, for example increasing from 0.80 (95% CI: 0.79-0.81) to 0.81 (95% CI: 0.80-0.82) for the logistic regression model from the emergency department survey. However, this effect was more substantial for cost capture, with an increase from 0.36 (95% CI: 0.33-0.39) to 0.41 (95% CI: 0.38-0.45). Overall, models were well calibrated. The decision curve analysis demonstrated that the enhanced models with EQ-5D-5L data provided the highest net benefit across a wide range of thresholds. The relative importance analysis found that for the inpatient care survey the EQ-5D-5L VAS was the among the most important predictors. For the emergency department survey, the usual activities and self-care dimensions were amongst the most important variables. Conclusion: Using routinely collected EQ-5D-5L data from British Columbians discharged from either inpatient care or emergency departments and administrative data, were found that models to predict subsequent HCUs demonstrated good discrimination and calibration. The addition of EQ-5D-5L data improved discriminative performance, particularly on cost capture, meaning that models were better able to predict the individuals with the highest health care costs. Prediction models using EQ-5D-5L data have the potential to identify individuals who could benefit from supports to improve outcomes and reduce health care costs.

Title: Evaluating Psychometric Properties of EQ-5D-5L Skin Bolt-On in Patients with Mild-to-Moderate Psoriasis: A Longitudinal Analysis of three Phase III Clinical Trial Data
Abstract: Aim: To enhance the sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L in assessing skin conditions, the EuroQol Group developed two skin-specific "bolt-on" dimensions -- skin irritation and self-confidence. In response to the EuroQol's 18th Call for Proposals by the Descriptive System Working Group, this study aims to evaluate the psychometric properties of the skin bolt-ons added to the EQ-5D-5L in patients with mild-to-moderate psoriasis. Specifically, we will assess construct validity, responsiveness to clinical changes over time, and measurement invariance across demographic subgroups. Methods: We will perform a secondary analysis of pooled data from three phase III international clinical trials (PSO-FAST, PSO-ABLE, PSO-LONG) involving 1,331 patients with mild-to-moderate psoriasis collected over 56 weeks. Measures include the EQ-5D-5L plus two bolt-ons, Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), Psoriasis Symptom Inventory (PSI), Psoriasis Quality of Life (PQOL-12) and clinical assessments such as the Physician Global Assessment (PGA) and modified Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (mPASI). Statistical analyses will follow COSMIN guidelines, assessing construct validity through convergent and known-groups validity, responsiveness using anchor-based methods, and measurement invariance via differential item functioning analysis. Significance: We will compare the EQ-5D-5L with the EQ-5D-5L plus two skin bolt-ons to assess whether the bolt-ons improve overall psychometric performance across three countries (UK, US and France). Findings will inform whether the skin bolt-ons have the ability to detect meaningful changes in dermatological conditions within a previously under-researched group of mild-to-moderate psoriasis patients. The results will support the integration of these bolt-ons into the EQ-5D framework, facilitate their advancement from Beta to Approved status, and encourage their adoption by the pharmaceutical industry in future clinical trials.

Title: A City-wide survey of HrQoL in children using EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: All City of York schools were invited to participate in a survey of children aged 11-16. A total of 5,750 children completed a specially designed questionnaire incorporating EQ-5D-Y and a graphic 0-100 rating scale. Results indicated higher rates of problems for the last 3 dimensions in girls compared with boys. This difference was most dramatically apparent in older girls on the worried/sad/unhappy dimension, where rates were double those of boys of the same age.Comparative data from surveys conducted some 10 years earlier in many of the same schools, deterioration in self-reported health status despite targeted programmes designed to mitigate mental health problems in the school population.

Title: 2-day entry level course describing development and current status of EQ-5D ”technologies” for Russia
Abstract: Russian researchers (in common with other countries of the former Soviet Union) have relatively little significant experience in the design and use of standardized health status measurement systems. The development of HTA and health economics methods in the Russian Federation and elsewhere in neighbouring countries requires a cadre of suitably qualified health status measurement practitioners. The leading role of EQ-5D provides the ideal basis for creating such a domestic, national resource. An entry-level workshop can provide the catalyst to encourage the adoption of EQ-5D technologies.

Title: Using EQ-5D to inform real-world decision making : a cross-sectoral perspective
Abstract: Multiple agencies responsible for planning and delivery of services in separate (and ostensibly unrelated) public sectors are being encouraged to share/exchange data. LARIA’s annual conference this year includes several speakers from PHE with workshops specifically targeting the central issue of improving information flows and data exchange. The perspective of researchers within separate sectors is largely limited by the scope defined by the services for which they are responsible. The historic emphasis on using EQ-5D for “health” applications has naturally reinforced the view within the health sector this is the specific role for which it is best suited. Alternative uses of EQ-5D – outside the health sector – are to be found and this suggests a possible role for such data in providing a linking mechanism between data sets on a cross-sectoral basis. This proposal is designed to test that challenge by bringing together relevant stakeholders, research academics and policy/planning advisors from Local Authorities, health and criminal justice sectors. LARIA has expressed a general willingness to support the proposal across its regional and national networks should funding support be made available.

Title: EQ-5D-5L Slovenia national value set
Abstract: The aim of this valuation study was to produce a value set to support the use of EQ-5D-5L data in decision making in Slovenia. The study design followed the published EuroQol research protocol, and a quota sample was defined according to age, sex, and region. Overall, 1012 adult respondents completed 10 time trade-off and seven discrete choice experiment tasks in face-to-face interviews. The Tobit model was used to analyse the composite time trade-off (cTTO) data in order to generate values for the 3125 EQ-5D-5L health states. The data showed logical consistency, with more severe states being given lower values. The greatest disutility was shown in the pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression dimensions. In the EQ-5D-5L value set, the values range from -1.09 to 1. With the exception of UA5 (unable to perform usual activities), all other levels on all health dimensions were statistically different from 0 and from each other. Compared with the existing EQ-5D-3L value set, there is a slightly lower share of 'worse than dead' states (32.1% compared with 33.7%) and the minimum value is lower. Results have important implications for users of the EQ-5D-5L in Slovenia and regions. It is a robust and up-to-date value set and should be the preferred value set used in adults in Slovenia and in neighbouring countries without their own value set.

Title: Revised title: Are there any challenges in valuing Y-5L arising from the descriptive system? A multi-country study Previous title: A multi-country pilot study of EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation
Abstract: Title: Are there any challenges in valuing Y-5L arising from the descriptive system? A multi-country study Psychometric evidence suggests some improved measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L (Y-5L) compared to the EQ-5D-Y-3L (Y-3L). In the same way that the EQ-5D-5L is considered to be the “flagship” instrument for measurement and valuation of health for adults, a similar role is possible for the Y-5L in paediatric populations. The Y-5L is planned to be launched as an approved instrument in 2024. However, to date no research has been undertaken to test the valuation of the expanded Y-5L descriptive system. The aim of this project was to (a) identify whether the descriptive system for the Y-5L presents any problems when states from it are presented in valuation tasks (e.g., preference reversals in severity levels); (b) establish the feasibility of eliciting stated preferences for the Y-5L from both adult and adolescent members of the general public; and (c) undertake initial exploration of the characteristics of stated preferences for the Y-5L across countries, with a focus on the implications of results for the descriptive system. The study was conducted among adults and adolescents from five countries: Australia, Canada, China, Netherlands and Spain, using DCE and response scaling tasks. Target samples included n = 1000 adults (>18 years) and n = 1000 adolescents (12-17 years) in each country, recruited from multiple panels via a market research company ‘Cint’. In the DCE tasks, adults used a 10-year-old perspective, and adolescents used their own perspective. Respondents undertook two response scaling tasks after the DCE, to arrange the labels for the Y-5L and Y-3L (for just one dimension, randomly assigned) on a VAS, to indicate their perceived level of severity. Results showed that, overall, adults can mostly interpret the level labels in their intended order of severity, and results were in general consistent from DCE tasks. We did not find statistically significant positive coefficients (i.e. ‘misorderings’ of coefficients) from DCE tasks, suggesting it is unlikely that the current descriptive system for the Y-5L presents problems when states from it are presented in valuation tasks using DCE without duration. However, we observed a few cases in which coefficients were negative but statistically insignificant in the DCE modelling results. These were found for moving between level 2 and level 3, on the first four dimensions of the Y-5L in Canada, Australia, China and the Netherlands, but not in the Spanish version. Response inconsistency based on the response scaling task analysis was more prevalent in adolescents compared to adults in all countries except for China. However, the overall patterns in dimension importance were broadly similar between adults and adolescents within each country: PD had the largest DCE decrement in all countries except China; SC and UA had the smallest decrements in all five countries. Adolescents valued MO as more important compared to adults. Our findings highlight further research on the best approach to value Y-5L is needed, and to explore the feasibility of eliciting adolescents’ preferences using different valuation methods, given the challenges in recruiting adolescents online and the increasing prevalence of fraudulent data in online, self-completion administration of valuation tasks.

Title: One Question Away: Using the EQ-5D-5L to Screen for Emotional Distress in Advanced Melanoma Care
Abstract: Imagine being able to triage cancer patients with emotional distress (ED) based on one simple question, allowing them to timely get the psychosocial care they need. Emotional distress (ED) is the mental or emotional suffering during the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, often presenting as anxiety, depression, or hopelessness. ED requires timely intervention, as it is associated with poorer health-related quality of life (HRQoL), outcomes, and even survival in patients with advanced-stage melanoma (stage III or IV). Clinical guidelines therefore recommend routine screening for depression, anxiety, and insomnia in cancer patients to facilitate timely referral to psychosocial care. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are validated questionnaires completed by patients that could be valuable tools for routine screening of ED. However, PROMs are currently not used for this purpose in clinical practice. Despite a recent successful pilot for PROMs-based ED screening in patients with advanced melanoma at the Netherlands Cancer Institute (NKI), its practicality has not yet been demonstrated. Importantly, this pilot was based on the EORTC QLQ-C30, while the EQ-5D-5L is a potentially more attractive PROM given its brevity. Yet, the EQ-5D-5L is currently not fit for clinical practice use, as healthcare professionals cannot interpret its scores without thresholds for determining clinically relevant ED. This project will lay the groundwork for implementing the EQ-5D-5L in routine clinical cancer care as a PROMs-based screening tool for ED in patients with advanced melanoma. The primary objective is to establish a clinically meaningful threshold for the EQ-5D-5L that enables the interpretation of ED, allowing it to replace the EORTC QLQ-C30 in PROMs-based ED screening. To secure the future implementation and use of the EQ-5D-5L in clinical practice, the secondary aim is to demonstrate the practicality of PROMs-based ED screening in routine clinical practice of advanced melanoma care.In the first work package (WP), we will implement the successfully piloted PROMs-based screening approach for ED in routine clinical care for advanced melanoma patients at the NKI. This screening builds on existing PROMs already in use at the NKI, including the EQ-5D-5L and the EORTC QLQ-C30, which are completed by melanoma patients every three months during diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. A research assistant will collect and interpret patients’ EORTC QLQ-C30 scores at diagnosis and three months post-diagnosis, using its validated clinical threshold values for ED that serve as the golden standard. Patients scoring below this threshold will be invited to complete more detailed assessments of anxiety, depression, and insomnia, providing a deeper understanding of the severity and nature of their ED. All patients who complete these in-depth assessments will be asked to share their views on the ED screening in a short debriefing interview with the research assistant. Patients are fed back their assessment results by the research assistant and offered referrals to appropriate supportive care services (e.g., social work, psychology, or psychiatry) depending on symptom severity. In the second WP, a PhD student will analyze the extensive data collected in the first WP. EQ-5-5L scores are analyzed in comparison to the EORTC QLQ-C30 to determine the most optimal threshold to detect clinically relevant ED for the EQ-5D-5L using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. The Youden’s J statistic (sensitivity + specificity − 1) will be used to identify the single cut-point maximizing correct classification. The added value of the developed threshold added to the EORTC QLQ-C30 or as standalone alternative will be determined through logistic regression models predicting the presence of ED by the EORTC QLQ-C30, EQ-5D-5L, or EORTC QLQ-C30 + EQ-5D-5L combined. To assess the value of the in-depth assessments, associations between ED and anxiety, depression, insomnia, and other domains of the EQ-5D and EORTC QLQ-C30 are as well analyzed in the logistic regression models. To demonstrate the practicality of PROMs based-screening for ED and use of supportive care resulting from PROMs-based ED screening, we will describe the demographic and clinical characteristics of patients that take part in each step of the ED screening, illustrating the potential impact on supportive care capacity for hospitals implementing PROMs-based ED screening in the future.This proposal directly addresses the PHSWG’s call for “research that explores the implementation of EuroQol instruments in routine outcome measurement.” As survival in advanced melanoma improves, care must increasingly focus on patients’ HRQoL. By developing clinically meaningful thresholds for interpreting ED using the EQ-5D-5L, this project will enable patient-centered care and embed the EQ-5D-5L into routine clinical practice. With steeply increasing melanoma incidence, this work will expand the reach and impact of the EuroQol Group’s measures across a growing patient population.

Title: Validity and feasibility of EQ-5D-Y-3L versus EQ-5D-Y-5L in Healthy and Diseased Children in Egypt
Abstract: Background: HRQOL (Health-Related Quality of Life) is becoming an important research topic for evaluating the impact of diseases on daily life in children and adolescents. The EQ-5D-Y (Youth Version) is a child-friendly, generic self-complete questionnaire that assesses HRQoL in children and adolescents from 8 to 15 years. There is growing interest in using HRQoL instruments in clinical practice to help detect health problems, as well as monitor changes in health over time and in patient decision-making including treatment decisions. As a result, it is important to critically evaluate the psychometric properties of new or updated HRQoL tools in different children health conditions prior to their widespread use. As far as we know, that there are no studies evaluating the psychometric properties of the Arabic version of the EQ-5D-Y to date. Aim: The aim of this study is to investigate the psychometric properties (validity, feasibility, reliability, and redistribution properties) of the Arabic version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L in children and adolescents with different health conditions in Egypt.Methods: Egyptian children between the ages of 12-15 who are healthy school children or with a chronic health condition (either diabetes or cancer) were eligible for recruitment. Children in all groups whose parents signed the consent were asked to self-complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L, PEDsQL, sociodemographic questions and the EQ-5D-Y-3L paper-based questionnaires. Since we used the self-administered version of the EQ-5D-Y questionnaires, we chose to recruit children between 12 and 15 to ensure that they were able to read and understand the questions without assistance. All children were asked to complete the questionnaires for the second time after 1-2 weeks to assess the test-retest reliability. Performance of both EQ-5D-Y Arabic versions was studiedthrough comparing feasibility, reliability, redistribution properties, and validity.Results: The Standard Arabic version of the EQ-5D-Y-5L was produced according to the EuroQol translation guidelines, with clear and appropriate severity qualifiers for the dimensions' levels that enabled children to differentiate between them in severity. The feasibility of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Arabic versions was confirmed by the absence of missing responses and a reasonable completion time of less than 5 minutes, with superiority of the EQ-5D-Y-5L according to children's preferences. There was a significant reduction (19.4%) of ceiling effect across all five dimensions (11111) from the EQ-5D-Y-3L to the EQ-5D-Y-5L. There was a significant moderate to strong correlation between dimensions of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L with related PedsQL items, supporting the convergent validity. The strong known-group discriminatory ability has been observed for the EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L LSS across groups known to have worse or better health states, depending on the VAS and PedsQL cut-off points. Additionally, there was a significant difference in EQ-5D-Y-3L/5L LSS and VAS scores between different health conditions. The inconsistent responses seen between the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L dimensions ranged from 1.8% for 'looking after myself' to 7.7% for 'worried, sad, or unhappy' dimensions. There was a significant moderate to substantial agreement across the dimensions of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, confirming the test-retest reliability. Also, the level sum scores of both versions and the VAS score showed excellent reliability ICC > 0.7. The VAS score showed good responsiveness to health improvements over time, as there was a significant improvement in the VAS score with a medium effect size among those with improved health. As per the nature of the chosen health conditions (type 1 diabetes and cancer), the number of participants who completed the second visit and reported significant changes in their health conditions was too small to make a meaningful conclusion about responsiveness at the dimension level, so future studies should be specifically designed to assess responsiveness.

Title: Comparison of DCE duration and EQ-VT in EQ-5D-Y-5L in Poland
Abstract: Background: The current proposal describes a replication study to the project 1923-RA (“Comparison of DCE duration and EQ-VT in EQ-5D-Y-5L in the Netherlands”). Two replication studies were planned in the original proposal (1923-RA), and preliminary accepted by the Exec in June 2024. The VWG and YPWG are jointly working on a protocol for the valuation of the EQ-5D-Y-5L. In the context of valuations of the EQ-5D-Y-5L instrument, we envisage that either an expanded version of the existing EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol will be used, or a protocol that relies on DCE with a duration attribute. However, it has never been tested whether these methods produce similar results when valuing paediatric utility instruments. This study aims to make such a comparison and to develop a value set for the EQ-5D-Y-5L. Methods: Three samples will be collected: 1) a sample of n=1000 respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 DCE split triplets. 2) a sample of n=500 respondents that are interviewed in a personal interview, with each respondent completing 10 cTTO tasks. 3) a sample of n=1000 respondents that complete an online survey, comprising of 15 latent scale DCE pairs. The DCE duration data will be analysed using a mixed logit model with an exponential discount rate. The latent scale DCE data is analysed using a mixed logit model. Predicted latent scale DCE values are anchored on the QALY scale using a mapping onto the mean observed cTTO values of each state included in the cTTO design. A value set is selected based consistency and discussion with the YPWG and VWG.

Title: Response Shift and Response Scale Heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L among Patients with Heart Failure
Abstract: Background: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) like the EQ-5D-5L are increasingly used to monitor healthcare performance and inform clinical decision-making. However, longitudinal validity is often threatened by Response Shift and Response Scale Heterogeneity. This is especially critical in heart failure  patients, who undergo long-term adaptation to chronic symptoms. Beyond technical validity, this study views these phenomena as meaningful indicators of patient adaptation. Despite increasing theoretical recognition, empirical evidence examining these mechanisms remains limited, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Ethiopia, where sociocultural factors significantly influence health reporting during the transition from acute to chronic care.  Using a mixed-methods approach, this research combines psychometric modeling with qualitative inquiry to capture the psychological and social realities of patient adaptation in a resource-limited setting. Objective: To assess how response shift and response scale heterogeneity influence the longitudinal validity and clinical interpretation of EQ-5D-5L outcomes among Ethiopian heart failure patients transitioning from hospital discharge through the 6-month recovery phase. Methods: A prospective multi-center longitudinal observational cohort study will be conducted at Ayder, Aksum, and Adigrat University Comprehensive Specialized Hospitals. A sample of 300 adult patients will be recruited at discharge (T0) and followed at 3 months (T1) and 6 months (T2). Response shift will be analyzed using a combined framework of then-test assessments, longitudinal measurement invariance testing, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), while scale heterogeneity will be evaluated via Latent Class Analysis (LCA). Clinical indicators and global rating of change measures will serve as external anchors to distinguish true health change from psychological adaptation and to provide a clinical context for score interpretation. A nested qualitative sub-study using cognitive and semi-structured interviews will triangulate these findings to explore the sociocultural drivers of health reconceptualization and response scale interpretation. All data will be captured electronically via KoboToolbox on encrypted tablets to ensure real-time validation and high data quality in a resource-limited setting.Expected Outcomes: This study will provide the first empirical quantification of response shift and scale heterogeneity in an Ethiopian HF cohort, assessing their impact on longitudinal EQ-5D-5L utility scores. By distinguishing true clinical change from measurement artifacts, and establishing how these shifts reflect patient adaptation, the findings will establish a methodological framework for the comprehensive interpretation of routine outcome monitoring. Ultimately, this research will provide the evidence-based guidance required to integrate the EQ-5D-5L into Ethiopia’s National non-communicable disease  Strategy, ensuring resource allocation reflects true health gains.Project duration (months):  24 months

Title: Investigating the Interpretation of EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S Response Options in the UK, USA, Germany, and China
Abstract: Background and aims: The EQ-HWB-S incorporates multiple response scales (difficulty, frequency, and severity) that require consistent interpretation for accurate scoring, health state description and valuation. Interpretations may also differ due to item translations or cultural aspects, potentially affecting the instrument's validity across diverse populations. This study aims to investigate the cross-cultural interpretation of modified (v1.2) and old version (v1.1.) response options in the EQ Health and Wellbeing Long and Short (EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S) instrument in four countries: UK, USA, China, and Germany.  Methods: A cross-sectional online survey will be conducted with a total of 1,200 participants (300 per country). Participants will complete: 1) response scale quantification tasks where they assign numerical values to each response option (e.g., specifying the number of days associated with "sometimes" on a frequency scale); 2) ranking exercises of response levels 3) slider tasks where they indicate the positions of response options on a continuous scale from 0 to 100 and ordinal ranking of response options; 4) the EQ-HWB/EQ-HWB-S instrument, which includes recent changes to formatting, instructional phrases, and item wording; Data analysis will involve descriptive statistics to summarize participant characteristics and response interpretations. Cross-country comparisons will be made using ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests for quantitative data, and intraclass correlation coefficients.  Significance: As EQ-HWB-S approaches its valuation phase, the findings will confirm whether the response options function as intended or identify where inconsistencies may arise, informing necessary refinements to the instrument. This research is important for enhancing the instrument's cross-cultural validity, ensuring accurate health state descriptions, and improving the comparability of data across diverse populations.

Title: Assessing Psychometric Properties and Implementation of EQ-HWB-S in Residential Aged Care Facilities: Evidence from Italy.
Abstract: In the UE, Italy has one of the highest percentage of residents older than 65 at 24.3% (around 14 million). Of these, around 28% have long-term needs that find limited responses in the public sector. The number of beds in public aged care facilities, indeed, can satisfy only 8% of those in need. Age, as a non-modifiable factor, increases the individual risk of diseases over the course of life, eventually resulting in disability, declined physical and mental functioning and reduced quality of life (QoL). Therefore, QoL is a critically important outcome measure in elderly care and represents a person-centered indicator of the quality of services provision. The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a new generic measure that extends the descriptive system of EQ instruments beyond health, capturing broader aspects of well-being. Two experimental versions are currently available: a 25-item long measure and a 9-item short-version (EQ-HWB-S). Although social care was one of the settings for which the measure was specifically developed, its appropriateness for routine use in residential aged care and for economic evaluations in this setting need to be further explored. Moreover, as half of the residents in aged care facilities have dementia (50.7% in Italy), there is a need for proxy-reporting and consequently for testing how feasible it is for proxies (e.g., family members, aged care staff) to report resident’s QoL. This study will use a mixed-methods design incorporating survey data and semi-structured interviews to investigate feasibility, content validity, convergent validity and know-group validity, and responsiveness of the EQ-HWB-S in older populations living in residential aged care facilities, and to gain insights on when and under what circumstances the different administration modes (i.e., self-reported, interviewer-administered and proxy-reported) should be used. Moreover, we will perform semi-structured in-person interviews with relevant stakeholders (i.e., managers, staff, informal caregivers) to identify key facilitators and challenges for implementing EQ-HWB-S as a routine outcome measure informing personalized care, and service quality evaluation in aged care facilities. The study is expected to recruit at least 6 facilities located in Northern Italy and hosting around 400 older residents.
