Cross-sectional data (plus a limited sample of longitudinal data) and interview data will be collected over a 6-month period after receiving approval from the Ethics Committee of Bocconi University.

Title: IHEA Pre-congress session on EQ-5D in the Indo-Pacific Region
Abstract: This IHEA pre-congress session - held on the afternoon of the 19th July in Bali - presented and promoted the use of EQ-5D instruments in the Indo-Pacific region. The focus of the workshop was to encourage capacity strengthening. The pre-congress session sought to build on the numerous EQ-5D valuation studies in the Indo-Pacific region by additionally promoting applications of the EQ instruments in national health surveys, large cohort studies and electronic health records. The pre-congress session presented three case studies that specifically focus on the development and use of EuroQol instruments in the Indo-Pacific region: Indonesia, Singapore, New Zealand. The session provided an overview of the research opportunities and research expertise that is available to support health economists to undertake research using EQ instruments.In addition to funding the pre-congress session, the grant also provided financial sponsorship to the LMIC and student attendees.

Title: EUROQOL Satellite Symposium - Applying Quality of life Measurements for Clinical and Economic Research
Abstract: n the Brazilian Public Health System, recommendations for the coverage and reimbursement of new medicines, devices, or equipment are centralized in a committee (National Commission for Technology Incorporation in the Unified Health System). To be approved, the claimant must provide health technology assessments (HTAs). These include measures of safety, efficacy, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness to substantiate the decision-making process. There is no restriction on the type of economic model that can be submitted for review. The recommendations are presented as legal documents and economic analysis guidelines.2 This document discusses focus on the possibilities of the utility measures, without any reference to sources or methods or the selection of the best evidence for utility parameters. Health insurance plans in the private sector have a similar process through an independent agency (National Regulatory Agency for Private Health Insurance and Plans) that is responsible for defining a mandatory list of procedures and medicines to be included in all plans. Brazilian preference research was sparse in both the public and private sectors. In this context, utility is a concept adopted from economics that refers to preferences for a specific health state or outcome. This preference (or weight) is usually based on a large group of people representing the general population. Utility is a proxy of quality of life and reflects the preferences of individuals or society for any particular set of health outcomes. Utility expresses the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in a single value scored on a scale anchored on 1 = “full health” and 0 = “death,” usually derived from “off-the-shelf” preference-based measures such as the EQ- 5D questionnaire. Some health states may be considered worse than death and given negative utility estimates.Utilities are used for informing cost–utility models and can sometimes be obtained from different sources; it is important to create a hierarchy when multiple estimates are available. In a cost–utility analysis, competing health technologies are compared in terms of their cost per “year in full health.” The quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) is one such widely used measure that combines a person’s life expectancy and the value of their HRQOL in a single estimate. The HRQOL can be expressed in utilities for economic analysis. It is important to distinguish between the utility weights and the profiles or health states. The measurement process using multiattribute instruments starts by asking for a description of individual health states, called profiles. The selected profiles are converted to utilities compared with a table called the value set, which contains weights for each profile. These weights are usually collected from the general population (valuation process) and represent preferences for each possible health state. In one Brazilian state, in 2011, value set was developed for the Short-Form Six-Dimension (SF-6D) instrument.9 For 3-level version of EQ-5D (EQ-5D-3L), the value set was developed nationally in 2013.10 Nonetheless, in the Brazilian HTA ecosystem, utility estimates based on Brazilian samples are limited. Considerations of the source and type of utility values are especially important in a modeling context, in which the lack of transparency, including the lack of a hierarchy for utility data sources, is a major issue for any estimation and could compromise model reliability. The absence of clear guidelines permits flawed modeling practices, given that an ad hoc evidence selection can result in cherry picking. An extreme example of this practice would be feeding a model with data to uphold the owner’s perspective, creating a false favorable impression of a particular technology. In recent years, the process of decision-making using cost–utility data in Brazil has improved. Because of the lack of confidence in some economic models, the cost–utility models have a mixed impact on real-world judgments. Transparently built models can hopefully support better decisions for the rational use of health resources. Few international guidelines discuss how to select the best utility data from different perspectives in the Brazilian context. This document aims to present the first version of the Brazilian guidelines for a utility measurement supporting an economic analysis. A glossary of technical terms was created. As an initial step, a rapid review of the literature was conducted on July 6, 2020, based on an adapted search strategy from MEDLINE,EMBASE, and LILACS databases and the websites of The University of Sheffield, the Decision Support Unit of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and the EuroQol Group. Additional individual search strategies were adapted for each recommendation to gather the main recommendations and debates previously published on utility measurement issues for economic analyses. Approximately 110 documents were reviewed. The experts were selected based on their previous experience with utility measurement instruments or economic models. The the external reviewer was selected for his experience with both topics. Another important criterion was to be a manager or member of the 2 incorporated sectors in Brazil: public health (Brazilian Public Health System) and insurance plans (National Regulatory Agency for Private Health Insurance and Plans). The review results were synthesized in a brief report. Then, in October 2020, these findings were discussed during a 5-hour online workshop, in which 5 lectures were presented by international speakers followed by debates. The complete program is available in the attached material. The expert group included a wide range of stakeholders—including government representatives, industry, academic groups, international guests, and a patient representative—and regulatory agencies, including the private health sector An adapted Delphi panel technique with 4 iterations was adopted for the construction of the final report. The draft report was sent to representatives, who used it to write the final report and who are listed here as coauthors. The recommendations are based on the proposal with the most approvals, but controversial topics are included in the recommendation or discussion. The text includes the rationale for the final decision

Title: Assessing the Appropriateness of the EQ-HWB-S: A Mixed-Methods Analysis from the Perspective of Informal Caregivers of People living with Dementia - A collaborative project between the Monash University (Australia) and the German Center of Neurodegenerative Diseases (Germany)
Abstract: This study explored the face validity and acceptability of the EQ-HWB-9 when used by informal caregivers as a proxy measure for community-dwelling people living with dementia (PlwD). Conducted as a collaboration between Monash University and the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases, and building on the EuroQol-funded project “Reliability of the EQ-HWB-S when health fluctuates,” (1592-RA) the project used qualitative data from 73 interviews with caregivers in Germany. The analysis of the qualitative data was done during a research stay at Monash University (Health Economics Group, School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine) from April to May 2025.Informal caregivers and their relatives with a form of dementia were randomly assigned to complete the EQ-HWB-9 using either a “today” or “7-day” recall period at three time points across 14 days. Afterwards, qualitative interviews with the caregivers were conducted to evaluate the appropriateness and usability of the EQ-HWB-9. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using a qualitative content analysis approach. Most caregivers found the instrument acceptable due to its clarity and broad health coverage. However, limitations were noted in its ability to capture internal emotional states and in the depth of assessment. The “7-day” recall period was associated with reduced adherence to the recall instruction compared to the “today” version.Findings suggest that the EQ-HWB-9 shows promise for proxy use in PlwD, though challenges remain regarding recall periods, proxy interpretation, and caregiver confidence in response selection. These insights contribute to improving the instrument's future application.

Title: Developing a User-Friendly EQ-5D Utility Index Score Calculator Using the Egyptian EQ-5D-5L Value Set
Abstract: Background: EQ-5D is a widely used tool for assessing health related quality of life. Health state profiles can be analysed using several methods, though commonly they are converted into a single utility index using country-specific value sets. Calculating EQ-5D utility values manually can be challenging, time-consuming and prone to errors. The Egyptian EQ-5D-5L was developed and published since 2021 and no EQ-5D utility index score calculator was developed.Aim: To develop a user-friendly EQ-5D Egyptian utility index score calculator that allows healthcare professionals and researchers to easily calculate EQ-5D utility values for different health states. This calculator will be made adaptable to be used by other researchers for other EQ-5D-5L value sets.Methods: This project will make use of the published value set using the prefered model in the Egyptian EQ-5D-5L valuation study. The calculator will be developed using Microsoft Excel , ensuring accessibility across various devices and platforms. Validation will be performed to ensure accuracy and ease of use. A detailed procedure will be developed and made available online for other researchers to be able to easily adapt the caclulator to other value sets as they emerge.

Title: Validation of the EQ-5D-5L Breathing Bolt-On: Longitudinal Evidence from a Large Randomized Controlled Trial
Abstract: : The EQ-5D is one of the most widely used tools to measure health-related quality of life; however, some important aspects of health may not be fully captured by its five core dimensions. For people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), breathing difficulties are a central concern. The EuroQol Group has therefore developed a “Breathing” bolt-on item, which may improve how well the EQ-5D reflects the lived experience of patients with COPD.This project will test the Breathing bolt-on using a rich longitudinal dataset of about 400 patients with COPD who were followed over time. We will examine whether the bolt-on provides new and useful information beyond the existing EQ-5D dimensions, whether it reflects differences in disease severity, and whether it is reliable and responsive to clinical changes over time.By applying established psychometric methods, we aim to show whether adding the Breathing dimension improves the measurement of health outcomes in COPD. The findings will directly support the EuroQol Group’s Bolt-On Toolbox initiative, which is developing guidance on when and how to use bolt-on dimensions. This unique secondary database of a large clinical trial in COPD is an opportunity to produce evidence of responsiveness, which is essential to demonstrate the value of the EQ-5D+B in clinical trials and registries where breathing is a critical outcome for conditions such as COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis and in many rare disease such as spinal muscular atrophy.  This will help researchers, clinicians, and policymakers better capture the impact of treatments and disease progression.

Title: Vision and Hearing Bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D- 5L: A Systematic Review
Abstract: This systematic review aimed to (i) identify the methods used to develop vision and hearing bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L, (ii) identify the wordings used in existing vision and hearing bolt-ons, (iii) categorise the populations in which these bolt-ons had been tested or applied, and (iv) summarise the available psychometric evidence. Following the protocol and methods described in 1703-RA, we conducted a systematic literature search in Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Findings for vision and hearing bolt-ons were summarised narratively using descriptive statistics and reported separately. Where available, psychometric properties of each bolt-on item were extracted and summarised descriptively. The review identified 21 publications relating to vision bolt-ons and eight publications relating to hearing bolt-ons.

Title: Understanding the routine collection and use of EQ-5D data in large-scale applications within the healthcare system (Apersu supports)
Abstract: See attached report

Title: Variability and ease of access in proxy quality of life interviews at the ICU
Abstract: This pilot seed grant study describes the process of implementing the EQ-5D in an Intensive Care setting and the differences EQ-5D responses between proxies. We report the pitfalls for implementation in this specific clinical setting and show that 217 out of 762 eligible patients could be included, resulting in 270 EQ-5D assessments. There are small but distinct differences between answers from the patient and the proxies (family members, physicians, general practitioners). When combining the logistical challenges of contacting healthcare professionals and the results of our study, family members appeared to be the most feasible and accurate proxies for estimating pre-admission QoL in incapacitated patients.

Title: Developing a EuroQol guidance for testing psychometric evidence for generic preference based instruments
Abstract: Background: There is no clear guidance as to how mixed methods psychometric approaches should be used to assess instruments with characteristics common to the EQ suite, such as descriptive systems measuring multiple dimensions and their associated value sets, and bolt-on dimensions. Discussions between the Descriptive System, Youth and EQ-HWB Working Groups highlighted this lack of guidance as a major gap for moving instruments forward. This is also recognized in the strategic plan, where a key objective is to “Support and encourage good practice in the analysis of EQ instruments’ data”.  Aims: This program of work aims to develop EuroQol guidance for testing psychometric properties of generic preference instruments. This includes two documents:  Guidelines for the use of qualitative methods for the testing of EuroQol instruments and modifications. Guidelines for the use of quantitative methods for the testing of EuroQol instruments and modifications  Methods: The program is organized into three complementary work packages (WP) that will inform the development of the psychometric guidance documents.  The three WPs are:  Work package 1 – Critical assessment of existing guidelines and literature A targeted review of the literature will be conducted to summarize existing guidelines for the psychometric analysis of patient reported outcome measures. The data extracted will be used to critically assess and synthesise the guidelines identified, and how they pertain to the analysis of GPBMs. This will be done using objective assessment of what the guidelines include and how they compare and differ, and subjective assessment of the strengths and weakness of the guidelines, the feasibility of the guidelines for GPBMs and any gaps for the assessment of GPBMs.  Learnings from this review will be triangulated with findings of a review of validation studies (1818-RA), which was conceive as part of this program of work.  Work Package 2 - Empirical comparison of methods for testing the EuroQol Suite of instruments We will empirically compare quantitative psychometric methods for testing EQ instruments. We will focus on issues specific to the EQ suite of instruments. We will conduct all analyses on the same datasets. These datasets include the EQ suite of instruments (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-Y-5L and bolt ons) alongside other non EQ instruments.  Examples of methods that will be applied include classical test theory, dimensionality assessment, Rasch analysis and item response theory. We will also compare approaches within each set of analyses, with a focus on CTT.  Work Package 3 - Development of psychometric guidance documents for the EuroQol Group We will develop guidance for testing EuroQol instruments and their possible modifications, through consensus based technique (Dephi). Responders will be the project team, other key EQ members, and non-members experts in psychometrics and in generic preference based measures. Responders will be presented a series of statements and will be asked to respond to them through open and closed ended questions. The objective will be to reach consensus on a final list of recommendations, through iterative rounds.

Title: Validation and Comparison of the Psychometric Properties of the EQ-5D-3L-Y and EQ-5D-5L-Y in the United States
Abstract: Aim:The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-3L-Y and EQ-5D-5L-Y in the United States are unknown.The aims of this study are to 1)test the psychometric properties (including feasibility, reliability, and validity) of the EQ-5D-5L-Y in children and adolescents with arthritis and leukemia and 2)compare the psychometric properties (including feasibility, redistribution, discrimination, and validity) of the EQ-5D-3L-Y and EQ-5D-5L-Y in children and adolescents with arthritis and leukemia.Methods:This study will recruit a total of 400 children and adolescents, including 100 patients with arthritis, 100 patients with leukemia, and 200 healthy individuals.Children and adolescents with arthritis and leukemia will be recruited from hospitals. Healthy individuals will be recruited from schools and matched with patients byage, gender, and race.Study participants will be asked to complete the survey in the order of 1) EQ-5D-5L-Y, 2) PedsQL, 3) self-rated health, 4) demographic questions, and 5) EQ-5D-3L-Y.They will be invited to complete the second survey seven to ten days after the baseline survey.The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L-Ywill be tested through feasibility(using missing values), reliability(using Cohen's kappa statisticandintra-class correlation coefficient), convergent validity(using Spearman's rho), and known-groups validity(using a priori hypotheses). The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-3L-Y and EQ-5D-5L-Ywill be compared through feasibility(using missing values and ceilingeffects), redistribution(using consistent response pairs), discrimination(using Shannon index and Shannon Evenness index), convergent validity (using Spearman's rho), and known-groups validity (using a priori hypothesesand relative efficiency statistic).

Title: 3.5 year PhD Studentship on ‘Identifying, developing and testing methods to generate EQ-5D-5L bolt-on value sets: What can and should be done?’
Abstract: EQ-5D-5L has been criticized for missing some important aspects of health in some specific populations. As a solution, the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system could incorporate additional descriptors - henceforth, bolt-ons - to improve measurement sensitivity and relevance in certain contexts. EuroQol protocol and guidance have been developed to guide identification, development and testing of bolt-ons; and recent work has focussed on the development of cognition, vision and hearing bolt-ons using mixed qualitative and quantitative approaches to be included in the proposed Bolt-on Toolbox. This PhD will contribute to the identification, development and testing of methods to generate EQ-5D-5L bolt-on value sets. EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons presents unique challenges for value set development. This may require some level of comparability and consistency with health states with only the core dimensions. The PhD will include a scoping review of health state valuation methods which could potentially be used for EQ-5D-5L bolt-on valuation. More importantly, the PhD will develop criteria to identify and select methods used to generate EQ-5D-5L bolt-on value sets. This will involve interviews and group discussions with key stakeholders (e.g. members of the EuroQol group and members of HTA bodies) about the desired properties ofEQ-5D-5L bolt-on value sets and associated methodological considerations and requirements. The methods identified in the scoping literature review will be mapped and assessed towards the criteria. Towards the end of the project an (online) survey will be conducted to determine the feasibility of the selected methods using a design building upon the findings from previous research.

Title: An investigation of the ‘shrinking factor’ model for predicting vision and cognition bolt-on values elicited from the general public
Abstract: Objective: In our previous research, we developed a "scaling factor model" – to estimate bolt-on value sets. The objective of this project was to investigate the feasibility of applying this model using a general public sample and a parallel design, specifically testing it with health states featuring vision or cognition bolt-ons. Methods: The study utilized three descriptive systems: the original EQ-5D-5L and two variations with bolt-ons – one involving vision ("EQ+VI") and another involving cognition ("EQ+CO"). A valuation study is conducted in Guizhou Province, China, with a general public sample using the composite time trade-off (cTTO) protocol. A team of interviewers collects data, both the scaling factor model and standard model were employed to estimate bolt-on value sets. To evaluate the model performance, we used a by-state cross-validation approach. Results: A total of 596 participants completed the valuation tasks, and the results indicated that adding a bolt-on dimension increases health state values for mild to moderate problems but decreased values for severe to extreme problems. The scaling factor model outperformed the standard models in predicting observed health state values, showing promise in estimating bolt-on value sets. However, differences were noted between vision and cognition bolt-ons, highlighting the importance of understanding the specific characteristics of bolt-on dimensions. Discussion: The findings confirmed the validity of the scaling factor model in estimating value sets for EQ-5D-5L health states with bolt-ons, preserving the relative importance of standard EQ-5D-5L sets. Future study should test this model with discrete choice experiment (DCE) method, which has also been used to generate EQ-5D-5L value set in some populations.

Title: Valuation study of EQ-5D-Y-5L in Japan
Abstract: This study aims to develop a Japanese value set for the EQ-5D-Y-5L following the international common protocol established by the EuroQol group, while examining the consistency between discrete choice experiment (DCE) and composite time trade-off (cTTO) valuation methods. Building on our previous success in establishing the Japanese EQ-5D-Y-3L value set and population norms, this research addresses the need for expanded measurement capabilities in pediatric health utility assessment. The study will employ a dual methodology approach: (1) face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviews for cTTO data collection (N=1000) and (2) online surveys for DCE with duration (N=2500). Participants aged 20-79 years will be recruited through quota sampling by sex and age. Methods should be compared based on such models accounting for heterogeneity, as that is the golden standard.Our research team, with extensive experience in developing EQ instruments in Japan and strong connections to the Center for Outcomes Research and Economic Evaluation for Health (C2H), is well-positioned to contribute to the broader implementation of EQ-5D-Y-5L in Japanese healthcare decision-making. This study will provide valuable insights into the comparability of different valuation methods and support the integration of pediatric health utility measurements into Japan's health technology assessment framework.

Title: {(RRM + RUM) + DCE} *EQ-5D-5L = Preference
Abstract: Objective: Traditionally, researchers extract latent coefficients using the conventional random utility maximization (RUM). Recently, a new model, the Random Regret Minimization (RRM) postulates that people making choices by minimizing the anticipated regret. This study aims to examine whether RUM or RRM better describes how people make decisions when faced with different levels of risks and survivals. Methods: A discrete choice experiment (DCE) was designed with 6 attributes including the 5 items of the EQ-5D-5L (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression) and out-of-pocket costs as % of annual household income (5%, 10%, 20% and 50%). The Amazon MTurk, a crowdsourcing web survey platform was used to collect data in September 2022. Modified Federov algorithm was used to design 16 different choice sets. For each choice set, respondents were presented with 3 different alternatives. Each choice set was described using a short 3-month survival or a relatively long 10-year survival. One dominant test choice set was included for each respondent’s choice sets for quality screening. Separate estimations of the traditional RUM and the three different RRM models were compared to understand how people make choices subject to different risks and survivals. The three RRM models included the general uRRM model, the classic RRM (assumes µ =1) and the pure RRM (assumes µ =0). Results: Out of 500 respondents, 47.6% (238/500) passed the screening test and included in the analysis. Respondents’ mean age was 36.5 years (SD ±10.8); 58% male; 89.5% white, 4.6% black and 76.9% of them were married. Further, 91.6% of them completed college degrees and, most of them have health insurances via commercial (32.8%), Medicare (44.5%), Medicaid (13.5%) and Affordable Care Act (3.8%). Estimated coefficients of all 5 EQ-5D-5L items were significant across all models in both survival scenarios except for self-care. The out-of-pocket cost showed significance when respondents faced with 3-month survival (p<0.05), and not significant in the 10-year survival scenario. Value of µ from the µRRM were closed to zero indicating that µRRM collapses into pure-RRM and that respondents showed a strong semi-compensatory behavior while making decisions in both 3-month (µ=0.001) and 10-year survival scenarios (µ=0.019). The log-likelihood estimations were comparable across different models suggested that these models had similar fittings to the data. Conclusion: Respondents were sensitive to the out-of-pocket costs when faced with short-term survival. When survival was emphasized in choice-making scenarios, regret minimization better described choice behaviors than utility maximization. Further investigation is warranted to assess how people make health choices when subject to different risks and survivals.

Title: Psychometric testing of E-QALY in China: a new study using face-to-face survey method
Abstract: Introduction: When developing the EQ-HWB, the face validation stage and psychometric stage were done in six countries including China. We noticed two problems when analyzing the China psychometric data: 1) over 70% of the 500 respondents had university or higher education level and the mean age of the sample was 35.9 years old, which suggests the sample was dominated by young and well-educated population; 2) the UK model achieved good fit with some modifications with all countries except for China, where many of the feelings sub-domains needed to be combined. It is not clear whether this CFA results was affected by the online sample of the E-QALY study. In this project, we aimed to redo the psychometric analysis using a F2F sample. Method: The existing questionnaire from the E-QALY was used in order to be consistent with previous study. A sample of 500 was used with 100 patients with lung cancer, 100 patients with diabetes, 100 patients with depression, 100 patients with schizophrenia and 100 general public were invited to participate the survey. Patients were mainly recruited in local hospitals and general public were recruited through personal invitations. All participants were recruited in Guizhou Province China. 14 undergraduate students were recruited as interviewers from Guizhou Medical University, China. All questionnaires were printed out before the interview. Participants were encouraged to respond to the questionnaire by themselves. Data were double entry by the interviewers using Epidata. For the 62 candidate items, the EFA (with EQ-5D-5L), CFA (bifactor model as reported in the E-QALY project), data distribution, known-group validity and item response theory results were reported. Additionally, we elicited 27 candidate items related to the EQ-HWB from the 62-item pool to explore the factor structure by EFA. Given that items about vision, hearing, sleep, and discomfort were identified as separate domains, they were excluded. Next, the CFA bi-factor model was constructed to confirm the domains of the EQ-HWB. Item performances were assessed by the IRT. Results: The data collection was conducted between December 2021 and September 2022 in Guizhou Province, China. The final sample size was 538, with n=98 patients with lung cancer, n=125 patients with diabetes, n=102 patients with depression, n=114 patients with schizophrenia, and n=101 general public. The mean age of our sample was 47.62 years old (SD: 17.19); 55.39% were male and only 16.17% had a university or higher education level. Seven items possessed a skewed distribution in the response option level 1, and five items had a lower than 5% response distribution in the response option level 5. The EFA results illustrate the six-factor structure explaining the structure of 62 items, in which items with positive phrasing were loaded with one separate factor. It prompted that a Bi-factor model would be appropriate in the CFA approach. The replicated UK bifactor model, reported in the E-QALY project, was optimized, with the model goodness-of-fit indexes of CFI 0.943, TLI 0.939, and RMSEA 0.052 (0.050,0.054). In lung cancer and diabetic subgroups, items about physical sensation (like pain frequency) were able to identify disease burden from healthy populations. Almost all items were sensitive to the burden of depression disease, but items did not present strong discriminability between schizophrenia patients and healthy people. For the 27 candidate items, a three-factor structure, which were psychological well-being, physical function, and physical sensation, was illustrated by the EFA. The model goodness-of-fit index of the three-bifactor model was CFI 0.964, TLI 0.955, and RMSEA 0.081 (0.074, 0.088). The item performances revealed that items ‘How difficult is it for you to wash, toilet, dress yourself, eat or care for your appearance?’, ‘I felt unable to cope with my day to day life’, and ‘I felt unsupported by people’ had less ability to be identified by respondents with different latent traits. Discussion: The optimized CFA model result confirms that the intended UK model structure can fit in China background. The candidate items of the EQ-HWB can measure health and well-being in patients with physical or mental diseases. The EQ-HWB has the potential to be used for measuring health and well-being in China.

Title: Comparative analysis of the EQ-HWB-S, CarerQoL, ASCOT, ICECAP-A, WIX and EQ-5D-5L among informal caregivers
Abstract: Background: Informal caregiving can substantially affect health and wellbeing, yet there is limited evidence on the comparative performance of preference-based and wellbeing instruments for capturing caregiver outcomes in economic evaluation. This study compared the EQ-HWB-9 with other commonly used measures to examine domain overlap and psychometric performance among informal caregivers.Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among adult informal caregivers of individuals with stroke, cancer, or dementia. Participants completed six instruments measuring health and wellbeing: EQ-HWB-9, EQ-5D-5L, ASCOT-Carer, CarerQoL-7D, ICECAP-A, and WiX. Descriptive statistics, floor and ceiling effects, convergent and divergent validity, known-group comparisons, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and test–retest reliability were assessed. Correlations were examined using Spearman coefficients, discriminatory power using Shannon indices, and reliability using intraclass correlation coefficients and weighted Cohen’s kappa.Results: Data from 487 caregivers were analysed. Mean EQ-HWB-9 utility was 0.801 (SD 0.211), comparable to ASCOT-Carer (0.791) and ICECAP-A (0.782). Ceiling effects were lower for EQ-HWB-9 (12%) than EQ-5D-5L (33%). Moderate to strong correlations were observed between EQ-HWB-9 and other instruments (ρ = 0.606–0.720), supporting convergent validity. Factor analysis identified three underlying constructs—psychosocial health, mental health, and physical functioning—with EQ-HWB-9 and WiX sharing mental health components. Known-group analyses showed lower wellbeing among caregivers with higher caregiving hours and those caring for recipients with greater disease severity. Informative response distributions were observed across most EQ-HWB-9 items (Shannon H′ = 1.25–2.11). Test–retest reliability for EQ-HWB-9 was acceptable (ICC = 0.69) with moderate item-level agreement.Conclusions: The EQ-HWB-9 demonstrates acceptable psychometric performance among informal caregivers and captures broader wellbeing domains beyond health status. Its conceptual overlap with other wellbeing measures, particularly mental health constructs, suggests it may provide a useful complementary outcome measure for economic evaluations involving caregiver populations.

Title: Measuring and Valuing Patient-Reported Outcomes in Economic Evaluations of Health Care Workshop
Abstract: The format of the presentation is outlined below, and the aims of the workshop. There are several strategic advantages to the EuroQol Group support of this workshop. This is the second annual conference for the China National HTA in Beijing. Approximately 800 attendees went last year, it is expected more will attend this year. There is interest in understanding approaches to valuing health in health technology assessment. Drs. Xie and Pickard are established academicians who have extensive experience presenting on this topic, and have previously co-presented workshops at ISOQOL, HTAi and ISPOR. Dr. Xie is an invited plenary speaker at the conference, and has established ties with the Chinese Ministry of Health that is involved in organizing the conference. This workshop is an opportunity to further build upon developing a relationship with the ministry and HTA organizations in China. The EuroQol Group has strategic interest in promoting understanding of approaches to valuing health. Although we are not explicitly “promoting” the use of the EQ-5D, a more nuanced approach is intentionally used here, where the EQ-5D will be used for exercises and featured as the foremost utility measure used globally. China has great strategic value for the group, as it is rapidly developing its own pharmaceutical industry, and this educational outreach initiative broaden efforts by the EuroQol group for goodwill relationships in Asian countries, particularly China.

Title: A multi-country EQ-5D-Y valuation study in Asia (Resubmission of project 154-2020RA)
Abstract: The importance of preference-based health-state utility values rises as countries shift towards using cost-utility analysis to inform healthcare priority setting. However, very few Asian value sets for child preference-based instruments are available. Thus, this study aimed to develop EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets for Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, and Vietnam. A multi-country EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation study was conducted using the international EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol with a larger composite time trade-off (cTTO) design. Two general population samples from Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, and Vietnam were surveyed to elicit their preferences for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states using either the cTTO method or a discrete choice experiment. A hybrid latent class model was used to estimate the EQ-5D-Y-3L value set for each participating country. Approximately 200 (range: 200-207) and 1000 (range: 1006-1047) respondents from each participating country completed the cTTO and DCE surveys, respectively. A latent class model with six classes fit the DCE data collected from Malaysia and Taiwan best; a model with four and five classes fit Singapore’s and Vietnam’s DCE data best, respectively. The model predicted value for the worst EQ-5D-Y-3L state (i.e. 33333) was -0.242 in Malaysia; -0.397 in Singapore; -0.582 in Taiwan; and -0.198 in Vietnam. The second highest value in all countries was for health state 12111, ranging from 0.928 in Taiwan to 0.966 in Malaysia. EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets for Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, and Vietnam were generated concurrently using a robust protocol for healthcare decision making involving child and adolescent populations. The hybrid latent class modelling approach may be considered in future EQ-5D-Y-3L value set studies.

Abstract: EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS are feasible metrics to measure in critically ill patientsBaseline, ICU admission & hospital discharge can be done routinely in patients in-hospitalLess data available at 1 week & 1 month in ICU (2nd to prior transfer out of ICU)3 months (70%) > 12 months (57%) follow-upGeneral trend of higher health utility at baseline, lower at admission, and rising again following critically illnessEQ-5D-5L is moderate-to-strongly correlated to EQ-VAS vs. SD-12 (conversion to SF-6D)Overall Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (rho): 0.74 (95% CI: 0.69-0.78) vs. 0.62 (95% CI: 0.56-0.68) [p 0.00001]EQ-5D-5L ranges: 0.50-0.74 (moderate-to-strong) [p 0.00001]EQ-5D-5L tends to underestimate health utility, but has a stronger correlation to patient reported EQ-VAS (not statistically different)Correlations strongest: baseline, hospital discharge & 3 & 12 month follow-upCorrelations only moderate: admission, 1 week & 1 month in ICUSF-12 (SF-6D conversions) tends to OVERestimate health utility, and has only a moderate correlation to patient reported EQ-VAS (statistically different)Proxy 2 scores for family members & healthcare workers performed better than Proxy 1 correlationsProxy 1 SDM & HCW both reported lower HRQoL vs. patients: mobility, self care & usual activities (domains) – statistically differentNo difference in domains of: pain/discomfort & anxiety/depression
