Title: Grant to develop the outcomes-research component of the intended Capacity-2 study
Abstract: Capacity-2 aims to extend the current multicenter Capa­city-clinical registration with 6 month outcome data, including EQ-5D/EQ-VAS; these data would allow to document whether - as suggested by preliminary imaging and pathophysiological findings - whether specific cardiovascular complications arise after a significant covid infection requiring hospital admission. Following the received information, about 30-40 (Dutch) hospitals participate in Capacity at large. The currently projected follow-up study aims to follow up at least 500 patients, with the option that more hospitals join (incl. international). The developmental award covers IT-associated costs which relate tot the projected outreach and data collection 6 month after first discharge of qualifying patients (see Capacity-2 protocol). Part of the data collection includes clinical parameters (incl. history taking), imaging data, and biomarkers. The other part of the data collection consists of a dedicated health questionnaire, primarily containing PROMs and some data required to process or interprete the outcome data. This questionnaire will also contain a.o. the EQ-5D and the EQ-VAS.

Title: The relationship between the EQ Health and Wellbeing short (EQ-HWB-S) and age in a large UK general population sample. A comparison with the EQ-5D-5L.
Abstract: Aim: This study descriptively examined the relationship between the EQ-HWB-9 experimental version (2022) and age, exploring the trajectories in utility, summary scores and dimensions across the life course. Comparisons were made with the EQ-5D-5L and ONS-4 life satisfaction and happiness scores. Methods. Using data from a large UK general population sample (n=12,401), age trajectories of EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L utility and summary scores were descriptively compared across continuous age categories and against ONS-4 life satisfaction and happiness item scores. EQ-HWB-9 item distributions and domain rankings were examined across age groups, with domains grouped into physical and psychosocial categories to compare overall patterns. Conceptually overlapping EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L domains were assessed to identify similarities and differences in age-related change. Ordinary least squares models tested linear, quadratic and cubic relationships between age and EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L scores, adjusting for gender, education, carer status, time and ethnicity, with interaction terms assessing age-gender differences. Gender differences in EQ-HWB-9 trajectories were also compared graphically. Results: The EQ-HWB-9 did not show the typical age-related decline seen with the EQ-5D-5L, rather age had a positive relationship with EQ-HWB-9 utility and summary scores. EQ-HWB-9 summary scores broadly followed the trends observed in the ONS-4 life satisfaction and happiness scores. Physical problems gradually increased with age in both instruments, whereas psychosocial problems generally decreased, resulting in distinct and contrasting life course trajectories across domains. Conclusions: Age-related expectations based on the EQ-5D-5L should not be assumed when interpreting the EQ-HWB-9. Recognising these differences is essential as the EQ-HWB-9 becomes more widely used in applied research and evaluation.

Title: Visualising EQ-5D-5L Outcomes for Routine Clinical Use: A Mixed-Methods Study in Sciatica Care
Abstract: Despite the increasing collection of EQ-5D data for measuring and monitoring patients' health in routine care, its implementation during clinical encounters remains limited. This project will employ a mixed-methods approach to address this issue. Work package 1 will involve creating a suite of diverse visualisation formats using real-world EQ-5D-5L data from the British Spine Registry for patients with sciatica. These visualisations will be informed by existing literature and data visualisation guidelines. Work package 2 will consist of qualitative focus groups with stakeholders (patients with sciatica, physiotherapists, and surgeons) to explore their preferences for the developed visualisation formats and to identify potential barriers and facilitators to their implementation in routine clinical use. Work package 3 will focus on integrating the preferred visualisation format into the British Spine Registry and developing best practice guidelines for EQ-5D-5L data visualisation based on the project's findings. This research seeks to create user-friendly visualisations that improve understanding and facilitate the use of EQ-5D-5L in decisions regarding patient care. The project directly aligns with EuroQol’s strategic research priorities concerning the 'reporting and implementation of EQ instruments in routine outcome assessment'.

Title: Establishment of a UK EuroQol Group and initial 1 day meeting
Abstract: We held a one-day meeting in the UK for researchers with an interest in the development and application of the EQ-5D and other EuroQol measures. The meeting was designed to be researcher-led and aimed at UK and Ireland based researchers primarily. The meeting discussed recent developments in EuroQol instruments (EQ-HWB, the latest UK valuation study, use of large EQ-5D datasets in England, changes in health state preferences over time and recent work on personal utility functions). The meeting was mainly attended by non-EuroQol members, including early career researchers and students.

Title: ### **USING THE OPUF APPROACH TO CREATE A VALUE SET FOR THE EQ-HWB-S – AN EXPLORATIVE FEASIBILITY STUDY**
Abstract: This project investigated the feasibility of using the Online elicitation of Personal Utility Functions (OPUF) approach to create value sets for the EQ-HWB-S. We constructed multiple value sets for the EQ-HWB-S in two countries (UK, Germany) and two patient groups (Germany) using the OPUF method, even in smaller sample sizes than traditionally required. We also conducted a test-retest study to assess the reliability of the OPUF method. While the results showed relative stability of model coefficients on an aggregate level, reliability on the individual participant level was low. Finally, we performed qualitative interviews to understand participants' experiences with the OPUF tasks. The interviews revealed confusion around some task instructions, and identified multiple areas for improvement. Overall, our project demonstrated that the OPUF method is a promising approach for estimating value sets for instruments with many dimensions, such as the EQ-HWB-S. However, the method requires further development to improve the reliability and validity of the derived preference weights.

Title: Towards A Continuum of Care for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis: Innovative Strategies regarding Monitoring and Treatment
Abstract: This is a formal request for support with the publication of my PhD dissertation, which describes innovative strategies for the care of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Data from the EQ-5D-Y-5L questionnaire have been of tremendous value for the research presented in this thesis regarding remote monitoring of patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis. By financially contributing to the publication costs of this dissertation you will directly support the dissemination of new insights into the most common rheumatic disease in children. Additionally, your support emphasizes the importance of these questionnaires as monitoring tools.

Title: Severity and EQ-5D (SEVQ). How can EQ5D-utilitites capture notions of severity for priority setting in health care.
Abstract: The two-page proposal on which this is based is attached. The EuroQol Exec requested a full-length proposal with more details, and for the requested budget to be capped at 150k €The urgent need for fair, equitable, and publicly acceptable priority setting criteria is attested to by an array of government white papers and scholarly works. QALY-based cost-effectiveness (utilitarian) alone is often considered insufficient. In order to accommodate other ethical concerns, various forms of severity criteria, to be applied on top of or alongside QALY models, have been suggested. However, there is no unambiguous answer to what severity is, and the topic has recently been debated byeconomists and philosophers in several publications.SEVQ aimstoinvestigate linksbetween the descriptive system of EQ-5D and ‘severity’, and to investigate to what extent respondents prioritise the most severely ill, the worst off, or tends towards utility maximization.

Title: Comparatively investigating sensitivity to change of the EQ-5D-3L and the EQ-5D-5L descriptive systems and seven country-specific value sets using different methodological approaches
Abstract: Introduction: Since the introductionof the EQ-5D-5L (5L) a growing body of literature comparedthe measurement properties of the 5L with the original three-level EQ-5D (3L). So far comparisons on responsiveness for change are rare. This study compares the responsiveness of the 3L and the 5L descriptive systems and (index)values, using two available longitudinal datasetsof rehabilitation patients with mild/moderate health problems,and of stroke patients with severe health problems. We separated descriptive from value effectsfollowinga previous 3L-5L comparative study, whichshowed that 3L descriptions systematically overestimate the presence of health problems, leading to biased 3L valuesand an over-or underestimation ofdiscriminatory power. Methods: First, descriptive results were compared cross-sectionally. Second, inconsistencies between 3L and 5L were determined (3L improves while 5L deteriorates within patient or vice versa). Descriptive responsiveness was tested through the% changed level responses (‘moves’) from baselineto follow-up, % of improved patients (a.o. according to the Paretianclassification of health change, PCHC), and the probability of superiority(PS), a non-parametric effect size measure. Subsequently wecalculated values based on ten country-specific value sets for both patient samples. Responsivenessof these values was assessed throughthe standardized response mean (SRM) and standardized effectsize (SES), using the level sumscore as reference. External anchors to classify patients into change categories were based on a self-rated health question (rehabilitation sample), and the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index (stroke sample).Relative efficiency of 5L over 3L was assessed by calculating ratios of the SRM and SES statistics.Results: Cross-sectional descriptive comparisons confirmedearlier evidence and showed an overestimation for health problems in 3L. Change inconsistencies between 3L and 5L were rare(average 1.0% bydimension for rehabilitation; 1.1% for stroke). Averagelevelmoves per respondent were 0.16 (3L) vs. 0.30 (5L) in rehabilitation, and 0.34(3L) vs. 0.58 (5L) in stroke (by dimension). 50% (3L) vs. 60% (5L) of patients improved in rehabilitation, while 51% (3L) vs. 44% (5L)in stroke (PCHC). The average PS,however,showed better performance of 5L over 3L in both samples (rehabilitation: PS3L= 0.57, PS5L= 0.59, stroke: PS3L=0.59, PS5L= 0.63). Using external anchors, 5L index values demonstrated larger responsiveness in rehabilitation patients, independently from value set and method. In stroke patients, however, 3L showed larger SES/SRMs compared to 5L, except for the SRM results on the mRS anchor, where results were similar. Relative efficiency results for rehabilitation indicated that 5L outperformed3L strongly for SRM and slightly for SESresults. In stroke 3L outperformed5L slightly (SRM) tomoderately (SES) for the Barthel Index anchor-based data while for mRS3L was moderately better for SES but similar to 5L for SRM. Conclusions: Descriptive responsiveness of 5L generally outperformed 3L in both clinical groups; the same was true for valueresponsiveness in rehabilitation, but not in stroke. As in previous cross-sectional comparisons, descriptive results were the main driver of the 3L/5L specific differences in responsiveness. Responsiveness of 3L was influenced by the 'confinedto bed' label. The overestimation bias of 3L affected all responsiveness results.Most likelythis bias will impact QALY estimations, leading to over-or underestimations of QALYs gaineddepending on the condition and condition severity.QALYs based on 5Lwill result in more precise estimates.

Title: UK value set HESG summer 2025 event
Abstract: The funded activity was a two-hour pre-conference session at the Health Economists’ Study Group (HESG) summer meeting in Brighton on 30 June 2025. The session, titled “Introducing an EQ-5D-5L Value Set for the UK”, aimed to disseminate early findings from the UK EQ-5D-5L valuation study and support its adoption by stakeholders. The event brought together researchers to discuss methodological considerations, governance processes, and implications for health technology assessment.Presentations covered the study’s objectives, design, and preliminary results, including the generation of a new UK value set based on preferences of 1,200 members of the public. Speakers addressed NICE’s perspective on implementation, industry concerns about predictability and impact on decision-making, and future methodological developments in health valuation. The session concluded with a panel discussion to encourage engagement and address questions from attendees. Overall, the event successfully informed participants about the forthcoming value set and fostered dialogue on its adoption and use in policy and practice.

Title: Assessing added values and psychometric performance of breathing, sleep, fatigue, EQ-HWB-25 and EQ-HWB-9 among obese individuals receiving weight-loss intervention
Abstract: Background: Despite the growing availability of obesity treatments and the rise in related clinical trials, significant gaps remain in how health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is routinely measured using patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). Existing instruments are costly, lengthy, or impractical for routine use. A more feasible, sensitive, and cost-effective PROM is needed for long-term HRQoL monitoring in obesity care and research. There is increasing demand for HRQoL measures that can support cost-utility analysis (CUA) in obesity; however, widely used tools, including the EQ-5D, may lack the content validity needed to fully capture the impact of obesity and its treatments.  One potential way is to include additional dimensions (‘bolt-ons’) that are related to obesity to be used together with EQ-5D-5L. We identified twelve potential bolt-on candidates in a previous qualitative study: breathing, sleep, tiredness, physical appearance, intimate relationship, discrimination / humiliation, social activities, self-confidence, burden to others, diet control, food enjoyment, gastrointestinal problems. Of these twelve bolt-on candidates, some have been shortlisted for the Experimental Bolt-on Toolbox (i.e. breathing problems, sleep, tiredness, self-confidence). Meanwhile, the newly developed 9-item EQ-HWB-S might also be more suitable than EQ-5D for measuring HRQoL of obese individuals as obesity is a multifaceted issue that affect both health and psychological well-beings.  Aims: The primary objective of this proposal is to evaluate the psychometric properties of the different versions of four bolt-ons in the experimental toolbox (breathing, sleep, fatigue, self-confidence), EQ-HWB-25, and EQ-HWB-9. The secondary objective of this proposal is to evaluate the psychometric performance of eight bolt-on items (physical appearance, intimate relationship, discrimination / humiliation, social activities, burden to others, diet control, food enjoyment, gastrointestinal problems) in individuals with obesity. The specific objectives are: To assess the psychometric performance of the different versions offour bolt-ons; To assess and compare the psychometric performance of EQ-HWB-25 and EQ-HWB-9 among individuals with obesity; andTo explore dimensionality underlying EQ-5D and bolt-ons using exploratory factor analysis and to assess the validity of the resulting scores. Methods: The study will recruit 150 adults (aged 21 years or above) with obesity defined by Asian BMI cut-off (BMI ≥37.5 kg/m2 or BMI ≥32.5 kg/m2 with an obesity-related health condition) who seek weight loss treatment (lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, or bariatric surgery) at the National University Hospital (NUH) and Alexandra Hospital (AH). Data will be collected from the participants at three time points: Baseline, 1 week after baseline, and 6 months after baseline. The baseline questionnaire will be answered when the participant visits the clinic and will include EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons, EQ-HWB-25, and other disease-specific HRQoL instruments (6 subscales from BODY-Q, IWQoL-Lite, the subjective sleep quality question from PSQI). A link of the follow-up questionnaires that include EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons and EQ-HWB-25 will be sent to the participant via their preferred contact method. Statistical analysis will be used to assess the distributional characteristics, divergent validity, convergent validity, known-groups validity, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness of the bolt-on items and EQ-HWB-25. In addition, we will explore potential non-preference-based scoring method of the bolt-ons using exploratory factor analysis.

Title: Visit to National University of Singapore
Abstract: This visit to Singapore included meetings with researchers and policymakers at NUS, Duke NUS, NUHS and Singhealth. I gave a presentation at the School of Public Health, NUS, and started the development of a new research grant on population norms for older adults. I was able to move forward some ongoing research grants using the EQ-5D and develop a number of opportunities with members of the HTA community for using the EQ-5D.

Title: Evaluating respondent burden for the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in prostate cancer
Abstract: Respondent burden is an important consideration for patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), and has motivated the development of shorter versions of PROMs. Despite its importance, respondent burden is ill-defined, and cannot solely be defined as length alone. Existing research on respondent burden, though limited and heterogeneous, indicates the that measuring content and difficulty can also contribute to an understanding of burden. The newly developed EQ-HWB has a shorter version, the EQ-HWB-S, but the perceived burden of both instruments is not clear. This study will use a mixed-methods approach to define, measure and evaluate burden for the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S for men with prostate cancer. Health and well-being is especially important for this population as survival continues to improve but treatments can have long-lasting impacts. This study will provide evidence on the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in a prostate cancer registry population, and on the perceived burden of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S. This information can guide decisions on the choice of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in the context of burden.

Title: Aversion to inequalities in health by EQ-5D domain
Abstract: BACKGROUND: On average, poorer people in the UK live shorter, and less healthy, lives than richer people. Evidence suggests the UK-public don’t like this inequality, and that they are willing to prioritise gains in life-expectancy to poorer people over richer people. Nobody has tested whether they are equally willing to prioritise poorer people for interventions that improve quality-of-life. If we want to include “inequality aversion”in cost-effectiveness analyses, it would be useful to know whether or not this is the case. We hypothesise that the UK-public are more willing to prioritise poorer people for life-expectancy gains than quality-of-life gains. METHODS: We fielded an online person-trade-off (PTO) study in 1,502 members of the UK-public. Participants were briefed on inequalities in health between socioeconomic groups, and then randomised to PTO exercises about one of ten health-gain types (nine forms of quality-of-life and life-expectancy). In each PTO, participants made choices between interventions that would benefit different numbers of people from either the poorest or richest fifth of society. We logically varied the number of people in each group in response to each participant’s response, in order to determine the relative priority they placed on improving the health of each group. Every participant completed two PTO exercises: one for a 3 QALY gain and one for a 0.5 QALY gain. We tested our hypothesis by comparing participant responses in the life-expectancy arm and each quality-of-life arms. This was done separately for the the two gain-magnitudes. RESULTS: The UK-public are more willing to prioritise poorer people for interventions that improve life

Title: Comparing the psychometric properties of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-Y-3L in children with osteogenesis imperfecta in China
Abstract: The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU-9D with the “standard” instrument, PedsQL, in a sample of children and adolescents with Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI). A web-based cross-sectional survey of pediatric OI patients was conducted to collect data. The EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, CHU-9D, and PedsQL were used to assess the health-related quality of life of the participants. Construct validity, including convergent and divergent validity, known-group validity, and test-retest reliability, were examined to confirm the psychometric properties of the instruments. A total of 157 children and adolescents with OI participated in the study. Few samples reported full health status. A strong ceiling effect was observed for all EQ-5D-Y and most CHU-9D dimensions. Both EQ-5D-Y and CHU-9D showed statistically significant correlations with the corresponding PedsQL subscales. A strong correlation was also identified between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L. The test-retest reliability for the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU-9D was acceptable. The EQ-5D-Y instruments showed a better known-group validity than CHU-9D in differentiating patients in different risk groups. The results show that the EQ-5D-Y instruments and CHU-9D are reliable and valid and that the EQ-5D-Y-3L performed slightly better than EQ-5D-Y-5L regarding convergent validity and its ability to discriminate.

Title: EQ-5D for proxy assessment of nursing home residents: A systematic review of feasibility and measurement properties
Abstract: Objectives: The accurate assessment of Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in residents of residential care facilities (RCF) necessitates the use of proxy-reported instruments that possess robust psychometric properties. Generally, these instruments are modified versions of self-reported tools, with adjustments made to pronouns and instructions to better suit the respondent. Among such tools, the EQ-5D has emerged as a prominent instrument for evaluating HRQoL within RCF settings. This review aimed to synthesize evidence on psychometric properties of the proxy version of EQ-5D. Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Setting and Participants: Residents in RCF. Methods: An extensive search was conducted across 8 databases, covering articles from inception to May 29, 2023. We included a total of 20 articles reporting data that can be used to evaluate psychometric properties of this instrument in RCF. The quality appraisal employed the COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist, and data synthesis followed COSMIN methodology. Results: Most of the included studies were conducted in Europe, with 75% using nursing staff as proxies. Missing data rates were 5% for EQ-5D and 26% for EQ VAS. Evidence of moderate certainty on construct validity of the EQ-5D index was inconsistent, although the EQ VAS showed sufficient construct validity supported by high certainty. EQ-5D index responsiveness evidence was limited, characterized by low certainty and inconsistency. Proxy-resident agreement ranged from poor to moderate, and improved with repeated administration for the “mobility” and “usual activities” dimensions. The lowest agreement was observed when staff served as proxies or the proxy-proxy perspective was adopted. Conclusions and Implications: This review offers an overview of the psychometric properties of EQ-5D as a proxy HRQoL measure in RCF. The suboptimal evidence on psychometric properties of EQ-5D indicated the need for more validation studies and cautious use of the instrument in RCF.

Title: EuroQol Data for Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE) for Egypt – A longitudinal study
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol Data for Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE) project aims to establish standardized, representative HRQoL datasets across diverse populations. Egypt, the most populous country in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, presents a unique opportunity for inclusion in the EQ-DAPHNIE initiative. With over 106 million residents, significant disparities in healthcare access, and a high burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), Egypt’s participation will enhance the project’s global representativeness and provide valuable insights into population health needs.Aim: This study aims to generate high-quality Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) data from the general adult population in Egypt to facilitate cross-country comparisons and contribute to EuroQol research.Methods: This longitudinal study will employ web-based self-administered surveys and face-to-face interviews to ensure inclusivity, particularly among elderly and illiterate populations. A quota sampling strategy will be applied to achieve national representativeness based on age, sex, and geographic distribution (urban or rural). The target sample size is 4,500 adults, with at least 500 face-to-face interviews conducted by trained interviewers. The survey will include 8 standardized HRQoL instruments namely, the EQ-5D-5L,  EQ Health and Wellbeing instrument-short (EQ-HWB-S), four EQ bolt-ons, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-10 (PROMIS-10), PROMIS-sleep disturbance short form, World Health Organization 5-items (WHO-5), Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2), and 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder questionnaire (GAD-2) along with socio-demographic and health-related questions, and response validation measures. A representative subset (N=1000) of the initial sample will be followed up after 6 months to offer additional insights on changes over time.

Title: Getting more from the core in bolt-on valuation
Abstract: The launch of the Bolt-on Toolbox necessitates development of valuation methods for bolt-ons. Subsequently, to equip this toolbox with country-specific value sets will be a big endeavour in view of the multiplicity of bolt-ons and countries. The core dimension value sets differ between countries, so offering a single bolt-on value set for multiple countries is guaranteed to result in gaming in at least some of the countries. The present proposal offers to seek a possible solution to the problem by studying the strength of association between preferences for core dimensions and for a selected bolt-on (cognition). Specifically, we plan to design and test a novel approach that will estimate the link between these two preferences. If the association between preferences is strong, then preferences for bolt-ons can be to some extent inferred from the core value sets which could perhaps reduce sample sizes in the bolt-on valuation studies of help with developing methods to transfer preference information between countries. We will recruit 300 respondents from prolific to online interviews. In these interviews, we will elicit preferences for health states defined using only core dimensions or also a bolt-on item using TTO in two arms: A) first core and then bolt-on health states; B) only bolt-on health states. In the modelling, we will use the CALE model specification, to reduce the number of parameters. For core dimensions health states, we will estimate the dimension importance and the relative importance of levels. For the bolt-on health states, we will estimate how the importance of bolt-on item is associated with the importance of core dimensions relative to the bolt-on-specific preferences.

Title: Measuring interactions in bolt-on valuation using lotteries
Abstract: In valuation studies, the interactions between core EQ-5D-5L dimensions are largely ignored: the utility is derived from individual dimensions in additive way. Such approach has pragmatic merits – e.g., a reduced number of parameters – but it is being questioned whether it can safely be extended to bolt-on valuation in view of possibly large overlap between bolt-ons and core dimensions. Meanwhile, a robust estimation of the interaction effects is challenging; as shown in the proposal, the interactions may be confounded with other phenomena, e.g., time preference. We aim to develop a method to test for the presence of interactions between a selected bolt-on and core dimensions using choices involving lotteries. The respondents will make choices from pairs of two-outcome, fair odds lotteries with outcomes being health profiles involving problems with none, exactly one, or two dimensions. The respondents will be interviewed online. Indifference points will be identified to verify how the disutility of combined problems relates to the sum of disutilities of individual problems, for instance, if disutility of 31111 health state plus the disutility of 13111 health state is equal to the disutility of 33111 (hence, if the dimensions interact in preferential sense). Based on test power calculations, we plan to recruit 130 respondents via Prolific. Additionally, to put the possible interactions between core dimensions and the bolt-on in a context, we will add tasks to elicit the interactions within the core dimensions.

Title: Multi-Country Quantitative Examination of Visual Analogue Scale Versions with the EQ-HWB-9
Abstract: Objective: Visual analogue scales (VAS) yield interval-level data that may complement an instrument's descriptive system. While existing EQ-5D instruments include the EQ VAS, the EQ-HWB-9 currently lacks an accompanying VAS. Prior mixed-methods evidence in a small US sample (n=34) suggested that candidate VAS constructs were perceived differently qualitatively yet did not differ meaningfully in quantitative ratings. To further inform the inclusion of an appropriate VAS with the EQ-HWB-9, this study examined whether construct specification produced measurable differences in VAS ratings and associations with the EQ-HWB-9 descriptive system across three countries.Methods: Responses were analyzed from an online survey of 916 adults from the US, UK, and Germany who completed the EQ-HWB-9 and three VAS versions specifying constructs of Health, Health and Wellbeing (HWB), and Quality of Life (QoL) with 7-day recall periods, in random order. Means, effect sizes, correlations, and agreement between ratings were compared across VAS versions. Construct-specific convergent validity was evaluated by correlations with EQ-HWB-9 items and external anchors. Multiple linear regression models estimated the variance in VAS ratings explained by EQ-HWB-9 items, with partial η² quantifying each item's unique contribution. Subgroup analyses by country and among caregivers and social care users were also explored.Results: Mean VAS ratings did not differ significantly across constructs (p = 0.195; all Cohen's d < 0.20), and inter-construct agreement was good (ICC = 0.77). EQ-HWB-9 items explained comparable variance across constructs (R² = 0.39–0.44), but with construct-specific differential sensitivity: Pain and self-rated health correlated most strongly with VAS-Health, while Sad/Depressed, Lonely, life satisfaction, and relationship satisfaction correlated most strongly with VAS-QoL. VAS-HWB was most explained by a balanced mix of physical and psychosocial items and was preferred by respondents, with 45.9% selecting HWB as best capturing EQ-HWB-9 content and 59.9% ranking HWB as the preferred construct.Conclusions: The three VAS versions yielded similar aggregate ratings and comparable overall explanatory power but differed in terms of which EQ-HWB-9 dimensions predicted their scores. VAS-HWB demonstrated the most balanced alignment with the EQ-HWB-9 in terms of coverage of items predicting ratings and was favored by respondents. These findings support VAS-HWB as a candidate for further investigation for inclusion with the EQ-HWB-9.

Title: The development of the national value set for the EQ-5D-Y-3L in Brazil
Abstract: BACKGROUND: There is an increasing growth of interest in the development of generic preference-based measures specific to children and adolescents in the last decades. The EQ-5D-Y-3L is a generic instrument developed by the EuroQol Group to measure health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents aged 8-15 years old. However, there is not an EQ-5D-Y-5L value set to estimate utility values in economic evaluations conducted for Brazilian children and adolescents. This study aims to cover this gap by following the International Valuation Protocol for the EQ-5D-Y-3L. This study aims at covering this gap by collecting preferences using a standardised protocol for deriving EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets. METHODS: Two independent sample of adults were recruited to the online discrete choice experiment and the face-to-face composite time trade-off by computer-assisted. Respondents completed the DCE (each respondent completed 15 pairs of the 150 pairs) and cTTO (each respondent completed 10 health states of the 28 health states) tasks considering your views for a 10-year-old child. The discrete choice experiment responses were analysed using a mixed-logit model. The discrete choice experiments values were mapped onto the mean observed composite time trade-off values to generate an EQ-5D-Y-3Lvalue set. Linear and non-linear mapping models were explored to estimate the most efficient model to generate this value set. RESULTS: Overall, 1,152 and 211 respondents completed the discrete choice experiment and composite time trade-off, respectively. The order the importance of each domain was pain/discomfort, followed by mobility, self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression. Furthermore, the final model ranged from 1 for “full health” (11111) to − 0.0059 for “the worst health state” (33333), which was the only negative utility value of the whole elicited value set. CONCLUSION: This study estimated the Brazilian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set, which can be used to estimate quality-adjusted life years in economic evaluations of healthcare interventions for Brazilian youth population. The linear mapping without intercept was the best model to generate a consistent value set for Brazilian youth.

Title: A comprehensive Psychometric Validation of EQ Instruments for Early Childhood Health-Related Quality of Life and Caregiver Spillover, including EQ-TIPS, EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-5L with Sleep and Fatigue Bolt-ons, and the EQ-HWB-S
Abstract: This study aims to address critical gaps in the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children under the age of five by conducting a comprehensive psychometric validation of the EQ-TIPS instrument, including both 3-level and 5-level versions. We will conduct a longitudinal study to assess the feasibility, face validity, known-groups validity, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness of both EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L in children aged 0–48 months. For children aged 25–48 months, we will also examine the comparability and potential transition between EQ-TIPS-5L and the proxy version of EQ-5D-Y-5L. In addition, we aim to explore spillover effects on family caregivers by evaluating the psychometric performance, such as known-groups validity, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness of two newly developed EQ-5D-5L bolt-on items (sleep and fatigue) and the EQ-HWB-S. Participants will be recruited from three tertiary hospitals in China across three health condition groups: acute illnesses, chronic conditions, and healthy controls. Caregivers will complete surveys twice with a follow-up interval of 1–3 weeks. The survey questionnaires will include two parts: 1) Child section: EQ-TIPS-3L, EQ-TIPS-5L, proxy EQ VAS, EQ-5D-Y-5L proxy version 1 (only for children aged 25-48 months), a 5-grade overall health assessment (OHA) proxy version, QQ-10 questionnaire, and children’s demographic information; 2) Carer section: carers’ EQ-5D-5L with sleep and fatigue bolt-ons, carers’ EQ VAS, carers’ EQ-HWB-S, and carers’ demographic information. Each clinical condition is selected for its high prevalence and clinical relevance in early childhood, as well as its suitability for stratifying health status by severity. Additionally, to assess face validity, caregivers will complete the QQ-10 questionnaire after completing the EQ-TIPS questionnaire to provide structured feedback on the clarity, relevance, and acceptability of EQ-TIPS. Findings will contribute essential evidence to support the use of EQ-TIPS in early childhood HRQoL assessment and of the EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons and EQ-HWB-S in evaluating caregiver spillover effects. The study data will be shared with the EuroQol Group to support future development and application of these instruments.

Title: Regional differences in health-related quality of life in England: EQ-5D in national surveys of the general population
Abstract: This research investigates regional differences in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) as described by EQ-5D in England over a 20 year period.Data will be extracted from the Health Survey forEngland (HSE), an annual survey of nationally representative residents in England that between 1996 and 2013 periodically included EQ-5D,supplemented by data from other national surveys, including ONS Omnibus and the General Household Survey (GHS) which also included EQ-5D. All surveys used essentially similar sampling methods and in total provide EQ-5D data on some 150,000 respondents. Regions will be classified in terms of the degree of urbanisation (village / town / urban), Government Office (North East / North West / Yorkshire / East Midlands / West Midlands / East/ London / South West / South East) and IMD quintile score (from least deprived to most deprived). Descriptive analyses by region will be conducted. Multiple regression models will be constructed to predict HRQoL (percentages of respondents reporting problems in each dimension of EQ-5D, VAS scores and utility scores) in separate regions and in different years.

Title: Malaysian EQ‐5D‐5L Value Set Symposium and Workshop
Abstract: A half-day symposium followed by a half-day workshop was organized to inform healthcare decision makers and researchers on the availability of a Malaysian EQ-5D-5L value set and provide guidance on its applications, specifically in economic evaluations and outcomes research.

Title: Developing guidance for best practice in collaborative involvement (CI) in health state valuation studies: An extension to CREATE (CREATE-CI)
Abstract: Background: Engaging and involving key collaborators beyond the research team is viewed as increasingly important in health research and practice. In health state valuation, non-researcher collaborators may include patients, members of the public, caregivers, clinical experts, and decision-makers, amongst others. Several benefits associated with collaborative involvement include enhanced outputs, increased buy-in from affiliated parties, and superior research impact. Best practice guidance on how to effectively involve and engage collaborators in health state valuation studies and to comprehensively and transparently report this process is lacking. Aim: Developing best practice methods guidelines is iterative. This project represents ‘Phase 2’ (building on project 1711-RA) and aims to develop guidelines for conducting and reporting collaborative involvement (CI) in health state valuation studies, as an extension to the EuroQol-funded Reporting Valuation Studies of Multi-Attribute Utility-Based Instruments (CREATE) reporting checklist (i.e., CREATE-CI). Methods: A three-stage, consensus-building methodology is proposed. First, a targeted review of associated literature (e.g., in comparative effectiveness research) will be combined with a framework of best practices for collaborative involvement derived from review project 1711-RA and draft recommendations developed. Second, focus groups will be held with EuroQol-affiliated experts, non-EuroQol experts, and collaborator representatives to refine the draft recommendations. Third, a modified international Delphi survey will be conducted to derive consensus on the guidelines. The guidelines will be finalised by a development committee, who will have oversight of the guideline development process. Key outputs include the CREATE-CI reporting guidelines and an aligned manuscript detailing best practice in collaborative involvement in health state valuation.

Title: Workshop to discuss the legitimacy, estimation, and uses of the Minimal Important Difference (MID) with EQ-5D
Abstract: There is clearly muddled language used in the literature and wide variations in methodologies. Despite this, there appears to be a tendency for researchers to quote one or two key papers when justifying the use of a single “off the shelf” MID despite the variation in MIDs across patient groups (e.g.the 0.074 averagefrom Walters & Brazier, 2005). In addition, there is no evidence of any exploration of how or whether a MID could be used with the descriptive systemrather than an index; the Pareto classification of change might provide a starting point for thisfor example(Devlin, Parkin and Browne, 2010).There appears to be some evidence that MIDs are different depending on whether they are used for an improvement or a deterioration in health, although this difference does not appear to be large. There is also a clear focus on the index (and EQ-VAS to a lesser extent) but this is not necessarily appropriate given that indices are typically based on general population values. It isalsocurrentlyunclear as to how the state transition approach might fit in alongside or compare with the more common anchor-based and distribution-based methods.

Title: Improving the way we ask children and young people to participate in paediatric valuation tasks – co-designing improvements to the EQ-5D-Y valuation and interview protocol with young people and experts
Abstract: Background: Recent stakeholder engagement suggests that young people, including children and adolescents, should be involved in health state valuations of paediatric health utility measures. However, valuation tasks may be too demanding for young people to complete, and adaptations may be required to make these tasks more accessible to them. Aims: This project aims to co-design an improved way of including children and young people in paediatric health state valuation tasks by adapting the existing EQ-5D-Y valuation protocol. Methods: This study will utilise a co-design methodology, whereby, parents, children and adolescents, paediatric experts (e.g., paediatricians, child psychologists, and ethicists) and valuation experts will be asked to co-design an improved, child-friendly version of the EQ-5D-Y valuation and interview protocol. During co-design, participants will help to design and refine an updated EQ-5D-Y valuation and interview protocol for young people (this is known as the ‘prototype’).

Title: Psychometric assessment of the E-QALY item pool in the United States
Abstract: This proposal is a subproject related to the psychometric validation phase of The ‘Extending the QALY’ collaboration between the EuroQol group and UK based researchers, centrally coordinated by Sheffield University, that aims to develop a broad measure of quality of life for use in economic evaluations across health and social care. The project consists of six stages, and this proposal concerns the fourth stage. The overall aim of this study is to test the psychometric validity of the E-QALY item pool using US data. We will collect online data from a sample of 500 US cancer patientsusing a range of instruments relevant to health and social care. This includes the E-QALY item pool measures of health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5LandPROMIS-29),and measures of wellbeing (WEMWBS). We will conduct psychometric analysis similar to that being conducted by the UK E-QALY team to better understand the generalizability of the findings of the UK to other predominant ly English speaking countries to support the item reduction and selection process. As health care policy and reimbursement in the USA can have global ramifications, it is useful to include the USA in the measure development process which may enhance the acceptability of the instrument in the future.

Title: Validating the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-HWB-9 in Inherited Bleeding Disorders in Canada
Abstract: Background: There is limited evidence on the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and the EQ-HWB-9 in Canada. Inherited bleeding disorders imposes significant impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of children, adults, and their families. Due to the genetic nature of these conditions, symptoms often appear in childhood and have a lifelong impact on patients. Some caregivers are also affected as patients. This unique population composition makes inherited bleeding disorders particularly well-suited for validating EQ instruments. Aims: To validate the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-HWB-9 among patients and caregivers living with inherited bleeding disorders in Canada. Methods: In collaboration with Canadian Hemophilia Society, a cross-sectional survey will be developed and administered online across Canada. The target respondents include two groups: 1) children and adult patients diagnosed with an inherited bleeding disorder; and 2) their caregivers. The survey will be distributed by email through the Canadian Bleeding Disorder Registry. It will contain three sections related to: 1) sociodemographic (e.g., age, gender, province of residence) and clinical characteristics (e.g., type of bleeding disorder, disease severity); 2) HRQoL burden; and 3) economic burden. HRQoL will be assessed using generic and disease-specific instruments. The generic instruments include the EQ-5D-5L (self-complete by adult patients) or EQ-5D-Y-5L (parent proxy) for pediatric patients, and the EQ-HWB-9 for caregivers. The disease-specific instrument is the Parent’s Index Version of the Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Children (Haemo-QOL). The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-HWB-9 will be assessed according to their health profiles, distributional properties, known groups validity, and convergent and divergent validity.Benefits to the group: Development of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and the EQ-HWB-9 are currently strategic priorities of the EuroQol Group. This research addresses a critical evidence gap in Canada, where more data is needed to support the use of the Y-5L in HTA and reimbursement decisions. The study also aligns with the Canadian Hemophilia Society’s priority to better measure disease burden. Including the Y-5L and EQ-HWB-9 offers opportunities to expand their psychometric evidence, explore transitions between EQ instruments, and build a sustainable partnership with CHS. By funding this work, the EuroQol Group can advance its global strategic goals and enhance its presence in Canadian policy and clinical settings.

Title: CANDOUR study: Using EQ-5D-5L to assess the impact of global use of COVID-19 vaccines on health-related quality of life
Abstract: Around 20,000 participants from a diverse group of up to 16 countries (approx. 1,200 per country) have responded to two online surveys (in 2020 and 2022), in which we asked questions about sociodemographic characteristics, health status, use of health care services, perceived health-related quality of life (HRQol) using the EQ-5D-5L instrument, prior to, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. These unique longitudinal international database, which will be followed imminently from a third survey, gives us the opportunity to explore how the COVID-19 pandemic and its legacy as well as current mutated economic circumstances (e.g. cost of living crises, wars) may differentially impact HRQol of different populations in different socioeconomics settings and countries.

Title: Estimating an EQ-5D-Y-3L value set in the United Kingdom
Abstract: The international EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol has now been successfully implemented in several studies. This experience was discussed in a three-day workshop organised by the EuroQol Group and summarised in a report. In general, there seems to be consensus that the use of discrete choice experiments (DCE) is appropriate to elicit preferences for health states that will be experienced by children. However, the most appropriate method to anchor latent scale DCE values onto the QALY scale is still uncertain. In addition, the report recommends a clearer engagement with relevant HTA agencies. This revised application has been prepared following these recommendations and present a research study to estimate a number of EQ-5D-Y value sets under different normative scenarios of perspectives and sample representativeness in the UK. The proposed methodology will be discussed before the study commences with an advisory group and relevant stakeholders and revised if necessary. We will conduct an online DCE with a representative sample of 1,000 adolescents (11-17 years old) and 1,000 adults (18 year and older). Participants will complete the DCE tasks using their own perspective or for a 10-year old child. An adult sample of 200 participants will complete a C-TTO task from the same two perspectives, which will be used to anchor DCE values onto the QALY scale. Finally, we will explore the impact of using value sets under different normative judgments of perspective and UK sample representativeness on QALY gains using patient-level data from a clinical trial with long-term follow-up.

Title: HRQoL and Health Literacy among informal caregivers to persons with dementia
Abstract: As part of a larger project financed by the Norwegian Research Council, PATHWAYS, on health and ageing, PhD candidate Kristin Häikiö has conducted a survey of ~200 informal carers for elderly people with dementia. Aside from demographics and other background variables regarding both careperson and the one receiving care, the survey was trained upon health literacy, time spent on various caring tasks, perceived carer burden(Relative Stress Scale), and quality of life(EQ-5D-5L). Preliminary analyses (regression models predicting utility scores using health literacy, including relevant background variables) indicate that health literacy is a statistically significant predictor of HRQoL as measured by the EQ-5D-5L among carepersons. This material has gone unused as of yet, the thesis focused elsewhere. As the PhD project funding is out in early2020, and Häikiöis set to deliver her thesis, there is risk that it will not be published upon. The proposal is for funding of three weeks of extra time for the PhD student to write up a paper on the findings regarding health literacy and utility scores, and two days of supervision on the interpretation and use of EQ-5D data.

Title: Comparing the psychometric performance of five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons in a multinational, longitudinal general population setting and their association with validated fatigue scales
Abstract: Background: Generic preference-based instruments like the EQ-5D-5L are widely used to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in both patient and general populations. However, its five core dimensions may not fully capture aspects of health that the general public considers important, such as energy and fatigue. To address this limitation, bolt-on dimensions have been proposed to enhance the EQ-5D-5L's relevance in population health surveys. EuroQol is planning to launch the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox as an instrument to accompany the EQ-5D-5L. Fatigue/energy and sleep are candidate bolt-ons for the Toolbox. For fatigue/energy, multiple different wordings have been proposed, and psychometric evidence is needed to support item development, refining and selection. Objectives: The aim of this study is to address gaps in evidence regarding the psychometric performance of five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons: tiredness, energy, fatigue, exhaustion, and sleep. Our main research questions are:  What are the comparative psychometric properties of the five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons: tiredness, energy, fatigue, exhaustion, and sleep in the adult general population? How do the five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons relate to each other and to widely used symptom-specific measures, such as the FACIT-Fatigue Scale and Rash-Transformed Fatigue Severity Scale (RT-FSS) in the adult general population? Do the five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons (tiredness, energy, fatigue, exhaustion, and sleep) demonstrate measurement invariance across the English, Spanish, German, Italian, and Japanese language groups? Which of the five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons is most preferred by the adult general population in terms of relevance of the content, and does the most preferred bolt-on also demonstrate the best psychometric performance?  Methods: We will conduct a secondary analysis of data from the GENESIS study, a multinational longitudinal survey of 10,500 adults representative of the general population in the US (n=3,000), UK, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Japan (n=1,500 each) starting in Q2 2025 (wave 1). A small subset from each country will be recontacted one month later (wave 2). This proposal is related to the analysis of waves 1 and 1 and 2 (~ 1 month after wave 1). Representativeness of the general population will be based on age, gender, region (interlaced), and education/socioeconomic status (overall). Data will be collected on demographics (age, sex, marital status, living situation, education, work situation, height, weight, use of mobility aids, need of a caregiver, chronic health conditions), EQ-5D-5L, bolt-ons, and a set of relevant patient-reported outcome measures including FACIT-Fatigue and Rash-Transformed Fatigue Severity Scale (RT-FSS). Psychometric performance of EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons will be evaluated using distributional characteristics (floor/ceiling effects, profile counts), informativity (Shannon H’ and J’), divergent validity, convergent validity, structural validity, explanatory power, responsiveness, and test-retest reliability. Measurement invariance testing will be conducted to identify differences in the five bolt-ons across languages. In terms of relevance, the most preferred of the five energy- and sleep-related EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons will be identified using average rank scores and the proportion of respondents selecting each bolt-on as the most preferred that reflects the best their HRQoL.

Title: The Relationship between Time, Sequencing, and Precision: Considerations for Choice Experiments
Abstract: Objective: This study estimatesthe effect of sequence on response precision and behaviorin health valuation studies.Methods: Time trade-off(TTO)and paired comparison responses from 6 health valuation studies—4 US, 1 Spanish, and 1 Dutch—were examined(22,225 respondents)to test whether task sequence influencesresponse precision(e.g., rounding),responsechanges and median response times.Each study used a computer-based instrumentthat randomized task sequence among a national sampleof adults, age 18 or older,from the general population.Results: For both TTO and paired comparisons, median response times decreasedwith sequence (i.e., learning), but tendedto flatten after the first 3 tasks. Although the paired comparison evidence demonstratedthat sequence hadno effect on response precision, the frequency of rounded TTO responses (to either 1-yearor 5-year units) increasedwith sequence. Conclusion: Based on these results, reducingthe numberor randomizing paired comparison tasksdoes not appear to influenceresponseprecision; however, generalizability, practicality,and precautionary considerations remain. Overall, participantslearnedto respondefficiently within the first 3tasksand didnot resort to satisficing, but may have roundedtheir TTO responses.

Title: The impact of overlap and color coding on response efficiency in discrete choice experiments
Abstract: Objective To test the hypothesis that level overlap and color coding can mitigate or even preclude the occurrence of attribute non-attendance in discrete choice experiments. Methods A randomized controlled experiment with five experimental study arms was designed to investigate the independent and combined impact of level overlap and color coding on respondents’ attribute non-attendance. The systematic differences between the study arms allowed for a direct comparison of observed drop-out rates and estimates of the average number of attributes attended to by respondents, which were obtained using augmented mixed logit models that explicitly incorporated attribute non-attendance. Results In the base-case study arm without level overlap or color coding, the observed drop-out rate was 14% and respondents attended on average only 2 out of 5 attributes. The independent introduction of level overlap and color coding both reduced the drop-out rate to 10% and increased attribute attendance to 3attributes. The combination of level overlap and color coding, however, was most effective: it reducedthe drop-out rate to 8% and improved attribute attendance to 4 out of 5 attributes. The latter essentially removed the need to explicitly accommodate for attribute non-attendance when analyzing the choice data. Conclusion Based on the presented results, the use of level overlap and color coding are recommendable strategiesto reduce the drop-out rate and improve attribute attendance in discrete choice experiments.

Title: The performance of EQ-5D-5L in various disease groups with different durations
Abstract: The EQ-5D-5L uses a “today” recall period, which may not fully capture health-related quality of life (HRQOL) for conditions with fluctuating symptoms. This study examined the performance of the EQ-5D-5L across different chronic diseases—tuberculosis (TB), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), HIV/AIDS—and periodic attack illnesses such as asthma and chronic skin disorders (CSD), while assessing how alternative recall periods influence HRQOL reporting.A total of 205 adult patients from hospitals in Bandung, Indonesia, completed up to three data collection sessions involving the EQ-5D-5L with varied recall periods (“today,” “past week,” “past month,” and “last time experiencing the illness”), disease-specific HRQOL questionnaires, and a General State of Health (GSH) question. Analyses included paired statistical tests, effect sizes, Gwet’s AC1, Bland–Altman plots, and correlations between EQ-5D-5L and disease-specific scores.Feasibility was excellent, with no missing responses. For TB, T2DM, and HIV/AIDS, EQ-5D-5L scores using “today” were generally stable across one month, particularly among participants reporting no change in health. Agreement coefficients showed substantial to almost-perfect concordance across sessions, and “past month” recall produced scores comparable to those collected one month prior. These findings suggest that the “today” recall period is adequate for stable chronic conditions.In contrast, patients with asthma and CSD showed significantly worse EQ-5D-5L scores when recalling their most recent illness episode compared with their “today” scores (p < 0.001 for EQ-VAS, utility, and LSS). This indicates that the standard recall period underestimates disease burden in episodic conditions. Correlations between EQ-5D-5L outcomes and disease-specific measures were significant across most groups and recall variations, supporting convergent validity.Patients with chronic conditions generally preferred the “today” recall period, while those with episodic illnesses demonstrated mixed preferences between “today” and “last illness experience.”Overall, the EQ-5D-5L performs reliably in stable chronic diseases but may miss important symptom variability in periodic attack illnesses, underscoring the need to consider disease trajectory when selecting or modifying recall periods.

Title: The EQ-5D-Y in a clinical sample of children and adolescents with asthma, diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis: convergent validity, agreement between self-and parent-reports as well as sensitivity to change
Abstract: Purpose: The EQ-5D-Y assesses child and adolescent health-related quality of life(HRQoL) by means of five items on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfortand anxiety/depression as well as a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) on the self-ratedcurrent health state. The present study investigates predictors of self-reported HRQoLaccording to the EQ-5D-Y in a mixed clinical sample of chronically ill children andadolescents based on longitudinal data.Methods: Data from the German Kids-CAT study on children and adolescents withasthma, diabetes and juvenile arthritis gathered over a period of six months wereanalyzed (n=310; aged 7 to 17 years; 48 % female). Socio-demographic as well asdisease- and health-specific predictors were investigated. Generalized linear mixedmodels and linear mixed models served to examine both the items and the VAS of the EQ-5D-Y.Results: Ceiling effects for the EQ-5D-Y were detected in the analyzed sampleindicating low burden of disease. Results of longitudinal regression-based analysesrevealed effects of health complaints on all investigated domains of HRQoL. Further,besides age- and gender-specific effects, associations of HRQoL with disease control,the duration of the disease as well as mental health problems were found.Conclusions: Our findings support the content validity of the EQ-5D-Y and underlinethe necessity to address subjective health complaints and mental health problems inthe care of children and adolescents with asthma, diabetes and juvenile arthritis.

Title: The Relative Value of Social Outcomes in Health Technology Assessment
Abstract: A key outcomein the evaluationof health technologies is the quality adjusted life year (QALY)which is oftenestimatedusing health measuressuch as EQ-5D. However, the impact of many interventions extends beyond a narrow definition of health to include non-health impactssuch associal care. This means that there are circumstances where the QALY doesnot capture the full value of an intervention.In response to this,instruments with a broaderperspective such as ASCOT, which measures social care related quality of life, havebeen developed. Given the growthin available measures, it is important that decision-makers have tools to assess value for money consistently. However, eliciting preferences for different aspects of QoL,to allow for the combined benefits to be captured within the same framework,has not been tested. We investigate the relationship between health and social care aspects of QoL when assessed jointly by combining theEQ-5D-5L and ASCOTin an online discrete choice experiment (DCE). Each respondent completed 15DCEtasks from an underlying design of 300 choice sets. Analysis used conditional logit regression to estimate coefficient decrements for each attribute and examine theirrelative importance. Latent class and mixed logit modelling were used to understand heterogeneity in preferences.Overall 975 people completed the survey. The results suggest evidence oftrading acrosshealth and social careaspects, as indicated by differences in the magnitude of the coefficients across the different aspectsincluded. There is evidence of preference heterogeneityacross the dimensions, particularly at the more severe levels.We have used an established valuation methodology to demonstrate that it is possible to value concepts measuring different aspects of quality of life on the same underlying scale. The results inform further valuation work eliciting preferences for instrumentscombining outcomes from multiple perspectives.

Title: Psychometric assessment of EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-Y-5L in rare genetic diseases: a mixed methods approach
Abstract: Background: Genomic testing is starting to be translated into clinical practice for people with rare genetic diseases. In England, the National Health Service launched a new Genomic Medicine Service. In Australia, Australian and Melbourne Genomics are supporting the Federal and State Governments in the translation of genomics. However, data on the outcomes of genomic testing is sparse, and there is uncertainty regarding the appropriate outcome measures to use. Data on the use of both established and new instruments, such as the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB and EQ-5D-Y-5L, would inform more robust health technology assessment decisions in this context. Aims: Assess the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-HWB, and EQ-5D-Y-5L instruments in adult patients and parents of children with lived experience of rare genetic diseases in Australia and England using mixed methods. Methods: The project comprises three phases:  Assessment of content validity, face validity, and feasibility of various instruments using think-aloud interviews, with semi-structured follow-up discussions; Assessment of convergent and known group validity in a large baseline sample of participants; Assessment of responsiveness in a sample of participants who will undergo genomic testing, with or without subsequent medical treatment or gene therapy.  Recruitment for all phases will take place in both Australia and England, leveraging large established rare disease cohorts and patient support networks via our partner institutions. Deliverables: Study report presented to the EuroQol Descriptive System Working Group and EuroQoL Group; 2-3 articles for submission to academic journals; presentations/dissemination of findings through the iHEA Econ-Omics group and collaborating institutions.

Title: Generation of an EQ-5D-5L value set for the Mexican population
Abstract: Aim: To develop an EQ-SD-SL value set for the Mexican general population. Background: There is strong interest in using EQ-SD-SL to support decision making in Mexico, for two reasons. First, HTA processes are used by the General Health Council of Mexico (CSG) to determine which new technologies are recommended for funding. To date, HTA has relied mainly on cost per life year gained and this is to be extended to include quality of life and QALYs. Secondly, the Mexican Secretariat of Health has as one of its main responsibilities monitoring of health care quality provided by public and private organizations. The General Directorate of Quality and Health Education, (DGCES) is in charge of such monitoring. Since 2013, the DGCES has been actively participating in the OECD Health Care Quality Indicators project. The DGCES has a well-established monitoring system based upon indicators that measure several aspects of health care quality from the provider perspective (DGCES, 2018) and wishes to extend that to include patient reported outcomes. An EQ-5D-SL value set for Mexico is required to support both uses of the EQ-SD-SL. Methods: The study will use the EQ-VT protocol and data quality monitoring processes that have emerged as best practice from previous value set studies. Value sets will be modelled from TTO data, DCE data, and both data combined via hybrid modelling. Deliverables: The principal deliverable will be a manuscript reporting the value set. Timelines: The project is planned to commence in September 2018 and to last for 18 months.

Title: A global survey of HTA agencies for their views on health utility instruments and data: protocol development
Abstract: Organizations which are most interested in using the EuroQol Group’s instruments are health technology assessment (HTA) agencies. However, to our knowledge, only limited formal ‘market’ research has been conducted to understand these users preferences with regard to the ‘science and technology’ underlying our instruments and/or their unmet needs. The ultimate goal of this research is to assess the preferences and needs of HTA agencies around the world with regard to the collection and use of health-state utility data. In this first phase of the project, we developed a study protocol for conducting a survey that can be sent to HTA agencies across the world. We first conducted a scoping review to understand the issues and challenges in collecting, evaluating, synthesizing, and using health utility data for reimbursement decision making. We then interviewed members of HTA agencies from Singapore, Indonesia, Canada, England, Norway, Australia, New Zealand, and Argentina, to understand the issues and challenges in their work with regard to the use of health utility instruments and to get their feedback on a draft survey. Based on this, we developed a survey that can be sent to HTA agencies to elicit this feedback.

Title: Advancing the Scaling Factor Approach for Bolt-On Valuation: A Research Program for Methodological Development, Model Refinement, and sample size requirement
Abstract: The Scaling Factor Approach (SFA), which applies previously estimated EQ-5D-5L coefficients as constants along with a scaling factor (λ) to bolt-on valuation data, has emerged as a promising method for producing consistent and cost-effective bolt-on value sets. While SFA has demonstrated strong predictive accuracy in previous studies, its broader adoption and methodological refinement remains limited. This research program addresses these gaps through four interrelated aims. First, we will develop a suite of user-friendly R functions to implement the SFA, complete with documentation and example datasets for cTTO and DCE applications. Second, we will explore relaxing the SFA’s core assumption by allowing separate scaling factors for different EQ-5D dimensions. Third, we will use simulation studies to identify the minimum sample size required for bolt-on valuation studies, guided by performance thresholds set by an expert panel. Together, these aims will strengthen the methodological foundation of the SFA, support its practical application, and evaluate its robustness in existing data. The findings will inform the development of a potential bolt-on valuation protocol.
