According to the Wilcoxon rank test, the index value and EQ-VAS scores of EQ-5D-5L improved by 0.04 and 7.0 post-treatment compared with baseline respectively. The Gwet’s AC2 ranged from 0.73 to 0.97 for EQ-5D-5L dimensions while the ICC for index value and EQ-VAS were 0.71 and 0.79, respectively indicating good test-retest reliability. The effect size ranged between -0.12 to 0.60 for the index value, indicating small to moderate responsiveness, and -0.12 to 1.16 for the EQ-VAS scores, indicating moderate to large responsiveness. Moreover, the average (range) MCID value of the EQ-5D index score was 0.10-0.15. The findings showed that only the MCID to MDC ratios at the group level were clinically meaningful than individual level. Conclusion: The EQ-5D-5L instrument was able to detect changes in health and discriminate between patients with different levels of health. While group-level MCIDs were established in this study, further studies need to be done to prove its usefulness at the individual level.

Title: Travel scholarship request to attend and present at the IHEA Congress 2025 in Bali, Indonesia.
Abstract: This travel grant application seeks funding support to attend and present at the IHEA Congress 2025. The accepted presentation “Are generic preference-based measures valid for use in informal carers? A psychometric investigation“ is part of my EuroQol funded PhD project (1481-PHD).  My participation (oral presentation) in the congress is part of an organised session titled: “The Hidden Costs of Caring: Unseen Economic, Health, and Quality of Life Impacts on Informal Carers.” This is an opportunity to share the results of this study on the performance of the EQ-5D-5L in informal carers in Australia. This is the first study that evaluated the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L in Australian informal carers, and also the first that evaluated the AQoL-8D performance.  This opportunity is a unique opportunity to share our findings and hear from researchers in the field of economics of informal care.

Title: Validity and Reliability testing of the EQ-5D-Y Proxy version 1 in young children.
Abstract: One of the key foci of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and its member states is the improvement of child health globally (1)(2). As a result there has been an increase in measures to monitor child health, including Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents has increased overthe last two decades (3).HRQoL measures aim to capture the subjective multi-dimensional constructs of HRQoL namely physical, social and psychological functioning which are relevant to health (4,5). By definition, an individual’s HRQoL is subjective and should be elicited by self-report whenever possible, even from children (6). This is not always possibly as there are those who are either too young or cognitively unaware to self-report and so it is necessary to rely onproxy report (6–12). Olderchildren can provide reliable and valid responses to measures like the EQ-5D-Y (13), Paediatric Quality of Life Measure (PedsQL) (14–16), Kidscreen (17–19), KINDL and Kiddy-KINDL (20). However, for younger children below the age of 7-8 years it is necessary to rely on proxy report. The EQ-5D-Y was developed and validated for children and adolescents aged 8-18 years by an international team under the EuroQol group (13,21–24). The youth version of the instrument was derived from the EQ-5D-3L, an adult HRQoL instrument. The primary use of the EQ-5D is to support the estimation of quality adjusted life years (QALYs) for economic evaluation. In recent years a large number of treatments have been developed for paediatric conditions which has increased the need for a child specific version of the EQ-5D, with an associated economic tariff. The EQ-5D-Y, like the adult version, includesfive dimensions but hasage appropriate descriptions.The EQ-5D-Y Proxy is a direct adaptation of the EQ-5D-Y for proxy completionand is currently recommended by the EuroQoL Foundation for use in children aged 4-8 years (25).Proxy version 1requires the respondent to rate the child’s health as the proxy perceives it to be. Proxy version 1 hasbeen validated in a Spanish study in children over six years of age (26)and the performance hasbeen examined in a few studies with children older than six years (27,28). Scalone et al (2011) tested the EQ-5D-Y proxy for suitability of the domains (from the child’s perspective) on ill children and healthy childrenattending kindergarten or school from age 4-11years (29). The authors concluded thatthe domains on the current EQ-5D-Y proxy self-careand usual activities are not considered suitable for younger children between the ages of 4-5 (29). Verstraete andJelsma (2017) report that the EQ-5D-Y Proxy version was acceptable tocaregivers of ill and typically developing children and performs well in children aged four years and older,but was not appropriate for very young children(30).

Title: Comparing a new TTO method with cTTO for valuation of EQ-5D-5L health states in a general population sample
Abstract: Objectives Composite time trade-off (cTTO) often exhibits issues such as a value clustering at -1, potentially due to suboptimal valuation task design. We developed a novel TTO which uses the “pits” state as an anchor state and enables a unified TTO procedure for all health states (referred to as “pTTO”). This study aimed to test the pTTO for valuation of EQ-5D-5L health states. Methods A total of 120 members of the general public were invited to value three pairs of dominant/dominated EQ-5D-5L states using both cTTO and pTTO and the “pits” state using cTTO. We compared the pTTO with cTTO in terms of feasibility (interviewer-rated task completing difficulty), acceptability (participant-reported task experience), value distribution, logical consistency, and discriminatory ability (using the standardized response mean [SRM], an effect size measure, derived from three pairwise comparisons of states with dominant/dominated relationship). Results The pTTO demonstrated similar feasibility to cTTO but slightly lower acceptability. The pTTO values exhibited a smoother and more continuous distribution than cTTO values. Relative to the cTTO, the pTTO showed higher individual-level logical consistency rate for the pair composed of severe states (stringent criterion: 53.04% vs 17.39%; less stringent criterion: 82.61% vs 78.26%). The SRM value based on pTTO values were higher than those based on cTTO values for the pair composed of severe states (0.388 vs -0.140). Conclusions The pTTO appeared to be feasible and acceptable to value EQ-5D-5L states. The pTTO values were less clustered, more logically consistent and discriminative than the cTTO values for severe health states.

Title: Measurement properties of the EQ-5D-5L among non-small cell lung cancer patients on active treatments in China
Abstract: Background: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in China and worldwide, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for 85% of cases. In recent years, numerous innovative NSCLC drugs (e.g., targeted therapies, immune checkpoint inhibitors) have been launched. China requires economic evaluations, preferably cost-utility analysis, to inform new drug reimbursement decisions. CUA relies on health utility values, but the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D, i.e., the only preference-based measures with Chinese value sets, lack reliability and validity evidence in NSCLC populations. This study aimed to examine the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L in comparison with SF-6D in patients with NSCLC in China. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted in 19 provinces across China from October 2022 to March 2024, recruiting NSCLC patients from 20 hospitals. Demographic and clinical data were collected, and participants completed the EQ-5D-5L, SF-6D, and QLQ-C30. The measurement properties were evaluated using response patterns (ceiling/floor effects), convergent validity with the QLQ-C30, known-groups validity (gender, age, cancer stage, surgery, brain metastasis), and Shannon (H’) and evenness (J’) indices. Results: Data from 947 eligible patients were analyzed (36.4% female; mean age 61.6 years; mean duration since diagnosis 1.81 years). Sixty-four percent were stage IV, 31.4% had surgery, and 18.9% had brain metastasis. The EQ-5D-5L ceiling effect was 24.87% vs 3.39% for the SF-6D. Moderate-to-strong correlations existed between EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D and QLQ-C30 dimensions with similar constructs (ρ 0.58–0.83, all p < 0.001). Known-groups validity hypotheses based on age, cancer stage, and surgery status were validated. The EQ-5D-5L showed strongest informativity and discriminatory power in “Pain/discomfort” (H’ = 1.75, J’ = 0.75) and weakest in “Self-care” (H’ = 1.10, J’ = 0.48). For the SF-6D dimensions, the Shannon index ranged from 1.93 for “mental health” to 2.23 for “social functioning”, and the Shannon evenness index ranged from 0.83 for “mental health” to 0.96 for “social functioning”.  Conclusions: The EQ-5D-5L demonstrated robust measurement properties, supporting its use in assessing health status of Chinese patients with NSCLC. Its performance was comparable with that of the SF-6D, though the EQ-5D-5L exhibited a higher ceiling effect.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: What are the additional benefits and challenges of collecting the 25 item EQ-HWB compared to the EQ-HWB-S in care home settings?
Abstract: Background: Measuring quality of life (QoL) in older adults residing in care facilities presents unique challenges, including cognitive impairment, the applicability of generic QoL instruments, and the burden of data collection. The EQ-HWB (EQ Health and Wellbeing Instrument) is a comprehensive international measure designed to assess health, carer, and social-care-related QoL, with both a full 25-item version and a condensed 9-item version (EQ-HWB-S). However, little research has been conducted on the performance and feasibility of the EQ-HWB instruments in residential aged care settings, particularly in the UK. Research aims: This study aims to evaluate the added value of the EQ-HWB (25-item) compared to EQ-HWB-S (9-item) in measuring QoL among older adults in UK residential care facilities. Specifically, it will assess (i) whether the additional 16 items improve measurement performance; (ii) the feasibility and burden of administering the full version; and (iii) the psychometric performance of modified EQ-HWB items appearing in the 25 version only. Additionally, this research will compare EQ-HWB (25 and 9 item versions) with the Adult Social Care Outcomes Toolkit self complete version (either ASCOT-SCT4 or the recently developed ASCOT-ER(OP), easy read older person version) to examine alignment with a policy-relevant social care and wellbeing measure. Methods: The study will recruit 120-150 residents from approximately 15 UK residential care facilities, utilizing trained social care researchers for data collection. The study design includes psychometric analyses to identify potentially redundant items, examine construct validity through known-group comparisons, and assess feasibility based on completion time, missing data, and respondent burden. Further analysis will compare the EQ-HWB and self complete ASCOT-SCT/ASCOT-ER(OP) instruments (at item and utility score level); interpreting differences in scores and psychometric properties in the context of the instruments theoretical frameworks. Findings from this study will provide critical insights into the applicability of EQ-HWB in care home settings, contributing to the refinement of the instrument and informing potential policy on QoL measurement for older adults in residential care. This research directly supports EuroQol’s strategic objective to advance the EQ-HWB to ‘Approved’ status by providing empirical evidence on its validity, feasibility, and distinct value compared to its short-form and another key social care measure.

Title: Assessing the impact of COVID-19 population health over time: a cross-country comparison between US, Sweden and Norway using the EQ-5D-5L repeated measures
Abstract: Background: The outbreak of COVID-19 global pandemic hit hard on global economy. Different countries implemented various policies in response, ranging from maximum, partial, to no lockdowns. Study objectives: To assess the impact of COVID-19 on population health using the repeated surveys in Sweden and Norway, and then perform a cross-country comparison with the data from US. Proposed methods: The same survey instrument was used in all 3 countries. The US study was funded by the EuroQol Group (84-2020RA) for 3 waves of data collection. To align with US, the 1st wave data in Sweden and Norway was collected also in April, 2020, and was paid out-of-pocket by the researchers. Findings from the 1st wave had been analysed, a working paper has been developed and available at: https://ihe.se/en/publicering/covid-19-quality-of-life/. Additionally, a comparison study between the 3 countries using the 1st wave data are currently being drafted, along with two manuscripts that are under peer review. To understand the change of COVID-19 impact over time, we aim to collect another wave of data in Sweden and Norway and then compare with US. The next wave of data collection will be aligned with the 3rd wave in US post-election. Main instruments used included: the EQ-5D-5L, the Veterans RAND 12 item health Survey (VR-12), the WPAI, and the PHQ-4. Others questions included respondents’ background, social-economic status, current known COVID-19 status, behaviour changes, and employment status changes due to COVID-19 were also included in the survey.

Title: Exploring the use of the EQ-5D-Y-5L for assessing mental health of children and adolescents aged 10-18 years in China
Abstract: This project, funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation, aimed to evaluate the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L, compare its performance with the EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D, and describe the current mental health status and its influencing factors among Chinese children and adolescents with mental health issues. The study was conducted as part of the Comprehensive Health and Relevant Factors Measurement among Chinese Young Populations (CHARMING) study, a large-scale repeated cross-sectional survey.A total of 8,292 respondents aged 8–18 years were recruited from ten cities across mainland China. Mental health issues were identified using the Mental Health Scale for Children and Adolescents (MHS-CA), with 931 respondents classified as having mental health issues and 7,361 as general population controls. Measurement properties including ceiling and floor effects, internal consistency (Cronbach's α), Shannon index and evenness, convergent validity with MHS-CA, and known-groups validity were assessed for all three instruments. Multiple linear regression was employed to identify influencing factors of EQ-5D-Y-5L score differences between children with and without mental health issues.Key findings revealed that the EQ-5D-Y-5L reduced ceiling effects compared with the 3L version (34.59% vs. 59.18%), but demonstrated limited overall psychometric performance in children with mental health issues. The CHU9D showed superior information capture (mean H'=0.873) and internal consistency (α=0.782), while the EQ-5D-Y-3L exhibited the strongest known-groups validity. All three instruments showed weak convergent validity with MHS-CA. Multiple regression identified parental depressive symptoms (higher PHQ-9 scores widened the health gap, β=0.23, P0.001) and social support (having more close friends attenuated the gap, β=−1.22, P0.001) as critical determinants of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) disparities. Family environment, physical activity, sleep duration, and parental mental health were consistently identified as key discriminators across all instruments.The findings provide crucial evidence on the comparative effectiveness of generic paediatric HRQoL measures for assessing mental health and highlight the importance of family and social support interventions in improving outcomes for children and adolescents with mental health issues in China.

Title: Partnership Agreement between Kemri-Wellcome Trust Research Programme and Euroqol Research Foundation
Abstract: Kemri-Wellcome Trust Research Programme and Euroqol Research Foundation set up a collaboration agreement, to establish the necessary arrangements for a synergistic partnership between the Parties in areas of mutual interest in order to promote public health in Africa through enhancing capacity of KWTRP to address public health challenges and ultimately promote the achievement of Africa’s health and wellness goals. The scope of the collaboration between Parties consists of the following: • Develop EQ-5D-5L value sets for selected countries (Kenya and Zambia) and an EQ-5D-Y-3L value set for Nigeria • Build capacity for African researchers and policy audiences to implement the collection and use of data from EQ-5D instruments.

Title: Interviewer Administered and Self-Complete versions of EQ-5D-5L: agreement and psychometric properties
Abstract: The Interviewer-Administered (IA) version of the EQ-5D-5L was developed to enhance accessibility for respondents unable to self-complete the questionnaire due to illiteracy, low education, illness, or vision-related issues. This study examined the psychometric performance of the newly adapted IA version in Bahasa Indonesia by assessing its agreement with Self-Complete (SC) and Assisted Self-Complete (ASC) modes, along with ceiling/floor effects and test-retest reliability across literate, illiterate, and patient populations. A total of 289 respondents were recruited, comprising literate adults (n = 189), illiterate or low-literacy individuals (n = 50), and patients with either tuberculosis (TB) or type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) (n = 50). All respondents completed two EQ-5D-5L modes—IA and either SC or ASC—followed by retest administration after two to four weeks. Agreement at the item level was assessed using Gwet’s AC2, while intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) evaluated EQ-VAS and utility scores. Across all groups and dimensions, the IA version exhibited a consistent ceiling effect but no floor effect. The IA version demonstrated high agreement with SC/ASC versions at the dimension level, with Gwet’s AC2 values ranging from 0.86 to 1.00 in most domains and populations. However, notable variations emerged in agreement for the EQ VAS and utility scores. For instance, the ICC for EQ VAS was excellent among TB patients (0.91) but poor among illiterate respondents (0.08). Utility scores similarly varied, with ICCs ranging from 0.12 in the illiterate group to 0.90 among TB patients. Test-retest reliability of the IA version also revealed strong performance at the domain level, with Gwet’s AC2 indicating almost perfect agreement in most cases. However, EQ VAS and utility scores again showed variation, where TB patients displayed the highest ICC values for test-retest reliability (0.77 and 0.87 for EQ VAS and utility, respectively), while illiterate respondents had the lowest (0.29 and 0.07, respectively). These findings suggest that the IA version of EQ-5D-5L is a viable alternative to self-complete modes for populations with limited literacy or physical constraints, particularly in LMIC settings such as Indonesia.

Title: Designing Visually Enhanced Anchoring Vignettes to Address Reporting Heterogeneity in EQ-5D Dimensions and EQ-VAS
Abstract: Comparison of EuroQol instruments of health outcomes across populations defined by clinical, demographic or socioeconomic characteristics is potentially confounded by reporting heterogeneity (RH), stemming from variations in respondents' reference points, perceptions, and biases. The anchoring vignette method can identify and adjust for RH, but its application to EuroQol instruments remains limited. Moreover, the validity of the method depends on two assumptions—Vignette Equivalence (VE) and Response Consistency (RC)—for which empirical support is mixed. This project will both extend application of the method to EuroQol instruments and investigate whether its validity is improved by presenting vignettes in visually enhanced formats, rather than text, with the aim of reducing variability in interpretation and aligning reporting styles. An experiment, employing within- and between-subject designs, will evaluate validity of the VE and RC assumptions with visual and text-only vignette presentations. Visual vignettes will be created using innovative AI tools, facilitating flexibility and broad applicability. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses will assess assumption validity. The experiment data will be used to expand knowledge on the nature and drivers of RH. This project aims to improve comparability of measures derived from EuroQol instruments – such as EQ-5D and EQ-VAS -and develop better-performing vignette designs that can be used, with EuroQol instruments, in health surveys.

Title: Health-Related Quality-of-life of the Pregnant and Postpartum Women during the COVID-19 Pandemic (Phase I)
Abstract: Since initial transmission of a novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV, or SARS-CoV-2) in December 2019, there have been over 78 million cases of COVID-19 and more than 1.7 million deaths worldwide. Nearly one-quarter of COVID-19 cases have been diagnosed in the US. In addition to the direct impacts of COVID-19 on morbidity and mortality, mitigation strategies to promote social distancing have disrupted standard healthcare in the US. Pregnant and postpartum healthcare delivery have been particularly impacted by these measures. These disruptions are likely to have adversely impacted maternal health. Although previous research has documented the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on mental health, limited data have documented the physical impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on maternal health and few studies have documented perceptions of prenatal and postpartum care. Through quantitative and qualitative data collection, this study will collect information on the experiences of pregnant women during the COVID-19 pandemic and how these experiences may influence health-related quality of life (as measured by the EQ-5D-5L instrument). Funding sought by this application would support baseline data collection for a web-based panel survey of 3,600 US pregnant and postpartum women. Results will inform the maternal health impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and the healthcare needs of families post-pandemic.

Title: Translation of EQ-HWB-9 10 most commonly requested languages
Abstract: Background and aim: The EQ Health and Wellbeing 9 is a new instrument that has undergone modification and testing with the aim to move from the current experimental status to approved effective status. Approved versions of any instrument require formal linguistic review and translation by translation agencies based on the appropriate forward and back translation (FT and BT) and cognitive debriefing with ranking exercise and proofreading. This project aims to support the translation of the ten most commonly requested languages for adult EQ instruments to prepare for the launch of the approved version. A secondary aim is to support researcher-led translations.  Methods: The ten most commonly requested languages (English - UK, USA, Australia, Canada; Spanish - Spain, USA; German, Simplified Chinese, French, Italian) have been identified by the Version Management Committee (VMC). An ISO-certified translation agency will be engaged to undertake formal translation of the finalised descriptive system of the EQ-HWB-9. In each language, linguistic review or translation will cover the self-complete (SC), interviewer-administered version (IA) and proxy 1 (P1). The initial translation will be for an English UK version which will be used as the source version for the other 9 languages. Available formally translated language versions will undergo linguistic review without FT and BT subject to there being no changes in the English source version, otherwise, full translation will be required. Cognitive debriefing will be undertaken with 8 participants (aged 18+, mixed gender and different socio-demographic strata and health conditions). VMC reviewers will support the translation process by reviewing reports from the translation agency at each stage of the translation.  Researcher-led translations will continue to be supported for languages that are not available. Researchers will undertake translations using EQ translation guides and processes developed by the VMC. This involves FT and BT, CD including ranking exercise and reporting on the findings including populating templates. VMC reviewers will undertake a light review of the results of the researcher-led translations before approval for use by the VMC liaison.  Outcome: Approved translations will be available for the EQ-HWB-9 for the ten most commonly requested languages with three modes of administration (SC, IA, P1) of each translation for the launch of the instrument.

Title: A study to evaluate the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox cognition items in Parkinson’s disease: content validity and psychometric testing
Abstract: Background:EuroQol has developed a global cognition bolt‑on for the EQ‑5D‑5L, alongside multiple exploratory cognition subdimension items (e.g., memory, concentration, decision making), which are now part of the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. Parkinson’s disease (PD)—a condition with heterogeneous cognitive profiles and frequent proxy reporting—is a well-suited population to psychometrically test these items including alternative item wordings, global, subdimension and composite cognition bolt-on items versions and potential overlaps with existing EQ‑5D dimensions (e.g., usual activities, anxiety/depression).Objectives:(1) Evaluate the content validity of the global cognition item from the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox and seven additional cognition items from the ‘exploratory’ Toolbox in PD via interviews with patients, caregivers, and clinicians; (2) evaluate the convergent validity, known‑group validity, test–retest reliability, responsiveness, and proxy–patient agreement.Methods:Mixed‑methods. Qualitative cognitive interviews with ~10 patients, ~7 caregivers, and ~7 clinicians following EuroQol topic guide. Quantitative prospective cohort of ~200 PD patient-proxy dyads (patients + their family members) at a tertiary hospital in China (baseline + 3 months follow-up). Measures: EQ‑5D‑5L (with EQ VAS), EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox (global cognition item and seven exploratory cognition items), the cognition items of Parkinson’s Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ‑39), Movement Disorder Society–Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS‑UPDRS), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox cognition items are currently being translated to Simplified Chinese under VMC oversight as part of EQ project 2183-RA (PI Xu) and will be available by the start of this project.Findings will provide evidence on the content validity and psychometric performance of cognition bolt-on items in Parkinson’s disease, informing the final selection of cognition bolt-ons for the EQ-5D.

Title: Developing Quality Adjusted Life Years Value Set for Kenya
Abstract: Kenya’s recent health financing reforms necessitate locally relevant health economic evidence to inform evidence-based decision-making processes in healthcare. This study developed Kenya's first EQ5D5L value set, based on the health preferences of its own population, to support economic evaluation and priority setting in healthcare.The study targeted a sample of 1,100 participants who were aged 18 or over, consented to participate, and were proficient in English or Swahili. A stratified random sampling approach selected 10 counties for a nationally representative sample. Data were gathered through computer-assisted, face-to-face interviews using laptops running EuroQol Portable Valuation Technology (EQ-PVT) software version 2.1.  Each respondent completed 10 cTTO and 12 DCE tasks. A cyclic quality-control process was conducted throughout fieldwork.Nine models were estimated, including hybrid models that account for left censoring at full health and for heteroskedasticity. A hybrid heteroskedastic Tobit model was selected as the final value set on the basis of logical consistency, statistical significance, and goodness-of-fit. The final model produced logically ordered and significant disutility coefficients for all levels. Based on the model reported in a manuscript currently under review, the predicted utility for full health (11111) was anchored at 1.00, while the worst state (55555) yielded a utility of -0.532. Pain/discomfort level 5 had the largest decrement (0.361), followed by mobility (0.347). Of the predicted 3,125 values of the EQ-5D-5L, 8.54% had negative values. Scatterplots confirmed strong agreement between observed and predicted values, supporting model validity.This is Kenya's first nationally representative EQ-5D-5L value set. The set provides a locally grounded input for cost-effectiveness analysis and strengthens the evidence base for health priority-setting in Kenya.

Title: Attendance at ISPOR Europe 2025 to deliver podium presentation “P18: Mixed-Method Exploration of VAS Variations to Measure Health, Social Care, and Carer-Related QoL”
Abstract: A presentation entitled Mixed-Method Exploration of Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) Variations to Measure Health, Social Care, and Carer Related Quality of Life was delivered on November 10th, 2025 as part of the programming for the 2025 ISPOR Europe Annual Meeting in Glasgow, Scottland. The presentation was part of a moderated session entitled "Incorporating Patients' Perspectives in HTA" with three other research presentations. The presentation lasted approximately 12 minutes with 3 minutes for questions from the audience. The presentation was attended by approximately 40 people and was also recorded for future viewing within the digital conference portal. The presentation showcased results from prior research into how the choice of VAS constructs and recall periods influence respondent comprehension of a VAS presented in conjunction with the EQ-HWB. This dissemination was important to highlight the ongoing development of the EQ-HWB, bring awareness to the instrument, and highlight usefulness of a potential VAS with the measure.

Title: Does EQ-5D cover the most undesirable health problems in different cultures? A study of seven countries using a mixed methods
Abstract: The research team conducted semi-structured interviews face-to-face and via Zooms with lay persons in seven countries including Argentina, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Netherlands, and Spain. Trained interviewers used a pre-tested interview guide to elicit important dimensions or concepts as characteristics of poor health and asked interviewees to nominate the five most important health dimensions using a card sorting exercise. The interviews were transcribed, translated into English, and pooled for thematic and frequency analysis. We found that the EQ-5D health dimensions were cross-culturally considered as the most important aspects for describing poor health. The study provides support for the idea that EQ-5D covers aspects of poor health which are broadly relevant to people in a range of geographical and cultural settings. This should give confidence to users who may have concerns about the fact that it was initially developed by researchers in Europe over 30 years ago.

Title: Understanding the relationship between health behaviors, attitudes and perceptions of HRQL using the EQ-5D
Abstract: Background: Strategies to improve public health may benefit from targeting specificlifestyles associated with poor health behaviors and outcomes. The aim of this studywas to characterize and examine the relationship between health and lifestyle-relatedattitudes (HLAs) and self-rated health and life-satisfaction.Methods: Secondary analyses were conducted on data from a 2012 communitywellness survey in Kirklees, UK. Using a validated HLA tool, respondents (n=9,130)were categorized into 5 segments: health conscious realists (33%), balancedcompensators (14%), live-for-todays (18%), hedonistic immortals (10%), andunconfident fatalists (25%). Multivariate regression was used to examine whetherHLAs could explain self-rated health (personal score) using the EQ-5D visual analogscale (EQ-VAS), the gap between personal and EQ-5D societal weighted score(societal score), and life-satisfaction. Health conscious realists served as the referencegroup.Results: Adjusted analyses found significant differences in the self-rating of health byHLA, with lowest mean EQ-VAS scores among unconfident fatalists (-9.0, 95% CI -9.9,-8.2) and live-for-todays (-2.0, 95%CI -2.8, -1.1). Unconfident fatalists had a largernegative difference between personal and societal scores (-0.027, 95% CI -0.017, -0.038), and were most likely to have low life-satisfaction (OR: 3.51, 95% CI 2.92, 4.23).Significance: Segmentation by HLA explains differences in self-rated health and life-satisfaction, with unconfident fatalists being a distinct segment with significantly worsehealth perceptions and life-satisfaction. In addition to informing conceptual frameworksof health, targeted health promotion efforts may benefit from considering the HLAsegment that predominates a patient group, especially unconfident fatalists, an areawhere further research is needed.

Title: Conceptual challenges in the valuation of health in children and adolescents
Abstract: Conceptually, the valuation of health states in children raises several questions, including: 1. Source: Whose preferences should be elicited? (adults, children, both?) 2. Perspective: Whose health should be valued? (self today, self as a child, own child, hypothetical child, etc.) If a child health perspective is taken, how should the age of the child be described, if at all? 3. Methods: How should be preferences be elicited and anchored? (TTO, DCE, etc.) Are there conceptual reasons why health state selection methods in a child health valuation study should differ from those for an adult health valuation study? This proposed project aims to study key conceptual issues in the valuation of health in children. This will be done via a combination of desk research, meetings to exchange/discuss ideas, and an expert workshop. It will contribute to the current debate and support the EuroQol Group in interpreting (and potentially expanding) its research agenda in this area. While several EuroQol-funded empirical studies in this area are likely to show how the choice of approach influences the outcomes of health state valuation, they are unlikely to provide a clear indication about which approach to prefer. The question of which approach to choose would then shift from an empirical one to a normative one, and our proposed research will provide insights into how such a question can be answered. The project is intended to be a collaboration between early career researchers who are actively working on EQ-5D-Y and conceptual issues in health state valuation research.

Title: Is there a need for bolt-on itching and fatigue beyond pain and discomfort? Empirical evidence to demonstrate whether specific symptoms are contained within the broader pain/discomfort dimension and development of a standard approach to reject/confirm a b
Abstract: Abstract of researchStudy aims:This study aims to investigate whether twospecific aspects of ‘discomfort’which are relevant to the patient groupinvestigated (itching, fatigue)are contained within/covered bythe broader EQ5D-5L pain/discomfort dimension. Secondly, wewilldevelop a standard approach to reject/confirm a bolt-in status.Data source:Pain, itching and fatigue are threecommonly reported symptoms among burn patients. Our research group may useexisting data from a large clinical survey in a nation-wide cohort of burn patients(self-assessment).The survey containsthe EQ-5D-5L and many additionaldescriptive items, including painand itchingon a VASof 1 (no pain/itch) to 10 (extreme pain/itch)andfatigue. Methods:First, we will assess to what extent variability in pain, itching and fatigue are captured by the EQ pain/discomfort dimension. Thenwe assess whatis, in a descriptive sense, the quantitative overlap (separately) of pain, itching and/or fatigue scores with the EQ-5D pain/discomfort dimension(regression methods).Subsequently,we determinethediscriminatory power of the EQ-5D-5L with and without the more specific pain and/or itching and/or fatigue items (recoded into five categories). Then, the redundancies with existing EQ-5D dimensions, notably pain/discomfort,will bedemonstrated using multiple methods, including dominance/dependence tables.Next, we explain variance in outcome(EQ-VAS), measured in severe burn patients by the EQ-5D5Lalone, to which pain, itching and fatigue data are added.Lastly,we will investigate towhat extent the addition of itching, pain and/or fatigue items (applying a plausible set of hypothetical valuation functions)influence rank orderings within burn severity groups.

Title: Valuing Health-Related Quality of Life: Developing an EQ-5D-5L Value Set for Ghana
Abstract: Introduction: The Ghanaian Ministry of Health and other stakeholders of health have initiated the process of requiring Health Technology Assessment (HTA) as a formal process for priority setting in Ghana. Progress made include an HTA pilot study, establishment of an HTA working group and development of a reference case to guide the conduct of economic evaluation as part of the HTA guidelines, which recommends the conduct of cost-utility analysis for health technologies using outcomes that include quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). There is no national value set available for the Ghanaian population to be used in estimating QALYs. The institutionalization and rise of HTA in the country necessitate that a value set be developed to allow estimation of QALYs to support HTA. This study therefore aimed to develop a value set for Ghana by eliciting Ghanaian general preferences using the EQ-5D-5L instrument. Methods: The study collected face-to-face preference data from 300 adult participants across three regions of Ghana using the adapted version of the EuroQol valuation technology (EQ-VT) standardised valuation protocol developed specifically for EQ-5D-5L valuation studies using composite time trade-off (cTTO) and discrete-choice experiments (DCEs). Additional qualitative data was collected to explore the ‘worse than death’ hypothesis to understand the contextual ‘value of life’ in Ghana and factors influencing respondents’ decision to opt to die rather than live in a particular health state. Different preference models were generated using both the cTTO and DCE data, either individually or together to provide complementary results on respondents’ utility preferences. Models explored were generalised least squares, Tobit, heteroskedastic, logit and hybrid. The best fitting model was selected for the value set based on its ability to account for the left censored and heteroscedasticity that was a feature of the data collected, logical consistency and on the statistical significance of the parameters. Inductive thematic analysis was used to analyse the qualitative data. Results: The 300 interviews provided 4500 cTTO responses and 4200 DCE responses. The demographic characteristics of respondents were representative of the Ghanaian population for religious background, level of education and marital status. It was not representative of the distribution of gender in Ghana. The preferred model chosen for the Ghana value set was Hybrid Tobit, random effect heteroscedastic, constrained model. The predicted value for the worst attainable health on the EQ-5D-5L (i.e. health state 55555) was -0.493 and that of the best health state (11112; except full health) was 0.969. The largest decrement was registered for level 5 mobility (0.369) followed by pain/discomfort (0.312), self-care (0.273), anxiety/depression (0.271) and usual activities (0.268). Findings from the qualitative study showed that health states perceived as ‘worse than death’ were those associated with impairment in mobility and anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort. Respondents preferred death under these circumstances because they wanted to avoid the financial burden on themselves and family, time spent in care giving by family, loss of personhood and loss of social status. Health and wellbeing were perceived as absence of illness and access to food. Conclusion: This is the first Ghanaian EQ-5D-5L value set based on social preference derived for a nationally representative sample in Ghana. The value set will play a key role in the institutionalization of HTA in Ghana and the use of economic evaluation studies to inform priority setting where different health technologies can be compared. The HTA working group has welcomed the findings of this study and have suggested dissemination to the broader stakeholders of health through a seminar or workshop.

Title: Advancing the interpretation and policy relevance of EQ-5D outcomes through methodological and empirical insights
Abstract: This project successfully disseminated new evidence on the interpretation, responsiveness, and cross-regional comparability of EQ-5D outcomes at the ISPOR Europe 2025 conference in Glasgow, United Kingdom. Two presentations were delivered. The first, an oral podium presentation titled "Exploring Variability in EQ VAS Scores: A Systematic Review and Meta-regression of Population Health Studies", identified that comorbidity prevalence and regional differences are key drivers of variability in EQ VAS scores. This has implications for cross-country comparisons and health system benchmarking. The second, a poster presentation titled "Differential Responsiveness and Minimally Important Difference of EQ-5D: Truth or Artefact?", presented results from a spine surgery registry study. This analysis highlighted significant methodological challenges in estimating Minimally Important Differences (MIDs), including the impact of response shift and baseline severity effects. The project engaged with health economists, clinicians, and policy-makers to discuss how these methodological advances can strengthen the application of EQ-5D in value-based healthcare and global health policy.

Title: The impact of COVID-19 on health status, based on the EQ-5D-5L, of adults visiting emergency departments and primary care clinics in Alberta, Canada
Abstract: **Background**: COVID-19 is placing a significant burden on individuals’ physical, mental, and social functioning. As such, it is imperative to explore the impact of this pandemic on the health-related quality of life (HRQL) of populations to inform public health policies and strategies. **Aims**: This proposed study aims to - Examine the impact of COVID-19 on health-related quality of life (HRQL), including physical and mental aspects of health, as measured by the EQ-5D-5L, of adults visiting emergency departments and primary care clinics in the province of Alberta. - Explore whether the impact of COVID-19 is disproportionate in certain groups of the population based on socio-demographic data and deprivation, and as such, identify the most adversely affected groups in this population. **Methods**: We will use data from two on-going large-scale surveys from health service users that have been conducted by the Health Quality Council of Alberta for several years; as such, these surveys will provide data “before”, “during”, and “after” COVID-19. EQ-5D-5L dimension level data and EQ-index and VAS scores before, during and after COVID-19 will be examined in the overall samples, and by population sub-groups to identify the most affected groups of the patient population. **Implications**: This study will provide evidence on the impact of COVID-19 on HRQL trends in adults with various health conditions. Quantifying this impact and identifying the most affected groups in the population will inform public health policies and strategies to alleviate the detrimental consequences of COVID-19 on population health status.

Title: Methods for development of a generic descriptive system
Abstract: Background: Hundreds of standardised instruments have been developed to measure health-related quality of life and health status, with a range of approaches used in the development. The EuroQol Group are currently exploring the potential for developing a new descriptive system. A key part of the process of this development will require the selection of items for inclusion in the instrument. Various methods for item selection are available and the Group will need to decide which to adopt in the development of any future EQ instrument. The aim of this study was to provide a contemporary overview of methods recommended in guidelines for item selection in instrument development and methods used by instrument developers. Method:A focused review of key standards and guidelines was used to identify recommended methods and psychometric evaluations. A systematic review of the literature was conducted to identify the methods actually used in empirical studies reporting development processes of descriptive systems and any additional methods not included in the guidelines. The search was conducted using COSMIN’s precise search filter for measurement properties, restricted to include health related quality of life studies and focusing on development of descriptive systems, and a total of 553 abstracts were identified. Supplementary searches were conducted by reviewing bibliographies and citations of the included studies to identify complete set of articles on development of the descriptive system where possible.Results: A total ofeleven guidance documents were consulted and a data extraction template was created. A total of 61 full text articles were included. Item generation involved three approaches: developing items de novo, identifying items from several existing measures or using a single measure to derive a short form measure. Item selection was determined by the instrument developers in few cases, but most reported use of empirical work. The guidelines describe two development phases after item generation: pretesting and field-testing of questionnaire but this was not always followed. Some studies determined items based on relevance and importance, assessed from interviews and rating studies. The most common approach was to apply statistical analyses to datasets containing completed questionnaires. Three general types of statistical models were applied: regression analysis, factor analytic techniques and item response theory models. These measurement models were used to establish construct validity, however in most cases further hypothesis testing was carried out to assess known group, convergent and divergent validity. The majority used a combination of statistical methods; with exploratory factor analysis and item response theory being the most common. Psychometric criteriaincluded descriptive statistics of the responses such as missing values, range and distribution of responses and internal consistency.Discussion: The methods used to identify items were similar across studies but differed considerably for item selection.Construct validity and internal consistency was assessed in most of the studies, but few instrument developers relied completely on content validity. Few of the statistical methods identified are interchangeable in terms of purpose, but may generate very different instruments. The developers seldom explained why one statistical model was chosen over another

Title: Investigating response heterogeneity in the EQ-5D
Abstract: Systematic differences in the ways that individuals interpret response categories may introduce bias when analysing self-reports to compare health or quality-of-life measures across heterogeneous patient and population groups. Inter-group comparisons using these self-reported measures which experience such variation may bring into question any resulting findings. Self-reported health measures can also be affected by response style; a respondent’s tendency to systematically respond to questionnaire items in a given way regardless of item content. Given the increased interest in the routine collection of self-reported health measures, such as the EQ-5D in PROMs programmes, registries, cohort studies and national surveys, there is value in understanding whether, and to what extent, the EQ-5D suffers from such response heterogeneity/bias. Moreover, such biases may vary widely across response items from the same individual, due to question wording, for example. This study developed open-source Julia package (MIOP.jl), which we have applied to the Multi-Instrument Comparison (MIC) data to evaluate response heterogeneity. The package MIOP.jl has been designed to estimate extensions of the generic inflation model, which consists of a single binary splitting equation – which in this context corresponds to mis-reporting – and then both inflation (into one, all, or a subset of the observed outcomes) and true health equation. In this way, the approach allows observed outcomes to arise from two sources: mis-reported and true. This nests the usual zero-and middle-inflated ordered probit models. These can be estimated on both cross-sectional and/or longitudinal data. Importantly such a range of bespoke models is not currently available in any other statistical software. In developing the package and applying it to the MIC data we are able to showcase the use of open-source software to explore response heterogeneity in EQ-5D self-reports.

Title: A qualitative study on respondent’s interpretation of the EQ-VAS in Ethiopia
Abstract: This study explored how the general public and people with physical/mental health problems use and interpret the EQ-VAS in a low-income country setting (Ethiopia). In-depth interviews were conducted with 15 individuals from the general public and 30 from a hospital setting, evenly split between physical (heart failure and/or hypertension) and mental health conditions (anxiety and/or depression). Separate content analyses were conducted for each participant group. The findings from each of the three participant groups were then compared using cross-case analysis. Key findings were categorised into four codes, exploring views towards (1) ease of completion, (2) interpretation of health, (3) representation of a meaningful change on the 0-100 scale, and (4) understanding of best/worst imaginable health states. The majority of the general public found completing the EQ-VAS challenging due to lack of explanations for the scale’s numbers. In contrast, the majority of participants with a health condition found it straightforward. General public often used past health as a benchmark and referred to past health conditions, work capacity, and social interaction, while those with physical or mental health problems focused on their current health and use of medication. Respondents suggested using 5- or 10-point hash marks over the current 1-point, which also reflected respondents’ interpretation of a meaningful change on the EQ-VAS. Participants with a physical health problem found that a change in health would correspond to a 5-point change on EQ-VAS, while those with a mental health problem suggested a 10-point change. The best health state for the general public involves being disease-free, financially stable, in full health, and having a healthy family. Individuals with physical and mental health problems often interpret it as full health or stable income, capability to work, and having a happier, pain- or disease-free life. The worst imaginable health state for the general public included being severely sick or having mental health problems. Those with cardiovascular issues often saw it as being bedridden, while individuals with mental health problems interpreted it as being unconscious. Achieving the best health state was considered unattainable by a few participants, with death infrequently mentioned as the worst imaginable health state. This study provided further evidence related to the interpretation of the EQ-VAS and underscores the necessity for explanations of numbers. Further quantitative research is needed to examine what denotes a meaningful change in EQ-VAS across different disease areas.

Title: Applying for travel scholarship to attend the 2025 ISPOR Europe Meeting: Country-related differential item functioning in the EQ-5D-5L: Insights from the EuroQol Data Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE)
Abstract: This proposal seeks support to disseminate findings at ISPOR Europe 2025 on country-related differential item functioning (DIF) in the EQ-5D-5L. I presented a poster titled “Country-related differential item functioning in the EQ-5D-5L: Insights from the EuroQol Data Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE)”. This work used the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset and a logistic regression framework to evaluate country-related DIF in the EQ-5D-5L. The analysis showed minimal DIF among countries sharing the same or similar languages but identified meaningful DIF across countries with different linguistic and cultural contexts, particularly in the mobility, self-care, and usual activities dimensions. These findings enhance understanding of how contextual factors may affect the comparability of EQ-5D outcomes and guide the planned analyses examining DIF across other instruments in the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset, including EQ-HWB and PROMIS-10. The feedback received from HTA bodies, researchers, industry stakeholders, and EuroQol members will further inform the next phase of multi-instrument DIF analyses. In addition, I delivered a podium presentation on behalf of my colleague Thao Nguyen on “Comparative Performance of the EQ-5D-5L and PROMIS-10 in the Elderly: Data From the EQ-DAPHNIE Project in Five Countries”  further contributing to the dissemination of research on instrument performance and applications of the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset. Overall, this travel support will foster knowledge exchange, international collaboration, visibility of research on EQ-5D instruments, and reflection on next research steps.

Title: Population norms and inequalities based on EQ-5D-5L general population surveys (POPS 2 Project)
Abstract: Populationnorms and inequalities based on EQ-5D-5L general public surveys (POPS 2 Project)One factor associated with the success ofthe EQ-5D instrument has been the ease of constructingcomparable international datasets, partlydue to the existence of user guides and standards of analysis. A book summarizing results from international EQ-5D-3L general population surveys on self-reportedhealth (“Self-Reported Population Health: An International Perspective based on EQ-5D”) continues to be in very high demand and has been downloaded over 50,000 timessince publication in 2014.A new edition of this book is necessary for a number of reasons. First, new population datasets have become available based on the EQ-5D-5L,including countries hitherto not being represented, including countries outside of Europe. These data were usually collected under higher quality control. Second, the selection of indicators (both economic and epidemiological) was elementary, where some amendments weremade due torecent guiding sources. The aim of the current proposal is to produce a new edition of population health data, including norms and inequality indicators based on EQ-5D-5L surveys conducted in representative samples of general populations. Specifically, the following are the key objectives:1)Identify EQ-5D-5L datasets from general population surveys. Create a database archive using standardized structure2)Generate EQ-5D-5L population norms3)Generate inequality indicators, both fromepidemiological and economic origin4)Make cross-country comparison of EQ-5D-5L population dataOutputs of the project will support future research activities of the EuroQol Group’s Health Inequalities Special Interest Group, such as future in-depth analyses of health inequalities using the dataset archive.The project would also have implications for other working Groups, such as the Valuation and the Education & Outreach Working Groups.

Title: Evaluating Performance of the Experimental EQ-TIPS (V3) for Assessing Infants and Toddlers with Acute Infections: A Mixed-Methods Approach of Cognitive Debriefing and Psychometric Testing
Abstract: This report summarizes the completed work done at the ISPOR Europe 2025 Conference from 9 to 12 November in Glasgow. The purpose of the travel scholarship grant is to support the dissemination of research findings through a poster presentation at the ISPOR Europe 2025 Conference.The following is the abstract accepted for poster presentation. This study is part of a EuroQol-funded multi-country research project (1928-RA). Objectives:The EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) was developed to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children aged 0–3 years. While the earlier 6-item,  3-level EQ-TIPS (V2) has been tested, the experimental 7-item version (V3) with 3- or 5-level response scales (EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L) has not yet been evaluated. This study assessed the updated experimental EQ-TIPS among caregivers of infants and toddlers with acute infections in Singapore. Methods:We used a mixed-methods design, comprising cognitive interviews and psychometric testing. Primary caregivers of children participated in interviews exploring clarity, comprehensiveness, and interpretation of EQ-TIPS items and the visual analogue scale (VAS), which were then analysed thematically. For psychometric testing, caregivers of children with acute infections such as rhinorrhoea or tachypnoea were recruited from a tertiary hospital’s emergency department.  At baseline, caregivers completed EQ-TIPS-3L, EQ-TIPS-5L, and PedsQL to assess ceiling and floor effects, as well as convergent validity. Two weeks later, follow-up assessments were conducted via Zoom to evaluate responsiveness to clinical change using standardized response means (SRM) of EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L level sum scores (LSS).Results:Caregivers (n=10) found EQ-TIPS acceptable, relevant, and easy to complete, although some ambiguity was noted in emotion and sleep items, with suggestions to extend the recall period and simplify the VAS. For the data from 77 caregivers of children (40 reassessed), ceiling effects (1111111) were 28.6% (3L) and 16.9% (5L), while floor effects were 0%. Both versions demonstrated strong convergent validity (ρ = 0.71). At follow-up, large SRMs among caregivers reporting HRQoL improvements indicated good responsiveness: –0.82 (EQ-TIPS-3L LSS), –0.81 (EQ-TIPS-5L LSS), and 1.47 (VAS). Conclusion:Both EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L demonstrated good content and construct validity, as well as responsiveness to recovery, for assessing acutely ill young children. Despite some item ambiguity, findings support their use in evaluating HRQoL in this population.

Title: ’Equimetrics’ of the EQ-5D. Measuring inequalities in health in the UK, Netherlands, and Italy to assess the potential of the EQ-5D-3L and 5L as outcome measures and determinants of income inequality
Abstract: Background: In datasets used for health inequality analysis, the selected indicators tend to have been used for decades: functional limitations, disabilities, and a simple subjective health evaluation. Little attention has been paid to consequences of using 'self-rated health' as an indicator to assess inequalities in health. Aims: The Equimetrics Project aimed to explore the potential of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L as outcome measures in health inequality analysis. We determined if there were differences in health status by country and by socio-economic status (SES) and by other stratifiers, such as gender and chronic disease status. We also compared the performance of the EQ-5D-3L and 5L in health inequality analysis. Methods: Data were collected from a multi-country cohort using a web-based survey that was administered to members of the general public aged 18 to 75 years from three European countries (United Kingdom (UK), Italy and the Netherlands). The survey included questions on sociodemographics, chronic disease and the EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, EQ VAS, QOLIBRI-OS. We compared health-related quality of life (HRQL) across strata, such as SES, country, gender and disease groups, but also across measures (EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, EQ VAS, QOLIBRI-OS). In addition, we calculated the slope index of inequality and relative index of inequality by country and by measure. Results: In total, 10,172 respondents completed the survey. Of these, 4,119 respondents were from the UK, 3,026 were from Italy and 3,027 were from the Netherlands. For each measure (EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L , EQ VAS and QOLJBRI-OS), HRQL was best for respondents from Italy and worst for respondents from the UK. Across countries, the UK had highest inequality with worse HRQL among those with a lower educational level and best HRQL among those with a high educational level, both for the total sample and stratified by gender. We observed the lowest inequality among respondents from Italy. For the EQ VAS and QOLIBRI-OS, country, gender and educational level patterns were mixed. The EQ-5D-5L outperformed the EQ-5D-3L in terms of ceilings (higher for EQ-5D-3L versus EQ-5D-5L) and absolute informativity. Conclusions: With regards to inequality analysis, the EQ-5D-5L showed larger contrasts compared to the EQ-5D-3L. However, these contrasts were smaller than expected. Most importantly, our study showed that EQ-5D instruments are suitable for assessing health inequalities in general population samples.

Title: Travel scholarship application to attend ISPOR Europe 2025
Abstract: This project successfully shared new evidence on how EQ-5D-5L value sets differ across regions and methods at ISPOR Europe 2025 in Glasgow, United Kingdom. I presented two posters. The first, “Beyond the Mean: Do Distribution-Based Metrics Offer Greater Insight into Predictors of Societal Health Preferences?”, examined 42 EQ-5D-5L value sets and showed that looking only at the mean hides important distributional patterns. Indicators like the IQR and pits state value performed better in explaining variability, and both EQ-VT version and region consistently influenced value-set characteristics. This reinforces that central tendency alone is not enough when comparing societal preferences. The second, “How Far Have We Come with EQ-5D-5L Value Sets? An Updated Systematic Literature Review of 55 Valuation Studies”, highlighted how rapidly the evidence base has grown. Value sets now span all major world regions, with strong growth in LMICs. The review also found clear methodological shifts towards hybrid valuation, wider use of EQ-VT 2 and above, and more advanced modelling approaches. Through these two presentations, I had the opportunity to speak with health economists, valuation experts, and HTA stakeholders about how these methodological developments can improve the interpretability, comparability, and policy usefulness of EQ-5D-5L value sets globally.

Title: Travel scholarship request to attend ISPOR Europe 2025 for findings dissemination
Abstract: I presented 3 posters at the ISPOR Europe 2025 Conference which was held between 9 and 12 November 2025, in Glasgow.My first study, “Assessing the Psychometric Performance of the Experimental EQ-TIPS (v2.0) in assessing the health-related quality of life of Stunted Children in Laos” [MSR41] assessed the known-groups validity and responsiveness of EQ-TIPS (v2.0) among 100 stunted children’s caregivers visiting emergency department in Laos. The second study, “Assessing known-groups and convergent validity of the EQ-5D-5L in assessing the health-related quality of life of individuals with obesity who have and have not received bariatric surgery” [MSR40] evaluated the known-groups and convergent validity of EQ-5D-5L among 82 patients with obesity who have not received bariatric surgery and 79 patients who have received bariatric surgery in Singapore. The third study, “Comparing Health-Related Quality of Life in Obese Patients With and Without Bariatric Surgery: A Cross-Sectional Study in a Multi-Ethnic Asian Population in Singapore” [PCR49] compared the health-related quality of life in a sample of obese patients who have and have not received bariatric surgery in Singapore using EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9.

Title: Validation of multiple EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox bolt-ons in older adults in China
Abstract: The EQ-5D instruments were designed as generic measures applicable across diverse health conditions and populations. Although they capture key aspects of health-related quality of life (HRQoL), they may not reflect all relevant impacts or improvements in specific groups. This limitation has prompted growing interest in extending the EQ-5D descriptive system by adding dimensions and items, known as EQ-5D bolt-ons. An experimental version of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox has been developed for the EQ-5D-5L to supplement measurement in specific clinical contexts. Given its experimental nature, psychometric testing is required.This project addresses the DSWG’s priorities in the latest call for proposals by testing the psychometric performance of multiple EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox items (including fatigue, hearing, sleep, vision, and an earlier versions of the cognition bolt-on) in older adults in China, and by generating evidence to support the further development of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox—particularly the cognition bolt-ons.The proposal builds on a piggyback data collection opportunity, incorporating the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-on items into the Early Dementia and Depression Screening Project for Adults Aged 65 and Older in Nanjing City, China, conducted by the Nanjing CDC. The survey employs a multistage, stratified cluster random sampling strategy, covering 12,000 adults aged 65 years and above from 12 districts (1,000 respondents per district) in Nanjing. The survey also includes the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), AD8 Dementia Screening Interview, PHQ-9, and self-reported questions on chronic conditions, sleep problems, and physical activity. The survey, including EQ-5D-5L and bolt-on items, are administered via face-to-face interviews. Data collection commenced in June 2025 and is expected to be completed by the end of 2025.We will conduct psychometric analyses of multiple EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox items in older adults in China, examining ceiling effects, divergent and convergent validity, known-group validity, and explanatory power, for individual items, and in combination and with EQ-5D-5L. We will further validate several alternative cognition bolt-ons from the Toolbox using analyses such as known-group validity testing, confirmatory factor analysis, principal component analysis, and uniform and non-uniform differential item functioning (DIF).As of end of Sep 2025, data has been collected for over 10,00 participants. We will provide timely evidence on the validity of multiple EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox items in older adults in China. Findings from this study will provide evidence on the use of bolt-ons to extend the EQ-5D-5L in specific contexts and inform future development of the Bolt-on Toolbox. This proposal strengthens the existing collaboration between the Nanjing CDC and the EuroQol Research Foundation, to support the collection, analysis, and use of EQ-5D measures in China.

Title: A head‐to‐head comparison of EQ‐5D‐3L and EQ‐5D‐5L index scores: more levels is better responsiveness?
Abstract: The EQ‐5D‐5L questionnaire (5L) has demonstrated better measurement properties than the EQ‐5D‐3L questionnaire (3L) in many cross‐sectional studies. In the only known head‐to‐head comparison of 3L and 5L using longitudinal data, the 5L index was not more responsive than the 3L index to health improvement experienced by stroke survivors. The 5L was found no more sensitive than SF‐6D. However, all these findings may be false because those were based on the interim ‘crosswalk’ algorithm for 5L. It is also unclear whether bolt‐on items can improve the responsiveness of EQ‐5D. This project is aimed to 1) compare the responsiveness of 3L and 5L index scores to the treatment benefit of cataract surgery (primary objective) ;2) compare the responsiveness of the two EQ‐5D index scores, the SF‐6D score, and the HUI3 score to cataract removal benefit (sedondary objective); and 3) evaluate the effect of a vision ‘bolt‐on’ item on the responsiveness of the 3L index score (secondary objective). We propose to interview 210 cataract patients face‐to‐face using a battery of questionnaires including the 3L with a vision ‘bolt‐on’ item, 5L, SF‐6D, and HUI3 before and after their cataract removal surgeries. Responsiveness of 5L, 3L, vision bolt‐on, SF‐6D, and HUI3 will be assessed in terms of Cohen’s effect size (d), standardized response mean, and Fstatistic (squared t statistic) based on the preoperative and postoperative scores generated from these instruments. Relevant country‐specific value sets of these intruments will be applied to the specific comaprisons.

Title: A qualitative study on the content validity of the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-PSO bolt-on in patients with psoriasis in Hungary
Abstract: Objectives: A number of bolt-ons have been proposed for the EQ-5D, including two psoriasis specific bolt-ons, skin irritation and self-confidence. The study investigates and compares the relevance and comprehensiveness of these psoriasis specific bolts and the EQ-5D-5L and explores the potential conceptual overlaps between the existing five dimensions and the two bolt-ons. Methods: Psoriasis patients were purposively sampled according to age and gender. Semi-structured interviews, where participants were asked to complete the EQ-5D-5L, the EQ VAS and the bolt-ons while thinking aloud, were conducted. Probes were used to investigate the thought processes of patients regarding the dimensions, wording, recall period and relevant concepts not captured by the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons. Data were analysed thematically. A focus group was used to confirm the findings. Results: Overall, 16 patients completed the interviews. Sixteen and fifteen patients considered skin irritation and self-confidence relevant areas to describe psoriasis problems. Three patients considered itching a form of discomfort, and thus, pointed out a potential overlap between pain/discomfort and skin irritation. Twelve patients reported overall 10 general health- or psoriasis-related concepts that are not captured by the EQ-5D-5L, including itching, social relationships and sex life. Eleven patients reported that the recall period of the EQ-5D-5L might be subject to bias because of the daily or within-day fluctuations of their symptoms. Conclusions: The skin irritation and self-confidence bolt-ons are particularly pertinent and contribute to improve content validity of the EQ-5D-5L in patients with psoriasis. There is only a minor conceptual overlap between the pain/discomfort and skin irritation dimensions.

Title: Beyond linear: Open-source software for DCE duration designs with non-linear time preferences
Abstract: Health state valuation using discrete choice experiments (DCEs) is increasingly applied as an alternative to traditional methods such as the standard gamble (SG) and time trade-off (TTO). A critical step in DCE studies is anchoring relative health state utilities onto the 0–1 quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) scale by including a duration-of-life attribute. Current DCE duration designs typically assume linear time preferences, despite behavioural evidence showing that individuals often value life years non-linearly. Generating DCE duration designs that account for non-linear time preferences while incorporating duration anchoring is technically complex, and no standardized, open-source tool exists to facilitate this process. This limits the broader implementation of the DCE duration protocol.This project builds on an existing DCE duration design generation package developed for the 10-item Well-being (WiX) instrument, which will be generalized and extended to support multiple health state valuation instruments, including EQ-5D and EQ-HWB. Released as an open-source, publicly accessible tool, it will simplify a technically demanding process, improve methodological rigor, enhance the behavioural realism of QALY valuations, and support the wider health economics research community in conducting DCE duration studies accommodating non-linear time preferences.

Title: Development and testing of EQ-5D-5L bolt-on descriptors for hearing
Abstract: The EQ-5D descriptive system could incorporate ‘bolt-on’ descriptors in order to improve measurement sensitivity and relevance in certain contexts. Research has demonstrated that the EQ-5D lacks sensitivity in hearing-related impairment. The aim of this project is to identify one or more items for a hearing bolt-on, using qualitative and quantitative methods. This international research study builds on learnings from the team’s previous and ongoing work developing and testing bolt-on descriptors for cognition, vision, and hearing. This mixed-methods study consists of three phases. In Phase 1a we will conduct a qualitative synthesis, based on a systematic review, to understand the dimensions of quality of life commonly identified by people with experience of hearing problems. Phase 1b will involve a series of group discussions that will be used to reduce, expand, and reformat the candidate domains and terminology identified in 1a. The result of Phase 1 will be the development of candidate bolt-on descriptors, guided by the development criteria used in our ongoing work in cognition and vision. In Phase 2, candidate descriptors will be tested in semi-structured interviews using cognitive debriefing to assess the acceptability and face validity of candidate bolt-ons for hearing. This will allow us to identify bolt-on descriptors to take forward to Phase 3, in which we will conduct an online quantitative survey and use psychometric analyses and item response theory to assess the properties of the candidate bolt-ons using a large sample of patients and the general population from the UK, Australia, and Norway.

Title: Applying narratives to reduce the time preference distortion in the time trade-off valuation of EQ-5D-5L health states
Abstract: The valuation of EQ-5D health states with the time trade-off method (TTO) requires the respondent to imagine living in hypothetical health states for some number of years. The durations of these imaginary lives span over many years: in lead-time TTO (LT-TTO), the durations of even 20 years are used. In the valuation of health states lasting into such far future, the results may be distorted by time preference: the willingness to trade-off life years for health-related quality of life may change depending on whether nearer or farther future is considered. This project will investigate a way to reduce this time-preference-related distortion by applying narratives to EQ-5D-5L health state descriptions. Narratives (or storytelling) is a widely used tool in public communication, which is demonstrated to increase recipient engagement and reduce the temporal distance from the objects presented in the communication (i.e., those objects are perceived to appear sooner). Specifically, it is proposed that the narrative form of health state descriptions reduces the temporal distance from the occurrence of the valued health states (as compared to the non-narrative form) and, in consequence, reduces the time preference distortion in the measured TTO utilities. That mechanism will be studied experimentally: 150 respondents will each value 5 EQ-5D-5L health states with LT-TTO under one of conditions, i.e., using either narrative or non-narrative descriptions. The elicited utility values will be compared between the conditions, also accounting for the demographic and sociocultural characteristics of the participants (including future-orientation). The results can help improve EQ-5D-5L valuation methodology by suggesting how to reduce time preference distortion.

Title: US population norms for the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: Aim: The EQ-5D-5L is usedin many health-related fields, including patientclinical assessmentand cost-utility analyses. Inthese applications, a set of norms would be useful to allow for comparisons betweenthe population of interestand the general population. The aim of this study is to estimate population normsfor the EQ-5D-5L visual analogue and index-based scores.Methods: Data from the US EQ-5D-5L face-to-face (andpotentially the online)valuation studieswhich used age, gender and race/ethnicity-based quota sampling forthe US adult general populationwill serve as the data source. Conceptual and statistical considerations will be evaluated for appropriateness of using the face-to-face and/or the online study. Descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation, interquartile range and 95% confidence intervals) will be reportedby gender/age bands for the VAS and EQ-5D-5L index-based summary scores using the value set based on the international protocol (Pickard et al, 2019).Significance: The availability of US 5L norms will help facilitate useand interpretationof the EQ-5D-5L in the United States for both economic and non-economic purposes, thereby encouraging use of the measure.

Title: Design and Analysis Considerations when using the EQ-5D alongside clinical trials or observational studies for economic evaluation: PhD studentship and development of tools for analysts and researchers
Abstract: The EQ-5D instrument is widely used alongside randomized controlled trials and as part of observational studies to inform the development of cost effectiveness models. Perhaps surprisingly very little guidance has emerged on design and analysis considerations for analysts who are interested in employing the EQ-5D instrument as part of their study. Trial sponsors commonly analyse EQ-5D by trial arm and report that there is no difference in HRQL (sometimes in contrast to findings for other PROs). But the structure of economic models is often described in terms of discrete disease states over a patients’ lifetime. Health economic modellers have long recognized the limitations of standard approaches to trial data analysis and have instead employed regression modellingto understand the impact of events and health states on utility. Prominent examples include the analysis of the UKPDS trial1; work in COPD 2; oncology3, and cardiovascular disease4. We believe a lot more work can be usefully conducted to provide guidance on a wide range of issues including modelling approaches, handling patient drop out and providing guidance regarding the optimal design of studies designed to measure the impact of events at random points in time. This application is seeking funding for a studentship at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine to explore this work using available datasets.

Title: Values for EQ-5D-Y-3L: a comparative analysis of value sets and meta-analysis of international valuation data
Abstract: Background: Since publication of the EQ-5D-Y valuation protocol (Ramos-Goni et al 2020), there has been considerable interest in undertaking valuation studies and rapid progress toward producing value sets. So far, more than 10 studies have completed data collection, and several others are on their way.
