As the EQ-5D-Y valuation protocol that is currently used may not be the final version, this first wave of studies may provide us with a wealth of information on various aspects of values for EQ-5D-Y-3L states, as well as on how respondents value these states. Furthermore, the availability of these value sets allows for a comparison of values for the EQ-5D-Y-3L instrument and for those of adults. Aims: This study has three aims: 1) conducting a comparative analysis of EQ-5D-Y value sets, 2) conducting a comparative analysis of EQ-5D-Y respondent-level valuation data, and 3) comparing EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets.  Methods: A comparative analysis of value sets will be undertaken, in which the EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets of at least 10 countries are extracted from their respective manuscripts. Following a similar methodology of previously published work by Olsen et al (2018) and Roudijk et al (2022), we will compare how EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets may differ between countries, and additionally, whether these differences may relate to methodological choices made in these studies. For the comparative analysis of valuation data, PI’s of valuation studies will be contacted and asked to collaborate. In each dataset, preferences will be explored using latent class models, and it is tested whether similar latent classes exist between countries. Furthermore, the agreement between the cTTO and DCE data is tested within countries. Lastly, for the comparison of youth and adult value sets, we will focus on ordinal information that can be extracted from the respective EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets. For each country included, we will compare characteristics such as scale length, relative importance of the 5 dimensions, percentage of negative states. Furthermore, we will compare the values directly, and provide illustrative examples of how values may differ when transitioning between the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L instrument. Relevance: The three proposed studies may help us better understand how values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states differ between countries, how respondents may differ in their responses between countries, and whether the two valuation methods agree within countries. Furthermore, these studies will provide information on the transition between youth and adult value sets. This is all relevant for potential future valuation protocol updates, and may also be informative for researchers that want to value EQ-5D-Y-5L in the future once it gains beta status.

Title: Qualitative Study for Fatigue Bolt-on (QSFB) in Collaboration with U.S. Adults Living with Multiple Sclerosis
Abstract: Background: Fatigue is one of the most common and burdensome symptoms for persons living with multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic neurological condition affecting nearly one million adults in the U.S. The EQ-5D-5L instrument does not include a fatigue item, motivating efforts to develop a bolt-on. Aims: This formative qualitative research is a collaboration with U.S. adults living with MS (acceleratedcure.org). It will explore critical questions regarding the development of a fatigue bolt-on as well as potential gains in coverage and application for the EQ-5D-5L instrument. Aim 1: Which bolt-on wording and framing options best capture fatigue? Specifically:Do alternative labels (“fatigue”, “tiredness”, “worn out”, “exhaustion”) differ in clarity and relevance?Might the inclusion of patient-centered examples improve bolt-on performance?Does first-person phrasing (“feel” vs. “am”) affect bolt-on interpretation and response?Aim 2: Which bolt-ons are needed to extend the coverage of the EQ-5D-5L instrument? Specifically:What aspects of health-related quality of life are not covered by the EQ-5D-5L instrument?Do the candidate bolt-ons effectively capture important aspects of the lived experiences of individuals with fatigue, and how should these bolt-ons be prioritized?Does adding candidate bolt-ons change the interpretation and responses to the core items?We hypothesize that the current labels (“fatigue”) will outperform other labels while the inclusion of examples will enhance the comprehension of the instrument. Furthermore, we hypothesize that individuals living with MS will endorse appending the fatigue, vision, and cognition bolt-ons and that doing so does not affect their interpretation of or responses to the core items.Methods: This study will employ semi-structured qualitative interviews following the DSWG recommendations, standardised topic guide, and templates (N=20; acceleratedcure.org). These heterogeneous respondents serve as patient experts in fatigue due to their unique lived experience with MS. Diversity is needed to benefit from a wealth of perspectives (i.e., quota sampling by gender, age, disease severity). Interviews (Zoom) will be conducted by trained interviewers, and they will be audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim (otter.ai). The descriptive analysis will summarize the characteristics of the respondents. In the primary analysis, the open-ended responses will be coded (with 50% overlap) and analyzed thematically (Atlas.ti), and the ranking/optimization responses will be summarized in aggregate (R). This patient-centered study was designed to produce actionable recommendations that guide bolt-on development and the future use of the Bolt-on Toolbox.

Title: Using TTO data to anchor DCE data and produce EQ-5D-Y value sets: comparing alternative approaches using existing and simulated data
Abstract: The valuation protocol for the EQ-5D-Y-3L recommends that both discrete choice experiment (DCE) data and composite time trade-off (cTTO) data are collected. The DCE provides the key information on the relative importance of the different levels and dimensions, and the cTTO is intended to provide data to anchor the DCE data onto the full health to dead scale. However, there are multiple ways in which to conduct this anchoring. These include rescaling based on the mean cTTO values ("worst state rescaling"), mapping DCE onto mean cTTO values ("linear mapping"), and hybrid modelling. To date, there has been little research into the relative merit of these approaches. This research aimed to fill these gaps by comparing the different anchoring approaches using previously collected EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation data. Overall, it was found that, whilst the value sets produced by each anchoring method are similar, there are some notable differences which are generalisable. For example: 1) Both worst state rescaling and linear mapping will maintain the relative importance scores from the DCE data as they are linear transformations of the DCE data. 2) Worst state rescaling will produce value sets with a larger scale than both linear mapping and hybrid modelling due to prediction error. 3) Hybrid modelling and linear mapping will produce value sets that better align with the cTTO data than worst state rescaling as they use more cTTO data. Based on the current EQ-5D-Y valuation protocol, the linear mapping approach is likely to be viewed as advantageous over the worst state rescaling approach (makes better use of the data collected) and the hybrid modelling approach (insufficient data). However, the final decision on which approach to use is likely to involve some normative considerations. To aid decisions, researchers should engage with relevant stakeholders and test the sensitivity of their results based on different anchoring approaches.

Title: The development of the national value set for the EQ-5D-5L in Brazil
Abstract: Objective: To develop an EQ-5D-5L value set for the Brazilian population. Methods: We will develop a value set using the composite time-trade-off (cTTO) and discrete choice experiment (DCE) approaches. One thousand adults from general population will be included in this valuation study. The study will be conducted in six urban centers: two in Southeast region (Ribeirão Preto and São Paulo - São Paulo) and one in each other regions: South (Uruguaiana - Rio Grande do Sul), North (Belém - Pará), Northeast (Fortaleza - Ceará), and Central-west (Distrito Federal - Brasília). Different model specifications will be tested using only cTTO data, only DCE data, and hybrid approaches combining both. Sensitivity analyses will be performed to assess the robustness of the model estimates.Discussion: Economic evaluations have been increasingly conducted in Brazil to support healthcare decision-making processes. The quality of these studies is considered satisfactory. However, improvements are needed especially in the methods used to estimate effect measures such as health-related quality of life considering the Brazilian scenario. Evidence shows that the EQ-5D-5L demonstrates superior measurement properties compared to the EQ-5D-3L. However, a value set for the EQ-5D-5L has not been developed for the Brazilian population yet. The development of this value set will facilitate the dissemination and use of this instrument in clinical and research settings across Brazil.

Title: Analysis of EQ-5D profile data and EQ VAS scores across patient groups in the Swedish National Quality Registers and use in developing alternative ways of summarizing EQ-5D data.
Abstract: This proposalaimsto investigate the evidence that the same EQ-5D state is valued differently across patient groups who experience that state because of different underlying conditions. Subsequently, we explore alternative ways of summarising EQ-5D profile data to reflect patients ́ views and experience of health. Swedish decision makers (its HTA body, TLV) prefer weightings based on the evaluations of the persons experiencing the health condition in question before calculations from an average of a population estimating a condition depicted for it. This raises the question of which patients’ preferences are relevant – patients’ overall or specific patients experiencing the illness under consideration, or the preferences of an individual patient? Little is known about how these experience-based values differ, which is the main topic of this proposal. Specifically we address the following research questions: •How do EQ-5D profile data differ across patient groups? •How do EQ VAS scores for EQ-5D profiles differ across patient groups? •To which extent does the importance of the dimensions, in explaining the EQ VAS scores, vary depending on the patients’ particular condition and experience of health? •How does the Swedish experience-based EQ VAS value set, estimated from models using self-reported EQ-5D profile data and EQ VAS scores performs in different patient groups?Hence, it is important to explore how patients’ preferences about HRQoL differ within and between disease areas. Swedish National Quality Registers data offers an opportunity to explore these questions. We will select 7-8 registers that represent diseases that affect different dimensions of health.

Title: Valuing health in children: an examination of age, perspective and methodological effects (REVISED)
Abstract: Introduction The first international protocol for valuing the EQ-5D-Y-3L recommends that valuation tasks are completed by adult general public respondents adopting the perspective of a 10-year-old child. This choice of perspective has been the subject of debate. Where values obtained under an own health perspective (the standard perspective used in valuing adult health states) have been found to differ from those obtained under a 10-year-old child perspective, it is unclear whether these differences are driven by the shift from thinking about adults to thinking about children, by the shift from thinking about oneself to thinking about another person, or both. It is also unclear whether the age of the child described or the valuation technique used matters. This study examines the impact on EQ-5D-Y-3L values of using different perspectives, child ages, and valuation techniques. The aim is to generate evidence that can be used to inform future methods and protocols for obtaining values for EQ-5D-Y-3L health states. Methods Two techniques (time trade-off; TTO and visual analogue scale; VAS) and four perspectives (own health, other adult’s health, 4-year-old child’s health, 10-year-old child’s health) were compared. Respondents each completed 24 valuation tasks, valuing 3 EQ-5D-Y-3L health states using both techniques and all four perspectives. They also completed debrief and priority setting questions designed to understand how they approached the valuation tasks and their wider views about how health care resources should be prioritised between adults and children, respectively. Data were collected via videoconference interviews with members of the public in England. Results 300 interviews were completed. In both the TTO and VAS tasks, and for all three health states examined, the difference in values/ratings observed between the 4-year-old child and 10-year-old child perspectives was negligible. For one of the severe health states, respondents gave substantially lower TTO values under their own health perspective than under the child health perspectives, with values under the other adult’s health perspective lying in between. These differences observed in the TTO data were not observed in the VAS data, where mean health state ratings were similar across all perspectives. Of the various statements presented to respondents describing factors they might have considered in completing the valuation tasks, the statement ‘I find it difficult to choose a shorter life for a child’ was the one that was most frequently selected. Conclusions Differences between the own health perspective and child health perspective TTO values appear to be in part due to differences in how people feel about health states for adults and health states for children, and in part due to differences in how people feel about health states for themselves and health states for other people. The fact that similar differences were not observed in the VAS data suggests that they may be an artefact of the TTO technique. Some of the study findings add to the existing evidence that adult TTO values tend to be lower than corresponding child TTO values because many people find trading life years for children more difficult. The age of the hypothetical child in the valuation tasks does not appear to substantially affect valuations.

Title: Parametric survival models for the analysis of cTTO data: accommodating asymmetry, heteroscedasticity, heterogeneity and censoring.
Abstract: The recent external review of the UK EQ-5D-5L valuation study identified that the Normality assumption made in the heteroscedastic Tobit models widely used to model cTTO in EQ-5D-5L valuation studies was not met; moreover this was also noted to be the case in other studies. Accordingly, the 20th RFP includes novel modelling approaches to cTTO data that can handle the asymmetric, heterogeneous, heteroscedastic and censored nature of this data as a current methodological need.We propose to use parametric survival models to fill this need. Specifically, defining indifference in the cTTO task as the event and disutility as the time, disutilities from cTTO data can be described as time-to-event data. There are well-developed parametric survival models that incorporate asymmetry and heteroscedasticity in addition to censoring; moreover, random effects can be added to accommodate heterogeneity. The proposed work will examine Weibull, Gompertz, and log-logistic survival models, and mixtures thereof. We anticipate that this approach will provide sufficient flexibility accommodate the asymmetry and heteroscedasticity present in cTTO data, thus permitting future valuation studies to produce more methodologically rigorous estimates.

Title: Validation of the EQ-HWB-S for measuring the health and wellbeing of informal carers
Abstract: Background: Informal caregivers provide essential support for people with chronic conditions, yet capturing their health and well-being in economic and outcomes research remains challenging. The EQ-HWB-9 is a recently developed instrument designed to measure broader health and well-being beyond traditional health-related quality of life. This study assessed the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-9 in informal caregivers and explored the performance of an EQ-HWB-9 visual analogue scale (VAS).Methods: An online survey was conducted among adults providing informal care to individuals with stroke, cancer, or dementia. Participants were recruited through an online panel and completed four instruments: EQ-HWB-9, EQ-5D-5L, CarerQol, and ASCOT-Carer. Baseline characteristics of caregivers, care recipients, and caring situations were collected. Psychometric evaluation included assessment of floor and ceiling effects, convergent and divergent validity, discriminatory ability using Shannon indices, known-group validity, and test–retest reliability. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses examined relationships among items across instruments. A subset of participants completed a follow-up survey after 14 days to assess reliability.Results: A total of 487 caregivers participated, with similar representation across the three caregiving groups. The mean EQ-HWB-9 utility score was 0.801, lower than EQ-5D-5L (0.907) but higher than ASCOT-Carer (0.791). Ceiling effects for EQ-HWB-9 (12%) were lower than those observed for EQ-5D-5L. EQ-HWB-9 scores were moderately correlated with other caregiver and health-related quality-of-life measures, supporting convergent validity. Factor analysis identified five underlying constructs relating to mental health, psychosocial well-being, physical functioning and pain, negative psychosocial health, and support and fulfilment. Known-group analysis showed lower well-being among caregivers providing more hours of care and those caring for individuals with greater disease severity. Test–retest reliability was acceptable (ICC=0.69), with moderate item-level agreement.Conclusions: The EQ-HWB-9 demonstrates acceptable validity, reliability, and discriminatory ability among informal caregivers and may provide a useful instrument for capturing broader caregiver well-being in research and evaluation.

Title: Content validity of EQ-5D-5L plus Bolt-ons for metastatic urological cancer patients: a qualitative investigation of patients and caregivers
Abstract: Background: Cancer care and treatment are often responsible for high healthcare spending worldwide, with substantial impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) both due to disease symptoms and treatment side-effects. Although the EQ-5D is often used in cancer research, it has often been criticized as being too generic. A recent qualitative study (Gibson et al 2024) examining the content validity of preference-based measures in cancer (including EQ-5D-5L) concludes that cancer-specific measures have better relevancy than generic measures. Gibson et al (2024) also points to a dearth of qualitative work addressing the content validity of the EQ-5D-5L for cancer patients. The “bolt-on” approach identifies particular dimensions/domains which are missing from EQ-5D (for specific populations of interest) and, given sufficient evidence of measurement properties, adds these dimensions (items) to the core EQ-5D. This approach may improve the EQ-5D’s relevance for cancer patients. An existing research relationship with the comprehensive cancer centers (CCC) and the and the Urology department at Universitätsklinikum Tübingen (UKT) presents an opportunity to study the HRQoL of patients with urological cancer. We therefore propose to advance content validity of the EQ-5D-5L and investigate whether a set of bolt-ons can improve its content validity for (urological) cancer patients.The aims of the study include:Examine the content validity of EQ-5D-5L plus bolt-ons for metastatic bladder, prostate and kidney cancer patients, Field test a final short set of bolt-on items MethodsThe project will be cross-sectional qualitative and will include three phases:translation/adaptation,content validity examination with cancer patients (main phase), andfield testing EQ-5D-5L pus a small set of cancer-relevant bolt-ons.Forward-Backward translation plus cognitive debriefing will be used in Phase 1 to translate all toolbox bolt-ons and a set of selected non-toolbox bolt-ons that have not yet been translated into German (Germany). Phase 2 will sample 30 metastatic bladder, prostate and kidney cancer patients, 5-7 family caregivers, and 7-13 formal caregivers (clinicians) from the Conservative Uro-oncology clinic at UKT. Patients and family caregivers will be recruited for semi-structured interviews and formal caregivers will be recruited for focus groups. Both interviews and focus groups will investigate the content validity (Relevance, comprehensiveness, comprehensibility) of the core EQ-5D-5L, toolbox and non-toolbox bolt-ons. Relevant bolt-ons will be identified using an iterative approach: (1) all toolbox plus three selected non-toolbox bolt-ons will be investigated in an initial step; (2) after 10 interviews, bolt-ons with poor relevance will be removed from the interviews and additional relevant dimensions identified by patients will be added; (3) the bolt-on set will be reassessed again after 20 interviews. In Phase 3, we will field test the final set of bolt-ons (along with the core EQ-5D-5L) with 8-10 urological cancer patients (recruited from the Uro-oncology clinic at UKT). The interviews and focus groups will be analyzed using thematic content analysis guided by an a priori framework: namely the COSMIN content validity checklist. This approach will enable specific categories to be extracted from the material, and underlying themes and meanings to be identified. Relevance for the EuroQol groupContent validity of a measurement instrument is considered the most important type of validity because it affects all other types of validities. For development of bolt-ons, it is crucial for the EuroQol group to establish content validity in various patient populations. Cancer patients is a crucial patient population and strategically important for the EuroQol Group due to the rapid development of treatments for this population. This study will both provide content validity evidence for the core EQ-5D-5L as well as identify relevant bolt-on dimensions for a particular (urological) cancer population.

Title: DOES THE EQ-5D-5L IMPROVE PREDICTIONS OF HOSPITAL READMISSION? AN EQUITY GUIDED ANALYSIS OF OVER 24,000 PATIENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
Abstract: Unnecessary hospital readmissions are a major challenge for all health systems. If patients at high risk for readmission can be identified early, effective interventions exist that can prevent episodes. Previous prediction models tend to rely on administrative data and have reasonable predictive ability. Previous studies have suggested Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) could improve these predictions, but have tended to be in smaller samples of patients with specific conditions.  This project proposes to use data from British Columbia, where surveys have been conducted on large numbers (~25,000) of patients discharged from inpatient care, asking the EQ-5D-5L along with demographics. In our earlier work (funded by the EuroQol group), we found that the EQ-5D-5L improved predictions of high cost users (presented at 2023 Plenary).  In this study, we seek to extend this work by:  Assessing the performance of models to predict unplanned hospital re-admissions within 1-year of completion of the EQ-5D-5L and Compare the performance of predictive models with and without EQ-5D-5L data  We will further:  Explore the prediction models in various patient subgroups with specific ages and clinical diagnoses (e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; heart failure). Evaluate whether the performance of the predictive models vary across groups of the population defined by levels of neighborhood income which is used as an equity stratifier.   Our analysis will use the BC Acute Inpatient survey data, linked with health administrative databases, including the Discharge Abstract Database (hospital separations), National Ambulatory Care Reporting System (emergency department, day surgeries, and day clinics), Medical Services Plan (physician services), PharmaNet (prescription medications and medical supplies), and Home and Community Care (long-term care and assisted living).  We will develop logistic regression, LASSO and random forest models for outcomes based first on only administrative data, and then adding the EQ-5D-5L. We will use cross-validation to select best performing models and assess comparative model performance by using discrimination, calibration and decision curve analysis. For final models, we will conduct subgroup analysis based on disease and age groups. We will also explore predictive performance across subgroups of patients based on their neighbourhood income decile that we are using in this analysis as an equity stratifier. This will allow us to explore whether predictive performance varies across these subgroups, and consider the equity impacts when choosing our final predictive model.  We hypothesize that including PROMs will improve the predictive performance of models, justifying the routine collection of the EQ-5D-5L post hospital discharge to inform readmission predictions.

Title: Translation and cognitive debriefing of Dutch version of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox vision bolt-ons
Abstract: The EuroQol Group aims to validate the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. An opportunity has come up at the Rotterdam Eye Hospital (the Netherlands) to include the translated vision bolt-ons in ongoing and new externally funded data collections in glaucoma and vitreoretinal surgery. These studies can provide evidence for validity of the vision bolt-ons. It is therefore important that the vision bolt-on items are translated soon. Thus, we are proposing the translation of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox vision bolt-ons to Dutch and seeking funding support for it from EuroQol.This study aims to conduct a full researcher-led translation of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox vision bolt-ons (Paper Self-complete versions) into Dutch to make it available for future validation or valuation work. We will translate all items (4 in total) from the ‘Best available’ and ‘Exploratory’ toolbox.In accordance, with the EuroQol VMC translation guidelines, this involves two forward and two backward translations by four independent translators, which are fluent in English and Dutch, followed by a total of 8 cognitive debriefing interviews to ensure the clarity, naturalness, and adequacy of the translations, while also confirming that respondents interpret the wording as intended.First, the translation process involves two independent forward translations into Dutch from the UK English source versions for the current vision bolt-ons, which will be reconciled afterwards followed by the production of the first consensus version. The selected forward translators are fluent in English and native Dutch speakers. Secondly, based on the first consensus version two independent back translations of that version will be produced and reconciled in a subsequent back translation meeting. The appointed backward translators are fluent in Dutch and English with no to little prior experience on EuroQol questionnaires. As a result of the back-translation meeting, a draft second consensus version will be generated. Upon approval of the translation stages by the VMC, the finalised second consensus version will be carried forward to conduct a cognitive debriefing on the translations. Overall, 8 respondents will be recruited. These 8 respondents will be recruited from the Rotterdam Eye Hospital: 4 males and 4 females with a variety of eye conditions and of various ages, of which 2 with lower education levels (only primary school education). The cognitive debriefing interviews will be conducted by an experienced qualitative researcher.The tentative timelines for this project will be October to December 2025.Generally, this study will follow the design proposed by the VMC for translation work.Note: After completion of this study, the Dutch version of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox vision bolt-ons will be checked in Belgium, to see whether a separate Flemish version of the vision bolt-ons is needed.

Title: Translation, Cultural Adaptation, and Psychometric Evaluation of Health-Related Quality of Life Instruments for Early Childhood (EQ-TIPS-5L) and Caregiver Spillover (EQ-HWB-9) in Egypt
Abstract: Aim: Given the substantial disease burden among Egyptian children under five—particularly hematologic malignancies, this study aims to fill critical gaps in the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in early childhood. This involves the translation and cultural adaptation of the Arabic 5-level version of the EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations instrument (EQ-TIPS-5L) for Egypt and conduct a comprehensive psychometric validation of EQ-TIPS-5L and three Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) scales in children aged 0–4 years. In addition, caregiver spillover will be assessed using EQ-HWB-9 EMV2.1 and WHO-5.Methods: Translation and cultural adaptation will follow EuroQol Research Foundation guidelines, including forward–backward translation, consensus meetings, cognitive debriefing with 8 caregivers, then face validity testing in a 24 caregivers using QQ-10 questionnaire.  A longitudinal psychometric validation study will be conducted in line with COSMIN standards. The sample will include 200 caregivers of children aged 0–4 years: 100 with malignancies (like acute lymphoblastic leukemia) and 100 healthy controls. Participants will be stratified  by severity. Instruments administered at baseline and at least two-week follow-up will include EQ-TIPS-5L, PedsQL generic modules, along with global health ratings to assess test-retest reliability. Additionally, the spillover effect of the child’s health on the caregiver will be assessed using EQ-HWB-9 EMV2.1 and World Health Organization Five-Item Well-Being instrument, WHO-5. Psychometric evaluation will cover feasibility, ceiling and floor effects, test-retest reliability, known-groups validity, and explanatory power. Data will be disaggregated by age groups, health status, and other relevant variables. The findings will generate robust psychometric evidence for two key EQ instruments and support their wider application in Egypt and the broader MENA region.

Title: Investigating the aspects of HRQoL covered by pain/discomfort and the added value of the psoriasis bolt-ons (EQ-PSO) among patients suffering from skin diseases (Revised).
Abstract: Introduction: Skin conditions do not constitute a direct threat to life, but their chronic and incurable character has a negative impact on the health-related quality of life (HRQoL). In the EQ-5D, physical discomfort, such as that associated with skin conditions (e.g., itching), is captured by the pain/discomfort item. While pain is clearly a very important aspect of physical discomfort, other aspects such as itching, skin irritation, and the indirect impact of this on skin appearance, self-confidence, and relationship difficulties are not explicitly mentioned. An EQ-5D-5L psoriasis bolt-on (EQ-PSO), which includes itching and self-confidence, has been shown to have face validity in studies undertaken in the global North, but no study has been undertaken in the global South. The objective of this study is to investigate how well aspects of HRQoL are captured by the EQ-5D descriptive system, and more specifically by the pain-discomfort item, and the additional advantage of using the psoriasis bolt-ons (EQ-PSO questionnaire) in people with skin diseases in Ethiopia.Method: Translation of both EQ-5D-5L and EQ-PSO was undertaken into Tigrinya language by two forward translators, two backward translators, one proofreader, four interviewers, and a project manager, in collaboration with the EuroQol version management committee (VMC). In-depth qualitative interviews were then undertaken to investigate how well the health aspects important for people with skin diseases (psoriasis) are captured by the EQ-5D descriptive system, the pain-discomfort item, and the additional advantage of using the EQ-PSO questionnaire. Both EQ-5D-5L and EQ-PSO questionnaires were administered to participants. The qualitative interviews were recorded using an encrypted audio recording device, transcribed, and translated. For the analysis, statements were grouped into thematically related groups based on aspects of content validation, including comprehension (understanding), relevance, and comprehensiveness.ResultsTwenty-nine adults with psoriasis participated in the interviews. Most reported moderate to severe disease burden with itching (51.7%), psychological distress (27.6%), and impaired daily functioning (34.5%) as major concerns. While the EQ-5D-5L was generally understood and relevant, several psoriasis-specific aspects, such as itching, self-confidence, and social stigma, were perceived as missing. The EQ-PSO bolt-on dimensions (itching and self-confidence) were consistently rated as highly relevant and reflective of participants lived experiences. Minor conceptual overlap was noted between the pain/discomfort and skin irritation dimensions, but each contributed distinct information.ConclusionThe EQ-PSO bolt-on for itching and self-confidence improves content validity and better reflects the lived experience of patients. Incorporating bolt-ons offers a more comprehensive assessment of HRQoL in this population and may support improved measurement in clinical and economic evaluations.

Title: EQALY International Psychometric Analysis: Argentina study
Abstract: The aim of thisproject is to support item selection for a new instrument development (Extending the QALY (E-QALY project) that aims tocapture the changes in quality of life from interventions in health and social care that would be fit for the purpose of inclusion in economic evaluations. The core domains for the instrument have been identified and a pool of potential items have been proposed. Face validity has been undertaken in 5 countries (Argentina, Australia, China, Germany and USA) as well as the UK. Psychometric work based on a large survey is being undertaken in the UK from September through to December 2018 in order to identify items for the new measure. This proposed study will collect and analyse additional Argentina data to support the psychometric work and future item selection. It is the only Spanish speaking country in this initial multi-country team, Spanishbeingthe second most common language in the world. We will also explore the relationship of HRQoL and finnancial coping, patient and family coststhe whole sample andin different disease groups.Data on the E-QALY test items, plus EQ-5D-5L and other existing instruments, will be collected from a sample of 500 members of the public, of whom 400willreport a health condition using a commercial panel. This data will be analysed in line with the analysisof the UK survey data using basic psychometrics and Item Response Theory (IRT). These findingswill be interpreted in the light of evidence from the face validity work, and country specific recommendations will be made. These will be discussed in conjunction with other international evidence to support item selection for the new instrument.

Title: Psychometric validation of the Chinese version of EQ‐5D‐Y for China in three medical conditions
Abstract: Aim: The Chinese version of EQ‐5D‐Y for china was not psychometrically validated. This project aimed to validate the Chinese version of EQ‐5D‐Y for China (both self-complete and proxy versions) in three populations, including school-attending children and adolescents, children with leukemia, and children with asthma. Methods: Three separate surveys were conducted. Chinese EQ‐5D‐Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L questionnaires were administered to Children and their health and medical information was retrieved from health records. Parents or legal guardians of children with Leukemia or asthma were asked to complete proxy version of Y-3L and Y-5L questionnaires. Validity, reliability and responsiveness of Y-3L and Y-5L self-complete and proxy versions were assessed. Results and conclusions: Both the self-complete and proxy versions of Y-3L and Y-5L questionnaires demonstrated validity, reliability and/or responsiveness in the study samples. The studies also generated some evidence for the agreement between self-reported and proxy-reported EQ-5D-Y health outcomes.

Title: Feasibility and application of the EQ-5D in elderly
Abstract: Due to the aging population and changes in the morbidity structure, health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measurement in the elderly gets more relevant. However, special characteristics of the elderly population, such as impaired cognitive functioning or visual impairments, seem to make an accurate measurement of HRQoL challenging. The EQ-5D is a widely used generic preference-based instrument, which is psychometrically sound with the general population, but it may not be suitable for use in elderly. Therefore, we need to examine whether the EQ-5D is a feasible measure applicable for the use in the elderly population. Hence, this study aims to systematically identify and analyse the available literature which examined feasibility properties of the EQ-5D specifically for the elderly. We conducted a systematic search in the PubMed, PsycInfo and the EuroQol database to identify articles published in English or German without any restrictions to the publication date. Studies were included, if (1) the minimum age of the sample was reported and included participants were at least 65 years old and (2) HRQoL as a primary or secondary outcome was measured by the EQ-5D. Two independent reviewers conducted the literature sifting process. We extracted the sample and study characteristics, including outcomes referring to the feasibility of the EQ-5D as a measure of HRQoL in the elderly in a qualitative synthesis. We identified 15 studies reporting information on feasibility based on four criteria: missing values, completion rates, time required to complete the instrument and -more broadly –qualitative statements referring to the completion of the measure. Only two of the included studies examined the EQ-5D-5L, the remaining 13 reported on the 3L version. Our findings suggest that missing values or comprehension problems (especially with the VAS) are slightly more prevalent in older age groups. However, these aspects are well within an acceptable range and still considerably lower than in other measures such as the SF-36 or ICECAP-O, which are frequently used in the elderly. Furthermore, older respondents seem to have a higher propensity of requiring some degree of assistance or even an interviewer-based approach, but still on a quite low level.Overall, evidence from the reviewed literature indicates that the EQ-5D is a comprehensible and short measure, which is also highly applicable in older respondents. The EQ-5D is a well-established instrument used to measure and evaluate health-related quality of life. Both versions the EQ-5D-3L and 5L demonstrated good measurement properties across many conditions and populations, strengthening the EQ-5D’s role as a basis for calculating quality-adjusted life years for use in clinical and economic evaluations. In the light of an aging population, the EQ-5D also showed adequate measurement properties in the elderly population. When evaluating healthcare services for elderly people, the measure should also be feasible and applicable to the use in an elderly population. The ease of applying the EQ-5D in an elderly sample may have an impact on data quality given that feasibility issues increase the risk of measurement error, i.e. missing responses ormulti-coded answers, or even complete study withdrawal. Yet, little is known about these properties of the EQ-5D in this population. This study aims to examine the feasibility of the EQ-5D-3L and 5L in the elderly general population by exploring the impact of age on the completion of the EQ-5D instruments further controlling for gender and the presence of long-term conditions. A prerequisite for this analysis is the availability of uncleansed, self-report EQ-5D health data from the general population. We pool across five waves of secondary datasets from the GP Patient Survey from years 2012, 2016 and 2017, where respondents self-report their health in either EQ-5D-3L or 5L depending on the wave of fieldwork. First, descriptive analysis was undertaken to analyse the distribution and proportion of missing values and completion rates stratified by age and EQ-5D version. Secondly, logistic regression models were specified to quantify the impact of age, gender and potential long-term conditions on the completion of each of the EQ-5D instruments. The total sample comprises around 4.36 million observations, of which 2.88 million respondents report their health in 5L and 1.47 million in 3L, respectively. Respondents being 65 years and above have marginally more missing values in each dimension compared to younger respondents. The highest share was observed for the oldest age group in the dimension anxiety/depression (3L 9.1% vs. 5L 7.6%), otherwise being below 5%. Consequently, completion rates (observed and predicted) decreased with age and at a higher rate after the age of 64. Evidence from our study suggests that both the EQ-5D-3L and 5L have good feasibility properties. The proportion of missing values is acceptably low across all age groups but compares more favourably for the 5LGiven the ongoing ageing trend in European countries, we expect a major increase in the proportion of elderly people with a corresponding increase in long-term care needs. While in Europe the majority of long-term care is provided by informal caregivers in a home-based setting, little is known about the impact of different care settings on the (health-related) quality of life (HRQoL) of care-dependents. Hence, this study aims to assess differences in (HR)QoL between elderly respondents receiving informal care and elderly respondents receiving formal care based on EQ-5D-3L, 5L and the age-specific WHOQOL-old. In addition to that, we aim to add to the scarce evidence of the EQ-5D’s feasibility and test-retest properties in the elderly population. Our findings suggest that differences in (HR)QoL between different care settings seem indeed to be prevalent, pointing towards higher levels of reported (HR)QoL in recipients of formal care and those in a nursing homes. Generally, the EQ-5D shows good properties in terms of response distribution, feasibility and test-retest statistics and this is irrespective of the version. Moreover, we conclude that using the WHOQOL-old alongside EQ-5D in this sample added further information ondifferent aspects of QoL from care-dependents.The EQ-5D is one of the most prominent instruments for the measurement and valuation of health-related quality of life. Due to its generic descriptive system it can be used to measure health across different disease areas and age groups. Given the growing demand of HRQoL data for clinical and economic appraisal targeted at the elderly age group the EQ-5D was extensively used in this population, too. Reference values are a helpful tool to facilitate comparisons against other groups. For example, to assess disease burden of patients, for researchers as baseline or control measurement or to determine the effects of treatments. In order to generate reference values for the German elderly population (≥65 years), we analysed a sub-set of data from the German valuation study to present benchmark values for mean utilities and VAS values as well as with regard to the response distribution stratified by age and gender. Instead of using only two age groups to characterise the elderly population, we used four age groups (65-69, 70-74, 75-79 and >79 years) to facilitate a more detailed examination of age-related HRQoL. Generally, our findings correspond well to earlier findings from a large German population norm study. Nonetheless, a more detailed provision of reference values for the elderly population seems helpful given that HRQoL in the oldest old is more volatile and differs from the young elderly, while the sought age categorisation of conventional population norms studies seems to mask these differences. Our findings may help researchers, clinicians and health economists to compare their results with those of the German general elderly population.

Title: Psychometric assessment of the eQALY item pool in Australia
Abstract: The ‘Extending the QALY’ project aims to develop a broad measure of quality of life for use in economic evaluation across health and social care. While the project consists of six stages, the proposed research plan is concerned with the fourth stage (psychometric validation).This follows assessment of the face-validity of the E-QALY items in Australia as part of stage 3 of the wider project. The overall aim of this study is to test the psychometric validity of the E-QALY item pool using data collected from Australian respondents. We will collect online data from a sample of 500 people in Australia with a self-reported health condition (covering a range of physical and mental conditions)and a healthy sample, using a range of instruments with different measurement frameworks. This includes the E-QALY item pool, measures of health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L and AQoL-8D), and a measure of wellbeing (WEMWBS). It is expected that this study will complement the psychometric analysis conducted by the UK E-QALY team for various reasons: (i) the E-QALY item pool will comprise additional items that were important to Australians in the face validity work, but were excluded by the UK E-QALY team; (ii) the item pool will include new items that were identified during the face-validity study in Australia; (iii) the inclusion of the AQoL-8D will extend the information available to psychometrically test the E-QALY item pool as it includes a number of domains that overlap with those developed by the E-QALY team; (iv) the Australian site will recruit additional patient groups that are not well coveredin the UK psychometric study. Overall, findings from the Australian psychometric study will provide additional data to support the item reduction and selection process.

Title: Guidance on methods for analysing data from EQ-5D instruments
Abstract: A complete draft of the book was completed in 2019. The deliverable from the project was a book, published by Springer in 2020, called 'Methods for analysing and reporting EQ-5D data'. Publication of the book was accompanied by a Euroqol-hosted online book launch/event where the authors presented. The book is available open access, and has been widely accessed and cited since its publication: https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-47622-9. To date, the book has been downloaded 70k times, and has an altmetric score of 41; in google scholar it has 220 citations.

Title: Validating the Vision Bolt-on for EQ-5D-5L in three health conditions: Content Validity (Patients, Caregivers, Clinicians) and Quantitative Psychometrics with Responsiveness to Intervention
Abstract: Background:Although a vision bolt-on has been developed to enhance the sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L in populations with visual impairment, evidence on its psychometric properties in relevant clinical populations remains limited. In particular, there is insufficient evidence on how well the bolt-on captures variation in vision-related health across different levels of impairment or between self- and proxy reports. Furthermore, uncertainties remain regarding the optimal wording (e.g., vision vs. seeing), the inclusion of visual aids (e.g., glasses or contact lenses), the use of examples or definitions to aid interpretation.Objectives:This study aims to evaluate the content and construct validity, known-group validity, responsiveness, test–retest reliability, and proxy–patient agreement of alternative versions of the vision bolt-on in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), cataract, and visual complications of diabetes, supported by insights from caregivers and clinicians.Methods:A mixed-methods design will be employed. The qualitative phase will involve approximately 21 patients (7 for each condition), 21 caregivers (7 for each condition), and 7 clinicians, using the topic guide to explore interpretation, relevance, and preferences concerning wording, aids, examples. The quantitative phase will include about 300 patients (≈100 AMD, ≈100 cataract, ≈100 visual complications of diabetes) assessed at two time points. Caregivers will be invited to provide proxy assessments, enabling patient–proxy agreement analyses assessed. Data will be collected at two time points: before and after intervention (anti-VEGF therapy or cataract surgery); two visits for managing visual complications of diabetes. Psychometric evaluation will cover construct validity, known-group validity, responsiveness and proxy–patient agreement, using the Chinese NEI-VFQ-9 and clinical indicators such as visual acuity and contrast sensitivity.

Title: Combining health and social outcomes using the EQ-5D-5L and the ASCOT – development of a pilot value set
Abstract: To allocate scarce health care resources equitably across a population we have to be able to measure and value all the outcomes that matter to the population. Current measurement systems focus mostly on health, and rarely on both health and social outcomes together. This project proposed and investigated a novel solution to combining the measurement of health and social outcomes, and to valuing them on the same scale. A key advantage of the approach is that it is based on combining the EQ-5D-5L with another well-established instrument – the ASCOT – to measure and value health-related quality of life and social care related quality of life together. The advantage of such an approach is that it uses the EQ-5D-5L as the basis for combining the domains of health and social care. This builds on earlier EuroQol funded work by the project team examining preferences for the EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT dimensions, using a discrete choice experiment approach. In this study we developed a conceptual framework for developing a combined instrument and conducted psychometric analysis to investigate overlap between EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT to identify key domains that should be included in a combined instrument. We conducted DCE research to explore interactions between the two instruments and qualitative research to refine wording for a valuation study using DCE methods.

Title: Content validity and measurement properties of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L in epilepsy patients in a low-income setting
Abstract: Abstract Introduction: Despite epilepsy affects health related quality of life significantly, there has been no study that assessed the content validity and measurement properties of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L in low-income settings, where the disease burden is highest. Therefore, the study aims to assess the content validity and measurement properties of the Amharic versions of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L among patients with epilepsy. Method: Mixed-method study was conducted from December 2025-May 2026 among 200 patients with epilepsy. The participants completed the EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS, and PHQ-9. Measurement properties were assessed in terms of feasibility, preferences, ceiling effects, redistribution and consistency, informativity, test-retest reliability, convergent and known groups’ validity. Test-retest reliability was assessed using ICC and Cohen’s weighted kappa coefficient. Convergent validity was assessed using the Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between EQ-5D index scores and the EQ-VAS scores, and known-groups validity was assessed using Mann-Whitney U/Kruskal-Wallis tests. Informativity was determined by calculating the Shannon index (H ′) and Shannon’s Evenness index (J ′). Content validity was explored using focus groups and in-depth interviews with health professionals and care-givers.  Thematic analysis was conducted for the qualitative data.Results: The EQ-5D-5L showed lower ceiling effects (24.0% vs. 29.5%) and higher absolute informativity with mean gain of 31.2% compared to EQ-5D-3L. Both versions index scores demonstrated strong convergent validity with EQ-VAS (3L: r= 0.706; 5L: r= 0.732). Both EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L indicated good known-groups validity with the EQ-5D-5L providing higher mean index score across the sub-groups. Both versions demonstrated acceptable test-retest reliability with slightly higher ICC for the EQ-5D-3L (3L ICC = 0.83; 5L ICC = 0.73). Feasibility was excellent with 100% completion rate for both the questionnaires and 93.5% of the participants preferred EQ-5D-5L. The qualitative findings confirmed that all EQ-5D dimensions as relevant. However, cognition, memory, fatigue, sleep, stigma and social relationship emerged as the most critical missing dimension requiring bolt-ons.Conclusion: Both EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L indicated good measurement properties and content validity. The EQ-5D-5L performed better in terms of ceiling, informativity and preferences and  the qualitative findings confirmed the relevance of all the existing EQ-5D dimensions. We recommend the use of EQ-5D-5L in HRQoL assessments and routine clinical practice in this setting. Further research on epilepsy-specific bolt-ons is needed to improve comprehensiveness and sensitivity.

Title: Comparison of the EQ-5D-5L to measures of well-being and capability in an older population
Abstract: Formal and informal social care support is an important input for individuals with long term conditions (LTCs) as they can help maintain well-being even where health is not improving. Health related quality of life measures such as EQ-5D may capture some of the impact of social care but may miss out on aspects such as independence and control and new measures such as the ICECAP-O, ASCOT or well-being have been recommended as alternatives. The overall aim of this study is to compare the new 5 level version of EQ-5D to these new ‘beyond health measures’ in a longitudinal study in order to examine the extent to which EQ-5D already captures the ‘beyond health’ domains covered in these measures. LTCs are more prevalent in older populations therefore participants aged over 65 with and without LTCs will be recruited from the South Yorkshire Cohort, an on-going study, and followed up for a year. The EQ-5D as well as the measures that go beyond health will be administered in a survey alongside health and social service use questions. The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L viz. reliability, validity and responsiveness will be tested against several indicators. The ability of the EQ-5D-5L to predict well-being compared to the other measures will also be tested. Results will provide information on the performance of the EQ-5D-5L in a large elderly population as well as whether it captures aspects that go beyond health such as social care use.

Title: Building in latent class support to xreg R package – simplifying access to linear and non-linear, latent class, random effects, censored/interval, and hybrid regression methods
Abstract: We have developed the R package hyreg2, which enables the estimation of EQ-5D-5L value sets based on the hybrid model. To account for preference heterogeneity, latent class estimation is implemented using the EM-algorithm, as available in the flexmix package. Our package adopts the data preparation and E-step from flexmix and introduces a new M-step incorporating the likelihood of the hybrid model. In addition, hyreg2 provides functions for summarizing and visualizing results (summary, plot). The package further allows for modeling heteroscedasticity and estimating partial coefficients, thereby extending the methodological possibilities beyond those available in hyreg (Stata) or xreg (R). Importantly, hyreg2 follows the typical input conventions of R. The package was submitted to CRAN on September 30, 2025. Until it is published there, it can be installed using use devtools::install_github("Selk19/hyreg2").Its functionalities were evaluated in a simulation and case study. For this purpose, two simulated datasets as well as the publicly available EQ-5D dataset (https://github.com/intelligentaccident/EQ5D_data) were used. The results demonstrated that controlling for groups (i.e. participants) is essential; without it, the model tends to group all TTO data to one class and all DCE data to the other. While group control is already available for the E-step, this functionality is unfortunately not yet implemented in the M-step. In particular, the analyses with the EQ-5D dataset highlight that hyreg2 is highly able to account for preference heterogeneity in the TTO data. Best results are generated using a two-step approach, which is also implemented in the package: First latent classes are uncovered only on the TTO data and afterwards on these classes the hybrid model is used on the TTO and DCE data to estimate the value sets.

Title: Longitudinal Assessment of the EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression Dimension in Cancer Patients with Emotional Distress: Structural Validity, Responsiveness, and Subgroup Performance Compared with PHQ-4 and HADS
Abstract: Depression and anxiety are common among individuals with cancer and significantly affect their quality of life and treatment outcomes. The EQ-5D-5L is a widely used instrument to measure health-related quality of life (HRQoL), but the performance of its Anxiety/Depression (A/D) dimension remains uncertain, particularly in oncology populations. This project aims to evaluate the validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L A/D dimension over time in patients experiencing emotional distress related to cancer.Using secondary data from the REDUCT clinical trial (N = 473), which followed participants at baseline, 4, and 7 months, we will apply longitudinal Item Response Theory (IRT) models to assess convergent validity, and responsiveness. The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4) will serve as reference measures. We will further examine differential item functioning (DIF) across age and psychiatric history subgroups to test for measurement bias.This study will provide the first longitudinal evidence on the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L A/D dimension in cancer care, supporting more accurate use of this measure in assessing mental health-related quality of life in clinical and economic evaluations.

Title: The sequential relief of child health problems: a preference path elicited by a kaizen task
Abstract: In the proposed PhD project, we conducted (1) a series of simulation studies of choice analysis (2 publications); (2) developed and implemented kaizen tasks for child health valuation (1 publication; 1 under review); (3) assessed the effects of child age and problem duration (1 under review); and (4) examined heterogeneity in preferences between subgroups (1 under review). With the support of this project, Maksat Jumamyradov completed his doctoral degree in Economics from the University of South Florida, Tampa, USA. His thesis is titled, "Essays in the Econometrics of Choice Analysis with Applications in Health Economics" (see attached).

Title: Mapping of Y5L from EQ-5D-5L in the population of orthopaedic paediatric patients in Hong Kong
Abstract: Background and objective The use of EQ-5D-5L has been demonstrated capable and reliable of rejecting the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of orthopaedic paediatric patients including those with idiopathic scoliosis. However, with the development of EQ-5D-Y-5L (Y5L) being more appropriate for children and young adolescents, currently there is a lack of an interim step for the transition from the adult form of EQ-5D-5L to the use of Y5L before Y5L can be well-established in multiple specialties of medicine. Proposed methods This is a mapping study of EQ-5D-5L and Y5L in the population of orthopaedic paediatric patients in Hong Kong. Specific conditions of interests include scoliosis, leg or limb length discrepancy, developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), and any orthopaedic fractures from trauma leading to consultation visits at the orthopaedic specialist clinics or being admitted to the orthopaedic wards. Patients must be 12 to 18 years of age. This study aims to establish prediction models for mapping EQ-5D-5L onto Y5L with adjustment for patient demographic and clinical characteristics in these orthopaedic paediatric patients. We propose to recruit patients in the orthopaedic specialist clinics and orthopaedic wards using quota sampling, based on treatment modality of initiation of treatment or pre-operation as compared to regular follow-up or observation only to obtain sufficient number of patients with severe, moderate or mild health state in the study population. Patients are asked to fill in the following questionnaires at the same visit: EQ-5D-5L, Y5L, Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 generic core scales and disease-specific Scoliosis-Research Society-22 items refined (SRS-22r) questionnaire for patients with scoliosis and Oxford Hip Score for patients with DDH. EQ-5D-5L and Y5L will each be tested for its relationship with PedsQL 4.0 and with disease-specific measures via correlation tests. The strength of correlation with other questionnaires will then be compared between EQ-5D-5L versus Y5L. The agreement of each dimension and index score of EQ-5D-5L and Y5L will also be examined. Prediction models for mapping of EQ-5D-5L and Y5L will be established using the response mapping method. Multiple mapping functions will be built through Bayesian networks and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, and these models will be compared before deriving the response mapping table and algorithm with best model performance for the Y5L conversion from EQ-5D-5L dimension responses. We will also use the adult EQ-5D-5L Hong Kong value set for estimating the utility scores from both the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L responses. Continuous mapping models between Y-5L utility scores and adult -5L utility scores will be established. It is expected such converting algorithm will be useful for clinical use of transferring previously captured HRQoL in EQ-5D-5L into Y5L from retrospective data, which can be compared with future assessment using the Y5L.

Title: Advancing the interpretation and dissemination of EQ-5D and EQ VAS outcomes across general populations and clinical contexts
Abstract: This project successfully disseminated findings from four distinct studies at two premier international conferences: the International Society for Quality of Life Research (ISOQOL) 32nd Annual Conference and the 11th Annual Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) International Conference, both held in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA, in October 2025.At the ISOQOL conference, two oral presentations were delivered. The first, "Exploring Variability in EQ VAS scores: A Systematic Review and Meta-regression of Population Health Studies", was selected as a 2025 New Investigator Oral Presentation Award Finalist. This meta-regression identified that comorbidity prevalence and geographical region (specifically Asia versus Europe) are significant drivers of variability in the EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale (EQ VAS), supporting its utility for cross-regional health comparisons. The second oral presentation, "Measuring What Matters in Primary Care: Health-Related Quality of Life and Its Predictors Among Users of Public Primary Care Clinics in Singapore Using the EQ-5D-5L", analysed data from public polyclinics in Singapore. It highlighted that higher health activation and the absence of comorbidities were linked to better health-related quality of life (HRQoL), whereas Malay ethnicity was associated with lower scores, underscoring significant health disparities.At the PROMIS conference, two poster presentations were delivered. The first, "Differential responsiveness and minimally important differences of patient-reported outcomes: truth or artefact?", revealed that Minimally Important Difference (MID) estimates for the EQ-5D index in spine surgery patients are highly dynamic. The analysis showed perioperative MIDs (0.42) were significantly larger than postoperative MIDs (0.09). This suggests that a response shift—a change in patients' internal standards of measurement—may be at play, urging caution when using global anchors to assess change. The second poster, "Patient-reported outcomes and their associated factors at 1- and 2-year follow-up after lumbar spine surgery", found that patients experienced the largest improvements in pain/discomfort and social functioning one-year post-surgery, with factors like poorer baseline Patient-Reported Outcomes (PROs) and higher education predicting better outcomes.Collectively, this project advanced the scientific understanding of EuroQol instruments by providing key evidence on population-level variability, primary care applications, and critical methodological considerations for interpreting MIDs in surgical populations.

Title: Comparing Bolt-On Item variants for Fatigue, Sleep, and Vision in the General Chinese Population
Abstract: Fatigue, sleep, and vision are among the most commonly used EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons, with multiple alternative wordings. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the psychometric performance of the following bolt-on variants: (1) fatigue (FA) vs. tiredness (TI); (2) vision without reference to vision aids (VI) vs. VI with aids (VI-A); and (3) sleep (SL) vs. sleep with examples in the dimension title (SL-E). A representative sample of 1,262 adults in Hong Kong completed an online survey including the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons. The following psychometric properties were assessed: ceiling/floor, informativity (Shannon indices), convergent validity (correlations with conceptually related items of PROMIS-29+2), agreement (Kendall’s tau), explanatory power (regression on EQ VAS and PROMIS-29+2 LSS), and known-group validity (effect sizes). Bolt-ons reduced EQ-5D-5L’s ceiling from 35% to 20-24% and improved relative informativity from 0.33 to 0.35–0.36. FA, TI, SL and SL-E demonstrated moderate-to-strong convergent validity (r=0.55–0.67) with PROMIS-29+2 items. All bolt-ons with the exception of VI-A enhanced explanatory power for both EQ VAS and PROMIS-29+2. Agreements between TI and FA (0.71), SL and SL-E (0.74), and VI and VI-A (0.78) were strong. For each of the three bolt-on pairs, differences in reducing the EQ-5D-5L’s ceiling, relative informativity and convergent validity were generally small. Based on known-group comparisons, TI, SL-E and VI slightly outperformed their counterparts.  All six bolt-on items showed good validity in a general population sample, with minimal differences between items belonging to the same bolt-on pair. These findings inform item development for the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox.

Title: The impact of partial profile designs on the valuation of health states
Abstract: Partial profile presentation of discrete choice experiment (DCE) choice tasks can be used to simplify health state valuations and reduce the burden on participating respondents. However, research has shown that presenting choice tasks with partial profilescan produce nonequivalent coefficient estimates to the case of presenting as full profiles. This study aimed to examine whether respondents’ tendency to infer missing attribute information can bring the discrepancy of parameter estimates between DCEs withfull versus partial profile presentation. At first, DCE data with two study arms (one with the full profile presentation and the other with the partial profile presentation) were used to examine the differences in EQ-5D-5L parameter estimates depending onthe presentation format. Then, three different models capturing the effect of respondents’ inference for absent attributes in choice tasks with the partial profile presentation were investigated based on three different data sets with varying methods to simulate respondents’ inference behavior. The results showed that DCEs with the partial profiles produced significantly different estimates from the case of the full profile presentation. However, we did not find significant evidence on the effect of inferring absent attributes in DCEs with the partial profile presentation. Nonetheless, we recommend being cautious about using choice tasks with partial profiles as respondents are likely to have structurally different health state values depending on the presentation format.

Title: Valuing Health Trajectories: Developing a Framework for Duration and Sequence-Adjusted Quality-Adjusted Life Years
Abstract: This research proposal investigates whether health state valuations should account for duration and sequence effects, rather than assuming values are independent of temporal context as current QALY calculations do. While standard practice values health states over fixed 10-year periods followed by death, real patient journeys involve dynamic health fluctuations, and evidence suggests people value health states differently depending on their duration and what follows them.The study proposes a mathematical framework where health state values depend on duration, sequence (improvement, deterioration, or death), severity, and potential interactions. The research comprises four stages: (1) developing a theoretical framework through systematic literature review, (2) conducting a discrete choice experiment across Netherlands and Australia to estimate temporal adjustment parameters, (3) validating findings against modified time trade-off studies, and (4) applying the framework to health economic models to assess impacts on cost-effectiveness analyses.This work aims to improve descriptive accuracy by capturing how people actually value health trajectories, while examining normative implications for resource allocation decisions. The framework could enable more realistic QALY calculations that better reflect preferences, though it may introduce challenges like path-dependent valuations requiring careful ethical consideration.

Title: An evaluation of the feasibility and acceptability of the use of the digital version of the EQ-5D 3L in routine care in a busy HIV care clinic in Harare, Zimbabwe.
Abstract: The study had three main aims. First, we translated and upgraded the EQ-5D from the 3L version to the 5L version. Next, we evaluated the measurement equivalency between the paper and digital versions of the EQ-5D 5L Shona version. Finally, we explored the feasibility and acceptability of the digital version, including the barriers and facilitators associated with its implementation in a busy HIV care clinic. Our findings showed the measurement equivalency of digital and paper versions of the EQ-5D 5L in Shona version. Thus, both versions can be used confidently in routine clinical care and research. Additionally, the anxiety/depression item on the EQ-5D 5L demonstrated strong diagnostic accuracy for screening anxiety and depression, outperforming multi-item and condition-specific screeners. Lastly, our pilot study indicates that integrating the digital version of the EQ-5D into HIV care in a low-resource setting is feasible and acceptable. Consequently, a follow-up definitive trial using the EQ-5D 5L is needed to assess the implementation and cost-effectiveness of digital mental health monitoring

Title: The impact of color coding and the optimal degree of overlap in discrete choice experiments
Abstract: 2016410 was an extension of 2015430 on overlap and color-coding, where we demonstrated that implementing overlap and color-coding improves DCE data a lot. That study resulted in two highly cited papers. The 2016410 extension project aimed to run a similar study with some extra’s, involving varying the amount overlap to identify the optimal amount. Data collection has been completed as planned.

Title: Comparison of patient and proxy reported global cognition, fatigue, and sleep bolt-ons in stroke
Abstract: BackgroundCognitive impairment is common after stroke and substantially affects patients’ independence and quality of life. While the EQ-5D-5L is widely used for assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL), it does not explicitly capture cognitive functioning, sleep disturbance, and fatigue. The recently developed global cognition bolt-on, along with sleep and fatigue items, may enhance measurement precision in this population. However, stroke often limits patients’ ability to self-report, necessitating proxy assessment. To date, no study has compared patient and proxy reporting using the EQ-5D-5L with the cognition and additional bolt-ons in stroke.Objective This study aims to quantify agreement and systematic differences between patient and proxy assessments of health-related quality of life measured using the EQ-5D-5L with the cognition, sleep, and fatigue bolt-ons, recognising that proxy ratings represent a distinct but complementary perspective. The secondary aim is to validate the bolt-ons by rater-type (self vs proxy).Methods Patients will complete the EQ‑5D‑5L with cognition, sleep, and fatigue bolt‑ons, while proxies will complete the proxy–proxy perspective (their own judgement of the patient’s HRQoL). Agreement will be assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for continuous outcomes, weighted Cohen’s κ for dimension‑level agreement, Bland–Altman plots for summary scores, correlations, and mean absolute error (MAE). Differences in mean Level Sum Scores (LSS) will be examined. Ceiling and floor effects will be evaluated. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted on the core EQ‑5D‑5L dimensions and bolt‑on items to assess construct validity.Expected outcomesThe study will provide the first evidence on the reliability and validity of proxy-reported EQ-5D-5L instruments incorporating cognition, sleep, and fatigue bolt-ons in stroke. Findings will establish baseline agreement between patient and proxy HRQoL assessments and evaluate the added value of these bolt‑ons for capturing broader aspects of post‑stroke HRQoL.ImpactResults will guide EuroQol’s further development of the cognition, sleep, and fatigue bolt-ons; strengthen their applicability in clinical and health technology assessment settings; and enhance the precision and comprehensiveness of HRQoL measurement in stroke and other conditions associated with cognitive or communication impairment.

Title: Using EQ-5D to measure health status in Chinese populations during the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: Since the new coronavirus (COVID-19) first emerged in Wuhan China at the end of 2019, the virus has spread to more than 200 countries and territories around the world. China was the first country to report COVID-19 cases and to impose strict lockdown, quarantine and outdoor restrictions. This research aims to investigate the health status of Chinese people during this pandemic. It can also show the usefulness of EQ-5D in describing health status in this global health crisis. We carried out an online questionnaire survey to collect health status information from the Chinese general population. EQ-5D-5L was used as the major component of our survey. Respondents’ sociodemographic information was also collected. The survey was distributed via the WeChat platform to Chinese mainland citizens living in Hubei (the lockdown province) and outside Hubei between February and March 2020, and to Chinese citizens living abroad between mid-March and April 2020. Data of the current survey will be compared with data collected in previous Chinese National Health Services Surveys, in terms of the likelihood of having any problems in all EQ-5D dimensions and mean VAS scores. Among respondents living in their home country, people living in Hubei province will be compared with those living outside Hubei. Health status of overseas respondents will be compared with that of respondents at home.

Title: Testing hearing bolt-on and other bolt-ons related to hearing function in individuals receiving hearing aids or cochlear implantation
Abstract: We propose a study to test the hearing bolt-on and other related bolt-ons in EuroQol's bolt-on toolbox. We will recruit individuals with clinically diagnosed hearing impairment who will receive hearing aids (n=200) or cochlear implantation (n=100) from a tertiary hospital in Finland. We will assess the patients before and after their hearing aid fitting or cochlear implantation using EQ-5D-5L, hearing bolt-on and other bolt-ons the bolt-on research programme recommends, hearing function questionnaires, and hearing tests. We will adopt the data analysis protocol developedby the bolt-on research programme to assess the acceptability, distributional characteristics, ceiling/floor effects, test-retest reliability, convergent validity, known-groups validity, and responsiveness of the bolt-ons. We will also assess the bolt-ons using exploratory factor analysis and item response theory (IRT) models. We have no plan to develop new bolt-ons, test bolt-ons outside the main and exploratory Toolboxes, or conduct qualitative assessment of any existing bolt-ons in this project, unless the bolt-on research programme wishes us to do so. We will follow the data analysis protocol developed by the bolt-on toolbox validation programme, if available and recommended, to assess the included bolt-ons.

Title: Assessing the Impact of Transitioning from Pediatric to Adult Care on the HRQoL of Adolescents with Complex Health Conditions: A 5-Year Longitudinal Registry Study in Los Angeles County Using the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: As medical technology has advanced, the population of children with special healthcare needs has steadily grown to nearly 20%. These children: “have or are at increased risk for chronic physical, developmental, behavioral or emotional conditions and who also require health and related services of a type or amount beyond that required by children generally”.  At Children’s Hospital Los Angeles (CHLA), the Center for Healthy Adolescent Transition (CHAT) is developing a registry to track pediatric patients with special healthcare needs as they age from pediatric (age 16) to adult care (age 21) with a 5-year follow-up. Medical specialties include, but are not limited to, hematology, rheumatology, medical genetics, cardiology, endocrinology, neurology, nephrology, and oncology. The CHAT registry presents a unique opportunity to assess children with special healthcare needs over time, including their health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL). The objectives of this study are to use the EQ-5D-5L in the CHAT registry to 1) assess the HRQoL of the medically complex children in Los Angeles County; 2) evaluate the sensitivity of EQ-5D-5L in detecting changes in HRQoL among these children transitioning to adult care; and 3) compare the sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L to that of the PedsQL in measuring HRQoL. In doing so, we hope to establish health state utility values among children with special healthcare needs; assess how HRQoL changes over time as adolescents transition into adulthood; and validate the EQ-5D-5L as an appropriate measure to assess health status in a transitioning pediatric population with special healthcare needs.

Title: Repeatability and validity of instructed and non-instructed EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-ons in age-related macular degeneration and diabetic eye disease
