Abstract: This project is a 12-month study aiming to test and validate the EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-on item. The EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-on has not been fully tested against existing, established measures in vision in clinical populations. A major point of debate is how to instruct patients about wearing glasses or contact lenses when answering the vision question.The project aim is to determine whether this vision bolt-on item is reliable and valid in people with two major eye diseases: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) and Diabetic Eye Disease (DED), and in comparison to responses from the general public who do not have these conditions.The project will test several versions of the vision bolt-on:Non-instructed bolt-on (Vision 1): The current "best available" version that does not mention glasses or visual aids.Instructed “exploratory” bolt-on (Vision 2 and 3): Exploratory versions that specifically tells the patient to answer with their visual aids ("with glasses or other aids if you use them") from the EuroQol bolt-on Toolbox.Exploratory bolt-on (Vision 4): One additional experimental version from the EuroQol bolt-on Toolbox.To assess and compare the validity of the bolt-ons, the project will also use a proven, established measure: the VILL-UI (Vision Impairment in Low Luminance questionnaire – utility instrument) derived from the VILL-33 patient-reported outcome measure. This instrument is already validated across multiple European countries in AMD and DED and serves as an ideal standard for comparison. The study will recruit participants from the UK (London) and Germany (Bonn) to ensure the bolt-ons work in different languages and contexts:1. Clinical Population (n=300)This core group includes 300 patients (150 with AMD, 150 with DED), split evenly between the UK and Germany. Each patient will complete the EQ-5D-5L and all vision bolt-ons, along with the VILL-33 (including the VILL-UI items), twice over a short interval (two to four weeks).2. General Population (n=2,000)A large market research panel of 2,000 adults (1,000 from the UK, 1,000 from Germany) from the general public will be recruited. This sample will be used to determine if the bolt-on is truly capturing vision problems related to eye disease or if similar response patterns are seen in the general, non-clinical population.In addition, since there is no German translation of the vision bolt-on candidate items (Vision 1,2,3,4) a small group of 10 patients will ensure the German translation of the bolt-on is culturally and linguistically accurate. Translation will follow the EuroQol Version Management Committee guidelines for Toolbox items. The analysis will follow EuroQol guidelines for psychometric analysis of the bolt-on toolbox and will focus on several areas, including:Convergent and divergent validity: Comparing the results of the instructed and non-instructed bolt-ons against the VILL-UI in clinical and general populations.Known group validity: Testing the bolt-on's ability to accurately distinguish between people with and without eye disease and across severity groups within AMD and DED.Test-retest reliability: Checking the consistency of the bolt-on results over time where vision has not changed in clinical populations. Ceiling effects: Examining the presence of ceiling effects of the vision bolt-ons against the VILL-UI in clinical versus general populations.Since there is currently no official value set for the new EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-on, the study will use a summary score (level sum score) for analyses.

Title: Think of the children: rationale for and implications of the perspective in EQ-5D-Y-3L health state valuation
Abstract: •The EQ-5D-Y facilitates the description and measurement of child and adolescent health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in economic evaluations of health technologies. The recently published standardized valuation protocol prescribes the use of a child perspective, rather than the individual perspective used for valuation of adult EQ-5D health states. An EQ-5D-Y value set is not yet available; however, the limited evidence so far indicates that a child perspective yields different utilities for similar EQ-5D health states. •The choice for and implications of using a child perspective for EQ-5D-Y health state valuation has received little attention. As it is important to understand the reasons for this change and what influence a different perspective has, the objective of this paper is to address this gap in the literature and discuss the rationale for using a child perspective, in comparison to using the conventional individual perspective, and the normative and practical implications of a child perspective for EQ-5D-Y value sets and estimation of HRQOL gains in children and adolescents in economic evaluations. •Although the use of an individual perspective for valuation of EQ-5D-Y health states is possible, it may not be suitable or desirable. However, the discussion of several implications of using a child perspective makes it clear that using this perspective may impact (the development of) EQ-5D-Y value sets and ultimately also reimbursement decisions in healthcare. Further research is necessary for gaining insight into the extent to which this impact is (not) empirically and normatively justified.

Title: HRQoL among patients seeking treatment for abuse of illicit substances
Abstract: The project has been severely delayed due to a number of factors. First, the regulations around patient data security were changed, resulting in a long process of getting everything approved. When this was in place, co-investigator Espen Arnevik had changed his formal position, and Rand was considerably more busy than anticipated. The result was an intermittent process of writing by relay, eventually resulting in submission of a manuscript in March of 2020. Fortunately for us (unfortunately for the field of research), there has been very little in the way of publication on HRQoL in SUD patients, and the manuscript is still relevant. Main methods 178 SUD patients were administered EQ-5D-3L at treatment start. SUD patients and a general population sample in the same age range were compared in terms of reported EQ-5D-3L health states, problems by dimension, UK index values, and EQ VAS scores. We investigated specific drug dependence, mental health disorders, sex, age, and education as predictors of EQ-5D-3L values and EQ VAS scores. Anxiety/depression dimension scores were compared to Hopkins symptom Checklist (HSCL-25) scores. Main results 91.6% of the patient sample reported problems on the EQ-5D-3L, with 29.8% reporting extreme problem. Corresponding proportions from the general population sample were 39.8% and 3.0%. The most frequently reported problems were for anxiety/depression, pain/discomfort, and usual activities. Mean UK index values were .59 (SUD) and .90 (general population). Mean VAS scores were 59.9 (SUD) and 84.1/general population). Regression analyses identified phobic anxiety diagnosis and cocaine dependence as statistically significant predictors of higher EQ-5D-3L index scores. Conclusions EQ-5D may be a useful and practical instrument for monitoring HRQoL in SUD patients, though there is need to demonstrate that the (ideally -5L version) instrument is sensitive to changes, not just to overall symptom burden.

Title: EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox exploration and validation in haematological malignancy. Example from a large UK population-based Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN)
Abstract: The project aims to assess the psychometric properties and performance of the best available items in the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox and compare the exploratory fatigue items among adults diagnosed with haematological malignancies (HMs) across all major subtypes (leukaemias, lymphomas, and myelomas) irrespective of treatment intent or disease stage. Data will be collected through the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN), a large UK population-based registry that includes all newly and previously diagnosed HM cases within a catchment of over four million people across 14 hospitals, offering an unique opportunity to capture the full spectrum of diagnosed HM patients and obtain representative real-world data beyond trials or online panels. Online survey will be administered through HMRN’s established infrastructure at two time points, following its routine six-monthly assessment schedule. Analyses will assess distribution characteristic, convergent validity, discriminant validity, known-group validity, structure validity, exploratory power and responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons, to provide evidence to support the development of the bolt-ons.

Title: Making LIFE simple: Exploration of a hybrid of best-worst scaling and visual analogue scale in valuing EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: The EQ-5D research community continues its endeavor in search for innovative methods to elicit preferences for health status measures such as the EQ-5D-5L, given the limitations and concerns among existing methods. Best worst scaling (BWS) is another choice-based technique which presents one health state at a time. This could potentially make the valuation task less cognitively demanding. Similar to other choice-based techniques, BWS also derives weights on a latent utility scale and thus cannot be directly used in quality-adjusted life year (QALY) calculation. In this proposal, we explore a new approach called BWS-VAS to directly deriving the impact weights on the full health-dead scale.

Title: Correcting bias in time trade-off within the EuroQol Valuation Technology
Abstract: Background: Time trade-off (TTO) valuation of EQ-5D-Y states by EuroQol will be performed using the perspective of a 10-year old child. However, TTO valuation is affected by several respondent characteristic (e.g. having children and subjective life expectancies) and time preference and loss aversion may lead to bias in TTO. We propose to study whether these effects are affected by movingthe perspective in TTO from adults valuing health states for themselves to that of a hypothetical child.Aim: To address existing questions faced by EuroQol andbridge the gap between earlier work onvariance andbias in TTO and EQ-VT, the aim of our proposal is to: i)Study to what extent TTO weights for EQ-5D-Y elicited in accordance with EQ-VT are affected by respondent characteristics suggested to lead to bias or variance in earlier work. ii)Compare the effect of such characteristics between valuation with a child or adult perspective.iii)Investigate the feasibility and validity of correcting for loss aversion and time preference in both perspectives.Methods:A general public sample will complete one of two EQ-5D-Y valuation tasks, where health states are either described to apply to themselves (self-perspective) or to a 10-year old child (child-perspective). Afterwards, demographics are collected and matched time preferences and loss aversion are elicited (i.e. for own life years or those of a child). The effects of (correcting for) these factors are compared between the two perspectives, and an extended feedback module is used to study validity of corrections.

Title: A fast-track proposal: write and publish a paper comparing DCE data from 11 Asian EQ-5D-5L valuation studies
Abstract: So far, 11Asian regions(China, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Philippine, Hong Kong, Vietnam, and Taiwan)have conducted their EQ-5D-5L valuation studies following EQ-VT protocol. Currently, there is no research comparing health preference focusing on Asian population. Notably, publishedresearchesaimedto compare the difference in the value set. A downside of directly comparing value set is that the differences identified may stem from 1) preference heterogeneity and 2) methodological differencesand it is difficult to detangle such differences .Despite the fact that all EQ-5D-5L valuation studies followed the EQ-VT protocol, different versions of EQ-VT protocol were developed to improve the quality of data collected using TTO method. Nevertheless,the design of DCE stayed intactfor all these valuation studies. Additionally, the DCE task was performed after the TTO task, which ensured that respondent already familiar with the EQ-5D-5L health description. Therefore, the highly standardized DCE data collection protocol offered a unique opportunity to study the health preference between countries.In this study, we utilize the DCE dataset of eleven Asian regions:first, each region’s data set wasmodelledusing a conditional logit main effect model. For comparison, we createddummy variable to represent different countries andmodelledtwo countries data together with the country variable as an interactionterm to test the differenceof the main effect variables. Next, Wecompared the relative importance of dimensions and relative utility decrements between each of the 5 levels for each country.

Title: Assessing older people's health related quality of life in aged care settings: unravelling the EQ-5D self-report proxy conundrum.
Abstract: This project focused on a program of work to address the unique challenges in measuring quality of life with older people in aged care. There is ongoing debate surrounding the ability of frail older people with cognitive impairment and dementia to self-report their own health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Despite increasing calls for inclusivity and self-assessment of HRQoL where ever possible, proxy-assessment of older people’s HRQoL (by family members or health/aged care professionals) is often used as the default option. This project applied an innovative mixed methods approach, incorporating qualitative think aloud and eye tracking technology in older people who self-completed the EQ-5D-5L, along with proxy family member data collection of HRQoL using the EQ-5D-5L from two proxy perspectives; proxy-proxy and resident-proxy. The project has facilitated a more detailed understanding of the impact of cognitive impairment and dementia on self-assessed HRQoL for older people in residential aged care settings using the EQ-5D-5L. The project has also provided an assessment of the impact of proxy perspective on the inter-rater agreement of self- and proxy-reported quality of life.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: Walk the talk: Would you let your child take part in health state valuation research?
Abstract: This study examined whether people involved in health valuation research would allow their own children to participate in health state valuation tasks. An online survey of 166 respondents, including EuroQol members and non-members, asked about consent for children aged 8–17 years to complete discrete choice experiment (DCE) and time trade-off (TTO) tasks, alongside questions on professional experience and views about child involvement in valuation. Willingness to consent increased with child age and was consistently higher for DCE than TTO. For DCE, consent rose from 53.4% among children aged 8–10 years to 95.3% among those aged 16–17 years; for TTO, it increased from 29.9% to 88.0%. Most respondents preferred valuation studies to include both adults and children rather than children alone. EuroQol members were more likely to support taxpayer-based arguments in valuation. Having a child in the relevant age range was strongly associated with willingness to consent to DCE participation, whereas being a parent alone was not. Respondents generally supported involving children in decisions about their health and quality of life, but those who viewed valuation tasks as ethically inappropriate for children or supported taxpayer arguments were less likely to consent. Overall, support for involving children in valuation research was substantial but depended on child age, valuation method, and respondents’ experience and views. The findings suggest that child health valuation studies should use age-appropriate, method-sensitive approaches and focus particularly on older adolescents, while also indicating that concerns about involving children may be less pronounced than often assumed.

Title: Writing a manuscript titled 'valuation of health outcomes using the time trade-off technique: the EuroQol protocols' for publication in the journal of Pharmacoeconomics
Abstract: The time trade‐off (TTO) valuation technique is widely used to determine utility values of health outcomes to inform calculations of quality adjusted life years (QALYs) for use in economice valuation. Protocols for implementing TTO vary in aspects including the trade‐off framework, iteration procedure and its administration model and method, training of respondents and interviewers, and quality control of data collection. The most widely studied and utilized TTO valuation protocols are the Measurement and Valuation of Health (MVH) protocol, the Paris protocol, and the EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ‐VT) protocol, all developed by members of the EuroQol Group. The MVH protocol and its successor, the Paris protocol, are developed for valuation of EQ‐5D‐3L health states. Both protocols are designed for a trained interviewer to elicit preferences from a respondent using the conventional TTO framework with a fixed time horizon of 10years and an iteration procedure combining bisection and titration. Developed for valuation of EQ‐5D‐5L health states, the EQ‐VT protocol adopts a composite TTO framework and makes use of computer technology to facilitate data collection. Training and monitoring of interviewers and respondents is a pivotal component of the EQ‐VT protocol. Research is under way aiming to further improve the EuroQol protocols which form an important basis for the current practice of health technology assessment in many countries.

Title: An online DCE study to support the development of an EQ-5D-Y value set for the UK
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D is the most widely used health-related quality of life questionnaire in cost-utility analysis internationally, and a version of it, the EQ-5D-Y, has been developed for use with young people. Recent work from members of the EuroQol Group has demonstrated that using existing adult EQ-5D-3L value sets for EQ-5D-Y states is inappropriate. New valuation exercises are needed for the EQ-5D-Y but these face a number of challenges not present in the adult counterparts. For example, if adults complete these new exercises, then what perspective should they use in evaluating the states: their own health or the health of a child? If children/adolescents’ preferencesare sought, what elicitation task should be used to obtain them? There is no clear guidance about these issues in the literature, but research conducted to date provide some directions. Such guidance suggests that if adults are asked to value EQ-5D-Y states, they should consider the health of a child and if children/adolescents are included in the task, then a choice-based method such as discrete choice experiment (DCE) might be preferable to approaches such as time trade-off or standard gamble. The aim of this study was to obtain latent scale discrete choice utilities from adults in the general population to develop a future EQ-5D-Y value set in the United Kingdom. Methods: Preferences were obtained using a DCE from a representative sample in terms of age, gender, social grade and nation, of adult members of the UK general population belonging to an online panel. Adults completed the valuation survey from the perspective of a 10-year-old child. A blocked Bayesian efficient design was used to identify pairs of health states, with fifteen pairs presented to each respondent. DCE data were modelled using a main effects multinomial logit and mixed logit models. Model performance was evaluated using goodness-of-it assessed with Akaike information and Bayesian information criteria, and probability prediction accuracy. Results: 1,000 participants completed the survey and overall the distribution of demographics was similar to the UK general population. The modelling exercise suggested consistent latent utilities forboth multinomial logit and mixed logit models. Mixed logit yielded better goodness-of-fit as indicatedby the smaller AIC and BIC and more accurate probability predictions compared to the MNL. Conclusion: Our paper has produced a latent scale EQ-5D-Y value set. The next step will be to combine this latent scale utility function with the most appropriate method to anchor it on the quality-adjusted life years (QALY) scale to obtain a potential EQ-5D-Y value set in the UK. A separate study is underway to test alternative approaches to anchoring.

Title: Investigating Boundary-Induced non-additivity in cTTO and DCE Valuation Models: A cross-study analysis of ten EQ-5D-5L valuation datasets
Abstract: Emerging research suggests that EQ-5D valuations may exhibit non-additive preferences, where the combined disutility of multiple health problems is smaller than the sum of their individual effects. Recent studies have shown that this pattern can arise not only from true preference structures but also from boundary-induced compression caused by the limited valuation range of bounded tasks such as composite Time Trade-Off (cTTO). This study aims to disentangle these two mechanisms by comparing how interaction effects manifest across cTTO and Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) data.Using ten existing EQ-5D-5L valuation datasets that each include both cTTO and DCE components collected with the standardized EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT 2.0), we will estimate four alternative model specifications: (1) dimension-specific interactions (e.g. pain/discomfort × anxiety/depression), (2) count-based severity terms (e.g. N45), (3) data-driven two-way severe-level interactions, and (4) a non-linear power model capturing general curvature in disutility. Model performance will be assessed by RMSE, AIC, BIC, and adjusted R².By comparing interaction patterns between bounded (cTTO) and unbounded (DCE) data, the study will quantify the extent to which observed non-additivity reflects genuine preferences versus boundary effects. Cross-study comparisons will then identify whether consistent interaction structures emerge across countries or if effects are context-specific.

Title: Content validity and cognitive debriefing of the EQ-5D-5L Vision bolt-on in patients with Inherited Retinal Dystrophies
Abstract: Background: Vision loss due to rare eye diseases (RED) such as inherited retinal dystrophies (IRD) has tremendous psychosocial, emotional and functional consequences, with attendant effects on quality of life. Generic Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) measures like the EQ-5D-5L may underrepresent these impacts. To inform cost-effectiveness analyses of new interventions, Health technology assessments (HTA) rely on accurate HRQoL data. In the absence of such data for novel gene therapies, HTA bodies rely on HRQoL estimates from unrelated ocular diseases, which poorly reflect the experiences of patients with IRD due to differences in pathology and age profile. To address these gaps, EuroQol has developed a Vision bolt-on within the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox, currently undergoing psychometric validation.Objectives: We aim to assess the content validity of four versions of the EQ-5D-5L Bolt-on Toolbox Vision bolt-on in adults affected with IRDs through in-depth patient interviews and cognitive debriefing. Methods: A qualitative study will be conducted using semi-structured cognitive debriefing interviews with approximately 30 adults diagnosed with IRD, recruited via the SUL registry (Irish national node of the ERN-EYE–coordinated European REDgistry, which collects harmonised pseudonymised data on rare eye diseases using a shared governance framework). Respondents will complete and discuss 4 different versions of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox Vision bolt-on, including variations in wording (e.g. 'vision' vs. 'sight') and the in- or exclusion of visual aids (e.g. 'with glasses/contact lenses') to confirm that bolt-on items are meaningful, understandable, and relevant to IRD patients’ real-world experiences. Data will be analysed thematically following EuroQol guidance to identify issues related to clarity, relevance, and conceptual coverage.Expected outcomes: This study is expected to deliver robust qualitative evidence on the appropriateness of Vision bolt-on wording in IRD populations to inform EuroQol’s selection and refinement of items for the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox.

Title: Understanding Self-perceived Health in Latin America
Abstract: Background:Some studies depict the relationships between self-reported health socio-demographic factors and clinical conditions in the general population. The relationship between self-reported health with broader life domains, like the perception of law and order, corruption, civic engagement, and others has been less studied. In Latin America and the Caribbean, notably, there have been very few studies looking into these issues. The Gallup World Poll is a survey conducted periodically in more than 160 countries around the world. In the 2007 and 2008 version, the poll included 130 countries (20 from LAC) and self-reported health using EQ-5D-3L instrument. Clustering is a term used to refer to a setoftechniques that find subgroups in a data set, such that observations within each subgroup are as similar to each other as possible and as different as possible to observations in other subgroups. “Similarity” between observation is determined by the selection of a similarity/dissimilarity measure. The choice of the appropriate measure is made based on the type of data and knowledge of the data being analyzed. After choosing the dissimilarity measure, the clustering algorithm must be selected. For our study, we chose partitioning algorithms which include the K-means clustering algorithm and the Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) algorithm. In PAM clustering, each cluster is associated with a medoid, the object with the smallest dissimilarity to all other objects in the cluster, and is named after it. Objectives:a) Sociodemographic segmentation: Find subgroups of respondents determined by patterns of sociodemographic variables and assess if belonging to such subgroups predicts a difference in the EQ-VAS score.b) EQ-5D segmentation: Find subgroups determined by response to all items of EuroQol combined with age, education and income.Methods:The Gallup World Poll is a Survey conducted in over 150 countries, with randomly selected, nationally representative adult samples using a set of core questions. Most items havea dichotomous response set and are organized into22indexes.Survey samples are nationally representative of adults over 15 years old. Survey data is weighted to account for sampling, design effects, and margin of error.We eliminated cases not corresponding to one of the following Latin-Americancountries. 1. Argentina2. Belize3. Bolivia4. Brazil 5. Chile6. Colombia7. Costa Rica8. Dominican Republic9. Ecuador10. El Salvador11. Guatemala12. Guyana13. Honduras14. Mexico15. Nicaragua16. Panama17. Paraguay18. Peru19. Trinidad and Tobago20. Uruguay21. VenezuelaWe chose to work with the R statistical package and to limit the amount of computing power necessary for clustering algorithms, we chose to work with data for the year 2008. We created two datasets, one for each previously specified objective. For sociodemographic segmentation, we used the22indexes that summarize information from different domains, and we created a dissimilarity matrix using Euclidean distance, given that all variables were numeric. For EQ-5D segmentation we used the following variables:• Household Income per capita (International Dollars) • Age• Own Health Today –Visual analog scale coded as a continuous variable with a range from 0 to 10. • Mobility• Self-Care• Usual activities• Pain/Discomfort• Anxiety/Depression• EducationSince the data included numeric and categorical variables, we generated a dissimilarity matrix using Gower distance.We later implemented a PAM algorithm, accounting for weighted observations for both objectives. We used weightedaverage Silhouette to determine the best way to cluster the data. This process was applied to both distance matrices. In both cases, a range of 2 to 10 clusters was explored. Once every observation was assigned to a cluster through the described methods,we assessed whether belonging to a specific cluster predicted a change in EQ-5D-VAS score through linear regression. We included the EQ-5D-VAS as an outcome variable, cluster as a categorical variable and age and education as covariables.Results:After selecting the variables to be analyzed and restricting the observations to those recorded in 2008, both datasets had 18,609 observations from 19 (Belize and Guyana were not included in 2008).For sociodemographic segmentation, average Silhouette was highestfor two clusters. Clustering produced clusters 7365and 18131. Cluster 18131concentrated 32,07% of observations and had better(statistically significant) values in all indicators included in the analysis. These clusters were significantly associated with a difference in the value of self-rated health on EuroQol. Belonging to cluster 18131was associated with an average increaseof 0.8994points in the EQ-VAS 0-10 scale, holdingsex,education and age constant, compared to belonging to cluster 7365.Using the criteria of the highest average Silhouette, we selected 8clusters as the best way to group the data for the EQ-5D-Based segmentation. Four clusters were predominantly male and four were predominantly female respondents. Clusters 15706 and 2016 gathered most of the respondents with no problems in any of the five domains and had the higher VAS score in males and females, respectively.We found a group of predominantly males with high EQ-VAS score that reported moderate anxiety depression.Discussion:In our study we explored different segmentation tools in a large Data set that includes data of self-reported health and other aspects from 19 LAC countries. These tools are increasingly used in healthcare to tailor clinical and public health interventions to heterogeneous populations In our first analysis, we showed thataclustering algorithm was able to identify a subgroup of observations defined by favorable values in the Index variables, andthatthese observations also correlated with higher values in the EQ-VAS. In our second analysis, we identifiedinteresting patterns defined by the five domains and VAS score of the EQ-5Daccording to sex. Our findings show that clustering analyses arenot only useful but are also versatile techniquesthat can be applied to the study of health-related quality of life and help to untangle the differences that lie within different cultural and social subgroups.

Title: Assessment of psychometric properties of EQ-TIPS in infants and toddlers with cerebral palsy in China
Abstract: The EQ-TIPS is a newly developed instrument designed to measure health-related quality of life in infants and toddlers, thereby facilitating economic evaluations. Although it holds significant promise, evidence on its psychometric properties in specific patient populations remains limited. To address this gap, the present study aims to evaluate the psychometric properties of the EQ-TIPS in a clinical sample of infants and toddlers with cerebral palsy, aged 1 to 5 years, in China. A cross-sectional survey design with a 2-week follow-up will be employed. Key assessments will include ceiling and floor effects, convergent validity, explanatory power, known-group validity, and test-retest reliability. The findings will provide the EuroQol Group with valuable insights into the EQ-TIPS's performance in children with cerebral palsy. An additional strength of this study is its evaluation of the instrument in Chinese, a strategically important language. Furthermore, the results will strengthen the evidence base supporting the EQ-TIPS's adoption as an official instrument.

Title: Validation of the EQ-5D plus respiratory bolt-on in the birmingham copd cohort study
Abstract: Objectives: Arespiratory bolt-on dimension for the EQ-5D-5Lhas recently been developed and valued by the general public. Thiscurrent study aimed to validate the EQ-5D-5L plusrespiratory dimension (EQ-5D-5L+R) in a large group of COPD patients. Methods: Validation was undertaken with data from the Birmingham COPD cohort study (BCCS), alongitudinal UK study of COPDprimary care patients. Data on the EQ-5D-5L+R were collected from 1,008 responding participants during a follow-up questionnairein 2017 and combined with (previously collected)data on patient and disease characteristics. Descriptive and correlationanalyses were performed on the EQ-5D-5L+Rdimensions and utilities,inrelation toCOPD characteristicsand compared to the EQ-5D-5L without respiratory dimension. Multivariate regression models wereestimated to test whether regression coefficients ofclinical characteristics differed between the EQ-5D-5L+Rutilityandthe EQ-5D-5L utility. Results:Correlation coefficients for the EQ-5D-5L+Rutility with COPD parameters were slightly highercompared to the EQ-5D-5Lutility. Both instruments displayed discriminant validitybut analyses in clinical subgroups of patients showed larger absolute differences in utilitiesfor the EQ-5D-5L+R. In the multivariate analyses,only the coefficientfor the CAT score was higher for the model using the EQ-5D-5L+R utilityas outcome. Conclusions:This study showed that the addition of a respiratory domain to the EQ-5D-5L led to small improvementsin the instrument’s performance. Comparability of the EQ-5D across diseases, currently considered one of its strengths, would have to be traded-off against a modest improvement in utilitydifference when adding the respiratory dimension.

Title: Insight into the higher health state valuation for children compared to adults: effect of 3 valuation methods
Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Available evidence comparing adult versus child stated preferences consistently report higher utility values for children, using the VAS, composite-TTO, DCE-with-death, DCE-with-duration, lag-time-TTO, and location-of-dead-approach, than for adult healthstates (HS). Explanations for these findings have been proposed but not verified.AIM: The aim of this research is to confirm the higher valuation for child compared to adult HS; and to investigate why respondents value child HS differently.METHODS: Eightygeneral public respondents from the UK, Belgium and The Netherlands were invited for a 1.5-hour face-to-face interview. Respondents valued four EQ-5D HS from two perspectives (8-year-old child, 40-year-old adult) using VAS and TTO. Thirty-two of the respondents participated in think-aloud interviewing. Quantitative analyses were carried out in SAS; audio-recorded interviews were transcribed,and a thematic analysis was conducted in NVIVO. Interviews were coded by two researchers using presumption-focused coding. Statements, nodes and themes were reviewed cyclically until consensus was reached within the research team. The aim was to obtain a framework with a limited number of sub-themes(nodes)and uniform statements within each node. A conceptual frameworkwasdevelopeddepicting the relationships between nodes, themes and the life years (LY) trade-off. Qualitative statements made by respondents were contrasted with their quantitative responses. RESULTS: Quantitative results: Statistically significantlyhigher utilitieswere found forchild versusadult TTO values: 0.026, 0.112, 0.377 and 0.294 higher utilities for mild, moderate, severe and worst HS (all p<0.001), whereas significantly higher VAS ratings were only observed for severe HS.Qualitative results:1,221 pages of transcripts were reviewed, resulting in 274coded statements. Fragments were categorised in 5 themes that were present both in child and adult valuation, though with a different interpretation. Two themes encompassed General principles on the value of life: Staying alive is important(Life is worth living even with impaired HRQoL, for children and adults)and Inter-generational responsibility and dependency(All lives are precious: childhood is the foundation yearsand a time for havingnew experiences; adulthood is an important time to take care of the family). Three themes were identified as ConversionFactors:Awareness of poor HRQoL and ability to make decisions(children have difficulties comprehending poor HRQoL and their parents are making choices for them, whereas adults are able to assess their HRQoL and decide for themselves); Adapting and coping(children being flexible and resilient; adults having experience with dealing with difficulties); and the Practical organisation of care(children being unconditionally cared for by their parents; adults being able to organise and pay for care).The five themes were combined into a conceptual framework, labelled the “Circle of life”.Mixed methods: Comparing statements on the value of childhood as a time for new experiences and adults’ roles in life to prepare their children for adulthood, with the same respondents’ TTO values, confirmed the concordance between the qualitative and quantitative results.CONCLUSION: Adult respondents revealed having a lower willingness-to-trade LY for achieving higher HRQoL in children. Child-specific value sets will pose a challenge for pharmacoeconomic evaluation and resource allocation as this might have implications for access to health care for children.

Title: Test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L in the general population of the UK, Italy and the Netherlands
Abstract: Background: EQ-5D-5L data of the general population is collected for multiple purposes, e.g. to monitor the health status of the general population or establish population norms. Essential for each of these purposes is that the EQ-5D-5L is reliable. Previously several studies have investigated the test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L in the general population administered via an in-person interview. Whether the test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L administered via a web-based survey is similar compared to the test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L administered via an in-person interview remains to be investigated. Aims: The aim of this study is to assess the test-retest reliability of EQ-5D-5L administered via a web-based survey for the general population of the UK, Italy and the Netherlands. Methods: The sample consists of 1864 members of the general population (aged 18-75 years) of the UK, the Netherlands and Italy who completed the EQ-5D-5L on two consecutive occasions. We will use Gwet’s agreement coefficient (GAC) test to determine the test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) to determine the test-retest reliability of the EQ-VAS, EQ-5D sum level score and the EQ-5D-5L index value. GAC and ICC will be assessed for the respondents of the UK, Italy and Netherlands separately and for specific subgroups within a country. Output: A paper submitted to a peer-reviewed international scientific journal that describes the test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-5L administered via a web-based survey in multiple countries and within subgroups of a country.

Title: Understanding caregiver perspectives: qualitative testing of EQ-TIPS among caregiver dyads for children with moderate and severe chronic skin disease
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) is a generic measure of HRQoL for children aged 0-4 years. The instrument is currently being developed as part of a large multicountry project involving mainly Western Europe, South Africa, Australia, Asia, and North and South America. The EQ-TIPS has never been translated or used in any Eastern European country or language. The instrument is proxy-assessed, but EuroQol has not yet provided guidance on who can serve as a proxy or how assessments may differ between caregivers. Such differences may depend on caregiver characteristics such as age, gender, relationship to the child, caregiving experience, health background, and time spent caring.Objectives: This study aims to translate and cognitively debrief the EQ-TIPS to Hungarian and to assess its content validity (relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness) among caregiver dyads of the same children (aged 0-4 years) diagnosed with moderate or severe atopic dermatitis. We further aim to qualitatively explore the factors potentially affecting proxy reporting among caregiver dyads.Methods: The study team will conduct a researcher-led translation and cognitive debriefing of the EQ-TIPS-5L following EuroQol VMC guidelines. A total of 15 dyads (30 respondents) will be recruited from two dermatology centers in two large Hungarian cities, Budapest and Pécs. One-on-one, semi-structured interviews will be conducted with two caregivers of the same child. A standardised topic guide will be developed for the interviews, which combine the elements of concurrent think-aloud and retrospective verbal probing. We will focus on the following aspects of content validity: relevance of the items to capture the construct of interest (HRQoL problems in children with moderate or severe AD aged 0-4 years), missing concepts, understandability of the instructions and response options, the appropriateness of item wording, response options and recall period. We will compare qualitative responses from the two caregivers of the same child to identify factors influencing proxy reporting.

Title: How “representative” are internet panels for general population health surveys?: a comparison of four UK/England population health surveys using different sampling approaches
Abstract: BackgroundThe EuroQol group seeks to provide population reference estimates (or “population norms”) for its suite of measures. While random sampling of the population of interest is a gold standard, it is debatable whether internet panel based quota sampling can achieve representativeness in its estimates, which may be achievable if distribution of key covariates approximates the population of interest. The EuroQol is currently (and may continue to) collect population level data using online panels but there are concerns about this approach (e.g. voiced by members at the 42nd Plenary). If the data collected through online panels are perceived as unrepresentative, this puts at risk a large body of EuroQol-funded research. Therefore, we proposed a secondary data analysis project, exploiting already collected data using different sampling approaches available for the UK/England, to evaluate the representativeness of online panel sampling. The aims of the project are:Using traditional regression and unsupervised community identification approaches to understand heterogeneity in health and sociodemographic distributions across datasetsApply adjustment techniques to derive EQ-5D-5L norms based on aim 1 results and assess any remaining differences in adjusted norms across included datasetsMethodsTarget datasets are:Health Survey of England (stratified random sampling)EuroQol Data for Assessment of Population Health Needs and Instrument Evaluation (EQ-DAPHNIE: online panel with quota sampling)POPulation health impact of the CORoNavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (POPCORN: online panel with quota sampling), andthe EQ-5D-5L UK valuation dataset (non-random quota sampling).Analyses approaches include traditional multivariable regression analyses using EQ-5D-5L profile responses, utility values and EQ VAS as dependent variables. Remaining variations in EQ-5D-5L across datasets, after adjusting for sociodemographic, SES and health data will be assessed. In parallel, unsupervised machine learning community identification will be used to uncover heterogeneity within each dataset with the goal of identifying whether certain health and SES subgroups are systematically underrepresented/overrepresented in each dataset (as compared to one another). Community detection algorithms will be used to ensure that identified patterns reflect meaningful population structure rather than sampling noise. After understanding the most relevant variables related to variations in EQ-5D-5L across datasets, we will test adjustment procedures for population EQ-5D-5L estimates including post-stratification weighting (both using joint distributions and ranking procedures), mixed-effects modeling, and weighted continuous norming. Relevance for the EuroQol groupThis project directly aligns with aim 2 of the call for research of the PHS Working Group: examine methodological approaches for estimating population health norms, particularity the inference of recruitment methods, survey administration modes, sample representativeness (20th Joint Call of EuroQol Working Groups, September 2025). This study will generate evidence of how two online panel (quota sampling) recruited samples and non-random quota sampling data compare to data generated from random sampling.

Title: A qualitative study to explore the interpretation and relevance of the EQ‐5D questionnaire in 4 Asian countries
Abstract: A large body of literature has demonstrated the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D questionnaire in many different cultures. In contrast, qualitative evidence on the content validity of the instrument (i.e. relevance and adequacy of the health dimensions included in its descriptive system) is very limited especially in Asia. This project aims to explore the appropriateness of the EQ‐5D questionnaire for use in a number of Asian populations including Chinese, Japanese, Koreans, Malays, and Indians. First, we aim to ascertain the relevance and adequacy, or content validity,of the EQ‐5D descriptive system in the target populations. Second, we aim to understand the thought processes these Asian populations use to rate their own health with the EQ‐VAS. We propose to collect qualitative data from nationals of China, Japan, SouthKorea,and Singapore on their views on health and EQ‐5D.In each participating country,personal and/or focus‐group interviews will be conducted to elicit what the important health dimensions are and how important the EQ‐5D dimensions are to local people, and how they interpret the EQ‐VAS and make decisions in the process of evaluating their health with the scale.All interviews will be recorded, transcribed verbatim, and translated into English for thematic analysis. the analysis will focus on identifying participants’ opinions about theEQ‐5D as a measure of health status, with a particular focus on the content and the relevance and appropriateness of the dimensions,how the measure could be improved, what is missing, the cognitive processes participants use when completing the instrument.

Title: Individual vs. proxy, child vs. adult – A systematic study of different perspectives applied in TTO valuation for EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: •EQ-5D-Y health states are valued by adults considering that the states affect a 10-year-old child. Earlier work has shown that this perspective may yield different valuations, compared to the perspective used in valuation of adult EQ-5D instruments. However, it is unclear exactly why these differences occur, as the perspective introduced for EQ-5D-Y involves two main changes: i) child health states are valued instead adults’ health states, and: ii) others’ health states are valued instead of valuing health states for oneself. Disentangling the influence of these two changes could be of empirical or normative importance. •In our study, we disentangled these effects by using four different perspectives in EQ-5D-Y valuation with visual analogue scale (VAS) and time trade-off (TTO) methods. Overall, differences between perspectives were consistent, but the direction of this impact depends on the health state and respondent. For VAS, the effect of perspective on outcomes of valuation depends on severity and variance was higher when deciding for children. EQ-5D-Y states valued with TTO on behalf of others (i.e. children or adults) receive higher valuations - but lower variances. •Our study suggests that the use of different perspectives may have a small effect on EQ-5D-Y valuation, but will lead to systematic heterogeneity. Seeing as it is unclear why differences between respondents occur, the search for the empirical and normative implications of perspective used in EQ-5D-Y is far from over.

Title: Validation of the breathing bolt-on for the EQ-5D-5L in patients with pulmonary fibrosis and patients with an acute COPD exacerbation
Abstract: Recently, the EuroQol group launched the bolt-on toolbox which includes additional dimensions of health that can be used to complement the EQ-5D-5L in specific, well-defined cases where a dimension that seems particularly relevant for a disease or population is missing. The breathing bolt-on was originally developed by the institute for Medical Technology Assessment (iMTA) of the Erasmus University Rotterdam and validated in the general population and patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The aim of the currently proposed study is two-fold. The first part aims to validate the breathing bolt-on for the EQ-5D-5L in a new patient population, namely patients with pulmonary fibrosis. The second part of the study aims to validate the breathing bolt-on in a COPD population hospitalized for an acute exacerbation and to estimate the utility impact of COPD exacerbations with and without breathing bolt-on. The latter is relevant when estimating QALY gains from interventions that prevent or reduce severity of such exacerbations. Validation exercises will be performed using data of two ongoing clinical trials in which the EQ-5D-5L plus breathing bolt-on has been included. The first trial, the SUITS trial, evaluates implementation of home-monitoring in care management of adults with pulmonary fibrosis versus hospital-based care only. The second study, the PRECISION trial is a randomized controlled trial comparing procalcitonin (PCT)-guided antibiotics with standard care (prednisone and/or antibiotics) in adults hospitalized for a severe COPD exacerbation. Both trials are conducted in the Netherlands. For both trials recruitment of patients is ongoing and for about 75% completed. Preliminary or total baseline data will be used for the current validation exercises without specification by treatment group (i.e. blinding of group-assignment is maintained). On the data from both trials, several descriptive statistical analyses will be performed for the EQ-5D dimensions and the breathing bolt-on to explore the response distribution and correlation with patient and disease characteristics. Divergent validity will be investigated by estimating the correlation between the breathing bolt-on and each of the EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Structural validity of the EQ-5D-5L plus breathing bolt-on will be tested using principal component analyses (PCA) to investigate the extent to which the breathing bolt-on measures a different construct than the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Known-group validity will be assessed by comparing the outcomes of the EQ-5D-5L with and without breathing bolt-on between clinically relevant subgroups of patients. To test content validity of the breathing bolt-on in pulmonary fibrosis, clarity, comprehensiveness and relevance of the breathing bolt-on will be evaluated in cognitive interviews with among five experts, consisting of pulmonary fibrosis patients and clinicians.To estimate the impact of a severe COPD exacerbation in terms of utility decrement compared to the stable state (disutility), the EQ-5D-5L data of the PRECISION trial measured at different time points will be used to estimate the disutility per patient both with and without the breathing bolt-on.  Future research after completion of the trials will focus on responsiveness of the breathing bolt-on over time (by treatment group). Responsiveness will be part of a future proposal because the timelines for completion of recruitment, follow-up and finalization of the main analyses are currently still uncertain.

Title: Exploring the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L and the breathing bolt-on in older adults at risk of influenza-like illness: a multi-country cohort analysis
Abstract: This study aims to (1) assess the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L and a breathing bolt-on in older adults experiencing influenza-like illness (ILI), and (2) examine age-related differences in measurement properties across subgroups (60–64, 65–74, 75–84, 85+). We will conduct a secondary analysis of data from a prospective, observational cohort study in Belgium, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom over two consecutive ILI seasons. Participants were recruited via 17 general practices and completed baseline assessments of demographics and HRQoL (EQ-5D-5L, breathing bolt-on, EQ VAS). During the ILI season, weekly monitoring captured ARI symptoms, PCR test results, medication use, absenteeism, and HRQoL. Psychometric evaluation will follow established frameworks for bolt-on assessment, comparing EQ-5D-5L alone versus EQ-5D-5L plus breathing bolt-on. To explore potential age-related differences in the performance of the EQ-5D-5L, we will stratify the older adult population into pre-specified age groups and replicate the psychometric assessments within each subgroup. We will also perform differential item functioning (DIF) analysis to examine whether EQ-5D-5L item responses exhibited DIF across age categories and language/country groups.

Title: The EQ-5D-5L Valuation Study in China
Abstract: Background: In order to estimate a country-specific EQ-5D-5L value set, time trade-off (TTO) values of a subset of EQ-5D-5L health states were recently elicited from a general population sample (N=1250) in China using the EuroQol Group’s EQ-VT system. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of various linear regression models to predict disutility (or utility) values of EQ-5D-5L health states.Methods: Characteristics of EQ-5D-5L health states were modelled to predict disutility values. Model specifications tested included main effects of different levels and types of EQ-5D-5L health problems, main effects with selected first-order interaction terms, and extended N3 and D1 models. All models were also tested with addition of one of two alternative terms, M1 (1, if slight problems in only 1 dimension and no problems in the remaining dimensions; 0, otherwise) and M2 (1, if slight problems in 1 or 2 dimensions and no problems in the remaining dimensions; 0, otherwise). Each model was estimated with 70% of the study sample and assessed for goodness of fit and prediction bias with the remaining 30% of the sample. Model prediction bias was visually examined by plotting the predicted and actual values for observed health states. Results: For all model specifications tested, the random-effects model was more efficient than the fixed-effects model (p>0.05 for all, Hausman test). The M1 and M2 terms were statistically significant in almost all models. However, the estimated effect of ‘slightly anxious/depressed’ turned negative in most models when the M1 term was added. All criteria considered, the model contained all main effects, the M2 term, and a fixed constant (defined as ‘M2 model’) or a varying constant as specified by the D1 term (defined as ‘D1-M2 model’) was most suitable for estimating the EQ-5D-5L TTO values in China. The two variants of the M2 model exhibited identical fit of the 30% of the sample which was not used for model estimation, with the mean absolute error being 0.0573 and the number of absolute errors >0.05 and >0.10 being 41 and 15, respectively. Conclusions: This study provides the algorithm for estimation of the EQ-5D-5L value set in China. The significance of the M terms suggests that Chinese rate the mildest EQ-5D-5L health states differently in the TTO exercise. Future studies should investigate whether this is the case in other populations and explore the reasons for this valuation behaviour.

Title: Performance of EQ-5D-Y in psychiatric/mental health conditions. Examples from autism and phobia
Abstract: Background The use of EQ-5D-Y in populations with mental health conditions is limited, resulting in insufficient knowledge/evidence concerning its performance and comparisons with other instruments. This study investigated the internal structure of EQ-5D-Y-3L and compared its psychometric properties with Child-Health-Utility-9D (CHU-9D) in children and young people (CYP) with specific phobias or autism spectrum disorders as examples. Methods Data for 268 CYP aged 7-16 years with phobia and 248 CYP aged 7-15 years with autism were obtained from two randomized controlled trials – ASPECT and I-SOCIALISE. In both trials, CYP, parents and teachers completed relevant clinical and symptoms impact measures, as well as EQ-5D-Y-3L (proxy in the I-SOCIALISE trial and self-completed in the ASPECT trial) and CHU-9D (both self-completed). The internal structure of EQ-5D-Y-3L was examined by three approaches, including reflective model, formative model, and reflective and formative combination model. The psychometric performance of EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU-9D was determined by assessing acceptability, validity (convergent and known-groups validity), and responsiveness, as well as explanatory power. Since no UK value set for EQ-5D-Y-3L exists, the Dutch value set was used in the main analysis and the German value set applied in sensitivity analysis Results The internal structures of EQ-5D-Y-3L from both trials differed from that of the parental EQ-5D (adult version). In terms of acceptability, the missing, non-complete and floor effects were low for both EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU-9D, but ceiling effect was larger in EQ-5D-Y-3L (>15%) for both CYP groups. Overall, in the autism trial, EQ-5D-Y-3L showed low to moderate convergent validity with most of SDQ scores (strong with the SDQ emotional symptom score), while CHU-9D showed, at best, weak association with SDQ scores. Both EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU-9D demonstrated a small to moderate known group validity. However, for responsive validity, except EQ VAS, none of the measures demonstrated responsiveness. In the explanatory power analysis, neither measure explained the variance of SSIS social skills score-T (primary outcome of the trial). In contrast, in the phobia trial both EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU-9 correlated well with RCADS scores, particularly with the CYP-completed version. Also both demonstrated moderate to large effect sizes in known group analysis. Depending on the chosen criteria to assess the responsiveness, both measures showed no responsiveness (as defined by BAT or ADIS/SUDS) and moderate/strong responsiveness (as defined by RCADS and CAIS). Similar to responsiveness, neither measure explained any variance of BAT (primary outcome) or ADIS/SUDS but managed to explain a proportion of variance in RCADS and CAIS, particularly in CYP-completed versions. Conclusion The findings suggest that amongst CYP with phobias, both EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU-9D demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, with effect size slightly larger in CHU-9D. Considering the number of dimensions and levels involved in each measure, EQ-5D-Y-3L showed a comparable result. However, less satisfactory psychometric properties were observed for either instrument for CYP with autism in the examined dataset. Our findings also suggest that compared to proxy version, self-completed version should be encouraged when using EQ-5D-Y-3L.

Title: Research visit to University of British Columbia, University of Alberta, and McMaster University to facilitate collaborative working and engage with local stakeholders to promote routine PROM data collection and analysis in the Canadian healthcare system
Abstract: Funding is requested to allow Nils Gutacker to visit several EuroQol members and local experts in the routine collection and use of PROM data at their respective universities for 3 weeks in 2026. The purpose of this visit is to deepen research collaborations, develop grant applications on comparative health system performance assessment and determinants of PROM instrument completion, and to promote knowledge exchange between Canadian policymakers and Gutacker, reflecting their respective expertise in PROM-based system management in Canada and England.
Working Group: Populations and Health Systems, Education and Outreach

Title: Testing EQ-TIPS using latent discrete choice experiments: a mixed-methods study
Abstract: The valuation of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments for infants and toddlers remains largely unexplored, limiting the inclusion of very young children in economic evaluations despite this being a critical period for early intervention. The EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) instrument was recently developed to measure HRQoL in children aged 0-3 years across six dimensions (movement, play, pain, social interaction, communication, and eating). However, no valuation studies have yet been conducted for EQ-TIPS, primarily due to methodological challenges related to the choice of elicitation method, respondent group, and framing of perspective.This study will assess the feasibility of applying latent discrete choice experiment (DCE) methods to EQ-TIPS-5L valuation through a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 will involve 20–30 cognitive interviews with parents and general adults to explore comprehension, interpretation, and feasibility of valuation perspectives (own vs. hypothetical child) and age framings within the 0–3-year range. Findings will inform the design of the DCE implemented in Phase 2, where a nationally representative sample of 1,000 Australian adults will complete DCE tasks framed across multiple perspectives and age specifications.Choice data will be analysed under random utility theory using multinomial logit (MNL) and mixed logit (MIXL) models to test for logical consistency, preference heterogeneity, and framing effects. Swait–Louviere tests will be used to assess preference and scale differences across perspectives.The study will generate empirical evidence on the feasibility of latent DCE valuation for EQ-TIPS-5L, identifying which respondent groups and perspectives yield the most logically consistent preferences. Results will inform the development of a standardised EQ-TIPS-5L valuation protocol and provide methodological foundations for incorporating infants and toddlers into economic evaluations.

Title: EuroQol past, present & future publication
Exploring the validity of EQ-5D-5L in older populations using SIPHER data from the UK
Abstract: Accurate measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in older adults is essential for fair and valid economic evaluation, clinical assessment, and population health monitoring. The EQ-5D-5L is widely used for these purposes, yet evidence on its validity and performance among the oldest age groups remains limited. While existing studies suggest that the EQ-5D-5L performs adequately overall, it is unclear whether its measurement properties differ across subgroups of older age or whether older respondents can reliably distinguish between all five severity levels. Moreover, aspects of life that gain importance in later years—such as autonomy, social participation, and cognition—are not directly represented within the EQ-5D descriptive system, raising questions about the need for age-relevant “bolt-on” dimensions.This project will examine the validity and psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L among older adults, with particular attention to differences between the “old” and “very old.” Using the UK SIPHER-HWMIC dataset (n≈12,000; ages 18–97), analyses will compare the performance of the EQ-5D-5L across the adult age range. These analyses will assess predictive validity for EQ-VAS and life satisfaction, evaluate ceiling and floor effects, convergent and construct validity, and explore age-related differences in the latent factor structure of health and wellbeing. The study will also test whether potential bolt-on domains (e.g., vision, hearing, cognition, fatigue) improve predictive performance for older adults, and whether such improvements differ from those observed in younger age groups.Findings will provide new empirical evidence on how the EQ-5D-5L functions across later life stages, informing EuroQol’s work on descriptive system validity and the potential development of age-relevant extensions.

Title: Psychometric Performance of the EQ-HWB in Individual with Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Background
Abstract: Background: Global migration has led to a growing number of migrants residing in host countries, and it is widely recognised that the migration experience significantly influences health and wellbeing. These population groups are often described as Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD), and referred to internationally as ethnic minorities, racial groups, or by other related terms. The EQ Health and Wellbeing Short version (EQ-HWB-S) is a recently developed instrument by the EuroQol Group, designed to evaluate outcomes across health, public health, and social care settings—covering patients, carers, and social care users. However, further evidence is needed regarding its psychometric performance across diverse populations. This study aimed to assess the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-S among CALD individuals in Australia, and compare these with non-CALD Australians. Methods: Data were drawn from an online survey administered to 877 Australians from CALD backgrounds and 2,175 Australians without CALD backgrounds. Respondents completed the EQ-HWB-S, the Recovering Quality of Life Utility Index (ReQoL-UI), the EQ-5D-5L, and the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6) in random order. Psychometric evaluation of the EQ-HWB-S included analysis of response distribution (floor and ceiling effects), convergent validity, and known-group validity. Convergent validity was assessed using Spearman’s rank correlations (interpreted as weak [≤0.4], moderate [0.4–0.7], or strong [>0.7]). Known-group validity was examined across 18 subgroups with and without physical or mental health conditions. Results: The EQ-HWB-S demonstrated similar response patterns among CALD and non-CALD Australians. Strong convergent validity was observed for the EQ-HWB-S when compared with the EQ-5D-5L, ReQoL-UI, and K6, using both sum and index scores. At the item level, the EQ-HWB-S items were moderately to strongly correlated with items of similar constructs from EQ-5D-5L, ReQoL-UI and K6. Known-group validity was generally supported, with the EQHWB-S effectively distinguishing between groups with and without health conditions, except in the cases of hypertension and osteoporosis. Conclusion: This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the psychometric performance of the EQHWB-S in a large sample of Australian adults from CALD backgrounds. The findings suggest that the EQ-HWB-S is a promising outcome measure for use in diverse population groups.

Title: Testing the partially-fixed model for bolt-on valuation: a multi-country study
Abstract: Introduction: Bolt-on dimensions can enhance the descriptive system of the EQ-5D by capturing additional treatment benefits not covered by the core five dimensions. Previous studies have shown improved psychometric properties with bolt-ons, but conventional valuation studies for bolt-ons are cost-prohibitive. The partially-fixed "scaling factor" model, which uses existing value set parameters adjusted with a scale parameter, offers a cost-effective alternative. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and performance of the scaling factor model in valuing bolt-on dimensions for the EQ-5D in China and Italy, using both cTTO and hybrid designs. Methods: Two bolt-ons, EQ-PSO (itching and self-confidence) and social relationships, were selected for valuation in China and Italy, respectively. In China, 401 participants valued EQ-7D health states using cTTO. In Italy, 200 participants completed cTTO tasks, and 1000 participants completed DCE tasks for EQ-6D states. Data was modeled using standard main-effects and scaling factor approaches in which parameters from existing national value sets were used. Model performance was evaluated by predicting observed, out-of-sample health state cTTO values. Results: The scaling factor model showed high predictive accuracy in both countries. In China, the scaling factor model using the new value set achieved similar accuracy to the standalone model. In Italy, the scaling factor model performed slightly worse than the standalone model, with marginal differences between cTTO-only and hybrid models. The scale parameters indicated a reduction in the size of coefficients for core dimensions, confirming bolt-on’s compression effect observed in previous studies. Discussions: The scaling factor model appears to be a viable and robust approach for developing bolt-on value sets. This method could facilitate cost-efficient application of bolt-ons in health economics and outcomes research when EQ-5D is considered to be inadequate due to its lack of specificity.

Title: Exploring psychometric properties and scoring approaches for the EQ-5D-5L psoriasis bolt-on: Supporting decisions on its IP status
Abstract: The psoriasis bolt-on – a disease-specific EQ-5D-5L measure which includes two additional dimensions of skin irritation and self-confidence – is a leading candidate to become an approved instrument and the first EuroQol endorsed bolt-on. We propose this project to support the advancement of the psoriasis bolt-on by addressing some crucial research gaps including the instrument’s responsiveness, potential conceptual overlap with core EQ-5D dimensions, performance across a range of languages and information important for non-preference based scoring.  Leveraging secondary data from clinical trials of psoriasis patients, we aim to:  examine the psychometric properties of the psoriasis bolt-on, with a focus on responsiveness, and comparison to the core EQ-5D-5L; investigate the structure of the psoriasis bolt-on items a) in relationship to other generic and skin-specific health measures (to assess item performance and construct validity), as well as b) in relationship to the EQ-5D-5L (to examine potential conceptual overlap with EQ-5D core dimensions and assessing the psoriasis bolt-on measurement model); explore non-preference based scoring based on findings of aim 2; and examine potential differences in responsiveness, structure and item functioning across language and country subgroups.  The results on psychometric properties and structure of the psoriasis bolt-on will provide support for the instrument advancing to approved status as well as provide the groundwork for future non-preference based scoring research. This project will also provide some of the first evidence of non-preference scoring of the psoriasis bolt-on, giving it a foundation for broader applications outside of health technology assessment and cost utility analyses.

Title: Testing fatigue and breathing bolt-ons in the EQ-5D toolbox in three different types of cancers
Abstract: We propose to test breathing and fatigue bolt-ons in the main toolbox and exploratory toolbox in lung, blood, and gastrointestinal cancers. In this multi-centred study, we will consecutively recruit 200 non-small cell lung cancer patients, 200 lymphoma patients, and 200 gastric/colorectal cancer patients who will receive active anticancer treatment in three different tertiary cancer centres in China. All eligible patients will complete EQ-5D-5L and 10 fatigue bolt-on variants before and after treatment, together with cancer-specific QLQ-C30 and a fatigue scale. Lung cancer patients will also complete the QLQ-C30 lung cancer module (LC13) and 2 breathing bolt-on variants. Patients' clinical characteristics and performance status before and after treatment will be evaluated or retrieved from medical records. We will evaluate the distributions, ceiling/floor effects, content validity, convergent validity, known-groups validity, and responsiveness of the breathing and fatigue bolt-ons. We will also evaluate fatigue bolt-ons by pooling data collected from the three cancer groups.

Title: Content Validity of the EQ-5D Bolt-On Toolbox: Hearing, Vision, and Respiratory Bolt-Ons in Patients in Argentina
Abstract: Background:The experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox comprises two subsets of items: a Best Available Version, which includes eight items recommended for current applied use, and an Exploratory Version, which contains additional items to support development and testing. This study will evaluate selected items from both subsets to provide a comprehensive assessment of the performance of bolt-ons across key health-related quality of life (HRQoL) domains. The proposal focuses on: 1) hearing  and 2) vision bolt-ons, addressing sensory functioning; and 3) bolt-ons capturing respiratory functioning (breathing and fatigue). Objectives:To translate the experimental EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox hearing, vision, breathing and fatigue bolt-ons to Spanish (Argentina) and to explore their content validity among people with relevant target conditions such as hearing conditions, vision impairment, and respiratory problems (for breathing and fatigue) in Argentina. The study will assess item comprehension, relevance, and comprehensiveness, providing essential evidence to inform the final wording of these bolt-on(s).Methods:In the first stage, the selected bolt-on items (HEARING 1–5, VISION 1–4, BREATHING 1–2 and FATIGUE 1–10) will be translated into Spanish (Argentina) following EuroQol VMC translation guidelines, which include two forward translations, two back translations, and 10 cognitive debriefing interviews. Subsequently, a qualitative study will assess the content validity of the selected bolt-ons from the “best available” and “exploratory” Toolbox.  The qualitative study will include adults aged 18 years and older with health conditions related to the selected bolt-ons. Across all groups, purposive sampling will be used to ensure diversity in gender, education level and disease severity, with severity assessed using condition-specific clinical or patient-reported scales for each condition.For the hearing bolt-ons, the sample will comprise 30 participants: 15 individuals with moderate to severe tinnitus and 15 with hearing loss associated with chronic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or autoimmune diseases. All participants will have a confirmed diagnosis. For the vision bolt-ons, 30 participants will be recruited: 15 with age-related macular degeneration (both dry and wet forms) and 15 with diabetes-related visual complications, primarily diabetic retinopathy or diabetic macular edema. Participants will have had a confirmed diagnosis for at least six months. For the respiratory bolt-ons, the sample will include 30 participants: 15 with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and 15 with pulmonary fibrosis, all with a confirmed diagnosis of at least six months’ duration.Cognitive interviews will follow EuroQol guidelines for content validity testing. The paper-based, self-completed version will be used for the EQ-5D-5L+ bolt-ons. For participants with visual impairment who are unable to complete the questionnaire independently, a paper-based interviewer-administered (IA) version will be used. Data will be analyzed thematically to identify patterns in comprehension, relevance, and comprehensiveness of the items.Significance:Testing the selected bolt-ons in Spanish (Argentina), one of the most widely spoken languages globally, is a strategic priority of the EuroQol Group. The project also has the potential to enhance the applicability of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) contexts. The results will provide the first evidence of linguistic and conceptual equivalence of Hearing, Visual, Breathing and Fatigue items in Latin America and inform future psychometric and valuation studies.

Title: Experimental Bolt-on Toolbox - Cognitive debriefing of the UK English source version
Abstract: Background: Currently, two versions of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox have been developed (the ‘best available’ and ‘exploratory’ versions). The ‘exploratory’ version of the Toolbox includes a range of other bolt-ons or modifications to the ‘best available’ that will be tested in future work to inform the ‘final’ set of Toolbox bolt-ons. As the Toolbox includes bolt-ons drawn from different sources, and developed following different procedures, there has been no systematic investigation of the bolt-on wording in the source language (UK English) using cognitive debriefing methods.Objectives: To conduct cognitive debriefing of the experimental ‘best available’ and ‘exploratory’ Bolt-on Toolbox in UK English in people who report problems on one (or more) of the bolt-ons. Methods: A two-phase study will be conducted. The first phase of the study will consist of an online survey.  A large sample of participants will complete the EQ-5D-5L and all of the bolt-ons, followed by demographic questions.  The target sample size will be N=500 older adults from the UK general population. Survey responses will be used to identify individuals reporting problems on each of the bolt-ons; these individuals will be invited to participate in an interview. The second phase of the study will consist of qualitative cognitive debriefing interviews. Interview participants will be asked to complete the bolt-on items (for which they had previously reported problems) whilst thinking aloud about how they are completing each question. Follow up questions will also be asked to ensure that relevant, appropriate and comparable information is elicited for each bolt-on, starting with the ‘Best Available’ bolt-on for each concept. The Skin Irritation and Self Confidence bolt-ons will be excluded given the extensive qualitative evidence supporting the current versions and their status as beta items with more than 50 existing translations.

Title: Understanding recall bias in health-related quality of life: the role of reference frames, response styles and life events
Abstract: This PhD project explores recall bias in self-reported health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using the EQ-5D-5L in the general population. Despite the widespread use of retrospective health assessments in health economics and outcomes research, little is known about their accuracy or the factors influencing them.
