This research addresses how reference points, response styles, and life events affect the validity and comparability of EQ-5D-5L data over time, using the multi-country, longitudinal POPCORN dataset.The project comprises five work packages (WPs):WP1 examines how accurately individuals recall their past HRQoL and identifies socio-demographic, clinical, and psychological predictors of recall bias.WP2 tests whether recall bias is stable across time points, suggesting a trait-like cognitive pattern.WP3 explores whether individuals who evaluate their health relative to age norms exhibit greater recall bias, linking internal standards to retrospective distortion.WP4 investigates whether response heterogeneity —measured using vignette evaluations— explains individual differences in recall bias, providing insight into interpretation of EQ-5D-5L response scales.WP5 studies whether major health events, specifically COVID-19 infection, serve as cognitive anchors that distort retrospective HRQoL assessments.Together, these work packages address core priorities of the EuroQol Foundation, including how response scale heterogeneity, changes in internal standards, and contextual factors affect EQ-5D data quality. By combining longitudinal data, vignette methodology, and detailed individual-level information, this research will generate actionable insights into the interpretation and use of EQ-5D instruments in longitudinal and population health studies. These insights will support better-informed decision-making in clinical research, health monitoring, and policy.

Title: Reporting heterogeneity in health description and valuation: identification, correction, and sources
Abstract: EuroQol instruments are often used to compare health (gains) across groups defined by disease, demographic, socioeconomic, and other characteristics. Systematic differences in the way in which groups respond to the instruments – reporting heterogeneity (RH) – bias comparisons. For example, socioeconomic health inequality will be underestimated if lower socioeconomic groups report health more positively. Such differences in reporting styles may, in part, arise from differences in health knowledge and beliefs.  RH is potentially present in EQ-5D descriptions of health levels within dimensions, in EQ VAS global assessments of health, and in EQ-5D value sets representing preferences between levels and across dimensions. To identify and correct RH in these EuroQol instruments, some external anchor is required. For example, a respondent’s evaluation of the health of a vignette description of functioning within a health domain identifies RH, which can then be purged from the respondent’s evaluation of their own health, using the same instrument. This method relies on the assumptions of vignette equivalence (VE) – all respondents interpret a vignette in the same way – and response consistency (RC) – a respondent uses the same style to report own health and that of the vignettes. There is limited and mixed evidence on the validity of these assumptions, particularly in the context of EuroQol instruments.  This PhD project will test for RH in data obtained with EuroQol instruments and it aims to develop methods to purge these instruments of RH. In collaboration with the research team, the student will review vignettes that have been developed for use with the EQ-5D descriptive system, with a view to developing new vignettes for which the identification assumptions (VE and RC) are more plausible (WP1). Next, we will develop and test methods that use vignettes data to identify and correct RH in categorical ratings of health obtained with EQ-5D (WP2). The project will also evaluate the use of vignettes to purge RH from EQ VAS scores (WP3). In addition to identifying RH and correcting for it in data obtained with EuroQol instruments, the project will explore sources of RH. In particular, we aim to test the hypothesis that it arises, in part, from differences in health knowledge and beliefs (WP4, WP5). Evaluation of a health state may be contingent on ability to recognize its risks and on beliefs about the relative position of that state. Finally, we will apply the methods developed in WP1-WP5 to purge RH from estimates of socioeconomic health inequality obtained with EuroQol instruments (WP6).

Title: Psychometric testing of cognition, fatigue and breathing bolt-ons in a cohort with long COVID
Abstract: Numerous studies have evaluated the impact of long COVID on health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) using the EQ-5D, and while there is an evidenced decline in HRQoL, the key symptoms of long COVID – brain fog, fatigue and breathlessness – may not be effectively captured by the EQ-5D. This chronic condition thereby offers an opportunity to evaluate items in the EQ-5D Bolt-On Toolbox. This project uses mixed methods to test bolt-on items for the EQ-5D-5L in a cohort of individuals with long COVID. The project will utilise Mātauranga Raranga | Long COVID Registry Aotearoa New Zealand, a registry which longitudinally tracks HRQoL using the EQ-5D-5L. Mixed-methods research will be employed, where the nature of the pschyometric testing will vary according to the bolt-on and in consultation with the DSWG Bolt-on sub-team using standardised protocols and analysis templates. This project will test the validity of cognition, fatigue and breathing bolt-ons in a population with a new and significant chronic condition, thereby contributing to the EuroQol Group’s scientific understanding and strategic positioning regarding bolt-ons.

Title: Extending the use of EQ-5D-Y-5L to Younger Children: Testing Comprehensibility and Interviewer-Assisted Administration in Indonesia
Abstract: The EQ-5D-Y is a standardized instrument developed by the EuroQol Group to measure health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents. Although designed for self-completion by children aged 8–15 years, its feasibility among younger children remains uncertain. Previous research in Indonesia suggests that even within the recommended age range, some children—particularly those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds—experience comprehension difficulties that may compromise response validity. Understanding whether younger children with chronic illness can meaningfully complete the EQ-5D-Y, and under what conditions interviewer assistance or simplified response structures may improve comprehension, is therefore essential for extending the instrument’s applicability.This study aims to examine the comprehensibility and feasibility of two modes of EQ-5D-Y administration (self-complete and interviewer-assisted) among children aged 6–10 years with chronic illness. Variations in literacy, age, gender, and socioeconomic status will be considered. Specifically, the study seeks to (i) determine whether children aged 6–10 years with chronic illness can understand and complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L, (ii) identify when interviewer assistance is required to support comprehension, and (iii) explore whether the EQ-5D-Y-3L may be more suitable than the 5L for some younger children due to reduced response-level complexity, thereby informing recommendations for administration mode and instrument choice in younger populations.Participants (n = 36) will be purposively selected across combinations of age group (6–7, 7–8, and 8–10 years), gender, and socioeconomic status. A literacy screening will guide assignment to administration mode. Children with adequate literacy will begin with self-completion of the EQ-5D-Y-5L, followed by interviewer assistance if difficulties arise. Children with limited literacy will begin directly with interviewer-assisted administration. If children are unable to complete the EQ-5D-Y-5L even with interviewer assistance, the EQ-5D-Y-3L will be offered to explore whether reduced severity-level complexity improves comprehension. All interviews will conclude with a retrospective, structured debriefing session to examine how children understood the questionnaire. Qualitative thematic analysis will identify patterns of misunderstanding, level inversion, and subgroup differences. Findings will generate evidence-based recommendations regarding minimum age, administration mode, and version suitability, contributing to EuroQol’s methodological work on extending EQ-5D-Y use to younger children with chronic illness.

Title: Scoring Methods for the EQ-5D instrument: theoretical background and empirical analyses (revised application)
Abstract: Introduction: The EQ-5D is a preference-based measure developed for economic analysis of health interventions. Yet, most of its applications are in other settings, where preference-based approaches have no more merit than other scoring approaches. In this study, we explore reflective and formative approaches to summarize the EQ-5D-5L for non-economic applications. Methods: We examined: 1) reflective approach modelling EQ-5D-5L items on one latent factor using confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) and item response theory (IRT); 2) formative approach conceptualizing the items as causal and health scales as reflective using Multiple Indicators, Multiple Causes (“external” MIMIC) models; and 3) hybrid approach which modeled some EQ-5D-5L items as formative and others as reflective indicators of one latent factor (“internal” MIMIC). Nine datasets [population (4), patient (3), mix (2)] containing the EQ-5D-5L were analyzed to examine the robustness of the results. Results: CFA showed all items loaded well (0.7 to <0.95) except for AD (loadings 0.192 to 0.619, excluding one outlier). The best fitting external MIMIC modelled the HUI3 and SF-36 subscales on two factors (RMSEA=0.147). The best fitting internal MIMIC model defined MO, AD and, PD as causal, and SC and UA reflective indicators, confirming the findings of Gamst-Klaussen et al. 2017. Conclusion: Neither the reflective or formative approach was best – the AD and SC dimensions were problematic, respectively. A hybrid model to scoring the EQ-5D-5L is suggested for future research. Most datasets analyzed were from Western, developed countries; despite similar findings across datasets, the results may not be generalizable to all countries.

Title: Validity, Responsiveness and Test-Retest of EQ-5D-3L-Y and EQ-5D-5L-Y and their proxy versions in Pediatric Patients in Indonesia
Abstract: The EQ-5D-Y-5L was developed to address the limitation of EQ-5D-Y-3L. It is clear in adults the 5L outperforms the 3L on psychometric criteria, yet it still has to be confirmed if the 5L of EQ-5D-Y outperforms the 3L version in the same way. The aim of this study was to compare the EQ-5D-Y-5L and the EQ-5D-Y-3L self-complete version and proxy-version measurement properties and sensitivity to change in pediatric patients. The study sample consisted of 286 children and their caregivers or someone who knew the child well. The children’s medical conditions were major beta-thalassemia, hemophilia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (AcLL), or acute illness. Data collection was done in 5 hospitals located in Jakarta and Bandung, Indonesia. Questionnaires being used were EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, PedsQL Generic Core Scale, PedsQL cancer module, TranQol, and Haemo-Qol. Missing responses were comparable between the two versions of the EQ-5D-Y and between self-complete and proxy version. The number of patients in the best health state (level profile 11111) was equal in both EQ-5D-Y versions. The projection of EQ-5D-Y-3L scores onto EQ-5D-Y-5L for all dimensions showed that the two additional levels in EQ-5D-Y-5L slightly improved the accuracy of patients in reporting their problems, especially if severe. Convergent validity with PedsQL and disease-specific measures showed that the two EQ-5D-Y versions performed about equally. Test–retest reliability and sensitivity for detecting health changes, were both better in EQ-5D-Y-5L. Except for acutely ill patients, agreement between the EQ-5D-Y-5L proxy and self-reports was at least moderate

Title: Advancing EQ-TIPS in Low and Middle-Income Countries: Evidence map, cultural adaptation, and psychometric validation in Indonesian infants and toddlers
Abstract: Background: Early childhood (0–47 months) is a critical period when illness disrupts everyday functioning, such as movement, play, feeding, interacting with others, and managing emotions, yet these outcomes are seldom measured in routine care in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Existing instruments provide valuable clinical information but often lack preference-based utility and robust LMIC validation. EQ-TIPS, EuroQol’s proxy-reported measure for infants and toddlers offers a life-course link to the EQ family but requires cultural adaptation and empirical testing in Indonesia. Parental spillover from child illness is also undermeasured despite its policy relevance.Aim: To adapt, validate, and implement EQ-TIPS for Indonesian infants and toddlers and to quantify caregiver spillover by linking child HRQoL (EQ-TIPS) with caregiver well-being (EQ-HWB-9), thereby extending EuroQol’s life-course measurement framework to early childhood in an LMIC.Methods: Five linked studies will be conducted. (1) An evidence map and COSMIN-based systematic review will profile instruments for ages 0–47 months and align domains with EQ-TIPS. (2) Cross-cultural adaptation of EQ-TIPS to Bahasa Indonesia will follow EuroQol procedures (forward–backward translation, expert review, cognitive debriefing). (3) Qualitative content-validity interviews with caregivers and health professionals will assess relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness. (4) Psychometric testing of the Indonesian EQ-TIPS will use a cross-sectional and short-term longitudinal design (baseline and 7–14-day retest) to examine distributional properties, reliability (ICC), construct and known-group validity, and responsiveness. (5) Parental spillover will be quantified via correlations, multivariable regression, known-groups comparisons, test–retest reliability, and responsiveness linking EQ-TIPS with EQ-HWB-9.

Title: Testing the psychometric properties of 9 bolt-ons for the EQ-5D
Abstract: Objectives: We aim to assess the psychometric performance and added value of nine existing bolt-ons (breathing problems, cognition, hearing, self-confidence, skin irritation, sleep, social relationships, tiredness and vision) for the EQ-5D-5L in a general population sample. Methods: The EQ-5D-5L, nine bolt-ons, SF-6Dv1, PROMIS-29+2, PROMIS Global Health and Satisfaction With Life Scale were completed in an online cross-sectional survey among a general adult population sample in Hungary (n=1587). The following psychometric properties were tested for the EQ-5D-5L+bolt-on(s): ceiling, informativity, divergent and convergent validity, factor structure, known-group validity and explanatory power. Results: Adding sleep (30%), tiredness (24%) or vision (21%) substantially reduced the ceiling of the EQ-5D-5L (41%). Cognition, sleep, social relationships and tiredness correlated with corresponding PROMIS and SF-6D items (rs=ǀ0.32ǀ-ǀ0.73ǀ). All bolt-ons, except cognition and self-confidence, loaded on a different factor from the EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Breathing, hearing, skin irritation and vision significantly improved known-group validity in relevant health condition groups. The sleep bolt-on improved known-group validity in 9 out of 13 chronic health conditions. Tiredness had the largest impact on explaining EQ VAS score variance in 8 out of 13 conditions. Hearing and vision improved the ability of the EQ-5D-5L to capture declining health with age, while self-confidence and social relationships were valuable for mental health and wellbeing assessment. Conclusions: This study established the validity of multiple bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-5L and highlights the usefulness of including relevant bolt-ons in population-based and patient surveys. Our findings inform the further development of these bolt-ons and the bolt-on item selection for clinical studies.

Title: Exploring outcome measure iteming order effects: An evidence synthesis of overall and dimension-specific questions
Abstract: With the development of the EQ-5D bolt-on toolbox, decision for placement of the bolt-on items relative to the EQ VAS of the core EQ-5D measures will be an important suggestion for end users. This decision will be informed both by practicality and the impact of any ordering effects. We propose supporting decision making about EQ VAS and bolt-on order by summarizing available information on:1) ordering effects of general health indicator and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) items, and items switching response scales and 2) how other HRQoL/PROMs measures with short/long forms and/or add-on modules, or items with different response scales, have operationalized item ordering.For Aim 1, we propose a rapid review (RR) to synthesize available evidence on ordering effects of self-reported health measures. The RR will be conducted following guidance from the Cochrane Rapid Review Methods Group, and in collaboration with an experienced biomedical librarian. Aim 2 will be guided by the expertise of the EuroQol Descriptive Systems Working Group (DSWG) and broader EuroQol membership. Synthesized evidence from the RR and ordering of other measures will be summarized in a report to support decision on the ordering of EQ VAS and bolt-on.This project will be conducted in close and active collaboration with the DSWG as decisions on the search strategy and data extraction will necessarily need to be optimized to support decision making. The proposal has been extensively discussed with the DSWG, and aligns with the strategic priorities for this RFP focused on the order of bolt-ons in relation to the EQ-VAS.

Title: Transitioning between the EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L in Chinese adolescents aged 12–18 years with atopic dermatitis or mental health problems
Abstract: Background The EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L are designed to measure health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in adults and younger populations, respectively. The EQ-5D-Y-5L maintains the same five dimensions as the EQ-5D-5L but uses child-friendly wording. Together, they enable consistent HRQoL measurement from childhood to adulthood. However, the user guide for the EQ-5D-Y-5L suggests that both the youth and adult EQ-5D instruments can be used in ages 12–15 years, while the adult version may be preferred for 16 years and above, but if all respondents are 18 or below, using youth instrument alone is preferred. Comparability of the two versions in adolescents aged 12–18 years with different health conditions remains inadequately known. Aims The study aims to generate evidence to inform the transition between the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in adolescents aged 12–18 years with atopic dermatitis (AD) or mental health problems (MHP), by examining their relationship in terms of response distributions and psychometric properties including construct validity, test–retest reliability, responsiveness and agreement.  Methods We aim to recruit 600 adolescents aged 12–18 years with AD or MHP from the Dermatology Hospital of Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China) and Shanghai Mental Health Center (Shanghai, China). Baseline data will be collected upon consent taking. Test–retest assessment will occur 2–5 days after baseline. For responsiveness assessment, AD patients will be reassessed 12 weeks post-baseline, and MHP patients will be reassessed 4 weeks post-baseline, in line with the typical time for the treatment regimens to take effect. Trained university students or nurses will collect data in clinics and wards using electronic devices. At baseline, participants will self-complete EQ-5D-5L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, either the Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index (CDLQI; for AD patients) or the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWBS for MHP patients), and a single item self-rated health (SRH); followed by demographic questions. The order of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L will be randomized. At follow-up, participants will self-complete the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and SRH, with the order of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L randomized. In addition, we will extract clinical information from medical records, including diagnosis, disease duration, treatment, comorbidities, and severity scores: the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) for AD, the Hamilton Anxiety (HAM-A) and Depression (HAM-D) Rating Scales for MHP. Response distributions and psychometric properties will be compared between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-Y-5L. Response distribution analyses will include ceiling and floor effects, redistribution, and informativity. Psychometric comparison will include convergent validity, known-group validity, agreement, test–retest reliability, and responsiveness.

Title: Speaking at an Issues Panel at ISPOR Europe (Glasgow, November 2025) in which transitions between EuroQol instruments (EQ-TIPs to EQ-5D-Y-5L to EQ-5D-5L) will be discussed "Handling Transitions Between Child and Adult HRQoL in Economic Evaluation"
Abstract: Speaking at an Issues Panel at ISPOR Europe (Glasgow) in which transitions between EuroQol instruments (EQ-TIPs to EQ-5D-Y-5L to EQ-5D-5L) will be discussed.ISPOR Europe Issues Panel: Handling Transitions Between Child and Adult HRQoL in Economic Evaluation. November 2025.https://www.ispor.org/conferences-education/conferences/upcoming-conferences/ispor-europe-2025

Title: Introduction to EuroQol Instruments and their various applications at the ISPOR UAE Chapter Annual conference
Abstract: While health technology assessment (HTA) infrastructure is steadily advancing across the MENA region, the routine use of standardized outcome measures—particularly those enabling quality-adjusted life year (QALY) estimation—remains limited and uneven. Several countries, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Jordan, the UAE, Morocco, and Qatar, have developed EQ-5D value sets, providing a strong methodological foundation for economic evaluation. However, challenges persist in translating these advances into consistent application in practice and policy. This 3-hour workshop will introduce the EuroQol instruments and discuss how they can be more effectively integrated into healthcare decision-making across MENA. Beyond their established role in cost-utility analysis, presentations will highlight the broader use of EQ measures in value-based healthcare, real-world evidence generation, and population health monitoring within the region’s evolving health systems. The workshop will bring together regional HEOR leaders and experts to identify gaps, research priorities, and capacity-building needs to support greater adoption of EQ-5D in economic and policy contexts. Importantly, it will also provide a platform for the EuroQol Research Foundation to expand its engagement in MENA, strengthen relationships with emerging HTA authorities, and foster new collaborations that promote EQ-5D research, education, and implementation.

Title: Testing the potential of multiplicative models for efficient EQ-5D bolton/off valuation study design
Abstract: Prediction of bolt-on/offEQ-5D health state valuescan be based on new value sets independent of original EQ-5D value sets. Nevertheless, it would be more efficient to link bolt-ons to existing EQ-5D value sets. For this purpose, the effect of bolt-on/off items on valuation of EQ-5D dimensions should be elucidated. Previous studies found the effect of bolt-on items on valuation of EQ-5D health states was complex and failed to inform efficient valuation designs for bolt-on/off EQ-5D. Recently, multiplicative models were found to be superior to addictive models (which was used in almost all previous bolt-on valuation studies) and have been used to estimate 5L value sets. This new type of models provides a new opportunity to exploring the relationship between bolt-on/off and valuation of EQ-5D health states. The purpose of this project is to test the multiplicative models for their potential in exploring the effect of bolt-on/off items on valuation of EQ-5D health states. The specific research questions are: 1) are multiplicative models superior to the additive main-effects models for modelingvisionbolt-on (5L+VI) and self-care bolt-off (5L-SC) valuation data? 2: Are common parameters of the multiplicative models for 5L, 5L-SC and 5L+VI or ratios of the parameters constant? We propose to elicit the utility values of 30 5L, 29 5L-SC, and 31 5L+VI health states from 600 members of the general public using the c-TTO method. Each respondent will be asked to value arandom block of 5L, 5L-SC, or 5L+VI health states (n=14 to 16). Data will be modeled with both additive and multiplicative models and the model results will be examined to answer the research questions raised.

Title: Guidance for qualitative studies to test the content validity of bolt-ons
Abstract: A number of possible bolt-ons to the EQ-5D-5L/3L have recently been propsed for the bolt-on toolbox. Testing the content validity of  proposed bolt-on items is important. This includes qualitative content validity testing. This project will produce a package of standardised guidance to support EuroQol funded research projects aiming to test the content validity of bolt-ons. This will be beneficial a) to ensure high quality data and analysis b) to share resources where it is cost-effective to do so c) to make it easier for findings across qualtiative studies to be synthesied.

Title: Developing and validating a copula-based method to transport aggregated EQ-5D utility values between value sets
Abstract: Health economic analyses and cost effectiveness models often employ health state utility values sourced from publications, wherein EQ-5D values are often reported with marginal statistics (mean, SD/SE) only. As such analyses are usually designed to fit within specific country settings, utility values should ideally be derived using a relevant value set. When sourced from publications, the reported values typically only reflect a single value set, and changing aggregate statistics from one value set to another would normally require access to individual level patient data (IPD). In the absence of IPD access, analyses and models are frequently populated with values reflecting several different value sets, most of which will not be relevant for the setting they are used. We have developed a promising proof-of-concept algorithm that allows estimation of mean values from any desired value set based on reported mean values from a known value set, including transportation between reported -3L and desired -5L value sets. The algorithm produces remarkably good estimates in small-scale testing using the multi-instrument comparison study dataset, but has not yet been tested in e.g. clinical trial data or observational study datasets. This proposed project aims to develop, refine, and formally validate the existing proof-of-concept method to transport aggregated EQ-5D utility values across value sets when IPD is not accessible. The project is structured as three relatively independent subprojects. Subproject 1 bring the crudely developed proof-of-concept code from functional sketch stage to a fully CRAN-compliant R package with a user friendly web front-end. The existing code allows, by a relatively complex procedure, transportation based on reported mean and reported value set to any other value set. The desired code will make this process simple and optionally allow inclusion of reported variance / uncertainty, to allow transportation including uncertainty. Subproject 2 we will engage pharmaceutical companies to identify relevant clinical trials; extract random subsamples of participants (60%-90% of the full samples), extract EQ-5D data, treatment allocation , timing of measurement, and broadly defined clinical group. The idea is to have a dataset of real data covering a wide range of clinical settings without allowing identification of which trials the data stems from. If successful, a publication is planned describing the collaborative dataset, which will be made publicly available. In parallel, we aim to collect a large number of patient subgroup-specific observational datasets including EQ-5D data, as such datasets are frequently used to publish mean utility values.Subproject 3 involves formal testing and validation of the utility transportation procedure. Briefly, as all the collected datasets include self-reported EQ-5D (either -3L or -5L), we can calculate “true” utility values using all available value sets. We can then, from each “true” value use the transportation procedure to produce estimates of all not-used value sets. These estimates can then be compared with the “true” values to determine the expected precision of the procedure, broken down by starting (reported) value set, target value set, and patient/disease group.

Title: Measurement properties of the EQ-5D-5L instrument and the CarerQoL instrument, when administered to the informal caregivers of patients with post-stroke aphasia
Abstract: The project that we are proposing is a psychometric analysis of the EQ-5D-5L and the CarerQoL instruments, for measuring the quality of life of informal caregivers. We are aware that relevant data has already been collected from the BIG CACTUS study (Palmer et al 2019). The BIG CACTUS study was a UK-based trial investigating a computer-delivered speech and language therapy intervention for patients with aphasia following a stroke.Participants: 278 patients were included in the study.Caregiver Involvement: Where available, a maximum of one informal caregiver per patient was invited to participate in self-reported data collection regarding their own quality of life.Measurement Tools: EQ-5D-5L: self-reported by informal caregiversCarerQol-7D: A specific instrument designed to measure the care-related quality of life of informal caregivers.Additional Data: The study also collected data on CaCoast, patient self-reported EQ-5D-5L, and patient primary endpoints.Following a 12-month follow-up period, complete EQ-5D-5L data was collected from 226 patients, and complete EQ-5D-5L data was collected from 125 informal caregivers. This dataset would make it possible to evaluate the construct validity and responsiveness of both the EQ-5D-5L and the CarerQol-7D for informal caregivers of post-stroke aphasia patients.The Lead Investigator of the BIG CACTUS study has already granted permission to obtain and use the dataset for this proposed analysis.

Title: Comparison of EQ-HWB versions with other preference-based measures of health and wellbeing in adults
Abstract: Several preference-based wellbeing measures, including the EQ-HWB-S, have been developed to measure outcomes beyond health-related quality of life (HRQoL) for economic evaluation. To operationalise this work, it is important to examine the level of the overlap between these different approaches. This can be achieved by comparing the content of these measures against an established conceptual framework and consulting with the community. Additionally, empirical evidence on the degree of overlap and differences in psychometric properties will help guide the use of these measures. Another key consideration for the application of the EQ-HWB-S is the consistency of responses and subsequent estimates of values from the standalone EQ-HWB-S compared to those derived from the full-length EQ-HWB. Understanding the consistency in responses, and therefore values, between the versions, will help to establish the flexibility of the EQ-HWB-S. This is especially relevant in situations where the full-length EQ-HWB may not provide additional information at the expense of respondent burden. Overall, this study aims to explore the validity and application of the EQ-HWB by providing a detailed understanding of its relationship with other preference-based measures of wellbeing in adults (ICECAP-A, ASCOT and WiX), and investigate the potential of the EQ-HWB-S as a standalone measure. Specifically, the aims of this study are to: A. Compare the content of the EQ-HWB and other wellbeing measures and examine the degree of conceptual and empirical overlap between them. B. Examine the consistency and validity of the EQ-HWB-S as a standalone measure compared to when derived from the EQ-HWB using primary data collected in Australia. C. Compare the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB and other wellbeing measures using data collected from the general Australian population. The item content of the EQ-HWB, ICECAP-A, ASCOT and WiX will be linked to categories of a conceptual framework (Olsen and Misajon, 2020) which expands on existing frameworks to integrate HRQoL within the broader context of subjective wellbeing. The number of codings per category will be descriptively analysed to identify distinct and overlapping conceptual areas across instruments.  We will also collect data from a sample of 1000 people in Australia, administering the EQ-HWB, EQ-HWB-S (as a standalone) and the other wellbeing measures. Psychometric properties will be analysed and compared, and the degree of overlap between measures will be assessed. Additionally, the consistency of responses between the EQ-HWB-S scores obtained from the standalone version and the full-length EQ-HWB will be evaluated by analysing the degree of agreement and stability of responses. This study meets the funding priorities listed by the EQ-HWB Group by contributing to understanding of the placement and value of the EQ-HWB-S alongside other social care and wellbeing measures used in economic evaluation, and alongside the full-length EQ-HWB. The study also supports the Strategic Plan’s objective to advance the development of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S to ‘approved’ status.

Title: Developing a National Value Set for the EQ-5D-Y-3L Instrument in South Korea: A Discrete Choice Experiment and Composite Time Trade-Off Study
Abstract: The EQ-5D-Y-3L is a paediatric health-related quality-of-life instrument designed for children and adolescents aged 8–15 years. A national value set is required to compute quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) for economic evaluations of healthcare interventions targeting younger populations in South Korea. This study will follow the international standardised protocol for EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation studies. Preferences will be elicited from a representative sample of the adult general population using two methods: (1) an online discrete choice experiment (DCE) in which 1,000 respondents each complete 15 paired comparisons, and (2) composite time trade-off (cTTO) interviews conducted with 200 respondents, each completing 10 cTTO tasks. In both tasks, respondents will be asked to consider what they prefer for a hypothetical 10-year-old child. DCE data will be analysed using mixed-logit models, and the resulting latent-scale values will be anchored to the QALY scale (0 = dead, 1 = full health) usinga mapping approach that links predicted DCE values to observed mean cTTO values across multiple health states. The resulting value set will enable cost-utility analyses of paediatric healthcare interventions in South Korea and will contribute to the growing body of international EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets.

Title: Compare the TTO and DCE modelling results on individual level
Abstract: Background So far, little attention has been given to the question what level of agreement is required to support the hybrid model, and what level of agreement can realistically be expected from DCE and TTO data. In this study we investigate the relationship of DCE coefficients and TTO coefficients on individual level. Methods A total of 210 university students were recruited from Guizhou Medical University, China to complete both TTO and DCE tasks. All participants valued 31 states using TTO and completed 55 choice tasks in the DCE. The set of states in the TTO tasks included a 25-state orthogonal design + 5 mildest states + 55555. A Bayesian efficient design algorithm was used to construct Bayesian D-efficient design with 60 pairs (55 unique pairs + 1 dominated pair + 4 repeated pairs) for the other respondents. The priors of the DCE design were from a sample of 36 students who completed a design of 40 pairs of DCE design constructed using priors from previous study. Students completed the TTO and DCE tasks in two separate face-to-face session, with the assistance of a trained interviewer. The interval between two sessions was <7 days. All responses were modelled by student using OLS (for TTO) and conditional logit (for DCE) using a 5-parameter (5P) model. 20-parameter (20P), 10-parameter (10P) main effects model were used to compare two sets of coefficients on aggregate level. Results 210 university students completed both sessions. For the TTO session. On average, each student spent 59.37 (SD: 18.93) minutes and used 8.97 (SD: 2.05) moves in the TTO tasks. 174 students completed the design of 60 DCE tasks (including 1 dominant pair test and 4 repeated pair tests) and 36 students completed the design of 40 DCE tasks. Among the 174 students of completing 60 DCE tasks, 166 students passed the dominant pair tests. 49, 67, 39 and 18 students passed 4, 3, 2, 1 repeated-pair tests, respectively. For the coefficients, the average Pearson correlation was 0.435 (SD: 0.462, median: 0.567, range: -0.859 to 0.999). Respondents whose DCE data was of better quality according to R2 showed better consistency in their TTO and DCE modelling results. On aggregate level, two sets of coefficients had a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.885 for the 5P model, 0.906 for the 10P model and 0.871 for the 20P model. Discussion Our results showed that on individual level, there are some evidence that the two sets of coefficients are associated, but not for all respondents. A main limitation of this study is the limited power of modelling coefficients on individual level. On aggregate level , it is clear that the linear relationship between two sets of coefficients exist, but varied with the severity levels of the coefficients.

Title: Psychometric comparison of experimental and experimental modified versions of the EQ-HWB-9 in the Netherlands and the USA
Abstract: BackgroundThe EuroQol Health and Wellbeing 9 (EQ-HWB-9) and EQ-HWB long form measures cover dimensions relevant for healthcare and social care users, and their caregivers. After initial testing of the experimental version (v1.1, 2022), areas for possible refinement were identified in item wording, response option labels, and item ordering. A modified experimental version (v1.2) was introduced in 2024. This study examines the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB-9 v1.2 and v1.1 in the Netherlands (NL) and the United States (USA).MethodsData from 3,783 adult participants (NL n=1,571; USA n=2,212) were collected via an online panel using quota sampling. All participants completed EQ-HWB-9 v1.2 as part of a longer survey and a subset was randomized to one of four arms, including EQ-HWB long form, EQ-HWB-9 v1.1 and its variants. Response distribution was explored, with instrument-level ceiling and floor effects defined as >15%. Known group validity was assessed using Mann-Whitney U test across five pre-defined subgroups, and convergent validity was assessed using Spearman’s correlations between EQ-HWB-9 versions, EQ-HWB long form, and EQ-5D-5L level sum scores.ResultsInstrument level floor/ceiling effects were not observed across versions, except for a marginal ceiling effect above threshold in the NL v1.1 (15.3%). v1.1 presented a higher proportion of Level 1 responses, particularly for day-to-day activities (USA - v1.2: 51.9%; v1.1: 60.5%; NL - v1.2: 51.8%; v1.1: 60.1%), and control (USA - v1.2: 53.4%; v1.1: 63.0%, v1.2: 56.0%; v1.1: 59.5%). All versions significantly discriminated across all known groups in both countries with large effect sizes in four out of five groups. v1.2 showed very strong cross-version correlations with v1.1 (rho=0.88 USA; rho=0.85 NL). Convergent validity was also demonstrated with external measures (EQ-5D-5L, EQ VAS, global health satisfaction, SWLS), with slightly higher correlations in v1.2 in both countries. Item-level convergent validity between matched v1.2 and v1.1 items was very strong to strong in both countries (rho=0.57 to 0.82) as well as with conceptually matched EQ-5D-5L items.ConclusionEQ-HWB-9 v1.2 demonstrated at least equivalent or slightly superior psychometric performance to v1.1 across all properties and consistently in both countries, supporting the modifications adopted in v1.2.

Title: Development of health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) value set for India
Abstract: The present study aims to develop EuroQol five-dimensional (EQ-5D-5L) health states value set for Indian population. A cross-sectional survey using the EuroQol Group’s Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) software will be undertaken in representative sample of 2700 respondents.The respondents will be selected from 12 districts in 6different states of India using a multistage stratified random sampling technique.The participants will be interviewed in a face to face setting using CAPI (computer assisted personal interviewing) technique. Time trade off (TTO) valuation will be done using 10 composite (cTTO) tasks and 7 discrete choice experiment (DCE) tasks.The demographic data will be analyzed by descriptive statistics. TTO values will be modeled using main effects model that will includeconstant and 20 main effectsderived from the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, using ordinary least squares (OLS)and tobit models. The DCE data will be modeled under random utility using the conditional logit model. Hybrid modeling approach using both c-TTO and DC data to estimate the potential value setwill be applied. This method will combine the utility values elicited in the c-TTO for the 86 health states with utility values elicited in the DC experiment for 196 pairs of states. Sensitivity analysis will be conducted to explore the impactof severely inconsistent responders.Value set for EQ-5D-5L health state will be estimated for the Indiangeneral population. This will be helpfulin clinical practice/research for better monitoring of health-relatedquality of life. The scores can be used as an important input that better reflect Indian population’s preference for health technology assessment research. In addition, the results can be used for international comparison in order to understand similarities and differencesof health preference across populations.

Title: Comparing test-retest reliability and responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L with four bolt-ons, PROMIS-29 and Skindex-16 in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis patients
Abstract: Poster presentation at ISPOR 2026:Objectives:Evidence supporting psychometric validity of EQ bolt-ons has been largely limited to cross-sectional studies. This study evaluated the impact of adding four bolt-ons—Skin Irritation (SI), Self-confidence (SE), Social Relationships (SR), and Sleep (SL)—on test-retest reliability and responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L in patients with Psoriasis(Ps) and Atopic Dermatitis (AD), and compared performance with PROMIS-29 and Skindex-16.Methods:This observational, single-center longitudinal study collected patient-reported data at baseline (N=236), 3–7 days later for test-retest reliability (N=180), and after 12 weeks for responsiveness (N=194). Test–retest reliability was assessed using weighted kappa (Kw) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). At week 12, patients were categorized as “stable,” “improved,” or “worsened” based on a combination of two external criteria (Global Rating of Change and clinical endpoints). Responsiveness was evaluated using effect sizes, standardized response mean, relative efficiency (RE), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).Results:EQ-VAS and standardized level sum scores showed good reliability with ICCs consistently >0.85 in Ps, and moderate to good reliability in AD (ICC=0.77–0.88). Kw values for SI, SE, SR, and SL were 0.69/0.63, 0.72/0.61,0.72/0.53, and 0.75/0.75 in Ps/AD, respectively. PROMIS-29 T-scores demonstrated moderate to good reliability (ICC=0.67–0.81 in Ps; 0.71–0.83 in AD). Individual inclusion of SI and SL more efficiently distinguished “improved” subgroups in Ps (RE=1.29 and 1.34), while inclusion of any single bolt-on was more efficient than EQ-5D-5L alone in AD. Skindex-16 showed the highest responsiveness among “improved” patients in Ps and AD ( RE=1.57 and 3.2, respectively). However, in “worsened” groups, EQ-5D-5L alone outperformed bolt-on versions and Skindex-16. All HRQoL measures were responsive (AUROC >0.6).Conclusion:Adding SI, SE, SR, and SL bolt-ons improved EQ-5D-5L responsiveness to smaller health changes while maintaining good test-retest reliability. Skindex-16 remained substantially more responsive than generic HRQoL instruments among improved groups.

Title: From Population Health to Valuation Methodology: Disseminating EQ-5D Research at ISPOR 2026
Abstract: This project successfully disseminated six EQ-5D research studies at ISPOR 2026, held 17–20 May 2026 at the Pennsylvania Convention Center, Philadelphia, PA, USA. All six abstracts were accepted as poster presentations and were presented in person, collectively advancing the evidence base for EQ-5D measurement, valuation, and application across population health, clinical outcomes assessment, health economic evaluation, and valuation methodology. Two presenters – Dr Cheng Ling Jie (Jeremy), EuroQol Group member, and Mr Xun Li (Ethan), researcher on EuroQol-funded project 2078-RA – shared presenting responsibilities to cover two pairs of overlapping poster sessions. The studies addressed: (1) declining population health and widening socioeconomic inequalities in a multi-ethnic Asian population using nationally representative EQ-5D-5L data (EPH179); (2) factors associated with preoperative EQ-5D outcomes among 1,194 patients undergoing degenerative lumbar spine surgery (EPH106); (3) the lack of standardisation in economic evaluations of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and the need for EQ-5D-based QALY estimation (EE173); (4) a systematic review of 138 value sets across six multi-attribute utility instruments (EPH226); (5) a methodological review of the evolution of EQ-5D-5L valuation practices and lessons from the 3L (MSR230); and (6) modelling of health system capacity and measurement dispersion as predictors of cross-national variation in EQ-VT utility values (MSR178). The project engaged health economists, clinicians, HTA practitioners, and policy-makers across dedicated discussion periods, supporting priorities of the Populations and Health Systems Working Group and the Valuation Working Group. All six posters are to be published in Value in Health. The project was supported by a EuroQol Travel Grant of €4,200 towards conference-related costs (registration, travel, and accommodation) for the two presenters.

Title: Establishing the optimal amount of Attribute Level overlap in 9D EQ-HWB instruments
Abstract: BackgroundIn EQ valuation, discrete choice experiments are becoming increasingly important, and the design of these tasks has direct consequences for both respondent burden and statistical efficiency. One important design feature is attribute level overlap, where one or more dimensions are held constant between alternatives within a choice task. Although overlap can reduce task complexity, it also reduces the statistical information generated by each choice. Determining the appropriate amount of overlap is therefore an important design question. This is especially the case for EQ-HWB-9, where the 9-dimensional structure makes unconstrained choice tasks substantially more demanding, while it remains unclear whether this is desirable. Project aimThe project aims to determine the optimal amount of attribute level overlap for the EQ-HWB-9 instrument. As no EQ-HWB-9 valuation data are currently available for this purpose, primary data will be collected. Different overlap conditions, defined by the number of dimensions held constant between alternatives within a choice task, will then be compared to identify the level that best balances task complexity and statistical efficiency.MethodsAn online DCE study will be conducted in a UK general population sample using the EQ-HWB-9 instrument. Respondents will be randomly allocated to one of eight experimental arms, each representing a different degree of attribute level overlap, ranging from 0 to 7 overlapping dimensions within a choice task. The overlap conditions will be compared using indicators of response efficiency, statistical efficiency, respondent behaviour, and data quality. The main analysis will use mixed logit models, with alternative estimation approaches examined where necessary to address the convergence and identification difficulties associated with high-dimensional EQ-HWB-9 data.

Title: Assessing psychometric properties and content validity of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L using IA and proxy‐report among school children aged 5-7 (Revised)
Abstract: Introduction: EuroQol Group has developed an experimental version of EQ-5D-Y-5L that has five severity levels for each dimension. The Younger Populations Working Group (YPWG) has expressed interest in evaluating psychometric performance in different childhood conditions considering of the views of children and their caregivers and potentially comparing EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L. Objective: To assess feasibility, test-retest reliability, responsiveness, known-group-validity and agreement between interviewer administration (IA) and proxy-report of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L among Ethiopian children with different disease conditions aged 5-8 years. Methods: Agreement, feasibility, test-retest reliability, responsiveness and known-group-validity of both EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were assessed and compared among children aged 5–8 years. First, children self-reported their health state through IA and thereafter, parents/guardians completed the corresponding EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L proxy-1 report Amharic version. Administration of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L versions was randomized and separated by an age-appropriate demanding cognitive task/problem- solving algebra. Repeated measures were taken by IA and proxy-report to assess test-retest reliability (for unchanged health status) and responsiveness (for changed health status) after ten days and one month, respectively, using a one-item global rating (GRS) scale to assess change in health status. Agreement and test-retest reliability of dimension scores (using percent agreement, Gwet’s AC and Cohen’s) and for LSS and EQ-VAS (using ICC), known-group validity (using Kruskal-Wallis rank test), and responsiveness (using mean change, standardized effect size (SES)). Results: A total of 356 participants were included in the study: 163 from the general school children, 95 with acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), and 98 with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). Most participants were school-aged children (mean age ~6.5 years), with 52.08% males. The highest proportion of reported problems reported in the “Feeling worried/sad/unhappy” and “Pain/discomfort” dimensions of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L, with proxy respondents consistently reporting fewer “no problems” responses than IA (χ² > 85, p < 0.001). Agreement between IA and proxy-reports ranging from moderate to almost perfect across all dimensions (Gwet’s AC = 0.61–0.91), with percent agreement between 67–91%. Known-group validity for both EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L was supported, with significant LSS differences across health conditions (χ² = 87.9–94.4, p < 0.001). Test–retest reliability (ICC) for IA and proxy LSS ranging from 0.62 to 0.80. Responsiveness was demonstrated in improved cases (n = 57), particularly for IA reports (ES = 1.04–1.18).  Conclusion: The EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L Amharic versions demonstrated good agreement and acceptable psychometric performance across IA and proxy-report. IA and proxy versions showed similar psychometric properties across all dimensions with greater variability for WSU and P/D. This study shows that both the Y-3L and Y-5L IA versions are valid and reliable for use in children aged 5-8 years where self-complete is not possible.

Title: Panel debate on QALY-based HTA and the EQ-5D at the Society for Medical Decision Making 48th Annual Meeting in Oslo
Abstract: The pharmaceutical industry and patient advocates argue that QALY-based HTA and the EQ-5D in particular serve to limit patients' access to care. Debates around QALY-based HTA, cost-effectiveness thresholds, and recommendations for the use of EQ-5D are ongoing in several countries.The Annual Meeting of the Society for Medical Decision Making is in Oslo, Norway, and I have been provided an opportunity to arrange a 75 minute panel debate around these issues, with representatives from the industry, HTA, academia, and EuroQol. The aim is to have an informed and exciting discussion, highlighting areas of controversy and how these should be tackled.SMDM is broadly attended by people involved in health-care decision making, including health economists, clinicians, and researchers.

Title: Cognition in EQ-5D-5L: A Content Validity Study in Dementia and Caregiving Contexts in the Netherlands
Abstract: This cross-sectional qualitative study aims to evaluate the content validity of the best available cognition bolt-on (Toolbox v1) and two related exploratory cognition bolt-ons on thinking and memory (Toolbox v1.5) to the EQ-5D-5L health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instrument in the context of dementia care. Interviews will be conducted with people living with mild to moderate dementia, and informal caregivers and healthcare professionals of people living with mild to severe dementia. Participants will engage in concept elicitation and cognitive debriefing while completing the EQ-5D-5L, cognition bolt-ons, ASCOT, and DEMQOL instruments using think-aloud. The study will assess the relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness of the cognition bolt-on.  Thematic analysis will be applied to interview transcripts. This study uniquely incorporates perspectives from both individuals living with dementia (community-dwelling and institutionalized) and their (formal and informal) proxies to ensure the bolt-on reflects diverse lived experiences and professional insights. Findings will contribute towards the validation of the Toolbox’s cognition bolt-ons and contribute to the item’s dossier with dementia-and caregiving-specific findings.

Title: Translation and cultural adaptation of 18 EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons into standard Arabic Language for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA)
Abstract: The EuroQol Research Foundation has recently developed the EQ-5D-5L Bolt-On Toolbox to enhance the instrument’s ability to capture health dimensions not fully represented in the core system, such as sleep, cognition, and fatigue. However, the global adoption of these bolt-ons depends on the availability of high-quality translations and culturally appropriate adaptations. Arabic is a strategic priority given its widespread use across the Middle East and North Africa, with Modern Standard Arabic enabling cross-country comparability. Saudi Arabia represents a particularly relevant context due to ongoing health system transformation under Vision 2030, emphasizing value-based care and patient-reported outcomes.This study aims to translate and culturally adapt 18 EQ-5D-5L bolt-on items into Modern Standard Arabic for use in Saudi Arabia, following EuroQol’s standardized translation and linguistic validation protocols under the supervision of the Version Management Committee. A subset of eight core and ten exploratory items will be translated and adapted to ensure conceptual equivalence and cultural relevance. The resulting Arabic toolbox will support future empirical validation through planned national studies and facilitate broader use in clinical research, health technology assessment, and real-world evidence generation across the region.

Title: Psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L for use in patients with autoimmune Graves’ disease
Abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L for use in patients with Graves’ disease (GD). Methods A prospective cohort of patients with relapsed GD recruited at three public hospitals in Hong Kong completed the EQ-5D-5L and ThyPRO-39 questionnaires at baseline, 1-month, and 6-month follow-ups. Construct validity was tested by examining the Spearman correlation between EQ-5D-5L and ThyPRO-39 scores at baseline. 1-month test-retest reliability was assessed by Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), Gwet’s Agreement Coefficient 2 (AC2), and percentage agreement. Responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L index and EQ-VAS scores was assessed using effect size statistics (standardized effect size [SES] and standardized response mean [SRM]). Results Of 125 recruited patients, 101 (80.8%) and 100 (80.0%) patients were followed up at 1- and 6-month, respectively. For construct validity, there was moderate negative correlation was found between EQ-5D-5L index score and ThyPRO-39 Overall QoL-impact score (-0.350), between EQ-VAS score and ThyPRO-39 overall QoL-impact score (-0.451), and between EQ-VAS score and composite score (-0.483), and a strong negative correlation between EQ-5D-5L index score and composite score (-0.567). The Gwet’s AC and percentage agreement were the highest in self-care (0.964 and 0.967), followed by mobility (0.952 and 0.962), usual activities (0.934 and 0.948), pain/discomfort (0.801 and 0.887), and anxiety/depression (0.788 and 0.882). The ICC for the EQ-5D-5L index and the EQ-VAS respectively was 0.707 and 0.700, showing moderate reliability. For patients who reported having ‘worsened’ health at 6-month follow-up, the SES and SRM were -0.66 and -0.42 for EQ-5D-5L index and -1.15 and -1.10 for EQ-VAS, respectively. For patients with ‘improved’ health, SES and SRM were -0.16 and -0.17 for EQ-5D-5L index and 0.19 and 0.20 for EQ-VAS, respectively. Conclusions The EQ-5D-5L demonstrated construct validity, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness to worsened health status among patients with GD. Responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L to health improvement warrants further investigation.

Title: Development of EQ-5D-Y-3L norms data based on a general population sample of children and adolescents in Sweden
