Title: Impact of mode of administration on responses agreement and measurement properties of the EQ-5D and other preference-based outcome measures: a systematic review
Abstract: Background: EQ-5D-3L/-5L and other preference-based outcome measures (PBMs) can be  administered using different modes of administration (MoAs), including self-complete (paper and pencil and digital survey) and interviewer administration (face to face, telephone, and computer-assisted personal interview). To compare EQ-5D-3L/-5L data obtained using different MoAs or to be able to pool data obtained using different MoAs, evidence on the extent to which they produce similar health responses is needed. Also, It is important to know whether using different MoAs affects key Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) measurement properties. Aims: To assess and compare the impact of using different MoAs on intra-rater response agreement and key COSMIN measurement properties of the EQ-5D and other PBMs.Methods: A systematic search of nine bibliographic databases will be conducted using a search strategy developed in consultation with a librarian. Studies comparing health responses, measurement properties including reliability, validity, and responsiveness across different MoAs for the EQ-5D or otherPBMs will be included. Two reviewers will independently screen titles/abstracts and full texts, and disagreements will be resolved through team discussion. Information on study characteristics, response distributions, key COSMIN measurement properties across different MoAs of EQ-5D and other PBMs will be extracted in duplicate using a pretested form. Following COSMIN guidelines, two reviewers will independently evaluate the measurement properties of the PBMs and rate the quality of evidence for each instrument per MoA. The study protocol has been developed in accordance with PRISMA-P guidelines, and the final report will follow PRISMA-COSMIN standards.

Title: The QALY under scrutiny: A systematic review and thematic synthesis of methodological, ethical, legal, and policy debates
Abstract: Despite widespread adoption in health technology assessment (HTA), the quality-adjusted life year (QALY) has faced persistent methodological and ethical critiques. Critics argue that QALYs discriminate against the elderly and individuals with disabilities, failing to account for equity or broader societal values. These debates have influenced the policy landscape, particularly in the US. The Affordable Care Act (2010) and the Inflation Reduction Act (2022) have banned the QALY-based decision making across federal programs.  Existing discussions are scattered across health economics, ethics, and policy literature. This systematic literature review aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize the diverse perspectives surrounding QALYs to provide a comprehensive analysis of the existing debate. Because the Group’s long-term financial sustainability is intrinsically linked to the continued recommendations of EQ instruments in the QALY framework for HTA, it is vital that the EuroQol Group actively engages in this debate and shape policy recommendations.

Title: An exploratory analysis of the Pain/Discomfort dimension of the EQ-5D-5L in people living with physical and mental health conditions
Abstract: Research into the Pain/Discomfortdimensionof EQ-5D instruments has identified problems with interpretation because two different aspects of health are combined in a single question. Studies have also shown that interpretation difficulties may arise because of the wording of response options, particularly concerning the differences between ‘slight’ and ‘moderate’ (levels 2 and 3), and ‘severe’ and ‘extreme’ (levels 4 and 5). This study will explore what is behind the Pain/Discomfort dimension of the EQ-5D-5L, drawing comparisons to other pain and discomfort items collected in the Extending the Quality-Adjusted Life Year (E-QALY) psychometric study in Australia. Analyses will include: descriptive statistics of response data; correlation analyses 2exploring the associations between EQ-5D-5L Pain/Discomfort and other E-QALY pain and discomfort questions; regression analyses assessing the extentto whichthe E-QALY pain and discomfort items are captured by EQ-5D-5L Pain/Discomfort; and discriminatory power analyses of the EQ-5D-5L with and without other E-QALY pain and discomfort questions. Furthermore, we will explore variation in reporting patterns for pain and discomfort questions across individuals living with mental health and physical health conditions, respectively. This sub-analysis arose from findings of the face validity study of the E-QALY project in Australia, which indicated that people with a mental health condition associated the Pain/Discomfort questions with emotionalpain or discomfort rather thanphysicalsensations. Overall, findings from this study will provide a better understanding of the Pain/Discomfortdimensionof the EQ-5D-5L, including implications for the complementary use of the EQ-5D-5L and E-QALY, and the future bolt-on agenda.

Title: Assessment of the EQ-5D-5L compared to EQ-5D-3L and generation of population norms in England
Abstract: There are two versions of EQ-5D, a brief preference-based utility measure that can be used in economic evaluation, one with 3 severity levels (3L) and one with 5 levels (5L). In England, EQ-5D-3L can be scored using the existing United Kingdompreference-based tariffwhile the EQ-5D-5L can be scored using a crosswalk to the 3L tariff or using the new English tariff. This study compared the performance of the EQ-5D-3L (n=930,200) against the EQ-5D-5L (n=881,810) using evidence from the GP Patient Survey (GPPS) in England. Comparison was based on feasibility (missing data) distribution across the dimensions, ceiling and floor effects, and discriminative properties using Shannon’s indices. Utility scores for the two versions were compared in terms of absolute and standardized effect sizes for groups with known differences categorised by self-reported long-term health condition, limitations in activity, and sociodemographic factors for the full samples. In addition, matched samples (age, gender and comorbidities) were used to compare utilities for subgroups with long-term health conditions. While the 3L and 5L had similar levels of missing data across dimensions, there was evidence of improved performance in the 5L compared to the 3L in terms of reduced ceiling effects (34.9%5Lvs. 44.4%3L) and re-distribution across the other levels, particularly for mobility, usual activities and pain/discomfort dimensions. There were very few respondents reporting the lowest level in either version (0.02%5Lvs. 0.03%3L). Mean (SD; range) 3L utility values were 0.804 (0.265; -0.594 to 1), mean 5L values from the cross-walk were 0.796 (0.237; -0.594 to 1) and mean utility values for the 5L were 0.859 (0.205; -0.281 to 1). The5L utility values tended to be higherthan corresponding 3L valuesbutthe variance in the 3L scores was larger(e.g. males means 0.8605Lvs 0.8083L; standard deviations 0.2055Lvs 0.2613L). Cross-walk values were smaller or equivalent to 3L values and smaller than 5L values(males,mean(SD):0.799 (0.236). Allversions were able to discriminate in the expected direction between groups with known differences e.g. younger respondents had higher utility scores than older respondents. The 3L had larger absolute mean differences between most groups with known differencesbutthis was mediated by the larger variances thus standardised effect sizes across the threeversions were comparable. For example, comparing those with arthritis/joint problems to those without, absolute differences were 0.3113Lvs. 0.273cwvs. -0.2325Landeffect sizes were 1.153Lvs. 1.13CWand -1.105L.Differences between those with and without a condition were smaller in the matched samples with small and similar differences across the three versionsfor some conditions (angina/heart problems, asthma/chest problems, cancer, blind/visual problems, deaf/hearing problems, diabetes, epilepsy, kidney/liver problems, learning difficulties). This study adds to what is known in terms of comparison based on utility values using the latest English tariff for the 5L

Title: DEVELOPMENT OF EQ-5D-Y VALUE SET FOR THAI CHILDREN AGED 8 – 15 YEARS OLD
Abstract: Currently, health technology assessment plays an important role in public health policy decision-making in Thailand, particularly in the process of policy decisions related to adding drugs to the National List of Essential Medicines by the Subcommittee on the National List of Essential Medicines, as well as decisions on adding diagnostic or treatment procedures to the benefit package for patients under the National Health Security scheme, overseen by the National Health Security Office (NHSO). This is due to budget constraints and the need to ensure fairness in access to public healthcare services. Cost-utility analysis is the recommended method for evaluating the economic value of public health interventions in Thailand. This requires utility data to calculate Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs), and the EQ-5D tool is recommended for utility assessments in Thailand. Although Thailand has an established value set for the EQ-5D tool, it is based on adult data and cannot be applied to children, as studies from other countries have shown that using adult value sets for children results in inaccurate utility values. This study aims to develop a utility value set for Thai children aged 8-15 using the EQ-5D-Y tool, which has been specifically developed for measuring utility values in children. This study will be conducted according to the International Valuation Protocol of EuroQol by randomly surveying the adult Thai population, who will act as representatives for children aged 8-15 years. This approach is due to ethical concerns that certain questions, such as those related to death or experiencing pain worse than death, may not be appropriate to ask children directly. The study will be divided into three parts. The study will consist of three parts: 1. An onsite survey of 1,400 Thai participants using the discrete choice experiment method to determine the weight between the five dimensions of the EQ-5D-Y tool. 2. A face-to-face interview of 280 Thai participants to find utility values for each health status using the composite time-trade-off method. 3. Mapping the results from both surveys to establish the utility weight (value set). The data collection tools will be supported by EuroQol, including EQ-VT, EQ-5D-Y, and their translation into Thai. In addition, EuroQol will provide training on the use of these tools as well as quality assurance for the data collection process. The population sampling will be conducted in cooperation with the National Statistical Office (NSO) to ensure the selection of appropriate and representative enumeration areas, and simple random sampling within these areas will be used to recruit participants with the specific characteristics required for the study, as determined by the National Statistical Office. The outcome of this study will be the development of a value set for EQ-5D-Y that can be appropriately applied to Thai children aged 8-15 years. This value set will be used for ongoing economic evaluations of public health interventions for children in Thailand.

Title: QC Tool as Web App (R/Shiny)
Abstract: The EuroQol Quality Control (QC) tool was initially developed by Juan M. Ramos-Goñi while working for the EuroQol Office. Its initial development started in 2013, and it has been in use in a lot of valuation studies up to nowadays. The current version keeps being Excel-based while it has turned out to be an EQ-VT2 Data Tool which downloads and parses data directly from EQ-VT2 servers. While during more than 10 years it has been a very powerful tool, it has several limitations including user’s control, cross-platform compatibility, especially with Mac users, and may be hindered by antivirus software and system configurations. This proposal aims to address these challenges by transitioning the Data Tool into a web-app solution implemented in R/Shiny. By doing so, we can achieve a more user-friendly experience, ensure compatibility across various devices, and implement enhanced security features like Two-Factor Authentication. The result will be a more robust, scalable, secure and accessible web-app platform keeping the same flexibility.

Title: Testing the validity and responsiveness to change of the EQ-HWB-9 in a population of young adults with chronic health conditions transitioning from paediatric to adult medical care - the Transition Compass Trial.
Abstract: The EuroQol Health and Wellbeing Short (EQ-HWB-9) is an internationally developed instrument for evaluating the impact of health, public health and social care interventions on patients and carers.(1,2)  Research is needed to evaluate the performance of the EQ-HWB-9 in younger populations (3) and the proposed study aims to address this evidence gap.The EQ-HWB-9 has been included in an Australian randomised controlled trial (Transition Compass (4)), which aims to improve the transition of young people with chronic disease from paediatric to adult health care. Currently, the processes and experiences of transition to adult care are often suboptimal with high rates of patients disengaging from specialist care as they enter adult services, resulting in increased reliance on crisis-driven and emergency care.  Transition Compass will evaluate a consumer-driven care model to improve transition, aiming to decrease healthcare disengagement and reduce crisis-driven care and its impact on both individual patients and the healthcare system. We know that young adults with chronic disease report poorer quality of life than the general population.  A recent study identified that half of the cohort of adolescents and young adults with chronic conditions experienced moderate to severe impact to their health-related quality of life (5).   Transition Compass will recruit approximately 400 young adults aged 16-18 years with chronic health conditions in their final year of paediatric care before transition to adult healthcare.  Participants will complete study surveys at baseline with follow up at one year post discharge from paediatric care. Participant quality of life and wellbeing will be measured using several psychological instruments, including EQ-HWB-9, PROMIS Scale Global Health (PROMIS-10), Emotion Thermometer: Distress, and On Your Own Feet Self-Efficacy Scale.  This provides a novel opportunity to examine the use of the EQ-HWB-9 in a population of young adults with chronic health conditions.  It is anticipated that the Transition Compass trial intervention will improve participants’ quality of life over time.The study for which EuroQol funding is sought aims to examine the validity and responsiveness to change of the EQ-HWB-9 in a population of young adults with chronic health conditions.  Specifically, we aim to validate the scale in this population using response distribution; convergent validity analysis and known group validity analysis across a range of known groups; and determine if the instrument is responsive to change over time (between baseline and follow-up).

Title: A Big Step Forwards for Health Policy in Indonesia: The Introduction of The EuroQol EQ-5D-5L Value Set and Other Recent Developments in Quality of Life Research and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis. (PI: Purba)
Abstract: This year in October the values set of the Indonesia 5 level version of the EQ-5D will be submitted to a scientific journal. We will also have the population norm scores. The arrival of the Indonesia 5 level value set and norm scores comes timely, as Indonesia has started in 2014 a societal health insurance system, and (cost-) effectiveness is determined as one of the leading principles for reimbursement. With this symposium/workshop we want to bring the stakeholders together how can benefit most from the introduction of the Indonesian value set and population norm scores, in order to facilitate the implementation of the EQ-5D-5L in Indonesia. The stakeholders will be the policy makers, physicians and scientists and other end users like representatives of industry. We will educate them about the principles of quality of life research, health economics and the added value of the now state-of-the-art Indonesian EQ-5D for those fields. The symposium is supported with budget and in kind by the Faculty of Psychology Universitas Padjadjaran (UNPAD). Given our network and that of UNPAD, we are able to attract key decision makers and scientific opinion leaders, who can support us in establishing a leading position of the EQ-5D in Indonesia. Given the present need of Indonesia to achieve valid cost-effectiveness and quality of life research, the symposium/workshop will have the effect a promotion of the EQ-5D in this country with 250 million citizens at the right moment.

Title: EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L Proxy Assessment in Neuropsychiatric Populations: Validating Patient-Proxy Agreement, Perspective Discordance, and the Role of Caregiver Burden
Abstract: Aim: This study's primary aim is to examine the validity of the EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L proxy versions in neuropsychiatric illness by assessing patient-proxy agreement, where the proxy is an informal caregiver. Secondary aims are to examine the extent to which the proxy-proxy perspective (caregiver rating from their own viewpoint) differs from the proxy-patient perspective (caregiver rating standing in the patient's shoes), with particular attention to conditions where the patient may not be engaged with reality, and to examine the role of caregiver burden in modifying the level of patient-proxy agreement.Methods: We will conduct a cross-sectional study involving patient-caregiver dyads plus healthcare provider assessments, recruiting 300 patient-caregiver dyads (neurology/ psychiatry departments from two academic medical centers in Lebanon). Patients will complete self-assessments using the EQ-HWB-9, EQ-5D-5L, and self-perceived burden. Their informal caregivers will complete both proxy-patient assessments and proxy-proxy assessments and a caregiver burden instrument. Primary analyses will assess item-level and scale-level agreement between patient self-reports and caregiver proxy-patient assessments using weighted kappa, intra-class correlation coefficients, and Bland-Altman plots. Secondary analyses will quantify differences between proxy-proxy and proxy-patient perspectives, and will examine how caregiver burden modifies proxy-patient agreement through regression models, including whether patient self-perceived burden moderates these associations. Significance: This project addresses a critical gap in health and wellbeing measurement in neuropsychiatric populations where proxy reporting is essential. By validating the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 proxy versions and distinguishing between two conceptually distinct proxy perspectives and the influence of caregiver burden on assessment accuracy,  findings will inform best practices for proxy use in clinical and research settings, supporting more accurate health measurement in populations least able to self-report.

Title: Whose Health Is It Anyway? Critically considering the role adults take in EQ-5D-Y valuation
Abstract: For cost-utility analyses for children, health-related quality of life (HRQOL) is commonly measured using paediatric instruments such as EQ-5D-Y, yet associated value sets are typically derived from adult preferences. This practice raises a fundamental normative question: whose preferences, and thus whose values, should count when valuing child HRQOL? Recent academic critique has focused on whether children have the fundamental right and ability to provide preferences and hence should be involved in valuing child HRQOL, yet the default position, that preferences of adult members of the general public should (at least partially) determine the importance of changes in child HRQOL, remains unchallenged. This perspective critically examines the role adults have in the valuation of child HRQOL. We first revisit the dominant justification for adult involvement in valuation, i.e., the taxpayer argument, and show that recent empirical evidence from public, stakeholder, and expert studies offers little support for this rationale. We then explore alternative normative arguments for involving adults, and propose a typology of 10 distinct roles adults can take in valuation of child HRQOL, ranging from the sole source of preference information to partners, caretakers, or only gatekeepers that enable children themselves to value child HRQOL. We argue that greater conceptual clarity about why and how adults are involved is essential for the future development of paediatric value sets for use in economic evaluations, thereby strengthening the legitimacy, transparency, and practical use of paediatric HRQOL instruments in policy and decision-making, and identify several high priority research gaps

Title: The EQ-HWB-S as a quality of life assessment tool in disability service support provision: An exploratory study
Abstract: The EQ‑HWB is a comprehensive tool designed to capture key aspects of health and wellbeing, but it remains an experimental instrument with limited evidence on its real‑world applicability, particularly in disability service settings. People living with disabilities represent a population for whom broader measures of quality of life (QoL) and wellbeing are highly relevant and the EQ-HWB has the potential to be a valuable routine QoL outcome measure in this space.This project aims to evaluate the comparative advantage of the interviewer‑administered EQ‑HWB‑9 as a routine outcome measure within a real‑world disability service context. Using an Australian not‑for‑profit disability service provider, Scope Australia, as a test case, the study will compare the EQ‑HWB‑9 with the WHOQOL‑BREF with Disability (DIS) addition, an instrument currently being trialled at Scope Australia. Mixed methods will be employed, including stakeholder workshops, longitudinal routine data collection, and qualitative interviews with clients, clinicians and support workers.Quantitative analyses will assess response rates, missing data, response distributions and reasons for non‑completion to determine comparative feasibility and data quality. Qualitative analyses will explore stakeholder perspectives on relevance, burden, and usability of the EQ‑HWB‑9, as well as its perceived value in informing care planning and service delivery. The project will also examine how EQ‑HWB‑9 data can be summarised and presented to support decision making in disability services, including potential dashboard approaches.Findings will inform practical guidance on the routine use of the EQ‑HWB‑9 in disability support settings, with relevance for value‑based health decision making and broader applicability to public and non‑for‑profit disability services internationally.

Title: Translation, cultural adaptation, and feasibility testing of the EQ-HWB-9 in Estonian and Russian languages within Estonia’s emerging integrated care networks (TERVIK)
Abstract: This project proposes a two-phase study to: (1) translate and culturally adapt the Experimental EQ-HWB-S (9-item) instrument into Estonian and Russian for use in Estonia, following the EuroQol translation methodology and ISPOR guidelines; and (2) conduct a preliminary feasibility assessment of the EQ-HWB-S within Estonia’s newly established regional integrated care service delivery networks (TERVIK).Estonia represents a strategically important setting for EQ-HWB development. The country is creating TERVIK networks which are county-level structures integrating primary healthcare, social care, and local hospital services with formal legislation anticipated in 2026. These networks are designed to manage populations with complex, multi-morbid conditions and coordinate care across health and social sectors—precisely the context for which the EQ-HWB-S was developed. Furthermore, Estonia’s substantial Russian-speaking minority (approximately 25–30% of the population) necessitates parallel language versions and offers a unique opportunity to examine cross-cultural measurement equivalence within a single-country setting.Phase 1 will produce officially approved Estonian and Russian (for Estonia) translations of the EQ-HWB-S Paper Self-Complete version through forward translation, back translation, cognitive debriefing (n=8 per language), and proofreading, with full Version Management Committee (VMC) oversight at each stage. Phase 2 will pilot the EQ-HWB-S in approximately 50 Estonian-speaking and 50 Russian-speaking respondents recruited through two TERVIK pilot sites, assessing feasibility, acceptability, response distribution, and preliminary psychometric properties. The project will deliver validated linguistic versions ready for larger-scale use, alongside evidence on the practical utility of the EQ-HWB-S in an integrated care context.

Title: Comparing the representativeness of population health surveys in Norway: a comparison of random probability sampling and online panel quota sampling (EQ-DAPHNIE)
Abstract: BackgroundPopulation health norms derived from EQ-5D instruments support health technology assessments, burden-of-disease studies, and economic evaluations. Random probability sampling remains the gold standard for generating representative population estimates, but rising costs and declining response rates have driven increasing use of online panel quota sampling. The EQ-DAPHNIE initiative uses online panel methods across multiple countries. Whether EQ-DAPHNIE samples are as representative as probability-based surveys is not yet established. A 2025 study of 53,000 randomly sampled adult individuals in the Norwegian population, recruited through the national health app, offers a unique opportunity for comparison.ObjectiveTo compare the representativeness and data quality of two Norwegian population health surveys using different recruitment strategies: (1) a large-scale random probability sample (N=53,000) recruited via national registries through Helsenorge, Norway's national digital health portal; and (2) a newly collected Norwegian EQ-DAPHNIE dataset using online panel quota sampling.MethodsCross-sectional comparison of survey performance metrics (response rates, completion rates, missingness, completion time, speeding), EQ-5D-5L outcomes (dimension scores, EQ VAS, index values, Level Sum Score), and chronic condition prevalence. Regression models will quantify unadjusted differences between samples. Sequential adjustment for sociodemographic and socioeconomic covariates (age, sex, education, income) will assess whether differences persist after controlling for composition. Post-stratification weighting, propensity score weighting, and calibration weighting will be explored as harmonization approaches.Expected outcomesThe study will produce methodological evidence on how sampling strategy affects data quality and population health estimates in a Norwegian context. Findings will directly inform the EuroQol Population Health Systems Working Group on sample representativeness, adjustment methods, and guidance for future EQ-5D population surveys and ongoing EQ-DAPHNIE data collection. Moreover, the Norwegian EQ-DAPHNIE data will be a valuable addition to the EQ-DAPHNIE data archive, providing a useful resource for population health research, instrument comparison and cross-country comparisons.

Title: Advancing EQ-5D-5L Application Through AI-Driven Full-Course Management Service for Breast Cancer Patients
Abstract: Background: The conventional administration of patient-reported outcome measures relies on predefined, fixed time points. This static approach presents methodological limitations when patients experience frequent and often unpredictable fluctuations in health status due to acute adverse events, treatment modifications, and disease progression. Can AI transform the administration of EQ-5D in routine clinical practice?Aims: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility of AI-driven, event-triggered EQ-5D-5L administration for measuring HRQoL in patients with breast cancer, and to compare HRQoL trajectories derived from event-triggered versus fixed-interval assessments. A secondary objective is to explore the relationship between AI-derived emotional phenotypes and the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression response.Methods: The proposed study will be embedded within a large-scale, multi-centre, prospective, controlled, real-world study evaluating AI-driven full-course breast cancer management in China. For the embedded study, 50 patients per group will be enrolled and randomized to the intervention and control groups. In the control group, EQ-5D-5L will be collected at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. In the intervention group, additional event-triggered assessments are automatically prompted by the AI system upon detection of clinically significant events in addition to the same fixed data collection schedule as in the control group. Feasibility will be evaluated through response rates, data completeness, and assessment adherence. We will investigate whether the patient's emotional state at the precise moment of EQ-5D-5L completion (as detected by the AI during the interaction in which the questionnaire is administered) systematically influences the response to anxiety/depression item, controlling for the underlying characteristics.

Title: Decomposing the socioeconomic gradient in health-related quality of life over the life course (DeQoL-LIFE)
Abstract: Reducing socioeconomic inequalities in health is a common social objective for policymakers. Differences between socioeconomic groups exist in terms of both health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and survival. These can result in large lifetime health inequalities. However, there is a lack of evidence on how inequalities accumulate over the life course and which dimensions of HRQoL contribute most to overall health inequality. This project will analyse how socioeconomic inequalities in HRQoL change with age and how these are determined by the different dimensions of the EQ-5D-3L. Our empirical analysis will yield population-level HRQoL scores for different socioeconomic groups, which can be combined with national life tables to produce estimates of quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE), a rich summary measure of lifetime health. We will analyse how much of the inequalities in QALEs can be attributed to each EQ-5D dimension. We will use HRQoL data from a long-running, nationally representative survey of the English population, the Health Survey for England, which has intermittently collected EQ-5D-3L data since 2003. We will use all waves that included the EQ-5D-3L to show how inequalities in both HRQoL and QALE have developed over the last 15 years. This project will demonstrate the usefulness of the EQ-5D instrument in measuring and explaining health inequalities over the life course, focussing specifically on the additional insights that can be gained from analysing the detailed EQ-5D health profile data. The results will also provide useful evidence to policymakers seeking to reduce health inequalities in England and internationally.

Title: Revisiting the MVH study: new methods for modelling UK valuations for the EQ-5D-3L
Abstract: Background: The 2017 English EQ-5D-5L value set differs substantially from the 1997 UK EQ-5D-3L value set recommended by NICE. Possible reasons include: (a) preferences of people have changed over the last 20 years (b) the composition of the general public has changed, affecting average preferences (c) differences in methods used to elicit preferences; (d) differences in the way preference data are modelled. Given the implications of using the 5L value set instead of the 3L value set, it is important to understand the contribution of each factor. Aims: To examine the effect on the value sets of the specific approaches taken to modelling. The innovative modelling approaches used in modelling the 5L value set are applied to the 3L data. Isolating the effect of the modelling methods provides a better basis for comparing the two value sets. Data: TTO data from 2,997 respondents and 912 respondents in the UK 3L and English 5L valuation studies respectively. Methods: 3L and 5L TTO data are modelled addressing data censoring; heteroscedasticity in the errors; and heterogeneity in preferences. Linear regressions provide the comparison baseline. Censored regressions without accounting for the heteroscedasticity nor heterogeneity are estimated using the maximum likelihood method. Censored models with no heteroscedasticity, heteroscedasticity alone, and both heteroscedasticity and heterogeneity being taken into account are estimated using Bayesian methods. Comparisons are made between estimated coefficients from different modelling methods, and between the predicted index values. Results: Results suggest differences between the UK 3L and English 5L value sets are primarily caused by differences in the underlying preference data, particularly the large number of values < 0 in the former. Applying the 5L modelling methods to 3L valuation data would yield a different value set with different properties than the existing UK 3L value set. However, the modelling methods exert a greater magnitude of difference on the 5L values than on the 3L values. Results raise questions about the interpretation of the constant in value functions.

Title: Initial psychometric testing of E-QALY and 3L-5L comparison in China

Title: Valuing Health-State: An EQ-5D-5L Value Set for Uzbekistan population
Abstract: This study aimed to develop an EQ-5D-5L value set for Uzbekistan to support the measurement and evaluation of health-related quality of life. The project, initially approved in April 2020, faced delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the loss of the original principal investigator. In 2023, a new research team was established and trained with the support of EuroQol researchers. Data collection was carried out between May and July 2024 in collaboration with four major medical universities across Uzbekistan. Overall 12 interviewers were requruited and one was dismissed from the study, due to not meeting quality requirements. More than 1,050 interviews were conducted, and 1,007 interviews are presented in the analysis, meeting EuroQol quality protocols. The results reveal that mobility is perceived as the most important health dimension in Uzbekistan, followed by self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression—contrasting with findings from other countries. Age and health experiences were found to be strong predictors of self-reported health on the EQ-VAS scale. The study highlights key policy lessons, including the need for better infrastructure for people with mobility limitations, enhanced support for individuals with reduced self-care ability, and increased investment in inclusive health technologies.

Title: Psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-9 in Brazilian frail and non-frail older adults
Abstract: Introduction: Long-term care for frail older adults represents an increasing challenge in the context of global population aging, with substantial implications for healthcare systems and resource allocation. Frailty is a multifactorial geriatric syndrome characterized by the accumulation of physiological deficits and diminished homeostatic reserve, leading to heightened vulnerability to adverse outcomes such as hospitalization, complications, institutionalization, and mortality. The hospital-to-home transition is a critical period, often influencing health outcomes and quality of life, and is frequently associated with readmissions. Health-related quality of life instruments generally assess limited range of health dimensions and often fail to encompass domains that are particularly relevant for older adults, such as autonomy, cognition, and social care. The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) instrument, comprising 25 items, was developed to address this conceptual gap by integrating health and wellbeing domains. A shorter version, the EQ-HWB-9, has been proposed to facilitate use in research and clinical settings. However, the psychometric properties of the proxy-interviewer administered version of the EQ-HWB-9 have not yet been evaluated in the Brazilian population. Objective: To assess the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-9 among frail and non-frail older adults in Brazil. Methods: This will be a longitudinal psychometric study including test-retest and 3-month follow-up assessment. Data collection will be conducted at the Hospital do Servidor Público Municipal of São Paulo, including 140 caregivers (aged over ≥18 years) of frail (n=70) and non-frail (n=70) older adults (aged ≥60 years). The Brazilian Portuguese proxy interviewer-administered versions of the EQ-HWB-9, EQ-HWB Visual Analogue Scale (EQ-HWB-VAS), and complementary instruments (EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, Short Warwick-Edinburgh mental well-being scale [SWEMWBS], Clinical Frailty Scale [CFS], Life-Space Assessment [LSA], Targeted Geriatric Assessment [TAGA], and Perceived of Change Scale [PCS]) will be administered. The psychometric properties will focus on reliability, measurement error, construct validity (convergent and discriminant), responsiveness, feasibility, and ceiling and floor effects. Discussion: This study will generate evidence on the validity of the EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-HWB-VAS in terms of reliability, measurement error, and construct validity and responsiveness, in a population of frail and non-frail older adults. This will generate important information on the feasibility of administration of the proxy interviewer administered version in a Brazilian context supporting its use in both clinical practice and health research.Keywords: Health-related quality of life; Older Adults; Frailty; Psychometric properties

Title: Travel Grant to support speakers of two EuroQol symposia focused on the Experimental Instruments (EQ-HWB-9, EQ-TIPS and ToolboxTM)
Abstract: This travel grant is on behalf of the YPWG and DSWG who coordinated the topics, speakers and abstract submission for two symposia at the 33rd Annual ISOQOL Conference (18-21 October 2026, Prague, Czech Republic). These symposia are respectively titled:- Challenges and triumphs of multi-national generic patient-reported outcome (PRO) measure development (Focus on EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-TIPS).- Introducing the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox: The EuroQol Groups' new approach to the development, valuation and use of bolt-ons to the EQ-5D-5L

Title: The translation of the EQ-TIPS instrument to Dutch
Abstract: Background: The EQ-TIPS is a standardized, proxy-reported experimental instrument developed by the EuroQol Group to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children aged 0–4 years. In the Netherlands, there is a lack of suitable HRQoL instruments for this age group, despite the growing importance of such measures in clinical research and economic evaluations. A Dutch version of the EQ-TIPS is needed to ensure linguistic and cultural appropriateness and to support future use in calculating quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).Aim: This study aims to translate the EQ-TIPS (5-level) from English into Dutch following EuroQol translation guidelines.Methods: The translation process includes forward translation by two Dutch-native translators, reconciliation into a first consensus version, and back translation by two English-native translators unaware of the original instrument. After producing a second consensus version, cognitive debriefing will be conducted with eight parents of children aged 0–4 years, ensuring variation in gender, education, and child health status. Findings will inform a pre-final version, followed by finalization, proofreading, and reporting.

Title: EQ DCE: Crowdsourcing innovation in valuation specification
Abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Health is not bought and sold openly. In order to understand the valueofits attributes, health preference researchers conductsurveys using paired comparisons (“Which do you prefer?”). In the absence of external data with which to validate their findings, resulting models, often based on conventional practices and assumptions,may be suboptimal in terms of predictive validity.Aims: To engage a large group of scientists in order to identify specifications and approaches to model selection that better predict health preferences. Methods: Announced in March 2016, the competition attracted 18 teams from around the world. In April,an exploratory survey was fielded:4074 US respondents completed 20 out of 1560 paired comparisons by choosing between two health descriptions (e.g., longer lifespan vs better health). The paired comparison data were distributed to all teams. By July, eight teams had submitted their predictions for 1600 additional pairs and described their analytical approach. After these predictions had been posted online, a confirmatory study was fielded (4148additional respondents).Results: In September, the victorious team, “Discreetly Charming Econometricians” led by Michał Jakubczyk, was announced at the EuroQol Plenary. This team achieved the smallest chi square 4391.54(a predefined criterion)usingtwo sub-models: one comparinga health descriptionvs immediate death and the other comparing twohealth descriptions.Conclusions: We demonstratedthe diversity of analytical approaches and highlighted the importance of predictive validity in health preference research. Although the generalizability to specific applicationsis unknown, the models that are more predictive, even if difficult to be immediately applied in health technology assessment (e.g. may not yield utilities directly assigned to specific health states), may inspireand informdebate among health preference researchers.

Title: Validation of Dutch translations of EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox vision bolt-ons in glaucoma and vitreoretinal surgery
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D-5L has been used frequently in ophthalmology, but sometimes lacks specificity and responsiveness in demonstrating changes over time or showing differences between ophthalmological conditions. EuroQol is seeking to validate the Bolt-on Toolbox, including bolt-ons for vision. EuroQol listed validation of the vision bolt-on as a priority for this grant round, especially testing of the multiple versions supporting the finalization of item wording, and providing evidence for validity and reliability. Objectives: We aim to validate the vision bolt-on in 2 ophthalmological disease populations (glaucoma and vitreoretinal surgery) in the largest eye hospital of The Netherlands.Methods: Translation of the vision bolt-ons from the Toolbox into Dutch is currently in progress by our study team. We will validate these vision bolt-ons through a "piggyback study": we will add the vision bolt-ons to existing studies using the EQ-5D-5L and to new externally-funded studies planning to use the EQ-5D-5L. We will focus on two disease areas: glaucoma (n = 80) and vitreoretinal surgery (n > 500). Study 1 & 2: two existing RCTs in glaucomaStudy 3: cross-sectional study in vitreoretinal surgery (QOL assessment)Study 4: cross-sectional study in vitreoretinal surgery (PROM validation)Study 5: prospective cohort in vitreoretinal surgery (real-world data)In glaucoma, 2 clinical trials assess surgical outcomes. In vitreoretinal surgery, our team is validating a disease-specific PROM. We will gather evidence on construct validity (correlations with NEI VFQ, visual acuity, and other relevant clinical measures), responsiveness (before and after surgery), and test-retest reliability.

Title: Estimating an EQ-5D-Y-3L value set for Brazil and comparing the measurement properties of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y- 5L and CHU9D in children and adolescents
Abstract: Introduction: Participation in the VI REBRATS Congress represents a strategic opportunity to disseminate EuroQol-supported research and strengthen the visibility and uptake of EQ-5D-Y instruments within the Brazilian health technology assessment (HTA) network. The REBRATS (Brazilian Network for the Evaluation of Health Technologies) and CONITEC (National Commission for the Incorporation of Technologies in the Unified Health System) play central roles in HTA decision-making, and presenting methodological advances on EQ-5D-Y valuation and validation will foster their integration into national economic evaluations and policy frameworks. Objectives and Methods: Five studies were presented in the VI REBRATS Congress, 1) the EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation study; 2) the qualitative arm of the EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation study to explore the valuation process from different perspectives (own-adult and child); 3) the qualitative arm of the EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation study to explore the valuation process from interviewers’ perspectives; 4) the study comparing the psychometric properties measurement of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D in children and adolescents; and 5) the study comparing the health-related quality of life of children and adolescents with and without musculoskeletal pain. The valuation study included discrete choice experiment (DCE) and composite time trade-off (cTTO) interviews with 1,376 Brazilian adults valuing child health states. Qualitative analyses explored participants’ reasoning and interviewers’ experiences with the valuation process. Additionally, cross-sectional psychometric studies were conducted with 441 children and adolescents (aged 8-18 years) with and without musculoskeletal pain to examine construct validity, reliability, and known-group validity and to investigate the impact of musculoskeletal pain in children and adolescents. Results and Discussion: A Brazilian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set was successfully developed (utilities ranging from 1 to -0.0059), with pain/discomfort identified as the most influential dimension. The qualitative studies identified cognitive and emotional aspects influencing valuations. The EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and CHU9D showed poor-to-moderate reliability, but EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L demonstrated good construct and known-group validity. Together, these studies provide the first comprehensive evidence base for pediatric health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measurement and valuation in Brazil. Impact: Disseminating these findings at REBRATS congress will promote awareness of EQ-5D-Y methodologies, support HTA capacity building in Latin America, and align Brazil’s economic evaluation practices with international standards. This presentation directly contributes to EuroQol’s mission of advancing the global use and methodological development of EQ-5D-Y instruments for children and adolescents.

Title: EUHEA preconference workshop: The Future of Health Preference Research
Abstract: Health preference research is undergoing structural renewal. The field is evolving in multiple directions at once: classic methods such as Time Trade-Off and Standard Gamble are increasingly complemented by modern approaches, including Discrete Choice Experiments. New protocols have been introduced to meet growing demand for internationally comparable value sets. At the same time, broader developments — including patient-centred definitions of value, consistent measurement across lifespan considerations, and expansion beyond traditional health outcomes — are reshaping how preference-based evidence is collected and used. Valuation research is happening at a larger scale and there is an increased need for mapping between instruments to retain a level of consistency and to ensure interoperability/ This session will provide a forward-looking exploration of health preference research, combining methodological innovation with practical and policy insights. We will highlight recent developments in valuation methods, examine the challenges of capturing preferences across different populations, and discuss how these methods inform evidence-based decision-making.

Title: Assessing the validity of the 86 health state selection for EQ-5D-5L VT studies: are we using the most efficient and valid set of health states to predict health states that exist in practice?
Abstract: Introduction When constructing an EQ-5D value set, a small number of health states will be directly valued by general public, and subsequently values for all health states are predicted using a regression model. A criterion that has been used for selecting health states for direct valuation, is whether the health states are ‘implausible’ for respondents. Health states being ‘implausible’ refers to those health states that respondent might find unrealistic. Inclusion of implausible states has been assumed to compromise respondents’ engagement with the task and to increase uncertainty around obtained health states’ values. Nevertheless, ‘implausible health states’ can be found in almost all valuation studies. In this study, we first, rated the ‘implausibility’ of all 3,125EQ-5D-5L health states using a student panel and explored the impact of ‘implausibility’ on data modelling; second, we explored the thought process of the respondents used to value ‘implausible’ health states. Methods1,600 students from Guizhou Medical University China, were recruited and each student valued around 200 EQ-5D-5L health states using EQ-VAS. Of those, 890 students provided feedback on the implausibility of health states they valued using a binary scale (implausible/plausible). In addition, 9 students were invited to share their views on ‘implausible health states’ in one on one semi-structured interviews and 12 students were invited in two focus group discussion (6 students each). An ‘implausibility’ score (ranging from 0 to 1, indicating the proportion of respondents who rated a health state as ‘implausible’; a higher score meaning more implausible) was calculated for each health state. Four OLS main effect model were fitted using implausible/plausible/all observations with/without additional implausible variable. Goodness of fit and misprediction effect were compared between models. Thematic analysis was performed for qualitative data by two independent researchers. ResultsApproximately 30% of the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states were rated as‘implausible’ by at least 50% of respondents. In the 20 dummy variables main effect model for estimating value set, adding the ‘implausibility’ information in the model as an addictive variable improved the model fit and lowered the MSE with a beta=-3.231(P=0.000) with 95% CI: -4.430, -2.032 (on EQ-VAS). Besides, excluding the implausible observations from the model will result in higher prediction error (MAE from 3.088 to 3.444). The qualitative work showed that some respondents encountered problems whenvaluing ‘implausible health states’. The most frequently reported categories of ‘implausible health states’ was: ‘health states with contradicting levels between dimensions’. The major reason for difficulty in valuing health states reported was ‘lack of experience/knowledge with severe health problems’. Respondents tended to give low value to ‘implausible health state’. Strategies respondents used to value ‘implausible’ state include ‘rewrite the health state to rationalize the contradictions’, ‘focus on certain dimensions and value’ and ‘refer to previous valued health states’.Discussions Our findings suggested that within the EQ-5D-5L set of 3,125 health states ‘implausible health states’ were not rare and respondents tended give low value to ‘implausible health states’. The understanding of ‘implausible health states’ differed over respondents. Nevertheless, inclusion of those implausible health states improves the model to estimated values sets. In cTTO task, the effect of the ‘implausible health state’ may not be problematic as respondent reactions can be controlled by the interviewer. In on-line DCE studies however, without further assistance from interviewers, the inclusion of implausible health state may irritate, confuse respondent and leads to more randomness in the data.ConclusionImplausible health states do exists, are more difficult to value and tent to have lower values, but excluding such state from modelling will result in higher prediction error in overall. Hence, it is not recommended to remove such states from a valuation study.

Title: Travel scholarship application to present EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 study findings at ISOQOL 33rd Annual Conference 2026
Abstract: This grant proposal requests funding to support the dissemination of research findings through an oral presentation and a poster presentation at the ISOQOL 2026 Conference, scheduled for 18–21 October 2026 in Prague, Czech Republic. The study titled “Are Preference-Based Cancer-Specific Measures More Sensitive than Generic Measures? A Comparison of EQ-5D-5L, SF-6Dv2, FACT-8D and QLU-C10D in Gastrointestinal Cancers”  has been accepted as an oral brief presentation. This study compared the psychometric performance of the generic EQ-5D-5L and SF-6Dv2 with the cancer-specific FACT-8D and QLU-C10D in patients with gastric, pancreatic, and colorectal cancers. Findings suggest that generic measures, especially EQ-5D-5L, performed better than or comparably to cancer-specific measures, although performance varied by cancer type. A second study, titled “Construct Validity and Responsiveness of the EQ-HWB-9 in Patients with Gastric, Pancreatic, and Colorectal Cancer,” has been accepted as an in-person poster presentation. This study demonstrated that the EQ-HWB-9 shows sufficient construct validity and responsiveness in gastrointestinal cancer populations. Both studies are conducted under the EuroQol-funded project [2120-RA], “Head-to-Head Comparison of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-S in Gastrointestinal Cancer Patients.”  The project received a small grant of €24,834, which covered personnel costs only and did not include any budget for dissemination activities. The two manuscripts have been submitted to Value in Health and Health and Quality of Life Outcomes, where they have received encouraging feedback and recognition from reviewers. Recognising the importance of these findings, we seek support to present them to a broader international audience at ISOQOL 2026.

Title: EQ-5D-5L Electronic Measurement Equivalence Project
Abstract: The overall aim of this study was to provide empirical evidence regarding the measurement equivalence of data collected with various data collection modes (paper, handheld, tablet,interactive voice response [IVR], and web) for the EQ-5D-5L. The objectives of this research were to:1.Collect and analyze test-retest data of the paper version of the EQ-5D-5L; and2.Quantitatively assess (via crossover studies) the measurement equivalence of various modes of data collection (i.e., paper, handheld, tablet, IVR, and web) of the EQ-5D-5L.The testing associated with these objectives involved a series of quantitative assessments of the various modes of the EQ-5D-5L. Several study samples were recruited from the UK general population to meet the objectives and conduct the quantitative assessments. The first group of participants consisted of 240 UK subjects divided across four independent samples (i.e., 60 subjects per sample). These four samples were used to assess the test-retest reliability of the paper EQ-5D-5L, as well as to test the agreement in the scores produced by the paper measureversus the three screen-based implementations of the EQ-5D-5L (i.e., handheld, tablet, and web). The second group of participants consisted of 61 UK subjects recruited to test the agreement in the scores produced by the paper, web, and IVR versions. Test-retest analysis of the paper EQ-5D-5L and analyses of the agreement of the scores of the original paper mode and the electronic modes (i.e., handheld, tablet, web, IVR) were conducted. Specifically, a two-period, repeated measures design was used for assessing the test-retest reliability of the paper form in one sample of 60 subjects. A three-period repeated measures design, with subjects equally allocated to order of completion, was used for testing the agreement among the various modes (i.e., handheld, tablet, web, IVR) in the separate samples of subjects. Statistical analysis consisted of testing mean differences based on a dependent sample t-test for the test-retest analysis, and repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) for the three period contrasts. Estimation of agreement was based on the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Analysis of the test-retest data resulted in mean differences near zero and ICC values above 0.90 for both the index and the global health rating scale (i.e., EQ VAS) scores. These data were also used to set the threshold values for the three period crossover assessments. For the mean differences, one-half of the standard deviations of 0.080 for the index and 8.0 for the EQ VAS was computed. Hence the equivalence intervals for mean differences were set as -0.040 to 0.040 for the index and -4.0 to 4.0 for the EQ VAS. The thresholds for denoting equivalence on the ICC for the three period comparisons were ICC lower 95% confidence interval (CI) ≥0.911 for the index and ≥0.940 for the EQ VAS.For the three period crossover designs, all of the mean differences for the index and EQ VAS were wholly contained in the equivalence intervals. Further, the ICC 95% lower CIs for the index and EQ VAS scores showed values above the thresholds for denoting equivalence across all comparisons in each sample. No significant mode-by-order interactions were present in any ANOVA model. These data, taken collectively, provide strong evidence that the data produced by the paper and electronic versions of the EQ-5D-5L are highly correlated and produce negligible differences in mean scores at the group level.

Title: Understanding participant’s responses to the EQ-VT tasks; A qualitative study
Abstract: Purpose: The EuroQol-Valuation-Technology (EQVT) uses traditional time-trade-off (tTTO) for health states better than dead and lead-time-TTO (LT-TTO) for states worse than dead to elicit a value (-1.0 to +1.0) for each health state. In the Canadian EQ-5D-5L Valuation studywhich used the EQVT platform, we observed an unexpected peak in frequency of “0” values and few negative values, particularly in the range of 0 to -0.5. To better understand this finding, we soughtto explore respondents’thought processeswhile valuing a health state, andtheir understanding of the tTTO andLT-TTOexercises.Methods: Qualitative semi-structured interviewswere conducted with EQVT task respondents. Questions focused on valuations of health states as:(a) Same as dead in tTTO, (b) Worse than dead in tTTO but changed to same as dead in the LT-TTO, (c) Worse than dead in LT-TTO, and (d) Worse than dead in LT-TTO with trading off all 10 years. Data were analyzed using content and thematic analysis. Results: Mean age ofparticipants (N=70) was 40±18.1years, 60%female, and 76% Caucasian. Participantsprovided similar reasons for valuing a health state same as or worse than dead. Many participants expressed confusion about worse than dead valuations, distinction between same as andworse than dead, and the transitionfrom tTTO to LT-TTO. A few indicated that theaddition of 10 years of full health in the LT-TTO influenced their valuations.Conclusions: The transition from tTTO to LT-TTO in the EQVT wasconfusing to participants, wherebysome health state valuations around this transition appeared to be arbitrary.

Title: Conceptualising bolt-ons: identifying key questions
Abstract: The notion of adding 'bolt-on' items to the EQ-5D has been discussed since its conception. However, there remains a lack of consensus on how bolt-ons should be developed and in what circumstances they ought to be used. This project aimed to develop a foundation for future bolt-on research by identifying key conceptual questions through a literature review, workshop, and survey.Following project initiation, significant strategic developments within EuroQol substantially altered the context for this work. Specifically, the development of the Bolt-on Toolbox concept and the inclusion of bolt-on research within EuroQol's Strategic Plan for 2024-2028 represented a major shift towards centrally coordinated bolt-on development and management. These organisational changed fundamentally expanded beyond the scope envisioned in the original project proposal.The project successfully completed a systematic literature review and developed a publicly accessible bibliographic database containing >60 research items. This database catalogues studies according to bolt-on dimensions, clinical contexts, EQ-5D instruments, research methods, countries, and funding sources. The review identified key conceptual areas requiring clarification: nomenclature, definitions, areas for future research, and the purpose and role of bolt-ons.The planned workshop and survey were not conducted, as the project stalled in early 2024 as sensitivities around bolt-on development prevented us from proceeding. Discussion between the research team, EuroQol Office, and the Executive Committee recognised that the strategic landscape had evolved significantly and completion of the project was not viable, resulting in its closure.

Title: Measurement Performance of the EQ-5D-5L in Hospitalised Older Adults: Routine PROMs Evidence
Abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is a cornerstone of person-centred care and outcomes-based healthcare evaluation, providing critical insights into patients’ perceptions of their own health and wellbeing. The EQ-5D-5L is among the most widely used patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) internationally; however, evidence on its measurement performance among hospitalised older adults remains limited. Older adults frequently experience multimorbidity, functional decline, and cognitive or sensory impairments, which may influence both their ability to self-report and the interpretability of responses. Ensuring that the EQ-5D-5L is valid, reliable, and responsive in this population is essential for its use in clinical decision-making, quality improvement, and economic evaluation. This study aims to examine the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L in hospitalised older adults using routinely collected PROMs data. Specifically, it will assess distribution properties (floor and ceiling effects), convergent validity, known-group validity, and responsiveness to change. Data will be drawn from an ongoing, co-designed PROMs collection system developed by the National Centre for Healthy Ageing, Monash University, and Peninsula Health. The system captures EQ-5D-5L data from patients aged 60 years and over at hospital discharge, 3-months and 6-months post-discharge, alongside demographic, clinical, and functional data. Utility scores will be derived using the Australian value set, and analyses will include descriptive, comparative, and longitudinal methods. Findings will generate robust evidence on the suitability of the EQ-5D-5L for use in older inpatient populations and inform best practice for PROMs implementation. This work aligns with EuroQol’s strategic priorities to advance HRQoL measurement across the lifespan.

Title: Quantification of EQ-5D health-state values by scaling similarity data (studies 1 and 2)
Abstract: Objective: It is assumed that the 'Q' in Quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) is unidimensional. However, this assumption has not been sufficiently tested which is what the current study aims to do. It is important to note that the response task might influence the dimensionality of the data. The current study should be considered a pilot study using a novel methodology to test the dimensionality of rank-ordered health states.Methods:The rank data of 2997 respondents from the Measurement and Valuation of Health (MVH) study was exploded into paired comparison data. Pairwise choice probabilities were transformed into proximity data by |,5.0ijijPwhere ijis the dissimilarity between health states iand jand ijPisthe probability of health state ibeing preferred to health state j. The proximity data were entered into a similarity matrix. Subsequently, this matrix scaled with metric and non-metric multidimensional PROXSCAL algorithms in SPSS in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions. Dimensional fit was assessed usinginterpretability,stress measures,and scree plots.Results:Based on interpretability the unidimensional solution had the best fit. State '33333' was scaled at the end of the continuum while all the states with a single attribute level at level 2 were scaled at the other end of the continuum. In terms of stress and the scree plot a two-dimensional solution would indicate a meaningful improvement over the unidimensional solution. However, the interpretability was lower compared to the unidimensional solutions. The three-dimensional solutions did not decrease stress measures meaningfully, nor increase the interpretability. Discussion: Based on the current findings we can infer that EQ-5D-3L rank-based data is scaled best unidimensionally, even though statistical fit leaves room for improvement. Other types of data could be put through the protocol of the current study to test the assumption of unidimensionality as well. The time trade-off data would seem like a prima candidate for this type of follow-up research.

Title: Evaluating the Performance of EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in Aged Care Setting: A Multicentre Study in Indonesia, China, and Hong Kong
Abstract: Background: The EQ Health and Well-being (EQ-HWB) and its shorter version, EQ-HWB-S, are newly developed tools for assessing health and well-being across health, social care, and public services. They provide a more comprehensive evaluation of quality of life (QOL) by capturing physical, emotional, cognitive, and social dimensions. With rapidly aging populations in China, Indonesia, and Hong Kong, reliable tools are needed to address the growing health and social care demands of older adults. However, further validation is required to determine the feasibility, validity, and responsiveness of these instruments in aged care settings. Objectives: This study aims to assess the feasibility of EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S, evaluate the validity and reliability of EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S, and assess responsiveness to detect meaningful changes in health and well-being over time. Methods: The study will involve dyads of elderly residents of aged care facilities and recipients of home care services, along with their caregivers in China, Hong Kong, and Indonesia, with a total of 450 participants (150 dyads from each country). Participants will be aged 65 and above, representing a range of chronic conditions and cognitive abilities. Data collection will combine quantitative and qualitative methods. It will be collected through self-report, proxy, and interviewer-administered methods. Follow-up data will be gathered from the same cohort, with 600 participants (including proxies) invited to complete a follow-up survey one to two weeks after the initial survey to measure responsiveness. Data analysis will assess (1) Feasibility by comparing refuse to participate rate, drop-out rate and completion rates, and identifying missing data patterns, (2) Validity and reliability, using correlation analysis, Cronbach’s alpha, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), (3) Responsiveness by tracking changes in EQ-HWB scores over time and correlating them with clinical outcomes, and (4) Known-group comparisons by evaluating the instruments’ ability to distinguish between participants with varying health conditions. Qualitative feedback will be gathered from 20 participants from each country through semi-structured interviews to explore the feasibility and perceived relevance of the instruments.

Title: Comparison of ‘DCE with duration’ and ‘EQ-VT’ to inform development of EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set in India: A pilot study
Abstract: Background: Value sets are essential instruments for conducting robust QALY-based health technology assessments (HTA) and cost-effectiveness analyses in any country. The EQ-5D-Y-5L instrument, designed to capture health-related quality of life in children and adolescents, extends health state measurement by incorporating five severity levels across five dimensions, however, the absence of country-specific value sets constrains its application in pediatric health evaluations. Given India’s sizable adolescent population, there is a pressing need to develop an India-specific EQ-5D-Y-5L value set to support evidence-based resource allocation. Nevertheless, no valuation protocol exists which can provide guidance on which method to use for developing the EQ-5D-Y-5L value set.   Objective: This study assessed different EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation methods, including the extended EQ-5D-Y-3L protocol, and the Discrete Choice Experiments (DCE) with a duration attribute (DCEd), to inform the development of the EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol, which can subsequently be used in developing the EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set for India. Additionally, this study also explored the impact of including the preferences of adolescents in the development of EQ-5D-Y-5L value-set. Methods: There are three key methodological considerations which have guided this study- first, to collect EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation data using an extended version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L protocol (cTTO and DCE) and assess feasibility for developing an India-specific value set.​ Second, collect DCE with duration (DCEd) data to compare results against the extended EQ-5D-Y-3L protocol.​ Third, incorporate adolescent (10–17 years) preferences in latent-scale DCE within the extended EQ-5D-Y-3L protocol to evaluate its impact on utility values across all health states. A cross-sectional EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation study was conducted in Haryana state of India using a 30-cluster sampling design with proportional representation of urban and rural areas. The study targeted adults aged 18 years and above for cTTO, DCE, and DCEd tasks, and adolescents aged 10–17 years for DCE tasks. Following a 5-day EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) and DCEd training, face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviews (CAPI) were carried out by eight trained interviewers. Of the 1,533 interviews completed, 1,524 were retained for analysis after excluding nine quality control–flagged cases. Among the interviews finally included in the analysis, 235 were cTTO, 441 were DCE, and 848 were DCEd interviews. The cTTO data was analyzed using a 20-parameter model that accounts for heteroskedasticity and a 20-parameter Tobit model. DCE data was modeled using a mixed logit model, while DCEd data was analyzed using a mixed logit model incorporating exponential discounting. Key results: The sample reflected national rural-urban proportions, with rural participants predominantly (69% in DCE, 72% in cTTO, 67% in DCEd) and balanced sex distribution across tasks. The 26–40-year age group was largest (42.3% of the total respondents), while 10–25-year-olds featured prominently (38%) in latent-scale DCE due to adolescent inclusion; most were married, with mean monthly household expenditure of ₹29,779 (ranging from ₹26,900 to ₹32,000 across cTTO, DCE and DCEd groups). Chronic ailments affected 22.9% (19–26% across the three groups of respondents), and reported substance use (tobacco, alcohol) was present among 20.9% of the study participants.​ In cTTO models, pain/discomfort (PD) was most important dimension (PD5 disutilities: 0.981 heteroskedastic, 1.090 Tobit), followed by mobility (MO; 0.376–0.428), with looking after myself (LAM) least important (0.133–0.186); minor ordering inconsistencies occurred, and worst-state value was –0.967 to –1.354. DCE confirmed PD > MO > LAM ordering (rescaled PD5: 0.806 full sample), with adolescents showing higher PD5 (0.896) and lower LAM5 (0.117) weights, plus lower choice consistency (gamma=0.706). DCEd mixed logit models yielded PD5 weights of 0.788–0.744, MO5 0.409–0.397, LAM5 0.202–0.205, and worst-state values of –0.952 to –0.881, with discount rates varying from –21.1% to 16.3%. Cross-method scatterplots showed high agreement but scale differences, with cTTO valuing mild/moderate states higher and severe states lower than DCE/DCEd. Implications: The findings are a step towards accurate QALY estimation for pediatric interventions, supporting transparent and equitable resource allocation in India's adolescent health programs and interventions. This study demonstrates a degree of methodological homogeneity across different valuation methods (cTTO & DCE versus DCEd) for EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation, with consistent pain/discomfort dominance, strong cross-method agreement, and no significant adult-adolescent preference differences. The findings of this study indicate that there are no statistically significant differences between adult and adolescent preferences in EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation tasks, nor are there meaningful differences in the utility values generated using different valuation approaches (extended EQ-5D-Y-3L protocol with cTTO and DCE vs. DCEd method). These results directly inform the design of the Indian EQ-5D-Y-5L main valuation study, supporting the use of a combined cTTO and latent-scale DCE design as the most suitable approach. Furthermore, the adoption of this design ensures methodological consistency with international EQ-5D-Y valuation studies, most of which rely on adult respondents, while also preserving alignment with the Indian EQ-5D-5L adult valuation study. This harmonization is expected to enhance comparability and facilitate robust application of the resulting value set in future health-economic evaluations. This pilot study in the Indian context as part of the broader EuroQol study programme of work for valuing EQ-5D-Y-5L in India, the Netherlands, Poland and Canada.The evidence thus generated will inform the development of a valuation protocol for the EQ-5D-Y-5L, which would serve as a guidance document to establish a value set for the EQ-5D-Y-5L in different countries.

Title: Deriving EQ-5D-5L preference weights for Denmark
Abstract: Deriving EQ-SD-SL preference weights for Denmark The project has two main aims: First, to derive a set of Danish preference-based weights for the EQ-SD-SL. The current weights were published in 2009 for the EQ-SD-3L (Wittrup-Jensen et al. 2009). We will follow the EuroQol Group's standardised valuation (EQ-VT) protocol to derive local preferences for the EQ-SD-SLquestionnaire, which includes two different tasks: composite time trade-off (TTO) and force-choice paired comparisons discrete choice experiment (DCE) (Oppe et al. 2014). Second, to further explore the DC methodology by adding a new task after the standard EQ-VT protocol. This is likely to be a head-to-head comparison of two DC approaches using a triplet format, one of which has been developed by the Dutch team, and the other by the Australian team. Specifically, we are interested in assessing the effect of duration in association with the choice task, and the use of dead. We will be discussing the details of these investigations with the EuroQol Group's Valuation Working Group (VWG).
