Title: Developing and testing a version of EQ-5D-Y for use in children aged 2-5 years using a mixed methods approach
Abstract: Background: Few preference-weighted health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) measures exist for use in children under 5 years of age limiting their inclusion in cost-utility analyses and resulting health care resource allocation decisions. This project sought to develop and assess a modification of the EQ-5D-Y HRQoL instrument for children aged 2-4 years. Methods Purposive sampling at the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne, Australia was used to recruit parents of children 2-4 years for online focus groups. Parents provided feedback on each dimension of the EQ-5D-Y. Qualitative findings guided the design of adaptations to the instrument that were then piloted and refined. Parents completed an online survey and a 4 week follow up to test the psychometric properties of the adapted versus original EQ-5D-Y instrument. Families were recruited from the Royal Children’s Hospital and via online panels. The distribution of responses was described for the total sample and children with and without special health care needs. Psychometric tests for ceiling effects (>15% of responses at highest level), known group validity (Cohen’s d effect sizes for pre-specified groups), test-rest (intraclass correlation coefficients) and responsiveness (standardized response mean effect sizes) were conducted using level sum scores. Results Online focus groups were conducted with 19 parents of well children and those with medical conditions. Parents provided a range of examples of how each domain related to their children, and suggested alternative wording to improve the applicability of the instrument to this age group. Modifications were made on this basis and tested again with a subset of original focus group participants to refine. 842 parents of children aged 2-4 years completed the online survey with 513 (61%) completing follow-up. Respondents reported more problems in each dimension with the adapted EQ-5D-Y than with the original instrument (for example, 66% reported no problems on the Usual Activities dimensions on the adapted EQ-5D-Y-5L version compared to 78% with the original instrument). The adapted instrument more strongly differentiated children with and without special health care needs based on Cohen’s D effect size compared to the original (EQ-5D-Y-5L adapted ES=1.01 (0.83-1.19), EQ-5D-Y-5L original ES=0.83 (0.52-1.14)). Test-retest was generally more reliable for the adapted versus original instrument. Responsiveness for children with improved and worsened health [assessed using a general health rating scale] at 4 weeks was consistent with size of effect expected (EQ-5D-Y-5L adapted- better health SRM=0.2, no change in health SRM=-0.05, and worse health SRM=-0.41). Conclusions and implications: It was possible to produce an adapted version of the EQ-5D-Y with considerable input from parents. The adapted EQ-5D-Y for 2-4 year olds was found to be more sensitive, valid and reliable than the original EQ-5D-Y, and thereby provides a means of extending measurement of HRQoL into this younger age group with a relatively simple modification. This in turn provides an important step towards valid and consistent measurement of HRQOL across the lifespan and may make it possible to obtain values for health states in these younger ages. However, important questions remain in relation to valuation of the adapted EQ-5D-Y, including whether a specific value set is required or a mapping approach, consistency across age for utility values generated, appropriate sample and perspective for valuation, and some feasible approaches for anchoring.

Title: EQ-5D-5L valuation in Poland: a methodological extension
Abstract: Objective Cost-utility analysis gain importance also in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). We aimed to develop Polish utility tariff for EQ-5D-5L health states.Methods Face-to-face, computer-assisted interviews were collected in the representative sample. Each respondent followed a standardizedprotocol to collect 10composite time trade off (cTTO) and 7discrete choice experiment (DCE) observations. In the Bayesian approach, several model specifications were compared based on model fit, the usabilityof the final value set, and how they reflect the elicitation procedure (e.g. censoring). A hybrid approach (using cTTO and DCE data) was employedin the final set, which wascomparedwith the existing ones: EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L cross-walk.ResultsData from 1252 respondents (11,480 cTTO valuations and 8764 DCE pairs) were collectedin June-October, 2016. The final model accounted for random parameters, error scaling with fattails, censoring at -1, unwillingness to trade in TTO by the religious, and Cauchy distribution in DCE. Pain/discomfort impacts the utility most: disutility equal to 0.575 when at level 5. In the value set, 4.4% of EQ-5D-5L states are worse than dead. Thenew value set has a comparable range (minimum at -0.590 compared to -0.523) and same ordering of the first three dimensions (pain/discomfort, mobility, self-care) as EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L cross-walk value sets. Moreover,it is more sensitive to mild health worsening.Conclusions The new value set guarantees consistency with past decisions in cost-utility studies,while offering betterassessment of even mild health gains. It can be an option for CEE countries lacking own value sets.

Title: Dutch translation of breathing, sleep, fatigue and cognition EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox items
Abstract: Background and aim: The EQ-5D-5L is a generic instrument used to describe and value health across a wide range of diseases. The EQ-5D-5L descriptive system includes five dimensions (Mobility, Self-Care, Usual activities, Pain / Discomfort and Anxiety/Depression), and has five response levels: no problems, slight problems, moderate problems, severe problems, unable to/extreme problems (1). The addition of other health dimensions to the EQ-5D-5L, referred to as Bolt-ons, has been explored by several studies as an opportunity to enhance the sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L in capturing aspects of health quality of life that may otherwise be missed in some populations (2). The systematic development and assessment of Bolt-ons, including their translation to other languages, is crucial for their broader application in research. The Post-COVID Network Netherlands (PCNN) is a collaborative initiative involving patients, scientists, healthcare professionals, and community partners. Its goal is to align scientific research and patient care for individuals affected by post-COVID condition (3). The PCNN patient portal, with over 15,000 registered patients, offers a valuable opportunity to collect longitudinal health data, including patient-reported outcome measures such as the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons. However, to include such bolt-ons in the portal, approved Dutch translations are first needed, most of which are not yet available. The aim of this proposal is to conduct a research-led translation of a selected set of Post-COVID relevant bolt-ons, from English to Dutch language. This includes a total of 22 items: 4 “best available” bolt-ons: Breathing problems, Fatigue, Sleep, and Cognition, and 18 “Exploratory items”:  1 Breathing item, 7 Cognition items, 9 Fatigue items, and 1 sleep item (see Appendix 1). Methods: The translation process will follow EuroQol’s Version Management Control (VMC) translation guidelines (4) and include the following steps:Two forward translations (English to Dutch) led by two independent translators (BE, DK) fluent in both English and Dutch. Followed by a discussion and merging of translations, and the production of a report. Review of the report by the research team and VMC representatives, followed by the production of a first consensus version.Two backward translations (Dutch to English) of the first consensus version led by two independent translators (SY, BB) fluent in both English and Dutch. Followed by a discussion and the production of a report. Review of the report by the research team and VMC, followed by a second consensus version.Cognitive debriefing interviews. A total of eight native Dutch speaking individuals (patients from PCNN and healthy individuals), will be recruited and interviewed by an experienced qualitative interviewer (MB). Data from the interviews will then be summarized and presented in a report. Review of report by VMC, followed by a third consensus version. Results: A final product in the form of a report with the final versions.Value to the EuroQol working groups: We anticipate that this project will provide substantial value to the EuroQol Research Foundation, as the development of bolt-ons is a priority within the EuroQol's strategic agenda (2024–2028). Moreover, translation of these bolt-ons will enable their application and assessment across multiple disease populations, as most items are generic rather than condition-specific. This initiative also supports EuroQol’s broader objective of developing the Bolt-on Toolbox®, which will include bolt-ons with certified VMC translations for research use.

Title: A Comparison Study of the New Discrete Choice Method and Traditional Composite Time Trade-Off in Japan
Abstract: This study aims to examine the consistency between a new discrete choice experiment (DCE) method including split-triplet choice tasks and conventional composite time trade-off (cTTO) methods in the Japanese context. While previous research in Trinidad and Tobago demonstrated similarity between these methods, their cross-cultural validity, particularly in Asian populations where different preference patterns have been observed, remains uncertain. The study will employ four valuation methods for EQ-5D-5L health states: cTTO with a sample size of 1000 and simple DCE with duration, normal triplet DCE, and split-triplet DCEwith 1500 respondents (for DCE). Data collection will involve face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviews for cTTO and online surveys for DCE methods. Analysis will utilize linear mixed or Tobit models for cTTO data and mixed logit models for DCE data. Non-linear time preference is also considered for DCE data. The research team's connection with Japan's health technology assessment agency (C2H) positions this study to directly inform policy decisions. Confirming consistency between these methods in a non-Western context would provide crucial evidence for their broad applicability and potentially influence methodological guidelines in Japan and other Asian countries.

Title: Extension EQ-5D-5L study England for other UK countries
Abstract: Earlier this year, our research team was awarded funding from the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) Policy Research Programme (PRP), supported by the Department of Health, to undertake an EQ-5D-5L value set for Englandstudy. The research is being undertaken as a collaboration between the Office of Health Economics and Sheffield University. Data collection is currently underway, with sampling and face to face interviews being undertaken throughout England by the social survey company Ipsos MORI. As the research funding is provided under the auspices of England’s Department of Health, we were advised by the Department of Health that the relevant definition of the ‘general public’, from whom to collect data, should be restricted to ‘the general public of England’ only –not the wider UK –and that funding could not be provided for the collection of any data outside England. This issue of whether this study should be focused just on England, or on the UK, had for some time been the subject of extensive discussion with the Department of Health –in the two years prior to submitting our proposal, this issue had been discussed in a number of key meetings between the EuroQol Group and the Department of Health. We had also consulted with colleagues in NICE (Carole Longson and Bhash Naidoo) and the Scottish Medicines Consortium (SMC) (Andrew Walker) on this issue.The 5L value set for England which we will produce for England as an outcome of our current work will be used by the Department of Health in England-specific applications -for example, in the analysis of data from the English NHS PROMs programme, and fromthe Health Survey for England. However, other decision making bodies that are very important users of the EQ-5D are responsible for slightly different populations. For example, NICE’s remit covers both England and Wales. The SMC makes decisions regarding health care technologies in Scotland. Both NICE and the SMC currently use the Dolan (1997) value set for the UK. Importantly, the system of value based pricing for new medicines, to be introduced in 2014, will be UK-wide -not just for England. As estimates of QALY gains (and therefore EQ-5D-5L data) will be central to VBP, a UK value set for EQ-5D-5L would ensure health states are valued in a manner fitting with the populations affected by VBP decisions.We are concerned that by restricting the value set to England, and failing to capitalise on the current opportunity to extend data collection efforts to Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, that this could potentially:(a)compromise the acceptability and perceived relevance of the new value set to key users such as NICE and in future decisions regarding VBP; and(b)adversely affect the use of the EQ-5D-5L in the UK.Because of these concerns, we sought advice from the England Department of Health on how to approach the Departments of Health in each of the ‘devolved governments’ of Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. Since funding for the EQ-5D-5L value set for Englandstudy was confirmed in May this year, we have been vigorously pursuing contacts in each of those countries, via email and teleconferences, to explain the study and to explore their willingness to provide funding to support data collection in each country.Initially, there was strong interest in principle from all three countries. The Office of the Chief Scientist in Scotland was subsequently confirmed the availability of funds to support the collection of additional data from the Scottish general public. Unfortunately, and despite the efforts of the people we were in contact with in Northern Ireland and Wales (which included the Chief Medical Officers and Chief Pharmacists in each case), they were unable to secure the (relatively modest) budgets required in each country to facilitate data collection.Having now exhausted all other avenues for seeking external funding for data collection in Wales and NI, we therefore ask the EuroQol Group to consider providing funding for that. Details of the aims and budget request are provided below.

Title: Using the EQ-5D to value the health-related quality of life of older adolescents: A feasibility and qualitative study
Abstract: Using 1000minds software, an online tool was created to value the EQ-5D-Y-5L and, separately, the EQ-5D-5L. The tool implemented the Potentially All Pairwise RanKings of all Possible Alternatives (PAPRIKA) method – an adaptive discrete choice experiment (DCE) – and a binary search algorithm to identify the location of ‘dead’ within each participant’s full ranking of health states. Convenience sampling was used to recruit 24 New Zealand adolescents aged 16-19 years (13 female; 50% Māori). Each adolescent completed two online DCE questionnaires (about 2 weeks apart, in random order), one comprising the EQ-5D-Y-5L and the other, the EQ-5D-5L. Both questionnaires included questions relating to health states worse than dead. The online questionnaires were completed in two face-to-face think-aloud sessions in the presence of a researcher (TS or SD) and a young research assistant. Each session concluded with a semi-structured interview to obtain feedback about the questionnaires and to explore adolescents’ views on including their preferences in decision making. There was no evidence of a difference (p>0.57) in mean differences in preference weights (by dimension) across the youth (Y-5L) and adult (5L) instruments; observed mean differences were small (diff≤0.01). The overall ranking of dimensions was similar between the two instruments with Worried, sad or unhappy (Y-5L) and Anxiety/Depression (5L) ranked 1st, Pain/Discomfort and Usual Activities 2nd or 3rd, Mobility 4th, and Looking after myself (Y-5L) and Self-Care (5L) 5th. The mean values for dead (i.e. before rescaling for dead = 0) was 0.410 for the EQ-5D-Y-5L and 0.417 for the EQ-5D-5L. The lowest health state values and the percentage of health states less than zero were ̶ 0.796 and 17.8%, and ̶ 0.884 and 21.2% respectively. Adolescents were capable of trading-off health states, including health states worse than dead. They think their preferences should contribute to social value sets and that completing the questionnaires in-person enhanced the quality of their responses.

Title: Exploring the potential of using EQ-5D-3L versus EQ-5D-5L to assess the value of a national large-scale health care improvement initiative in rheumatology in Sweden
Abstract: Several national quality improvement programs are under development in Sweden. In rheumatology, two person-centered care pathways have been developed. The Swedish Rheumatology Quality Register (SRQ) is closely linked to the care-pathways and data from the registry will be used to assess the consequences of the implementation. SRQ has been collecting EQ-5D-3L data since 2008 and EQ-5D has been discussed as a potential measure in the assessment of the pathways. Nevertheless, the responsiveness of 3L has been questioned and the registry is considering replacing it with EQ-5D-5L. The aims of the current study are: 1) to make recommendations regarding a replacement of EQ-5D-3L with the 5L version 2) to assess commensurability of 5L compared to 3L in this patient population and to develop a mapping function to enable comparability between newly collected 5L data and historical 3L data. Data will be collected in at least three rheumatology units in Sweden in patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) during the first year of disease (early RA) as well as in patients with established RA and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) on one-two occasions. Cross-sectional 3L and 5L data will be compared in terms of distributional characteristics, known groups and convergent validity. Responsiveness of longitudinal 3L and 5L data will be assessed on descriptive data (inconsistencies, level moves, PCHC, index of superiority) and values (standardized response mean, standardized effect size, relative efficiency). A mapping function will be estimated, based on descriptive data and values. Findings will be validated in a separate cohort of SLE patients.

Title: Exploring experience and perception of valuation tasks for valuing EQ-5D-Y-5L health states: a qualitative study of adults and adolescents
Abstract: Background: Preferences for child health states can be derived from adults, adolescents, or a combination of these age groups. The Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health and Ethiopian Public Health Institute has expressed an interest in developing a value set for the EQ-5D-Y-5L. However, there is no currently established protocol for involving adolescents in EQ-5D-Y valuation tasks. Evidence on whether adolescents can successfully complete DCE with duration or TTO tasks is lacking, and it has yet to be determined which valuation tasks (DCE, TTO, or DCE with duration) should be used in the EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol. Aims: The objective of this study is to explore the perceptions and experiences of adults and adolescents with the valuation tasks (DCE, TTO, or DCE with duration) being considered for the EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol in Ethiopia. Methods: This study will be conducted using a qualitative descriptive study design. A purposive sample of adults (≥ 18 years) and adolescents (12-17 yeas) will be recruited from the Ethiopian general population. Participants will be asked through face to face interview using EQ-VT to complete a series of DCE tasks followed by DCE with duration, and TTO based on EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol. As they go through the valuation tasks, they will be instructed to verbalize their thought process following a think-aloud approach. After completion of the valuation tasks, the participant will participate in a semi-structured individual interview to gain a deeper understanding of their perceptions and understanding of these tasks. Participants will be stratified into age bands to explore age-related differences in completing valuation tasks using predefined indicators. Abraham Welie will conduct the interviews with male participants, while a pediatrician female researcher will conduct the interviews with female participants. The interviews will be audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The data will be analyzed using content analysis. Findings from the think-aloud and semi-structured interviews will then be combined using a narrative synthesis.

Title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Properties Testing of the EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) Health-Related Quality of Life Measure in Brazilian Children
Abstract: Background: Health-related quality of life measures represents individuals’ preferences for a specific health state and are used to estimate one of the most common clinical outcomes in economic evaluations, the quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs). The PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, and Child Health Utility 9-Dimension (CHU9D) are the most common health-related quality of life measures used in children and adolescents. Although these instruments were validated for Brazilian population, the EQ-5D-Y instruments were developed for children and adolescents aged 8-15 years and CHU9D was developed for children and adolescents aged 7-17 years. The EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) as a generic measure of health-related quality of life for children aged 0-3 years. However, the assessment of the psychometric properties of this instrument has not been tested in Brazilian population yet. Objective: To cross-culturally adapt and assess the psychometric properties of the EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L in Brazilian children. Methods: Caregivers of children aged 0 to 48 months will be recruited from Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo, Brazil. The sample will include children with and without health conditions. The EQ-TIPS-3L and EQ-TIPS-5L will be translated and cross-culturally adapted into Brazilian-Portuguese. All caregivers will answer the proxy interviewer administration versions of the EQ-TIPS-3L, EQ-TIPS-5L, and PedsQL. Furthermore, caregivers of children with a health condition will answer specific-disease measures. All caregivers will also answer the EQ-HWB-9 considering their health. The psychometric properties assessed in this study will be test-retest reliability (based on reliability and measurement error), construct validity (convergent and discriminative), responsiveness, ceiling and floor effects, acceptability, feasibility, and distribution of responses of the EQ-TIPS-3L EQ-TIPS-5L, and PedsQL in Brazilian children. Furthermore, the impact of the child's health on the caregiver will be assessed using the EQ-HWB-9. Discussion: Economic evaluations have been increasingly conducted in Brazil to support healthcare decision-making processes. Although the quality of these studies is considered satisfactory, Brazilian guidelines suggest improvements in the methods used to assess health-related quality of life. The translation and cross-culturally adaptation into Brazilian-Portuguese and the psychometric properties testing of the EQ-TIPS instruments in Brazilian children will facilitate the dissemination and use of this instrument in clinical and research settings across Brazil.Keywords: Health-related quality of life; Infant; Toddler; Psychometric properties

Title: Creating a laboratory for testing differences between the 3L and 5L Index in patient populations: simulating profile and valuation data
Abstract: We created the ‘simulation laboratory’ as a suite of modules with associated data sets by iterative development of software. In doing this, the specific form and structure of the laboratory evolved from the prototype plan but resulted in the same functionality. We presented our initial plan at the mid-year meeting in Budapest in 2018 and demonstrated the results of the final structure at the plenary meeting in Lisbon later that year. Since then, we have concentrated on making the software more user friendly, written a user guide and added to the associated data sets.

Title: Health-Related Quality of Life in children living with cystic fibrosis (CF)
Abstract: Background: The advent of Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) has resulted in a need to motivate for access to life saving therapy with a reliance on measurement of Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) for health policy decision making. In regions where drugs are accessible HRQoL is key in monitoring real world outcomes. This study aims to assess the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, PedsQL and Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire Revised (CFQR) in children living with CF in South Africa. Methods: One-hundred and fifty eight children living with CF aged 0-18 were eligible for recruitment. Despite 103 caregivers and children providing consent/assent responses were received from 49 children aged 8-18 years and 90 caregivers of children aged 0-18 years. Children and/or their caregivers completed all four HRQoL measures, in random order, at routine medical visits and at a maximum of three subsequent medical visits. The psychometric performance of the measures was assessed regarding the known group validity, concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, responsiveness and patient-caregiver agreement. Results: The median age of the participants who self-completed the measures was 14 years with an even distribution of gender (Female, n=24). The majority of the sample was CFTR modulator naïve (n=45) and generally well with a median FEV1 of 79.2% . This was reflected in the similarly high report of no problems across the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL. The CFQR self-report showed good discriminant validity for known groups according to chronic lung infection (U=183.0 p=0.025) and pulmonary exacerbations (U=105.0 p=0.025) whereas the self-report EQ VAS discriminated between severity of lung function (H=9.91, p=0.010). The total scores of all self-report measures were highly associated and there were moderate to high associations for all dimensions hypothesized to be associated. Repeat self-report measures on the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL showed fair to moderate reliability in those with a stable health condition according to the CFQR score (n=38). The self-report EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L were both able to detect improvements in health with a large effect size. Whereas the self-report EQ VAS and PedsQL had a small to moderate effect size for detecting improved or worsened health. Children reported higher overall HRQoL than their caregivers on all measures. There is overall good agreement (ICC>0.70) between patient and caregiver on all measures considering their total scores. At a dimension level the EQ-5D-Y-5L and CFQR showed better agreement between the patient and caregiver than the EQ-5D-Y-3L and PedsQL. Conclusion: Despite good association between dimensions and total scores on the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, PedsQL and CFQR the CFQR was able to discriminate between known clinical groups. However, the PedsQL, EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L showed promising reliability and responsiveness results in children living with CF. Although there was good patient-caregiver agreement for the total scores of all measures the EQ-5D-Y-5L and CFQR showed better agreement at a dimension level. Further research with larger samples is warranted before a recommendation can be made on selection of a generic HRQoL measure to use alongside the disease-specific CFQR.

Title: Facing death to understand the construct validity of the (c)TTO method: a conceptual approach
Abstract: The construct validity of health utilities, e.g. the (c)TTO, is an under researched area. Existing determinants of (c)TTO are ill-understood. The search for (c)TTO-determinants and their interpretation has not been guided by theory. This proposal focusses on the role of death. In the search for concepts or determinants related to the (c)TTO, the word "dead" has been hopelessly missing. This is an omission as preferences for death as well as trading life are central to the (c)TTO, and this will induce death thoughts. Our proposal focusses on the thoughts of dead induced by the (c)TTO. Terror Management Theory (TMT) is used to understand psychological responses to thoughts of dead. TMT starts from death related anxiety, that occurs after death thoughts. Defense mechanisms, such as bolstering cultural values, are called into action to reduce this anxiety. As both TMT and the (c)TTO involve thoughts of death, we aim to study whether TMT can be used to improve our understanding of (c)TTO determinants. Relevance 1) This proposal is about the construct validity of the (c)TTO. 2) TMT enriches the construct validity of the (c)TTO by embedding it in the concepts of TMT. 3) Connecting (c)TTO and TMT guides the search for new (c)TTO-determinants, as well as interpreting previously found (c)TTO-determinants.

Title: Extension of Variability in DCE Results Ð October 2016
Abstract: Background: To date, most models of health preferences are based on logits or probits. Alternatively, ratio-or angle-based models may perform better, such as Zermelo-Bradley-Terry (ZBT). Aims: to comparelogit and ZBT models for the analysis of health preferences. Methods: Using paired comparison responses from seven EQ-5D-5L valuationstudies (Netherlands, China, Singapore, Spain, Canada, Uruguay and Korea), we estimated each model separately (i.e., 20 level and one ancillary parameter) and predicted 3125 EQ-5D-5L values. Specifically, fourteen models (7 countries ×2 models) were estimated by maximum likelihood with respondent-level clusters and evaluated by their predictive validity as well as the sign and significance of their parametersand values. Results: The ZBT produced fewer disordered levels (0 vs. 8) and fewer insignificant parameters (p-value<0.01; 5 vs. 32) compared to the logit. Apart from content and statistical considerations, the logit and ZBT estimates were significantly different for 92 (65.7%) level parameters and 6816 (31.2%) EQ-5D-5L values (p-value<0.01). Across the seven countries, ZBT consistently produced a higher pseudo-likelihood and found moredifferences between countries (109 vs. 86parameters, 27696vs. 2090027696X values). Conclusions: Compared to the logit, ZBT fit the choice databetter and producedfewer inconsistencies between levels.The EQ-5D-5L values were significantly different between the models.With improved fit and content validity, differences between countries became more evident. The results here confirm previous findings and hint at the potential benefits of geometric analysis in other forms of health preference research.

Title: Prediction of injury recovery patterns: can multiple measurements of EQ-5D data be used in dynamic prediction models?
Abstract: Background:The understanding of recovery patterns of acute onset conditions supports timely identification of specific patient groups with poor prognosis.Speed of recovery may depend on many factors, including complications that may develop after onset.To predict who faces a poor prognosis, one can use dynamic prediction models. These models use time-fixed data that is available at baseline as well as time-dependent data that is measured longitudinally. Multiple measurements of EQ-5D data have not yet been used in dynamic prediction models of prognosis. Aims:The aims of our study are 1) to assess performance of dynamic prediction models that use the EQ-5D data (summary index, EQ-VAS score, dimensions, cognition bolt on) as time-dependent covariate to predict injury prognosis; and 2) to compare performance of dynamic prediction models that use EQ-5D data versus health utilities index (HUI)data. Methods:We will use data from a large cohort of trauma patients who filled out the EQ-5D and HUI at 1 week, 1, 3, 12 and 24 months post-injury to develop dynamic prediction models that provide individual estimates of good recovery probabilities given patient’s current health status using various time-fixed predictors (e.g. gender) and time-dependent predictors. We will use the landmark approach to develop the dynamic prediction models. Output:Testing the use of multiple EQ-5D measurements in dynamic prediction models and assessing the performance of these models in a patient group with varying recovery patterns may pave the way for further application of longitudinal assessments of EQ-5D data (e.g. PROMs) in prediction modeling.

Title: EuroQol Early Career Researcher (ECR) Meeting 2026: Bridging Research Generations Across EuroQol Working Groups
Abstract: We propose an online ECR thematic meeting to be held in conjunction with the EuroQol PhD Network in late September/early October 2026, timed strategically after the 2026 Plenary and before the return of the Academy meeting in 2027. This meeting aims to provide a dedicated platform for early career researchers (ECRs) to present and discuss their EuroQol-related research across five Working Group domains: Descriptive Systems, EQ-HWB, Population and Health Systems, Valuation, and Younger Populations.The meeting will adopt a structured format where ECR presenters share their work (including repurposed abstracts not accepted at the EQ Plenary 2026), followed by designated discussants from the relevant Working Group who provide constructive feedback and discussion points. This format has proven effective in online settings and fosters meaningful mentorship between senior EuroQol members and emerging researchers.Key objectives include: (1) showcasing ECR research spanning the breadth of EuroQol’s scientific agenda; (2) strengthening the pipeline of early career talent within the EuroQol network; (3) facilitating cross-Working Group dialogue and collaboration, including through the Buddy Program; and (4) coordinating with the PhD Network to maximize reach and impact. The meeting will be conducted online via Zoom to ensure global accessibility, including for researchers in low- and middle-income countries.We anticipate 80–100 attendees across two half-day sessions, featuring 12–16 ECR presentations, 4–6 senior discussants, and networking breakout rooms. The programme will include a plenary keynote on career development in health economics research, thematic parallel sessions aligned with WG priorities, and a collaborative session with the PhD Network Core Panel.

Title: Extending the QALY project – testing the face and content validity of candidate items within the Australian context
Abstract: Summary of issues from face validity interviews•Most items were perceived positively •Problematic items that we considered for removal included: oQ6 (I could do the things I wanted to do) and Q8 (I was able to do what I needed) because of difficult wordingoQ19 (I was able to communicate with others with no difficulty) was removed because of misunderstanding of the word communication. oQ20 (Because of hearing and/or speech, how difficult did you find it to have a conversation?) was removed as people could have difficulties with having a conversation for other reasons. oQ22 and Q24 removed because the layout of Q21 and 23 was preferred (same content)•Potential amendments that we suggest for some items:oQ9: Change layout to difficulty across the top & refer to day-to-day rather than daily oQ16: Change layout to difficulty across the top and clarify the incorporation of health care aids (“I was able to get around inside my house with no difficulty (using any aids or equipment you need e.g., a wheelchair, frame or stick)”) oQ17: Change layout to difficulty across the top, clarify the incorporation of health care aids, clarify radius of distance, and add my house (“I was able to get around outside my houseto go shopping etc. with no difficulty (using any aids or equipment you need e.g., a wheelchair, frame or stick)”) oQ18: Change “How well did you communicate with others” to “How well did you interact with others (e.g., having a conversation)” •Response options: For Q10 and Q11 the frequency item scale was generally preferred•The recall time was generally acceptable, except for hearing and vision, where some participants felt that the recall time was irrelevant.

Title: Identification, development and assessment of a single sleep bolt on item o the EQ-5D-5L health-related quality of life measure – a sequential mixed methods study
Abstract: Background: The EQ-5D-5L is a widely used measure of people’s quality of life relating to their health (HRQoL). The EQ-5D-5L questionnaire is used among many populations with different medical conditions, but has been criticized for missing some important aspects of health for some specific populations, such as those with sleep disorder. The EQ-5D-5L descriptive system can be adapted to incorporate ‘bolt-on’ descriptors in order to improve measurement sensitivity and relevance in certain contexts as a solution. EuroQol is planning to develop a Bolt-on Toolbox containing several bolt-ons, one of which is sleep problems. However, so far, no definitive sleep bolt-on has been developed in accordance with EuroQol protocols and guidance for bolt-on identification, development and testing. Aims and Objectives: Our research proposal aims to identify and develop a single sleep bolt-on item for inclusion in the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. We aim to develop a bolt-on item that is relevant across diverse populations living with sleep problems (e.g. those with mental illness, chronic pain, asthma or diabetes), as well as for individuals with specific sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea or insomnia. Development work plan: The study will use mixed qualitative and quantitative methods that have built on learning from previous and ongoing work on developing and testing bolt-on descriptors for cognition, vision, sleep and hearing, and draws from the developmental work for the EQ-HWB. The study will have three phases. These will be delivered one after the other. The full programme is expected to take 18 months. Phase 1 aims to identify experiences and potential items related to sleep problems for Phase 2. Phase 1 will have two components: 1A and 1B. Phase 1A will include a scoping literature review to understand existing evidence about the experiences of people with sleep problems, and identify existing items that measure this. We will liaise with EuroQol colleagues who have done systematic reviews of bolt-on items to EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L to improve efficiency of our review. Phase 1B will refine the candidate items identified in Phase 1A through interviews with people who have sleep disorder and people with other chronic diseases that cause sleep problems. Phase 2 will include one to one interviews to assess how acceptable the potential items are to people with sleep disorders and people with other chronic diseases that cause sleep problems, and how well they describe their HRQoL. Phase 3 will assess how well the items work in larger and more diverse samples of people. An online survey will be conducted to assess how well the candidate items work among a group of people with sleep disorders and people with other chronic diseases that cause sleep problems (around 300 participants) and the general population in the UK (around 300 participants).
