A slight decrease in discriminative properties for caregivers was observed when transitioning from EQ-HWB to EQ-HWB-S.

Title: A German Tariff for the EQ-5D-5L - an explorative pre-study
Abstract: The objective of the approved study “A German Tariff for the EQ-5D-5L” is to derive a preference valuation set for the EQ-5D-5L health states from the German general public. Due to the results of the completed EQ-5D-5L valuation studies in five countries, it was decided to postpone the data collection in Germany and to apply funding for an experimental pre-study. So, the objective of the proposed pre-study is to test the effect of adding three modifications to the current EuroQol Valuation-Technique (EQ-VT). In the proposed study the implementation of the following three add-ons will be analysed: separate Time-Trade-Off (TTO) tasks for health states Better Than Dead (BTD) and Worse Than Dead (WTD), allow for change of TTO answers and ranking task. The study sample consists of a control group (N=100; current EQ-VT) and an intervention group (N=100; modified EQ-VT). The methodological procedure of the approved main study will be based on the results of the proposed pre-study (after consulting the Valuation Methodology Working Group [VMWG]).

Title: Vision, Hearing, Sleep, Fatigue/Energy and Social Relationships Bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L: A Systematic Review
Abstract: Previous studies explored and suggested that the addition of the bolt-on items would impose improvements in EQ-5D, but only the cognition bolt-on was systematically reviewed to date. The project aimed to review the development, application, psychometric properties, and valuation of the prevalent EQ-5D bolt-ons.  A systematic review following PRISMA 2020 was conducted. Searches on PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science, supplemented by citation tracking and manual Google Scholar and EuroQol conference searches, were used. Key study characteristics, bolt-on specifications, psychometric properties, and valuation evidence were summarized narratively.  The project uncovered the abundance of EQ-5D format bolt-on wordings (sleep=12; fatigue/energy=14; social relationship=23), demonstrating the popularity of EQ-5D bolt-on research. Findings on content validity confirmed the relevance of the bolt-ons with the EQ-5D core dimensions. In many cases, the bolt-ons reduced the ceiling of the EQ-5D, and enhanced the psychometric performance of EQ-5D in terms of exploratory power, informativity, and known-group validity. Despite progress, the evidence in qualitative development, test-retest reliability, responsiveness, differential item functioning, patient-proxy agreement and valuation was still limited. The systematic review of sleep, fatigue/energy and social relationship bolt-ons demonstrated the common lack of qualitative input, but the majority of existing psychometric evidence supported their added value to the EQ-5D in specific populations. Future mixed-methods bolt-on development and refinement studies are needed for bolt-on constructs.

Title: Characterising and Explaining Socioeconomic Gradients in EQ VAS: A Multinational Analysis of Response Heterogeneity and Health Inequality Underestimation (Project UNVEIL - UNcovering VAS-Education Inequalities in heaLth states)
Abstract: Background: The EQ VAS shows substantial variation across populations that cannot be fully explained by health status or demographic characteristics. The PI’s recent systematic review of 127 studies (N≈980,000) reported a pooled mean EQ VAS of 79.0 (95% CI 78.2 to 79.8) with extreme heterogeneity (I²=99.83%), of which meta-regression analyses explained only 12.55% using study-level and population characteristics. In addition, recent evidence from Olsen et al. (2025) demonstrated that individuals reporting identical EQ-5D-5L profiles exhibit marked education gradients in EQ VAS scores. Together, these findings suggest that reliance on EQ-5D-5L index values alone may understate the magnitude of education-related differences in self-reported health, potentially due to socioeconomic differences in adaptation processes and the omission of key psychosocial dimensions.Methods: Project UNVEIL will analyse the harmonised EQ-DAPHNIE dataset (15 countries; N≈67,000) using a two-phase design. Phase 1 quantifies cross-country and individual-level variation in EQ VAS using multilevel modelling. Phase 2 extends the within-profile framework by investigating heterogeneity in EQ VAS among individuals with identical EQ-5D-5L health states, explained by key socioeconomic proxies: education, relative income (country-specific quartiles), and employment. Furthermore, it calculates country-specific underestimation factors and investigates the influence of health behaviours and bolt-on dimensions such as fatigue/energy and sleep.Impact: By identifying when and why EQ-5D-5L underestimates health inequalities, this study will inform EuroQol’s work on response heterogeneity and provide empirical evidence to guide bolt-on development priorities. Key outputs will include country-specific underestimation factors, a decision framework for equity sensitive analyses, and a policy brief for health technology assessment bodies. These outputs will help ensure that population norms and priority setting decisions do not systematically understate the burden of socioeconomic disadvantage.

Title: Assessing the health of the general population in England: how do the EQ-5D 3L and 5L versions compare?
Abstract: not available

Title: Development of an Estonian EQ-5D-5L Value Set Using Discrete Choice Experiment with Duration
Abstract: Estonia does not have a national EQ-5D value set for neither the 3L nor 5L version of the instrument, despite the EQ-5D-3L being included in the Estonian Survey on Health Behaviour among Adult Population (HBEP) since 2002. This absence represents one of the last remaining gaps in Europe and limits Estonia’s ability to conduct locally relevant cost-utility analyses for health technology assessment, develop valid population norms, and support evidence-based health policy. The proposed study aims to develop the first EQ-5D-5L value set for Estonia using a discrete choice experiment with duration (DCEd).The DCEd component will adopt the methodology established by the DCE duration valuation protocol, as approved recently by EuroQol’s Executive Committee, employing 15 non-randomized split-triplet choice tasks plus 8 supplemental pairwise anchoring tasks administered via an online panel to 1,000 adults representative of the Estonian population. The study will leverage the existing survey infrastructure at National Institute for Health Development in Estonia, with sample frame for the DCEd study being drawn from population registry. Data will be modelled using mixed logit with exponential discounting (DCE). The resulting value set will enable valid cost-utility analyses, support the development of Estonian EQ-5D-5L population norms, and position Estonia at the forefront of EQ-5D valuation methodology by being among the first countries to use the emerging stand-alone DCE with duration protocol.

Title: Discrete choice modeling from a different angle
Abstract: Introduction: Preference-based measurement methods are frequently used to obtain values expressing the quality of health-state descriptions. A crucial assumption in these methods is that respondents pay equal attention to all information components presented in the response task. So far, there is no solid evidence that respondents are fulfilling this condition or are using shortcuts. The aim of our study is to explore the attendance to various information cues presented in the discrete choice response tasks. Methods: Eye tracking was used to study the eye movements and fixations on specific information areas. This was done for seven discrete choice response tasks comprising health-state descriptions. A sample of 10 respondents participated in the study. Videos of their eye movements were recorded and are presented here graphically. Statistics were computed for length of fixation and number of fixations, so differences in attendance were demonstrated for particular attributes in the tasks. Results: All respondents completed the survey. Respondents were fixating on the left-sided health-state descriptions slightly longer than on the right-sided health-state descriptions. Fatigue was not observed, as the time spent did not decrease in the final response tasks. We noted that the time spent on the tasksdepended on the difficulty of the task and the amount of information presented. Conclusion: Eye tracking proved to be a feasible method to study the process of paying attention and fixating on health-state descriptions in the discrete choice response tasks. Eye tracking facilitates the investigation of whether respondents fully understand the information in health descriptions or whether they ignore particular elements.

Title: Development of a proxy English Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) instrument for children under six years of age, derived from the EQ-5D-Y: Part 1
Abstract: Background and Aim: Although the EQ-5D-Y was developed for self-report by children over the age of seven years, there is no instrument in the EuroQoL stable developed and validated specifically for younger children and infants. In order to investigate the need for the development of such an instrument, a systematic review of Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) measures for children under seven years of age was undertaken. The COSMIN (1)checklist for reviewing outcome measures was used as a framework.Study Design:The search strategy was based on published literature and expert knowledge. A data abstraction form was developed, following COSMIN (2). Information on bibliographic details, instrument development, completion by self/proxy, domains, number of items, response options, frame of reference, recall period, scoring and psychometric results pertaining to validation, reliability and practicality was recorded. Results:Fifteen generic HRQoL measures were identified. The development procedure for most of the instruments was based on the existing literature and expert opinion and all authors claimed to have taken age-appropriateness into account. Many of the measures were extended for proxy use to five years of age but few were developed specifically for children under the age of seven years. Domains were similar across measures and in accord with WHO’s definition of health and components of the HRQoL namely: physical; emotional; social and cognitive. Content validity was judged from the developmental process of the measure. Face validity was reported based on results of the pilot or field testing during the development process. Despite therequirements of FDA guidelines for proxy measures, observable characteristics of the domains were poorly defined and no measure was based purely on observable behaviour. The majority of measures rely on either domain scoring and/or a single summary score.The scoring algorithms for the measures are generally poorly defined. The criterion validity of most of the instruments was established through comparison to a previously developed and validated HRQoL measure. The divergent validity was generally examinedby confirming differences between known-groups. The reliability as measured by internal consistency was reported α≥0.70 for only eight of the measures. Conclusion:There is a need to develop a comprehensive generic, preference-based HRQoL measure for children under the age of seven years as none of the measures reviewed satisfy all of the criteria. The specific aspects that were deficient included: a) The development procedure did not include focus groups of parents of children in the age group to establish the age appropriate behaviour which would represent the HRQoL construct and b) observable domains were not explicitly included and observable behaviour that would inform proxy report was not defined; c) the scoring systems were not necessarily psychometrically sound and the scoring algorithms, where developed, where opaque. There is a lack of preference based measures and several of the instruments were lengthy and valuation sets would be difficult to develop. There may be a need to develop more thanone instrument to measure HRQoL in different age categories for children under the age of seven years.

Title: EQ-5D-3L valuation study with crosswalk to EQ-5D-5L in Georgia
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol methodology (EQ-5D) has been used several times in Georgia, with a recent surge in interest in economic evaluation alongside their world-leading viral hepatitis elimination program. In 2021, the EQ-5D-5L was included in a nationally representative health survey in Georgia. However, the absence of a Georgian value set for either the EQ-5D-3L or 5L limits its application in health policy and economic evaluation.Objective: This study aimed to develop a Georgian value set for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L to enable more accurate and culturally relevant health economics studies, which will be crucial for policy-making and healthcare improvements in the region. Methods: The EuroQol EQ-VT version 2 standardised valuation protocol was used to gather EQ-5D-3L related preferences from the Georgian population. A total of 300 interviews were conducted. The interviews included both composite time-trade-off (cTTO) and discrete choice experiment (DCE) questions. Data were analyzed, accounting for the heteroskedastic nature and censoring at -1 of the cTTO data, using a Tobit model. This model was combined with a logit model for the DCE data in a hybrid model and compared to other modeling methods. The EQ-5D-3L values were used to estimate EQ-5D-5L values using a crosswalk method.Results: Within the Georgia value set, mobility level 3 had the largest disutility, followed by pain/discomfort level 3. In contrast, for level 2 responses, self-care had the largest disutility, with mobility having the lowest disutility of level 2 responses. The lowest state (33333) had a predicted value of -1.16.

Title: Travel scholarship request to attend the EuHEA conference 2024 in Vienna, Austria - Jan Faller
Abstract: This travel grant application sought funding support for an accepted abstract as part of Jan Faller’s EuroQol funded PhD study (1481-PHD). This was presented at the 2024 European Health Economics Association (EuHEA) Conference held in Vienna, Austria from 1-3 July 2024. Jan’s PhD programme aims to address methodological issues concerning the inclusion of informal carer outcomes in economic evaluations, particularly using the EQ-5D tools. Jan’s accepted presentation was titled: How well do generic preference-based measures perform in informal carers: a psychometric study in Australia. The study reported findings on the performance of the EQ-5D-5L and the AQoL-8D in terms of convergent validity, known-groups, ceiling effects and test-retest reliability. Furthermore, the conceptual overlap between the generic preference-based measures and carer-specific measures (CarerQoL, ASCOT-Carer, and the Carer Experience Scale) was also presented. The study concluded that both the EQ-5D-5L and AQoL-8D were valid generic preference-based measures for use in the informal carer population. Questions were also fielded after the presentation along with further discussions among the attendees. Outside of the presentation, Jan was also able to attend a pre-conference workshop titled: “Choice Modelling in Health: Eliciting and Modelling Stated Preferences for Health Interventions” delivered by Professor Esther de Bekker-Grob and Associate Professor Jorien Veldwijk of the Erasmus Choice Modelling Centre. The workshop aimed to help participants to familiarize ourselves with the steps of conducting a stated preference study and modelling choice data. Learnings from this workshop will be valuable for the subsequent studies of Jan’s PhD programme. During the conference, Jan was able to also network with Professor Hareth Al-Janabi, a leading researcher in the informal carer field. Jan and Professor Al-Janabi discussed the potential collaboration in future research as he had similar areas of interests with Jan and PhD supervisor Lidia Engel.

Title: EQ-5D for monitoring population health: a comparison of general population survey data in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay
Abstract: Objectives: To describeself-reportedhealth related quality of life (HRQL) fromgeneral population of Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay and to report population norms based on EQ-5D.Methods:We included data from the 2009 national health risk survey in Argentina (n=41,392) and from the participants of theEQ-5Dvaluation studies Brazil(n=3,362, Viegas Andrade 2013),Chile (n=2000, Zárate 2011) and Uruguay (n=792). We estimated mean VAS values and EQ-5D index by age, gender and the presence of limitations in any of the EQ-5D domains. We also explored the most frequent health states (those which include at least 90% of the population). Results:Self-rated mean VAS was 76.5 (IC95% 76.2-76.8), 83.8 (83.3-84.3), 75.7 (74.8-76.6) and 80 (78.6-80.9) in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay respectively. The percentage of individuals without limitations was 60.9%, 44.3%, 49.8%, and 44.6% in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay respectively. The EQ-5D TTO-based index valuesshowed slightly higher values in Argentina and Uruguay (0.910; CI95% 0.907-0.913 and 0.957; CI95% 0.951-0.962) than in Brazil and Chile (0.892, CI95% 0.888-0.897 and 0.80, CI95% 0.79-0.81). In all countries, both VAS and EQ-5D index values decreased with increasing age, andwere lowerin females. Out of the 243possible EQ-5D-3L health states only eight were present in at least 90% of the populationin Argentina, nine in Brazil, and 19 in Chile. In Uruguay, only 33 out of the possible 3125EQ-5D-5L health states were referred at least by 90% of the participants. In general, the prevalent states were the ones with mild limitations in pain-discomfort, anxiety-depression ormobility. Conclusions: This is the first collaborative work between Latin-American EQ-5D researchers from four countries. This study summarizespopulation norms for the region that can be used in decision-makingas well as in research

Title: The distribution of the EQ-5D-5L Index in patient populations
Abstract: Background:EQ-5D data are often summarised by anEQ-5D index, whosedistribution foritsoriginal version, the EQ-5D-3L,often shows in patient populations two distinct groups, arising fromboth the distribution of ill health and how the index is constructed (Parkin et al., 2016). Todate, there is little evidence about the distribution of the EQ-5D-5L index.Aims:The aimsof this study are:to explore whether or not the EQ-5D-5L index distribution also demonstrates clustering; to test the extent to which clustering of EQ-5D-5L profile data drivesany observed clustering of the EQ-5D-5L index,and the extent to which clusters result fromthe value sets used to create the index; and to discussthe implications of our results for statistical analysis of EQ-5D-5L index data.Data:Data from Cambridgeshire Community Services NHS’s electronic patient records data warehousewere analysed.EQ-5D-5L profiles before treatmentwere obtained for30,284 patients across three patient groups: community rehabilitation services (N=6,919); musculoskeletal therapy services (N=19,999); and nursing services (N=3,366).Methods:The EQ-5D-5L indexis calculated using both a ‘mapped’ (crosswalk) value set (MVS) and the English value set (EVS).We examinedthe distribution of 1,730 of the 3,125 profiles described by the EQ-5D-5L to check forclustering of the EQ-5D-5L index. The k-meanscluster method and the Calinski–Harabaszpseudo-F indexstopping rule were used to search for the clusters in the index. We examined the impact on the results of using different initial values in the clustering analysis. Results:Clustering within the EQ-5D-5L index distribution is suggested by both clustering methods, forthe three patient groupsand all patients together.For the all patients’data, we foundtwo robust clusters for the MVS-based index, compared to three robust clusters for the EVS-based index. The EQ-5D-5L profile dataalonedonotobviously drive the index clusters.Conclusion:The results highlight the importance of undertakingcareful exploratory data analysisfor health related quality of life measures such as the EQ-5D,to ensure that statistical testingtakesaccount ofclusteringand other features of the data distribution.Key words:EQ-5D; EQ-5D-5L Index; EQ-5D-5L profile; EQ-5D-5L value sets; Clustering Analysis; Patient Reported Outcomes (PROs); NHS PROMs.

Title: Making composite time trade-off method sensitive for worse-than-dead states
Abstract: Objective The utility values elicited with composite time trade-off method (cTTO) for health states worse-than-dead (WTD) correlate poorly with other measures of state severity. Various explanations for this lack of sensitivity have been put forward in the literature. We aimed to explore if various modifications of cTTO influence the correlation between utility and severity to better understand the reasons for the lack of sensitivity and identify possible methods for improvement. Methods A total of 480 respondents completed an online TTO interview, valuing 12 EQ-5D-5L health states. The respondents were randomly split into four arms, A--D. Arm A served as the benchmark and followed the cTTO implementation for EQ-5D valuation studies. Notably, cTTO has three characteristics. First, it uses two choice tasks to identify whether a given health state is WTD (henceforth, sorting questions): 1) a comparison of living for 10 years in this state with immediate death; 2) an analogous comparison with 10 years in full health added to both alternatives. Second, the lead-time TTO (LT-TTO) part of cTTO used for WTD states censors the utility values at -1. Third, the first negative utility value offered in LT-TTO amounts to -0.5. In arm B, we removed the first sorting question. In arm C, we allowed for utility values <-1 by reducing the time in the valued state in the choice task. In arm D, we randomized the starting negative utility between -0.2, -0.4, -0.6, and -0.8. We compared the distributions of elicited utilities, inspected the association between utilities and level sum score (LSS) using linear regression, and assessed the proportion of inconsistencies between logically ordered states at the individual respondent level. We assessed the impact of selected personal characteristics, including religiosity and numeracy skills. Results Arm A replicated the lack of a statistically significant association between LSS and negative utility. In arm B, a statistically significant negative association emerged (slope =-0.018), while it remained absent in arms C and D. In arm A, the negative association seemed to emerge for respondents with above-average numeracy skills or those non-religious, yet remained non-significant (however, p-values <0.1). Arm B resulted in greater proportion of states being WTD than arm A (46.5% vs 26.3%) and slightly fewer inconsistencies (3.7% vs 5.7% for better-than-dead states, and non-significant 10% vs 12.1% for WTD states). Arm B also yielded a slightly lower utility for the 55555 health state than arm A in the estimated value set: -0.588 vs -0.479. Conclusion The observed lack of correlation between LSS and utility for WTD states appears linked to the sorting question using the immediate death comparison. LT-TTO is capable of eliciting utility values in a way that is sensitive to severity. However, when only very severe states are considered WTD and subject to LT-TTO, this sensitivity is compromised. Dropping the first sorting question in cTTO could be considered.

Title: Psychometric performance of preference-based instruments in older adults: a systematic review
Abstract: Background: Population ageing is a major public health concern. Preference-based instruments are widely used to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and evaluate the cost-effectiveness of interventions. With multiple instruments available, it is important to identify the most suitable for older adults. This study systematically reviewed evidence on the psychometric properties of preference-based measures in older adults.Methods: Four databases (Medline, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL) were searched, supplemented by citation tracking. Peer-reviewed studies assessing the psychometric properties of preference-based measures in adults aged ≥60 were included. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Methodological quality was assessed using the COSMIN risk of bias checklist, and evidence was graded using a modified GRADE approach.Results: A total of 106 studies met the criteria, covering EQ-5D-3L (48), EQ-5D-5L (34), ICECAP-O (29), ASCOT (15), QOL-ACC (9), HUI3 (8), HUI2 (7), QWB (5), EQ-HWB-9 (5), WOOP (3), SF-6D (3), AQoL-8D (2), AQoL-4D (1), and 15D (1). EQ-5D versions were most frequently evaluated and generally performed well, though ceiling effects, inter-rater reliability, and responsiveness issues were reported. Strong evidence supported ICECAP-O and ASCOT, but both need further testing on responsiveness. Limited and mixed findings were available for other measures. Early evidence for QOL-ACC and WOOP, both developed for older adults, was promising but incomplete.Conclusions: Preference-based measures are widely used with older adults, but psychometric evidence remains incomplete. Further research, particularly head-to-head comparisons using consistent methods, is needed to guide instrument selection in economic evaluations.

Title: Population health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic (POPCORN): fourth wave
Abstract: The POPCORN wave 4 project investigated the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and mental well-being (MWB) in the general population the EQ-5D-5L and explored which country level and individual factors were associated with lower HRQoL. We collected data using an online survey among the general population of six countries (Greece, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US)) in May-July 2023 (POPCORN wave 4). We merged POPCORN wave 4 dataset with wave 1-3 datasets resulting in one longitudinal dataset.  Next, two complementary studies were conducted within the multinational POPCORN cohort across six countries:Study 1: Examined the association between worry related to future pandemics, global geopolitical events and environmental threats and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and assessed whether resilience and social connectedness moderated these associations. We found that worry about global threats were consistently linked to lower HRQoL, while resilience and social connectedness were associated with better outcomes. However, their buffering effects differed by threat type.Study 2: Identified longitudinal HRQoL trajectories over three years using latent Markov modeling. Six distinct states were observed, ranging from no problems to multiple problems across EQ-5D-5L dimensions. HRQoL remained largely stable, with older age and chronic disease strongly associated with poorer states, and country-level differences favoring healthier profiles in the Netherlands and the US.

Title: An empirical analysis of the EQ-5D Anxiety/Depression dimension : investigating the Humpty Dumpty phenomenon using general population data
Abstract: Health Survey of England (HSE) data were  used  to explore the relationship between AD responses and (a) a standard measure of mental health (GHQ-12) and (b) a recognized measure of wellbeing (WEMWBS). Respondent-level data obtained in a nurse-led intereview conducted as part of the HSE survey, were used to create empirically defined categories of "caseness" which were used to verify psychometric performance of both these measures and dichotomised AD responses. The study also examined the feasibility of synthesizing AD responses using respondent-level covariate data. The study results show that AD performs well as a single-item indicator of depression “caseness” – outperforming both GHQ-12 and WEMWBS. However, analysis of potential association with anxiety proved infeasible. Most importantly, AD demonstrates a strong association with negative-worded items in GHQ-12, suggestive of it measuring psychological distress. However, the results of multidimensional analysis places AD centrally between GHQ-12 and WEMWBS, and lends support for identifying AD as a hybrid construct.

Title: Testing the skin irritation, self-confidence, social relationships, social participation and social connectedness bolt-on items for the EQ-5D-5L in German patients with chronic skin diseases associated with shame
Abstract: The EQ-5D-5L has shown potential limitations in capturing key aspects of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in dermatological diseases. The project investigated the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L and five bolt-ons – skin irritation (itching, IT), self-confidence (SE), social relationships (SR), social participation (SP) and feeling connected (FC) – in two prevalent chronic inflammatory dermatological conditions, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with n=180 German atopic dermatitis (mean age: 37 years) and n=285 psoriasis patients (46 years) including the EQ-5D-5L, five bolt-ons, and various (skin-specific) patient-reported outcome measures (e. g., Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), Skin Shame Scale (SSS-24), Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure (POEM), Psoriasis Signs and Symptoms Diary (PSSD), Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-4)). Analyses comprised distribution patterns (including number and proportion of "no problems" (ceiling) and missing values (feasibility)), convergent, divergent and known-groups validity, as well as explanatory power.

Title: Psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB in patients with breast cancer in Indonesia
Abstract: Objectives The EQ Health and Well Being is a new generic measure of health and wellbeing, with two versions: a 25-item long form (EQ-HWB) and a shorter 9-item version representing a subset of items (EQ-HWB-S). This study aims to test the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in breast cancer. Methods A single-center longitudinal survey was conducted in Bandung, Indonesia in 2023-24. Soft quotas were used to ensure variability in cancer stage and treatment cycles. Patients undergoing active treatment at baseline were invited for the 2-to-3-week follow-up (test-retest subsample), while those in their final treatment cycle were invited for the 2-to-3-month follow-up (responsiveness subsample). The interviewer-administered paper-and-pencil questionnaires included the following outcome measures: EQ-HWB, EQ-5D-5L, Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G), Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), and questions on socio-demographic and clinical characteristics. The 25-item EQ-HWB was administered, from which the EQ-HWB-S responses were derived. Index values were computed using the pilot UK (EQ-HWB-S), Indonesian (EQ-5D-5L), and Australian (FACT-8D) value sets. The following psychometric properties were tested: ceiling and floor, convergent validity with corresponding items and scales of other outcome measures, known-group validity (Cohen’s d effect sizes), test-retest reliability (Gwet’s AC2 coefficients and intraclass correlations [ICC]) and responsiveness (standardized response means [SRM] and effect sizes [SES]). Known-groups were defined as follows: patients with EQ VAS scores ≥80, 5-point self-perceived health scale, number of symptoms, and metastasis status. Test-retest analysis was conducted on patients with unchanged health status, while responsiveness analysis was performed on those with improved health, as evaluated by the Global Rating of Change scale. Results Overall, 300 female patients (aged 51.3±10.3) completed the baseline questionnaire. Across the 25 items of the EQ-HWB, the ceiling ranged from 29.0% (‘Exhausted’) to 88.3% (‘Unsupported’). For overall scores, the EQ-HWB-S exhibited a significantly lower ceiling (10.7%) compared to EQ-5D-5L (35.0%) albeit higher than FACT-8D (7.67%), while EQ-HWB and FACT-G yielded 2.3% and 0.7%, respectively. Convergent validity was established between conceptually-overlapping items, e.g., EQ-HWB Getting around inside and outside and EQ-5D-5L Mobility (r=0.60) and EQ-HWB-S Pain and FACT-8D Pain (r=-0.56). EQ-HWB level summary scores correlated at least moderately with FACT-G (r=0.69) and WEMWBS (r=-0.49). Strong correlations were found between the index values of EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L (r=0.73) and FACT-8D (r=0.70). The EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S effectively discriminated across known-groups with large effect sizes, ranging from -0.72 to -1.11 for EQ-HWB and -0.83 to -1.18 for EQ-HWB-S. In test-retest reliability (n=32), 17 EQ-HWB items demonstrated strong to almost-perfect agreement (Gwet’s AC2=0.60-0.97), with Sleep, Exhausted, and Anxious as the lowest performing items (Gwet’s AC2=0.32-0.35). Excellent test-retest reliability was observed at instrument level for EQ-HWB (ICC=0.83, 95%CI 0.68-0.91) and EQ-HWB-S (ICC=0.79, 95%CI 0.61-0.89]. Further, EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S showed small but significant responsiveness to change in health (n=75, SRM=-0.29, 0.24; SES=-0.19, 0.14, respectively). Conclusions This is the first study to validate the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S in breast cancer, and also the first to provide test-retest reliability and responsiveness evidence about the two instruments. Our findings add to the growing body of positive psychometric evidence supporting the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S.

Title: Comparison of the EQ-5D-Y-5L, EQ-5D-Y-3L and PedsQL in Paediatric Patients with Congenital Heart Disease in China
Abstract: Background: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is defined as a gross structural abnormality of the heart and/or great vessels at birth and is the leading birth defect. With increasing numbers of patients surviving through childhood and into adulthood, growing interest has been given to the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of patients with CHD. The EQ-5D-Y is one of the most commonly used generic preference-weighted measures for assessing a child’s HRQoL. Currently, there is no evidence about the feasibility and validity of the EQ-5D-Y-3L or EQ-5D-Y-5L for paediatric patients living with CHD. Aim of research: To examine the feasibility, validity, and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L in measuring HRQoL of paediatric CHD patients in China, and to compare their psychometric properties with PedsQL. Proposed methods: This prospective, longitudinal, study will recruit CHD patients aged 6 – 15 years from two tertiary general and children’s hospitals in China. At baseline, participants will self-complete a paper questionnaire that includes the EQ-5D-Y-3L, EQ-5D-Y-5L, generic PedsQL scale (PedsQL 4.0), and PedsQL cardiac-specific modules (PedsQL 3.0). Interviewer administered versions of the EQ-5D-Y-5L and PedsQL instruments will be available for children aged 6 and 7 as well as those unable to complete the self-administered version on their own. Participants who will receive surgery will be followed up at 3-months after the surgery. Feasibility, known-groups validity, convergent validity, and responsiveness will be assessed for both the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L-Y. Benefits to the group: This study addresses several research priorities highlighted in the current call for proposals of the EuroQol Research Foundation. It will be the first validation study for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and the EQ-5D-Y-5L in paediatric patients in China. The results from this study will generate important evidence about the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y and in comparison with PedsQL, a potential competitor of the EQ instruments. In addition, this study would potential be useful in either developing or validating the mapping function between EQ-5D-Y-3L and Y-5L.

Title: Scientific Summer Exchange Program to the Alberta PROMs and EQ-5D Research and Support Unit (APERSU)
Abstract: This final report documented my month-long residency with the Alberta PROMs and EQ-5D Research and Support Unit (APERSU) from September to October 2023, I engaged in a productive research exchange and internship at the School of Public Health, University of Alberta. This period was marked by significant growth in my skills, knowledge, and research capabilities related to the applications of EQ-5D and other Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) in clinical practice and health systems. The objectives were successfully met through a series of comprehensive activities. Firstly, I enhanced my research expertise by participating in an internship program, where I had the opportunity to learn from leading experts in the field. I attended and contributed to research seminars, presenting my PhD research proposal and the preliminary findings to a scholarly audience. Secondly, I visited and interacted with experts from APERSU and the Institute of Health Economics in Edmonton. These visits facilitated the exploration of PROMs data integration into health systems, aimed at promoting sustainability and efficiency. Advocacy for routine collection of PROMs data within healthcare system in Singapore was a significant aspect of these discussions, paving the way for future collaborative efforts. Thirdly, my attendance at the APERSU Annual End-user Meeting and the ISOQOL Annual Conference was instrumental. Not only did I stay updated with the latest research and practices in the field, but I also contributed significantly by presenting my PhD work alongside two oral and one poster presentation. Additionally, it provided an excellent platform for networking and establishing collaborations with renowned professionals and researchers, thereby contributing to my professional growth and the expansion of my research network. The completion of this funded travel has been a cornerstone in advancing my career as a researcher. It has equipped me with invaluable insights and expertise on PROMs in clinical practice and health systems. The visit has not only enhanced my capacity to contribute to improving patient outcomes and satisfaction through evidence-based decision-making but has also laid a robust foundation for my forthcoming post-doctoral pursuits and the achievement of my long-term career objectives. The benefits reaped from this grant-funded travel will resonate throughout my future endeavors in healthcare research.

Title: Examining the internal structure of the EQ-HWB with a focus on positively and negatively framed items: analysis of three general population datasets
Abstract: Our previous study (EQproject 127-2020RA) rigorously investigated the internal structure of the EQ-HWB using the psychometric study data (60+ items from which the final EQ-HWB items were drawn). More than half of the items selected for the EQ-HWB instrument have undergone revision, some substantively, and it is unknown whether the found structures would hold for the current version of the instrument. Furthermore, potential issues posed by the three positively worded items (all remaining items are negatively worded) have been noted by users of the experimental EQ-HWB. While we did not previously find positively/negatively worded items to pose a concerning methods effect, it is unknown whether using the 25 items divorced from the 60+ item bank changes item performance.  Given the limitations of the previous study, we propose to:   confirm the structure(s) found for the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S from project 127-2020RA using data on current version of the EQ-HWB, determine the extent of the measurement effect posed by including both positive/negative items in the 25-item EQ-HWB, and  examine stability of structural findings across subgroups with a focus on comparisons across two languages (English and Chinese) and three countries (Ireland, Australia, China).   Results are important for moving the EQ-HWB to approved status, especially providing measurement evidence on the three positively worded items (and whether they need revision). Furthermore, advancing non-preference based scores, especially for the long-version of the EQ-HWB for which preference-based scoring will not be developed, will support application of the instrument across a broad spectrum of settings.

Title: Using the Online elicitation of Personal Utility Functions (O)PUF approach to value EQ-5D-5L bolt-ons: an exploratory methodology study
Abstract: We completed all the tasks proposed in the application, including an online (O)PUF survey of over 800 members of general public in the UK, data analysis and report as well as delivery of presentation in the EuroQol Academy meeting 2025. We required no cost extension to complete the survey and write up the final report

Title: Quantifying Health Inequality: Systematic literature review of the application of EuroQol instruments
Abstract: To address the EuroQol strategic goals of understanding the measurement properties of its suite of instruments, increasing international relevance, and the call by the PHS WG to understand how these instruments can be used to assess health inequalities, we propose a **systematic literature review aiming to**: 1. systematically search and review published and grey literature on that used (approved) EuroQol suite of instruments to assess social inequalities in health; 2. evaluate how these instruments have been applied to assess health inequalities in both population and clinical settings; 3. synthesize the evidence on the sensitivity of these instruments for inequalities including potential differences across EQ-measures and socioeconomic indicators; and 4. (when feasible) conduct meta-analysis on particular inequality stratifiers. Understanding social inequalities in health is an important research topic and the EuroQol suite of instruments can play an important role as outcome measures. This review will provide the state of play of the use of these instruments in this field of research and identify knowledge gaps. Project results will include the existing evidence on the sensitivity of EQ-instruments to capture health inequalities across sociodemographic/-economic subgroups and identify populations (across and within cultures/countries) for which EQ-instruments have been used to address inequalities. Crucially, gaps in the existing literature will be identified. We will also assess the level of quality of existing published and grey literature. These results are relevant for the EuroQol Group as population level use of its instruments become more prominent (e.g. POPCORN and DAPHNIE studies).

Title: System-level PROM collection and EQ instruments: the current state of play
Abstract: An increasing number of health systems have signalled interest in routine collection of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) data to support health system development and value-based care. Widespread implementation of PROM data collection may be hindered by health system stakeholders’ capacity and capability to analyse and interpret the data collected. There is currently no systematic overview of the data, evidence and policy landscape in this space. This project plans to undertake a comprehensive review of current and planned routine PROMs collections internationally. The review will help to document the current state-of-play and to identify knowledge gaps and research opportunities to promote the use of EQ instruments in routine PROM data collection internationally. The work is led by members of the PHS WG and will result in a position paper for internal use by the WG and the wider EuroQoL membership and a peer-reviewed journal article.

Title: Validating the EQ-HWB and its modifications among informal carers of people living with dementia
Abstract: This qualitative study assessed the content validity of the EQ-HWB instrument among informal carers of people living with dementia in Ireland. Seventeen family carers (13 current, 4 former) participated in cognitive interviews between May and July 2025, using think-aloud protocols and verbal probing to evaluate comprehension, relevance, and comprehensiveness of the 25-item EQ-HWB. A second phase tested 10 wording and format modifications.Results showed the EQ-HWB was generally answerable, though several challenges emerged. The most prevalent issue was perspective ambiguity; carers were uncertain whether items referred to their own health or the care recipient's, particularly for physical function items. Caregiving phase effects influenced responses, with former carers contrasting current answers against active caregiving experiences. Response mapping difficulties arose from double-barrelled phrasing and ambiguous severity quantifiers. While emotional items (loneliness, anxiety, frustration) were universally relevant, physical health items were often judged irrelevant by those in good health. Carers identified missing constructs including identity loss, anticipatory worry, and complex grief. Modification testing revealed strong preferences for less severe wording ("lacked control" over "no control"), frequency-based scales, and plainer language ("some" over "moderate").The EQ-HWB demonstrates promising content and face validity for dementia carers but would benefit from targeted refinements, for example adding perspective anchors to clarify self-report focus, addressing caregiving phase in instructions, reducing double-barrelled phrasing, refining response labels, and considering a caregiver-specific supplement to capture domains such as fatigue, autonomy constraints, and anticipatory worry. These findings support the use of EQ-HWB with dementia carers while highlighting the importance of population-specific adaptation to optimise measurement validity.

Title: A Scoping Review of Stakeholder Engagement in Health State Valuation: What Is Currently Being Done and What Could Be Done Better?
Abstract: In the design, delivery, and dissemination of health research, collaboratively engaging with individuals invested in or affected by the research – beyond researchers themselves – is considered best practice. While collaborative engagement is common in many areas of health, the degree to which it is undertaken in health state valuation is unclear. The aim of this research was to: (i) identify best practice recommendations for collaborative engagement in the health economics and related patient-reported outcome (PRO) literature; (ii) identify valuation studies that featured examples of collaborative engagement; and (iii) map (ii) onto (i) to identify the degree of alignment between the two, to inform future practice and recommendations. A scoping review was conducted following best practice guidance, featuring database and grey literature searching. For aim (i), manuscripts or reports featuring at least one best practice recommendation for collaborative engagement were identified; recommendations were extracted and thematically synthesised. For aim (ii), health state valuation manuscripts published since 2019 featuring collaborative engagement were identified and key details extracted, before being mapped against synthesised recommendations (aim (iii)). Twenty-one papers featuring recommendations were included and fifteen best practice recommendations for collaborative engagement synthesised. Fifteen papers featuring examples of collaborative engagement in health state valuation were included. Most examples involved engaging patients and/or experts when informing health states. There was no evidence that 11 out of 15 synthesised recommendations had been applied in the valuation studies, with only nominal evidence provided for the remaining four. In conclusion, collaborative engagement in health state valuation appears misaligned with emerging recommendations from the health economics and PRO literature. The recommendations synthesised in this review represent a strategic starting point for developing guidance to improve practice.

Title: ISOQOL Dissemination of the of the adapted (modified) EQ-5D-Y validation study
Abstract: PhD student, and EuroQol PhD network member, Alexander van Heusden successfully presented his research titled "Psychometric validation of the adapted EQ-5D-Y (-3L and -5L) against PedsQL for use in children aged 2-4 years" at the ISOQOL 2023 conference in Calgary, Canada. Alexander van Heusden met and fostered social connections with other EuroQol PhD network members that attended the conference.

Title: HTAi Workshop: Engaging patients and general public in health technology assessment: Measuring and valuing health preferences
Translation of the EQ-HWB into Dutch language
Abstract: This project aimed to translate the EQ-HWB original (OG), EQ-HWB-9 OG, EQ-HWB Modified and EQ-HWB-9 Modified from English into the Dutch language. We followed the EQ-HWB translation guidelines developed by the EuroQol Research Foundation and were supported by the Version Management Committee (VMC). The steps of the translation process included forward translation, backward translation and cognitive debriefing interviews.

Title: Hong Kong participation BTD-WTD split experiment
Request for a travel scholarship to attend ISPOR Europe 2024 to present and disseminate findings
Abstract: Before attending the conference, I prepared and printed a poster for my project. At the ISPOR conference, I conducted a one-hour poster presentation, during which I stood by my poster the entire time, explaining its content to attendees and answering their questions. I also took the opportunity to introduce the EQ-HWB to fellow presenters in the surrounding poster exhibition area. Most of my audience consisted of professionals and experts working in the field of instrument development or related industries.

Title: Reintroduction of the ranking task in EQ-5D valuation. Improved data quality and reduced level of inconsistencies?
Abstract: Background:The EuroQol group has observed several problematicissues related to the quality of valuation data collected using the EQ-VT system. The objective of this study was to test if reintroducing a ranking task prior to TTO valuation could help to reduce inconsistencies and improve the quality of thedata in future valuation studies.Method:The study was performed in Spain (Canary Island). Respondents were assigned to three different study arms. Thecontrol group (Arm 1) wasthe current EQ-VT version, which did not include a ranking task. The second arm (Arm 2)wasthe EQ-VT preceded by a ranking task similar to the one used in the MVH protocol, in which the respondents wereasked to rank the target health states using physical cards. The last arm (Arm 3)wassimilar to the second, with ranking prior to the EQ-VT. Unlike the second branch, the ranked states remainedvisible through the Composite TTO (C-TTO) tasks, and the C-TTO states order weredetermined by the rank order. We usedjust one specific block of 10 C-TTO states. A total sample size of 600(~200 per experimental arm) respondentswererandomly selected with representatives in term of age and gender ofCanary Islands population. All interviews wereperformed face to face. The interviewers performed similar number of interviews in the different experimental branches. We comparedthe number of C-TTO-based inconsistencies.Results:The final sample size was 600 respondents (196, 205 and 199 for arms 1, 2 and 3 respectively). The percentages of times when the state 55555 was not valued as the worst state on C-TTO responses by study arm were 13.27%, 10.73% and 13.57% for arms 1, 2, 3 respectively. However, none of the observed differences in levels of inconsistent responses were statistically significant.Conclusions:Under the light of theseresults it does not make sense to increment the current burden of EQ-VT by adding the ranking task as it does not improve the data quality neither the spikes on C-TTO observed values distributions.

Title: Health-related quality of life among Ukrainian war refugees in Estonia: A comparative analysis with the general population using EQ-5D-3L
Abstract: This Project provided a comparative analysis of HRQoL and its health-related and socio-demographic correlates among Ukrainian refugees and in general population. Using data from two representative population health surveys from 2024, the Project aimed to be one of the first to use EQ-5D-3L in the context of current refugee crisis in Europe. The two deliverables - submitted manuscript of academic article and conference paper -  reported significantly lower HRQoL among refugees compared their age and sex-matched peers from general population even after adjusting for socio-demographic and health-related covariates. Project also demonstrated higher prevalence of behavioral risk factors among refugees compared to general population (female only sub-analysis) with each risk factor decreasing the EQ-5D index value by 0.04 in both groups. These findings contribute to the understanding of health impact of recent refugee crisis in Europe, as well as contribute to knowledge on the use of the EQ-5D instrument among vulnerable groups.

Title: Exploring perceived interactions between EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons: a qualitative valuation study using EQ-PVT
Abstract: This study qualitatively explored how bolt-ons affect the perception of EQ-5D-5L core dimensions in a valuation context. Sixty Indonesian adults (aged 20-67, 50% female) each valued 10 health states using composite Time Trade-Off (cTTO). States were presented in either forward (EQ-5D-5L, then with one bolt-on, then two) or backward (reversed sequence) order. Participants were assigned to one of three bolt-on dyads: vision and tiredness, cognition and social relationships, or skin irritation and self-confidence. In semi-structured qualitative interviews, respondents described how adding or removing bolt-ons changed the perceived importance of the five core dimensions. We classified these changes as related either to measurement or to valuation, with the latter further categorized as a relative or absolute shift in importance. Our results showed that cognition and vision generated the most shifts in perceived importance in the forward and backward groups, respectively. Regardless of ordering group, most shifts occurred between the EQ-5D-5L alone and the version with one bolt-on (first presented in the dyad), with significantly fewer shifts observed between the one-bolt-on and two-bolt-on states. In the forward group, most shifts were classified as measurement (56%) or relative preference (29%), while the reverse was true in the backward group: relative preference (53%) or measurement (31%). Absolute preference was least common across both groups. In summary, this is the first study to explore how individuals reason when valuing EQ-5D-5L+bolt-on health states. Our findings suggest that interactions between dimensions are complex and may be influenced by presentation order. Further qualitative research should directly investigate absolute preferential reasoning, and additional quantitative work may help distinguish between the effects of measurement-based and preference-based reasoning.

Title: Variation in health state preferences across local and international populations: East doesn't meet West
Abstract: The 2016 CADTH Symposium is the main scientific venue for researchers who conduct health technology assessment/health economics in Canada and government agencies that are involved in decision making in health care. It provided an excellent opportunity to: (1) promote awareness of The EQ-5D-5L Canadian Valuation study and the availability of the value set; (2) present research on geographic variation of preferences, and differences in the relationship between elicitation methods across regions and discuss its implications; (3)highlight the relationships between different preference-based elicitation techniques based on international valuation studies using a standardized protocol (EQ-VT) that demonstrates the state of the science supported by the EuroQol group to inform HTA around the world. Both are areas of scientific and policy-based interest to the EuroQol Group. These topics were of specific interest to policy makers and researchers in Canada, given that provinces are responsible for the delivery of health care services.

Title: Killing two birds with one stone? Psychometric assessment of EQ-HWB-S, cognition bolt-ons and EQ-5D-5L in a large nursing home setting in Argentina.
Abstract: This research explores the light cultural adaptation/cognitive debriefing, and psychometric performance of the latest cognition bolt-ons version (as provided by the DSWG-BM) for the EQ-5D, as well as of the EQ-HWB-S, in an elderly nursing home population. The study will be set in LeDor VaDor, a leading institution in Buenos Aires, Argentina, known for its comprehensive care and robust academic involvement. Housing approximately 300 residents, LeDor VaDor offers a rich setting for deploying significant health-related research due to its diverse resident profile and advanced medical facilities. Our study will initially perform a light cultural adaptation/cognitive debriefing interviews to adapt the cognition bolt-ons (and produce the changes needed to have an interviewer and a proxy -version 1- EQ-HWB-S Argentine versions), and assess the construct validity, and psychometric comparability of the EQ-HWB-S and cognition bolt-ons alongside the EQ-5D-5L. The project involves two main phases: (1) “light” cultural adaptation/cognitive debriefing interviews and content validity assessment of cognition bolt-ons in Argentina Spanish to a sample of 5-7 persons, (2) a cross-sectional psychometric validation study of the EQ-HWB-S, cognition bolt-ons, and EQ-5D-5L with a sample of 100-150 nursing home residents. If the project is successful, we plan to apply for a project extension to assess responsiveness on 80-120 subjects from this inception sample at 6-12 months follow-up. This study will contribute to further developing tools from the EuroQol set (cognition bolt-ons for EQ-5D, EQ-HWB-S) targeted to answer questions of the current RFP, for measuring quality of life in populations where the cognitive dimension is relevant.

Title: Development of Argentinean Spanish Mock-up Versions of the Experimental and Modified EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S Instruments
Abstract: **Background:** The EQ-HWB is a comprehensive tool developed to assess the impact of health and social care, as well as the role of informal caregiving on quality of life. Developed by an international team led by Prof. John Brazier, this tool was initially created in collaboration with multiple countries including Argentina and is now transitioning from experimental to approved status, pending further validation. **Objective:** The research proposal focuses on developing Argentinean Spanish mock-up versions of the EQ-Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) and its shorter form, EQ-HWB-S, both in their experimental and modified versions. **Methods:** The project will be executed through a series of methodical steps. Initially, a local researcher will use a previously translated 60-item Spanish version as a foundation to create the initial drafts of the EQ-HWB instruments. These drafts will then be adjusted based on the modifications identified in the English experimental versions. After the initial drafting, the drafts will be refined further through a collaborative review process. This involves another local researcher and a VMC reviewer fluent in Spanish. Their insights will be integrated during an online consensus meeting aimed at finalizing the drafts. Following this, the drafts will undergo a back translation process conducted by a qualified translator. This translator, fluent in both Spanish and English, will translate the Spanish versions back to English to ensure the translations maintain fidelity to the original meanings. Discrepancies identified between the back-translated English texts and the original drafts will lead to further adjustments. To assess the clarity and appropriateness of the translations, cognitive interviews will be conducted with a small sample of participants. This step is vital as it targets items that are known to be problematic or have undergone significant modifications. The insights and recommendations gathered from the cognitive debriefing will inform the final revisions to the drafts, leading to the production of the third consensus versions of the EQ-HWB instruments. These final versions will ensure accuracy and cultural relevance, making them suitable for use in the Argentinean context.

Title: Organizing a EuroQol workshop in Singapore to engage Asian HTA leaders and practitioners
Abstract: We developed and delivered a 2-hour workshop titled "Measurement and Valuation of Children's Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) for Health Technology Assessment: Methods and Instruments" on 19 Aug 2026 in Singapore, as a preconference workshop for the 12th HTAsianLink conference. We also had several face-to-face meetings with HTAsiaLink leaders and members to explore research collaborations with them at the institution and individual levels.

Title: Content Validity of the Experimental and Modified EQ-HWB S versions in Argentina: Moving One Step Closer to Prime Time.
Abstract: Objectives: The EuroQol Health and Wellbeing Questionnaire (EQ-HWB) is a generic instrument designed to measure health and wellbeing in diverse populations, including patients, social care users, and informal caregivers. Its short version (EQ-HWB-S), comprising nine items, was developed to suit valuation endeavors. The initial “Experimental” version has undergone minor adjustments, resulting in a “Modified” version. This study aimed to assess the content validity of the Spanish (Argentina) modified version of the EQ-HWB-S in a sample of patients, social care users, and informal carers, as well as inform whether the modifications are understood or preferred by the target population. Additionally, we aimed to evaluate the comprehension of the frequency scale in the EQHWB-S, which is also used by other Euroqol instruments. Methods: This was a qualitative study employing cognitive interviews. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling strategies. Interviews were conducted face-to-face, or via video conferencing. Trained qualitative researchers used a semi-structured interview guide with open-ended questions and targeted probes. Participants were asked to complete the questionnaires and verbalize their thoughts. Moreover, we included a card-sorting exercise that aimed to explore how the participants understand and order the frequency scale options, and to assess both the conceptual equivalence and preferences in the wording used in the modified version compared to the experimental version. Content analysis was conducted using a framework adapted for face validity studies, supported by data extraction matrices. The protocol was approved by a local Institutional Review Board (IRB) in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and participants provided verbal informed consent to participate. Results: A total of 20 participants were included, comprising patients (n= 11), informal carers (n= 3), and members of the general public (n= 4). From them, 9 were social care users. The median age was 64.5 years (range 25–88); 12 participants were women. Seventeen interviews were conducted face-to-face, and three were held via video conferencing. Content validity was summarized into the following themes: comprehension, interpretation, acceptability, relevance, response options, and exhaustiveness. Participants generally found the questionnaire easy to understand. Items were deemed relevant, and the response options were considered appropriate. Regarding exhaustiveness, some participants noted the absence of questions addressing leisure activities, social interactions, or close relationships. Additionally, participant feedback suggested revising the item related to self-control to enhance its clarity and relevance. The findings do not show a clear preference for how the questions are formulated between the experimental and modified versions. The modified version was considered appropriate. Regarding the frequency scale exercise, the modified version seems to be appropriate. Most participants located “never” and “most or all of the time” at the extremes as expected. There was somewhat more item misplacing in the intermediate labels (for example reversing the order of “a little of the time” and ‘sometimes’). Conclusion: This study shows the content validity of the modified Argentine version of the EQ-HWB-S for measuring health and wellbeing in a mixed population, including patients, social care users, and informal caregivers. In the majority of participants the modified frequency scale exercise did not reveal major wording or comprehension issues. No clear preference emerged between the experimental and modified versions assessment. These findings will support the use of the modified version in diverse contexts within Argentina and contribute to the increasing evidence base of the EQ-HWB-S.

Title: Meeting of EQ-5D researchers in the UK and Ireland

Abstract: The initial preparation of the study was undertaken between November 2012 and September 2013. Due to the results of the first wave of EQ-5D-5L valuation studies in 2012/2013and the following moratorium, it was decided to postpone the data collection of the main study in Germany and to conduct an initial experimental pre-studyto test the protocol updates in Germany.The final report was already signed-off and the results were published (Ludwig et al.
