Title: Assessing bolt-ons in cognition (ABC): a secondary analysis
Abstract: Purpose This study assessed the psychometric performance and response burden of five cognition bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-5L - one composite item (CO) and four components (Concentration (CC), Memory (ME), Confusion (CF) and Reasoning (RE)) in a U.S. general population sample. We aimed to determine whether specific cognition items or combinations offer meaningful psychometric improvements relative to added response burden. Methods A cross-sectional online survey collected data from 6,018 adults. Item-level properties included informativity (Shannon’s indices), ceiling reduction and divergent validity (polychoric correlations). Instrument-level properties assessed explanatory power (R² for EQ-VAS prediction) and dimensionality using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Response burden was estimated from median item completion times. Bolt-ons were presented in fixed order after EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Results J' values ranged from 0.403 (RE) to 0.629 (ME), showing diverse response distributions. Cognition bolt-ons moderately correlated with EQ-5D-5L items (highest with Anxiety/Depression, r=0.722 for CC). R² values for EQ VAS prediction ranged from 0.0855 (RE) to 0.1575 (CC). Adding cognition items reduced the ceiling effect by up to 3.63% (ME-CC module). Median response times increased modestly: by 9 seconds for CO and around 13 seconds for ME-CC. EFA identified three factors, with cognition items clustering separately from physical and subjective health dimensions. Conclusion The ME-CC module demonstrated slightly better psychometric performance and ceiling reduction than the composite item, with minimal added burden. These findings support further qualitative and valuation research to refine cognition bolt-ons for integration into generic preference-based measures like the EQ-5D-5L.

Title: Test of reference dependency in EQ-5D-5L health state valuations
Abstract: Background: Health state valuations provided by patients (i.e. experienced-based preferences) and non­ patients are generally not the same. Ultimately, the decision of which health-state values to use is a normative one, and research into the similarities and differences of values obtained from both perspectives is generated as basis for such decision. Thus far, the discussion has largely overlooked the fact that general population samples are very heterogeneous and comprise many respondents in impaired health states. Similar as patients, these respondents have a unique vantage (or reference) point that can influence their preferences. This potential source of bias is usually not recognized and even when it is acknowledged, the empirical implications are not investigated. This study seeks to address this issue by investigating the existence and empirical relevance of health state reference dependency in health state valuations. Methods: The reference dependency hypothesis is tested in a discrete choice experiment (DCE). A Bayesian DCE design consisting of 8 sets of 24 (matched pairwise) choice tasks was used, each set providing full identification of the EQ5D parameters for individual respondents. Mixed logit models were used to estimate the utility decrements associated with the severity levels in each dimension of the EQ5D. Reference dependency was subsequently modeled relative to respondents' own (self-assessed) EQ-5O health states using 5 additional parameters. These reference dependency parameters capture, separately for each EQ5D dimension, the multiplicative increase or decrease in health state utility as a result of valuing health state levels that are better than or equal to respondents' own health. Results: The DCE was administered to a Dutch nationally representative sample of 799 respondents. The majority of respondents in our sample was in good health, reflected by the share reporting problems in any of the dimensions: 24% in MO, 4% in SC, 27% in VA, 48% in PD and 22% in AD. Modeling the respondents' choices without taking reference dependency into account produced statistically significant and logically consistent parameter estimates. When reference dependency was taken into account, statistically significant and consistent parameters estimates were obtained for all severity levels and reference dependency parameters, except for self-care (where 96% of the sample reported not to have any health problems). Our results indicate that respondents in impaired health lower than or equal to the health state levels under evaluation have, on average, approximately 30% smaller health-state decrements. Despite these differences, a correction for reference dependency did not result in a social tariff with stronger health-state decrements; in fact, the social tariffs obtained from the models with and without reference dependency are close to identical. Conclusion: The results confirm our hypothesis that reference dependency can be observed in a random sample from the general population. On the one hand, reference dependency is found to have a major impact on respondents' individual preferences. On the other hand, the limited number of respondents with health impairments does not appear to bias the social tariff as obtained from a random sample of the general population, which is reassuring evidence.

Title: A VMC research proposal: developing and testing online Cognitive Debriefing interviews: these are ‘necessary’ – but are they ‘feasible’?
Abstract: Introduction: Cognitive debriefing (CD) is an essential component of the translation process from English into a target language for all EuroQol self-complete instruments. It is traditionally conducted through face-to-face (F2F) interviews. However, since F2F interviews are not always feasible, there is increasing interest in the use of virtual CD approaches. To date, the feasibility of conducting CD interviews, especially the administration of the qualifier ranking task via online panels, has not been systematically explored. This study aimed to assess the feasibility, as well as the strengths and limitations, of online CD interviews.Methods: A website was developed for online ranking tasks and tested prior to formal data collection. Sixteen respondents were recruited in accordance with the Version Modification Committee (VMC) requirements; eight from China using the Simplified Chinese EQ-5D-5L version and eight Singapore who used the English version. Online CD interviews consisted of three sequential components: the severity qualifier ranking exercise, independent completion of the EQ-5D-5L, and a follow-up CD interview. Two local research assistants were recruited to help disseminate the interview information and recruit respondents. Eligible respondents received a meeting invitation if they consented to participate. Interviews were conducted via Zoom in Singapore and Tencent Meeting in China and were recorded with automatic transcription. Throughout the interviews, the interviewer observed participants’ responses and independently recorded reflections on the strengths and limitations of the virtual format.Results: The respondents were recruited for each country fulfilling the sample requirement as suggested by the EuroQol Translation Guideline. The mean age of respondents was 48.6 years in China and 46.6 years in Singapore, with mean interview durations of 44 minutes (range: 34.0–53.2) and 38 minutes (range: 30.3–44.0), respectively. All Singaporean participants completed the ranking tasks correctly, whereas two respondents in China did not rank all items correctly (but were able to self-complete the EQ-5D-5L and complete the cognitive debriefing interview). All respondents completed the interviews and demonstrated adequate understanding of the interview instructions.Discussion: In general, online CD was feasible in Singapore and among the six younger respondents in China. The two respondents were a 30-year-old woman with a low level of education and a 74-year-old man with a low level of education. Key advantages of online CD included broader geographic reach and greater scheduling flexibility compared with F2F interviews, and rigorous quality control. However, limitations remain, particularly in reaching vulnerable populations who may lack the digital skills or resources required for online participation, and in managing potential internet disruptions. While online CD can provide information equivalent to F2F interviews when applied to appropriate populations, F2F approaches remain more suitable for older and less technically proficient populations.

Title: Bolt-on proposal
Abstract: Over the last few years there has been discussion within the EuroQol Group about the development of condition specific "bolt-ons" to the standard EQ-5D. Bolt-ons are extensions of the standard five dimension instrument, implying that a dimension or multiple dimensions will be added to the EQ-5D as to broaden the coverage of the health measurement continuum. Bolt-ons can be of substantial scientific and strategicinterest to the EuroQol group. There are several reasons for this interest. The most obvious and arguablymost important reason is user demand. Disease specific utility measures have begun to be developed and published in the literature. Also, agencies outside the EuroQol group are interested in funding research in this area. From a scientific point of view there are further grounds for exploring the development of condition specific bolt-ons to the EQ-5D. There is evidence that the EQ-5D does not capture all possible variations in disability caused by various conditions, in areas such as cognition (Krabbe et al, 1999), vision or hearing loss, (Espallargues et al, 2005; Brazier et al 2004), but also sexual function, incontinence or changes in someone’s appearance (Kaarlola et al, 2004). Two recent studies by Pickard and Lin (2010) and Solem et al (2011) show a number of condition areas where developingbolt-ons to the EQ-5D could be justified.Moreover, more and more so-called ‘mapping’algorithms to the EQ-5D are being used that are based on a link function between the EQ-5D and a condition specific non-preference based measure, often by means of a simple regression on the index values. Two recent review studies showed that many of these mappings are of very poor quality (Brazier et al, 2010, Mortimer et al, 2008), but the increasing use of these mappingsindicates that there is an interest for index values for extensions to the EQ-5D.There are two known studies that can be seen as initial bolt-on endeavours. The first is the addition of a cognitive dimension (Krabbe et al, 1999) and the second a sleep dimension (Yang et al, 2008). Both were not condition specific. In the cognition study valuations were performed and showed systematically different values compared to the standard EQ-5D, whereas content validity improved. It was concluded that the addition of the cognition dimension was justified. The secondbolt-on valuation study showed that the sleep dimension had no significant incremental disutility and therefore adding a sleep dimension to the EQ-5D was discouraged. Two recent studies aimed at the development of bolt-ons to the EQ-5Din the areas of vision and psoriasis (Yang et al, 2012; Swinburn et al, 2012). Vision had a significant impact on the EQ-5D-3L although differences between the EQ-5D-3L states and the corresponding states including the Vision dimension were not significant. Two psoriasis related dimensions (Skin irritation and Self-confidence)had a significant impact on the EQ-5D-5L.

Title: ’Decolonizing health’: Perception and development of a conceptual health framework among children and adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa and its content comparison with the EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: Aims Many existing generic health measures were originally based on conceptual frameworks that originated in high income countries and many (though not all) were originally developed for adults. There is little documentation of how health is perceived by children and adolescents in low-income countries (LICs) particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aimed to investigate how health is understood by children and adolescents in Malawi, develop a conceptual framework of child health in Malawi, and compare its content with that of the EQ-5D-Y. Methods We invited children and adolescents (aged 8-17years) from Blantyre, Malawi to take part in four focus group discussions (FGD) between December 2019-February 2020. Consent and assent were obtained from both parents and children before discussions. Each FGD was conducted using a standard topic guide, though prompt questions allowed individual ideas to be pursued. Data was audio recorded and transcribed verbatim in English before being analyzed by open and selective coding to identify concepts and sub-concepts of the conceptual framework. Results We recruited 37 participants (21 female; 16 male; mean age 10.4years). Qualitative analysis produced nine initial domains. Subsequent rounds of analysis refined this into a conceptual framework with seven domains: existence/functionality, self-care, strength/energy, peace of mind, absence of illness, God-given, and acceptance of illness. Four of these (existence/functionality, self-care, peace of mind and mobility) showed similarity with domains from the EQ-5D-Y (usual activities, self-care, anxiety/depression and mobility respectively). There was no equivalent in the Malawi conceptual framework to the EQ-5D-Y domain of pain. Three domains (God-given, strength/energy, acceptance of illness) were unique to the Malawi context. Conclusion A new conceptual framework of health developed among children and adolescents in Malawi has been developed including seven domains. There is some overlap with domains found in the EQ-5D-Y, though not all EQ-5D-Y domains are represented in the Malawi conceptual framework and three domains are unique to the Malawi context. The EQ-5D-Y is a valid utility instrument for use in economic evaluation but may lack content validity in LICs such as Malawi.

Title: Exposure and psychological responses to climate change and their association with EQ-5D: a secondary data analysis from the POPCORN study
Abstract: Background and aims: Climate change is increasingly recognized as a significant public health concern, affecting both physical and mental health worldwide. While extreme weather events such as floods, wildfires, and heatwaves are known to cause psychological distress, including anxiety, guilt, and worry, the link between these psychological responses and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) remains underexplored. This study will investigate the relationship between climate change exposure and psychological responses to climate change, and their impact on health outcomes measured by the EQ-5D-5L, GAD-7, and PHQ-9, using data from the POPulation health impact of the CORoNavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (POPCORN) study. Additionally, the study will evaluate the known-group validity of the EQ-5D-5L in differentiating between subgroups with varying levels of exposure and psychological responses to climate change. Methods: A cross-sectional secondary data analysis will be conducted using the fourth wave of the POPCORN study, which surveyed 3,572 respondents from the United States, the United Kingdom, Italy, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Greece between May and July 2023. Climate change exposure was assessed through five binary questions capturing personal and vicarious experiences, and psychological responses were measured using six items on a 5-point Likert scale. Health outcomes were assessed using the EQ-5D-5L, GAD-7, and PHQ-9 instruments. Descriptive analysis for the EQ-5D-5L, GAD-7, and PHQ-9 outcomes will be conducted for subgroups with different levels of exposure and different levels of psychological responses. Logistic and linear regression models will be employed to examine the relationships between climate change exposure, and psychological responses, and their impact on the health outcomes, adjusting for socio-demographic factors. Interaction terms will be tested. Known-group validity will be assessed using Cohen's d for effect size and the Kruskal-Wallis test to compare scores across subgroups. Results: The analysis is expected to explore how exposure to climate change impacts psychological responses and how these responses are associated with EQ-5D-5L, GAD-7, and PHQ-9. By analyzing data from six countries, this study will contribute to the understanding of how well the EQ-5D-5L can capture the psychological responses triggered by climate change across diverse populations and assess its validity in distinguishing between different subgroups. Conclusion: This study will help emphasize the relevance of EQ-5D-5L in measuring the health effects of climate change. The findings will inform future research on improving EQ-5D regarding the sensitivity for assessing the public health implications of climate change, while also providing evidence on the known-group validity of EQ-5D-5L, particularly in capturing the mental health effects triggered by climate change.

Title: Translating the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S for Germany
Abstract: Introduction The EQ-HWB is a newly developed generic tool designed to assess the effects of health, social care, and caregiving on quality of life. Currently classified as 'experimental,' additional research is urgently required to evaluate its performance within these target populations and across diverse countries and cultural settings. Therefore, an update German translation is needed to support the large-scale EQ DAPHNIE project, which includes Germany, as well as to facilitate additional testing in a key market for EuroQol questionnaires. Methods The translation of the original and modified EQ-HWB for Germany followed the protocol for researcher-led translations established by the Version Management Committee. First, the translation work was conducted based on two independent forward translations from the UK English source version into German. Afterwards, two independent backward translations were conducted from German back to English to identify potential translatability issues. Both after the forward and backward translation, a reconciliation meeting was conducted to harmonise the resulting translations and to discussion any issues that emerged. Consequently, the resulting consensus version was carried forward to a cognitive debriefing exercise, for which respondents were divided into two groups. The groups were structured to ease the cognitive burden during the cognitive debriefing exercise, as both the current (original) and modified self-complete versions were evaluated. In the first group, participants were initially debriefed on the current (original) self-complete version before being asked their preference regarding the modifications. Conversely, the second group reviewed the modified version first and was then asked whether they preferred any elements of the official wording. The cognitive debriefing interviews consisted of seven parts: introduction, demographic background questions, ranking exercise, self-completing the EQ-HWB, debrief of the general impression of the EQ-HWB, detailed cognitive debrief regarding the understanding of each item and, lastly, eliciting the respondents views on the item modifications or their original counter-parts depending on the debrief group. Results The translation work was conducted by four independent translators and a fifth researcher for proofreading the finalised versions. The forward translations were done by two researchers who are German native speakers and fluent in English, whereas the backward translators were English native speakers (one UK English and one US English speaker) and fluent in German. A total of 16 respondents were cognitively debriefed about the German EQ-HWB versions. Respondents were aged between 21 and 83 years with a mean age of 48.5 years including 9 female and 7 male participants. Moreover, 10 respondents had a health condition including ADHD, hypertension, skin cancer, various allergies, polymyalgia rheumatica, autoimmune disease, diabetes, a blood clotting disorder and asthma. Respondents seemed generally confident in ranking the response scales. The few observed problems related to some difficulty differentiating levels 2 and 3 in the difficulty and frequency response scales. The proposed response scale modifications were mostly preferred, since they allowed a clearer response scaling. In general, the German translations worked as intended and there was no item, instruction or response scale identified that was consistently misinterpreted. From the translation phase, there were concerns that translations for the items ‘feel anxious’ and ‘feel unsafe’ may be overlapping, but for both items respondents had a clear understanding of their intended meanings. It became evident from the debriefing that the item ‘feel unsafe’ almost exclusively tapped into physical insecurity or fear of physical harm. Moreover, respondents from the first group were highly aware of the switch from negative to positive items and voiced their concerns over the potential problems this may cause. Consequently, there was much greater endorsement to switch to the modified items. On the other hand, this was not as evident in group 2. Conclusion The EQ-HWB was successfully translated for Germany following the researcher-led translation protocol established by the VMC. Following this translation project four self-complete versions of the EQ-HWB are available in German. This includes the EQ-HWB long form and EQ-HWB-S both in the original and modified version. Translated constructs were easily understood and well perceived by respondents participating in the rigorous cognitive debriefing process. In this regard, the translation protocol for researcher-led translations worked as anticipated providing guidance in conducting the translation and cognitive debriefing for new translations. Overall, the researcher-led translation protocol is a cost-efficient process for generating new language versions in a timely manner.

Title: Hybrid model in R
Abstract: This was not a study in the normal sense, but the process has been helpful in identifying several issuesrelated to hybrid modelling that call for further investigation. The R hyreg command will make hybrid regression available to a larger audience, and unlike STATA, is completely free. The xreg function will hopefully simplify future modelling efforts both related to EQ-5D, and in general.

Title: AI Preferences for Health? Characterizing LLM Responses to DCE-Based Valuation Tasks and Evaluating Strategies for Detecting Automated Survey Respondents
Abstract: [A revised proposal and response to reviewers documents has been uploaded. No changes to the abstract]Online health preference surveys using Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs) are increasingly threatened by automated response systems. While traditional bots and browser add-ins have long posed a data quality risk, large language models (LLMs) now represent a qualitatively new category of threat: automated responders capable of generating contextually plausible, human-like responses to complex health scenarios in ways that standard detection systems such as reCAPTCHA are unlikely to identify. Unlike classical automated responders, which produce random noise or simple patterns, LLM-based systems process the semantic content of survey items and produce responses whose statistical properties may closely resemble those of genuine respondents. Two complementary categories of LLM-based tooling amplify this threat: AI coding assistants (e.g. Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) that enable rapid development of custom survey bots, and fully autonomous LLM-powered agent systems (e.g. OpenClaw, ClawdBot) that can complete surveys directly without custom development.This project aims to (1) characterise how currently available LLMs respond to DCE-based health valuation tasks and associated DAPHNIE background questions, and (2) evaluate candidate methods for detecting LLM-based automated respondents in online health preference surveys. This is not an investigation of AI preferences per se, but a methodological study to protect the integrity of online preference research.Methods include: development of one or more bespoke surveys on the EQ-VT platform with DCE valuation and DAPHNIE elements; deployment of multiple automated response systems (autonomous LLM agents, a bespoke LimeSurvey API-based responder, and non-LLM browser bots as a baseline); embedding of candidate detection mechanisms; and analysis of response patterns by system and model. Outputs are (a) a scientific paper characterising LLM response patterns across models and (b) a confidential report for the EuroQol Group on the effectiveness of specific detection strategies and recommended next steps. Together, these outputs will equip EuroQol with evidence to evaluate the growing threat from LLM-based automated responders and to guide investment in bespoke, durable countermeasures.

Title: Investigating validity and responsiveness to change of the EQ-HWB-S in a sample of people living with dementia with mild cognitive decline; the I-CHARD study
Abstract: The EQ-HWB-S has been included in an innovative new study from University of Sydney, which aims to optimise the functional and social independence and safety of older people living with dementia in aged care homes, titled: Implementation Research of Interdisciplinary Care Home-bAsed Reablement Program (I-CHARP). This NHMRC funded program aims to implement an intervention previously developed for home-based care (Interdisciplinary Home-bAsed Reablement Program (I-HARP)). The I-HARP intervention was a community-based rehabilitation program for people with mild-to-moderate cognitive decline, living at home. The study found a significant impact for people living with mild dementia specifically for better functional independence in the intervention group(1). I-CHARP builds on I-HARP to transfer the program logic from home-based care to residential aged care settings. The intervention includes 8-12 full individual sessions and eight brief follow-ups per resident, tailored to their needs, and delivered by a team of occupational therapists, registered nurses, and allied health staff. The I-CHARP program is a bio-behavioural-environmental intervention that includes a comprehensive assessment of the person and the environment, minor environmental modifications and assistive devices/technologies/communication aids, training in use of compensatory strategies, medication review and adherence support, strength and balance training and exercise, activity engagement, problem solving for depression intervention, pain management, cognitive rehabilitation, communication rehabilitation/communication partner training, nutrition management, carer support (family and care staff), alongside consultation/referrals as necessary for physiotherapist, psychologist, dietitian, speech pathologist, GP, and other specialist appointments. Data collection is currently underway. The study will contain 188 participants at baseline (already collected), an estimated 150 participants at 4-6 months follow-up (completed by April 2025), and 120 participants at 12-months follow-up (completed by the end of 2025). The longitudinal nature of this study and the relevant population of people living with dementia with mild cognitive decline, makes this study invaluable for determining the validity of the EQ-HWB-S in this hard-to-reach population. There are three quality-of-life instruments included (Quality of Life in Alzheimer’s Disease (QoL-AD) for overall quality of life (mapped to the AD-5D(2)), the EQ-5D-5L, and the EQ Health and Wellbeing instrument for health and wellbeing related quality of life (EQ-HWB-S), making this study ideal for measuring convergent validity. A wide range of dementia specific instruments have been included making this study ideal for measuring known-groups validity. The longitudinal nature of the study makes this ideal for measuring the responsiveness of the EQ-HWB-S to change. The EQ-HWB-S was included in this study as an instrument that is potentially responsive to change in QoL over time and between groups in this population. A pilot value-set from the UK is now available (3) for the EQ-HWB-S, valued on the zero to one scale necessary to calculate Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs). As data collection for this study is not yet completed, we will also be able to include different versions of the EQ-HWB-S within the study design, enabling testing of potential changes to the EQ-HWB-S that are currently being considered. We will work with the EQ-HWB-S working group regarding the versions of the EQ-HWB-S to be included in the final data collection rounds. This data presents an opportunity to investigate the validity and, most importantly, the responsiveness to change, of the EQ-HWB-S in a population of people living with dementia with low cognitive decline. Baseline and follow-up data will be available, and it is anticipated that the intervention will improve participants’ quality-of-life over time. Aims The aim of the research for which funds are requested in this grant application is to measure the validity and responsiveness to change of the EQ-HWB-S in data from a trial to evaluate the effects of specific program for people living with dementia with mild cognitive decline. Specifically, we aim to: 1. Validate the scale in this population using: a. Feasibility and response distribution, b. Convergent validity analysis against a range of relevant self-complete scales c. Known groups validity analysis across a range of known groups 2. Determine if the instrument is responsive to change over time (between baseline and post intervention, 4-6 months and 12 months) 3. Investigate differences between versions of the EQ-HWB-S following the EQ-HWB Working Group guidelines. Method Data will be collected as part of the NHMRC funded I-CHARP study. Data collection for this innovative study is staggered over three cycles, with each cycle taking 12 months, and including data at baseline, follow up at 4-6 months, and final data collection at 12 months. We expect approximately a 20% attrition at each collection of the follow up data.. 65% of the data will use the modified version of the EQ-HWB-S, and 35% will use the original version. Data collection will be completed at the end of 2025 for all cycles; however, to provide timely results to EuroQol we anticipate writing an interim report on the data that has completed collection by April 2025. We also note that any reference to outcomes of the intervention cannot be published until after the I-CHARP study main results have been published. This will not stop us from writing the report for EuroQol but will mean that we hold off publishing the responsiveness data if we include the intervention in this analysis. Baseline survey will include: Socio-demographic data: (Age, Sex, Ethnicity, Education), Dementia diagnosis information including: Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (ACE-III)(49) for cognitive status; Clinical information (health and cognitive conditions, medications, GP and specialist consults; Global Deterioration Rating Scale for Assessment of Primary Degenerative Dementia (GDRS) for dementia severity; Disability Assessment for Dementia (DAD) to assess daily function and self-care ability; Primary outcome, Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB)(50) for objective physical function. There will be three quality-of-life instruments included, which can be use for convergent validity analysis: Quality of Life in Alzheimer’s Disease (QoL-AD) for overall quality of life, mapped to the AQ-5D(2), EQ-5D-5L, EQ Health and Wellbeing instrument (EQ-HWB-S). Statistical Analysis Using the baseline data, the EQ-HWB-S items will be assessed in terms of feasibility (missing data), response distribution (across items), convergent validity (using Spearman’s correlations comparing the EQ-HWB-S to the AQ-5D and the EQ-5D) and known groups validity (across pre-hypothesised groups using t-tests and one-way ANOVAs). Using the longitudinal data, we will analyse responsiveness to change as per our previous study(4) where changes in dementia status will be compared to changes in health and wellbeing (EQ-HWB-S). We will conduct an evaluation of the potential differences between the two versions of the EQ-HWB-S using the Working Group guidelines: “Guidance for Testing EQ-HWB Modifications”.

Title: EQ-5D and population disability profiles in Estonia: patterns of inequality and its implications for disability-free life expectancy
Abstract: The project uses EuroQol’s EQ-5D instrument to study the temporal trends and sociodemographic inequalities in self-reported disability patterns that underlie disability-free life expectancy (DFLE). With a focus on the Estonian adult population, where total life expectancy (TLE) has increased substantially since the mid-1990s, the project aims to: a) analyse socio-demographic inequalities and temporal changes of EQ-5D and disability indicator GALI during 2002–2024, b) decompose the activity limitations into specific health profiles and assess their impact to inequalities in DFLE by combining self-reported and registry data, c) develop HRQoL population norms based on EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L for Estonia. The project will extend the currently available data on population-level HRQoL by conducting a repeated, EQ-5D focused study on 2020 survey respondents complemented by individual-level data linkage from health registries. Resulting multilayered longitudinal data opens a unique opportunity for detailed study of individual trajectories and temporal changes in both activity limitations and EQ-5D to decompose activity limitations into specific health profiles. The project will also analyse the role of reporting heterogeneity and have overarching focus on health inequalities. Additionally, the project would result in development of population norms for Estonia, filling the current gap on the lack of EQ-5D specific population norms in the Baltic region. The main deliverables of the project are five academic papers submitted to peer-reviewed journals during the project period of 27 months. The project aims, closely aligned with the priority areas of EuroQol’s Population and health systems working group, are expected to provide significant academic value to EuroQol Consortium and will provide data-driven support for national public health policy in improving population health and addressing health inequalities in Estonia.

Title: HTA and quality of life measurement in patients
Assessing Validity, Test-retest Reliability and Responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L with Bolt-ons in Patients with Atopic Dermatitis in China: A Mixed-methods study
Abstract: Background Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a highly prevalent chronic skin disease that significantly impacts patients' health-related quality of life. Two bolt-ons (skin irritation and self-confidence) have improved the content validity and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L in psoriasis. While their content validity has been shown in AD patients, other psychometric properties remain unclear. Other items like sleep and social difficulties may also be important but have not been well-explored. The majority of available evidence and ongoing studies are from European or African populations, which may not be applicable to Asian populations. Cultural differences may impact reporting problems in the self-confidence bolt-on. Aims This study aims to assess the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L with bolt-ons in Chinese AD patients. Methods A mixed-methods approach incorporating qualitative and quantitative methods will be employed in this study. The content validity (relevance, comprehensibility and comprehensiveness) of the bolt-ons—skin irritation, self-confidence, sleep, and social/relationship difficulties—will be evaluated through cognitive debriefing, with interview data analysed thematically. Results will inform the finalization of the bolt-ons for psychometric testing. The psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L+bolt-ons will be tested among 300 Chinese AD patients. Factor analysis will be performed to explore latent factors underlying the EQ-5D-5L+bolt-ons. Convergent validity will be assessed against the EQ-5D-5L, Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), and Atopic Dermatitis Control Tool (ADCT), while divergent validity will be compared to core EQ-5D-5L dimensions. The Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) will be used to compare the known-group validity of the EQ-5D-5L vs EQ-5D-5L+bolt-ons. Responsiveness will be assessed by correlating score changes from baseline to 12-week follow-up with EASI. Test-retest reliability will be assessed by evaluating the consistency of scores between baseline and the 3-day retest. Impacts This study will generate new evidence on psychometric performance of bolt-ons for skin conditions, expanding their use to Asian populations.

Title: Cross-cultural adaptation of the EQ-TIPS into Chichewa (Malawi): preliminary findings
Abstract: Objectives: The EuroQol Toddlers and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) was developed as a generic health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instrument for children aged 0 - 3 years. While the EQ-TIPS V3 has been used in various high-income settings across different disease with promising results, research in resource-poor settings has been limited. The aim of this work was to crossculturally adapt and validate the EQ-TIPS into Chichewa for Malawi. Methods: EQ-TIPS was forward translated into Chichewa and back translated into English by two sets of translators. The translated version was reviewed by a member of the EuroQol version management committee and after several iterations, an agreement was reached for a consensus version. The version was piloted through cognitive debriefing with five caregivers of infants and children aged 0-3 years two of which tow were at home and three in hospital. Changes were made accordingly based on their feedback to inform the next version. Results: The translation process was relatively straightforward although two items: “managing emotions” and ”interacting with others” were found to be difficult concepts to translate accurately. Further, we found that adding a pronoun such as he/she to response levels was necessary in comparison with the source language standalone options. Cognitive debriefing (CD) indicated that combining both “kumasuka (freeness)” and “kulankhulana (speaking)” would be ideal to accurately translate “interacting with others” which was also noted during translation. Additionally, CD identified issues with translation of ”sleep”, “pain”, and “managing emotions” items. For sleep, some respondents suggested that the examples included to explain the concept referred to different phases of sleep thereby making it difficult to rate it. Kuphwanya m’thupi (pain) was suggested to be replaced with ‘kupweteka’ or ‘kuwawa’ which also refers to pain but thought to be more age-appropriate translation for infants and toddlers. The EQ-5D-Y versions, however, uses “Kuphwanya m’thupi” for “pain” because they carry the thought of someone ably expressing pain for themselves as opposed to a proxy version. Lastly, it was suggested that “dongosolo la malingaliro” (managing emotions) may benefit from expansion of examples. For example, adding ‘ngati mwana amatha kuonetsa mkwiyo (unhappy), chisoni (sadness), chisangalalo (happiness)’ would enrich the meaning. Conclusion: These are only preliminary results of the EQ-TIPS Chichewa version for Malawi. The next steps will be to refine the items and come up with a final approved version. As this is the first study, to the knowledge of the team, attempting to establish a conceptual and linguistic equivalence of the EQ-TIPS into an African spoken language outside South Africa, this work will not only be useful to EuroQol’s Strategic Plan but also other settings. The study found that observable items were more easier to translate and understand as opposed to emotional items. The underlying cause for this could be due to a limited vocabularly of the Chichewa language which may be a common thread for the Bantu languages spoken in most of the sub-Saharan 2 of 3 Africa. As such, some emotional concepts such as pain, may be adapted with more examples for younger children in these settings.

Title: Reducing biases in adaptive Time Trade-Off using non-transparent methods
Abstract: This paper offers a new explanation of the disparity between utilities elicited using standard (or Classic) and Time Trade-Off (TTO) and utilities elicited using Chaining. we refer to “Classic” as the utility of a health state obtained from a Time Trade-off question where the end points are Full Health and Death. We refer to “Chained” as the utilities that are obtained from a TTO question where at least one of the end points is neither Full Health or Death. Previous literature has observed that the two sets of utilities are different, and they have been explained by anchoring effects. We present and alternative explanation based on the different Evaluation Mode that Classic and Chained TTO use, namely, Separate Evaluation Mode in the case of TTO and Join Evaluation Mode in the case of Chained TTO. In this paper, we present the result of a study conducted among the Spanish general population (n=346) to separate the role of anchoring from the role in the Evaluation Mode as potential explanations of the disparity between Classic and Chained utilities. All subjects had to estimate the utility of three health states (say A, B and C) using the standard TTO. They also had to answer three direct TTO questions (A vs B, A vs C and B vs C) to estimate Chained utilities. The Chained procedure always started with a comparison between two health states with the same duration (10 years). Our study also observed differences between Classic and Chained utilities. The disparity was explained by the large amount of preference reversals observed. People preferred one health state in standard TTO and another one in the choice between (A, 10 years) vs (B, 10 years). The discrepancy between Classic and Chained utilities vanished for those subjects who did not do preference reversals. Those results suggest that the difference between Classic and Chained utilities is mainly produced by the different Evaluation Mode and not so much because of anchoring effects. We present the implications of our results for preference elicitation methods for health states.

Title: Exploring Targeted Support for the International Academy of Health Preference Research (IAHPR) 2025
Abstract: This education and outreach project explored targeted support mechanisms for the International Academy of Health Preference Research (IAHPR) 2025 meeting, with the aim of increasing visibility and engagement of EuroQol within the health preference research community. EuroQol’s support was formally acknowledged throughout the conference, including sponsor recognition in the programme and presentation materials, verbal acknowledgements by session chairs during relevant sessions, and a post-conference LinkedIn communication. Registration data confirmed uptake of the EuroQol free registration code by two participants, with an estimated additional six to seven EuroQol members attending the meeting, although precise numbers were difficult to ascertain due to multiple institutional affiliations. Overall, the grant supported enhanced awareness of EuroQol among attendees and strengthened links between EuroQol and the IAHPR community.

Title: Directly eliciting personal utility functions: a feasibility study of an innovative approach to valuing HRQoL
Abstract: Introduction: In 2015, we introduced the concept of Personal Utility Functions (PUFs) at the Scientific Plenary meeting (Devlin et al 2015), and shared some promising early results from pre-piloting.In contrast to existing valuation methods –all of whichrely on presenting health states and inferring from respondents’responses what their preferences are with respect to the descriptive system, the PUF approach asks respondentsto consider the dimensions and levels of the EQ-5D, and takes them through a series of tasks to help them attach weights to reflect the importance of these relative to each other.We also ask respondentsto identify their anchor for dead = 0.An important emphasis of the approach is on helping respondentsreflect and deliberate on their answers as they construct their PUF. Subsequent to the Plenary, we further improved our methods for eliciting PUFs, and conducted pilot interviews with n=76 members of the general public in England and a convenience sample of n=30health outcomes professionals working for Pharmerit (various locations). The aimsof this paper areto (a) report the results from the pilot and (b) demonstrate the way in which the PUFs of individuals can be modelled to obtain a value set. Methods:The method allows for the estimation of each respondent’s own 20 parameter utility function. Descriptive statistics for each element of the PUF tasks are reported as well as distributions of the 20 parameters. Descriptive statistics from the various validation tasks built into the interview are reported and correlated with PUF data on a within-respondent basis to establishinternal face validity.Preference types identified in the dimension and level weighting tasks, and in the placement of dead, are identified and used to inform modelling. An average utility function will be calculated. Additionally cluster analysis will be applied to find whether there are typical groups of respondents.Results:Overall, PD and MO are the highest ranked dimensions (as is the case in many of the value sets generated using other methods) and UA is the lowest ranked dimension.There was a high level of consistency in respondents’responses to the various dimension-weighting tasks. The ratings for intermediate improvements in each dimension (e.g. from MO3 to MO2) shows heterogeneity, both within (i.e. most respondents’ratings differed between dimensions) and between respondents. The results of the validation exercises demonstrate that the PUF algorithm works as intended. The task to identify the individual’s location of dead within the descriptive system worked well.23.7% of respondentsindicated that no EQ-5D health states are worse than dead.The data allow the reporting of individual respondents’ PUFs, and a social value set to be constructed as an average of the PUFs.Conclusion: APUF approachis feasible, and haspotentialto (a) yield meaningful, well informed preference datafrom respondentsand (b) provide individual preference data that can be aggregatedto yield a value set for the EQ-5D. The deliberative approach to health state valuation which it entails also has the potential to complement and improve existing valuationmethods. Further improvementof some elements of the tasks are required, e.g., regarding interactions, and a more systematic approach to the capture and use of qualitative data would be beneficial.

Title: Modelling dependence in EQ-VT DCE data: impact on value sets
Abstract: Background.In health economics, there has been interest in using discrete-choice experiments (DCEs) to derive pre-ferences for health states in lieu of previously established approaches like time tradeoff (TTO). We examined whetherpreferences elicited through DCEs are associated and agree with preferences elicited through TTO tasks.Methods.We used data from 1073 respondents to the Canadian EQ-5D-5L valuation study. Multivariate mixed-effects modelsspecified a common likelihood for the TTO and discrete-choice data, with separate but correlated random effects forthe TTO and DCE data, for each of the 5 EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Multivariate latent class models allowed separatebut associated latent classes for the DCE and TTO data.Results.Correlation between the random effects for the 2tasks ranged from20.12 to 0.75, with only pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression having at least a 50% posteriorprobability of strong (.0.6) correlation. Latent classes for the TTO and DCE data both featured 1 latent class cap-turing participants attaching large disutilities to pain/discomfort, another capturing participants attaching large disu-tility to anxiety/depression, and the third class capturing the remainder. Agreement in class membership was poor(kcoefficient: 0.081; 95% credible interval, 0.033–0.13). Fewer respondents expressed strong disutilities for problemswith anxiety/depression or pain/discomfort in the TTO than the DCE data (17% v. 55%, respectively).Conclusions.Stated preferences using TTO and DCEs show association across dimensions but poor agreement at the level of indi-vidual health states within respondents. Joint models that assume agreement between DCE and TTO have been usedto develop national value sets for the EQ-5D-5L. This work indicates that when combining data from both tech-niques, methods requiring association but not agreement are needed.

Title: Understanding the effects of preference-weights on the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB short form through comparing sum- and preference-based scores.
Abstract: The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a new generic measure that has been developed internationally for evaluating interventions in health, public health, and social care, including the impact on patients, social care users, and carers. A range of recent validation studies have evaluated the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB-S, suggesting that it is reliable and valid. When the EQ-HWB-S instrument is finalised we expect a range of preference weights (value-sets) will be produced across countries to generate utility values for calculating QALYs (quality adjusted life years) for use in Health Technology Assessment. In preparation for this, there have been several studies conducted over the past few years that have tested different methods for generating preference weights. This work has been undertaken due to the differences in valuing the EQ-HWB-S measure with its wide range of domains that move beyond health, and the large number of items (9 items). Preference weight generation methodologies that have been tested to date, and which have produced indicative value sets for the EQ-HWB-S include: 1) composite time trade-off (cTTO) and a discrete choice experiment (DCE), known as the UK pilot preference weights 2) PAPRIKA, which stands for “Potentially All Pairwise RanKings of all Possible Alternatives” and 3) DCE with a duration attribute and DCE-triplet design with “dead” (a EuroQol funded PhD project). The UK pilot preference weights have been used extensively in recent validation studies; however, the effect of the preference weights on psychometric properties is not yet well understood. In much of the data we have on caregivers, we see high levels of exhaustion, loneliness, anxiety and lack of control. However, the preference weights for exhaustion, loneliness, cognition, anxiety and lack of control (psycho-social items) are smaller compared to pain, mobility and daily activities (the physical items). By this, we mean that utility decrements are smaller for the items where more severity is observed for caregivers, suggesting that impairment for these items will have a relatively smaller impact on utilities and hence QALYs. Aims In our proposed study, we are interested in whether the differences in EQ-HWB-S scores calculated when preference weights are applied affect relevant psychometric outcomes. We aim to investigate whether study outcomes and psychometric outcomes (including known-group validity and change over time) are affected by how the EQ-HWB-S is scored. Abstract Method Procedure We will use five high quality datasets from a range of countries (including Australia, Canada, Europe, United Kingdom (UK), United States (US)), from cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. Our studies include a range of relevant populations, such as caregivers of children where families have experienced adversity, parents of children with health conditions, participants with mental health conditions, and general population samples. We will assess three indicative preference-weights: UK pilot, PAPRIKA, and DCE-duration/DCE-triplet. Abstract Statistical Analysis We will compare sum-scores and preference-weighted scores through: 1) assessing mean differences, 2) comparing rate of agreement between index- and sum-scores using Bland-Altman plot and Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), 3) comparing Cohen’s d scores from known-group validity analysis, and 4) assessing differences in change over time data.

Title: Agreement between proxy EQ‐5D‐Y and self‐reported EQ‐5D‐Y in a paediatric patient group
Abstract: Study Design.Prospective cohort study.Objective.To compare feasibility of self-reported and proxy-reported youth version of EuroQoL Five-Dimension Three-LevelQuestionnaire (EQ-5D-3L-Y), to estimate the agreement of healthoutcome between patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis(AIS) and their proxies, and to examine factors that may affectpatient-proxy agreement.Summary of Background Data.The EQ-5D-3L-Y question-naire has both self-reported and proxy-reported versions. Despiteprevious studies have indicated that proxies tended to respondwith higher or lower levels of severity in specific dimensionsthan patients report, the level of agreement between childrenwith AIS and their proxies remained unknown.Methods.A consecutive sample of patients with AIS and theircaregivers were recruited. Feasibility was tested according to theproportion of missing responses. Agreements between self-reportand proxy EQ-5D-3L-Y were evaluated using percentage agree-ment, Gwet agreement coefficients and the intraclass correlationcoefficients. Linear regressions and logistic regressions were con-ducted to assess the factors associated with the agreement in healthoutcome between self-reported and proxy-reported EQ-5D-3L-Y.Results.A total of 130 patient-proxy pairs were involved in thestudy. Agreement of EQ-5D-3L-Y responses between the self-report and proxy version was good for ‘‘Feeling worried/sad/unhappy’’ dimension, and very good for other dimensions. Pooragreement in visual analog scale score was observed betweenpatient and proxy versions. Proxy’s education level, patient’scurvature type, and treatment modality were the significantdeterminants of the agreement in ‘‘Mobility,’’ ‘‘usual activities,’’and ‘‘pain/discomfort’’ dimension, respectively.Conclusion.Proxy-reported EQ-5D-3L-Y demonstrates goodfeasibility and satisfactoryagreement with patient version.Proxy’s education appears to have positive influence in agree-ment between patient-proxy dyads.Key words:adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, agreement, EQ-5D-3L-Y, feasibility, proxy.Level of Evidence:2Spine 2020;45:E799–E807
