Title: Measuring Quality of Life in the general population in Romania: an EQ5D-5L value set and population norms for Romania (QoLRO
Abstract: Clear, transparent and consistent criteria for decision-makingand healthcare resource allocation have recently become the focus of many health system strategic plans across the globe. In the last few years, in Romania, several factors have converged to create a more favourable environment for the development of health technology assessment (HTA). However, some challenges still remain. This research aims to simultaneously elicit value setsand develop population norms for both EQ-5D-3L and 5L in the same sample of Romanian respondents. Amulti-stage stratified sampling procedure will be used to recruit 2,016people representative of the Romanian general population in terms of historical region, degree of urbanisation, age and sex. Data will be collected through face-to-face interviews conducted in respondents’ homes. Preferences for EQ5D3L and 5L health states will be elicited from the same respondents using composite time trade-off(cTTO)techniques. Additionally,discrete choice experiments (DCE) will be used to elicit preferences for the 5L version. Linear regression models will be used to estimate the 3L value set based on the cTTO data. A hybrid model using the data from both the cTTO and DCE will be used to estimate the 5L value set. This project will enable local expertise development, thus addressing one of the challenges highlighted as potentially hindering theeffective implementation of HTA in Romania. Additionally, it will benefit the EuroQoL Foundation by creating a new demand for EQ-5D as the instrument will be the only utility measure in Romania for which a local value setand population normswill be available.

Title: Estimation of the EQ-5D-5L value set for Portugal
Abstract: Aims:Any decision-making, mainly in a context of limited resources, has to have arationaleand be transparent. The EQ-5D is a generic preference-based quality of life measure considereduseful to support clinical and policy decisions, by providing utility values that can be easily converted into QALYsto be integrated in cost-utility economic evaluations.However, its first 3L version showssignificant ceiling effect. Therefore, a 5L version was designed with five levels ofproblems intensity for each dimension, allowing utility values for all 3,125 health statesmeasured.The purpose of this study was to estimate the value system for Portuguese population in what concernsthe different health states described by the EQ-5D-5L description system.Methods: Health states values were elicited according to the EuroQoL Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) protocol using composite time trade-off (cTTO) and a discrete choice experiment (DCE). Data were collected between October’2015 and July’2016 using computer-assisted personal interviews in arepresentative sample of the Portuguese population aged above 18 years andstratified by age and gender.cTTO data weremodelledby fixed and random effects models, such as OLS, variable effects GLS, censored GLS, censored Tobit, interval GLS censored at 1, and interval GLS censored at 1 and 0. Model performance was assessed according to specific criteria: internal consistency, statistical significance of the estimated coefficients, and goodness of fit evaluation.The ability for the model to tackle censored data was also evaluated. DCE data were not modelled.Results: A sample of 1,451 respondents revealed aVAS mean score of78.9 in a 0-100 scale from the worst to the besthealth. Themodels showed no inconsistenciesand the models with best performance was the interval GLS censored at 1.Conclusions: This research provided the Portuguese value set for the EQ-5D-5L based on cTTO and these findings are to be usedin economic evaluationsto be conducted in Portugal.

Title: Qualitative study of the modified EQ-HWB in cancer patients.
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a broad, generic instrument designed for use across health, social care, and public health contexts. The developer team proposed wording, ordering, response level and layout modifications to improve conceptual clarity and cultural fit; however, evidence regarding the modified items in clinical populations, especially in LMICs remains limited.Objective: To evaluate the relevance and comprehensibility of modified EQ-HWB-9/EQ-HWB items compared with the experimental (original) versions among Indonesian cancer patients and their caregivers.Methods: Semi-structured, one-to-one qualitative interviews were conducted with 60 participants (30 patient-caregiver dyads) recruited from oncology outpatient services. All patients were undergoing active treatment (radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy) and temporarily resided in patient lodging houses near the hospital. Diagnoses included breast, thyroid, colorectal, cervical, ovarian, bone, and nasopharyngeal cancers, and hematologic malignancies. The mean age of patients was 40.07 years (SD = 15.50; 72.41% female), and of caregivers 39.37 years (SD = 12.90; 53.33% female). All interviews followed the EQ-HWB Working Group’s standardized qualitative testing protocol. Participants completed the modified EQ-HWB (which includes the EQ-HWB-9 items) and subsequently compared each modified item with its original version using structured probes. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed thematically by two independent coders using the WG coding framework for understanding, relevance, and preference.Key results: Comprehensibility was high across EQ-HWB-9 items for both groups, though interpretation issues arose for a small number of participants depending on the item. Relevance was consistently strong, with most participants linking items to treatment effects, functional limitations, emotional strain, and caregiving demands. Clear preference patterns emerged: (1) Activities-first ordering was favoured by most respondents who perceived it as a more natural “general-to-specific” flow; (2) the shorter, non-repeating stem was preferred by nearly all participants for reducing redundancy; (3) the modified Mobility wording (“or”) and the inclusion of bracketed examples improved clarity for both patients and caregivers; and (4) the modified frequency label (“a little of the time”) was consistently understood more clearly than “only occasionally”. Positive-framed long-form EQ-HWB items were also administered and generally understood. Implications: The study provides item-level qualitative evidence supporting several proposed refinements to the modified EQ-HWB-9/EQ-HWB and demonstrates the feasibility and acceptability of the modified items in an oncology population in an LMIC setting. Results from this study contributed to the pool of evidence for the finalisation of the EQ-HWB-9 and the dossier development.

Title: Evaluating consistency between DCE and TTO valuations using multivariate mixed models and multivariate latent class analysis
Abstract: Background: In health economics there has been interest in using discrete choice experiments (DCEs) to derive preferences for health states in lieu of previously established approaches like time trade-off (TTO). We examined whether preferences elicited through DCEs correlate and agree with preferences elicited through TTO tasks. Methods: We used data from 1073 respondents to the Canadian EQ-5D-5L valuation study. Multivariate mixed effects models specified a common likelihood for the TTO and discrete choice data, with s eparate but correlated random effects for the TTO and DCE data, for each of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions. Multivariate latent class models allowed separate but correlated latent classes for the DCE and TTO data. Results: Correlation between the random effects for the two tasks ranged from 0.17 for usual activities to 0.57 for anxiety and depression, reaching statistical significance for all dimensions except usual activities. Latent classes for the TTO and DCE data both featured one latent class capturing participants attaching large disutilities to pain/discomfort, another capturing participants attaching large disutility to anxiety/depression, and the third class capturing the remainder. Agreement in class membership was poor (kappa coefficient: 0.081; 95% Credible Interval 0.033 to 0.13). Fewer respondents expressed strong disutilities for problems with anxiety/depression or pain/discomfort in the TTO than the DCE data (17% vs. 55%, respectively).Conclusions: Stated preferences using TTO and DCEs show reasonably strong association across dimensions, but poor agreement at the level of individual health states within respondents. J oint models that assume agreement between DCE and TTO have been used to develop national value sets for the EQ-5D-5L. This work indicates that when combining data from both techniques, methods requiring association but not agreement are needed.

Title: Translation, Cultural Adaptation, and Validation of EQ-TIPS for Bangladeshi Infant and Toddler Populations
Abstract: This project aims to co-develop and validate the Bangla version of the EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations instrument (EQ-TIPS) for the first time in Bangladesh. In collaboration with the EuroQol Youth Working Group, the proposed study will adapt the EQ-TIPS-5L version to ensure cultural relevance and assess its psychometric performance in both healthy and ill children aged 2-4 years. In addition, caregivers' HRQoL will be measured using the EQ-5D-Y-5L and explore the relevance of potential sleep bolt-ons for improved content validity. The study will be prospective and longitudinal in design, with data collection conducted in collaboration with local partners: the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b), and the ARK Foundation. Approximately 750 caregivers will be recruited, with 500 from hospital settings (ill children) and 250 from community settings (healthy children). The study will focus on two common infectious conditions: diarrhoea and pneumonia, in children under five. Recruitment will ensure a balanced representation across four age groups: 0-12 months, 13-24 months, 24-36 months, and 36-59 months, with at least 70 children per group to facilitate meaningful subgroup analyses. Quantitative data will include HRQoL measures and socio-demographic characteristics, while qualitative feedback will be gathered through Likert-scale ratings and open-ended questions. Psychometric properties will include feasibility (response rate, missing data, time taken), test-retest reliability, known-group validity (e.g., compare EQ-TIPS scores between children with mild versus severe cases), and responsiveness to clinical outcomes (comparing changes before and after clinical treatment). Data will be disaggregated by age groups, health status, and other relevant variables. Additionally, the spillover effect of the child’s health on the caregiver will be assessed using the EQ-5D-Y-5L with sleep bolt-ons. This study will provide critical insights into the psychometric properties of the Bangla EQ-TIPS and its potential for use in Bangladesh and similar contexts.

Title: Assessment of the Psychometric Properties of Candidate items for the EQ-5D-5L hearing bolt-on alongside the “Listening with Unilateral verses bilateral Cochlear Implants in Adults (LUCIA)" randomised controlled trial.
Abstract: This research will assess the acceptability (data quality, distributional properties), reliability (test-retest, internal consistency), validity (convergent, divergent, known group, structural) and responsiveness of the EQ-5D-5L hearing bolt-on question(s). Research will be conducted alongside the NIHR-funded LUCIA trial in the UK. The EQ-5D-5L and candidate hearing bolt-on questions will be assessed at multiple time-points during the trial and be compared with the York Binaural Health Related Quality of Life measure, the Health Utilities Index mark 3, as well as a range of patient-reported hearing questionnaires and audiometric measures.

Title: Screen size & data quality
Abstract: IntroductionThe EQ-5D is frequently used to understand the development of health-related quality of life (HRQL) following injury. However, the lack of a cognition dimension is generally felt as disadvantageous as many injuries involve cognitive effects. We aimed to assess the added value of a cognitive dimension in a cohort of injury patients.MethodsWe analyzed EQ-5D-3L extended with cognition (EQ-5D + C) dimension responses of 5346 adult injury patients. We studied dimension dependency, assessed the additional effect of the cognitive dimension on the EQ-VAS, and, using the EQ-VAS as a dependent variable, determined the impact of EQ-5D and EQ-5D + C attributes in multivariate regression analyses.ResultsExtreme cognitive problems combined with no problems on other dimensions are uncommon, whereas severe prob-lems on other dimensions frequently occur without cognitive problems. The EQ-VAS significantly decreased when cognitive problems emerged. Univariate regression analyses indicated that all EQ-5D + C dimensions were significantly associated with the EQ-VAS. Exploratory analyses showed that using any set of five of the six EQ-5D + C dimensions resulted in almost identical explained variance, and adding the remaining 6th dimension resulted in a similar additional impact.ConclusionsThe addition of the cognition dimension increased the explanatory power of the EQ-5D-3L. Although the increase in explanatory power was relatively small after the cognition dimension was added, the decrease of HRQoL (meas-ured with the EQ-VAS) resulting from cognitive problems was comparable to the decreases resulting from other EQ-5D dimensions.

Title: Using EQ-5D-Y to capture children’s HRQoL in economic evaluation: conceptual and empirical challenges for cost effectiveness modelling and implications for modellers and decision makers.
Abstract: The specific consideration of health-related quality of life in children is extremely important in Health Technology Assessment, but also raises a number of challenging questions in terms of interpretation and use of data in policy making. Treating QALYs in child and adult populations as equivalent is a strong assumption due to differences in descriptive systems, in valuation, and in framing. Importantly, the range of scores in youth instruments are typically smaller than observed for adults, which can lead to higher ICERs for quality of life improving interventions in children, a consequence that may be unreasonable. Considering children differently can also lead to perverse effects in economic evaluation, such as significant artefactual discontinuities in health-related quality of life in models of cost effectiveness that span childhood into adulthood. This proposal brings together experts from within and outside the EuroQol Group to build a conceptual framework for consideration of such issues, and will lay out a roadmap to help researchers and policy makers. This will identify the range of interpretations of data that we observe in EQ-5D-Y value sets, and identify a range of innovative, practical solutions based on each interpretation. We will explore the perspectives on these matters that already exist, and build in the views of our world-leading methodologists and practitioners in our Expert Advisory Panel.

Title: 3rd EuroQol Asia Academy Meeting 2026: sharing and networking among EQ-5D researchers of Asian countries
Translation of the EQ-TIPS experimental version (V.3.0) in Spanish for Argentina and development of the digital and paper-based version mok-ups both for 3L and 5L versions.
Abstract: The EuroQol Toddler and Infant Populations (EQ-TIPS) is a generic measure of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) developed for children aged 0–3 years. Designed to complement the EQ-5D instruments for adult and youth populations, EQ-TIPS contributes to a comprehensive measurement system across all life stages. Argentina has actively participated in the development and refinement of EQ-TIPS, contributing to its translation, adaptation, and validation. In 2024, Argentina took part in a cognitive debriefing study to assess the instrument’s face and content validity. The results of that study led to modifications in the descriptive system, item wording, and response scale labels, which were integrated into version 3.0 of the instrument. This project reports on the Spanish translation of EQ-TIPS version 3.0 (including 3L and 5L versions) for use in Argentina. These translated versions will be employed in upcoming psychometric validation studies both in Argentina and internationally.

Title: Examining the psychometric performance of the EQ-HWB in caregivers of persons living with dementia.
Abstract: Introduction The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a generic new instrument developed internationally to use in evaluating interventions across health, public health, and social care, and enabling the inclusion of impacts on caregivers. Evaluations of the instrument’s performance in a range of informal caregiver populations is now needed. We know that for caregivers of people living with dementia, providing informal care can significantly impact their health and wellbeing; whether the EQ-HWB is able to capture these impacts remains unclear. Using data collected through an Australian study of caregiver quality-of-life, this project aimed to investigate the psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB in caregivers of persons living with dementia. Method An online survey was developed which included demographic questions, informal care-related questions, and a range of quality-of-life measures suitable for caregivers (C-DEMQOL and CarerQol) as well as the 25-item EQ-HWB. The psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-S (9-item short form) were assessed for acceptability (missing data), distribution (ceiling and floor effects), known groups and convergent validity analysis, and an exploration of dimensionality using exploratory factor analysis. Results Whilst some items were highly skewed, there were no floor or ceiling effects for either EQ-HWB instrument (answers to all items were at lowest (ie 111111111) or highest response level (ie 555555555)). Caregivers chose the two most severe responses for exhaustion (34.7% of responses were in the two most severe response categories, often or most/all of the time) and loneliness (25.7%)). In known group validity analysis, both EQ-HWB instruments performed well against the C-DEMQOL and CarerQol in terms of effect sizes (Cohen’s d and Eta-squared); however, the C-DEMQOL had higher effect sizes for dementia severity, and shared caregiving. At the item level, 13 of the 25 items were significantly different between groups when comparing caregiving time (2-groups), and 23 of 25 items were significant when comparing general health (2-groups). Most hypothesised correlations in convergent validity analysis were found to be above 0.3. Four items failed to load on to the EFA model (seeing, hearing, sleep, exhaustion), of which only exhaustion was from the EQ-HWB short form. Conclusion Our results suggest that the EQ-HWB instruments, both as sum-scores and index-scores, performed well in this population.

Title: Spillover Effects in Health-Related Quality of Life in Parents/Caregivers of Children 0 to 4 years old. Testing the Measurement Properties of the EQ-HWB-S in a multinational study in Argentina, Australia, Canada, Germany and Singapore
Abstract: The health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of children can significantly impact their parents and caregivers, a phenomenon known as the spillover effect. Generic HRQoL tools often fail to capture this dynamic. To address this, the EQ-HWB-S was developed to measure both individual and caregiver HRQoL. While preliminary validations and spillover assessment exist, broader evidence on its utility in caregiver contexts of young children is scarce.  This study proposes a secondary analysis of pooled data from an ongoing multinational project evaluating HRQoL in children aged 0–4 years and their caregivers across five countries: Argentina, Australia, Canada, Germany and Singapore. The aim of the current proposal is to assess the EQ-HWB-S’s capacity to reflect the spillover effects of children’s health status on caregivers’ HRQoL.  When data will be available in early 2026, we will perform descriptive, regression, and segmentation analyses to examine: (1) overall caregiver HRQoL; (2) correlations between child and caregiver HRQoL; (3) the magnitude and drivers of spillover effects; and (4) caregiver typologies. Analyses will be conducted in R, with adjustments for relevant clinical and sociodemographic variables, and country included as a random effect.  By funding this proposal, the EuroQol Group will obtain novel insights into the spillover body of knowledge, and the EQ-HWB-S’s application across diverse populations and contexts, reinforcing its potential for inclusion in both public health and population studies as well as in economic evaluations for informing health policy and decision-making.

Title: EQ-HWB-9 modifications testing using a one-at-a-time approach
Abstract: Objectives: EuroQol is currently developing a suite of new instruments, including the EQ-HWB-9. Little is known about the impact of single modifications (e.g. a one-word change in an item or a single response level) on quantitative psychometric performance of the instrument. This tests the effect of individual modifications on quantitative performance of EQ-HWB-9, applying a one-at-a-time approach.Methods: In 2025, an online cross-sectional survey was conducted in a representative general population sample in Hungary (n=2,000). The study used a mixed design with between- and within-subject components. Respondents were randomised into five arms examining differences in EQ-HWB-9 item wording, response levels and ordering, with balanced distribution across age, gender, education, place of residence, region and general health. Arm 1 used EQ-HWB-9 v1.2 (‘modified’, 2024) items and response levels. Arm 2 used modified items with v1.1 (‘experimental’, 2022) response levels. Arm 3 used experimental items with modified response levels. Arm 4 used modified items and response levels with reversed ordering of the activities and mobility items. Arm 5 used the modified items and response levels with a mobility item not referencing aids. Additional variants of the mobility, cognition and control items were administered across all arms. Psychometric properties were assessed across all arms, including distributional characteristics, convergent validity, agreement (Kendall’s tau) and known-groups validity (Cohen’s d effect size). Subgroup analysis was conducted by mobility aid use in the past 7 days (n=186).Results: Replacing ‘only occasionally’ with ‘a little of the time’ and ‘some difficulty’ with ‘moderate difficulty’ produced no significant differences in mean item scores for any item. The use of ‘and’ vs ‘or’ in the mobility item (‘getting around inside and/or outside’) or reversing the order of the mobility and activities items did not result in statistically significant differences in mean item scores or ceiling. Agreement between the with-aids and without-aids mobility items was lower among respondents who used mobility aids (0.448-0.731) than among those who did not (0.755-0.793). Known-groups validity for musculoskeletal diseases was similar between the with-aids and without-aids mobility items. Testing of the cognition item yielded inconclusive results, with one arm showing significantly more frequent problems with ‘trouble’ and the other with ‘difficulty’. Simplifying the parenthetical explanation of the control item led to more frequent experiences of problems. At the instrument level, EQ-HWB-9 showed very similar mean level sum scores across the 5 arms (range: 15.98-17.18; p=0.140). For known-groups validity, EQ-HWB-9 variants with either experimental items or response scales (arms 2 and 3) often yielded lower effect sizes than fully modified variants (arms 1, 4 and 5).Conclusion: For many individual wording, response option or item order modifications, only minor differences were observed in psychometric performance, suggesting that these refinements have a limited impact on instrument performance in the general population. These findings provide direct, quantitative evidence to guide finalisation of the EQ-HWB-9.

Title: Deriving Social Values for the EQ-5D 5L in Peru implementing a “Lite” protocol
Abstract: The main deliverablesplanned were: a draft of preliminary results and a draft of report/paper to be shared with the EuroQol team, that was accepted and going to be presented at the Brussels plenary; technical report published with the peruvianauthorities with the study details, analysis, results, and the peruvian eq-5d-3l value sets.We aimed to deliver at least 2 papers to be published in an international peer reviewed journal: a) one about the valuation set using the lite protocol and hybridmodelling (to be undertaken in the near future)b) about the comparison of the DCEvariants. A collaboration was done with Australian and Danish team and another paper sent to the plenary lead by Alice Yu about the DCE triplet comparison. After the revision of the project, and resubmission, the teaching-distance learning material was not planned nor produced.

Title: Testing the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-on in a large cross-sectional sample of patients with type 2 diabetes and a control group with no diabetes (SMART India study)
Abstract: AbstractObjectives: To evaluate the psychometric performance of the EQ-5D-5L and its vision bolt-on in adults with type 2 diabetes in India.Methods: Data from the cross-sectional SMART India diabetes cohort were analysed (n=7,910). Data collected included the EQ-5D-5L, vision bolt-on, EQ VAS, VisQoL, visual acuity, diabetic retinopathy (DR) severity with grading for presence of Diabetic Macular Oedema (DMO), demographic and clinical variables. DR severity was categorized as no DR, non-vision threatening diabetic retinopathy and vision threatening DR. Visual acuity was categorised as visual impairment (visual acuity>0.3 to 1.0 logMAR) and blindness (visual acuity>=1.0 logMAR) based on the US criterion. Additional variables considered included age, sex, diabetes duration, rurality, education level and epidemiological transition level. A comprehensive psychometric analyses was conducted including calculation of ceiling effects, informativity, convergent validity, explanatory power, known-groups validity, as well as a subgroup analysis on convergent validity were assessed.  These were done at the bolt-on and instrument levels using calculated level sum scores.Results: Of the 7,910 participants, 1,213 (15.3%) had visual impairment and 126 (1.6%) were blind. By diabetic retinopathy severity grade, 490 (6.2%) had non-vision threatening diabetic retinopathy (non-VTDR) and 365 had vision threatening DR. The mean age of the study sample was 58.6 years (SD 10.6). Compared with those with normal vision, blind participants more often had diabetes duration ≥10 years (46% vs 29%), vision-threatening DR (13% vs 4%), and ungradable retinal images (50% vs 20%). Problems on the vision bolt-on was reported by 28% (n=1,855), 60% (n=733) and 100% (n=126) of participants with normal vision, visual impairment and blindness. The bolt-on reduced ceiling effects (absolute reduction 7.1% points; relative reduction 13.4%) and improved informativity (Shannon’s H’ 3.55 to 4.46). VA (ρ =0.43) and visQOL mean score (ρ=0.51) showed stronger correlations with the bolt-on than core EQ-5D-5L dimensions (VA: ρ=0.22-0.31; VisQOL: ρ=0.32-0.49). The bolt-on improved model fit for VisQoL (ΔR2=0.103), VA (ΔR2=0.107), any visual impairment (Δ pseudo-R2=0.057), and blindness (Δ pseudo-R2=0.183; all p0.001). Discriminatory ability improved for blindness (Relative efficiency [RE]=1.50), vision-threatening DR (RE=1.42), and DMO (RE 1.41).Conclusions: In this nationally representative cohort of people with diabetes in India, the vision bolt-on demonstrated improved the psychometric performance compared to the EQ-5D-5L alone. These findings support its use in HRQoL measurement and HTA, particularly in LMIC settings in diabetes related visual complications.

Title: Learning and promoting health measurement and valuation using EQ instruments across continents
Summer Research Visit to Singapore: Advancing EuroQol Fatigue/Sleep Bolt-ons among adults living with Obesity
Abstract: Background: Fatigue is one of the most common and burdensome symptoms experienced by persons living with multiple sclerosis (MS), yet it is not currently captured in the EQ-5D-5L. The project 2035-BT: Qualitative Study for Fatigue Bolt-on (QFSB) aims to inform the development of the fatigue bolt-on through semi-structured interviews with persons living with MS. As one of the interviewers of the project, Minh Pham (MP) conducted a research visit to the National University of Singapore to receive qualitative training under the guidance Professor Nan Luo and his PhD student, Jia Jia Lee.Aim: The visit aimed to develop and pilot qualitative research materials including the interview guide, survey instrument, and coding framework, and to receive training in interviewing, transcription, and thematic coding.Methods: During the two-week visit, the research team reviewed the study proposal and addressed feedback from the EuroQol Executive Committee. The interview guide and survey instrument were developed and refined. Mock interviews and alpha testing were conducted to assess these materials.Results: Overall, the visit provided practical experience with interview procedures and data analysis. In addition to drafting the materials, MP was able to shadow a PhD student conducting in-person qualitative interview and assisted a nursing student in coordinating two group interviews. MP also received training in transcription using otter.ai and thematic coding using atlas.ti. During the visit, MP began drafting the protocol paper for the study, which is planned for abstract submission to the 2026 EuroQol Plenary Meeting.

Title: Exploring health system stakeholders’ preferences for visualizing routinely collected EQ-5D data in hip and knee arthroplasty in Canada
Abstract: Background: Data from EQ instruments are widely collected in routine care settings. Despite the recognized importance of this type of patient-reported outcome data, its use remains limited. Effective visualization of EQ-5D data is essential for enhancing their interpretation and ultimately promoting their uptake and use in health systems.  Aims: While previous studies have focused on EQ-5D data presentation and visualization for clinical end-users, this study aims to identify effective visualization formats of routinely collected EQ-5D data for health system administrators and decision-makers through a two-part approach: (1) conducting a scoping review to identify current visualization formats for routinely collected EQ-5D data in any clinical setting, and (2) using the visualization formats identified from the review to explore Canadian health system stakeholders’ preferences for visualizing routinely collected EQ-5D data in hip and knee arthroplasty, as part of the Canadian National PROM program. Methods: The scoping review (part 1) will summarize literature related to the graphical display of EQ-5D data collected in routine care. Searches will be performed across multiple databases and grey literature sources, complemented by information from the EuroQol office regarding registered projects on routine EQ instrument collection. The most common visualization formats identified from the review will be used to create samples for part 2 of the study. For the second part, national and provincial health system stakeholders (e.g., PROM program leads, administrators) from five Canadian provinces participating in the national PROM program will be interviewed about their preferences for EQ-5D data visualization. The interviews will be analyzed using directed content analysis, based on pre-determined themes including ease of interpretation, usefulness of the content, and visual appeal.  Benefit of the research: Understanding stakeholders’ preferences for presenting EQ-5D data in hip and knee arthroplasty will help improve data visualization, ultimately promoting the routine collection and use of EQ-5D data in health systems.

Title: Preference Inversion in the EQ-5D-5L
Abstract: Background: Evidence on preference inversion(i.e., where respondent preferences contradict the adjectival scalein health-related quality of life [HRQoL])has become increasingly apparent for the EQ-5D-5L, specifically in the last level of each item. This perception has anecdotally deteredthe adoption of the 5Lin the United States. Aims: 1.To directly test preference inversion between levels 4 and 5 of each itemby asking single intradomain pairs:Pr(L4>L5)  L5) > Pr(L3>L4) Methods: To test for these inversionsempirically, I propose to create a survey containing a series of paired comparisons(listed below)using a nationally representative sample of the United States respondents. For each of the 10 intradomain and 200 interdomain pairs, 50 responses will be collected such that 2,635 respondents each complete 4 pairs (i.e., 50x(10+200)= 2635x4).Implications: Regardless of outcome, a better understanding of preference inversion has substantial implications for the EQ-5D development, particularly for its valuation and dissemination.

Title: Testing the face and content validity of E‐QALY domains and items: a study of the Chinese population
Abstract: This project aims to test the face and content validity of the items generated in stage 2 of the E‐QALY project in a groups of Chinese respondents from Shanghai, China. The project will use the standard study protocol developed by the E‐QALY team. It is part of the international study of the E‐QALY instrument approved by the EuroQol Group.

Title: Can social care needs and well-being be explained by EQ-5D? Analysis of the Health Survey for England dataset.
Abstract: Introduction: It is becoming increasingly important for decision makers to be able to measure and compare diverse outcomes arising from health and socialcare interventions. Use of different outcome measures for assessment in the two sectors creates difficulties for comparisons and for capturing the multiple outcomes in a single metric. EQ-5D is the preferred measure of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) by key decision-makers in the UK. However, there is currently little clarity about how it is associated with other outcomes used in social care. Method: We empirically compared responses to EQ-5D with responses to measures of social care needs and subjective wellbeing using a large cross-sectional dataset of the UK general population, the Health Survey for England.Bivariate and multivariate regression analyses wereused to examine whethersocial care needs,measured by the Barthel Index,in people aged 65 years and over could beexplained by EQ-5Dresponsesand wellbeing measures; and how much ofthe variation in mental health and subjective well-being in the general population, as captured by GHQ-12 and WEMWBS, are explained by the EQ-5D. Results: Our study found that responses indicating poor health and wellbeing in EQ-VAS, EQ-5D Index, GHQ-12 summary score and WEMWBS pointspredicted a need for social care. Investigation of dimensions used to construct the measuresfound that two of the EQ-5D dimensions -self-care and pain/discomfort -were significantly associated withneed for social care. In addition, individuals with extreme anxiety/depression(compared to notanxious/depressed) and unable to perform usual activities (compared to no problem in performing usual activity) were more likely to report need for social care. None of the GHQ-12 dimensions were significantly associated with the Barthel Index. Two dimensions from WEMWBS,‘been feeling useful’ and ‘had energy to spare’ were significantly associated with the Barthel index. Amongst background characteristics, age and limiting longstanding illness were significant predictors of social care need across all the models. Conclusion: The need for social care,which largely depends on one’s ability to perform personal day-to-day activities,appears to be significantly associated with those EQ-5D dimensions that capture physical health and mental health.This offers the EuroQol group a strong ground to pursue how best EQ-5D instrument could be made available in capturing outcomes of social care, increasing comparability in economic evaluations between the health and social care sectors. This may includereviewingdescriptive system and/or any future development of additional or amended EQ-related questionnaire.

Title: Evaluation of different methods for handling missing EQ-5D-5L data – an explorative simulation study and empirical application
Abstract: Background: As a self-reported index instrument, the EQ-5D-5L (5L) has a considerable risk of missing data, potentially leading to biased estimates when not handled adequately. To address this issue, multiple imputation strategies (MI) and longitudinal linear mixed models (LLM) have shown to be promising. MI can be divided into two broad categories, Joint Modelling (JM) and Fully Conditional Specification (FCS). However, it remains unclear which MI approach best suits longitudinal 5L data and whether to impute missing 5L data at the response or index level. In this study, we explored the performance of the aforementioned methodological strategies to handle 5L data in clinical trials using simulated and empirical data. Methods: 2,000 complete data sets were simulated based on empirical trial data, including 5L responses at baseline and two time points. Missing data was introduced at rates of 10%, 25%, and 50% under Missing At Random (MAR), Missing Completely At Random (MCAR), or Missing Not at Random (MNAR). Different missingness patterns were applied at index and response levels. Six strategies were evaluated: complete-case analysis with ordinary least squares (CCA-OLS), LLM alone, FCS with LLM at index-level (FCS-LLM index), FCS with LLM at response-level (FCS-LLM response), JM with LLM at index-level (JM-LLM index), JM with LLM at response-level (JM-LLM response). Performance was assessed using empirical bias (EB), root-mean-square error (RMSE), and coverage rate (CR). Furthermore, the six strategies were applied to empirical trial data to descriptively assess the generalizability of our results. Results: CCA-OLS resulted in highly biased estimates. LLM alone had similar and oftentimes slightly smaller EBs and RMSEs than JM-LLM at 10%, 25%, and 50% missing data, irrespective of missingness pattern. FCS-LLM is outperformed by LLM alone and JM-LLM in all scenarios. Among MI strategies, JM-LLM had smaller EBs and RMSEs than FCS-LLM. In all scenarios, all method were slightly overfitted, with FCS-LLM having CRs closest to the nominal level. At 50% missing data, all strategies resulted in high EBs and RMSEs. MI performed worse when imputing at the response-level rather than on index-level MI, and LLM could not be performed at all on response-level. The MCAR results aligned with the MAR findings, whereas the MNAR results exhibited larger EBs and lacked a clear pattern indicating a superior or inferior strategy. In the empirical trial data, estimates from CCA-OLS deviated considerably from those of the other strategies, whereas estimates derived using LLM and MI at index-level were highly similar. The latter, however, was not the case for MI at the response-level. Conclusions: CCA-OLS yields biased estimates, whereas LLM seems to perform slightly better than MI strategies for handling missing 5L data in trial-based evaluations, provided that baseline data are complete. If this assumption does not hold, among MI strategies, JM-LLM is preferred, and index-level imputation is advised.

Title: Valuation of bolt-ons using measurement data
Abstract: ObjectiveIn some health conditions, the EQ-5D-5L core dimensions (CDs) are supplemented with bolt-ons (BOs) to increase sensitivity. For BOs to be usable in cost-utility analysis (CUA), BO value sets must be developed, and their application should ensure consistency with CD value sets and avoid double-counting. This study aimed to (1) define a consistency criterion, (2) propose a method to achieve it, and (3) assess its empirical properties.MethodsWe define consistency through the distribution of disutility values in measurement data. The definition separates the disutility corresponding to added sensitivity from that reflecting the BO-CD overlap. Consistency can be achieved by contracting the disutilities in BO value sets. We analyse 9 BOs using data from the general population (GP, 14 countries) and patient populations (PP, 6 disease areas). CD disutilities were based on the Polish EQ-5D-5L value set, and the BO disutilities were based on published studies.ResultsObservation counts ranged from 10,395 (hearing) to 42,206 (self-confidence) in GP, and from 312 (cognition) to 2,486 (breathing, sleep, tiredness) in PP. Level 5 disutilities ranged from 0.037 (sleep) to 0.385 (cognition). Spearman correlations between CDs and BOs ranged from 0.14 (mobility--self-confidence) to 0.55 (anxiety/depression--self-confidence or social relationships) in GP, and from -0.02 (self-care--cognition) to 0.58 (usual activities--tiredness) in PP. Achieving consistency required contraction factors between 0.864 (cognition) and 0.981 (sleep) in GP, and 0.829 (breathing) to 0.989 (sleep) in PP. Stronger contraction was needed for BOs with larger disutilities (significant) and more strongly correlated with CDs (non-significant).ConclusionConsistency between EQ-5D-5L and BO value sets is attainable through modest disutility reductions (2--17%), eliminating double counting while preserving increased measurement sensitivity.

Title: EuroQol workshops back-to-back with ISPOR 7th Asia-Pacific Conference in Singapore on September 3, 2016
