Title: Investigating the difference between the item-by-item and the grid version of EQ-HWB-9 and the performance of two potential EQ-HWB VAS versions
Abstract: The EQ-HWB-9 descriptive system was finalized in September 2025. However, supporting evidence for certain methodological aspects requires further testing in the coming year to facilitate the planned launch in 2027. In web-based questionnaire design, the grid/matrix and item-by-item formats are two common approaches for presenting items with shared response scales. Although each offers distinct advantages, they also have limitations. It is essential to understand the differences between these formats in terms of response distributions, completion time, data quality, respondent burden, and device compatibility, particularly for online surveys using the EQ-HWB-9. Additionally, all EuroQol instruments—including the adult and youth versions of the EQ-5D, as well as the EQ-TIPS—incorporate a visual analogue scale (VAS). However, no VAS has yet been proposed for the EQ-HWB(-9). This study aims to explore the impact of layout changes (item-by-item vs. grid) on the measurement properties of the EQ-HWB-9; and the measurement performance and potential differences between two versions of an EQ-HWB VAS in a representative sample of the Hong Kong general population. This proposed analysis will provide empirical evidence on how the EQ-HWB-9 item format and modifications to the cognition response options affect its psychometric properties in the general population. Moreover, this study is among the first to compare two versions of the HWB VAS within the same population. It will also investigate the relationship between the HWB VAS and the EQ VAS of the EQ-5D-5L, along with their broader associations with the EQ-HWB-9 and EQ-5D-5L items.

Title: EQ-HWB translation and cognitive debriefing methodology: Disseminating methodology, experiences and findings from Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Slovenia
Abstract: Background:The EQ Health and Wellbeing (EQ-HWB) is a new generic measure intended to capture health-, social care-, and carer-related quality of life. Following developmental testing, additional work was required to assess the comprehensibility, translatability, and performance of both the Experimental and Modified versions of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 across broader linguistic and cultural settings.Objectives:Primarily, this project aimed to analyse the understanding of the EQ-HWB-9 across four languages - German, Hungarian, Slovene and Dutch - to help inform an evidence-based decision towards the finalisation of the EQ-HWB-9 descriptive system made by the EQ-HWb working group. Secondly, this project aimed to summarise the experiences and findings from researcher-led translations and cognitive debriefing (CD) of the EQ-HWB and EQ-HWB-9 and to extract methodological lessons to support future instrument refinement and translation guidance. Methods:To investigate comprehension of the EQ-HWB-9 components, i.e. items, responce scales and instructions, results from the country team's CD interviews among a diverse convenience sample (N=64) of adults with varying health conditions were used. CD involved a structured ranking exercise of qualifier hierarchies (difficulty, frequency, severity), line-by-line item probing, and qualitative coding based on the EQ-HWB Working Group framework. Responses from translation, CD and ranking exercises in the four countries were transcribed and compiled into exercise specific Excel files. The EQ-HWB Working Group coding framework  was applied to categorize issues with understanding.  An on-line session was held to establish consensus on the nature of each code and to standardise the coding during which the Research Team collectively examined a sample of responses. In coding each item, researchers considered respondents’ interpretations and examples, as well as feedback from interviewers, translation teams, and VMC reviewers. Attention was given to translation quality, conceptual clarity, and formatting.Subsequently, each item was double-coded: one researcher conducted the initial coding, and another verified it. To ensure consistency, the team held further online consensus meetings where sample responses were reviewed, coding was standardized, and discrepancies were resolved.Analysis of the reports from the four countries provided a summarised qualitative view of the understanding of the original experimental and modified items and acceptability of the modifications over the original experimental items and response scales. Final grading of each item (red, orange and green) and recommendations as to possible amendments were based on reaching a shared consensus based on the frequency and the narrative data.Results:Overall, the EQ-HWB-9 was well understood across languages, though several cross-linguistic challenges emerged. Respondents frequently struggled to differentiate frequency qualifiers—particularly “only occasionally” versus “sometimes”—with one-third misordering these levels. Double-barrelled items (“getting around inside and outside”, “concentrating or thinking clearly”, “sad or depressed”) produced substantial interpretation difficulties, especially due to ambiguous constructs and problematic examples (e.g. mobility aids). Several terms (e.g. “anxious”, “exhausted”) showed language-dependent ambiguities. Qualifier hierarchies for difficulty and severity were generally well understood, whereas frequency qualifiers performed least well. Modified phrasings sometimes improved clarity (e.g. replacing “only occasionally” with “rarely”), though language-specific variation was substantial. Issues related to fluctuating symptoms (pain, sadness, depression) highlighted challenges in the 7-day recall period for certain constructs.Conclusions:The cross-country evaluation confirms good overall comprehensibility of the EQ-HWB-9 but identifies recurring linguistic and conceptual issues that warrant refinement before finalising the descriptive system. Key recommendations include revising or splitting double-barrelled items, reconsidering problematic qualifiers (especially frequency terms), reviewing examples involving mobility aids, and aligning stems with intensity-based response options. Addressing these issues now will strengthen cross-cultural validity and ensure robust future implementation of the EQ-HWB measures.

Title: Statistical analysis and preparation of a manuscript describing the responsiveness, and impact on outcomes of administering the EQ‐5D‐Y via internet to children/youths with Type I Diabetes Mellitus in clinical practice.
Abstract: OBJECTIVEThe objective of the study was to assess the potential for using an internet-administered version of EQ-5D-Y as a routine outcome measure in children/youths with T1DMin clinical practice. Specifically, to assess its capacity to detect changes in health comparing with other measures of Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQOL). METHODSThis is a secondary data analysis of a longitudinal study designed totest whether the systematic monitoring of HRQOLin Spanish pediatric patients with T1DM helps improve their daily life measured with KIDSCREEN-27. Of 205 potential candidates, 136 were consecutively recruited between July and December 2014 from a list of outpatient with T1DM attending to paediatric endocrinology departments at 5 hospitals in the Barcelona province (Spain). Paediatricians were randomly allocated to either the intervention or the control group. The intervention consisted of discussing HRQOL scores between the doctor and the patient at each routine visit. The EQ-5D-Y, the KIDSCREEN-27, and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) were completed, and clinical variables were collected, during the first and last visit of the study in both groups. Changes between evaluations on dimensions of the EQ-5D-Y, EQ-VAS, EQ-5D-YSummaryscore, KIDSCREEN-27 physical and psychological well-being dimensions, KIDSCREEN-10 index, and SDQ were described and compared between groups. Sensitivity, Specificity, and Positive and Negative Predictive Values (PPV/NPV) of the EQ-5D-Y dimensions were estimated. Multivariate models of repeated measures were constructed to assess the HRQL impact of monitoring health over time. RESULTSAt the end of follow-up response rate was 82.6%. Mean of age was 14 years old, and mean time from diagnosiswas 5.56 years.The comparisonbetween 1stand 4thfollow-up visits showed statistically significant improvement in the intervention group for: ‘Worried/Sad/Unhappy dimension’(28.6% and 15.7%, p=0.035), the SummaryEQ-5D-Y score (9.29 and 5.29, p=0.013), the EQ-VAS (78.5 and 83.2, p=0.009), the KIDSCREEN-10 index,and the two KIDSCREEN-27 dimensions. No differences between both visits were found in the control group, except for the SDQ. The GEE showed no differenceson EQ-5D-Y change between groups.EQ-5D-Y dimensions and Summaryscore showed good sensitivity to detect stability (38.5%-95.5%) in health status and high specificity to detect worsening (89.7%-100%) and improvement (77.4%-100%) when using changes in theKIDSCREEN as the criterion measure.EQ-5D-Y dimensions and Index also showed a very high PPV (70.4%-100%) for detecting improvement and a high NPV to discard worsening (71.2%-82.7%) and stability (75%-96.6%).CONCLUSIONThe electronic EQ-5D-Y is wellaccepted by children/youths with T1DMto be used as a routine outcome measure in clinical practice.Results confirm ourhypothesis that mental health improved in the intervention group,as measured by Worry/Sad/Unhappy of EQ-5D-Y and Psychological Well-Being of KIDSCREEN-27. Also, as hypothesized,the EQ-5D-Y shows a high capacity for the detection ofHRQL improvement in these patients, but our results did not confirm the hypothesis about its capacity to detect worsening.Since this latest issue is related to the low proportion of patients experiencing worsening in our sample, further studies are needed to test this capacity.

Title: An exploratory study of alternative recall periods for EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-S and possible ‘health and wellbeing’ VAS versions in a representative sample of Hong Kong Chinese general population
Abstract: Both EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 are generic, preference-accompanied instruments by EuroQol that use different recall periods. This study aimed to explore the impact of recall period on the measurement properties of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9, including a possible EQ-HWB VAS. An online cross-sectional survey was conducted with a representative general population sample in Hong Kong (n=1262). Respondents completed both a ‘today’ and a ‘last week’ version of the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9, including the EQ VAS and a ‘health and wellbeing’ VAS for EQ-HWB-9. Psychometric properties (e.g., ceiling, convergent validity with ReQoL-10 and PROMIS-29+2, and known-group validity) were assessed for both the descriptive systems and the VAS versions. The ‘last week’ versions of EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 (28.8% and 14.6%) showed lower ceiling than the ‘today’ versions (34.8% and 18.2%). More respondents had identical ‘today’ and ‘last week’ profiles on EQ-5D-5L (52.4%) than on EQ-HWB-9 (17.7%). The longer recall improved convergent validity for most EQ-HWB-9 items. Both instruments’ ‘last week’ versions showed slightly better known-group validity. The mean ‘today’ EQ VAS and ‘last week’ EQ-HWB VAS scores were 76.7 and 73.5 (p<0.001), with a strong correlation between them (r=0.88). EQ-HWB-9 items explained more variance in EQ-HWB VAS than EQ-5D-5L items in EQ VAS. Recall periods affect EQ-HWB-9 more than EQ-5D-5L; however, overall effects are small. ‘Last week’ versions perform slightly better in the general population. We provide the first evidence of the EQ-HWB VAS’s validity and its ability to capture distinct concepts from the EQ VAS, supporting its potential added value to the EQ-HWB-9.

Title: Indonesian valuation and validation study of the EQ-5D-5L and its application in families living in unhealthy circumstances and in breast cancer patients
Abstract: Indonesia is with more than 238 million people the world’s fourth’s most populous country. Given the large gap between its under-resourced health care system and its strong and persistent economic growth (6% per year), a rise in new pharmaceutical products,and illness prevention projects with corresponding cost-effectiveness analyses are to be expected in the coming years. The introduction and use of the validated EQ-5D-5L can perform a pivotal role here. Therefore, the aimsof this study are:1. To translate the EQ-5D-5L in Bahasa Indonesia (BI), to obtain age and gender norms, and to derive a preference valuation set for the translated EQ-5D-5L health states from the Indonesiangeneral public. 2. To validate the EQ-5D-5L by its application inan impoverished population group in Jakarta. Methods: Ad 1. Translationof the 5 levels versionof the EQ-5D, the EQ-VT and the guide book will be carried out according to guidelines of the EuroQol Group Executive office. Next, arandom sample (N=1,000) representative forthe Indonesianpopulationwill be asked to value a subset of EQ-5D-5L health states usingthe EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT). Regression techniques will be used to estimate anIndonesianvalue set of all possible 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states from the empirical validated subsample of health states. Test-retest reliability of the valuationswill be determined in a subgroup (n=200)and there we will examine the relation between the quality of the interviews (adherence to the protocol) and the valuation task (EQ-VT).Age and gender (distribution) norms of the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and EQ-VAS for the general population will be obtained as well. Ad 2: Validation: The construct validity of the EQ-5D-5L will be determined in boththe general population and in 250 families, living in unhealthy circumstances in the urban area of Jakarta and/or Bandung. The construct validity will be based on the comparison of the EQ-5D-5L with a number of additional quality of life measures (among which the WHOQOL-Bref) and a comparison between the healthy population and the impoverished sample.In addition, the EQ-5D-5L will be completed by about 200 Indonesian patients with breast cancer in Bandungwho participate in a Dutch Cancer Foundation funded project that ischaired by two of the principleinvestigators of the presentEUROQOLproposal(SS and JP). The patients’scores will be stratified according to cancer stage (I-IV) and compared with the scores of the other samples. Reports and presentations will be provided for the Indonesian stakeholders (government officials, physicians and water sanitation companies)and for the international scientific community.

Title: Investigating the validity of values worse than dead estimated using DCE with duration
Abstract: Background: DCE with duration (DCEtto) is an alternative protocol for deriving population value sets for instruments such as the EQ-5D-5L. Valuation studies of the EQ-5D-5L so far have used the EQ-VT which only included DCE without duration questions. In Canada, we sought to estimate the DCEtto by combining the EQ-VT with additional DCEtto questions. Our objectives were twofold: 1) to determine the feasibility of generating the DCEtto from this combination of EQ-VT and DCEtto questions; and 2) to further investigate the validity of the DCEtto. The latter involved comparing individual values from the conventional TTO and the DCEtto.Methods: Data from 1107respondents in the Canadian EQ-5D-5L valuation survey are used. Each respondent completed the EQ-VT (composite TTO, and DCE without duration) followed by an additional survey which included 2 DCEtto tasks. These DCEtto tasks where selected using experimental design theory whereby the DCE without duration tasks were assumed to have equal duration, and combined with the DCEtto data to create a single dataset amenable for the analysis. For our first objective we useda conditional logit modelto estimate coefficients from the combined data. For our second objective ran mixed logit models and used hierarchical bayes to estimate individual values from the DCEtto. We then compared these to the TTO values.Results: The DCEtto provided coefficients that were statistically significant and logically ordered. Values ranged from 1 to -0.71(for health state 55555). Thiscontrasted to a range of 1 to 0for the TTO, suggesting clear differences in cardinal values derived from the two different protocols. The DCEtto values were better distributed than the TTO, which for severe health states suffered from clusters of values at 1, 0.5, 0 and -1. However, there was limited consistency between severe health states between the DCEtto and TTO. Conclusions: Values for the EQ-5D-5L were successfully generated using the DCEtto by simply adding two questions to the EQ-VT. The model generated plausible values, and the model coefficients were similar to those seen in previous DCEtto studies.The DCEtto values for severe health states were lower than those generated from the conventional TTO.

Title: Improving DCE design efficiency with monotonicity constraints
Abstract: Bayesian efficient designs improve the statistical efficiency of discrete choice experiments (DCEs) by optimizing a chosen design criterion over a prior distribution of anticipated preference parameters; their performance therefore depends critically on how well that prior reflects respondents' actual preferences. When reliable pilot data are not yet available, researchers often do already know the expected sign or ordering of some or all attribute-level coefficients on theoretical grounds. This paper introduces such qualitative information into Bayesian efficient design by truncating the prior to the admissible polyhedron Aβ>0, where A encodes the imposed sign and monotonicity restrictions, and subsequently integrating the design criterion over this constrained space. This approach is evaluated in an EQ-5D health-state valuation study with six designs arms (n = 2,648). Imposing sign and monotonicity constraints on a diffuse standard normal prior reduced the conditional and panel mixed logit D-error by 60% and 50%, respectively, recovering most of the efficiency gain that typically requires informative priors and more than halving sample size requirements. Imposing these constraints on an already accurate informative prior yielded no further improvement. Notably, the observed efficiency gains came at minimal behavioral cost, with dropout, speeding, and fatigue remaining unaffected. Sign and monotonicity constraints therefore provide an easily implemented and potentially performant extension for Bayesian efficient designs when more precise prior parameter information is not yet available.

Title: An EQ-5D-5L value set for the Vietnam population
Abstract: Data collection was implementedfrom November –December, 2017.The value set was disseminated in a national conference on Health Technology Assessment in Nov 27, 2018. Detail of the conference can be found here. The value set has been introduced to the research network in Vietnam.Manuscript was developedand submitted to “Value in Health”in Nov 14, 2017. The current status is “Waiting for reviewer selection”.An abstract of study results has been sent to iHEA conference and currently waiting for their decision.

Title: Generation of a National EQ-5D-5L Value Set for Zambia to Support Economic Evaluation and Policy: A study protocol
Abstract: This work addresses the increasing demand for locally generated health preference data in the context of the country’s transition from donor‑dependent health financing to domestically funded systems. This transition necessitates more efficient domestic resource allocation and demands evidence‑informed priority setting, including the application of health technology assessment (HTA).A cross-sectional, in-person survey of about 1260 adults aged 18 years and older was undertaken utilising a multistage stratified sampling method to account for variations among provinces, encompassing urban-rural and socioeconomic disparities. The study adhered to the standard EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) protocol, that includes both Composite Time Trade-Off (cTTO) tasks (10 per participant) and Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) tasks (12 per participant).Actual data collection commenced on the 15th September 2025 after extensive enumerator training, pilot testing, and pre-testing, utilising computer-based EQ-PVT software under organised supervision. A stringent quality control framework was implemented, encompassing daily monitoring via the Quality Control (QC) tool, evaluation of protocol compliance (including accurate elucidation of worse-than-dead tasks, minimum time thresholds, and logical coherence of responses), and systematic retraining as well as exclusion of subpar interviewers. Data quality assessments were performed at critical milestones during the data collection process.The study was conducted in conjunction with the EQ-VT Support Team and national stakeholders, including the Ministry of Health and the Zambia Immunisation Advisory Board, under the supervision of the Principal Investigator. All data were securely administered, anonymised, and prepared for submission to the EuroQol SAVED repository in accordance with national data protection rules.The analysis utilised hybrid modelling techniques that integrated cTTO and DCE data through Stata software, with model selection grounded in logical consistency, statistical fit, and robustness assessments. The principal deliverables comprise a nationally representative EQ-5D-5L value set, draft manuscript and stakeholder workshops.The resultant value set will serve as an essential instrument for cost-effectiveness analysis, aiding health technology assessment and policy decisions in domains such as vaccine prioritisation, while also acting as a standard for other low- and middle-income nations.

Title: Cognition bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L: a systematic review
Abstract: Despite the frequent use of cognition bolt-ons with the EQ-5D, no systematic review had previously summarised their development, use and psychometric properties, creating uncertainty for researchers and decision-makers in selecting appropriate items. Our systematic literature review has identified 181 publications with cognition bolt-ons for the EQ-5D-3L or EQ-5D-5L. We identified 52 distinct wordings (three-level: 23, five-level: 29), with the most common dimension titles being cognition (29%) and thinking ability (19%), and examples being concentration (60%), memory (39%) and remembering (31%). The methodological quality of bolt-on development was heterogeneous, often lacking qualitative input in item wording or clear phrasing. Bolt-ons were used in 28 languages across 24 countries, with 64% of the studies originating from the Netherlands. Overall, 16% of the studies used proxy-reporting. Most studies developed (n=38) and used or psychometrically tested EQ-5D+bolt-on(s) (n=120), with fewer valuation and disability weight studies (n=27). These studies covered 71 patient populations, most commonly injuries, dementia, depression, HIV, schistosomiasis and stroke. The most frequently reported psychometric properties were item-level ceiling (n=75) and known-groups validity (n=54). Fewer studies explored convergent or divergent validity (n=8 for each), responsiveness (n=3), patient-proxy agreement (n=2) and test-retest reliability (n=1). None reported on content validity. Five-level bolt-ons generally outperformed three-level bolt-ons in terms of overall psychometric performance. The most-tested bolt-ons were the Janssen 2013 (5L, cognition) and Haagsma 2005 (3L, thinking ability) versions. Future research should prioritise testing the psychometric properties of the most promising bolt-ons using both qualitative and quantitative methods across different populations.

Title: Application for a grant to prepare and conduct a workshop in ISPOR Real-World Evidence Summit 2025 on 30 September in Tokyo, Japan
Abstract: We prepared an issue panel for discussing the necessity of using culture-specific preference-based measure versus generic PBMs in the ISPOR real world evidence conference in Tokyo, Japan on 30 September 2025. After the issue panel proposal was accepted, we had several zoom meetings to discuss the content and structure of the 1-hour issue panel. The final issue panel consisted of three presentations and a general discussion with audience. The first presentations provided information about two Asian culture-specific PBMs, namely, CHROM-G for China and AP-7D for Asia. The last presentation was an advocacy of using the generic EQ-5D in Asia. After the presentation,

Title: Establishing population norms and assessing the usefulness of EQ-5D in studying health inequalities: a cross-sectional and longitudinal study based on Stockholm public health cohort
Abstract: EQ-5D is widely used in economic evaluations and population health assessments. This study used a large population-based cohort with EQ-5D-3L data to describe health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in the general population, examine variations across sociodemographic factors, prevalent health conditions and risk factors, and assess temporal trends and how inequalities developed over time (2002–2021). The cross-sectional analyses included 52,714 respondents aged 23–104 years from the 2021 Stockholm Public Health Cohort (SPHC), larger than most studies on population norms to date. The trend analyses were based on 149,439 observations aged 23–84 from five waves (2002, 2006, 2010, 2014, and 2021).   Calibration weights constructed using registry data of the whole population were applied to reduce non-response bias and improve representativeness. Differences in EQ VAS and EQ-5D-3L index values were examined using multivariable regression models, and modified Poisson regression was used to estimate the likelihood of reporting problems across EQ-5D dimensions. Nonlinear associations between age and HRQoL were modelled using splines, and interactions between survey wave and socioeconomic status were included to evaluate changes in socioeconomic disparities over time.The HRQoL of the general population was generally good but variations across sociodemographic and risk factor groups were observed. HRQoL demonstrated a non-linear relationship with age, with relatively lower scores observed among the youngest adults, increasing through midlife, followed by a marked decline in older age, particularly among those aged 80 years and above. The mean EQ-5D-3L index was lower among females (0.79 [95% CI: 0.79–0.80]) than males (0.83 [95% CI: 0.83–0.84]), and a similar pattern was observed for the mean EQ-VAS scores (75.96 [95% CI: 75.59–76.33] vs. 78.3 [95% CI: 77.62–78.42], respectively). People with lower education, low disposable income as well as those born outside of the European union and UK reported relatively lower HRQoL. Adjusting for age attenuated but did not eliminate these demographic and socioeconomic differences. Persistent associations between behavioral risk factors and HRQoL were also observed. Similarly, people with chronic health conditions, particularly those with long-term illness or multiple health conditions, exhibited markedly lower HRQoL. The preliminary results from analyzing data over two decades indicate that, overall, the mean index values and EQ-VAS scores remained stable throughout the study period. Among females, the EQ-5D index was 0.80 (95% CI 0.80–0.81) in 2002 and 0.80 (95% CI 0.80–0.80) in 2021, and EQ VAS scores were 0.77 (95% CI 0.77–0.78) in 2006 and 0.76 (95% CI 0.76–0.77) in 2021. Among males, the EQ-5D index was 0.85 (95% CI 0.85–0.86) in 2002 and 0.84 (95% CI 0.83–0.84) in 2021, and EQ-VAS scores were 0.79 (95% CI 0.79–0.80) in 2006 and 0.78 (95% CI 0.78–0.79) in 2021. However, distinct patterns across sociodemographic subgroups were observed, indicated by significant interactions with survey years. HRQoL patterns differed by age group, with a relative decline in the younger cohort, relative stability in the middle-aged and older population. Income-related differences also appeared to widen over time, with lower-income groups showing a more marked decline in HRQoL.In conclusion, this study demonstrated substantial variations in HRQoL across sociodemographic groups, behavioral risk factors, and self-reported health conditions, providing insights that can inform healthcare planning and future investments in health and research. The results may also serve as reference values in clinical and economic evaluations, and for comparing outcomes from specific patient subgroups with the general population. Over time, HRQoL seems stable albeit not for all. Notably, HRQoL seemed to decline for younger people and those with low income.

Title: EQ-5D-5L UK Valuation Educational Session - HESG Summer 2025
Abstract: The Health Economics Study Group (HESG) UK in Brighton was held between 30th June and 2nd July.  An educational session, "Introducing an EQ-5D-5L value set for the UK: practical and methodological considerations", was held on 30th June where the lead PI, Professor Donna Rowen presented findings from the study. In addition, other study stakeholders including a representative from NICE and separately from industry presented their views. Finally, a non-study researcher presented a different view. The session was well attended and offered the opportunity for questions and answers related to the new value set. This enabled knowledge transfer in the session and in subsequent discussions outside the session. There were also other sessions focused on EQ-5D and EQ Health and Wellbeing. I chaired one session focused on severe mental health that used EQ-5D and I attended and contributed to the session on the EQ-HWB and application of Q methodology in a mixed population from China. It was also valuable to attend sessions on valuation: a) analysing DCE data, b) valuing condition specific measures, c) adolescents undertaking valuation.

Title: EQ-DAPHNIE Project - request for extension of funding period
Abstract: The EQ-DAPHNIE Project is well known to the EQ Executive. It was originally funded as a major infrastructure investment for the EuroQol Group. There are two major aspects to this infrastructure: 1) the data arising from the measurement of population health with EQ instrument-based surveys in countries around the world; and 2) the survey and data storage infrastructure that can be used by EQ members for future population-level studies. This later aspect is analogous to the investment made in valuation infrastructure to support the creation of preference-based value sets for EQ instruments.

Title: Assessing the health-related quality of life of adolescents in Ethiopia: Mixed method study (quantitative and qualitative)
Abstract: As for the adult population, measuring the health status of children and adolescents is vital for describing and monitoring the health of a population, for public health research, and evaluation of treatments. In Ethiopia, where 24% of the population is aged 10-18 years, it is particularly important to have information about the health status of adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this PhD project is increase knowledge on measuring health among adolescents aged 12-17 years in Ethiopia using the EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L instruments. Mixed methods will be employed. First, a systematic scoping review will be undertaken to identify: the approaches (modes of administration), instruments used, and factors associated with child and adolescent HRQoL in Sub-Saharan Africa. Then, extensive analysis of the (n=5000) adolescents HRQoL data will be undertaken. Other than the common income and employment status measures of socio-economic status (SES), a new method of adolescents SES classification adopted from Ghanaian researchers will be tested in Ethiopia from the collected data set. Third, adolescent population norms will be presented using both the Y-3L and Y-5L instruments and the performance of the instruments will be compared. Fourth, factors associated with the HRQoL of adolescents, as measured using Y-3L and Y-5L instruments, will be assessed. Finally, a qualitative study exploring the content validity and acceptability of EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L among children and adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes will be conducted pending outcome of a current grant application.

Title: Exploring older people's understanding of the  EQ-5D-5L: a qualitative study
Abstract: Globally, older people (aged 65 and over) are the fastest growing age cohort, with 830 million older people, currently representing 10% of the world’s population expected to double to approximately 1.5 billion, representing 17% of the world’s population by 2050. Older people are heavy users of health and social care services, already accounting for nearly half of total healthcare expenditures in OECD countries. The EQ-5D-5L has been used extensively to measure and value health related quality of life in economic evaluation and is increasingly being used in quality assessment with older populations across health and social care settings. This research project builds upon our team’s previous qualitative work to assess older aged care residents' understanding of the EQ-5D-5L, funded by the EuroQol group, and our collective extensive experience in the measurement and valuation of quality of life in older people using the EQ-5D-5L, Quality of Life-Aged Care Consumers (QOL-ACC) and other preference-based measures. By use of a qualitative think-aloud protocol with older people of different age groups in community settings, we aim to [1] investigate face and content validity of the EQ-5D-5L in older people, and inform which age-subgroup(s) to target for any further analysis, and [2] subsequently investigate how older people assess bolt-ons in the Toolbox when presented alongside the EQ-5D-5L. An initial deductive framework analysis will be undertaken using the well-established Tourangeau framework.

Title: Proposed 1-week visit to EuroQol offices & Erasmus University, Rotterdam, November 2025
Abstract: This travel grant supported me to visit Rotterdam for one week, capitalising on the fact that I was already in Europe for ISPOR. Three days were spent as a visitor at ESHPM, Erasmus University. The time there was used to progress various projects I am working on in collaboration with Stefan Lipman, and to have a series of face to face meetings with Erasmus PhD students and various senior colleagues. (A detailed calendar of activities and meetings is provided as an attachment). Two days were spent as a visitor in the EuroQol offices in Rotterdam. The time was in the office divided between (a) working with Bram Roudijk to progress various projects, including progress toward the EQ-5D-Y-5L valuation protocol and (b) face to face meetings with Bernhard Slaap to discuss various Board matters.  Just as importantly, being in the office was an important opportunity to meet new members of the staff, take part in various informal team activities, and to get a good sense of how the office works as a team. I would strongly recommend such visits to future Board chairs.

Title: Assessing the Relevance of EQ-TIPS Compared with EQ-5D-Y in Children Aged 4–6 Years with Severe Health Conditions in Argentina: A Qualitative Study with Primary Caregivers
Abstract: Background: Measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in early childhood presents important methodological challenges due to rapid developmental changes, reliance on proxy respondents, and the limited availability of age-appropriate instruments. Within the EuroQol family of instruments, the EQ-5D-Y is currently recommended for children aged 4–18 years, while the new instrument being developed, the EQ-TIPS, is designed for children aged 0–4 years. However, the conceptual overlap and transition between these instruments in early childhood remain poorly understood. This gap is particularly relevant for children with severe health conditions whose developmental trajectories may extend the applicability of instruments designed for younger ages. Objectives: To explore  how primary caregivers of children aged 4–6 years with severe health conditions perceive the relevance of the EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y descriptive systems for capturing key aspects of HRQoL,and to inform recommendations on  on which instrument is more appropriate at each developmental stage, particularly for children with severe health conditions. Methods: A qualitative study using cognitive interviews will be conducted with approximately 21–30 primary caregivers recruited from a tertiary pediatric hospital in Argentina. A purposive quota sampling strategy will ensure variation by age (4, 5, and 6 years) and condition (cerebral palsy, neuromuscular disorders, and oncological conditions). Participants will complete both instruments in randomized order using think-aloud techniques and targeted probing. Interviews will explore  instruments' relevance, comprehensiveness, and caregiver preferences, as well as which instrument is perceived as more relevant and suitable according to the child's health condition and developmental stage. Data will be audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic content analysis with a directed coding approach informed by content validity frameworks. Expected Results and Impact: This study will generate novel evidence on how caregivers interpret and value HRQoL domains across early childhood in children with severe conditions, identifying gaps, overlaps, and factors influencing perceived relevance. Findings will directly inform EuroQol guidance on the upper age limit of EQ-TIPS and the lower age limit of EQ-5D-Y, particularly for children with severe health conditions. By providing evidence from a Spanish-speaking, low- and middle-income country context, this research will also contribute to improving the cross-cultural validity and global applicability of pediatric HRQoL instruments.

Title: Creating a EuroQol Research Knowledge Graph
Abstract: EuroQol has funded over 900 research projects, producing a large body of publications on EQ-5D and related instruments. This literature contains detailed evidence on how these instruments perform across populations, countries, clinical areas, and methods. However, this information is distributed across individual papers and is not easily searchable or aggregable at the portfolio level.We propose to build a research knowledge graph of EuroQol's funded projects and their associated publications. Using large language models (LLMs), we will extract structured data from full-text papers: study designs, sample characteristics, instrument versions, methods, countries, and key findings. The extracted data will be stored in a graph database and made accessible through a web application that supports structured search, visual summaries, and natural-language queries.The project will proceed in three stages: (1) assembling the corpus from EuroQol's project database and identifying associated publications; (2) developing and iteratively refining the extraction pipeline; (3) building the web application. A preliminary demonstration, based on 944 project abstracts, produced a graph of over 2,000 nodes and 8,000 edges. The seed grant will go further by extracting from full-text publications and providing an interactive interface.If the approach proves useful, the knowledge graph can be expanded to cover the broader EQ-5D literature (over 17,000 publications in PubMed). The seed grant produces the working system and the evidence needed to assess whether such an expansion is warranted.

Title: Does a spoonful of honey improve a barrel of tar? Comparing 33333+1 with 33333
Abstract: Objectives: The EQ-5D Bolt-on ToolboxTM is intended to improve the sensitivity of health-related quality-of-life measurement in areas insufficiently captured by the five core dimensions of EQ-5D-5L. However, it remains unclear whether adding information that a person has no problems on a bolt-on dimension changes the perceived value of health states that include problems on the core dimensions. This study examined whether appending a bolt-on at level 1 affects preferences for EQ-5D-5L health states.Methods: An online discrete choice experiment was conducted in a representative sample of the United Kingdom general population recruited via Prolific. Respondents were recruited to one of four arms: core EQ-5D-5L only, or EQ-5D-5L plus one of three bolt-ons (social relationships, vision, or appetite). Respondents chose between living for 10 years in a health state with problems across core dimensions and living for a shorter duration in full health (3, 6, or 9 years). Core states were 22222, 33333, and 44444, with corresponding bolt-on states 22222+1, 33333+1, and 44444+1. Odds ratios comparing choices in each bolt-on arm with the core-dimension arm were pooled using the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel method.Results: Data from 2,391 respondents were analysed. Choice patterns were consistent with expected monotonicity in duration and health-state severity. Adding a level-1 bolt-on did not significantly affect the probability of choosing the impaired health state over full health. Pooled odds ratios were 0.921 for social relationships, 1.038 for vision, and 0.944 for appetite, with no statistically significant effects.Conclusions: Appending information on no problems in a bolt-on dimension did not change the perceived attractiveness of EQ-5D-5L health states with problems in core dimensions. These findings contrast with evidence from studies using the scaling factor approach in bolt-on valuation. Further research is needed to understand how respondents integrate bolt-on information into health-state preferences.

Title: Evaluating and comparing the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L, five bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB-S in injury patients
Abstract: Background: The EuroQol Group is exploring extending the EQ-5D with bolt-ons and embarked upon developing entirely new instruments, such as the EQ-HWB. Evidence on psychometric performance of bolt-ons alongside EQ-5D-5L and the EQ-HWB(-S) in general and patients populations is needed to ensure their reliability and validity before they can be adopted in clinical practice or research. Aims: The aims of this proposal are to evaluate and compare the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-5L, five bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB-S in injury patients and determine factors associated with worse scores in these instruments and bolt-ons. Methods: We will use data from a stratified sample of patients who presented to the emergency department because of an injury. The 12 month follow up survey will include the EQ-5D-5L, five bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB-S. We will evaluate and compare distributional characteristics, structural validity, differential item functioning, known group validity, exploratory power analysis and analysis of interchangeability. Where possible, psychometric properties will be evaluated for the total sample and for specific sub-groups (e.g. those with low health literacy level). We will use linear regression models to determine factors that are associated with worse EQ-5D-5L, EQ-5D-5L + bolt-ons and EQ-HWB-S scores. Deliverables: The project will produce at least three scientific manuscripts. In addition, the project will produce evidence on the psychometric performance of EQ-5D-5L, bolt-ons and the EQ-HWB-S in a diverse patient population.

Title: Dissemination seminar on Bangladesh value sets for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L study and piloting of EQ-5D-Y
Abstract: A dissemination seminar on the development of the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets (Project ID: 1996-VS), as well as the piloting of the EQ-5D-Y (Project ID: 1646-RA), was conducted in Bangladesh. The audience included representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, potential HTA bodies (e.g., the Directorate General of Health Services, and the Health Economics Unit, Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics), researchers and academicians, national and international development partners, members of the print and electronic media, public health advocates, and civil society representatives.During the seminar, presentations covered the methodology and process of the valuation survey, challenges encountered, the resulting EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L tariffs, the feasibility of the EQ-5D-Y, and their practical applicability for HTA in Bangladesh. A Q&A session was carried out, focusing on the usefulness of these value sets. To evaluate the impact of the seminar, pre- and post-event surveys assessing participants’ knowledge of the “value of health” and the EQ-5D instrument were conducted. In addition, print and electronic media and social media covered the dissemination session.

Title: A travel grant to support the psychometric evaluation and cultural relevance of EQ instruments in China
Abstract: The visit will support three primary areas of work: (1) conducting psychometric analyses of the EQ-HWB and EQ-5D using an existing dataset collected during the COVID-19 pandemic; (2) exploring the EQ-DAPHNIE dataset, with a specific focus on outcomes related to long COVID; and (3) developing a qualitative study to investigate perceptions of quality of life and the content validity of the EQ-HWB among ethnic minority populations in China. Additionally, this visit will provide valuable hands-on experience in data collection through participation in an ongoing study involving older adults residing in social care facilities. The visit aims to enhance research skills, finalize ongoing studies, and initiate new projects related to the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQoL), with a particular focus on the psychometric evaluation and cultural relevance of EQ instruments.

Title: Measuring the strength of preferences on bolt-ons: a DSWG/VWG collaboration
Abstract: Background: The current EQ-5D-5L Bolt-on Toolbox includes "best available" items across eight dimensions. While these have been identified by the Descriptive Systems Working Group (DSWG) as promising candidates for official inclusion, there is currently insufficient preference evidence to support their development, approval, and valuation.Objective: To generate actionable preference evidence for the eight candidate bolt-ons using a multi-arm, latent-scale discrete choice experiment (DCE) survey. Specifically, we aim to:Measure the strength of preference for each candidate bolt-on (main effects).Assess differences in main effects across the eight candidates (differential effects).Examine how adding a bolt-on changes the importance of the five core dimensions (relative effects).This project is a collaboration between the DSWG and the Valuation Working Group (VWG) designed to provide timely evidence that will inform bolt-on development, Toolbox approval, and the design of future valuation studies.Ideally, a candidate bolt-on should broaden HRQoL descriptions into areas where the core dimensions may be insufficient. This means it should possess strong measurement properties and have an impact on values (Aim 1), while minimizing distortion of the relative effects of the 5 core dimensions (Aim 3). Candidates that exert larger effects on choices are more relevant to economic evaluations (Aim 2), strengthening the case for their development and approval. Conversely, distortions (Aim 3) imply a conceptual overlap, redundancy, or double-counting between the bolt-on and core dimensions. Consequently, adopting such bolt-ons may compromise the structural integrity and independent valuation of the core dimensions, complicating comparisons with the original instrument.Methods: This formative study will recruit a nationally representative sample of 5,000 US adults (Dynata) for an online DCE survey (LimeSurvey). Data quality will be ensured via geographic validation, automation detection, and attentiveness checks. The DCE survey consists of nine arms: a baseline arm with the five core attributes of the EQ-5D-5L (N=1,000) and eight candidate arms where one "best available" bolt-on is appended (N=500 per arm). Each candidate arm utilizes a common D-efficient design (24 paired comparisons, 10 blocks, 50 respondents per block). In the primary analyses, conditional logit models will be estimated on a latent scale (log-odds) to characterize three effects:Main effects: Differences in latent-scale disutilities (log-odds) between successive dimension levels (Aim 1).Differential effects: Differences in bolt-on main effects across candidate arms (Aim 2).Relative effects: Differences in the ratios of core-dimension main effects between the baseline and candidate arms (Aim 3).Furthermore, we will conduct sensitivity analyses using Bayesian estimation of mixed logit models to ensure the robustness of our frequentist findings. We will also estimate scale-factor models that decompose the main effects of each arm into dimension-specific scale factors and cross-attribute level effects (CALEs). As a secondary analysis, we will evaluate whether appending a bolt-on affects respondent burden (e.g., completion time) or data quality (e.g., left-right bias, task sequence effects) relative to the baseline arm.Beyond these aims, we offer an optional supplement to estimate attribute interactions (bolt-on vs. core, core vs. core). While this supplement doubles data collection costs, it does not increase personnel costs (see budget), thereby leveraging economies of scale to provide more granular preference evidence.

Title: Reporting heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L: Sociodemographic and cognitive drivers and their impact for population health measurement
Abstract: All self-reported health indicators are susceptible to reporting heterogeneity — the systematic variation in how individuals with the same underlying health use the instrument's response categories. The potential consequences of ignoring response scale heterogeneity extend beyond academic measurement concerns. In the context of EuroQol's EQ-5D instruments, which hold a prominent position in health economics and outcomes research, reporting heterogeneity might bias population health norms and health inequality estimates, undermining both clinical and health technology assessment applications.This Project studies reporting heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L data in Estonia. The primary aim is to examine whether sociodemographic characteristics systematically shift EQ-5D-5L response thresholds after adjustment for objectively validated health status, and to quantify the resulting bias in unadjusted population health norms. The secondary aim is to investigate the specific role of cognitive functioning in EQ-5D-5L reporting heterogeneity among older adults (65+), with implications for the concurrent validity of EQ-5D-5L and the Cognition bolt-on in this population.The Project uses registry-linked longitudinal survey data from study "Health and quality of life 2025" conducted under EuroQol grant 1960-RA. Reporting heterogeneity will be investigated using the Hierarchical Ordered Probit (HOPIT) model, testing alternative specifications of the latent health equation based on self-reported, registry-validated, and registry-only health indicators.The Project delivers two outputs: a peer-reviewed article on reporting heterogeneity in EQ-5D-5L across sociodemographic groups, and a conference paper — to be developed into a full article — on cognitive functioning as a driver of reporting heterogeneity. Both deliverables directly address PHSWG Priority 3 of the current Call and generate evidence relevant to the DSWG Cognition bolt-on programme.
Working Group: Descriptive Systems, Populations and Health Systems

Title: How should fatigue be phrased in the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox? A qualitative study of wording, meaning, and patient language in cardiovascular and selected cancer contexts in Indonesia
Abstract: Background: The current EuroQol call prioritises conceptual and methodological evidence for development of the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. Within this priority, the DSWG specifically requests conceptual and qualitative proposals addressing how fatigue should be measured and how fatigue items should be described. Fatigue is highly relevant in cardiovascular disease and selected cancer contexts, primarily gynecologic cancer and, where feasible, lung cancer, but it is not explicitly represented in the five core EQ-5D-5L dimensions. This raises a practical instrument-development question for EuroQol: what wording best captures illness-related fatigue in a way that is clear, relevant, and distinct from nearby concepts and existing EQ-5D-5L dimensions [1,4-7]?Objectives: The study will generate patient- and healthcare-professional-informed qualitative evidence that may inform possible refinements to fatigue wording in the EQ-5D Bolt-on Toolbox. It will explore how adult patients with cardiovascular disease and selected cancer populations (primarily gynecologic cancer and, where feasible, lung cancer) understand and describe illness-related fatigue, how they distinguish it from related concepts such as tiredness, weakness, low energy, sleepiness, and vitality, and how they interpret candidate wordings drawn from the 10 translated Toolbox fatigue items and any additional DSWG/Bolt-On Toolbox-recommended alternative phrasings. The study will also consider the broader applicability and limitations of Bahasa Indonesia findings in relation to the English source-language Toolbox and other language versions.Methods: A two-stage qualitative methodological design will be used. Stage 1 will involve open-ended concept elicitation interviews to explore the lived meaning and language of illness-related fatigue. To avoid priming participants' terminology, Stage 1 interviews will begin with spontaneous discussion of symptoms and daily-life impacts before fatigue-related terms, candidate items, or any fatigue-specific scale are introduced. A fatigue scale will not be administered immediately before the Stage 1 concept elicitation interview as an inclusion criterion; if a fatigue measure is used, it will be administered 1-2 weeks earlier for sampling support or after the open-ended elicitation component as a descriptive indicator. In each clinical context, Stage 1 will target 8 patients and 4 healthcare professionals. Stage 2 will involve cognitive debriefing interviews to assess the comprehensibility, relevance, acceptability, and conceptual distinctiveness of candidate wordings drawn from the 10 translated Toolbox fatigue items, with one or two additional alternative phrasings included only if recommended by the DSWG/Bolt-On Toolbox team before Stage 2 commences. Stage 2 will use the same target structure in each clinical context, giving 24 planned interviews per stage and 48 planned interviews overall across cardiovascular and cancer contexts. A small number of patients and healthcare professionals will also be consulted during piloting to support protocol design, topic guide refinement, and interview flow.Expected contribution: The study will provide EuroQol with development-focused evidence on how fatigue is understood and phrased in Bahasa Indonesia and how candidate wording may function across cardiovascular and selected cancer contexts. The study will not claim to determine whether the current UK English Toolbox items are adequate on its own. Instead, it will generate evidence that may inform possible refinements to fatigue wording when considered alongside DSWG guidance, Toolbox team input, and evidence from other languages and patient groups.
